name: Netherlands

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; Low Saxon and Limburgish are recognised regional languages, and Papiamento and English are official in the Caribbean Netherlands

people: Most people are Dutch, with a distinct Frisian minority in the north and large communities with roots in Indonesia, Suriname, the Dutch Caribbean, Turkey and Morocco, alongside many newer arrivals from across Europe and beyond. Over half the population now reports no religious affiliation; roughly a fifth are Catholic (mainly in the south), around 15% Protestant (strongest in a 'Bible belt' running from Zeeland to the north-east) and about 5% Muslim. It is one of the most densely populated countries in Europe and overwhelmingly urban, with the Randstad ring of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht at its heart.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Port of Rotterdam and logistics expertise
Agricultural and horticultural innovation
Water management and delta engineering know-how
Highly educated, multilingual workforce
North Sea wind and natural gas
Rich artistic and museum heritage
struggles: Severe housing shortage and high rents, especially for young people
Long-term sea-level rise and land subsidence in a low-lying delta
Nitrogen pollution and tension between farmers, nature protection and government
Political polarisation and difficult debates over migration and integration
Earthquakes and damaged homes in Groningen caused by decades of gas extraction
Loneliness among older people and pressure on youth mental health
prayFor: For young people and families searching for a home they can afford, that they may find stability and welcome
For farmers, scientists and policymakers seeking a just path between livelihoods and the health of land and water
For the people of Groningen, still living with damaged homes and broken trust, that they receive repair and peace
For newcomers and long-settled neighbours alike, that the Dutch tradition of tolerance may deepen into genuine friendship
For those who are lonely or burdened in mind, that they may be seen, accompanied and loved

summary.history: Hunter-gatherers and later farmers lived on the higher sandy grounds and the mounds (terpen) of the coast long before the Romans held the Rhine as their frontier. Through the Middle Ages the people drained peat, built dikes and windmills, and grew rich towns on trade, until a sixteenth-century revolt against Habsburg Spain produced the Dutch Republic. Its seventeenth-century Golden Age of trade, science and painting was financed in part through colonial rule in Indonesia, Suriname and the Caribbean and through the transatlantic slave trade, which was abolished only in 1863. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945, and around three quarters of its Jewish population were murdered, among them Anne Frank; after the war came the hunger of 1944–45, reconstruction and a violent, long-unacknowledged war against Indonesian independence. Today the country is a prosperous, densely populated delta nation still negotiating with the water and with its own past.
summary.politicalHistory: The northern provinces declared their independence from Philip II of Spain in 1581, and the Dutch Republic was formally recognised in 1648 at the Peace of Münster. After the French period, the Kingdom of the Netherlands was founded in 1815 under the House of Orange-Nassau, and Belgium broke away in 1830. Johan Rudolph Thorbecke's constitution of 1848 created a parliamentary system with ministerial responsibility, and universal suffrage followed in 1917 for men and 1919 for women. Today it is a constitutional monarchy with a ceremonial monarch, a two-chamber States General elected by proportional representation, and governments that are always coalitions.
summary.art: Dutch painting reached extraordinary heights in the seventeenth century with Rembrandt, Vermeer and Frans Hals, and later with Vincent van Gogh and Piet Mondriaan's De Stijl movement. Crafts such as Delftware, tile-making and design traditions from Gerrit Rietveld to today's Dutch Design remain vibrant. Its literature runs from the medieval Reynard the Fox and Vondel's plays to Multatuli's anti-colonial Max Havelaar and the diary of Anne Frank.
summary.monuments: The Amsterdam canal ring, the windmills of Kinderdijk-Elshout and the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht are all UNESCO World Heritage sites that show the Dutch genius for living with water and for design. The Wadden Sea, shared with Germany and Denmark, is a UNESCO-listed tidal wilderness of mudflats and islands. The Anne Frank House in Amsterdam and the Afsluitdijk and Delta Works in the north and south-west tell, in turn, of the country's darkest wartime chapter and its long struggle to hold back the sea.

highlights.title: Rijksmuseum
highlights.line: Stand before Rembrandt's Night Watch and Vermeer's Milkmaid in the national treasure house; book a timed ticket and go at opening or in the last two hours.

highlights.title: Anne Frank House
highlights.line: Climb behind the bookcase into the Secret Annex where Anne wrote her diary; tickets are released online only, about six weeks ahead, and sell out fast.

highlights.title: Van Gogh Museum
highlights.line: The world's largest collection of Van Gogh's paintings and letters traces his short, luminous life; reserve a time slot and leave space to linger over the sunflowers.

highlights.title: Amsterdam canal ring
highlights.line: The seventeenth-century UNESCO-listed canals are best seen from a small open boat or on foot at dusk, when the gabled houses glow.

highlights.title: Begijnhof and Our Lord in the Attic
highlights.line: Find quiet in Amsterdam's hidden courtyard of the Beguines, then visit Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder, a whole Catholic church secretly built into a canal-house attic.

highlights.title: Kinderdijk windmills
highlights.line: Nineteen eighteenth-century mills stand along the polder waterways; arrive early by water bus from Rotterdam and walk or cycle the dike path.

highlights.title: Zaanse Schans
highlights.line: Working windmills grinding paint pigments and spices sit beside green wooden houses just north of Amsterdam; go early before the tour buses.

highlights.title: Keukenhof gardens
highlights.line: Around seven million bulbs flower here each spring from late March to mid-May; rent a bike to ride through the surrounding striped bulb fields.

highlights.title: Mauritshuis, The Hague
highlights.line: An intimate palace-museum holding Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft; pair it with a walk past the Binnenhof parliament buildings.

highlights.title: Scheveningen beach
highlights.line: The Hague's seaside resort has a pier, dunes and fish stalls; go at sunset for a long walk on the wide North Sea beach.

highlights.title: Delft
highlights.line: A small canal city of blue-and-white pottery and Vermeer's birthplace; climb the Nieuwe Kerk tower and visit the Royal Delft factory.

highlights.title: Rotterdam architecture
highlights.line: Rebuilt after the 1940 bombing, the city is a showcase of bold design, from the Cube Houses to the arched Markthal food hall and the Erasmus Bridge.

highlights.title: Utrecht Dom Tower and wharves
highlights.line: Climb the 465 steps of the country's tallest church tower, then eat on the unique sunken canal wharves along the Oudegracht.

highlights.title: Rietveld Schröder House
highlights.line: A small 1924 home in Utrecht that became a manifesto of De Stijl design; visits are by guided ticket only, so book ahead.

highlights.title: Haarlem
highlights.line: A gentler Amsterdam fifteen minutes away by train, with the soaring Grote Kerk, the Frans Hals Museum and the Corrie ten Boom House.

highlights.title: Leiden
highlights.line: The oldest Dutch university town, with almshouse courtyards (hofjes), the Pilgrim Fathers' story and the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden of antiquities.

highlights.title: Giethoorn and Weerribben-Wieden
highlights.line: A village of thatched farmhouses linked by canals and footbridges; rent a silent electric 'whisper boat' and head into the national park beyond the crowds.

highlights.title: Hoge Veluwe and Kröller-Müller Museum
highlights.line: Borrow a free white bicycle to cross heath, sand drifts and forest to a superb museum with Van Gogh paintings and a sculpture garden.

highlights.title: Wadden islands
highlights.line: Take the ferry to Texel, Vlieland or Terschelling for dunes, seals and bird life; in summer join a guided mudflat walk (wadlopen) only with a certified guide.

highlights.title: Afsluitdijk
highlights.line: Drive or cycle the 32-kilometre dam that sealed off the Zuiderzee in 1932, with the open Wadden Sea on one side and the IJsselmeer on the other.

highlights.title: Delta Works at Neeltje Jans
highlights.line: Walk inside the Eastern Scheldt storm surge barrier, built after the 1953 flood, to grasp how the Dutch live with the sea.

highlights.title: Maastricht
highlights.line: The southern city feels almost Burgundian: pray at the Basilica of Our Lady Star of the Sea and browse Boekhandel Dominicanen, a bookshop inside a Gothic church.

highlights.title: Limburg hills
highlights.line: Walk the rolling South Limburg countryside of half-timbered farms and orchards, and taste vlaai fruit tart in a village café.

highlights.title: St John's Cathedral, 's-Hertogenbosch
highlights.line: A flamboyant Gothic cathedral full of carved figures; afterwards try a chocolate-coated Bossche bol, the city's cream-filled treat.

highlights.title: Groningen
highlights.line: A lively northern student city with the Martinitoren tower, a striking modern museum and easy access to the quiet villages of the north.

highlights.title: Friesland and the Eleven Cities
highlights.line: Cycle or sail between the small historic towns of the legendary Elfstedentocht skating route, and hear Frisian spoken in daily life.

highlights.title: Cheese markets of Alkmaar and Gouda
highlights.line: On summer market days carriers in white uniforms weigh and carry wheels of cheese on wooden barrows; check the season dates before you go.

highlights.title: Fresh herring
highlights.line: From late spring a fish stall will serve raw Hollandse Nieuwe herring with onions and pickles; Amsterdammers often eat it in a soft roll.

highlights.title: Stroopwafels at a market
highlights.line: Buy a warm syrup waffle pressed fresh on the spot, best at Gouda, where they originated, or at Amsterdam's Albert Cuyp market.

highlights.title: Borrel in a brown café
highlights.line: Join locals for an early-evening drink and crisp bitterballen in a candle-lit, wood-panelled bruin café, a cornerstone of Dutch gezelligheid.

highlights.title: Indonesian rijsttafel
highlights.line: A legacy of colonial history and of the Indonesian-Dutch community, this spread of many small dishes is best shared with friends in Amsterdam or The Hague.

highlights.title: Cycling like a local
highlights.line: Rent a city bike and use the dedicated red cycle lanes, signalling with your hand and keeping right so faster riders can pass.

highlights.title: King's Day
highlights.line: On 27 April the whole country turns orange for street markets, music and boat parties; book lodging early and expect huge crowds in Amsterdam.

funFacts: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by dunes, dikes and pumps.
Flevoland, the twelfth province, was created almost entirely from land reclaimed from the sea in the twentieth century.
There are estimated to be more bicycles in the Netherlands than people.
Utrecht Centraal station has the world's largest bicycle parking garage, with room for around 12,500 bikes.
Amsterdam is the constitutional capital, but the government, parliament and king's working palace are in The Hague.
The Dutch are among the tallest people in the world on average.
Schiphol Airport sits about three metres below sea level on the bed of a drained lake, the Haarlemmermeer.
The Netherlands was the first country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2001.
The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, issued shares to the public and is often called the world's first publicly traded company.
New York began as the Dutch colonial settlement of New Amsterdam.
English words such as cookie, boss, yacht and landscape all come from Dutch.
West Frisian, spoken in Friesland, is one of the closest living relatives of English.
The national colour is orange, after the royal House of Orange-Nassau, even though the flag is red, white and blue.
The Wilhelmus, the Dutch national anthem, dates from the sixteenth century and is one of the oldest national anthems in the world.
Despite its size, the Netherlands is the world's second-largest exporter of agricultural products by value, after the United States.
Rotterdam is the largest seaport in Europe.
The Peace Palace in The Hague houses the International Court of Justice, the principal court of the United Nations.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek of Delft was the first person to observe bacteria and other microorganisms through his handmade microscopes.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Saturn's moon Titan in 1655 and built the first pendulum clock.
Bluetooth technology was developed largely by the Dutch engineer Jaap Haartsen while working for Ericsson.
Tulips are not native to the Netherlands; they arrived from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century and sparked the famous 'tulip mania' of 1637.
Delftware began as a local imitation of the Chinese blue-and-white porcelain brought to Europe by Dutch traders.
Many old canal houses have a hoisting beam at the top of the gable because furniture is lifted in through the windows rather than up the narrow stairs.
Over a thousand historic windmills still stand in the Netherlands, and many still turn.
Rembrandt's Night Watch was trimmed on all sides in 1715 so that it would fit on a wall in Amsterdam's town hall.
The Afsluitdijk, finished in 1932, turned the salty Zuiderzee into the freshwater IJsselmeer.
The Elfstedentocht, a 200-kilometre skating race through eleven Frisian towns, can only be held when the ice is thick enough and was last held in 1997.
Chocolate sprinkles called hagelslag are a common topping on buttered bread for breakfast and lunch.
Sinterklaas arrives each November by steamboat, and families exchange gifts and poems on the evening of 5 December.
Most Dutch children earn a swimming diploma at a young age, a practical necessity in a land full of water.
Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten are constituent countries within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
The word 'gezellig', describing a cosy, convivial atmosphere, is so central to Dutch life that it has no exact English equivalent.
The Dutch famine of the 'Hunger Winter' of 1944–45 has been studied for decades for its lasting effects on the health of children born afterwards.

languageGuide.intro: Dutch uses 'u' as the polite form of 'you' with strangers and older people and 'je/jij' with friends, though people switch to informal speech quickly; the guttural 'g' and 'ch' are pronounced in the throat like a soft clearing sound, and 'ui' and 'ij' have no exact English equivalent. English is spoken very widely, especially in cities, but a greeting or thank-you in Dutch is warmly received.

culture.history: Born from a long struggle with the sea and a sixteenth-century revolt against Habsburg Spain, the Dutch Republic became a seventeenth-century trading power whose Golden Age was financed partly through colonial rule in Indonesia, Suriname and the Caribbean and through the transatlantic slave trade. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945, and around three quarters of its Jewish population were murdered, among them Anne Frank. After the war came decolonisation, including a violent war against Indonesian independence that the Dutch state has only recently begun to reckon with openly. Today the country is known for its land reclaimed from water and a culture of negotiated consensus.
culture.politics: The Netherlands is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy in which the monarch's role is ceremonial and the cabinet answers to a two-chamber States General. Proportional representation produces many parties, so governments are always coalitions built through long negotiation. The 'polder model' of consultation between government, employers and unions remains a defining civic ideal.
culture.arts: Dutch painting reached extraordinary heights with Rembrandt, Vermeer and Frans Hals, and later with Vincent van Gogh and Piet Mondriaan's De Stijl abstraction. Its architecture ranges from gabled canal houses to the Amsterdam School and bold contemporary design. Literature includes Multatuli's anti-colonial novel Max Havelaar and the diary of Anne Frank.

love.expression: Affection tends to be shown through reliability, honesty and shared time rather than grand gestures; directness is often a sign of trust. Friendships are built slowly, frequently around planned coffee, bicycle rides or birthday circles, and once made are deeply loyal. Couples often value equality and sharing everyday tasks.

etiquette: Arrange visits in advance; spontaneous drop-ins and dinner invitations are less common than planned appointments.
Directness is not rudeness; an honest opinion is usually meant as respect.
Watch for bicycle lanes (often red asphalt) and never stand or walk in them.

name: Belgium

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. regional languages such as Walloon and Limburgish and many immigrant languages; three official languages

people: Belgium is home to Dutch-speaking Flemings in the north (about 60% of the population), French-speaking Walloons in the south, a small German-speaking community in the east, and officially bilingual Brussels, one of Europe's most international cities, where a large share of residents have roots abroad, from Morocco, Turkey and Congo to the rest of the EU. Catholicism has shaped the culture deeply and remains the largest faith, with very roughly half identifying as Catholic but far fewer practising; Muslims make up around 7%, and a growing share have no religion. It is one of the most urbanised countries in the world, a dense network of cities and towns linked by rail and road.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; Type E sockets have a protruding earth pin, so older Type F (Schuko) plugs without the matching hole may not fit; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe's largest
Central location and the institutions of the EU and NATO in Brussels
Chemical, pharmaceutical and biotech industries
Multilingual, highly skilled workforce
Fertile farmland and a celebrated food, beer and chocolate culture
Extraordinary medieval and artistic heritage
struggles: Deep linguistic and regional divides that make forming governments slow and difficult
Poverty, unemployment and post-industrial decline in parts of Wallonia and Brussels
Drug trafficking through the port of Antwerp and the violence and corruption it brings
Discrimination and unequal opportunities for people of migrant background
Expensive housing, heavy traffic and air pollution around the cities
Recovery from the deadly 2021 floods in the Vesdre valley and rising climate risk
prayFor: For Flemings, Walloons, German speakers and the people of Brussels, that they may keep choosing to listen to one another across language and region
For families in struggling neighbourhoods and former industrial towns, that they find good work, dignity and hope
For young people drawn into or harmed by the drug trade around Antwerp and Brussels, and for all who work to protect them
For newcomers and their children, that they meet open doors, fair treatment and true belonging
For the communities rebuilding after the 2021 floods, that their homes and hearts be restored

summary.history: Julius Caesar called the Belgae the bravest of the Gauls, and after Roman rule the region became a heartland of the Franks. In the Middle Ages Flemish cloth cities such as Bruges, Ghent and Ypres grew rich and proud, and under the Dukes of Burgundy and then the Habsburgs the southern Low Countries became a centre of art and commerce, while also suffering repeated wars and religious repression. After Spanish, Austrian, French and Dutch rule, Belgium won independence in 1830; under King Leopold II the Congo Free State (1885–1908) was run as a personal possession marked by forced labour, mutilation and mass death, before becoming a Belgian colony until 1960, with Rwanda and Burundi also under Belgian administration. Belgium was invaded and occupied in both World Wars, its fields around Ypres became a byword for slaughter, and over 25,000 Jews and Roma were deported from the Mechelen barracks to Auschwitz. In the decades since it has become a prosperous federal state and the home of the European Union's main institutions.
summary.politicalHistory: The Belgian Revolution of 1830 broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, and the 1831 constitution, then one of the most liberal in Europe, made Leopold of Saxe-Coburg the first King of the Belgians. Suffrage widened from a narrow elite to plural male voting in 1893, equal male suffrage in 1919 and women's suffrage in national elections in 1948. The 'Royal Question' over Leopold III's wartime conduct led to his abdication in 1951, and from 1970 a series of state reforms transformed the unitary state into a federation, formally in 1993. Today Belgium is a federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy with powerful regions (Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels) and language communities.
summary.art: The Flemish Primitives Jan van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden and Hans Memling pioneered oil painting, followed by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Rubens and Van Dyck, and later by James Ensor and the surrealist René Magritte. Victor Horta made Brussels a capital of Art Nouveau, while lace-making, tapestry and the 'ninth art' of comics, from Hergé's Tintin to Peyo's Smurfs, are proud national crafts. Music runs from the Renaissance polyphony of Josquin-era Flemish composers to Adolphe Sax's saxophone, Django Reinhardt's jazz and the chansons of Jacques Brel.
summary.monuments: Brussels' Grand-Place, the historic centre of Bruges and the Flemish béguinages are UNESCO World Heritage sites that preserve the beauty of the medieval and Renaissance Low Countries. The belfries of Belgium and France and the Plantin-Moretus printing house in Antwerp tell of civic pride and of the early age of print. The Atomium recalls the optimism of Expo 58, while the Menin Gate and the war cemeteries of Flanders keep vigil over the dead of the First World War.

highlights.title: Grand-Place, Brussels
highlights.line: One of the most beautiful squares in Europe, ringed by gilded guild houses; see it lit at night and, in August of even years, carpeted in flowers.

highlights.title: Magritte Museum and Royal Museums of Fine Arts
highlights.line: Bruegel, Rubens and the world's largest Magritte collection share one complex on the Mont des Arts; allow half a day.

highlights.title: Horta Museum
highlights.line: Victor Horta's own home in Saint-Gilles is an Art Nouveau masterpiece of light and curving iron; book a slot, as visitor numbers are limited.

highlights.title: Comic strip walls of Brussels
highlights.line: Follow the comic strip route of over fifty murals, then visit the Belgian Comic Strip Center in a Horta-designed department store.

highlights.title: Atomium
highlights.line: Ride up inside a 102-metre model of an iron crystal built for Expo 58, with views across Brussels from the top sphere.

highlights.title: Bruges canals and Belfry
highlights.line: Wander a perfectly preserved medieval city by canal boat and climb the 366 steps of the Belfry; stay overnight to enjoy it after the day-trippers leave.

highlights.title: Basilica of the Holy Blood, Bruges
highlights.line: A small, jewel-like chapel venerating a relic of Christ's blood, carried through the streets each Ascension Day in a great procession.

highlights.title: Béguinage of Bruges
highlights.line: Whitewashed houses around a lawn of trees and spring daffodils, still a place of silence where Benedictine sisters now live.

highlights.title: Ghent Altarpiece
highlights.line: The Van Eyck brothers' Adoration of the Mystic Lamb in St Bavo's Cathedral is one of the turning points of Western art; the visitor centre uses augmented reality to tell its story.

highlights.title: Gravensteen and Graslei, Ghent
highlights.line: Explore a moated twelfth-century castle, then sit by the river among the guild houses of the Graslei, lively with students in the evening.

highlights.title: Antwerp Cathedral of Our Lady
highlights.line: Four Rubens masterpieces hang beneath the tallest church spire in the Low Countries.

highlights.title: Rubens House and Plantin-Moretus, Antwerp
highlights.line: See where Rubens lived and painted, then the UNESCO-listed printing house with the world's oldest surviving printing presses.

highlights.title: Antwerp Central Station
highlights.line: A cathedral of a railway station with a vast dome and marble halls; arrive by train to get the full effect.

highlights.title: Leuven
highlights.line: A university town since 1425, with a flamboyant Gothic town hall, the rebuilt university library and the Oude Markt, called the longest bar in Europe.

highlights.title: Mechelen
highlights.line: Climb St Rumbold's Tower for wide views, then visit Kazerne Dossin, the sobering memorial and museum of the Holocaust deportations from Belgium.

highlights.title: Menin Gate Last Post, Ypres
highlights.line: Every evening at 8 pm buglers sound the Last Post beneath the names of more than 54,000 missing soldiers; arrive early and stand in silence.

highlights.title: In Flanders Fields and Tyne Cot
highlights.line: Learn the story of the First World War at the Ypres museum, then walk among the white headstones of Tyne Cot, the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world.

highlights.title: The Belgian coast by tram
highlights.line: The Kusttram runs the whole length of the coast from De Panne to Knokke; hop off at Ostend for fish and the seafront promenade.

highlights.title: Dinant
highlights.line: An onion-domed church beneath a cliff-top citadel on the Meuse, and the birthplace of Adolphe Sax, inventor of the saxophone.

highlights.title: Namur citadel
highlights.line: One of Europe's largest fortresses commands the meeting of the Sambre and Meuse; ride the cable car up for the views.

highlights.title: Caves of Han-sur-Lesse
highlights.line: Take a historic tram into vast limestone caverns carved by an underground river in the Ardennes.

highlights.title: Ardennes forests
highlights.line: Hike or kayak around Durbuy, La Roche-en-Ardenne and Bouillon among wooded valleys and castle ruins; autumn colours are spectacular.

highlights.title: Hautes Fagnes
highlights.line: Walk the boardwalks of Belgium's highest plateau, a wild landscape of raised bogs and heath near the German border.

highlights.title: Waterloo battlefield
highlights.line: Climb the Lion's Mound and visit the underground memorial to understand the 1815 battle that ended Napoleon's rule.

highlights.title: Liège
highlights.line: A gritty, warm-hearted city: climb the 374 steps of the Montagne de Bueren and taste the original Liège waffle with pearl sugar.

highlights.title: Banneux and Beauraing
highlights.line: Two quiet Marian shrines in Wallonia, places of the 1932–33 apparitions, where pilgrims come to pray for the sick and the poor.

highlights.title: Orval Abbey
highlights.line: Walk the ruins of a medieval abbey beside the working Trappist monastery whose monks support their life through cheese and beer.

highlights.title: Trappist and abbey beer
highlights.line: Belgian beer culture is UNESCO-listed; drink slowly from the right glass and try a Trappist ale in a traditional café.

highlights.title: Fries from a frietkot
highlights.line: Belgian fries are double-fried and served in a paper cone; choose from dozens of sauces at a roadside frietkot.

highlights.title: Moules-frites
highlights.line: A steaming pot of mussels with fries is a national favourite, traditionally best in the colder months.

highlights.title: Chocolate in the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert
highlights.line: Browse elegant chocolatiers in the nineteenth-century glass-roofed arcade where the praline was born.

highlights.title: Carnival of Binche
highlights.line: On Shrove Tuesday the Gilles, in wax masks and ostrich plumes, dance through the streets in a UNESCO-listed carnival tradition.

highlights.title: Tournai
highlights.line: One of Belgium's oldest cities, with a five-towered UNESCO cathedral and the country's oldest belfry.

funFacts: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.
After its 2010 election, Belgium went 541 days without a newly formed government, a record at the time.
The saxophone was invented by Adolphe Sax, born in Dinant, who patented it in 1846.
Tintin first appeared in 1929, created by the Brussels artist Hergé.
The Smurfs were created by the Belgian cartoonist Peyo in 1958.
The filled chocolate praline was created by Jean Neuhaus in Brussels in 1912.
The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître first proposed the theory that became known as the Big Bang.
Voting is compulsory in Belgium, and has been since 1893.
The Atomium represents an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
Manneken Pis has a wardrobe of more than a thousand costumes, changed regularly for festivals and causes.
Belgian beer culture was added to UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity in 2016.
Belgium brews well over a thousand different beers.
Brussels hosts the main institutions of the European Union and the headquarters of NATO.
One panel of the Ghent Altarpiece, the Just Judges, was stolen in 1934 and has never been found.
The mapmaker Gerardus Mercator was born in Rupelmonde, in Flanders, in 1512.
The actress Audrey Hepburn was born in Ixelles, Brussels, in 1929.
The town of Spa in the Ardennes was so famous for its healing waters that its name became the English word for a health resort.
Belgian fries are traditionally fried twice, first to cook them through and then to make them crisp.
Belgium was the second country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2003.
The Kusttram along the Belgian coast is one of the longest tram lines in the world, at about 67 kilometres.
The cyclist Eddy Merckx won the Tour de France five times.
René Magritte's painting of a pipe captioned 'This is not a pipe' is one of the most famous images of surrealism.
The 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels gathered Einstein, Marie Curie, Bohr and many other physicists for one of science's most famous photographs.
The Belgica expedition of 1897–99 was the first to spend a winter in the Antarctic.
Brussels sprouts take their name from the Brussels area, where they were widely grown.
The Battle of Waterloo in 1815 was fought just south of Brussels.
KU Leuven traces its origins to a university founded in 1425, making it one of the oldest in Europe.
The Last Post has been played at the Menin Gate in Ypres every evening since 1928, except during the German occupation of the Second World War.
The Palace of Justice in Brussels was one of the largest buildings constructed in the nineteenth century.
In the village of Baarle-Hertog, Belgian enclaves are scattered inside the Netherlands, so the border runs through houses and cafés.
Belgium's highest point, Signal de Botrange, is just 694 metres above sea level.
Liège waffles are made from a yeasted dough with pearl sugar that caramelises in the iron, unlike the lighter, rectangular Brussels waffle.
Paul Otlet's Mundaneum in Mons, a vast card index of world knowledge begun in the 1890s, is often described as a paper forerunner of the internet.

languageGuide.intro: French is spoken in Brussels and Wallonia, while Flanders (Bruges, Ghent, Antwerp, Leuven) speaks Dutch, so switch to English or Dutch there rather than starting in French; use 'vous' with strangers and always greet shopkeepers with 'Bonjour'. Belgian French says 'septante' for 70 and 'nonante' for 90, calls lunch 'le dîner', and often uses 's'il vous plaît' when handing something over; English is widely spoken in Brussels and among younger people.

phrases.local: Un billet pour Bruges, s'il vous plaît

culture.history: The lands of Belgium were among medieval Europe's richest, with Flemish cloth cities such as Bruges and Ghent, and later passed through Burgundian, Spanish, Austrian, French and Dutch rule before independence in 1830. Under King Leopold II the Congo Free State was run as a personal possession marked by forced labour and atrocities that cost a vast number of lives, and Belgian colonial rule continued until 1960. Belgium was invaded and occupied in both world wars, and its fields at Ypres and elsewhere hold some of the First World War's deepest scars. Since then it has become a home of European institutions and a country patiently negotiating between its language communities.
culture.politics: Belgium is a federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a ceremonial monarch and a government responsible to parliament. Power is shared between the federal level, three regions (Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels-Capital) and three language communities (Dutch, French, German), an unusually layered structure. Balancing linguistic and regional identities is the defining civic theme, and coalition formation can take a long time.
culture.arts: Flemish masters such as Jan van Eyck, Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Peter Paul Rubens shaped European painting, and Belgium later gave the world René Magritte's surrealism and Victor Horta's Art Nouveau houses. It is a heartland of the comic strip, from Hergé's Tintin onward. Music runs from Renaissance polyphony to Jacques Brel's chanson.

love.expression: Belgians are often reserved with strangers but warm and generous once a bond forms, with hospitality centred on long meals, good food and a shared drink. Friendship and family time, especially Sunday gatherings, carry real weight. Expression differs between Flemish, Walloon and Brussels circles, from understated to more effusive.

etiquette: Use the language of the region you are in (Dutch in Flanders, French in Wallonia); English is a tactful fallback if you are unsure.
Greetings among acquaintances often include one cheek kiss; follow your host's lead.
Bring a small gift such as flowers or chocolates when invited to someone's home.

name: France

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue) in metropolitan France, incl. regional languages such as Occitan, Breton, Basque, Corsican and Alsatian and many immigrant languages; far more are spoken in the overseas territories

people: France's people include strong regional identities, from Bretons, Basques, Corsicans and Alsatians to Occitans, alongside the peoples of its overseas departments in the Caribbean, the Indian Ocean and South America, and generations of immigrants and their descendants from Italy, Spain, Portugal, North and West Africa, Vietnam and beyond. The state is secular (laïcité) and does not count religion, but surveys suggest roughly half identify as Christian, mostly Catholic, around 8–10% as Muslim, with significant Protestant and Jewish communities (the largest Jewish population in Europe) and a large and growing non-religious share. About four in five people live in towns and cities, while many rural areas face ageing and depopulation.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; Type E sockets have a protruding earth pin; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Fertile farmland, wine and gastronomy
Nuclear and hydroelectric power
Aerospace, rail and engineering industries
Luxury, fashion and design houses
Tourism and one of the world's richest cultural heritages
The French language and a worldwide Francophone community
struggles: Deep social and political polarisation, with frequent mass protests over pensions, cost of living and policing
Inequality and isolation in poorer suburbs (banlieues) and in declining rural areas
Debates over laïcité, immigration and the place of Muslims in national life, alongside rising antisemitism
Lasting trauma from terrorist attacks such as those of 2015 and 2016
Droughts, heatwaves and wildfires linked to climate change, and farmers struggling to make a living
Poverty and unrest in overseas territories such as Mayotte and New Caledonia
prayFor: For a divided society, that people of every view may rediscover the fraternité at the heart of their national motto
For young people in the banlieues and in quiet rural towns, that they may find opportunity, respect and a future
For Muslims, Jews, Christians and those of no faith, that they may live free from fear and hatred, as neighbours
For farmers and all who tend the land, that their work may be honoured and their burdens lightened
For the peoples of the overseas territories, especially in Mayotte and New Caledonia, that justice and peace may grow

summary.history: People painted the caves of Lascaux and Chauvet tens of thousands of years ago, and Celtic Gaul was conquered by Rome in the first century BC before the Franks, under Clovis and later Charlemagne, gave the land its name and Christian kingship. Medieval France built great cathedrals and suffered the Hundred Years' War, in which Joan of Arc rose and died, and the Wars of Religion, including the massacre of Protestants on St Bartholomew's Day in 1572. The Revolution of 1789 proclaimed the rights of man yet also brought the Terror; Napoleon spread its laws across Europe through war, and France built a vast colonial empire in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Pacific, profiting from the enslavement of Africans until abolition in 1848 and fighting bitter wars of decolonisation, above all in Algeria (1954–62). The First World War devastated a generation, and under German occupation in the Second the Vichy regime collaborated in the deportation of around 76,000 Jews, while many others resisted or sheltered the persecuted. After 1945 France rebuilt, helped found what became the European Union, and remains a nation shaped by its ideals and its unfinished reckoning with them.
summary.politicalHistory: The Capetian kings slowly gathered France into a centralised monarchy that reached its height of absolutism under Louis XIV. The Revolution of 1789 overthrew it, declaring a republic in 1792, but the following century swung between empire, restored monarchy and republic: the First Empire of Napoleon, the Restoration, the July Monarchy, the Second Republic of 1848, the Second Empire, and the long-lived Third Republic from 1870. After defeat in 1940 the Vichy regime replaced democracy, and liberation led to the Fourth Republic in 1946 (when women voted nationally for the first time, after gaining the vote in 1944). The crisis over Algeria brought Charles de Gaulle back and the Fifth Republic of 1958, a semi-presidential system with a directly elected president and a prime minister answerable to parliament.
summary.art: French culture gave the world Gothic architecture, the classical theatre of Molière and Racine, and the novels of Victor Hugo, Flaubert and Proust. In painting it was the cradle of Impressionism and modern art, from Monet and Renoir to Cézanne and Matisse, while Rodin reshaped sculpture and the Lumière brothers invented cinema. Its living crafts include haute couture, perfumery, pastry and a gastronomic meal that UNESCO lists as world heritage, and its music ranges from Gregorian chant and Debussy to the chanson of Édith Piaf.
summary.monuments: Mont-Saint-Michel, the Palace of Versailles and Chartres Cathedral, all UNESCO World Heritage sites, embody in turn medieval pilgrimage, royal absolutism and the summit of Gothic art. The Roman Pont du Gard and the cave paintings of the Vézère valley, including Lascaux, reach much further back into the human story. In Paris, the Eiffel Tower is the emblem of modern engineering, and Notre-Dame, reopened in December 2024 after the 2019 fire, remains the spiritual heart of the city.

highlights.title: Eiffel Tower
highlights.line: Go up at dusk to watch Paris turn golden, and book lift tickets well in advance or climb the stairs to the second floor.

highlights.title: The Louvre
highlights.line: One of the world's great museums, from the Mona Lisa to Egyptian antiquities; reserve a timed entry and choose a few wings rather than trying to see everything.

highlights.title: Musée d'Orsay
highlights.line: Impressionist masterpieces in a former railway station, with a view of the Seine through its great clock window.

highlights.title: Notre-Dame and Sainte-Chapelle
highlights.line: Visit the restored cathedral, then the nearby Sainte-Chapelle, whose thirteenth-century stained glass glows best on a sunny morning.

highlights.title: Montmartre and Sacré-Cœur
highlights.line: Climb the hill of artists to the white basilica, where perpetual adoration has continued day and night since 1885.

highlights.title: A Paris café and boulangerie
highlights.line: Take a morning croissant and café crème at a pavement table, and buy a warm baguette from a neighbourhood bakery, a UNESCO-listed craft.

highlights.title: Versailles
highlights.line: Walk the Hall of Mirrors and the vast gardens; go early on a weekday, and visit the musical fountains on spring and summer weekends.

highlights.title: Giverny
highlights.line: Monet's house and water-lily garden bloom from April to October; arrive at opening to see the pond before the crowds.

highlights.title: Chartres Cathedral
highlights.line: A Gothic marvel with intact medieval stained glass and a labyrinth on the floor that pilgrims still walk.

highlights.title: Mont-Saint-Michel
highlights.line: The abbey rising from the tidal bay is unforgettable; check the tide tables and consider staying on the island to see it at night.

highlights.title: D-Day beaches
highlights.line: Walk Omaha Beach and the American Cemetery at Colleville, Juno and Pegasus Bridge, to remember those who died in 1944.

highlights.title: Étretat cliffs
highlights.line: Hike the clifftop paths above the chalk arches on the Normandy coast that inspired Monet.

highlights.title: Brittany coast and crêpes
highlights.line: Explore the Pink Granite Coast and the standing stones of Carnac, and eat buckwheat galettes with a bowl of cider.

highlights.title: Loire Valley châteaux
highlights.line: Cycle between Chambord's double-helix staircase and Chenonceau's arches over the River Cher.

highlights.title: Lourdes
highlights.line: Join pilgrims from across the world at the grotto of Massabielle, and walk in the candlelit procession on spring and summer evenings.

highlights.title: Lascaux IV and the Dordogne
highlights.line: See a faithful replica of the prehistoric cave paintings, then wander the golden medieval town of Sarlat and canoe the Dordogne river.

highlights.title: Rocamadour
highlights.line: A pilgrimage village clinging to a cliff face, with a chapel of the Black Madonna at the top of its long stairway.

highlights.title: Bordeaux and Saint-Émilion
highlights.line: Stroll Bordeaux's elegant riverside, visit the Cité du Vin, and take a day among the vineyards of Saint-Émilion.

highlights.title: Basque Country
highlights.line: Surf in Biarritz, eat pintxos and gâteau basque in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, and hear the Basque language in village squares.

highlights.title: Carcassonne
highlights.line: A restored walled medieval city of turrets and ramparts; walk the walls in the evening after day visitors leave.

highlights.title: Albi
highlights.line: A red-brick fortress cathedral and the Toulouse-Lautrec Museum in a quiet southern town.

highlights.title: Pont du Gard
highlights.line: Swim or picnic beneath the three-tiered Roman aqueduct, nearly two thousand years old.

highlights.title: Avignon
highlights.line: Tour the vast Palace of the Popes, seat of the papacy in the fourteenth century, and the famous half-bridge of Saint-Bénézet.

highlights.title: Provence lavender
highlights.line: The fields of the Valensole plateau flower from late June to mid-July; respect farmers' fields and photograph from the edges.

highlights.title: Gorges du Verdon
highlights.line: Kayak the emerald river through Europe's deepest canyon, or drive the dramatic rim roads.

highlights.title: Marseille
highlights.line: Eat bouillabaisse by the Vieux-Port, climb to Notre-Dame de la Garde, and take a boat to the white limestone calanques.

highlights.title: Nice and the Côte d'Azur
highlights.line: Walk the Promenade des Anglais, browse the Cours Saleya flower market, and visit the Matisse and Chagall museums.

highlights.title: The Camargue
highlights.line: See white horses, black bulls and pink flamingos in the Rhône delta, and the Romani pilgrimage at Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer each May.

highlights.title: Lyon
highlights.line: France's food capital: eat in a traditional bouchon, explore the hidden traboules passages, and climb to the Fourvière basilica.

highlights.title: Burgundy and Taizé
highlights.line: Taste wine around Beaune and its medieval Hospices, then join the sung prayer of the ecumenical community of Taizé.

highlights.title: Chamonix and Mont Blanc
highlights.line: Take the Aiguille du Midi cable car for close views of Western Europe's highest peak; weather changes fast, so check forecasts.

highlights.title: Annecy
highlights.line: Cycle around one of Europe's cleanest lakes and wander the canals of the old town.

highlights.title: Strasbourg and Alsace
highlights.line: Gaze at the cathedral's astronomical clock, visit the Christmas market in December, and follow the wine route through Colmar and Riquewihr.

funFacts: France is the most visited country in the world by international tourist arrivals.
Thanks to its overseas territories, France spans twelve time zones, more than any other country.
France's longest land border is with Brazil, via French Guiana.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was meant to stand for only twenty years.
The Eiffel Tower can grow by up to around 15 centimetres in summer as its iron expands in the heat.
The internal iron framework of the Statue of Liberty, a gift from France, was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
The Louvre was a royal fortress and palace before it opened as a public museum in 1793.
The craft of making the French baguette was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2022.
The French gastronomic meal was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
The Lumière brothers held the first public, paid screening of films in Paris in 1895.
Louis Braille, blinded as a young boy, invented the braille reading system as a teenager.
Louis Pasteur developed the first rabies vaccine and gave his name to pasteurisation.
Marie Curie, working in Paris, was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
After 1066, French was the language of the English royal court for around three centuries, which is why so many English words come from French.
The first Tour de France was held in 1903.
The tides in the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel are among the strongest in continental Europe, with a range of up to about 14 metres.
The Lascaux cave paintings were discovered in 1940 by four teenagers following their dog.
Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 shaped legal systems across Europe, Latin America and beyond.
Many entrances to the Paris Métro, which opened in 1900, still have their original Art Nouveau designs by Hector Guimard.
In 2016 France became the first country to ban supermarkets from throwing away or destroying unsold edible food.
Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region may legally be called Champagne.
The croissant was inspired by the Austrian kipferl, brought to Paris by Viennese bakers in the nineteenth century.
Nice and Savoy only became part of France in 1860.
Corsica became French in 1769, the same year Napoleon was born there.
The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles has 357 mirrors.
The Paris Catacombs hold the remains of around six million people.
The Millau Viaduct in southern France has the tallest bridge pier in the world, rising about 343 metres.
The metric system was created in France in the 1790s.
When the Bastille was stormed in 1789, it held only seven prisoners.
Distances from Paris are measured from a bronze 'Point Zéro' set in the square in front of Notre-Dame.
The Montgolfier brothers launched the first crewed hot-air balloon flight in 1783.
More than 3,000 prehistoric standing stones line the fields at Carnac in Brittany.
Roman Paris was called Lutetia.

languageGuide.intro: Always open with 'Bonjour' (or 'Bonsoir' in the evening) before any question in a shop, café or ticket office, and use the polite 'vous' with anyone you don't know; final consonants are usually silent and 'r' is softly rolled in the throat. English is common among younger people and in tourist areas, but a sincere attempt at French is greatly appreciated, especially outside Paris.

culture.history: From Roman Gaul and the Frankish kingdoms grew a powerful monarchy whose cathedrals, courts and language shaped much of Europe. The Revolution of 1789 proclaimed liberty, equality and fraternity, yet also brought the Terror, and Napoleon's empire spread both reforms and war across the continent. France built a vast colonial empire in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean, including participation in the slave trade, and its end came through painful wars, above all in Algeria. Occupied in the Second World War, the country lived through both collaboration under Vichy, including the deportation of Jews, and the courage of the Resistance.
culture.politics: France is a semi-presidential republic under the Fifth Republic constitution of 1958, with a directly elected president holding significant powers alongside a prime minister responsible to the National Assembly. The state is historically centralised, though regions have gained powers. Laïcité, the strict separation of religion and state, is a defining and much-debated civic principle.
culture.arts: France has shaped world culture through Gothic cathedrals such as Chartres and Notre-Dame, the Impressionism of Monet and Renoir, and the literature of Molière, Victor Hugo and Marcel Proust. Its music spans Debussy and Ravel to Édith Piaf's chanson. French cinema, from the Lumière brothers to the New Wave, remains a cornerstone of the art form.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed through conversation, shared meals and time given generously, with long lunches and dinners as places of intimacy. Friendships may take time to deepen but are valued for their depth and candour. Romance is less about public display than about attentiveness, wit and presence.

etiquette: Always say 'Bonjour' when entering a shop or starting any conversation; skipping it reads as rude.
Use 'vous' with people you do not know well until invited to use 'tu'.
At meals, keep hands visible on the table and wait for the host before beginning to eat or drink.

name: Spain

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. regional languages such as Asturian and Aragonese and immigrant languages; Catalan/Valencian, Basque and Galician are co-official in their regions

people: Spaniards share a strong national life alongside proud regional identities, especially among Catalans, Basques, Galicians and Andalusians, and Spain is also home to one of Europe's largest Roma (Gitano) communities and to millions of residents born abroad, notably from Latin America, Morocco and Romania. Catholicism has profoundly shaped its culture, festivals and calendar, and around 55–60% still identify as Catholic, though regular practice is much lower and a large, growing share, especially among the young, describe themselves as non-religious; Muslims make up roughly 4%. About four in five people live in cities, while much of the interior, the 'España vaciada', has been steadily emptying.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

basics.say: GRAH-thyahs (GRAH-syahs in the south and Canaries)

resources: Tourism, sunshine and Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts
Olive oil, wine, fruit and vegetables
Abundant solar and wind energy
One of the world's largest high-speed rail networks
Spanish, a global language shared with Latin America
An immense artistic, architectural and spiritual heritage
struggles: High youth unemployment and insecure, low-paid work
Soaring rents and housing shortages, intensified by mass tourism in cities and islands
Drought, extreme heat, desertification and deadly flash floods
Depopulation and ageing in rural interior regions
Tensions over regional identity and independence, especially in Catalonia
Migrants risking and losing their lives on sea routes to the Canary Islands and the southern coast
prayFor: For young Spaniards seeking stable work and an affordable home, that they may be able to build families and futures
For farmers and rural villages facing drought and emptiness, that the land may be renewed and communities revived
For migrants crossing dangerous seas, and for the rescuers and islanders who receive them, that every life be treated with dignity
For understanding between Spain's peoples and regions, that difference may become a gift rather than a wound
For the healing of memories from the Civil War and dictatorship, that truth and reconciliation may walk together

summary.history: Human fossils at Atapuerca reach back over a million years, and the painted ceiling of Altamira was made by Ice Age artists; later Iberians, Celts, Phoenicians, Greeks and Carthaginians settled before Rome made Hispania one of its richest provinces. After Visigothic rule, Muslim armies crossed in 711 and al-Andalus flourished for centuries, with Córdoba and Granada among the most brilliant cities of Europe, as Christian kingdoms in the north slowly pushed south. In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs took Granada, expelled Jews who would not convert, and sponsored Columbus, opening an empire across the Americas and the Philippines that brought enormous wealth along with conquest, the collapse of Indigenous populations and the enslavement of Africans; the Inquisition and the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609 deepened religious persecution at home. After centuries of decline, Napoleonic invasion and the loss of its last major colonies in 1898, Spain was torn apart by the Civil War of 1936–39, with atrocities and repression on both sides, followed by Franco's long dictatorship. Since his death in 1975 Spain has become a democracy and a dynamic member of the European Union, still working through the memory of its twentieth-century wounds.
summary.politicalHistory: The marriage of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 united the crowns that became Spain, ruled first by the Habsburgs and from 1700 by the Bourbons, who centralised the state. The liberal Constitution of Cádiz of 1812 began a turbulent century of military coups, Carlist wars and a short First Republic (1873–74), followed by the restored monarchy, the dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera (1923–30) and the Second Republic of 1931, which gave women the vote. General Francisco Franco's victory in the Civil War led to a dictatorship until 1975, after which King Juan Carlos I supported a negotiated transition to democracy. The 1978 Constitution created a parliamentary monarchy with seventeen autonomous communities, and a 1981 coup attempt failed, confirming democratic rule.
summary.art: Spain's painters include El Greco, Velázquez, Zurbarán, Murillo and Goya, and in the twentieth century Picasso, Dalí and Miró, while Antoni Gaudí transformed Barcelona with his organic architecture. Its literature runs from the medieval Poem of the Cid and Cervantes' Don Quixote to the mystics Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross and the poet Federico García Lorca. Flamenco, with its song, guitar and dance rooted in Andalusia's Gitano communities, is UNESCO-listed, alongside crafts such as Moorish-inspired tiles (azulejos), Toledo metalwork and Valencian ceramics.
summary.monuments: The Alhambra in Granada, the Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba and the cathedral, Alcázar and archives of Seville are UNESCO World Heritage sites that tell of al-Andalus and of the Christian kingdoms that followed it. Santiago de Compostela, goal of the Camino pilgrimage for over a thousand years, and Gaudí's Sagrada Família in Barcelona are two of Europe's great sacred places. The Roman aqueduct of Segovia and the cave of Altamira reach back to antiquity and prehistory.

highlights.title: Sagrada Família, Barcelona
highlights.line: Gaudí's basilica, under construction since 1882, fills with coloured forest light; book a timed ticket and aim for late afternoon sun through the west windows.

highlights.title: Park Güell and Casa Batlló
highlights.line: See Gaudí's mosaic terraces and dragon-scaled house; Park Güell's monumental zone needs a pre-booked slot.

highlights.title: Montserrat
highlights.line: Ride the rack railway to the mountain monastery of the Black Madonna and hear the Escolania boys' choir, one of Europe's oldest.

highlights.title: Girona and the Costa Brava
highlights.line: Walk the old Jewish quarter and city walls of Girona, then swim in the rocky coves around Cadaqués and Calella de Palafrugell.

highlights.title: Museo del Prado, Madrid
highlights.line: Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights; free entry in the last two hours most evenings.

highlights.title: Reina Sofía and Retiro Park
highlights.line: Stand before Picasso's Guernica, then join Madrileños rowing on the lake in Retiro Park on a Sunday.

highlights.title: Tapas in Madrid
highlights.line: Hop between bars in La Latina and the Huertas quarter, and end with churros con chocolate at San Ginés.

highlights.title: Toledo
highlights.line: A hilltop city where cathedral, synagogues and mosque stand within a few streets; stay overnight to see it lit and quiet.

highlights.title: Segovia
highlights.line: Walk beneath the Roman aqueduct, visit the fairy-tale Alcázar and taste roast suckling pig, a local speciality.

highlights.title: Ávila
highlights.line: Walk the complete medieval walls and visit the convents linked to St Teresa, the great mystic and reformer.

highlights.title: Salamanca
highlights.line: Golden sandstone, one of Europe's oldest universities and the most beautiful Plaza Mayor in Spain, best at night.

highlights.title: El Escorial
highlights.line: Philip II's monastery-palace in the hills near Madrid combines a basilica, royal tombs and a magnificent library.

highlights.title: The Alhambra, Granada
highlights.line: The Nasrid palaces' carved stucco and fountains are timed to the minute; book months ahead in high season and watch sunset from the Mirador de San Nicolás.

highlights.title: Free tapas in Granada
highlights.line: Many bars still serve a free tapa with each drink, so an evening of small glasses becomes a meal.

highlights.title: Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba
highlights.line: Walk among the forest of red-and-white arches, with a Renaissance cathedral rising in the middle; mornings are calmest.

highlights.title: Seville
highlights.line: Climb the Giralda, explore the Real Alcázar's gardens and lose yourself in Santa Cruz; in spring the city's courtyards smell of orange blossom.

highlights.title: Holy Week in Andalusia
highlights.line: During Semana Santa, brotherhoods carry ornate floats through the streets of Seville, Málaga and Granada in processions of deep devotion.

highlights.title: Flamenco
highlights.line: Hear raw cante jondo in a small tablao or peña in Seville's Triana or Jerez de la Frontera rather than a large tourist show.

highlights.title: Ronda and the white villages
highlights.line: Cross Ronda's dramatic bridge over its gorge, then drive through whitewashed villages such as Grazalema and Zahara de la Sierra.

highlights.title: Cádiz
highlights.line: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Western Europe, with golden beaches and fried fish eaten from paper cones.

highlights.title: Doñana National Park
highlights.line: Wetlands, dunes and pine forest of the Guadalquivir delta, home to the endangered Iberian lynx; visit with an authorised guide.

highlights.title: Mérida
highlights.line: Sit in a Roman theatre still used for summer performances in the former capital of Lusitania.

highlights.title: Camino de Santiago
highlights.line: Walk at least the last 100 kilometres to Santiago de Compostela to receive the Compostela, sharing the road with pilgrims from every nation.

highlights.title: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral
highlights.line: Attend the pilgrims' Mass, and you may see the giant thurible, the botafumeiro, swing smoking across the transept.

highlights.title: Galicia's coast and pulpo
highlights.line: Explore the green rías and wild Costa da Morte, and eat octopus a feira with paprika and olive oil.

highlights.title: Picos de Europa and Covadonga
highlights.line: Hike limestone peaks and visit the cave shrine of Our Lady of Covadonga, cradle of the Asturian kingdom.

highlights.title: San Sebastián
highlights.line: Swim at La Concha beach, then join locals going from bar to bar for pintxos in the old town.

highlights.title: Guggenheim Bilbao
highlights.line: Frank Gehry's titanium-clad museum transformed a post-industrial city; walk the riverside to see it from every angle.

highlights.title: La Rioja
highlights.line: Visit wineries and medieval villages such as Laguardia and Haro, and taste the region's celebrated reds.

highlights.title: Valencia
highlights.line: Eat true paella valenciana near the Albufera lagoon, see the futuristic City of Arts and Sciences, and, in March, the fiery Fallas festival.

highlights.title: Cuenca
highlights.line: Houses literally hang over a gorge in this hilltop town, which also hosts a fine museum of abstract art.

highlights.title: Mallorca's Serra de Tramuntana
highlights.line: Hike the UNESCO-listed mountains of olive terraces and stone villages such as Valldemossa and Deià.

highlights.title: Mount Teide, Tenerife
highlights.line: Ride the cable car up Spain's highest peak and stay for stargazing; a permit is needed to hike to the very summit.

funFacts: Spain is the world's largest producer of olive oil.
Spain's national anthem, the Marcha Real, has no official lyrics.
Spain has the longest high-speed rail network in Europe.
Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, founded in 1725, is recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest restaurant in the world still operating.
Spanish is the second most widely spoken native language in the world, after Mandarin Chinese.
Mount Teide in Tenerife, at about 3,715 metres, is Spain's highest peak and lies outside mainland Europe.
Spain has two cities on the African mainland, Ceuta and Melilla.
Every New Year's Eve, Spaniards eat twelve grapes, one for each stroke of the midnight bell.
Spain has the largest area of vineyards in the world.
Spain is geographically in line with Britain and Portugal but has kept Central European Time since 1940.
Don Quixote, first published in 1605, is often called the first modern novel.
Picasso's Guernica only came to Spain in 1981, after democracy was restored, as the artist had wished.
Basque, spoken in northern Spain and south-western France, is a language isolate unrelated to any other known language.
Spaniards usually carry two surnames, the first from their father and the first from their mother, and women keep their own surnames after marriage.
Spain has led the world in organ donation rates for more than three decades.
Spain has one of the highest life expectancies in the world.
The cave of Altamira is often called the 'Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art'.
Fossils at Atapuerca, near Burgos, include some of the oldest human remains found in Western Europe.
The Chupa Chups lollipop logo was designed by Salvador Dalí.
The modern floor mop with a wringing bucket, the fregona, was popularised by the Spanish engineer Manuel Jalón in the 1950s.
Spain has around fifty UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among the most of any country.
Flamenco was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
Catalonia's human towers, castells, can rise up to ten levels of people standing on each other's shoulders.
The Spanish silver dollar, or 'piece of eight', was a global currency and helped inspire the United States dollar.
English words such as mosquito, patio, canyon and plaza come from Spanish.
Every August in Buñol, near Valencia, thousands of people pelt each other with ripe tomatoes in La Tomatina.
A chalice in Valencia Cathedral has been venerated for centuries as the Holy Grail.
Spain was among the first European countries to drink chocolate, which arrived from Mexico in the sixteenth century.
On Lanzarote, vines grow in pits dug into black volcanic ash, each sheltered by a small stone wall.
Many spaghetti westerns were filmed in the Tabernas desert of Almería.
The Royal Palace of Madrid, with over 3,000 rooms, is one of the largest royal palaces in Europe.
Toledo has been famous for its steel blades since Roman times.
Spain is one of the most mountainous countries in Europe, and Madrid is one of its highest capitals.

languageGuide.intro: Spanish is spelled almost exactly as it is spoken, with clear vowels; in most of Spain 'c' before e/i and 'z' sound like the 'th' in 'think', and 'j' is a breathy throat sound. Use 'usted' for older people and formal settings, though Spaniards move quickly to the informal 'tú'; English is common in tourist areas and among the young, and in Catalonia, the Basque Country and Galicia a word in the local language (such as 'gràcies', 'eskerrik asko' or 'grazas') is a lovely gesture.
