phrases.say: ah lah eeth-KYAIR-dah / ah lah deh-REH-chah

phrases.local: Una mesa para dos, por favor
phrases.say: OO-nah MEH-sah PAH-rah DOS, por fah-VOR

culture.history: Iberia was shaped by Romans, Visigoths and nearly eight centuries of Muslim al-Andalus, a period of remarkable learning in which Christians, Muslims and Jews lived together, though not always in peace. The completion of the Christian 'Reconquista' in 1492 coincided with the expulsion of Jews and, later, Muslims, and with Columbus's voyage, which opened an empire in the Americas built on conquest and immense suffering for Indigenous peoples. The twentieth century brought a brutal civil war (1936–1939) and nearly four decades of dictatorship under Franco. Spain's peaceful transition to democracy after 1975 remains a defining achievement.
culture.politics: Spain is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy under the 1978 constitution, with a ceremonial monarch and a prime minister accountable to the Cortes Generales. Seventeen autonomous communities hold substantial self-government, with their own parliaments and, in several, co-official languages. The balance between national unity and regional identity, notably in Catalonia and the Basque Country, is a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Spain's Golden Age gave the world Cervantes's Don Quixote and the painting of El Greco and Velázquez, followed by Goya's searing images of war and later Picasso, Miró and Dalí. Its architecture runs from the Alhambra and Córdoba's Mezquita to Gaudí's Sagrada Família. Flamenco, rooted in Andalusian Romani culture, is one of its most powerful living art forms.

love.expression: Affection is often warm and openly expressed, with embraces, two cheek kisses and close physical presence common among friends and family. Time together, especially around late meals and evening walks, is the fabric of relationships. Family ties remain strong across generations, though styles vary across regions.

etiquette: Meals run late: lunch around 2 pm and dinner often after 9 pm.
Greet friends and new acquaintances in social settings with two cheek kisses, starting on the right.
In Catalonia, the Basque Country and Galicia, a word or two of the local language is warmly received.

name: Portugal

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; Mirandese is officially recognised in the north-east

people: Most of Portugal's people share a Portuguese identity shaped by Celtic, Roman, Germanic and Moorish layers, joined today by sizeable communities from Brazil, Cabo Verde, Angola, Ukraine, South Asia and elsewhere. Around four in five identify as Catholic, with growing numbers of non-religious people and small Protestant, Muslim, Hindu and Jewish communities. Two thirds live in towns and cities, especially around Lisbon and Porto, while millions more of Portuguese descent live abroad in France, Switzerland, Brazil, the US and beyond.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

basics.local: Obrigado (said by a man) / Obrigada (said by a woman)

resources: Atlantic coastline, fisheries and ports such as Sines
Wind, solar and hydro power
Cork oak forests and the world's largest cork industry
Wine, especially Port, Douro and Alentejo wines
Tourism and a rich living heritage
A global Portuguese-speaking community and a growing tech and talent base
struggles: Severe housing shortage and rising rents, especially in Lisbon and Porto
Low wages relative to Western Europe, driving emigration of young graduates
An ageing population and depopulating interior villages
Wildfires and drought intensified by climate change
Pressure on the national health service and long waits for care
Integrating a fast-growing immigrant population fairly and humanely
prayFor: For young families searching for an affordable home, and for wisdom for those shaping housing policy
For young people weighing whether to stay or leave, that they may find meaningful work close to those they love
For elderly people in emptying villages of the interior, that they be visited, cared for and not forgotten
For firefighters, farmers and forest communities facing drought and fire
For newcomers from Brazil, Africa and Asia, that they find welcome, dignity and fair work

summary.history: Celtic and Iberian peoples, then Romans, Suebi, Visigoths and, from 711, Muslim rulers shaped the land before the Kingdom of Portugal emerged in the twelfth century and fixed its borders by the 1290s. From the fifteenth century Portuguese navigators reached Africa, India, Brazil and Japan, building a vast maritime empire that also pioneered the Atlantic slave trade and carried millions of enslaved Africans across the ocean. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Napoleonic invasions and the loss of Brazil in 1822 weakened the kingdom through the nineteenth century. In the twentieth century the Estado Novo dictatorship ruled for over four decades and fought long colonial wars in Africa until the Carnation Revolution of 1974 restored freedom and brought independence to the colonies. Democratic Portugal joined the European Community in 1986 and has since become an open, outward-looking society.
summary.politicalHistory: Portugal became an independent kingdom under Afonso Henriques, recognised by the Pope in 1179, and remained a monarchy, apart from Spanish rule from 1580 to 1640, until the revolution of 5 October 1910 proclaimed a republic. The unstable First Republic fell to a military coup in 1926, leading to António de Oliveira Salazar's authoritarian Estado Novo from 1933. On 25 April 1974 a largely bloodless military uprising, the Carnation Revolution, ended the dictatorship, and the 1976 constitution founded today's semi-presidential democracy with an elected president, a prime minister and a single-chamber Assembly of the Republic.
summary.art: Fado, the soulful song of Lisbon and Coimbra carried to the world by Amália Rodrigues, gives voice to saudade, a longing for what is absent. Blue-and-white azulejo tiles, Manueline stone carving and filigree gold from the north are signature crafts. Literature runs from Luís de Camões's epic The Lusiads to the many-voiced poet Fernando Pessoa and Nobel laureate José Saramago.
summary.monuments: The Jerónimos Monastery and Tower of Belém in Lisbon celebrate the age of discovery in exuberant Manueline stone. Sintra's cultural landscape, with the romantic Pena Palace and the Moorish castle, and the Gothic monasteries of Batalha and Alcobaça are UNESCO-listed treasures of faith and royal memory. Porto's historic centre, the terraced Douro wine region and the Sanctuary of Fátima speak of trade, toil and devotion.

highlights.title: Jerónimos Monastery
highlights.line: A masterpiece of Manueline stonework where Vasco da Gama lies; go early on a weekday to avoid queues, and pair it with the Tower of Belém nearby.

highlights.title: Pastéis de Belém
highlights.line: Taste custard tarts warm from the oven at the bakery that has followed the monks' recipe since 1837; sit inside, where the table queue moves faster.

highlights.title: Alfama and fado
highlights.line: Wander the oldest quarter of Lisbon by day, then hear live fado in a small tasca at night, keeping quiet while the singer performs.

highlights.title: Tram 28 and the miradouros
highlights.line: Ride the vintage yellow tram through Lisbon's hills, then watch sunset from Miradouro da Senhora do Monte; mind your pockets on crowded trams.

highlights.title: Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
highlights.line: A serene collection from Egyptian art to Lalique jewellery set in calm modernist gardens, perfect for a quiet Lisbon afternoon.

highlights.title: Sintra
highlights.line: Explore the fairytale Pena Palace and the mystical Quinta da Regaleira; book timed tickets and go by train rather than car.

highlights.title: Cabo da Roca
highlights.line: Stand on the westernmost point of mainland Europe, high above the Atlantic, and bring a windproof layer.

highlights.title: Porto's Ribeira
highlights.line: Stroll the riverside quarter of a UNESCO-listed city and cross the Dom Luís I bridge on the upper deck for the views.

highlights.title: Port lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia
highlights.line: Tour the cellars where Port wine ages in oak, and taste a tawny alongside a white Port and tonic.

highlights.title: Francesinha in Porto
highlights.line: Try Porto's hearty layered sandwich drowned in beer-and-tomato sauce; share one if you plan to eat again that day.

highlights.title: Douro Valley
highlights.line: Ride the scenic train or a river boat through terraced vineyards, and visit a quinta during the September harvest.

highlights.title: Guimarães
highlights.line: Walk the medieval streets of the town called the birthplace of Portugal, up to the castle linked to its first king.

highlights.title: Bom Jesus do Monte, Braga
highlights.line: Climb the zigzag Baroque staircase of this pilgrimage sanctuary, or ride the water-powered funicular from 1882.

highlights.title: Peneda-Gerês National Park
highlights.line: Portugal's only national park offers granite peaks, waterfalls, Roman milestones and wild garrano horses.

highlights.title: University of Coimbra
highlights.line: Visit one of Europe's oldest universities and its gilded Joanina Library; tickets are timed, so book ahead.

highlights.title: Aveiro
highlights.line: Glide through canals on a painted moliceiro boat and taste ovos moles, a sweet egg-yolk treat in wafer shells.

highlights.title: Sanctuary of Fátima
highlights.line: Join the candlelight rosary procession where Mary is believed to have appeared in 1917; 13 May and 13 October draw vast crowds.

highlights.title: Batalha Monastery
highlights.line: A soaring Gothic monastery built to give thanks for victory in 1385, with the haunting Unfinished Chapels open to the sky.

highlights.title: Alcobaça Monastery
highlights.line: See the carved tombs of the tragic lovers King Pedro I and Inês de Castro beneath vast Cistercian vaults.

highlights.title: Convent of Christ, Tomar
highlights.line: Explore the Templar round church and the famous Manueline window of this UNESCO-listed fortress-convent.

highlights.title: Óbidos
highlights.line: Walk the walls of this whitewashed medieval town and sip ginjinha cherry liqueur from a chocolate cup.

highlights.title: Nazaré
highlights.line: Watch the giant winter waves from the lighthouse fort and look for women in traditional seven-layered skirts drying fish on the beach.

highlights.title: Ericeira
highlights.line: Surf or learn to surf in Europe's first World Surfing Reserve, then eat fresh seafood in the old fishing town.

highlights.title: Évora
highlights.line: Wander a walled UNESCO city with a Roman temple and the sobering Chapel of Bones; summer afternoons are very hot, so start early.

highlights.title: Monsaraz and Alqueva
highlights.line: Stay in a hilltop village above Europe's large Alqueva lake and stargaze in one of its certified dark-sky areas.

highlights.title: Alentejo wine and cork country
highlights.line: Visit a family winery and learn how cork is harvested by hand from living trees every nine years or so.

highlights.title: Ponta da Piedade and Benagil
highlights.line: Kayak among golden sea arches and caves on the Algarve coast with a licensed guide, choosing calm morning waters.

highlights.title: Rota Vicentina
highlights.line: Hike wild clifftop trails on Portugal's south-west coast, among storks nesting on sea stacks and quiet fishing villages.

highlights.title: Sagres
highlights.line: Watch the sunset at Cabo de São Vicente, once thought the edge of the world, and try fresh percebes (goose barnacles).

highlights.title: Madeira's levadas
highlights.line: Walk beside centuries-old irrigation channels through laurel forest, a UNESCO-listed ecosystem; carry a torch for tunnels.

highlights.title: São Miguel, Azores
highlights.line: See the twin lakes of Sete Cidades and taste cozido cooked underground by volcanic heat at Furnas.

highlights.title: Mount Pico, Azores
highlights.line: Climb Portugal's highest mountain with a registered guide, and see the UNESCO-listed vineyards walled with black lava stone.

highlights.title: Santo António festivities
highlights.line: Join Lisbon's June street festival of grilled sardines, basil pots, paper garlands and neighbourhood parades.

funFacts: Portugal and England share the oldest diplomatic alliance still in force, dating back to a treaty of 1373.
Portugal's borders have changed very little since the thirteenth century, making them among the oldest in Europe.
Portugal produces around half of the world's cork, much of it from oak forests in the Alentejo.
Cork oaks are never cut down for harvest: the bark is stripped by hand roughly every nine years and grows back.
Livraria Bertrand in Lisbon, founded in 1732, is recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest operating bookshop.
The largest wave ever surfed, according to Guinness World Records, was ridden at Nazaré.
Mirandese, spoken around Miranda do Douro, has been officially recognised since 1999 as Portugal's second language.
Catherine of Braganza, a Portuguese princess who married Charles II, helped make tea fashionable at the English court.
In 2001 Portugal decriminalised the personal possession of all drugs, treating addiction primarily as a health issue.
Portuguese is spoken by more than 250 million people worldwide, most of them in Brazil.
Portugal's highest point, Mount Pico at 2,351 metres, is a volcano in the Azores, not on the mainland.
The Douro was one of the world's first legally demarcated wine regions, established in 1756.
The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, tsunami and fire shook European thought and prompted Voltaire to write about it.
The Pombaline buildings that rebuilt Lisbon after 1755 used a wooden lattice frame, one of the earliest earthquake-resistant designs.
The University of Coimbra, founded in 1290, is one of the oldest universities in the world still in operation.
A colony of small bats lives in Coimbra's Joanina Library and eats the insects that could damage the old books.
The Japanese word for bread, 'pan', comes from the Portuguese 'pão', brought by traders in the sixteenth century.
Portuguese traders are widely credited with introducing frying techniques to Japan that influenced tempura.
Portuguese ships helped carry chilli peppers from the Americas to India and the rest of Asia.
Portugal's national anthem once urged citizens to march 'against the Britons', later changed to 'against the cannons'.
Many everyday Portuguese words, like 'azeite' (olive oil) and 'alface' (lettuce), come from Arabic.
The word 'azulejo' is generally traced to the Arabic for a small polished stone, not to 'azul', blue.
In May 2016 Portugal ran on renewable electricity alone for four consecutive days.
Portugal abolished the death penalty for civil crimes in 1867, one of the first European countries to do so.
Cabo da Roca, near Sintra, is the westernmost point of mainland Europe.
Évora's Chapel of Bones greets visitors with the inscription: 'We bones that are here, await yours.'
Fado was inscribed on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011.
'Obrigado' literally means 'obliged', and women say 'obrigada' to match.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge across the Tagus estuary is about 12 kilometres long, among the longest in Europe.
Alqueva in the Alentejo became the world's first certified Starlight Tourism Destination in 2011.
A popular Portuguese saying claims there is a different way to cook bacalhau (salt cod) for every day of the year.
Madeira's laurel forest, the Laurisilva, is a relic of forests that covered much of southern Europe millions of years ago.
The Tenshō embassy, the first official Japanese mission to Europe, landed in Lisbon in 1584.

languageGuide.intro: European Portuguese swallows many unstressed vowels and turns final 's' into a soft 'sh', so it can sound quite different from Brazilian Portuguese or Spanish; people warmly appreciate any attempt, and using 'o senhor / a senhora' is the polite way to address strangers. English is widely spoken in Lisbon, Porto, the Algarve and among younger people, while a few words of Portuguese go a long way in rural areas.

culture.history: One of Europe's oldest nation-states, with borders largely fixed since the thirteenth century, Portugal launched the age of maritime exploration, reaching India, Brazil and East Asia. Its empire also pioneered the Atlantic slave trade, carrying millions of enslaved Africans, chiefly to Brazil. From 1933 the Estado Novo dictatorship under Salazar ruled for four decades and fought long colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau. The almost bloodless Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 restored democracy and led to the independence of the African colonies.
culture.politics: Portugal is a semi-presidential republic with a directly elected president, who can dissolve parliament and veto legislation, and a prime minister and government accountable to the single-chamber Assembly of the Republic. The autonomous regions of the Azores and Madeira have their own governments. The memory of 25 April 1974 and the value of democratic freedom remain central to civic life.
culture.arts: Fado, the melancholic song of Lisbon and Coimbra, made famous by Amália Rodrigues, expresses the untranslatable longing called saudade. The Manueline style of the Jerónimos Monastery and the blue-and-white azulejo tiles define its architecture. Literature runs from Camões's epic The Lusiads to Fernando Pessoa and Nobel laureate José Saramago.

love.expression: Affection is gentle and steady, often shown through hospitality, food lovingly prepared and time spent with extended family. People may seem reserved at first, but friendships become warm and enduring. Small kindnesses and practical care are quiet signs of love.

etiquette: Speak Portuguese or English, not Spanish; Portugal has its own distinct language and identity.
Greet friends and acquaintances with two cheek kisses among women and mixed company, and a handshake between men.
Bread, olives and cheese placed on the table at restaurants are usually charged if you eat them.

name: Italy

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; regional languages such as Sardinian, Friulian, Neapolitan and Sicilian are widely spoken, with German, French, Slovene and Ladin protected in border regions

people: Italians share a strong national culture alongside deeply rooted regional identities, dialects and cuisines, and long-standing linguistic minorities live in South Tyrol, the Aosta Valley, Friuli and the south. Most people are Catholic by tradition, roughly three quarters, with a growing non-religious share and Muslim, Orthodox, Protestant and Jewish communities, many linked to migration from Romania, Albania, Morocco, China, Ukraine and elsewhere. About seven in ten live in towns and cities, and tens of millions of people of Italian descent live abroad, especially in the Americas.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; some sockets are Type L (three pins in a line), so a universal adapter is useful; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: An unrivalled artistic, architectural and archaeological heritage
World-renowned food, wine and agricultural traditions
Advanced manufacturing, machinery and design-led industries
Tourism across cities, coasts, lakes and mountains
Alpine hydropower and growing solar energy
Creative, entrepreneurial people and strong family-run businesses
struggles: One of the world's lowest birth rates and a rapidly ageing population
A persistent economic gap between the north and the south
High public debt and years of slow growth
Youth unemployment and the emigration of young graduates
Organised crime and corruption in some sectors and regions
Earthquakes, floods, heatwaves and the challenge of receiving migrants arriving across the Mediterranean
prayFor: For young couples longing to build a family, that work, housing and support make it possible
For the people of the south, that opportunity, justice and hope grow where they have been held back
For those who resist organised crime, and for communities seeking freedom from fear
For migrants crossing the Mediterranean, for those who rescue and receive them, and for towns that welcome strangers
For the elderly and lonely, and for families caring for them across generations

summary.history: Etruscans, Greeks, Italic peoples and others flourished on the peninsula before Rome rose to rule the Mediterranean world, an empire built on conquest and slave labour that also spread law, roads and, later, Christianity. After the western empire fell, the land fragmented into kingdoms, papal domains and rich city-states such as Venice, Florence and Genoa, whose wealth fed the Renaissance. Foreign powers dominated much of Italy until the Risorgimento unified it between 1859 and 1871, followed by mass emigration from the poor south. Fascism under Mussolini brought dictatorship, brutal colonial wars in Libya and Ethiopia, racial laws against Jews and alliance with Nazi Germany, until defeat and the partisan Resistance ended it in 1945. Post-war Italy became a founding member of the European Community and a major economy, while carrying the wounds of political violence, organised crime and regional inequality.
summary.politicalHistory: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861 under the House of Savoy, with Rome becoming its capital in 1871. A liberal parliamentary monarchy gave way in 1922 to Benito Mussolini's Fascist dictatorship, which collapsed during the Second World War. In a 1946 referendum, the first national vote in which women took part, Italians chose a republic, and the 1948 constitution established a parliamentary system with two chambers, a president as head of state and a strong constitutional court. Italy's democracy has since seen frequent changes of government and a major overhaul of its party system in the 1990s after the 'Clean Hands' corruption inquiries.
summary.art: Italy shaped Western art, from Giotto and the Renaissance genius of Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael to the Baroque drama of Bernini and Caravaggio. Opera was born here and flowered with Monteverdi, Verdi and Puccini, while Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio laid the foundations of Italian literature. Living crafts range from Murano glass and Cremona violin-making to Sicilian puppet theatre and the neorealist and auteur cinema of De Sica and Fellini.
summary.monuments: Rome's Colosseum, Forum and Pantheon recall the ancient capital of an empire, while the buried cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum preserve daily Roman life beneath Vesuvius's ash. Florence's cathedral with Brunelleschi's dome and Venice with its lagoon are UNESCO-listed centres of Renaissance and maritime civilisation. Further south, the Sassi of Matera and the Greek temples of Agrigento testify to thousands of years of human endurance and faith.

highlights.title: Colosseum and Roman Forum
highlights.line: Stand where ancient Rome gathered and governed; book a combined timed ticket and go at opening time.

highlights.title: Pantheon
highlights.line: Look up through the open oculus of this nearly 2,000-year-old temple, now a church; a small entry fee now applies.

highlights.title: Trastevere
highlights.line: Wander Rome's ivy-draped lanes at dusk and eat cacio e pepe or supplì in a family trattoria.

highlights.title: Florence's Duomo
highlights.line: Climb the 463 steps inside Brunelleschi's dome for close-up frescoes and a view over terracotta roofs; reserve your slot.

highlights.title: Uffizi Gallery
highlights.line: See Botticelli's Birth of Venus and masterpieces of the Renaissance; book ahead and allow at least three hours.

highlights.title: Michelangelo's David
highlights.line: Meet the colossal marble at the Accademia in Florence; early evening slots are often quieter.

highlights.title: Siena and the Campo
highlights.line: Sit in the shell-shaped piazza that hosts the Palio horse race each July and August, and visit the striped cathedral.

highlights.title: Val d'Orcia
highlights.line: Drive or cycle through the UNESCO-listed Tuscan hills of cypress lanes and stone farmhouses, pausing in Pienza for pecorino.

highlights.title: Assisi
highlights.line: Pray at the tomb of St Francis beneath Giotto's frescoes and walk the quiet Umbrian lanes above the plain.

highlights.title: Venice
highlights.line: Ride the vaporetto down the Grand Canal, then get lost in the back canals; check if a day-tripper access fee applies on your date.

highlights.title: Padua's Scrovegni Chapel
highlights.line: Giotto's luminous fresco cycle that changed painting; visits are timed and short, so book ahead.

highlights.title: Verona Arena opera
highlights.line: Hear opera under the stars in a Roman amphitheatre during the summer festival; bring a cushion for the stone steps.

highlights.title: The Dolomites
highlights.line: Hike or ski among dramatic pale peaks, UNESCO-listed, and stay in a mountain refuge serving canederli dumplings.

highlights.title: Lake Como
highlights.line: Hop between lakeside villages like Bellagio and Varenna by ferry and visit villas with terraced gardens.

highlights.title: Milan's Last Supper
highlights.line: Leonardo's fragile mural at Santa Maria delle Grazie is shown in 15-minute slots that sell out weeks ahead.

highlights.title: Langhe and Barolo
highlights.line: Taste Barolo and Barbaresco wines in Piedmont's vine-covered hills, and look for white truffles in autumn in Alba.

highlights.title: Cinque Terre
highlights.line: Walk coastal trails between five colourful villages; check which paths are open and travel by train, not car.

highlights.title: Bologna food culture
highlights.line: Eat tagliatelle al ragù and mortadella in the city of porticoes, and join a market tour in the Quadrilatero.

highlights.title: Parma and Modena
highlights.line: Visit a Parmigiano Reggiano dairy at dawn and taste traditional balsamic vinegar aged for decades.

highlights.title: Ravenna's mosaics
highlights.line: See dazzling early Christian and Byzantine mosaics in San Vitale and the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.

highlights.title: Loreto
highlights.line: Visit the Holy House within the basilica, honoured by pilgrims as the home of Mary of Nazareth.

highlights.title: Naples pizza
highlights.line: Eat a true Neapolitan pizza, whose art of the pizzaiuolo is UNESCO-recognised, in the historic centre.

highlights.title: Pompeii and Herculaneum
highlights.line: Walk Roman streets frozen in AD 79; bring water and sun protection, and consider smaller Herculaneum for detail.

highlights.title: Amalfi Coast
highlights.line: Take the ferry or bus between Positano, Amalfi and Ravello, and hike the Path of the Gods above the sea.

highlights.title: Matera's Sassi
highlights.line: Explore ancient cave dwellings and rock churches, once a symbol of poverty and now a reborn UNESCO city.

highlights.title: Alberobello's trulli
highlights.line: Stay in a whitewashed cone-roofed trullo in Puglia's Itria Valley and cycle among olive groves.

highlights.title: Lecce
highlights.line: Admire golden Baroque façades carved in soft local stone, and try a pasticciotto custard pastry for breakfast.

highlights.title: Valley of the Temples
highlights.line: Watch the Greek temples of Agrigento in Sicily glow at sunset among almond trees.

highlights.title: Mount Etna
highlights.line: Hike the craters of Europe's highest active volcano with a guide, and taste wines grown on its black soils.

highlights.title: Palermo street food
highlights.line: Try arancine, panelle and sfincione in the Ballarò market, and see the golden mosaics of nearby Monreale.

highlights.title: Aeolian Islands
highlights.line: Island-hop by hydrofoil and watch Stromboli's eruptions at night on a guided trip.

highlights.title: Sardinia's coast and nuraghi
highlights.line: Swim in clear turquoise coves and visit the Bronze Age stone towers of Su Nuraxi at Barumini.

highlights.title: The passeggiata and aperitivo
highlights.line: Join locals for the evening stroll through the piazza and an aperitivo with small bites, a lovely slice of everyday life.

funFacts: Italy has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country.
Two independent states, San Marino and Vatican City, lie entirely within Italy.
Campione d'Italia is a small Italian town entirely surrounded by Switzerland.
Mount Etna in Sicily is the highest active volcano in Europe.
The University of Bologna, founded in 1088, is considered the oldest university in continuous operation in the Western world.
Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded in 1472, is regarded as the oldest bank still operating.
The piano was invented in Florence around 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori.
Musical terms used worldwide, such as allegro, forte and piano, are Italian.
Standard Italian is based largely on the Florentine Tuscan used by Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio.
By one scholarly estimate, only about 2.5 percent of Italians spoke standard Italian at unification in 1861.
Venice is built on more than 100 small islands linked by around 400 bridges.
Coins thrown into Rome's Trevi Fountain, over a million euros a year, are collected and given to the charity Caritas.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to lean during construction in the twelfth century, and engineers reduced its tilt between 1990 and 2001.
The 1946 referendum that created the Italian Republic was the first national vote in which Italian women took part.
The first espresso machine patent was filed in Turin by Angelo Moriondo in 1884.
The Po is Italy's longest river, flowing about 650 kilometres from the Alps to the Adriatic.
Italy's sports teams wear blue, 'azzurro', the colour of the former royal House of Savoy.
Guglielmo Marconi, a pioneer of radio, shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909.
Maria Montessori opened her first Casa dei Bambini in Rome in 1907.
The Vespa scooter was launched by Piaggio in 1946.
Sardinia is one of the world's 'Blue Zones', known for an unusually high number of centenarians.
In South Tyrol, German is the first language of most residents.
The Italian one-euro coin shows Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man.
Bologna's porticoes stretch for about 62 kilometres and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Pinocchio's author, Carlo Collodi, was born in Florence, and the story was first serialised in 1881.
Italy's constitution explicitly forbids the reorganisation of the dissolved Fascist party.
Lake Garda is the largest lake in Italy.
Nutella was developed by Ferrero in Alba, Piedmont, rooted in the local tradition of hazelnut chocolate spreads.
The cappuccino takes its name from the brown habits of Capuchin friars.
Italy has around 1,500 kilometres of high-speed rail on which Frecciarossa trains run at up to 300 km/h.
Mont Blanc, Western Europe's highest mountain, rises on the border between Italy and France, where it is called Monte Bianco.
Cremona's traditional violin-making craft is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Italy has dozens of officially protected (DOP) cheeses, from Parmigiano Reggiano to Gorgonzola and Pecorino Sardo.

languageGuide.intro: Italian is pronounced much as it is written, with every vowel clear and double consonants held a little longer, and greeting people with 'Buongiorno' or 'Buonasera' on entering a shop or bar is expected courtesy. Use the formal 'Lei' with strangers and elders until invited to use 'tu'; English is common in major tourist areas and among younger people, less so in rural areas and the south.

phrases.local: Un biglietto per Firenze, per favore
phrases.say: oon bee-LYET-toh pehr fee-REN-tseh, pehr fah-VOH-reh

phrases.local: Un tavolo per due, per favore
phrases.say: oon TAH-voh-loh pehr DOO-eh, pehr fah-VOH-reh

culture.history: The heartland of the Roman Empire and later of the Renaissance, the Italian peninsula was for centuries a patchwork of city-states, kingdoms and the Papal States, until unification in the Risorgimento, completed in 1870–1871. Fascism under Mussolini from 1922 brought dictatorship, colonial wars in Libya and Ethiopia marked by atrocities, antisemitic racial laws and alliance with Nazi Germany. Liberation in 1945 owed much to the partisan Resistance, and in 1946 Italians voted to become a republic. Post-war Italy rebuilt into a major economy while contending with deep north–south disparities and the violence of organised crime.
culture.politics: Italy is a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state, elected by parliament and regional delegates, and a government led by a prime minister that must hold the confidence of both houses. Twenty regions, five with special autonomy, share power with the national state. Frequent changes of government, balanced by strong constitutional institutions, are a long-standing feature of civic life.
culture.arts: Italy is the cradle of the Renaissance, home to Giotto, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael, and of Baroque Rome shaped by Bernini and Caravaggio. Dante's Divine Comedy founded Italian literature, and opera was born here, flowering with Verdi and Puccini. Its cinema, from Fellini to De Sica's neorealism, remains deeply influential.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed openly, through embraces, animated conversation and the long shared table, where cooking for someone is an act of love. Family bonds are central and often span generations living close to one another. There is wide regional variety, from more reserved northern manners to effusive southern warmth.

etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees when visiting churches.
Cappuccino is traditionally a morning drink; after meals, locals usually order an espresso ('un caffè').
Greet shop staff with 'Buongiorno' or 'Buonasera' on entering, and validate train tickets before boarding regional trains.

name: Vatican City

languages.note: Italian is the everyday and administrative language; Latin is the official language of the Holy See; residents and staff come from many nations and speak many languages

people: Vatican City's few hundred residents are mostly clergy, members of religious orders, the Pontifical Swiss Guard and some lay employees and their families, drawn from many countries; most citizenship is tied to an office and ends with it. Almost everyone is Catholic, and several thousand more lay and religious staff, mostly Italians, commute in daily from Rome. Every year millions of pilgrims and visitors from across the world pass through its square, basilica and museums.

plug.note: Same as Italy: UK and US travellers need an adapter, and a universal one handles Type L sockets; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: St Peter's Basilica and the tomb of the Apostle Peter, heart of Catholic pilgrimage
The Vatican Museums, one of the world's greatest art collections
The Vatican Apostolic Library and Archive, treasuries of manuscripts and history
A worldwide diplomatic network through the Holy See
The spiritual and moral voice of the papacy for over a billion Catholics
Skilled custodians: restorers, archivists, mosaicists, astronomers and musicians
struggles: Budget deficits and a strained pension fund
Rebuilding trust after financial scandals and ongoing reforms of financial oversight
The Church's continuing reckoning with clerical abuse and its care for survivors
Overcrowding and wear on fragile art and buildings from millions of visitors
Holding together a global Church marked by deep differences and tensions
prayFor: For survivors of abuse within the Church, that they be heard, believed, healed and accompanied with justice
For all who serve here — guards, clergy, sisters, cleaners, restorers and guides — that their work be joyful and sustained
For integrity and transparency in the stewardship of resources entrusted for the poor and the mission of the Church
For pilgrims who arrive weary, grieving or searching, that they meet consolation and hope
For unity and charity across a worldwide Church, and for peace among the nations

summary.history: In Roman times the Vatican Hill lay outside the city, with gardens and Nero's circus, where by ancient tradition the Apostle Peter was martyred and buried around AD 64. Emperor Constantine raised a great basilica over the tomb in the fourth century, and pilgrims have come ever since. For over a thousand years the popes also ruled the Papal States across central Italy, a temporal power that ended when the Kingdom of Italy took Rome in 1870. The present basilica, built between 1506 and 1626, and the surrounding palaces became a world centre of art, learning and faith, while the Church's history here also holds grievous chapters for which recent popes have publicly asked forgiveness. Since 1929 the Vatican has existed as a tiny sovereign state supporting the spiritual mission of the Holy See.
summary.politicalHistory: After Italian troops captured Rome in 1870, the popes refused to recognise the loss of their territory and remained within the Vatican for nearly six decades, a dispute known as the Roman Question. The Lateran Treaty of 1929, signed by the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy, created Vatican City State as an independent territory and was later confirmed in Italy's republican constitution. Vatican City is an elective absolute monarchy: the pope, elected for life by the College of Cardinals in conclave, holds supreme legislative, executive and judicial power, exercised day to day through a pontifical commission and governorate. Its Fundamental Law was revised in 2000 and 2023, while the Holy See, a distinct sovereign body, maintains diplomatic relations with most of the world's states.
summary.art: The Vatican holds summits of Western art: Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling and Last Judgement, Raphael's Rooms and the classical sculptures of the Pio-Clementino such as the Laocoön. Sacred music lives on in Gregorian chant and the Sistine Chapel Choir, heir to Palestrina's polyphony. The Vatican Mosaic Studio, which renders the basilica's altarpieces in durable stone mosaic, keeps a centuries-old craft alive.
summary.monuments: The whole of Vatican City is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, centred on St Peter's Basilica with Michelangelo's dome and Bernini's bronze baldachin above the tomb of Peter. Bernini's colonnaded St Peter's Square opens like embracing arms to the world, with an ancient Egyptian obelisk at its centre. The Sistine Chapel, the Vatican Museums and the Vatican Necropolis beneath the basilica carry the memory of faith, art and the earliest Christian community of Rome.

highlights.title: St Peter's Basilica
highlights.line: Enter one of the largest churches on earth, built over Peter's tomb; arrive at opening time to pray in near-silence and pass security quickly.

highlights.title: Michelangelo's Pietà
highlights.line: See Mary cradling her Son in marble, carved when Michelangelo was in his twenties; it is behind glass just inside the right-hand entrance.

highlights.title: Climb the Dome
highlights.line: Climb, or take a lift part-way, up Michelangelo's dome for a sweeping view over Rome; the last stretch is narrow and steep.

highlights.title: Bernini's Baldachin
highlights.line: Stand beneath the soaring bronze canopy over the papal altar, directly above the tomb of St Peter.

highlights.title: Chair of St Peter
highlights.line: Look toward the apse where Bernini's golden glory surrounds a dove of the Holy Spirit in alabaster glass, especially lovely in afternoon light.

highlights.title: Vatican Necropolis (Scavi)
highlights.line: Descend to the Roman cemetery beneath the basilica toward the traditional tomb of Peter; small group tours must be booked well ahead through the Excavations Office.

highlights.title: Vatican Grottoes
highlights.line: Walk through the crypt beneath the basilica where many popes are buried; entry is free and usually from inside the basilica.

highlights.title: St Peter's Square
highlights.line: Find the round paving stones near the fountains where Bernini's four rows of columns line up into one.

highlights.title: Papal General Audience
highlights.line: Join pilgrims from every nation for the pope's Wednesday audience; tickets are free but must be requested in advance.

highlights.title: Sunday Angelus
highlights.line: Gather in the square at noon on Sunday when the pope usually prays the Angelus from a window of the Apostolic Palace.

highlights.title: Mass at the Altar of the Chair
highlights.line: Join an early-morning or daily Mass in the basilica, often celebrated in Italian or Latin, a calm way to experience it as a living church.

highlights.title: Sistine Chapel
highlights.line: Gaze at Michelangelo's ceiling and Last Judgement in silence; photography is forbidden, and a small pair of binoculars helps.

highlights.title: Raphael Rooms
highlights.line: See the School of Athens and other frescoes painted by Raphael and his workshop for Pope Julius II.

highlights.title: Vatican Museums at opening
highlights.line: Book the first entry slot or a Friday evening opening in season to see the galleries with fewer crowds.

highlights.title: Gallery of Maps
highlights.line: Walk the 120-metre gallery of painted maps of sixteenth-century Italy under a richly gilded ceiling.

highlights.title: Laocoön and the Apollo Belvedere
highlights.line: Visit the Octagonal Court of the Pio-Clementino, where the ancient Laocoön has stood since its rediscovery in 1506.

highlights.title: Belvedere Torso
highlights.line: See the muscular fragment that Michelangelo is said to have deeply admired and studied.

highlights.title: Round Hall
highlights.line: Admire the vast porphyry basin and mosaic floor in this domed hall modelled on the Pantheon.

highlights.title: Pinacoteca
highlights.line: Find Raphael's Transfiguration, Caravaggio's Entombment and Leonardo's unfinished St Jerome in the picture gallery.

highlights.title: Gregorian Egyptian Museum
highlights.line: Explore mummies, statues and papyri gathered by popes since the Renaissance.

highlights.title: Gregorian Etruscan Museum
highlights.line: Discover the gold and bronze of ancient Etruria, including the treasures of the Regolini-Galassi tomb.

highlights.title: Braccio Nuovo
highlights.line: See the Augustus of Prima Porta, a celebrated portrait statue of Rome's first emperor.

highlights.title: Collection of Modern Religious Art
highlights.line: Find works by Matisse, Chagall, Dalí and Van Gogh exploring faith in modern times.

highlights.title: Courtyard of the Pinecone
highlights.line: Rest beside the giant ancient bronze pinecone and Arnaldo Pomodoro's modern Sphere within a Sphere.

highlights.title: Bramante Staircase
highlights.line: Photograph the famous double-helix spiral staircase near the Museums' exit, designed by Giuseppe Momo in 1932.

highlights.title: Anima Mundi Museum
highlights.line: See art and sacred objects from Indigenous peoples of the Americas, Africa, Asia and Oceania in a thoughtful ethnological collection.

highlights.title: Carriage Pavilion
highlights.line: View papal carriages, early cars and popemobiles in a quieter corner of the Museums.

highlights.title: Vatican Gardens
highlights.line: Explore groves, fountains and grottoes covering about half the state on a guided tour or open-air bus tour.

highlights.title: Swiss Guard
highlights.line: Spot the guards in their striped Renaissance-style uniforms at the Arch of the Bells and the Bronze Door; please do not ask them to pose.

highlights.title: Vatican Post Office
highlights.line: Send a postcard with a Vatican stamp from the post office in the square, beloved by collectors.

highlights.title: Holy Door
highlights.line: Look for the bronze Holy Door of the basilica, opened only during Jubilee years as a sign of mercy.

highlights.title: Christmas and Easter in the Square
highlights.line: Experience the nativity scene and Christmas tree in the square, or the Easter 'Urbi et Orbi' blessing; arrive very early.

highlights.title: Castel Gandolfo
highlights.line: Take the train to the papal summer residence in the Alban Hills, where the Barberini Gardens are open to visitors.

funFacts: Vatican City is the world's smallest independent state, covering about 44 hectares.
It is the only country whose entire territory is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Vatican City is completely surrounded by the city of Rome.
The Pontifical Swiss Guard was founded in 1506 and is one of the oldest military units still in service.
Swiss Guards must be Catholic Swiss men, and new recruits are sworn in each year on 6 May.
The 6 May swearing-in remembers the 147 guards who died defending the pope during the Sack of Rome in 1527.
The Vatican Museums trace their founding to 1506, when Pope Julius II displayed newly acquired ancient sculptures.
Michelangelo was called to examine the Laocoön statue soon after it was unearthed in Rome in 1506.
Vatican citizenship is generally granted because of an office or role, not by birth.
Latin is the official language of the Holy See, and a Vatican ATM has offered instructions in Latin.
The Vatican mints its own euro coins under an agreement with the European Union.
The Vatican issues its own postage stamps, prized by collectors around the world.
Vatican Radio began broadcasting in 1931 with a transmitter built by Guglielmo Marconi.
L'Osservatore Romano, the Holy See's daily newspaper, was founded in 1861.
The Vatican Observatory is one of the oldest astronomical institutes in the world and runs a telescope in Arizona.
The Vatican Apostolic Library was formally established in 1475 under Pope Sixtus IV.
The former Vatican Secret Archives were renamed the Vatican Apostolic Archive in 2019; 'secret' had meant 'private'.
The Pietà is the only work Michelangelo ever signed, his name carved across the sash on Mary's chest.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling standing on scaffolding he designed, not lying on his back.
Conclaves to elect a new pope are held in the Sistine Chapel, and white smoke announces the election.
The word 'conclave' comes from the Latin 'cum clave', meaning 'with a key'.
The obelisk in St Peter's Square was brought from Egypt by Emperor Caligula and moved to its present spot in 1586.
The obelisk also serves as a giant sundial gnomon, with a meridian line marked in the paving of the square.
Bernini's colonnade around St Peter's Square has 284 columns topped by 140 statues of saints.
Markers set into the floor of St Peter's show the lengths of other great churches of the world for comparison.
Most of the 'paintings' above the altars in St Peter's are actually mosaics made of tiny pieces of coloured glass and stone.
The Vatican has its own railway station, linked to the Italian network by one of the world's shortest national railways.
Vatican City has a heliport but no airport.
Roughly half of Vatican City's territory is taken up by gardens.
In 2008 some 2,400 solar panels were installed on the roof of the Paul VI Audience Hall.
The Holy See, not Vatican City, holds permanent observer status at the United Nations.
The Holy See maintains diplomatic relations with more than 180 states.
The central bronze doors of St Peter's, made by Filarete in the 1440s, were carried over from the old basilica.

languageGuide.intro: Italian is the everyday language inside Vatican City, and the courtesy of greeting with 'Buongiorno' or 'Buonasera' and using the formal 'Lei' with staff, guards and clergy is warmly received. Italian is pronounced much as it is written, with every vowel clear and double consonants held a little longer; English and many other languages are widely spoken at the Museums and Basilica, while Latin appears on inscriptions and in solemn liturgy.

culture.history: Vatican Hill was the site of Nero's circus and, by ancient tradition, of St Peter's martyrdom and burial, over which Constantine built the first basilica in the fourth century. For more than a millennium popes also ruled the Papal States across central Italy, a temporal power that ended when Italian troops took Rome in 1870. The 'Roman Question' was settled by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, signed with Mussolini's government, which created the independent Vatican City State. The Church's own history here includes both great works of charity and art and grievous chapters it has publicly acknowledged and asked forgiveness for.
culture.politics: Vatican City is an elective absolute monarchy in which the Pope, chosen by the College of Cardinals in conclave, holds supreme legislative, executive and judicial authority. Day-to-day administration is delegated to a Pontifical Commission and a governorate, while the Holy See, a distinct sovereign entity, conducts diplomacy with most of the world's states. It exists chiefly to guarantee the spiritual independence of the papacy.
culture.arts: The Sistine Chapel holds Michelangelo's ceiling and Last Judgement alongside frescoes by Botticelli and Perugino, while the Raphael Rooms and the Vatican Museums house one of the world's great art collections. St Peter's Basilica, with Michelangelo's dome and Bernini's colonnade and baldachin, is a summit of Renaissance and Baroque architecture. Sacred music lives on in the Sistine Chapel Choir and the Gregorian chant heritage.

love.expression: Life here is shaped by Italian warmth and by a Catholic vision of love as self-giving, expressed in service, prayer and hospitality to pilgrims. Many who live and work here are clergy, religious and lay staff from around the world, so expressions of affection are as varied as their homelands. Kindness to the poor and the stranger, through the work of papal charities, is a central expression of care.

etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees to enter St Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Museums; dress codes are enforced.
Keep silence in the Sistine Chapel, where photography is not allowed.
Book Vatican Museums tickets in advance and allow for security checks before entering the basilica.

name: Germany

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages such as Turkish, Arabic, Russian and Polish; Danish, Sorbian, Frisian, Romani and Low German are recognised regional or minority languages

people: Germany is home to a German majority with strong regional identities, from Bavaria and Saxony to the Rhineland and the north coast, and to recognised minorities including Danes, Sorbs, Frisians and Sinti and Roma. Around a quarter of residents have a migration background, with large communities of Turkish, Polish, Russian-German, Syrian, Ukrainian, Italian and other heritage. Christians, divided roughly evenly between Catholics and Protestants, now make up under half the population, alongside a large non-religious share, especially in the east, and a Muslim community of around five to six million; three quarters of people live in towns and cities.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: A world-leading engineering, automotive and machinery industry
A skilled workforce trained through the dual vocational system
Strong research universities and institutes
Fertile farmland, forests and the Rhine and Elbe waterways
Wind and solar power at the heart of the energy transition
A deep cultural heritage in music, literature, philosophy and design
struggles: Economic stagnation and pressure on its export and car industries
An ageing population and shortages of skilled workers, carers and teachers
Affordable housing shortages in major cities
Political polarisation and a rise in far-right extremism, antisemitism and racist hostility
Integrating refugees and migrants with fairness and mutual trust
Lingering economic and social gaps between east and west
prayFor: For workers and families anxious about jobs as industries change, that they find security and new purpose
For nurses, carers and teachers carrying heavy loads, and for the elderly in their care
For Jewish, Muslim and migrant communities, that they live free from hatred and fear
For refugees from Syria, Ukraine, Afghanistan and elsewhere, that they find healing and home, and for neighbours who welcome them
For reconciliation between east and west and across political divides, rooted in truth and remembrance

summary.history: Germanic peoples lived beyond and alongside the Roman frontier, and from the Middle Ages the German lands formed the core of the Holy Roman Empire, a patchwork of principalities, bishoprics and free cities. The Reformation began here in 1517, and the Thirty Years' War that followed devastated much of the land. Unified in 1871, Germany briefly held colonies where its forces committed genocide against the Herero and Nama in present-day Namibia, and after defeat in the First World War its fragile Weimar democracy fell to the Nazi dictatorship. The Nazi regime waged a war of conquest and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust, together with Sinti and Roma, disabled people and many others. Divided during the Cold War, Germany was peacefully reunited in 1990 after the fall of the Berlin Wall, and its culture of remembrance seeks to face this past honestly.
summary.politicalHistory: Under Otto von Bismarck, Prussia united most German states into the German Empire in 1871, a monarchy that collapsed in the revolution of 1918. The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, was destroyed after 1933 by Adolf Hitler's Nazi dictatorship, which ended with total defeat in 1945. In 1949 the democratic Federal Republic in the west, founded on the Basic Law, and the communist German Democratic Republic in the east were established, and the peaceful revolution of 1989 led to reunification on 3 October 1990. Today Germany is a federal parliamentary republic of sixteen states, with a chancellor accountable to the Bundestag, a largely ceremonial federal president and a powerful Constitutional Court.
summary.art: Germany's musical heritage runs from Bach, Handel and Beethoven to Brahms, Wagner and today's vibrant electronic scene. Its literature and thought include Goethe, Schiller, Kant, the Brothers Grimm, Thomas Mann and the post-war voices of Heinrich Böll and Günter Grass, while art spans Albrecht Dürer, Caspar David Friedrich and Expressionism. The Bauhaus school, founded in Weimar in 1919, reshaped modern architecture and design across the world.
summary.monuments: Cologne Cathedral, a Gothic masterpiece begun in 1248 and completed in 1880, and Aachen Cathedral, the resting place of Charlemagne, are among Germany's most beloved UNESCO sites. Berlin's Brandenburg Gate and the remains of the Berlin Wall stand as symbols of division and reunification, while Museum Island holds treasures of world civilisations. Dresden's rebuilt Frauenkirche and the Wartburg, where Luther translated the New Testament, speak of destruction, reconciliation and faith.

highlights.title: Brandenburg Gate and Reichstag
highlights.line: Walk through Berlin's symbol of reunification, then climb the glass dome of the Reichstag; registration is free but required in advance.

highlights.title: Berlin Wall Memorial
highlights.line: Visit the preserved border strip on Bernauer Strasse to understand life in a divided city, then see the murals of the East Side Gallery.

highlights.title: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
highlights.line: Walk among the concrete stelae in silence, and visit the information centre below to meet individual stories.

highlights.title: Museum Island
highlights.line: See the Ishtar Gate and the bust of Nefertiti among five world-class museums; a day pass saves money.

highlights.title: Potsdam's Sanssouci
highlights.line: Wander the palaces and terraced vineyards of Frederick the Great's summer retreat, an easy trip from Berlin.

highlights.title: Dresden's Frauenkirche
highlights.line: See the Baroque church rebuilt from its rubble after 1945, a symbol of reconciliation; join an evening organ prayer.

highlights.title: Saxon Switzerland
highlights.line: Hike to the Bastei Bridge among sandstone towers above the Elbe, best early morning before the crowds.

highlights.title: Leipzig
highlights.line: Hear the boys' choir at St Thomas Church, where Bach worked, and visit St Nicholas Church, cradle of the 1989 peaceful revolution.

highlights.title: Weimar
highlights.line: Visit the homes of Goethe and Schiller and the Bauhaus Museum, and reflect at the nearby Buchenwald memorial.

highlights.title: Wartburg Castle
highlights.line: Explore the hilltop castle above Eisenach where Martin Luther translated the New Testament into German.

highlights.title: Quedlinburg
highlights.line: Stroll more than a thousand half-timbered houses in a UNESCO-listed town at the edge of the Harz mountains.

highlights.title: Harz and the Brocken
highlights.line: Ride the steam narrow-gauge railway up the Brocken, the mountain of witches' legends and Goethe's Faust.

highlights.title: Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie
highlights.line: Take the free plaza access for harbour views, and walk the red-brick canals of the Speicherstadt nearby.

highlights.title: Lübeck
highlights.line: Enter the medieval Hanseatic city through the Holsten Gate and taste its famous marzipan.

highlights.title: Rügen's chalk cliffs
highlights.line: Walk the beech forest of Jasmund National Park to the white cliffs painted by Caspar David Friedrich.

highlights.title: Wadden Sea
highlights.line: Join a guided mudflat hike at low tide in this UNESCO-listed sea, and watch for seals; never go without a guide.

highlights.title: Cologne Cathedral
highlights.line: Climb the 533 steps of the south tower and see the shrine of the Three Kings, then try a Kölsch beer in a brewhouse.

highlights.title: Aachen Cathedral
highlights.line: Stand in Charlemagne's Palatine Chapel, consecrated around 805 and one of Germany's first UNESCO sites.

highlights.title: Rhine Gorge
highlights.line: Cruise past castles, vineyards and the Lorelei rock between Bingen and Koblenz, or hike the Rheinsteig trail.

highlights.title: Moselle Valley
highlights.line: Taste Riesling grown on some of Europe's steepest vineyards, and visit Burg Eltz in its forested valley.

highlights.title: Trier
highlights.line: Walk through the Porta Nigra, a Roman city gate, in Germany's oldest city with a wealth of Roman sites.

highlights.title: Heidelberg
highlights.line: Climb to the romantic castle ruins and walk the Philosophers' Way across the river at golden hour.

highlights.title: Black Forest
highlights.line: Hike through dark pine forests and waterfalls at Triberg, and taste a slice of Black Forest cherry cake.

highlights.title: Lake Constance
highlights.line: Visit the flower island of Mainau and the UNESCO-listed monastic island of Reichenau, travelling by ferry.

highlights.title: Ulm Minster
highlights.line: Climb the 768 steps of the world's tallest church steeple for views reaching the Alps on clear days.

highlights.title: Rothenburg ob der Tauber
highlights.line: Walk the complete medieval town walls, and stay overnight to enjoy the quiet streets after day visitors leave.

highlights.title: Würzburg Residence
highlights.line: See Tiepolo's vast ceiling fresco above the grand staircase, and taste Franconian wine from its round Bocksbeutel bottles.

highlights.title: Bamberg
highlights.line: Wander a UNESCO-listed old town built on seven hills, and try the city's distinctive smoked beer, Rauchbier.

highlights.title: Nuremberg
highlights.line: Explore the imperial castle and the Documentation Center on the former Nazi Party Rally Grounds, a powerful place of learning.

highlights.title: Munich beer gardens
highlights.line: Sit under chestnut trees with a Mass of beer and a pretzel; in traditional beer gardens you may bring your own food.

highlights.title: Dachau Concentration Camp Memorial
highlights.line: Visit the first Nazi concentration camp with a guide or audio guide, allowing time for quiet reflection.

highlights.title: Neuschwanstein and the Bavarian Alps
highlights.line: Book timed tickets for King Ludwig II's fairy-tale castle, and see the turquoise Königssee or the Zugspitze, Germany's highest peak.

highlights.title: Christmas markets
highlights.line: Warm up with mulled wine and gingerbread at markets like Dresden's Striezelmarkt or Nuremberg's Christkindlesmarkt from late November.

funFacts: Germany borders nine countries, more than any other country lying wholly in Europe.
German bread culture is on Germany's national list of intangible heritage, with more than 3,000 registered bread varieties.
Ulm Minster has the world's tallest church steeple, at about 161 metres.
Large stretches of the German Autobahn have no general speed limit, only an advisory 130 km/h.
Johannes Gutenberg developed movable-type printing in Mainz around 1450.
The word 'kindergarten' was coined by the German educator Friedrich Fröbel in 1840.
Dresden's Striezelmarkt, first held in 1434, is among the oldest documented Christmas markets.
In German, every noun is written with a capital letter.
German has three grammatical genders, and 'das Mädchen', the girl, is grammatically neuter.
The Bavarian Beer Purity Law of 1516 allowed only water, barley and hops in beer.
Germany has around 1,500 breweries, many of them small and family-run.
Gummy bears were invented by Hans Riegel, founder of Haribo, in Bonn in 1922.
Fanta was first created in Germany in 1940, when Coca-Cola syrup could not be imported during the war.
Currywurst is credited to Herta Heuwer, who sold it in Berlin in 1949.
The döner kebab sandwich as many know it was popularised in Berlin by Turkish immigrants in the 1970s.
Karl Drais of Mannheim invented the 'running machine', an ancestor of the bicycle, in 1817.
In 1888 Bertha Benz made the first long-distance car journey, driving about 100 km to visit her mother.
Aspirin was first synthesised in a stable form at Bayer in 1897.
The MP3 audio format was developed largely at the Fraunhofer Institute in Erlangen.
Albert Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879.
Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770.
Heidelberg University, founded in 1386, is the oldest university in present-day Germany.
The Venus of Hohle Fels, carved from mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, is one of the oldest known figurative sculptures.
Bone and ivory flutes found in Swabian caves are among the oldest known musical instruments in the world.
The Berlin Wall stood for 28 years, and since 2018 it has been gone for longer than it stood.
Hamburg has around 2,500 bridges, more than Venice and Amsterdam combined.
Hamburg's Speicherstadt is the largest historic warehouse district of its kind in the world.
The border on part of Lake Constance between Germany, Switzerland and Austria has never been formally agreed.
Germany's deposit system, the Pfand, returns money for most drink bottles and cans, and almost all are brought back.
Most shops in Germany close on Sundays, which are protected by the constitution as days of rest.
The Brothers Grimm collected many of their fairy tales in Hesse, now traced by the German Fairy Tale Route.
Germany has won the men's FIFA World Cup four times and the women's World Cup twice.
The decorated Christmas tree tradition spread from Germany across the world in the nineteenth century.

languageGuide.intro: German uses the formal 'Sie' for strangers, shop staff and older people and the informal 'du' among friends and young people, and pronunciation is fairly regular: 'w' sounds like English 'v', 'ei' like 'eye', 'ie' like 'ee', and 'ch' is a soft breathy sound. English is widely spoken, especially by younger people and in cities, but starting with a German greeting is appreciated; in Bavaria and the south you will often hear 'Grüß Gott'.

phrases.en: A glass of tap water, please

culture.history: For centuries the German lands were a mosaic of principalities within the Holy Roman Empire, and the Reformation began here in 1517 with Martin Luther. Unified in 1871, Germany briefly held colonies in Africa and the Pacific, where its forces committed genocide against the Herero and Nama in present-day Namibia. Defeat in the First World War was followed by the Weimar Republic and the Nazi dictatorship, which waged a war of conquest and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust, along with Roma, disabled people and many others. Divided into East and West during the Cold War, Germany reunified peacefully in 1990, and its culture of remembrance is a deliberate reckoning with this past.
culture.politics: Germany is a federal parliamentary republic under the Basic Law of 1949, with a largely ceremonial federal president and a chancellor elected by and accountable to the Bundestag. Sixteen federal states (Länder) hold strong powers and are represented in the Bundesrat. Constitutional safeguards for human dignity and democracy, designed in response to the Nazi era, shape its civic identity.
culture.arts: Germany's musical legacy is immense, from Bach and Beethoven to Brahms and Wagner. Its literature includes Goethe, Schiller, Thomas Mann and the Brothers Grimm, and its art ranges from Albrecht Dürer to Expressionism. The Bauhaus school, founded in 1919, transformed modern architecture and design worldwide.

love.expression: Affection is often shown through reliability, honesty and keeping one's word, with friendships formed slowly but held with great loyalty. Time spent together, in walks, shared meals or a long conversation, carries meaning. The shift from the formal 'Sie' to the familiar 'du' is itself a quiet sign of closeness.

etiquette: Be punctual; arriving on time is a basic form of respect.
Use 'Sie' and surnames with titles until invited to switch to 'du'.
Respect quiet hours, especially on Sundays and late evenings, and sort recycling carefully.

name: Austria

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; Croatian, Slovene and Hungarian are recognised regionally

people: Most of Austria's roughly 9.2 million people are German-speaking Austrians, alongside long-rooted Burgenland Croat, Carinthian Slovene, Hungarian, Czech, Slovak and Roma minorities; about a quarter of residents have a migrant background, with large communities from Germany, Turkey, the former Yugoslavia, Romania, Syria, Afghanistan and Ukraine. Roughly 55% are Roman Catholic, about 8% Muslim, around 5% Orthodox and 4% Protestant, while over a fifth profess no religion. About one in five Austrians lives in Vienna, yet Alpine villages and small towns still shape much of the national character.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Alpine landscapes and year-round tourism
Hydropower, supplying well over half of its electricity
Forests and a strong timber industry
Skilled family-owned manufacturing and engineering firms
A towering musical and cultural heritage
Vienna's role as a diplomatic hub (UN, OSCE, OPEC, IAEA)
struggles: Long dependence on Russian gas and the cost of the energy transition
Polarised debate over migration, asylum and integration
Rising housing and living costs, especially in cities
An ageing population and a shortage of carers and nurses
Shrinking glaciers, landslides and floods in a warming Alpine climate
prayFor: For warmth and fairness in the energy transition, so no household is left cold or overburdened
For newcomers and long-settled Austrians to meet one another with patience, dignity and real welcome
For carers and nurses, and for the elderly they tend, that none would be lonely or neglected
For the mountains, rivers and villages facing floods and melting ice, and for wise stewardship of creation
For a culture of honest memory, so that remembrance of the Holocaust keeps hearts awake to every form of hatred

summary.history: The Alpine lands of Austria were home to the Iron Age Hallstatt culture and later to Celtic Noricum, absorbed by Rome with frontier towns such as Carnuntum and Vindobona (Vienna) along the Danube. From 1278 the Habsburg dynasty made Austria the heart of a vast multinational realm that withstood Ottoman sieges of Vienna in 1529 and 1683 and dominated central Europe for centuries. Defeat in the First World War broke up the empire, and the small republic that remained slid into civil strife in 1934 and was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938. Many Austrians took part in Nazi crimes; around 65,000 Austrian Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, and the country long sheltered behind the myth of being Hitler's 'first victim' before a fuller reckoning began from the 1980s. Allied occupation ended with the State Treaty of 1955, after which a neutral Austria rebuilt itself into a prosperous democracy that joined the European Union in 1995.
summary.politicalHistory: Austria emerged as a Babenberg margraviate and duchy within the Holy Roman Empire, became the Austrian Empire in 1804, and shared power with Hungary in the Dual Monarchy from 1867. The First Republic was proclaimed in 1918 and given a federal constitution drafted largely by Hans Kelsen in 1920, but parliament was suspended in 1933 and Engelbert Dollfuss set up an authoritarian corporate state before the 1938 Anschluss. The Second Republic was restored in 1945, regained full sovereignty through the 1955 State Treaty and declared permanent neutrality the same year. Today Austria is a federal parliamentary republic of nine states, with a directly elected president and a chancellor-led government answerable to the National Council.
summary.art: Vienna nurtured Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, the Strauss family, Mahler and Schoenberg, and the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert still carries that legacy to the world. Around 1900 Gustav Klimt, Egon Schiele, Otto Wagner and the Wiener Werkstätte reshaped painting, architecture and design, while writers such as Stefan Zweig, Arthur Schnitzler and Ingeborg Bachmann gave voice to a changing society. Folk traditions endure in yodelling, Schuhplattler dancing, Advent crafts and the coffee-house culture of conversation.
summary.monuments: The Palace and Gardens of Schönbrunn and the Historic Centre of Vienna, both UNESCO sites, embody Habsburg power and its baroque splendour. The Historic Centre of Salzburg and the Hallstatt–Dachstein/Salzkammergut cultural landscape tell of prince-archbishops and seven millennia of salt mining. The Wachau with Melk Abbey, the pioneering Semmering Railway and the Mauthausen Memorial—where tens of thousands died in a Nazi concentration camp—complete a portrait of beauty and sorrow.

highlights.title: Schönbrunn Palace
highlights.line: The Habsburgs' summer palace is a masterpiece of baroque grandeur; book a timed ticket and climb to the Gloriette for the best view over Vienna.

highlights.title: St Stephen's Cathedral
highlights.line: Vienna's Gothic heart with its glazed-tile roof; climb the 343 steps of the south tower, then sit quietly at a weekday Mass.

highlights.title: Viennese coffee houses
highlights.line: Linger for hours over a Melange and newspaper in Café Hawelka or Café Central; no one will rush you, and a glass of water comes free.

highlights.title: Kunsthistorisches Museum
highlights.line: One of the world's great painting collections, with the largest group of Bruegels anywhere; the domed café is a treat in itself.

highlights.title: Klimt at the Belvedere
highlights.line: See 'The Kiss' in the Upper Belvedere and stroll the terraced baroque gardens; arrive at opening time to avoid the crowds.

highlights.title: Standing room at the State Opera
highlights.line: World-class opera for a few euros: queue for Stehplatz tickets on the day and tie a scarf to the rail to save your spot.

highlights.title: Spanish Riding School
highlights.line: Watch the white Lipizzaner horses at morning exercise in the Hofburg—far cheaper than a gala performance and just as moving.

highlights.title: A Heuriger in Vienna's vineyards
highlights.line: Take the tram to Grinzing, Nussdorf or Stammersdorf and drink young local wine under a pine branch with a simple cold buffet.

highlights.title: Naschmarkt
highlights.line: Vienna's lively market for spices, olives, cheese and street food; go on Saturday morning when the flea market spills alongside.

highlights.title: Salzburg's old town
highlights.line: Mozart's birthplace, baroque domes and the Getreidegasse's wrought-iron signs; walk up the Kapuzinerberg for a quieter view.

highlights.title: Hohensalzburg Fortress
highlights.line: One of Europe's largest medieval castles crowns Salzburg; ride the funicular up and stay for an evening chamber concert.

highlights.title: Hallstatt
highlights.line: A lakeside village of salt-mining history beneath steep mountains; visit early or out of season, and tour the ancient salt mine above town.

highlights.title: Melk Abbey
highlights.line: A golden baroque Benedictine abbey on a bluff above the Danube, with a breathtaking library; combine it with a boat trip through the Wachau.

highlights.title: Cycling the Wachau
highlights.line: Ride the gentle Danube cycle path between Melk and Krems past vineyards, apricot orchards and ruined castles; rent a bike at either end.

highlights.title: Grossglockner High Alpine Road
highlights.line: A spectacular 48-km pass road to the foot of Austria's highest peak; go early on a clear day and watch for marmots at Kaiser-Franz-Josefs-Höhe.

highlights.title: Krimml Waterfalls
highlights.line: Austria's highest waterfalls thunder 380 m in three tiers; the well-built path up alongside them takes about an hour and a half.

highlights.title: Eisriesenwelt ice cave
highlights.line: The vast ice cave above Werfen glitters by lamplight; bring warm layers even in August, as it stays below freezing inside.

highlights.title: Innsbruck's old town
highlights.line: Pastel houses and the Golden Roof against a wall of mountains; the Hofkirche's bronze statues around Maximilian's tomb are unforgettable.

highlights.title: Nordkette from Innsbruck
highlights.line: Ride the Hungerburg funicular and cable cars from the city centre to over 2,000 m in about twenty minutes for alpine views and walks.

highlights.title: Alpine hut hiking
highlights.line: Walk hut to hut in Tyrol or Salzburgerland and eat Kaiserschmarrn at a mountain Hütte; Alpine Club membership gives cheaper beds.

highlights.title: Skiing in the Arlberg
highlights.line: St Anton and Lech are the cradle of alpine skiing; even non-skiers can enjoy the snowy villages and après-ski warmth.

highlights.title: Zell am See and Kaprun
highlights.line: A lake town for swimming and boating in summer with a glacier for year-round snow just above; buy a summer card for free lifts and boats.

highlights.title: Mariazell Basilica
highlights.line: Central Europe's great Marian pilgrimage shrine since 1157; walk part of a pilgrim route or ride the narrow-gauge Mariazellerbahn.

highlights.title: Admont Abbey library
highlights.line: The world's largest monastic library hall, in white and gold rococo, sits in the green Gesäuse valley of Styria.

highlights.title: Graz
highlights.line: Austria's second city pairs a red-roofed old town with the 'friendly alien' Kunsthaus; climb the Schlossberg to the clock tower.

highlights.title: South Styrian Wine Road
highlights.line: Rolling vineyard hills on the Slovenian border; taste Sauvignon Blanc at a Buschenschank and buy dark green pumpkin-seed oil.

highlights.title: Lake Neusiedl
highlights.line: A shallow steppe lake shared with Hungary, rich in birdlife; cycle the reed-fringed shores and taste Burgenland's sweet wines.

highlights.title: Wörthersee
highlights.line: Carinthia's warm, turquoise lake is perfect for summer swimming; take the Pyramidenkogel tower lift for a view to Slovenia.

highlights.title: Wiener Schnitzel in a Beisl
highlights.line: Try the real thing—veal, thin and golden—in a traditional Viennese tavern, with potato salad and a squeeze of lemon.

highlights.title: Sachertorte and cake culture
highlights.line: Compare the chocolate Sachertorte at Hotel Sacher with Demel's version, and order it 'mit Schlag' (with whipped cream).

highlights.title: Advent Christmas markets
highlights.line: From Vienna's Rathausplatz to Salzburg's cathedral square, markets glow with mulled wine and crafts; bring your mug back for the deposit.

highlights.title: Ars Electronica Center, Linz
highlights.line: A playful museum of art, science and technology on the Danube; on weekend evenings its façade lights up in changing colours.

highlights.title: Mauthausen Memorial
highlights.line: A sobering former concentration camp near Linz; allow half a day, consider a guided tour, and leave time afterwards for silence.

funFacts: Vienna's Tiergarten Schönbrunn, founded in 1752, is the oldest zoo in the world still in operation.
'Silent Night' was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 in the village church of Oberndorf near Salzburg.
Vienna has hundreds of hectares of working vineyards within its city limits, more than almost any other capital.
Austria completed a nuclear power plant at Zwentendorf but never switched it on after a 1978 referendum rejected nuclear energy.
The snow globe was developed in Vienna around 1900 by Erwin Perzy, and his family still makes them there today.
By Austrian food rules, a dish may only be sold as 'Wiener Schnitzel' if it is made from veal.
When Austria joined the EU, a special protocol protected 23 Austrian food words, such as Erdäpfel (potatoes) and Paradeiser (tomatoes).
Vienna is one of only four main UN headquarters cities, alongside New York, Geneva and Nairobi.
The Grossglockner, at 3,798 m, is Austria's highest mountain.
The Krimml Waterfalls, falling about 380 m, are the highest in Austria.
Eisriesenwelt near Werfen is considered the largest known ice cave in the world, with about 42 km of passages.
Salt has been mined at Hallstatt for around 7,000 years, making it one of the oldest known salt mines anywhere.
Although landlocked today, Austria-Hungary once had a sizeable navy based on the Adriatic coast.
Austria's national anthem was changed in 2012 to honour 'great daughters' as well as sons.
The red-white-red Austrian colours go back to the coat of arms of the Babenberg dukes in the 13th century.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, in a house on the Getreidegasse.
Lake Neusiedl, shared with Hungary, is so shallow that in most places you could stand up in it.
Vienna's giant Ferris wheel, the Riesenrad in the Prater, was built in 1897.
Sigmund Freud lived and worked at Berggasse 19 in Vienna for nearly half a century; it is now a museum.
Vienna-born actress Hedy Lamarr co-invented a frequency-hopping technique that underlies later wireless technologies.
The energy drink Red Bull was founded in Austria in the 1980s and is still headquartered near Salzburg.
Ötzi the Iceman was discovered in 1991 by hikers in the Alps on the Austrian–Italian border and turned out to lie just inside Italy.
About one in five people in Austria lives in Vienna.
Austria has been permanently neutral since 1955 and is not a member of NATO.
Around two-thirds of Austria's territory lies in the Alps.
The Semmering Railway, opened in 1854, was the first mountain railway in the world to be declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Vienna's coffee-house culture is listed in Austria's national inventory of intangible cultural heritage.
The Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert is broadcast every year to audiences in dozens of countries.
Graz was European Capital of Culture in 2003 and Linz in 2009.
Mariazell's basilica has received pilgrims since the 12th century, making it one of central Europe's oldest shrines.
Austria abolished the death penalty entirely in 1968.
The Danube flows for roughly 350 km through Austria, passing Linz and Vienna.
