Austrians often greet each other with 'Servus', a Latin word meaning 'at your service', for both hello and goodbye.

languageGuide.intro: Austrians speak German with their own warm accent and vocabulary, and politeness matters: use 'Sie' and 'Grüß Gott' with strangers, and save 'du' and 'Servus' for friends. Pronounce 'w' like English 'v', 'ei' like 'eye' and 'ie' like 'ee'; English is widely spoken in cities and tourist areas, but a few German words are warmly received everywhere.

culture.history: For more than six centuries Austria was the core of the Habsburg realm, which grew into a multinational empire spanning much of central Europe and twice withstood Ottoman sieges of Vienna. The empire collapsed after the First World War, leaving a small republic that slid into authoritarian rule in the 1930s. In 1938 Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany, and many Austrians took part in the regime and its crimes, including the persecution and murder of Austrian Jews; the country only gradually moved past the myth of having been simply Hitler's 'first victim'. After occupation by the Allies, Austria regained full sovereignty in 1955 and declared permanent neutrality.
culture.politics: Austria is a federal parliamentary republic with a directly elected federal president and a government led by a chancellor accountable to the National Council. Nine federal states (Bundesländer) share power with the federal level. Permanent neutrality, enshrined since 1955, and a long tradition of social partnership between employers and labour shape its civic life.
culture.arts: Vienna was the home of Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and the Strauss family, and later of Mahler and Schoenberg's new music. Around 1900 the Vienna Secession of Gustav Klimt and Egon Schiele and the architecture of Otto Wagner redefined modern art. Its Baroque abbeys, such as Melk, and the coffee-house literary culture are cherished legacies.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed through gentle courtesy, shared rituals such as coffee and cake, and time together outdoors in the mountains or at a Heuriger wine tavern. Austrians may be formal at first, but friendships run deep and loyal. Hospitality and attentiveness to small comforts are quiet signs of care.

etiquette: Greet with 'Grüß Gott' in shops and villages; 'Servus' is the friendly informal hello and goodbye.
Use academic and professional titles (such as 'Frau Doktor') where known; they are still valued.
Most shops close on Sundays, so plan errands ahead.

name: Ireland

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Shelta, Irish Sign Language and immigrant languages; English is spoken by virtually everyone

people: Ireland's roughly 5.4 million people include the Irish majority, the Irish Traveller community (recognised as an ethnic minority in 2017), and about one in five residents born abroad, notably from Britain, Poland, India, Lithuania, Romania, Brazil, Nigeria and Ukraine. About 69% identified as Catholic in the 2022 census, around 14% as having no religion, with smaller Church of Ireland, Orthodox, Muslim and other communities. Most people live in towns and cities, especially greater Dublin, and tens of millions of people worldwide claim Irish ancestry through centuries of emigration.

plug.note: UK travellers need no adapter; continental European and US travellers need a Type G adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: A young, highly educated and globally connected workforce
Green grasslands supporting world-renowned dairy and beef
A major hub for technology, pharmaceutical and medical-device firms
Strong Atlantic winds for renewable energy
A rich literary, musical and storytelling heritage
A vast, loyal global diaspora
struggles: A severe housing shortage, high rents and rising homelessness
Long waiting lists and overcrowding in the public health service
Heavy reliance on tax from a small number of multinational companies
The lasting wounds of abuse in Church and state institutions
Tensions over asylum accommodation and integration amid rapid change
Cutting agricultural emissions while sustaining rural livelihoods
prayFor: For homes for those without one, and for young people and families struggling to find a secure place to live
For survivors of institutional abuse, that they would know truth, justice and deep healing
For nurses, doctors and patients in an overstretched health system
For newcomers and host communities to build trust, friendship and a shared future
For lasting peace and reconciliation across the whole island

summary.history: People have lived in Ireland for over 10,000 years, and farming communities built great passage tombs such as Newgrange more than 5,000 years ago. Gaelic Ireland embraced Christianity from the 5th century, and its monasteries became renowned centres of learning, later raided and then settled by Vikings who founded Dublin and other towns. From the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1169, English and later British rule deepened through conquest, plantation and penal laws against Catholics, and the Great Famine of 1845–52 killed about a million people and drove a million more abroad. Revolution and war brought independence for 26 counties in 1922, followed by a bitter civil war, while Northern Ireland remained in the UK and endured decades of violence until the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Modern Ireland has grown prosperous and diverse while reckoning honestly with abuses in Church and state institutions.
summary.politicalHistory: Ireland was joined to Great Britain by the Act of Union in 1801, and after long campaigns for Home Rule, the 1916 Easter Rising and the War of Independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty created the Irish Free State as a dominion in 1922, amid a civil war over its terms. The 1937 constitution, Bunreacht na hÉireann, established the state as Éire with an elected president, and the Republic of Ireland Act took effect in 1949, ending ties with the Commonwealth. Ireland joined the European Economic Community in 1973, and in 1998 voters approved the Good Friday Agreement and changes to the constitution's claim to Northern Ireland. Today it is a parliamentary republic in which the Taoiseach leads a government answerable to the Dáil, elected by proportional representation, and constitutional changes require a referendum.
summary.art: Ireland's literature runs from early sagas and monastic poetry through Jonathan Swift to W. B. Yeats, James Joyce, Samuel Beckett and Seamus Heaney, and its theatre includes Synge and Shaw. Traditional music—fiddle, tin whistle, uilleann pipes, bodhrán and unaccompanied sean-nós singing—thrives in pub sessions and festivals. Illuminated manuscripts such as the Book of Kells, high crosses, Celtic metalwork and Aran knitting are treasured crafts.
summary.monuments: Brú na Bóinne, with the passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth, is a UNESCO site older than the Pyramids, and Skellig Michael's clifftop monastery is another. The Rock of Cashel, monastic Glendalough and Clonmacnoise speak of Ireland's early Christian and royal past. Trinity College Dublin's Book of Kells and Kilmainham Gaol, where leaders of the 1916 Rising were executed, tell of learning and the struggle for independence.

highlights.title: Book of Kells and the Long Room
highlights.line: See the 9th-century illuminated gospels and Trinity College's soaring old library; book a morning slot online to skip the queue.

highlights.title: Kilmainham Gaol
highlights.line: A moving tour of the prison where Irish rebels were held and executed; it sells out, so reserve days ahead.

highlights.title: A Dublin trad session
highlights.line: Live traditional music fills pubs nightly; sit near the musicians, listen quietly, and never clap along off-beat.

highlights.title: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
highlights.line: An imaginative museum on the Irish diaspora in Dublin's docklands; good on a rainy afternoon.

highlights.title: Newgrange
highlights.line: A 5,000-year-old passage tomb aligned to the winter solstice sunrise; it can only be visited by guided tour from the Brú na Bóinne centre.

highlights.title: Glendalough
highlights.line: A 6th-century monastic city of round tower and ruined churches in a glacial valley of the Wicklow Mountains; walk the lakeside trails.

highlights.title: Kilkenny
highlights.line: A medieval city with a grand castle, St Canice's Cathedral and lively craft studios; climb the round tower for the view.

highlights.title: Rock of Cashel
highlights.line: A dramatic cluster of medieval church buildings on a limestone outcrop in Tipperary; arrive early for soft light and few crowds.

highlights.title: Cork's English Market
highlights.line: A covered food market trading since 1788; try buttered eggs, local cheese and the famous spiced beef.

highlights.title: Kinsale
highlights.line: A colourful harbour town known for seafood; walk out to Charles Fort along the water.

highlights.title: Ring of Kerry
highlights.line: A classic coastal loop of mountains and sea; drive anti-clockwise as tour buses do, or cycle part of the Kerry Way.

highlights.title: Killarney National Park
highlights.line: Lakes, oak woods and red deer beside town; take a jaunting car to Muckross House or hire a bike to Ross Castle.

highlights.title: Skellig Michael
highlights.line: An early medieval monastery clinging to a sea rock; boats run in summer only and are weather-dependent, so book early and stay flexible.

highlights.title: Slea Head on the Dingle Peninsula
highlights.line: A breathtaking drive past beehive huts and Blasket views in an Irish-speaking area; stop in Dingle town for music and seafood.

highlights.title: Cliffs of Moher
highlights.line: Sheer cliffs above the Atlantic; walk part of the coastal path from Doolin for a quieter and more dramatic approach.

highlights.title: The Burren
highlights.line: A lunar limestone landscape blooming with rare wildflowers in late spring; look for the Poulnabrone dolmen.

highlights.title: Galway
highlights.line: A bohemian city of buskers, pubs and festivals; wander Shop Street and catch a session in a pub off Quay Street.

highlights.title: Aran Islands
highlights.line: Stone walls, cliffs and Irish-speaking communities; hire a bike on Inis Mór to reach the prehistoric fort of Dún Aonghasa.

highlights.title: Connemara
highlights.line: Wild bogs, mountains and white beaches; drive the Sky Road near Clifden and watch for Connemara ponies.

highlights.title: Kylemore Abbey
highlights.line: A Benedictine abbey in a lakeside castle with a restored Victorian walled garden; allow a few hours.

highlights.title: Croagh Patrick
highlights.line: Ireland's holy mountain above Clew Bay, climbed by pilgrims on Reek Sunday; wear proper boots for the loose scree.

highlights.title: Knock Shrine
highlights.line: Ireland's national Marian shrine in County Mayo, a place of quiet prayer since the 1879 apparition.

highlights.title: Achill Island
highlights.line: Reachable by bridge, with dramatic Keem Bay and the deserted village of Slievemore; perfect for a slow day of walking.

highlights.title: Slieve League cliffs
highlights.line: Among Europe's highest sea cliffs in Donegal; walk up from the viewing point for vast Atlantic views.

highlights.title: Glenveagh National Park
highlights.line: A remote Donegal valley with a castle, gardens and reintroduced golden eagles; take the shuttle bus or walk in.

highlights.title: Lough Derg pilgrimage
highlights.line: St Patrick's Purgatory, a three-day barefoot penitential retreat on a lake island in summer; one-day retreats are offered too.

highlights.title: Clonmacnoise
highlights.line: A great early Christian monastic site on the River Shannon with high crosses and round towers; peaceful at sunset.

highlights.title: Hurling at Croke Park
highlights.line: Watch the world's fastest field game at the GAA's stadium in Dublin; summer championship matches are electric.

highlights.title: Waterford Greenway
highlights.line: A 46-km traffic-free cycle path on an old railway line from Waterford to Dungarvan, over viaducts and through a tunnel.

highlights.title: Hook Lighthouse
highlights.line: One of the oldest working lighthouses in the world, on a wild Wexford headland; climb the medieval tower on a guided tour.

highlights.title: Seaweed baths
highlights.line: Soak in hot seawater and fresh seaweed at Strandhill or Enniscrone—a century-old Irish tradition of renewal.

highlights.title: Brown bread and chowder
highlights.line: Try seafood chowder with soda bread in a harbour pub; each kitchen has its own family recipe.

highlights.title: A Gaeltacht summer
highlights.line: Spend time in an Irish-speaking region like Connemara or Gweedore to hear the language as everyday speech.

funFacts: Newgrange in County Meath is older than both Stonehenge's great stone circle and the Great Pyramid of Giza.
At the winter solstice, the rising sun shines through a roof-box at Newgrange to light its inner chamber.
Ireland has no native snakes because they never recolonised the island after the last Ice Age.
In 2015 Ireland became the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by popular vote.
Irish is the first official language under the Constitution, with English as the second.
Irish became a full working language of the European Union in 2022.
The Irish language has no single words for 'yes' or 'no'; people answer by repeating the verb.
The word 'whiskey' comes from the Irish 'uisce beatha', meaning 'water of life'.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol, appearing on its coins and passports.
Halloween has roots in the Gaelic festival of Samhain, when turnips were carved into lanterns.
Ireland has won the Eurovision Song Contest seven times, a record it shares with Sweden.
Four Irish writers have won the Nobel Prize in Literature: Yeats, Shaw, Beckett and Heaney.
Dublin was designated a UNESCO City of Literature in 2010.
Dracula's author, Bram Stoker, was born in Dublin.
Hurling, one of the world's oldest field games, was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2018.
Players in Gaelic games are amateurs who are not paid to play, even in national finals.
The green of the Irish flag represents the Gaelic tradition, the orange the Protestant tradition, and the white the hope of peace between them.
Ireland introduced the world's first nationwide ban on smoking in workplaces in 2004.
A levy on plastic shopping bags introduced in 2002 cut their use by more than 90%.
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland or Britain, at about 360 km.
The Wild Atlantic Way coastal touring route stretches some 2,500 km from Donegal to Cork.
Ogham, the earliest form of written Irish, was carved as notches along the edges of standing stones.
Saint Patrick was born in Roman Britain and first came to Ireland as an enslaved captive.
St Brigid's Day became a public holiday in 2023, the first Irish holiday named after a woman.
The Titanic's last port of call was Cobh (then Queenstown) in County Cork in April 1912.
Skellig Michael featured as Luke Skywalker's island refuge in the later Star Wars films.
In 2022 Ireland's population passed five million for the first time since 1851.
The whole island still has fewer people today than it did before the Great Famine.
Ireland is militarily neutral and is not a member of NATO.
The Book of Kells is written on around 340 calfskin vellum leaves.
Phoenix Park in Dublin, home to the President's residence and a herd of wild fallow deer, is one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks.
Only about 11% of Ireland is covered by forest, one of the lowest shares in Europe.
Hook Lighthouse in County Wexford has guided ships for some 800 years.

languageGuide.intro: English is spoken by everyone in Ireland, but Irish (Gaeilge) is the first official language, heard daily in the Gaeltacht regions of the west and on signs everywhere—and even a few words are met with delight. Spelling follows its own rules (bh and mh often sound like 'v' or 'w', and 'si' like 'shi'), and pronunciation varies between Munster, Connacht and Ulster dialects, so the guides below are approximate.

culture.history: Celtic Ireland became an early centre of Christian learning, its monasteries preserving and illuminating manuscripts through the early Middle Ages. From the twelfth century English, and later British, rule deepened through conquest, plantation and penal laws against Catholics, and the Great Famine of 1845–1852 killed about a million people and drove a million more to emigrate. The 1916 Easter Rising, the War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty led to an independent state in 1922, followed by a bitter civil war and the partition of the island. Recent decades have brought prosperity, the Northern Ireland peace process of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, and a painful public reckoning with abuses in Church and state institutions.
culture.politics: Ireland is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president as largely ceremonial head of state and a Taoiseach (prime minister) accountable to the Dáil, the lower house of the Oireachtas. Elections use proportional representation by single transferable vote, and constitutional changes require a referendum, which gives citizens a direct voice on major social questions. Relations with Northern Ireland and the wider island remain a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Ireland's literary tradition is extraordinary, from early Irish sagas to W. B. Yeats, James Joyce, Samuel Beckett and Seamus Heaney. Traditional music, with fiddle, uilleann pipes and sean-nós singing, thrives in sessions across the country. The Book of Kells, an illuminated gospel book from around 800, is a masterpiece of medieval art.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed through humour, teasing and storytelling, with warmth carried in the gentle 'slagging' of close friends. Hospitality, a cup of tea offered and time made for a chat, matters deeply, as do strong family ties across the diaspora. Sentiment may be understated in words but shows up in loyalty and presence when it counts.

etiquette: In a pub group, take your turn buying a round for everyone.
Self-deprecating humour and gentle teasing are signs of friendliness; respond in good spirit.
Avoid lumping Ireland in with Britain, and approach Northern Ireland and the Troubles with sensitivity.

name: Poland

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; Kashubian is a recognised regional language

people: Most of Poland's roughly 37.5 million people are ethnic Poles, alongside Silesians, Kashubians, Germans, Belarusians, Lithuanians, Lemkos, Roma and centuries-old Tatar Muslim communities, while well over a million Ukrainians have made Poland home, especially since 2022. In the 2021 census about 71% identified as Roman Catholic, with small Orthodox, Lutheran, Jehovah's Witness, Muslim and Jewish communities, though religious practice is falling fast among the young. About 60% live in towns and cities, and a large diaspora is spread across the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom.

plug.note: UK and US travellers need an adapter; Type E sockets have a protruding earth pin; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Fertile farmland—one of Europe's largest producers of apples and poultry
Copper and silver deposits, among the largest in the world
A skilled workforce of engineers and IT specialists
Baltic ports such as Gdańsk and Gdynia
Ancient forests, lakes and mountains, from Białowieża to the Tatras
A deep cultural, religious and literary heritage
struggles: Heavy reliance on coal and some of the EU's worst winter air pollution
Deep political polarisation and disputes over the rule of law
A rapidly ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in Europe
Bearing the strain of war next door and hosting refugees from Ukraine
Rising housing costs and gaps between cities and rural regions
prayFor: For clean air and a just energy transition for mining communities in Silesia
For reconciliation and listening across a divided public life
For Ukrainian refugees and the Polish families and towns who have welcomed them
For young families, that they would find homes, stability and hope for the future
For honest remembrance and healing of the wounds of war, occupation and the Holocaust

summary.history: Slavic tribes settled the lands between the Oder and Vistula, and Poland enters written history with the baptism of Duke Mieszko I in 966. Under the Piasts and then the Jagiellonians, Poland grew into the vast Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a multi-faith realm long known as a refuge for Jews, before neighbouring Russia, Prussia and Austria partitioned it out of existence between 1772 and 1795. Restored as an independent state in 1918, Poland was invaded by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939; some six million Polish citizens died in the Second World War, including about three million Polish Jews murdered in the Holocaust, much of it in German-run death camps on occupied Polish soil. After the war, borders shifted west, millions were expelled or resettled, and a Soviet-backed communist regime ruled until the Solidarity movement helped bring peaceful change in 1989. Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004 and has since become one of Europe's fastest-growing economies.
summary.politicalHistory: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was an elective monarchy with a powerful noble parliament, and in 1791 it adopted the Constitution of 3 May, Europe's first modern codified constitution, shortly before the final partitions. The Second Republic, founded in 1918, began as a parliamentary democracy until Józef Piłsudski's 1926 coup led to authoritarian rule. After the Second World War a communist People's Republic was imposed; martial law in 1981 tried to crush Solidarity, but the Round Table talks of 1989 led to partly free elections and the first non-communist government in the Soviet bloc. Under the 1997 constitution Poland is a parliamentary republic with a bicameral parliament (Sejm and Senate), a prime minister-led government and a directly elected president.
summary.art: Fryderyk Chopin's mazurkas and polonaises carry Polish folk rhythms into the concert hall, and the International Chopin Competition still draws the world's pianists to Warsaw. Literature runs from the Romantic poet Adam Mickiewicz to Nobel laureates Henryk Sienkiewicz, Czesław Miłosz, Wisława Szymborska and Olga Tokarczuk, while Jan Matejko painted the nation's history and directors such as Andrzej Wajda and Krzysztof Kieślowski shaped world cinema. Folk crafts include colourful paper cut-outs (wycinanki), painted Easter eggs, wood carving and the polka-dot pottery of Bolesławiec.
summary.monuments: Kraków's Old Town and Wawel Hill and the nearby Wieliczka Salt Mine were among the very first UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1978. Auschwitz-Birkenau, the German Nazi concentration and extermination camp, is preserved as a memorial to the more than one million people murdered there, most of them Jews. Warsaw's Historic Centre, painstakingly rebuilt after its wartime destruction, Malbork's vast Teutonic castle and the Jasna Góra monastery in Częstochowa, home of the Black Madonna, complete the story of Polish endurance and faith.

highlights.title: Kraków's Main Market Square
highlights.line: One of Europe's largest medieval squares, with the Cloth Hall and St Mary's Basilica; listen for the hourly trumpet call from the tower.

highlights.title: Wawel Castle and Cathedral
highlights.line: Seat of Polish kings for centuries; buy timed tickets early and climb to the great Sigismund Bell.

highlights.title: Kazimierz
highlights.line: Kraków's historic Jewish quarter of synagogues, cafés and courtyards; visit the Old Synagogue and eat at Plac Nowy's zapiekanka stalls.

highlights.title: Wieliczka Salt Mine
highlights.line: Underground chapels and chandeliers carved entirely from rock salt; the tour involves about 800 steps, mostly downhill.

highlights.title: Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial
highlights.line: The most solemn place in Europe to remember the Holocaust; book a guided visit well ahead and allow a full, unhurried day.

highlights.title: Zakopane and the Tatras
highlights.line: Poland's mountain capital with wooden highland architecture; ride the cable car to Kasprowy Wierch on a clear morning.

highlights.title: Morskie Oko
highlights.line: A glacial lake beneath granite peaks in Tatra National Park; it is a 9-km walk each way on a paved road, so start early.

highlights.title: Warsaw Old Town
highlights.line: Rebuilt from rubble after 1944 and now a UNESCO site; climb the bell tower of St Anne's Church for the view.

highlights.title: POLIN Museum
highlights.line: A profound museum of a thousand years of Polish Jewish life in Warsaw; allow at least three hours.

highlights.title: Warsaw Rising Museum
highlights.line: An immersive account of the 63-day uprising of 1944; visit before walking the rebuilt city to understand what was lost.

highlights.title: Chopin in Łazienki Park
highlights.line: Free open-air Chopin piano recitals beside his monument on summer Sundays; bring a blanket and come early.

highlights.title: Gdańsk Main Town
highlights.line: Gabled merchant houses along the Long Market and the Motława river; look for Baltic amber in the shops of Mariacka Street.

highlights.title: European Solidarity Centre
highlights.line: The story of the movement that began in the Gdańsk shipyard and helped end communism, told in a striking rust-coloured building.

highlights.title: Malbork Castle
highlights.line: The world's largest castle by area, built by the Teutonic Knights in red brick; take the audio guide and allow half a day.

highlights.title: Baltic beaches and the Hel Peninsula
highlights.line: Long white beaches and pine forests; cycle the Hel Peninsula path and visit the seal sanctuary.

highlights.title: Słowiński moving dunes
highlights.line: Sand dunes up to 30 m high that shift across the coast near Łeba; rent a bike for the forest approach.

highlights.title: Masurian Lakes
highlights.line: A land of a thousand lakes for sailing, kayaking and quiet; rent a sailing boat or paddle the Krutynia river.

highlights.title: Białowieża Forest
highlights.line: One of Europe's last primeval lowland forests, home to wild European bison; the strict reserve can only be entered with a guide.

highlights.title: Toruń
highlights.line: Copernicus's Gothic hometown on the Vistula; bake your own spiced gingerbread at the living gingerbread museum.

highlights.title: Wrocław
highlights.line: A city of islands, bridges and a colourful market square; hunt for the hundreds of bronze dwarf statues hidden around town.

highlights.title: Churches of Peace
highlights.line: The vast timber Lutheran churches of Jawor and Świdnica, built without nails or stone towers under 17th-century restrictions.

highlights.title: Jasna Góra, Częstochowa
highlights.line: Poland's spiritual heart, home to the Black Madonna icon; attend the unveiling of the image, held several times a day.

highlights.title: Wooden churches of Lesser Poland
highlights.line: Centuries-old larch churches with painted interiors in villages like Dębno; check opening times or ask locally for the key.

highlights.title: Zalipie, the painted village
highlights.line: Cottages, wells and even dog kennels painted with bright flowers; visit in spring when the painting contest is held.

highlights.title: Pierogi at a milk bar
highlights.line: Eat hearty pierogi, soups and pancakes in a bar mleczny, the cheap cafeteria loved since communist days.

highlights.title: Żurek and Polish soups
highlights.line: Try sour rye żurek served in a bread bowl, or beetroot barszcz; soup is the soul of a Polish lunch.

highlights.title: Bieszczady Mountains
highlights.line: Remote, wild hills in the southeast with bears, wolves and wooden Orthodox churches; hike the open polonina ridges.

highlights.title: Lublin Old Town
highlights.line: A charming, uncrowded old town with a Holy Trinity Chapel of rare Byzantine-Ruthenian frescoes inside the castle.

highlights.title: Zamość
highlights.line: A Renaissance 'ideal city' with an arcaded market square, designed by an Italian architect in the 16th century.

highlights.title: Poznań's goats
highlights.line: Watch two mechanical goats butt heads on the town hall tower every day at noon, then taste a croissant-like St Martin's roll.

highlights.title: Łódź
highlights.line: An industrial city reborn: stroll Piotrkowska Street and visit the Manufaktura complex in a converted red-brick textile mill.

highlights.title: Pączki on Fat Thursday
highlights.line: On the last Thursday before Lent, queues form at bakeries for rose-jam doughnuts; join them for a taste of tradition.

highlights.title: Christmas Eve Wigilia
highlights.line: If invited, share the opłatek wafer and a meatless twelve-dish supper beginning when the first star appears.

funFacts: Marie Skłodowska-Curie, born in Warsaw, was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
Nicolaus Copernicus, who placed the Sun at the centre of the solar system, was born in Toruń in 1473.
Poland's Constitution of 3 May 1791 is regarded as Europe's first modern codified national constitution.
Polish mathematicians first broke the German Enigma cipher in the 1930s and shared their work with the Allies in 1939.
Warsaw's Old Town was rebuilt after the war partly with the help of 18th-century paintings by Bernardo Bellotto.
The Białowieża Forest is home to the world's largest population of free-roaming European bison, which were once extinct in the wild.
St Kinga's Chapel in the Wieliczka Salt Mine, including its chandeliers, is carved entirely from rock salt.
Malbork Castle is the largest castle in the world measured by land area.
Many Poles celebrate their name day (imieniny) as warmly as their birthday.
At Christmas Eve supper, many Polish families set an extra place for an unexpected guest.
On Easter Monday, Śmigus-dyngus, people playfully drench each other with water.
On Fat Thursday before Lent, Poles eat pączki doughnuts in vast numbers.
Poland is the largest producer of apples in the European Union.
Chopin's heart is preserved in a pillar of Holy Cross Church in Warsaw, by his own wish.
Pope John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła in Wadowice, was the first non-Italian pope in over 450 years.
More Poles have been recognised by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations than people of any other nationality.
The Solidarity trade union had around ten million members at its peak in 1980–81.
Kraków's hourly trumpet call, the Hejnał, breaks off mid-melody in memory of a legendary trumpeter struck by an arrow.
Wrocław has hundreds of small bronze dwarf statues scattered across the city.
The Vistula, about 1,050 km long, is Poland's longest river.
Poland's highest peak, Rysy (2,499 m), sits on the border with Slovakia.
The 'Crooked Forest' near Gryfino has hundreds of pines with mysteriously curved trunks.
The dunes of Słowiński National Park can move several metres a year.
Polish surnames often change form by gender, as with Kowalski and Kowalska.
Polish women gained the right to vote in 1918.
Poland was the only EU country to avoid recession during the 2008–09 financial crisis.
Tatar Muslims have lived in Poland since the 14th century, and wooden mosques still stand at Bohoniki and Kruszyniany.
Kashubian is recognised as a regional language, and some towns in Pomerania have bilingual signs.
Kraków's Old Town and the Wieliczka Salt Mine were on UNESCO's very first World Heritage List in 1978.
The Black Madonna of Częstochowa bears two scars across her cheek.
The 1944 Warsaw Uprising lasted 63 days.
Toruń has been famous for its spiced gingerbread since the Middle Ages.
The Polish tongue-twister 'W Szczebrzeszynie chrząszcz brzmi w trzcinie' ('In Szczebrzeszyn a beetle buzzes in the reeds') is a classic test for learners.

languageGuide.intro: Polish uses polite forms such as 'Pan' (sir) and 'Pani' (madam) with strangers, and 'proszę' does triple duty as please, here you are and you're welcome. Spelling is consistent once you learn a few rules—'w' sounds like 'v', 'ł' like 'w', 'cz' like 'ch', 'sz' like 'sh' and 'rz' like the 's' in 'pleasure'; English is common among younger people and in cities.

culture.history: Baptised in 966, Poland grew into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, a vast, multi-faith realm with an elected monarchy and a notable tradition of religious tolerance. Partitioned out of existence by Russia, Prussia and Austria in the late eighteenth century, it regained independence in 1918. In the Second World War Poland was invaded by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union; the German occupiers built death camps such as Auschwitz on Polish soil, about three million Polish Jews were murdered, and millions of other Polish citizens died. After decades of Soviet-backed communist rule, the Solidarity movement led a largely peaceful transition to democracy in 1989.
culture.politics: Poland is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president, who holds a legislative veto, and a government led by a prime minister accountable to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament. A member of the EU and NATO, it has a bicameral parliament with the Senate as the upper chamber. Debates over the independence of courts and the rule of law have been a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Frédéric Chopin's piano music is woven into Polish identity, as is the poetry of Adam Mickiewicz and, in the twentieth century, Nobel laureates Czesław Miłosz and Wisława Szymborska. Kraków's Gothic and Renaissance heritage and the painstakingly rebuilt old town of Warsaw speak to resilience. Polish cinema, from Andrzej Wajda to Krzysztof Kieślowski, and its poster art are celebrated worldwide.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed through generous hospitality, where guests are fed abundantly and urged to take more. Flowers, given in odd numbers, are a cherished gesture for hosts, birthdays and name days. Formality with strangers gives way to deep warmth and loyalty among family and friends.

etiquette: Bring flowers in an odd number when visiting someone's home; even numbers are associated with funerals.
Use 'Pan' (Sir) or 'Pani' (Madam) with people you do not know well.
Remove your shoes when entering a home unless your host says otherwise.

name: United Kingdom

languages.note: ≈ established living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Scots, Cornish, Irish and British Sign Language; hundreds more are spoken by immigrant communities, especially in London

people: The UK's roughly 69 million people live in four nations—England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland—each with its own identity, and about one in five belongs to an ethnic minority, including large South Asian, Black African and Caribbean, Chinese, Polish and Irish communities. In the 2021 census of England and Wales about 46% described themselves as Christian and 37% as having no religion, with Muslims around 6.5% and smaller Hindu, Sikh, Jewish and Buddhist communities; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own distinct Presbyterian and Catholic traditions. More than four in five people live in towns and cities, with London one of the most diverse cities on earth.

plug.note: The three-pin Type G plug is used almost nowhere else in Europe, so EU and US travellers need an adapter; US devices that are not dual-voltage also need a converter.

resources: World-leading universities and scientific research
London as a global centre of finance, law and culture
Offshore wind, among the largest capacity in the world, and North Sea energy
Creative industries—music, film, theatre, publishing and games
The English language and wide global cultural reach
A diverse, multicultural population with ties across the world
struggles: High living costs and rising child poverty
Long NHS waiting lists and an overstretched social-care system
A housing affordability crisis and rising homelessness
Deep regional inequalities between London and much of the North, Wales and coastal towns
Post-Brexit divisions and debates over the future of the Union
Loneliness and mental-health strain, especially among young and old
prayFor: For families stretched by rising costs, that children would be fed, warm and free to flourish
For NHS and care workers, and for patients waiting in pain or uncertainty
For people without a safe home, and for communities working to welcome and house them
For unity and mutual respect among England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and lasting peace in Northern Ireland
For the lonely and isolated, that neighbours and churches would become places of belonging

summary.history: Britain's prehistoric peoples raised monuments like Stonehenge, and Celtic Britons later lived under Roman rule for nearly four centuries before Anglo-Saxon, Viking and Norman newcomers reshaped the land, culminating in the Norman Conquest of 1066. England and Wales were united by conquest and law, England and Scotland joined as Great Britain in 1707, and Ireland was added in 1801. Britain led the Industrial Revolution and built the largest empire in history, enriching itself also through the transatlantic slave trade, colonial violence and famine, before abolishing the slave trade in 1807 and slavery across most of the empire in 1833. After two world wars and the loss of most of Ireland in 1922, the empire gave way to decolonisation, the post-war welfare state and NHS, and migration that made Britain multicultural. The UK joined the European Communities in 1973, devolved power to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland in the late 1990s, and left the European Union in 2020.
summary.politicalHistory: Royal power was gradually checked by Parliament, from Magna Carta in 1215 to the Civil War of the 1640s, when Charles I was executed and Oliver Cromwell ruled a short-lived republic, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688, whose Bill of Rights established parliamentary supremacy. The Acts of Union of 1707 and 1800 created Great Britain and then the United Kingdom, and the partition of Ireland in the early 1920s left Northern Ireland within it. The vote expanded step by step until equal suffrage for women and men in 1928, and devolution in 1998–99 created parliaments or assemblies for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Today the UK is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy with an uncodified constitution, in which a prime minister governs with the confidence of the House of Commons.
summary.art: Britain's literature spans Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton, Jane Austen, the Brontës, Charles Dickens, Robert Burns and Dylan Thomas, and its theatre tradition remains among the world's liveliest. In painting, Turner and Constable transformed landscape art, while music runs from Purcell, Handel and Elgar to the Beatles and a constant stream of popular music. Welsh choirs and the National Eisteddfod, Scottish piping and ceilidhs, and crafts such as tartan weaving and Harris Tweed carry the distinct traditions of each nation.
summary.monuments: Stonehenge and Avebury, Hadrian's Wall on Rome's northern frontier, and the Tower of London are all UNESCO World Heritage Sites spanning five millennia of history. Westminster Abbey and the Palace of Westminster stand at the heart of the nation's coronations and parliamentary life, and Canterbury Cathedral has been a pilgrimage centre since Thomas Becket's martyrdom in 1170. Edinburgh's Old and New Towns, the castles of Edward I in north Wales and Northern Ireland's Giant's Causeway show the variety of the four nations.

highlights.title: British Museum
highlights.line: Two million years of human history, free to enter; pick one or two galleries rather than trying to see it all.

highlights.title: Tower of London
highlights.line: Nearly a thousand years of royal fortress, prison and Crown Jewels; join a Yeoman Warder's tour, included in the ticket.

highlights.title: Westminster Abbey
highlights.line: The coronation church of English and British monarchs and resting place of Newton and Darwin; attend Evensong to experience it free, in prayer.

highlights.title: Choral Evensong
highlights.line: Sung evening prayer in a cathedral or college chapel is one of Britain's great free treasures; check service times and arrive early.

highlights.title: West End theatre
highlights.line: London's theatre district rivals Broadway; check official day-seat and lottery schemes for cheap same-day tickets.

highlights.title: Shakespeare's Globe
highlights.line: A reconstruction of Shakespeare's open-air theatre on the Thames; standing 'groundling' tickets cost just a few pounds.

highlights.title: Borough Market
highlights.line: London's historic food market under railway arches; graze on cheese, pies and street food, ideally on a weekday morning.

highlights.title: Stonehenge
highlights.line: The famous prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain; at the solstices the site opens for gatherings at sunrise.

highlights.title: Bath
highlights.line: Roman baths and honey-coloured Georgian crescents; soak in the rooftop pool of the modern Thermae spa.

highlights.title: Oxford
highlights.line: Dreaming spires, ancient colleges and the Bodleian Library; climb the tower of the University Church for the view.

highlights.title: The Cotswolds
highlights.line: Rolling hills and golden-stone villages; walk a stretch of the Cotswold Way between villages and stop for a pub lunch.

highlights.title: Canterbury Cathedral
highlights.line: Mother church of the Anglican Communion and site of Thomas Becket's martyrdom; walk the old city walls too.

highlights.title: Cornwall's coast
highlights.line: Fishing harbours, surf beaches and St Ives' art galleries; follow the South West Coast Path for wild clifftop walks.

highlights.title: Jurassic Coast
highlights.line: Dorset and East Devon cliffs with 185 million years of geology; hunt for fossils on the beach at Charmouth after a storm.

highlights.title: Lake District
highlights.line: England's most loved mountains and lakes, inspiration of Wordsworth; take a steamer on Ullswater and walk back along the shore.

highlights.title: Hadrian's Wall
highlights.line: Walk sections of Rome's northern frontier near Housesteads Fort; the Hadrian's Wall Path crosses the whole country.

highlights.title: York
highlights.line: Medieval walls, the narrow Shambles and the great Gothic Minster; walk the city walls for free.

highlights.title: Lindisfarne (Holy Island)
highlights.line: The cradle of Christianity in northern England, reached by a tidal causeway; always check the safe crossing times.

highlights.title: Liverpool waterfront
highlights.line: The Beatles' city, with the Royal Albert Dock and excellent free museums including the International Slavery Museum.

highlights.title: Peak District
highlights.line: Britain's first national park, with gritstone edges and limestone dales; hike Mam Tor or visit Chatsworth House.

highlights.title: Edinburgh Old Town and Castle
highlights.line: The Royal Mile runs from the castle to Holyrood; climb Arthur's Seat at dawn for the best view of the city.

highlights.title: Edinburgh Festival Fringe
highlights.line: Every August the world's largest arts festival fills the city; book accommodation many months ahead.

highlights.title: Glencoe and the Highlands
highlights.line: A brooding glen of mountains and history; drive or take the bus through Rannoch Moor and walk to the Lost Valley.

highlights.title: Isle of Skye
highlights.line: Jagged Cuillin peaks, the Old Man of Storr and the Fairy Pools; visit in spring or autumn to avoid summer traffic.

highlights.title: West Highland Line
highlights.line: One of the world's great rail journeys from Glasgow to Mallaig over the Glenfinnan Viaduct; sit on the left going north.

highlights.title: Iona
highlights.line: The island where St Columba founded his monastery in 563; join the Iona Community's simple worship in the abbey.

highlights.title: Speyside whisky
highlights.line: Tour a distillery along the River Spey and learn how single malt is made; designate a driver or take the bus.

highlights.title: Eryri (Snowdonia)
highlights.line: Climb Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), the highest peak in Wales, or ride the mountain railway; start early in summer.

highlights.title: Castles of north Wales
highlights.line: Conwy and Caernarfon castles, built by Edward I, are among Europe's finest medieval fortresses; walk Conwy's town walls.

highlights.title: St Davids
highlights.line: Britain's smallest city, with a cathedral in a hollow and the Pembrokeshire Coast Path on its doorstep.

highlights.title: Giant's Causeway
highlights.line: Some 40,000 interlocking basalt columns on the Antrim coast; walk the clifftop trail and come down by the Shepherd's Steps.

highlights.title: Titanic Belfast
highlights.line: An outstanding museum on the slipways where the Titanic was built; walk on to the murals and peace walls with a local guide.

highlights.title: Cream tea and Sunday roast
highlights.line: Debate jam-first (Cornwall) or cream-first (Devon) with scones, and join locals at a pub for a Sunday roast.

funFacts: The UK has no single written constitution; its rules come from statutes, court rulings and conventions.
'Big Ben' is the name of the great bell, not the clock tower, which was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, was the world's first underground railway.
The Welsh village of Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch has one of the longest place names in Europe.
No place in the UK is more than about 115 km (70 miles) from the sea.
Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
The Penny Black of 1840 was the world's first adhesive postage stamp, and British stamps still show no country name.
Greenwich in London was chosen as the Prime Meridian of the world in 1884.
Ben Nevis, at 1,345 m, is the highest mountain in the UK.
Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland is the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles.
The British Museum has been free to enter since it opened in 1759.
Scotland has around 800 islands, of which roughly 90 are inhabited.
Hadrian's Wall stretched about 117 km across northern England.
The National Health Service, founded in 1948, provides care free at the point of use.
Four original copies of the 1215 Magna Carta survive.
Liverpool is a UNESCO City of Music, birthplace of the Beatles.
The Giant's Causeway is made up of around 40,000 interlocking basalt columns.
Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin are both buried in Westminster Abbey.
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is the largest arts festival in the world.
The first commercial Christmas card was produced in London in 1843.
The Football Association drew up the first codified rules of modern football in London in 1863.
The Channel Tunnel has the longest undersea section of any tunnel in the world, about 38 km.
Stonehenge is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and the sunset at the winter solstice.
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown Dependencies, not part of the UK.
Kew's Millennium Seed Bank holds the world's largest collection of wild plant seeds.
British people drink an estimated tens of millions of cups of tea every day.
Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, invented the World Wide Web in 1989.
Welsh is an official language in Wales, and road signs there are bilingual.
Scots and Scottish Gaelic are both recognised minority languages in Scotland.
Women in the UK gained the vote on equal terms with men in 1928.
The River Severn, at about 350 km, is the longest river in Britain.
Red post boxes carry the royal cipher of the monarch reigning when they were installed, so some date back to Queen Victoria.
The Shard in London is the tallest building in the UK, at about 310 m.

languageGuide.intro: English is spoken everywhere, but British English has its own vocabulary, understatement and politeness—'please', 'thank you' and 'sorry' are used constantly, and queuing is taken seriously. Accents vary enormously between regions, and you will also hear Welsh in much of Wales and Scottish Gaelic in parts of the Highlands and Islands; the phrases below give everyday British usage plus a few Welsh greetings.

phrases.local: Could I have the bill, please?
phrases.say: kood eye hav thuh BIL, pleez

culture.history: England and Scotland joined in a single kingdom in 1707, and Ireland was added in 1801; most of Ireland left in 1922, leaving Northern Ireland within the union. Britain led the Industrial Revolution and built the largest empire in history, an enterprise inseparable from conquest, famine policy and a central role in the Atlantic slave trade until its abolition. Having stood against Nazi Germany in the Second World War, the country rebuilt itself around a welfare state and the National Health Service, founded in 1948. Decolonisation, migration from the Commonwealth, and the Troubles in Northern Ireland have shaped a plural, still-negotiating national identity.
culture.politics: The UK is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy with an uncodified constitution built from statute, convention and case law. Government is formed by whoever commands the confidence of the elected House of Commons, alongside an appointed House of Lords. Devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland makes the balance between union and nations a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Its literary tradition runs from Chaucer and Shakespeare through Jane Austen, the Brontës, Dickens and Virginia Woolf. Painting found landscape voices in Turner and Constable, while Gothic cathedrals like Durham and York sit beside the modern galleries of London. In music, choral tradition from Purcell and Elgar meets the global reach of the Beatles and British pop.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed with understatement: a dry joke, a cup of tea made without asking, turning up when it matters. Warmth deepens slowly and loyalty runs long, though regional and generational styles vary widely, from reserved to openly effusive.

etiquette: Queue patiently and never jump the line.
Say please, thank you and sorry often; politeness is woven into everyday speech.
In pubs, buying rounds is customary; take your turn.

name: Croatia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. minority and immigrant languages such as Serbian, Italian, Hungarian and Romani

people: About nine in ten people identify as Croats, alongside Serbs (around 3%), Bosniaks, Italians in Istria, Hungarians, Roma and other communities. Roughly 79% are Catholic, about 3% Orthodox and just over 1% Muslim, with a growing share of people of no religion. Most live in towns and cities, the population is ageing, and a large diaspora lives in Germany, Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Americas and Australia.

plug.note: Standard European two-pin sockets; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: An Adriatic coastline with more than a thousand islands
Tourism and hospitality skills
Clean karst rivers, springs and groundwater
Forests and timber
Wine, olive oil and fisheries
The Port of Rijeka and Adriatic shipping links
struggles: Emigration of young people and a shrinking, ageing population
Heavy dependence on seasonal tourism, with rising rents and overcrowding in Dubrovnik and Split
Lingering wounds of the 1990s war: missing persons, mine-suspected land and slow reconciliation between communities
Concerns about corruption and trust in institutions
Summer wildfires, drought and heat on the coast
High living costs after the inflation surge of 2022–23
prayFor: For young Croatians weighing whether to leave, that they may find good work, homes and a future close to their families
For island and village communities emptied outside the summer, that year-round life, schools and care for the elderly may flourish
For families still searching for missing loved ones from the 1990s war, and for healing between Croats, Serbs and Bosniaks
For firefighters and coastal towns facing heat and wildfire, and for wise care of forests and sea
For honest leadership and institutions worthy of the people's trust

summary.history: Illyrian peoples and Greek colonies were followed by Roman rule, whose grandest trace is the palace Emperor Diocletian built at Split around 300 AD. Slavic Croats settled in the seventh century, embraced Christianity and formed a medieval kingdom that entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102, while Venice came to hold much of Dalmatia and the Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) thrived as a merchant city-state. Habsburg rule, Ottoman wars on the frontier and the nineteenth-century national revival shaped modern identity, and after 1918 Croatia joined Yugoslavia. In the Second World War the fascist Ustaše regime committed grave crimes against Serbs, Jews and Roma, notably at Jasenovac, while many Croats fought with Tito's Partisans; independence in 1991 was followed by a war until 1995 that brought deep loss and displacement on all sides.
summary.politicalHistory: After centuries within the Hungarian and Habsburg crowns, Croatia entered the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918 and became a republic of socialist Yugoslavia after 1945. The first multi-party elections were held in 1990 and independence was declared on 25 June 1991, with Franjo Tuđman as its first president. A constitution of 1990, later amended in 2000 to curb presidential power, made it a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president and a unicameral Sabor. Croatia joined NATO in 2009, the European Union in 2013 and both the eurozone and Schengen area in 2023.
summary.art: Dalmatian klapa a-cappella singing, Pag and Lepoglava lace and the painted gingerbread hearts of the north are recognised by UNESCO as living heritage. The Renaissance poet Marko Marulić and the Ragusan playwright Marin Držić founded a literary tradition later carried by the children's writer Ivana Brlić-Mažuranić and the novelist Miroslav Krleža. The sculptor Ivan Meštrović and the naïve painters of Hlebine gave Croatian visual art its most beloved forms.
summary.monuments: Diocletian's Palace in Split, the walled Old City of Dubrovnik and the medieval town of Trogir are UNESCO World Heritage Sites that tell the story of Roman, Ragusan and Venetian Croatia. The Euphrasian Basilica in Poreč preserves sixth-century Byzantine mosaics, and the Cathedral of St James in Šibenik is a Renaissance masterpiece built entirely of stone. Plitvice Lakes and the ancient Stari Grad Plain on Hvar show how nature and patient farming have shaped the land.

highlights.title: Dubrovnik City Walls
highlights.line: Walking the nearly 2 km circuit of walls above terracotta roofs and open sea is unforgettable; go at opening time or late afternoon to avoid heat and cruise crowds.

highlights.title: Diocletian's Palace, Split
highlights.line: A Roman emperor's retirement palace that became a living town, with cafés, homes and a cathedral inside its walls; wander the cellars and the Peristyle at dusk.

highlights.title: Plitvice Lakes National Park
highlights.line: Sixteen turquoise lakes linked by waterfalls and wooden boardwalks; book tickets online in summer and start early from the upper lakes.

highlights.title: Krka National Park
highlights.line: Travertine cascades and the tiny monastery island of Visovac make a lovely day from Šibenik; swimming at Skradinski Buk is no longer allowed, so bring a picnic instead.

highlights.title: Hvar Town and the island's lavender fields
highlights.line: Beyond the lively harbour, Hvar's inland villages and early-summer lavender fields reveal a quieter island; visit in late June for the bloom.

highlights.title: Korčula
highlights.line: A compact walled town built in a fish-bone street pattern to catch the breeze; catch a performance of the Moreška sword dance in summer.

highlights.title: Rovinj
highlights.line: A pastel fishing town on a hill crowned by the Church of St Euphemia; climb the bell tower for sunset over the Istrian coast.

highlights.title: Pula Arena
highlights.line: One of the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world, still used for concerts and a summer film festival.

highlights.title: Euphrasian Basilica, Poreč
highlights.line: Glittering sixth-century Byzantine mosaics in a working church; dress modestly and look up at the golden apse.

highlights.title: Motovun and Istrian truffles
highlights.line: A hilltop town above oak forests where truffles are hunted with dogs; taste fuži pasta with truffle in a konoba and look for autumn truffle fairs.

highlights.title: Zagreb's Upper Town
highlights.line: Gaslit lanes, the tiled roof of St Mark's Church and the Stone Gate shrine, where locals light candles before an image of Mary.

highlights.title: Dolac Market, Zagreb
highlights.line: Red umbrellas, farmers from the hills and fresh cheese with cream (sir i vrhnje); come before noon for the liveliest stalls.

highlights.title: Museum of Broken Relationships, Zagreb
highlights.line: A tender, often funny collection of objects donated by people after breakups, which began as a travelling art project.

highlights.title: Marija Bistrica
highlights.line: Croatia's national Marian shrine in the Zagorje hills, with its Black Madonna and a hillside Way of the Cross; pilgrims gather especially around 15 August.

highlights.title: Zadar Sea Organ and Greeting to the Sun
highlights.line: Waves play music through pipes beneath marble steps, and at night a solar-powered glass circle glows in colour; sit and listen at sunset.

highlights.title: Cathedral of St James, Šibenik
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed Renaissance cathedral built entirely of stone, ringed by 71 carved heads of ordinary townspeople.

highlights.title: Trogir
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed medieval island town of Romanesque churches and palaces, easy to visit from Split by bus or boat.

highlights.title: Kornati Islands
highlights.line: A stark, beautiful archipelago of some 140 islands best explored by boat from Murter or Zadar; bring water and sun protection.

highlights.title: Pag cheese and lace
highlights.line: On the windswept island of Pag, salty pastures give paški sir its flavour and women still make fine needle lace in Pag town.

highlights.title: Ston walls and oysters
highlights.line: Climb one of Europe's longest medieval defensive walls, then eat oysters fresh from the bay at Mali Ston.

highlights.title: Pelješac wines
highlights.line: Steep vineyards on this peninsula produce bold Plavac Mali reds like Dingač; book a family cellar tasting and arrange a driver.

highlights.title: Vis and the Blue Cave
highlights.line: Remote Vis keeps a slower rhythm; from there, boats visit the Blue Cave on Biševo, which glows best around late morning.

highlights.title: Mljet National Park
highlights.line: Saltwater lakes and a twelfth-century Benedictine monastery on an islet; rent a bicycle and swim in the warm inner lakes.

highlights.title: Klapa singing
highlights.line: Close-harmony male (and increasingly female) choirs sing of the sea and love; listen in Omiš at its July festival or in a Split church courtyard.

highlights.title: Peka
highlights.line: Meat or octopus slow-baked under an iron bell covered in embers; order a day ahead at a konoba, as it takes hours.

highlights.title: Paklenica National Park
highlights.line: Limestone canyons on the slopes of Velebit, loved by climbers and hikers; start early in summer for shade.

highlights.title: Varaždin
highlights.line: An elegant baroque town of palaces and a moated castle; in late summer the Špancirfest street festival fills its squares.

highlights.title: Trakošćan Castle
highlights.line: A romantic castle above a lake in the Zagorje hills, with a lakeside walking path and period interiors.

highlights.title: Vukovar Water Tower
highlights.line: A shell-scarred tower preserved as a memorial to the 1991 siege; visit quietly and with respect for all who suffered.

highlights.title: Kopački Rit Nature Park
highlights.line: One of Europe's great river floodplains where the Drava meets the Danube, rich in birds; take a boat tour in spring or autumn.

highlights.title: Đakovo Cathedral
highlights.line: The red-brick twin-towered cathedral of Slavonia, with an annual summer folklore festival celebrating the region's costumes and music.

highlights.title: Zlatni Rat, Bol
highlights.line: A tongue of pebbles on the island of Brač whose tip shifts with wind and current; windsurfers come for the afternoon maestral breeze.

highlights.title: Sinjska Alka
highlights.line: A knightly tournament held in Sinj each August since the eighteenth century, in which riders aim a lance at a ring at full gallop; listed by UNESCO.

funFacts: The word 'cravat' and the necktie itself trace back to the neckscarves worn by Croatian soldiers in seventeenth-century France.
Hum in Istria calls itself the smallest town in the world, with only a few dozen residents inside its walls.
Croatia has more than a thousand islands, islets and reefs, yet only about fifty are inhabited.
The Dalmatian dog takes its name from the Croatian region of Dalmatia.
Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in the village of Smiljan, in present-day Croatia.
Slavoljub Penkala, working in Zagreb, patented a mechanical pencil in 1906, and 'penkala' became a Croatian word for pen.
Faust Vrančić of Šibenik published a design for a parachute, the 'Homo Volans', in his book Machinae Novae around 1615.
Ivan Vučetić, born on the island of Hvar, developed a fingerprint classification system while working for the police in Argentina.
The Republic of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, outlawed the slave trade in 1416.
Dubrovnik introduced one of the world's first quarantine laws in 1377, isolating arrivals before they could enter the city.
The pharmacy of Dubrovnik's Franciscan monastery has operated since 1317, making it one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe.
Zadar's Sea Organ, completed in 2005, makes music from waves pushing air through pipes beneath its stone steps.
Plitvice's lakes are separated by travertine barriers that are still slowly growing from minerals deposited by moss and algae.
The Baška Tablet from the island of Krk, carved around 1100, is one of the oldest inscriptions in the Croatian language, written in Glagolitic script.
The Glagolitic alphabet appears on Croatia's 1, 2 and 5 euro cent coins.
The former currency, the kuna, was named after the marten, whose pelts were once used in trade, and a marten now appears on Croatia's 1 euro coin.
Croatia adopted the euro and joined the Schengen area on the same day: 1 January 2023.
Pula's Roman amphitheatre is the only surviving one that still has all four of its side towers.
The cathedral in Split was originally Emperor Diocletian's mausoleum, making it one of the oldest buildings in continuous use as a cathedral.
Zagreb's funicular, opened in 1890, runs just 66 metres and is one of the shortest public funiculars in the world.
Croatian dialects are named after their word for 'what': što, kaj and ča.
In 1999 a white truffle weighing 1.31 kg was found near Buje in Istria and entered the Guinness World Records.
The walls of Ston, about 5 km long, were built to protect the Republic of Ragusa's precious salt pans, which are still worked today.
Croatia has eight national parks, from the Brijuni islands in the north to Mljet in the south.
Tito used the Brijuni islands as a summer residence and kept a small safari park stocked with animals gifted by world leaders.
Korčula claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo, a claim that Venice and historians still debate.
Croatia's men's football team reached the World Cup final in 2018 and won bronze medals in 1998 and 2022.
The red-and-white checkerboard, or šahovnica, has been a Croatian heraldic symbol for over five centuries.
Painted gingerbread hearts (licitar) from northern Croatia are on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
Large parts of Dubrovnik's old town served as King's Landing in the television series Game of Thrones.
The shape of Zlatni Rat beach on Brač shifts with the wind and currents.
The Sinjska Alka tournament commemorates a 1715 victory in which the town of Sinj resisted an Ottoman siege.
The Croatian mainland coastline is about 1,800 km long, but with the islands it stretches to roughly 6,000 km.

languageGuide.intro: Croatian is written exactly as it sounds: c is 'ts', č and ć are 'ch', š is 'sh', ž is 'zh', đ is like 'j' in 'jam' and j is 'y'. Use the polite Vi (and greetings like Dobar dan) with strangers and elders; English is widely spoken by younger people and in coastal tourist areas, less so in rural Slavonia.

culture.history: Slavic Croats settled the region in the seventh century and formed a medieval kingdom that entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102, later falling within the Habsburg world while Venice held much of the Dalmatian coast. After 1918 Croatia became part of Yugoslavia; during the Second World War the fascist Ustaše regime committed grave atrocities, including at the Jasenovac camp, while many Croats fought with the Partisans. Croatia declared independence in 1991 and endured a war until 1995 that brought deep loss and displacement on all sides. It joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013.
culture.politics: Croatia is a parliamentary republic in which the government is accountable to the unicameral Sabor, while a directly elected president serves as head of state with limited powers. Membership of the EU, the eurozone and Schengen anchors the country in European institutions. Reconciliation after the 1990s war and the vitality of coastal and rural communities remain important civic themes.
culture.arts: Klapa, unaccompanied harmony singing from Dalmatia, is recognised by UNESCO, as is the lace-making of Pag and Lepoglava. Diocletian's Palace in Split and the walled city of Dubrovnik hold layers of Roman, Venetian and Ragusan architecture. Marko Marulić, the father of Croatian literature, the novelist Miroslav Krleža and the sculptor Ivan Meštrović are cherished names.

love.expression: Friendship is lived around long coffees, shared meals and family gatherings where hospitality is generous and time is given freely. Affection is warm and direct, often shown through food, help and simply showing up, with styles differing between the Mediterranean coast and the continental interior.

etiquette: Greet with a handshake and eye contact; use titles until invited to first names.
Coffee is a social ritual meant to be lingered over, not rushed.
Cover shoulders and knees when visiting churches.

name: Greece

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Turkish and Pomak in Thrace, Arvanitika, Aromanian, Romani and immigrant languages such as Albanian

people: Most people are Greek, alongside a long-standing Muslim minority of Turkish-speakers, Pomaks and Roma in Thrace, and newer communities from Albania, Eastern Europe, South Asia and the Middle East. Around nine in ten identify with the Greek Orthodox Church, with small Muslim, Catholic, Protestant and Jewish communities. About a third of the population lives in greater Athens, and a large diaspora thrives in the United States, Australia, Germany and Cyprus.

plug.note: Standard European two-pin sockets; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Unrivalled archaeological and cultural heritage
Seas, islands and sunshine that sustain tourism
One of the world's largest merchant shipping fleets
Olive oil, feta, wine and Mediterranean agriculture
Strategic ports such as Piraeus
A deep tradition of hospitality (filoxenia) and a talented diaspora
struggles: The long shadow of the debt crisis: lower wages, high youth unemployment and emigration of young graduates
A falling birth rate, an ageing population and emptying villages
Wildfires, heatwaves, drought and floods intensified by climate change
Housing pressure in Athens and the islands from short-term rentals
The plight of refugees and migrants arriving by sea, and the strain on island communities
Low trust in institutions after tragedies such as the 2023 Tempi rail crash
prayFor: For young Greeks who left during the crisis, and for work and homes that make it possible to return
For firefighters, farmers and villages living with fire, drought and flood, and for wise care of the land
For refugees and migrants on perilous journeys, and for the islanders and volunteers who receive them
For families grieving those lost in disasters, and for justice and accountability that rebuild trust
For elderly people in remote villages and islands, that they may not be alone

summary.history: The Minoan civilisation of Crete and the Mycenaean world flourished in the Bronze Age, followed by the classical city-states whose philosophy, drama, science and democracy shaped much of the world. Alexander the Great carried Greek culture across Asia, Rome absorbed Greece, and for a thousand years the Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire bore Orthodox Christianity until Constantinople fell in 1453. Nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule ended with the War of Independence begun in 1821, after which the state expanded and the 1923 population exchange with Turkey uprooted over a million people. The twentieth century brought brutal Nazi occupation and famine, the deportation and murder of most of Greece's Jews, a bitter civil war, and a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974, followed by democracy, European membership and the hardship of the 2010s debt crisis.
summary.politicalHistory: Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire with recognition by the Great Powers in 1830 and became a kingdom under Otto of Bavaria in 1832, gaining its first constitution in 1844. The twentieth century saw sharp divisions between monarchists and Venizelos's liberals, the Metaxas dictatorship from 1936, occupation, civil war and the colonels' junta of 1967 to 1974. After the junta fell, a 1974 referendum abolished the monarchy and the 1975 constitution established a parliamentary republic with a 300-seat parliament and a largely ceremonial president elected by parliament. Greece joined NATO in 1952, the European Community in 1981 and the eurozone in 2001.
summary.art: Homer's epics, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, and the sculpture of Phidias and Praxiteles laid foundations for Western art. Byzantine icon painting and chant flourished for centuries, and the Cretan painter Domenikos Theotokopoulos carried that tradition into his work as El Greco. Modern Greece gave the poets Cavafy, Seferis and Elytis, the composers Mikis Theodorakis and Manos Hadjidakis, and the soulful urban music of rebetiko, recognised by UNESCO.
summary.monuments: The Acropolis of Athens, crowned by the Parthenon, is the supreme symbol of classical Greece and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Delphi, Olympia and the theatre of Epidaurus recall the religious, athletic and dramatic life of the ancient world, while Knossos on Crete preserves the Minoan palace culture. The monasteries of Meteora and Mount Athos and the Byzantine churches of Thessaloniki and Mystras witness to Greece's long Orthodox Christian heritage.

highlights.title: Acropolis and the Parthenon
highlights.line: The temple of Athena above Athens is a wonder in any light; book a timed ticket and go at opening or in the last hours before closing to avoid heat and crowds.

highlights.title: Acropolis Museum
highlights.line: See the Parthenon sculptures at eye level in a glass gallery aligned with the temple itself, and walk over excavated streets visible through the floor.

highlights.title: Plaka and Anafiotika
highlights.line: Wander lanes of neoclassical houses below the Acropolis, then climb into Anafiotika, a whitewashed village built by island stonemasons.

highlights.title: Ancient Agora of Athens
highlights.line: The heart of ancient civic life, where Socrates taught; visit the reconstructed Stoa of Attalos and the beautifully preserved Temple of Hephaestus.

highlights.title: Temple of Poseidon, Sounion
highlights.line: Marble columns on a cliff above the Aegean; time your visit for sunset, about an hour's drive from Athens.

highlights.title: Delphi
highlights.line: Once called the navel of the world, the sanctuary of Apollo clings to the slopes of Mount Parnassus; the museum's bronze Charioteer is unmissable.

highlights.title: Meteora
highlights.line: Monasteries perched on towering sandstone pillars in Thessaly; dress modestly, check each monastery's closing day and stay overnight in Kalambaka for dawn light.

highlights.title: Ancient Olympia
highlights.line: Walk through the stone tunnel into the original stadium where the Games began in 776 BC, then visit the excellent museum.

highlights.title: Theatre of Epidaurus
highlights.line: A fourth-century BC theatre with astonishing acoustics that still hosts summer performances of ancient drama.

highlights.title: Mycenae
highlights.line: Pass through the Lion Gate into the citadel associated with Agamemnon, and step into the vast beehive tomb known as the Treasury of Atreus.

highlights.title: Nafplio
highlights.line: Greece's first capital, with Venetian fortresses, elegant squares and a seaside promenade; climb the long stairway, said to have 999 steps, to Palamidi in the cool morning.

highlights.title: Monemvasia
highlights.line: A medieval walled town hidden on a rock island linked to the mainland by a causeway; stay overnight when day visitors leave.

highlights.title: Mystras
highlights.line: A hillside Byzantine city of frescoed churches and palaces near Sparta; wear good shoes for the climb.

highlights.title: Santorini caldera
highlights.line: Cliffside villages above a flooded volcanic crater; walk the trail from Fira to Oia and visit the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri.

highlights.title: Naxos
highlights.line: The greenest of the Cyclades, with mountain villages, marble quarries, long beaches and the great Portara gate framing the sunset.

highlights.title: Delos
highlights.line: The sacred island of Apollo, one of the richest archaeological sites in Greece, reached by boat from Mykonos; there's no overnight stay, so bring water and a hat.

highlights.title: Tinos
highlights.line: Pilgrims come to the Church of Panagia Evangelistria, some on their knees from the harbour; the island also has beautiful marble-carving villages and Catholic communities.

highlights.title: Patmos
highlights.line: Visit the Cave of the Apocalypse, where tradition holds St John received the Book of Revelation, and the fortified Monastery of St John above it.

highlights.title: Rhodes Old Town
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed medieval city of the Knights of St John, with the Street of the Knights and the Palace of the Grand Master.

highlights.title: Knossos, Crete
highlights.line: The labyrinthine Minoan palace near Heraklion; pair it with the Heraklion Archaeological Museum to see its frescoes and treasures.

highlights.title: Samaria Gorge, Crete
highlights.line: A 16 km walk down one of Europe's longest gorges to the Libyan Sea, open roughly May to October; finish with a ferry from Agia Roumeli.

highlights.title: Chania
highlights.line: A Venetian harbour with a lighthouse, old quarters and covered market; try bougatsa for breakfast.

highlights.title: Thessaloniki
highlights.line: A lively northern city of Byzantine churches, the Roman Rotunda and the White Tower, renowned for its food scene and seafront promenade.

highlights.title: Vergina
highlights.line: The royal tombs of the Macedonian kings, displayed in an atmospheric underground museum, including the tomb attributed to Philip II.

highlights.title: Zagori and the Vikos Gorge
highlights.line: Stone villages and arched bridges in the Epirus mountains, with hiking into one of the world's deepest gorges relative to its width.

highlights.title: Corfu Old Town
highlights.line: Venetian fortresses, arcaded streets and a British-era cricket ground give the Ionian capital its unique layered charm.

highlights.title: Mount Olympus
highlights.line: Hike from Prionia through forests toward the home of the gods; the summit Mytikas requires experience and a night at a mountain refuge.

highlights.title: Hydra
highlights.line: A car-free island where donkeys and water taxis carry everything; walk the coastal path to swim off the rocks.

highlights.title: Greek Easter (Pascha)
highlights.line: The most important feast of the year: candlelit midnight services on Holy Saturday, then lamb on the spit and red eggs on Sunday; dates follow the Orthodox calendar.

highlights.title: The kafeneio and Greek coffee
highlights.line: Sit in a village coffee house with a small cup of thick Greek coffee, ordered sketo (no sugar), metrio (medium) or glyko (sweet).

highlights.title: Meze, ouzo and tsipouro
highlights.line: Share small plates in a taverna or ouzeri, with ouzo in the islands or tsipouro in the north; meals are long and meant to be shared.

highlights.title: Mount Athos
highlights.line: The self-governing monastic peninsula of twenty monasteries admits only men with a permit, but anyone can see its monasteries from boat cruises out of Ouranoupoli.

highlights.title: Summer panigyria
highlights.line: Village saints' day festivals with live music, dancing and shared food, especially around 15 August; everyone is welcome to join the circle dance.

funFacts: The Greek national anthem, the 'Hymn to Liberty', has 158 verses, though only the first two are usually sung.
Greece has around 6,000 islands and islets, of which only about 200 are inhabited.
Greece has the longest coastline of any country in the Mediterranean.
The Antikythera mechanism, found in a shipwreck in 1901, is an ancient geared device for predicting astronomical positions and eclipses.
The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896 in the Panathenaic Stadium, built almost entirely of marble.
Spyridon Louis, a Greek water carrier, won the first modern Olympic marathon in 1896.
The Olympic flame for every modern Games is lit at Olympia using the sun's rays focused by a parabolic mirror.
In the EU only cheese made in certain regions of Greece, from sheep's milk with up to 30% goat's milk, can be called feta.
Many Greeks celebrate their name day, the feast of the saint they are named after, as much as or more than their birthday.
In Greek, 'ne' means yes, while a slight upward nod with raised eyebrows means no.
Greek has around 3,400 years of written records, going back to the Linear B tablets of the Mycenaeans.
The Greek alphabet, adapted from the Phoenician script, is the ancestor of both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets.
The nine stripes of the Greek flag are popularly said to stand for the nine syllables of 'Eleftheria i Thanatos' (Freedom or Death).
The olive tree of Vouves on Crete is estimated to be at least 2,000 years old and still bears olives.
Santorini's caldera was formed by a massive volcanic eruption around 1600 BC that buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri in ash.
Cars and motorbikes are banned on the island of Hydra, so goods are carried by donkeys, mules and boats.
The theatre of Epidaurus seats around 14,000 people, yet a coin dropped on the stage can be heard from the upper rows.
Retsina, a wine flavoured with pine resin, is thought to descend from the ancient practice of sealing wine jars with resin.
Greece celebrates 'Ochi Day' on 28 October, remembering its refusal of Mussolini's ultimatum in 1940.
At New Year, Greek families cut a vasilopita cake with a coin hidden inside, bringing luck to whoever finds it.
At Easter, Greeks crack red-dyed eggs against each other, and the owner of the last unbroken egg is said to have good luck.
