Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the gods, rises to about 2,918 metres and is Greece's highest mountain.
Greek Orthodox Easter is calculated using the Julian calendar, so it often falls on a different Sunday from Western Easter.
The name of the continent Europe comes from Europa, a princess of Greek mythology.
Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, built the Achilleion palace on Corfu in the 1890s.
The island of Kalymnos has a centuries-old tradition of sponge diving.
Mount Athos has been a monastic community for over a thousand years and still keeps Byzantine time, with the day beginning at sunset in some monasteries.
Greek shipowners control one of the largest merchant fleets in the world.
Words like 'democracy', 'theatre', 'music' and 'philosophy' all come from ancient Greek.
Thessaloniki was once home to one of the largest Sephardic Jewish communities in the world, most of whom were murdered in the Holocaust.
The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey uprooted around 1.5 million people in total, reshaping both nations.
Rebetiko, the urban blues of Greek port cities, was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2017.
Greek is one of the official languages of the European Union and of Cyprus.

languageGuide.intro: Greek uses its own alphabet, but many signs also appear in Latin letters; stress matters and is marked with an accent on every word. Use the polite plural (Γεια σας, 'yia sas') with strangers and elders; English is widely spoken in cities and on the islands, and a few Greek words are warmly received.

phrases.en: What time does the ferry leave?

culture.history: Ancient Greek city-states gave the world foundational philosophy, drama and the idea of democracy, and Greek culture later carried the Byzantine Empire and Orthodox Christianity for a thousand years. Nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule ended with the War of Independence that began in 1821. The twentieth century brought the 1923 population exchange with Turkey, brutal occupation in the Second World War, a civil war from 1946 to 1949 and a military junta from 1967 to 1974. Democracy was restored in 1974, and Greece joined the European Community in 1981 before weathering a severe debt crisis in the 2010s.
culture.politics: Greece is a parliamentary republic: the government is formed from the 300-seat Hellenic Parliament, and a largely ceremonial president is elected by parliament. The monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1974. The memory of the junta and the hardships of the debt crisis keep democratic accountability and economic dignity at the heart of civic life.
culture.arts: Homer's epics and the tragedies of Aeschylus and Sophocles still shape Western storytelling, and the Parthenon remains a touchstone of architecture. Byzantine icon painting flowered for centuries, and the Cretan-born Domenikos Theotokopoulos carried it into his work as El Greco. Modern voices include the poet Cavafy, the Nobel laureates Seferis and Elytis, and the soulful urban music of rebetiko.

love.expression: Affection is expressive and social: long tables, lively conversation, and hospitality (filoxenia) offered even to strangers. Family bonds are close and touch is natural among friends, though warmth takes quieter forms on islands, in villages and between generations.

etiquette: Accept offered food or drink graciously; refusing hospitality can feel cold.
Dress modestly in monasteries and churches; some provide wraps at the door.
An open-palm gesture toward someone's face (the moutza) is an insult, so wave with care.

name: Mexico

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), counting many Zapotec, Mixtec and other Indigenous varieties separately; the state recognises 68 Indigenous languages

people: Most Mexicans are of mixed Indigenous and European (mestizo) heritage; around a fifth identify as Indigenous, about 7 million speak an Indigenous language such as Nahuatl, Maya, Tseltal, Mixtec or Zapotec, and some 2% identify as Afro-Mexican. Roughly 78% are Catholic, about 11% Protestant or evangelical and around 10% have no religion, with devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe shared far beyond church walls. About four in five live in cities, and some 37 million people of Mexican origin live in the United States.

plug.note: Same flat-pin plugs as the US; UK and EU travellers need an adapter, and devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Extraordinary biodiversity: one of the world's megadiverse countries
Silver, copper and other minerals (the world's largest silver producer)
Oil and gas in the Gulf of Mexico
A large manufacturing and automotive sector integrated with North America
Maize, avocados, tomatoes, cacao and a cuisine recognised by UNESCO
Living Indigenous cultures, archaeological heritage and a young, creative population
struggles: Violence by organised crime, with more than 100,000 people registered as disappeared
Deep inequality and poverty, especially in the rural south and in Indigenous communities
Violence against women, including femicide
Danger and exploitation faced by migrants crossing the country
Water scarcity and subsidence in Mexico City and drought in the north
Corruption and impunity, with most crimes never resolved
prayFor: For the mothers and families searching for their disappeared loved ones, that they may find truth, consolation and justice
For women and girls, that they may live free from violence and be honoured in every home and street
For migrants passing through Mexico, and for the shelters, parishes and families who welcome them
For Indigenous and rural communities, that their lands, languages and dignity be protected
For peace in towns living under the shadow of violence, and courage for journalists, judges and police who serve honestly

summary.history: For thousands of years Mexico was home to great civilisations, including the Olmec, the builders of Teotihuacan, the Zapotec, the Maya and the Mexica (Aztecs), whose island capital Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 to Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies. Three centuries of colonial rule brought conquest, devastating epidemics, forced labour and the evangelisation of New Spain, along with a new mestizo culture and the devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe. Independence came in 1821 after a long war begun by Miguel Hidalgo in 1810, but the young nation lost about half its territory to the United States in 1848 and endured a French intervention in the 1860s. The Revolution of 1910 to 1920 cost perhaps a million lives and reshaped land and labour, while the twentieth century brought industrialisation, the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre of students and, more recently, a painful wave of cartel violence.
summary.politicalHistory: Mexico declared independence in 1810 and won it in 1821, briefly became an empire under Agustín de Iturbide, and adopted a federal republican constitution in 1824. Conflicts between liberals and conservatives led to Benito Juárez's Reform laws, the 1857 constitution and the defeat of the French-backed Emperor Maximilian in 1867, followed by Porfirio Díaz's long rule. The Revolution produced the 1917 constitution, still in force, and from 1929 a single party, later the PRI, governed for 71 years until the opposition won the presidency in 2000. Today Mexico is a federal presidential republic of 31 states and Mexico City, with a bicameral Congress and presidents limited to one six-year term.
summary.art: Pre-Hispanic sculpture, codices and murals were followed by baroque churches, the poetry of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz and the brilliant folk arts of Talavera, alebrijes and textiles. In the twentieth century Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted the nation's history on public walls, while Frida Kahlo turned the self-portrait into testimony, and Juan Rulfo, Octavio Paz and Rosario Castellanos shaped its literature. Mariachi, son jarocho, the Day of the Dead and Mexican cuisine are all recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage.
summary.monuments: Teotihuacan, with its Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, and the Maya cities of Chichén Itzá and Palenque reveal the grandeur of pre-Hispanic Mexico and are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The historic centres of Mexico City, Oaxaca, Puebla and Guanajuato preserve colonial cathedrals and plazas built over and beside ancient foundations, as at the Templo Mayor. The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac, one of the most visited Marian shrines in the world, is the spiritual heart of the nation.

highlights.title: Teotihuacan
highlights.line: Climb the Pyramid of the Sun and walk the Avenue of the Dead in the vast ancient city near Mexico City; arrive at opening and bring a hat and water.

highlights.title: Zócalo and Templo Mayor
highlights.line: Mexico City's great square sits beside the excavated main temple of Tenochtitlan; the site museum shows how the Aztec capital lies beneath the colonial one.

highlights.title: National Museum of Anthropology
highlights.line: One of the world's great museums, home to the Aztec Sun Stone and rooms for every Indigenous region; allow at least half a day.

highlights.title: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe
highlights.line: The image on St Juan Diego's tilma draws millions of pilgrims, especially on 12 December; a moving conveyor beneath the image lets visitors pass slowly.

highlights.title: Palacio de Bellas Artes
highlights.line: An art nouveau palace with murals by Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros; try to see the Ballet Folklórico performance on Sundays or Wednesdays.

highlights.title: Frida Kahlo's Casa Azul, Coyoacán
highlights.line: The cobalt-blue house where Frida lived and died; book tickets online well ahead, then stroll Coyoacán's plazas.

highlights.title: Xochimilco
highlights.line: Glide through ancient canals on a painted trajinera with mariachis and food boats; visit an axolotl sanctuary run by local chinampa farmers.

highlights.title: Street tacos in Mexico City
highlights.line: Tacos al pastor carved from a spinning spit, with pineapple, cilantro and onion; busy stands with high turnover are the best sign.

highlights.title: Chichén Itzá
highlights.line: The great Maya city of the stepped pyramid El Castillo; come at opening, and at the spring equinox see a shadow serpent descend the stairs.

highlights.title: Palenque
highlights.line: Maya temples rising out of the Chiapas rainforest, with howler monkeys calling at dawn; the Temple of the Inscriptions held King Pakal's tomb.

highlights.title: Tulum
highlights.line: Maya ruins on a cliff above the Caribbean; go early, then swim at a nearby beach.

highlights.title: Cenotes of the Yucatán
highlights.line: Swim in crystal-clear sinkholes sacred to the Maya; use biodegradable sunscreen or none, and shower before entering.

highlights.title: Mérida
highlights.line: A gracious Yucatecan city of plazas, free Sunday dances and cochinita pibil; use it as a base for Uxmal and Maya villages.

highlights.title: Oaxaca City and Monte Albán
highlights.line: A colonial city of markets, churches and galleries, overlooked by the Zapotec hilltop capital of Monte Albán.

highlights.title: Oaxacan food and mezcal
highlights.line: Taste seven moles, tlayudas and chapulines (grasshoppers) in the markets, and visit a family palenque where mezcal is distilled.

highlights.title: Guelaguetza
highlights.line: In July, communities from across Oaxaca share dances, music and gifts in a joyful festival rooted in Indigenous reciprocity.

highlights.title: Day of the Dead in Michoacán
highlights.line: Around 1–2 November, families keep candlelit vigils in cemeteries around Lake Pátzcuaro and Janitzio; observe quietly and ask before photographing.

highlights.title: Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve
highlights.line: From roughly November to March, millions of monarchs cluster on fir trees in the mountains of Michoacán and the State of Mexico; walk or ride with local guides.

highlights.title: Copper Canyon and El Chepe
highlights.line: A network of canyons deeper in places than the Grand Canyon, crossed by a spectacular railway, and home to the Rarámuri people.

highlights.title: San Miguel de Allende
highlights.line: A pink-stone parish church, colonial streets and a vibrant arts scene; nearby Atotonilco's sanctuary is a UNESCO-listed baroque gem.

highlights.title: Guanajuato
highlights.line: A colourful university city built in a ravine, with tunnels for streets, the Cervantino arts festival each October and student callejoneada serenades.

highlights.title: Puebla and Cholula
highlights.line: Taste mole poblano and chiles en nogada, see Talavera pottery workshops, then visit the church atop the huge pyramid of Cholula.

highlights.title: Tequila and the agave landscape
highlights.line: Blue agave fields around the town of Tequila in Jalisco are a UNESCO site; tour a distillery and travel back by train from Guadalajara.

highlights.title: Guadalajara and mariachi
highlights.line: Hear mariachis in Plaza de los Mariachis or Tlaquepaque, and see Orozco's fiery murals in the Hospicio Cabañas.

highlights.title: Gray whales of Baja California
highlights.line: From about January to March, gray whales calve in the lagoons of Baja; in San Ignacio, curious mothers sometimes approach the small boats.

highlights.title: Sea of Cortez
highlights.line: Called the 'world's aquarium', with sea lions, whale sharks and coral reefs around La Paz and Cabo Pulmo.

highlights.title: San Cristóbal de las Casas
highlights.line: A highland town of cobbled streets where Tsotsil and Tseltal communities gather; visit San Juan Chamula's church only with respect and no photos inside.

highlights.title: Sumidero Canyon
highlights.line: Take a boat between cliffs up to a kilometre high near Tuxtla Gutiérrez, watching for crocodiles and spider monkeys.

highlights.title: Lucha libre
highlights.line: Join the cheering crowd at Arena México for masked wrestling, a beloved family spectacle with deep roots in popular culture.

highlights.title: Markets and tianguis
highlights.line: Every town has a market of fruit, flowers, herbs and food stalls; eat where the locals eat and carry small change.

highlights.title: Bacalar
highlights.line: The 'lagoon of seven colours' in Quintana Roo, a calmer alternative to the Caribbean coast; protect the fragile stromatolites by not standing on them.

highlights.title: Campeche
highlights.line: A pastel walled port city with Spanish bastions built against pirates; walk the walls at sunset and visit the nearby Maya site of Edzná.

highlights.title: Zacatecas
highlights.line: A silver-mining city of pink stone with a stunning baroque cathedral, a cable car and an old mine you can tour.

funFacts: Maize was domesticated in what is now southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago from a wild grass called teosinte.
Chocolate, tomato, avocado, chile and coyote all come into English from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.
The Great Pyramid of Cholula is the largest pyramid in the world by volume, though it now looks like a hill topped by a church.
Mexico has more native Spanish speakers than any other country.
Parts of Mexico City are sinking by tens of centimetres a year as groundwater is pumped from beneath the old lakebed.
Mexico City was built on the island city of Tenochtitlan, in the middle of Lake Texcoco.
The axolotl, a salamander that can regrow limbs, lives in the wild only in the canals and lakes around Xochimilco.
Guillermo González Camarena, a Mexican engineer, patented an early colour television system in the 1940s.
Chemist Luis E. Miramontes, working in Mexico City in 1951, co-synthesised norethisterone, used in early oral contraceptives.
The Caesar salad was created in Tijuana in the 1920s by restaurateur Caesar Cardini.
Vanilla comes from an orchid native to Mexico, first cultivated by the Totonac people around Papantla.
The poinsettia is native to Mexico, where it is called flor de Nochebuena.
The Chihuahua dog takes its name from the Mexican state of Chihuahua.
The Chicxulub crater, linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs, lies buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula, and a ring of cenotes traces its edge.
In 1943 the volcano Parícutin erupted from a farmer's cornfield in Michoacán and grew over 300 metres in its first year.
Pico de Orizaba, at about 5,636 metres, is Mexico's highest peak and the third-highest mountain in North America.
Monarch butterflies migrate up to about 4,000 km from Canada and the United States to overwinter in the forests of central Mexico.
Mexico is home to roughly a tenth of the world's known species.
Traditional Mexican cuisine was the first national cuisine recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, in 2010.
The eagle on a cactus eating a snake on Mexico's flag recalls the sign said to have shown the Mexica where to found Tenochtitlan.
Tequila may only be produced in Jalisco and designated municipalities in four other states.
Mexico City has over 150 museums, among the most of any city in the world.
The official name of the country is Estados Unidos Mexicanos, the United Mexican States.
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, the seventeenth-century poet and nun, appears on Mexico's 100-peso banknote.
The central campus of UNAM, Mexico's national university, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with murals by Siqueiros and a library covered in mosaics by Juan O'Gorman.
Mexico City hosted the 1968 Olympics, the first held in Latin America.
Estadio Azteca hosted World Cup finals in both 1970 and 1986, and Mexico is a co-host of the 2026 World Cup.
Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City is often called the only castle in the Americas that housed reigning sovereigns.
The state of Oaxaca alone is home to around sixteen distinct Indigenous peoples.
Mexico is the world's largest exporter of avocados.
Mexico's Day of the Dead marigold, cempasúchil, is believed to guide souls home with its colour and scent.
Real de Catorce, a former silver town, is reached through a 2.3 km single-lane tunnel cut through the mountain.
Mexico is one of the world's largest producers of silver, mined continuously since colonial times.

languageGuide.intro: Mexican Spanish is clear and melodic, with every vowel pronounced and the stress usually on the second-to-last syllable; use usted with elders and strangers, and you will often hear the courteous '¿Mande?' for 'Pardon?'. English is common in tourist areas and big cities, but a little Spanish opens hearts everywhere.

phrases.say: DOHN-deh es-TAH lah es-tah-SYOHN del MEH-troh

phrases.local: Un boleto a Oaxaca, por favor
phrases.say: oon boh-LEH-toh ah wah-HAH-kah, por fah-VOR

phrases.en: What time does the bus leave?
phrases.say: ah keh OH-rah SAH-leh el kah-MYOHN

phrases.local: A la izquierda / a la derecha
phrases.say: ah lah ees-KYEHR-dah / ah lah deh-REH-chah

phrases.local: Unos tacos al pastor, por favor
phrases.say: OO-nohs TAH-kohs ahl pahs-TOR, por fah-VOR

phrases.en: Could you give me a small discount?

culture.history: Mexico was home to Olmec, Maya, Zapotec and Mexica (Aztec) civilisations, whose capital Tenochtitlan fell to Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies in 1521. Three centuries of colonial rule brought conquest, epidemic, forced labour and a new mestizo culture before independence was won in 1821. The country lost roughly half its territory to the United States in 1848, and the Revolution of 1910 to 1920 reshaped land, labour and national identity. For most of the twentieth century a single party dominated politics, until a democratic transition in 2000.
culture.politics: Mexico is a federal presidential republic of 31 states and Mexico City, with a bicameral Congress and an independent judiciary. Presidents serve a single six-year term, the sexenio, with no re-election. Questions of security, inequality and the rights of Indigenous communities are central civic themes.
culture.arts: The muralists Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted national history onto public walls, while Frida Kahlo turned the self-portrait into testimony. Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Juan Rulfo and Octavio Paz anchor its literature. Mariachi, son jarocho and Día de Muertos altars are living traditions recognised by UNESCO.

love.expression: Love is lived through family, food and fiesta: long Sunday meals, serenades, and care that extends to grandparents and godparents alike. Affection is warm and openly expressed, with hugs and a kiss on the cheek common, though customs differ between cities, regions and Indigenous communities.

etiquette: Greet everyone in a room, not just the person you came to see.
Use usted with elders and in formal settings until invited otherwise.
Social invitations run on relaxed time, but business meetings expect punctuality.

name: Argentina

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Guaraní, Quechua, Mapudungun, Wichí, Qom, Welsh in Chubut and immigrant languages

people: Most Argentines descend from Spanish and Italian immigrants mixed with criollo and Indigenous ancestry, alongside Indigenous peoples such as the Mapuche, Qom, Wichí, Guaraní and Kolla, Afro-Argentines, and newer communities from Paraguay, Bolivia, Peru and Venezuela. Around six in ten are Catholic, some 15% evangelical and nearly a fifth have no religion, and Argentina has Latin America's largest Jewish community. More than nine in ten live in cities, about a third in Greater Buenos Aires.

plug.note: Angled Type I sockets dominate, with Type C in older buildings; most travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: The fertile Pampas, producing soy, wheat, maize and beef
Vaca Muerta shale oil and gas
Lithium in the high Andean salt flats
Mendoza's vineyards and a world-famous Malbec
Patagonia, the Andes and Iguazú, sustaining tourism
A highly educated population, free public universities and rich cultural life
struggles: Chronic inflation and repeated debt crises that erode savings and wages
Poverty affecting over 40% of people in 2023, with many in informal work
Deep political polarisation, often called 'la grieta' (the rift)
Droughts and floods that hit farming and rural communities
Indigenous land rights and poverty in the north and Patagonia
Unresolved justice for victims of the 1994 AMIA bombing
prayFor: For families struggling with rising prices, that they may have bread on the table, stable work and hope for tomorrow
For children and young people in poor neighbourhoods (villas), and for the parishes, soup kitchens and teachers who serve them
For healing of the rift that divides families and friends, and for leaders who seek the common good
For Indigenous communities in the Chaco and Patagonia, that their land, water and dignity be honoured
For all who still mourn the disappeared and the victims of terror, that truth and justice bring peace

summary.history: Indigenous peoples such as the Diaguita, Guaraní, Qom and Mapuche lived across the land for millennia, leaving traces like the hand paintings of the Cueva de las Manos, before Spanish colonisation in the sixteenth century and the founding of Buenos Aires. After the May Revolution of 1810 and independence in 1816, decades of civil war followed, and the 'Conquest of the Desert' in the 1870s and 1880s seized Indigenous lands in the Pampas and Patagonia with great loss of life. Millions of European immigrants, mostly Italian and Spanish, arrived between 1870 and 1930, making Argentina one of the world's richest countries for a time. The twentieth century swung between Peronism and military coups, culminating in the dictatorship of 1976 to 1983, when thousands were disappeared, and the 1982 Falklands/Malvinas war; democracy returned in 1983, though economic crises, especially in 2001, have caused deep hardship.
summary.politicalHistory: The May Revolution of 1810 created a self-governing junta in Buenos Aires, and independence was declared at Tucumán on 9 July 1816, followed by long struggles between unitarians and federalists. The 1853 constitution established a federal republic, and the 1912 Sáenz Peña law brought secret, compulsory male suffrage, with women voting from 1951. From 1930 to 1983 elected governments, including those of Juan Perón, were repeatedly overthrown by military coups, and the last dictatorship ended after defeat in the Falklands/Malvinas war. Since 1983 Argentina has been a stable federal presidential democracy of 23 provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, whose 1985 Trial of the Juntas became a landmark for human rights worldwide.
summary.art: Tango, born in the port neighbourhoods of the Río de la Plata, was carried around the world by Carlos Gardel and reinvented by Astor Piazzolla, and folk music voiced by Atahualpa Yupanqui and Mercedes Sosa sings of the land and its people. Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar and Ernesto Sabato reshaped world literature, while José Hernández's gaucho poem Martín Fierro is the national epic. Fileteado porteño, the swirling sign-painting of Buenos Aires, and the silverwork and weaving of the provinces are cherished crafts.
summary.monuments: Iguazú Falls and the Perito Moreno Glacier in Los Glaciares National Park are UNESCO natural sites of overwhelming beauty. The Jesuit missions of the Guaraní, such as San Ignacio Miní, and the Jesuit Block of Córdoba recall a remarkable chapter of colonial history and faith. In Buenos Aires, the Plaza de Mayo, the Teatro Colón and the former ESMA detention centre, now a museum of memory listed by UNESCO, tell the story of a nation's power, art and hard-won commitment to human rights.

highlights.title: Recoleta Cemetery
highlights.line: A city of marble mausoleums where Eva Perón and many national figures rest; wander freely and look for the Duarte family tomb.

highlights.title: La Boca and Caminito
highlights.line: Brightly painted tin houses, tango dancers and the Boca Juniors stadium; stay in the main tourist streets, especially after dark.

highlights.title: San Telmo Sunday Fair
highlights.line: Antiques, street tango and empanadas fill Calle Defensa every Sunday; end the day at the evening milonga in Plaza Dorrego.

highlights.title: Teatro Colón
highlights.line: One of the world's great opera houses, famed for its acoustics; take the guided tour or catch a performance.

highlights.title: A tango milonga
highlights.line: Watch or join locals dancing late at night in a traditional milonga; beginner classes often run before the dancing starts.

highlights.title: An asado
highlights.line: The Argentine barbecue is a weekend ritual; at a parrilla, order bife de chorizo, provoleta and chimichurri, and expect generous portions.

highlights.title: Café Tortoni and the bares notables
highlights.line: Buenos Aires protects its historic cafés; linger over a cortado and medialunas as porteños have for generations.

highlights.title: Plaza de Mayo
highlights.line: The political heart of the nation, facing the Casa Rosada; the white headscarves painted on the ground honour the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo.

highlights.title: ESMA Museum and Site of Memory
highlights.line: A former clandestine detention centre turned into a sober museum and UNESCO site; a profound place to understand the dictatorship years.

highlights.title: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
highlights.line: A former theatre turned bookshop, with balconies of books and a café on the old stage.

highlights.title: Tigre Delta
highlights.line: Take a train and boat into the labyrinth of river islands north of Buenos Aires, with stilt houses and rowing clubs.

highlights.title: Basilica of Luján
highlights.line: Argentina's national Marian shrine; each October thousands of young people walk about 60 km overnight from Buenos Aires in pilgrimage.

highlights.title: Iguazú Falls
highlights.line: Some 275 waterfalls on the border with Brazil; walk the Argentine side's trails to the Devil's Throat, and allow two days.

highlights.title: San Ignacio Miní
highlights.line: The red-stone ruins of a Jesuit mission where Guaraní people once lived, prayed and made music; stay for the evening sound-and-light show.

highlights.title: Esteros del Iberá
highlights.line: Vast wetlands of Corrientes with caimans, capybaras and marsh deer, where reintroduced jaguars now roam again.

highlights.title: Salta
highlights.line: A colonial city of pastel churches, empanadas salteñas and folk music in the peñas; the Museum of High Mountain Archaeology is extraordinary.

highlights.title: Quebrada de Humahuaca
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed Andean valley of striped mountains and adobe villages; see the Hill of Seven Colours at Purmamarca in morning light.

highlights.title: Cafayate and the Quebrada de las Conchas
highlights.line: Drive past red rock formations to high-altitude vineyards and taste crisp Torrontés white wine.

highlights.title: Salinas Grandes
highlights.line: A dazzling white salt flat at around 3,400 metres; bring sunglasses and warm layers, and go slowly at altitude.

highlights.title: Mendoza and Malbec
highlights.line: Cycle or drive between wineries at the foot of the Andes; book tastings ahead and remember lunch is long.

highlights.title: Aconcagua
highlights.line: The highest mountain outside Asia; even non-climbers can walk to the Laguna Horcones viewpoint in the provincial park.

highlights.title: Córdoba's Jesuit Block
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed complex of church, university and college, with rural Jesuit estancias nearby.

highlights.title: Bariloche and the Lakes District
highlights.line: Alpine-style lakes, forests and mountains in Patagonia; enjoy chocolate shops in town and the panoramic Circuito Chico.

highlights.title: Seven Lakes Route
highlights.line: A scenic road between San Martín de los Andes and Villa La Angostura, best driven slowly with stops to swim and picnic.

highlights.title: Perito Moreno Glacier
highlights.line: Watch towering blocks of ice crash into the lake from the walkways near El Calafate, or join a guided ice trek.

highlights.title: El Chaltén and Fitz Roy
highlights.line: Argentina's trekking capital; the day hike to Laguna de los Tres offers an unforgettable view of the granite spires.

highlights.title: Ushuaia and the Beagle Channel
highlights.line: Sail among sea lion colonies and lighthouses at the edge of the continent, and walk in Tierra del Fuego National Park.

highlights.title: Península Valdés
highlights.line: Southern right whales from about June to December, plus elephant seals, sea lions and orcas; Puerto Pirámides is the base.

highlights.title: Ischigualasto and Talampaya
highlights.line: Twin parks of strange eroded rock and Triassic fossils in San Juan and La Rioja, sometimes called the Valley of the Moon.

highlights.title: Sharing mate
highlights.line: Being offered mate is a sign of welcome; drink it all, hand it back to the host, and only say 'gracias' when you want no more.

highlights.title: San Antonio de Areco
highlights.line: A gaucho town in the Pampas with silversmiths, saddlers and an annual Day of Tradition festival each November.

highlights.title: Rosario
highlights.line: A lively river city where the Monumento a la Bandera marks the place the national flag was first raised in 1812.

highlights.title: Gaiman's Welsh tea houses
highlights.line: In Chubut, descendants of nineteenth-century Welsh settlers serve afternoon tea with torta negra, a rich black cake.

funFacts: Argentina's name comes from the Latin argentum, meaning silver.
Aconcagua, at about 6,961 metres, is the highest mountain in the Americas and in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.
In 1892 Argentina became the first country to solve a murder case using fingerprints, thanks to the system of Juan (Ivan) Vucetich.
The ballpoint pen was patented in Argentina in 1943 by László Bíró, and Argentines still call a pen a 'birome'.
The world's first known animated feature film, El Apóstol (1917), was made in Argentina by Quirino Cristiani.
Argentina has five Nobel laureates, including Bernardo Houssay, the first Latin American Nobel winner in the sciences.
Pope Francis, elected in 2013, was born in Buenos Aires, the first pope from the Americas.
Line A of the Buenos Aires Subte, opened in 1913, was the first underground railway in Latin America and the Southern Hemisphere.
Avenida 9 de Julio in Buenos Aires is one of the widest avenues in the world, about 140 metres across.
Argentina is the eighth-largest country in the world by area.
Argentina is the world's largest producer of yerba mate.
Argentinosaurus, found in Patagonia, is one of the largest land animals known to have ever lived.
The hand stencils of the Cueva de las Manos in Patagonia were painted up to around 9,000 years ago.
Emilio Palma, born in 1978 at Argentina's Esperanza Base, was the first person known to be born in Antarctica.
Welsh settlers arrived in Chubut in 1865, and Welsh is still spoken by some families in Patagonia today.
Argentina's men's football team has won the World Cup three times: in 1978, 1986 and 2022.
Tango was declared part of humanity's intangible heritage by UNESCO in 2009, jointly with Uruguay.
Fileteado porteño, the ornate sign-painting style of Buenos Aires, is recognised by UNESCO.
The 'Sun of May' on Argentina's flag is a sun with a face, said to recall the Inca sun god Inti.
Argentines celebrate Friend's Day on 20 July, an idea inspired by the 1969 Moon landing.
Argentina is one of the countries with the most psychologists per person in the world.
Buenos Aires is home to the largest Jewish community in Latin America.
Ushuaia is often called the southernmost city in the world.
The Iguazú Falls system includes around 275 individual cascades.
Argentina is a polo powerhouse, and its national Open at Palermo is one of the sport's most prestigious tournaments.
Mendoza produces most of Argentina's wine, and Malbec, originally from France, became the country's signature grape.
Dulce de leche, a milk caramel, is used in everything from alfajores to ice cream.
Lionel Messi and Che Guevara were both born in the city of Rosario.
The Perito Moreno Glacier periodically dams a lake arm until the water breaks through the ice in a dramatic rupture.
Argentina's 1985 Trial of the Juntas was one of the first times a democracy tried its own former military rulers in civilian court.
Buenos Aires residents are called porteños, 'people of the port'.
Argentine Spanish pronounces 'll' and 'y' as 'sh', so 'calle' (street) sounds like 'CAH-sheh'.
In Argentina, dinner commonly begins after 9 pm, and restaurants fill up close to midnight.

languageGuide.intro: Argentine Spanish uses 'vos' instead of 'tú' (vos sos, vos tenés) and pronounces ll and y as 'sh', with an Italian-like lilt. Use usted with elders and in formal settings; English is spoken in tourist areas and by many younger porteños, less so in the provinces.

phrases.en: Where can I top up my SUBE card?

phrases.local: Un pasaje a Mendoza, por favor
phrases.say: oon pah-SAH-heh ah men-DOH-sah, por fah-VOR

phrases.en: What time does the coach leave?
phrases.say: ah keh OH-rah SAH-leh el MEE-kroh

phrases.local: A la izquierda / a la derecha
phrases.say: ah lah ees-KYEHR-dah / ah lah deh-REH-chah

phrases.local: Una mesa para dos, por favor
phrases.say: OO-nah MEH-sah PAH-rah dohs, por fah-VOR

phrases.en: A coffee with milk and croissants
phrases.local: Un café con leche y medialunas
phrases.say: oon kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh ee meh-dyah-LOO-nahs

phrases.en: Is there a discount for cash?

culture.history: Indigenous peoples including the Diaguita, Guaraní and Mapuche lived across the land before Spanish colonisation, and independence was declared in 1816. Nineteenth-century campaigns pushed Indigenous communities from the Pampas and Patagonia, while a vast wave of European immigration transformed the country's cities. The twentieth century swung between Peronism and military coups, culminating in the dictatorship of 1976 to 1983, when thousands were disappeared; the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo became a global symbol of resistance. Defeat in the 1982 Falklands/Malvinas war hastened the return to democracy in 1983.
culture.politics: Argentina is a federal presidential republic of 23 provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, with a bicameral National Congress. The trials of the dictatorship's leaders made memory, truth and justice a defining civic commitment. Recurring inflation and debt crises keep economic stability at the centre of public debate.
culture.arts: Tango, born in the port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, was carried worldwide by Carlos Gardel and reinvented by Astor Piazzolla. Jorge Luis Borges and Julio Cortázar reshaped world literature with labyrinthine stories. Folk music from the northwest, voiced by Mercedes Sosa and Atahualpa Yupanqui, carries the country's Andean soul.

love.expression: Affection is close and physical: friends, including men, greet with a kiss on the cheek, and long conversations over mate or late dinners are the stuff of friendship. Family and friends are intertwined, and feelings are often spoken openly and with passion, with quieter styles in the provinces.

etiquette: Greet with a single kiss on the right cheek once you are introduced.
Dinner often begins after 9 pm; plan meals later than you might expect.
If mate is shared, do not say gracias until you are finished, as it signals you want no more.

name: Brazil

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. some 150+ Indigenous languages and immigrant languages such as German and Japanese dialects

people: Brazilians are one of the world's most mixed peoples: in the 2022 census about 45% identified as pardo (mixed), 43% as white and 10% as Black, alongside some 1.7 million Indigenous people from more than 250 peoples and large communities of Italian, German, Arab and Japanese descent. Roughly half are Catholic and around a third Evangelical or Protestant, with Spiritism and Afro-Brazilian religions such as Candomblé and Umbanda woven through the culture. About nine in ten live in towns and cities, concentrated along the Atlantic coast.

plug.note: Voltage varies by state and even by building, so check before plugging in; the three-pin Type N socket also accepts two-pin Type C plugs, and most travellers need an adapter.

resources: The Amazon rainforest and world-leading biodiversity
Vast freshwater and hydropower
Agricultural powerhouse: soy, coffee, sugar, beef and orange juice
Iron ore and offshore 'pre-salt' oil
Music, dance and a joyful festival culture
A young, creative and diverse population
struggles: Deep inequality, with stark racial and regional gaps
Deforestation and fires in the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal
Urban violence and organised crime, especially in poorer neighbourhoods
Sharp political polarisation
Extreme weather, such as the catastrophic 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul and severe droughts in the Amazon
Threats to Indigenous lands and health, including illegal gold mining on Yanomami territory
prayFor: For families in favelas and peripheries, that children may grow up safe, schooled and free from the pull of violence
For Indigenous peoples and forest communities, that their lands, languages and health be protected
For the Amazon and all who depend on it, and for wisdom in caring for creation
For those who lost homes and loved ones to floods and drought, and for lasting rebuilding
For healing across political and racial divides, and for a shared hope that includes everyone

summary.history: For thousands of years Tupi-Guarani, Gê, Arawak and many other peoples lived across the forests, savannas and coasts, and their populations collapsed through war, enslavement and disease after Portuguese navigators arrived in 1500. Sugar plantations, then gold mining in Minas Gerais and later coffee were built on the labour of roughly four to five million enslaved Africans, more than any other country in the Americas received. In 1808 the Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio de Janeiro, and Brazil became independent in 1822, abolishing slavery only in 1888 without land or redress for the freed. The twentieth century brought industrialisation, mass migration from Europe, the Middle East and Japan, rapid urbanisation and a military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985. Today Brazil is a continental democracy of enormous creativity, still wrestling with inequality and the fate of its forests.
summary.politicalHistory: Brazil gained independence in 1822 as an empire under Pedro I, becoming a republic after a military coup in 1889. Getúlio Vargas dominated mid-century politics, including the authoritarian Estado Novo of 1937–1945, and a military coup in 1964 led to two decades of dictatorship marked by censorship, torture and exile. Redemocratisation culminated in the 1988 'Citizen Constitution', and since then two presidents have been removed by impeachment, in 1992 and 2016. Brazil is today a federal presidential republic of 26 states and a Federal District, with a bicameral National Congress and compulsory voting for literate adults aged 18 to 70.
summary.art: Samba, born in Rio's Afro-Brazilian communities, bossa nova from Antônio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto, and the Tropicália movement of Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil carried Brazilian music around the world. Machado de Assis, Clarice Lispector and Jorge Amado lead a rich literature, while Aleijadinho's soapstone prophets crown the baroque of Minas Gerais and Tarsila do Amaral and Candido Portinari shaped modern painting. Capoeira, forró, frevo and the woodcut-illustrated cordel booklets of the Northeast show the depth of popular art.
summary.monuments: Christ the Redeemer above Rio de Janeiro has become a symbol of the nation and of welcome. The UNESCO-listed historic centres of Ouro Preto and Salvador's Pelourinho preserve baroque churches built with gold and enslaved labour, while Valongo Wharf in Rio, the largest landing site of enslaved Africans in the Americas, is a World Heritage site of memory. Oscar Niemeyer's modernist Brasília and the thundering falls of Iguaçu National Park are also inscribed by UNESCO.

highlights.title: Christ the Redeemer
highlights.line: The Art Deco statue on Corcovado is Rio's embrace of the city; take the cog train early in the morning to beat clouds and crowds.

highlights.title: Sugarloaf Mountain
highlights.line: Two cable cars lift you over Guanabara Bay; go late afternoon and stay for sunset as the city lights come on.

highlights.title: Copacabana and Ipanema
highlights.line: Rio's beach life is a democratic living room; at Arpoador, locals applaud the sunset, and carry only what you need to the sand.

highlights.title: Escadaria Selarón and Santa Teresa
highlights.line: Jorge Selarón's tiled staircase links Lapa to the bohemian hills of Santa Teresa; visit by day and ride the restored bonde tram.

highlights.title: Iguaçu Falls
highlights.line: Some 275 cascades plunge along the Argentine border; walk the Brazilian side for the panorama and get soaked on the Devil's Throat walkway.

highlights.title: Meeting of the Waters, Manaus
highlights.line: The dark Rio Negro and sandy Solimões run side by side for kilometres before mixing; a short boat trip from Manaus shows it best.

highlights.title: Amazon lodges
highlights.line: Stay a few nights at a jungle lodge on the Rio Negro or in the Mamirauá reserve to hear howler monkeys and see pink river dolphins.

highlights.title: Teatro Amazonas
highlights.line: Manaus's rubber-boom opera house, with its tiled dome, still hosts performances; join a guided tour if you can't catch a show.

highlights.title: Pantanal
highlights.line: The world's largest tropical wetland is the best place on Earth to see wild jaguars; go in the dry season, roughly July to October.

highlights.title: Pelourinho, Salvador
highlights.line: Pastel colonial streets ring with drums and capoeira in the heart of Afro-Brazilian culture; visit the gilded São Francisco church.

highlights.title: Acarajé from a baiana
highlights.line: Black-eyed-pea fritters fried in dendê oil by women in white dress are Salvador's sacred street food; ask for it 'frio' if you dislike chilli.

highlights.title: Lençóis Maranhenses
highlights.line: Rain fills turquoise lagoons between white dunes; they are fullest from about June to September, reached via Barreirinhas.

highlights.title: Chapada Diamantina
highlights.line: Table mountains, caves and waterfalls in inland Bahia; hike to Cachoeira da Fumaça with a local guide from Lençóis.

highlights.title: Fernando de Noronha
highlights.line: A protected archipelago with some of Brazil's clearest waters and spinner dolphins; visitor numbers are limited and a daily environmental fee applies.

highlights.title: Ouro Preto
highlights.line: A hilly gold-rush town of baroque churches and Aleijadinho sculpture; wear grippy shoes on the steep cobblestones.

highlights.title: Inhotim
highlights.line: A vast garden-museum of contemporary art near Belo Horizonte; give it a full day and use the internal carts to cover ground.

highlights.title: Paraty
highlights.line: Colonial streets that flood gently at high tide sit between rainforest and bay; take a schooner to nearby islands and taste local cachaça.

highlights.title: Ilha Grande
highlights.line: A car-free island of trails and beaches; hike to Lopes Mendes beach and leave no trace in the Atlantic Forest.

highlights.title: Brasília
highlights.line: The planned capital is an open-air museum of Niemeyer modernism; don't miss the crown-shaped Cathedral and the Palácio do Itamaraty.

highlights.title: Avenida Paulista and MASP
highlights.line: São Paulo's main avenue closes to cars on Sundays; see MASP's paintings hung on glass easels and wander into Liberdade's Japanese quarter.

highlights.title: Mercadão de São Paulo
highlights.line: The Municipal Market's stained glass shelters fruit stalls and the famous towering mortadella sandwich; share one, they are enormous.

highlights.title: Carnival
highlights.line: Rio's samba schools parade in the Sambadrome, while Salvador and Olinda celebrate in the streets; book far ahead and keep valuables minimal.

highlights.title: Olinda
highlights.line: Hilltop colonial churches look over Recife; at Carnival giant papier-mâché puppets dance through the lanes to frevo.

highlights.title: Bonito
highlights.line: Float down crystal-clear rivers among fish in Mato Grosso do Sul; tours are capped and booked through local agencies to protect the waters.

highlights.title: Feijoada
highlights.line: Black-bean stew with pork, rice, greens, farofa and orange is a leisurely Saturday ritual; pace yourself and pair it with a caipirinha.

highlights.title: Churrascaria rodízio
highlights.line: Waiters bring skewers of grilled meat until you turn your card to red; in the South try gaúcho barbecue and a gourd of chimarrão.

highlights.title: Pão de queijo in Minas Gerais
highlights.line: Cheese bread with strong coffee is mineiro hospitality at its simplest; buy it warm from a padaria.

highlights.title: Basilica of Aparecida
highlights.line: One of the world's largest Marian shrines houses the small dark clay image found by fishermen in 1717; 12 October is a national feast.

highlights.title: Círio de Nazaré, Belém
highlights.line: On the second Sunday of October, millions accompany Our Lady of Nazareth through Belém in one of the world's largest processions.

highlights.title: Ver-o-Peso market
highlights.line: Belém's riverside market sells açaí, tucupi, Amazon fish and herbal remedies; try tacacá soup and its tingling jambu leaves.

highlights.title: Jericoacoara
highlights.line: A dune village in Ceará where everyone climbs the big dune at sunset; it is also a world-class kitesurfing spot.

highlights.title: Festas Juninas
highlights.line: In June the Northeast dances forró around bonfires, with Campina Grande and Caruaru hosting the biggest São João festivals.

highlights.title: Football at the Maracanã
highlights.line: Watching a match in Rio's legendary stadium is pure collective emotion; buy official tickets and choose a neutral sector if unsure.

funFacts: Brazil is the fifth-largest country in the world by area and borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
Brazil takes its name from pau-brasil, a tree whose red dye was the colony's first major export.
Brazil is the only country in the Americas whose official language is Portuguese, and it has far more Portuguese speakers than Portugal.
From 1808 to 1821 Rio de Janeiro was the seat of the Portuguese empire, the only time a European empire was ruled from the Americas.
Brazil has the largest Catholic population of any country in the world.
Brazil has been the world's largest coffee producer for more than 150 years.
Brazil has won the men's FIFA World Cup five times, more than any other nation.
Pelé is the only player to have won three World Cups, in 1958, 1962 and 1970.
The capital moved from Rio de Janeiro to the newly built city of Brasília in 1960.
Seen from above, Lúcio Costa's plan for Brasília resembles an airplane or a bird with outstretched wings.
About 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies within Brazil.
The Amazon River discharges more water than any other river on Earth, roughly a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans.
Brazil is home to more known plant species than any other country.
Christ the Redeemer was completed in 1931 and stands about 30 metres tall, not counting its pedestal.
Brazil has the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan, centred on São Paulo.
Most of Brazil's electricity comes from renewable sources, chiefly hydropower.
Most new cars sold in Brazil are flex-fuel and can run on ethanol made from sugarcane.
The Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River, shared with Paraguay, is one of the most productive hydroelectric plants in the world.
The English words jaguar, piranha and tapioca came from the Indigenous Tupi language by way of Portuguese.
Brazil abolished slavery on 13 May 1888 with the 'Golden Law', the last country in the Americas to do so.
Brazil was the only South American country to send combat troops to Europe in the Second World War, fighting in Italy.
The 27 stars on Brazil's flag show the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the morning of 15 November 1889, with one star for each state and the Federal District.
The flag's motto, 'Ordem e Progresso' (Order and Progress), was inspired by the philosophy of Auguste Comte.
Many Brazilians regard Alberto Santos-Dumont as the father of aviation for his public flight of the 14-bis in Paris in 1906.
Snake Island off São Paulo's coast is the only home of the golden lancehead viper, and public visits are forbidden.
The golden lion tamarin lives only in the Atlantic Forest of Rio de Janeiro state.
In the Amazon region of Pará, açaí is traditionally eaten unsweetened as a savoury side with fried fish and cassava flour.
The caipirinha, Brazil's national cocktail, is made with cachaça, a spirit distilled from fresh sugarcane juice.
Each year surfers ride the pororoca, a tidal bore that pushes up rivers near the mouth of the Amazon.
Rio's Sambadrome, where the samba schools parade at Carnival, was designed by Oscar Niemeyer and opened in 1984.
Brazil's instant-payment system Pix became so popular within a few years of its 2020 launch that street vendors commonly accept it.
Voting is compulsory in Brazil for literate citizens aged 18 to 70.
Capoeira, the Afro-Brazilian art blending fight, dance and music, is recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

languageGuide.intro: Brazilian Portuguese is friendly and informal: 'você' works for almost everyone, while 'o senhor / a senhora' shows respect to elders, and a 'tudo bem?' opens most conversations. Final 'de' and 'te' often sound like 'jee' and 'chee', nasal vowels hum through the nose, and English is limited outside hotels and big-city business areas, so a few words go a long way.

culture.history: Hundreds of Indigenous nations lived in the territory before Portuguese colonisation began in 1500. Brazil received more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas, and in 1888 it became the last nation in the hemisphere to abolish slavery, a legacy still felt in its inequalities. Independence came in 1822 as an empire, followed by a republic in 1889. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, and the 1988 constitution established today's democracy.
culture.politics: Brazil is a federal presidential republic of 26 states and a Federal District, with a bicameral National Congress and powerful state governments. Voting is compulsory for literate adults between 18 and 70. Inequality, racial justice and the protection of the Amazon and its Indigenous peoples are defining civic themes.
culture.arts: Samba, bossa nova from Antônio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto, and the Tropicália movement made Brazilian music a world language. Machado de Assis and Clarice Lispector stand among its great writers, and Aleijadinho's sculpture crowns the baroque churches of Minas Gerais. Oscar Niemeyer's curving modernism gave form to the capital, Brasília.

love.expression: Warmth is expressive and tactile: hugs, cheek kisses and lingering goodbyes are common, and friendships often feel like family. Love is shown in shared time at long lunches, beach days and celebrations, with styles that vary across a vast and diverse country.

etiquette: Expect warm greetings with cheek kisses; the number varies by region.
The OK hand gesture can be read as rude, so give a thumbs-up instead.
Social times are flexible, but be punctual for business.

name: Peru

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. some 45 Amazonian languages and many Quechua varieties

people: Most Peruvians identify as mestizo, while more than a quarter are Quechua or Aymara peoples of the Andes, joined by dozens of Amazonian nations such as the Asháninka, Awajún and Shipibo-Konibo, Afro-Peruvian communities on the coast, and well-rooted Chinese (tusán) and Japanese (Nikkei) Peruvians. Roughly three-quarters are Catholic and about one in seven Evangelical, with Andean traditions honouring Pachamama often lived alongside Christian faith. About four in five people live in cities, nearly a third in metropolitan Lima, and a large diaspora lives in the United States, Spain, Argentina, Chile and Italy.

plug.note: Many sockets accept both US flat pins and European round pins, but the voltage is 220 V, so US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter; UK travellers need an adapter.

resources: Copper, gold, silver and zinc mining
Extraordinary biodiversity from Pacific coast to Andes and Amazon
Rich Pacific fisheries fed by the cold Humboldt Current
Ancient agricultural diversity: thousands of potato varieties, quinoa, maize and a booming fruit-export sector
A world-renowned cuisine
Inca and pre-Inca heritage and living Andean and Amazonian cultures
struggles: Chronic political instability, with repeated clashes between presidents and Congress
A largely informal economy, leaving most workers without contracts or pensions
Illegal mining, logging and coca cultivation damaging the Amazon and endangering forest defenders
Deep gaps in services between Lima and rural Andean and Amazonian communities
Melting glaciers, El Niño floods and water scarcity in the desert coast
Rising crime and extortion in cities
prayFor: For a political life marked by honesty, stability and service, and for trust between citizens and their institutions
For Andean and Amazonian communities, that their voices be heard and their lands and waters protected
For workers in the informal economy, that they may find dignity, security and fair wages
For families still seeking truth and the remains of loved ones lost in the years of violence
For those living with water shortage, floods and retreating glaciers, and for wise stewardship of creation

summary.history: Caral, on the desert coast, flourished nearly 5,000 years ago as one of the oldest cities in the Americas, and later Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Wari and Chimú cultures shaped the coast and highlands. In the fifteenth century the Inca built Tawantinsuyu from Cusco, the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, linked by thousands of kilometres of roads. Spanish conquest from 1532, led by Francisco Pizarro, brought war, epidemics and forced labour in the mines, and the Viceroyalty of Peru governed much of South America from Lima. Independence was declared in 1821 and secured at the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824, but the nineteenth century brought the guano boom, Chinese indentured labour and defeat in the War of the Pacific. Between 1980 and 2000 an internal armed conflict involving the Shining Path, the MRTA and state forces left an estimated 69,000 dead, most of them Quechua-speaking rural people.
summary.politicalHistory: José de San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence in 1821, and Simón Bolívar's forces completed it in 1824, after which decades of rule by military strongmen followed. A military government under Juan Velasco Alvarado from 1968 to 1975 carried out sweeping land reform and made Quechua co-official, and civilian democracy returned in 1980. Alberto Fujimori's 1992 self-coup led to the 1993 constitution and an increasingly authoritarian decade, and since 2016 repeated confrontations between the executive and Congress have seen several presidents resign or be removed. Peru is a unitary presidential republic with a unicameral Congress, which a 2024 reform is set to replace with a two-chamber legislature.
summary.art: Andean textiles, from the Paracas mantles to living weaving traditions around Cusco and Lake Titicaca, rank among the finest in the world, alongside Moche portrait ceramics and the Cusco School's fusion of Indigenous and European painting. César Vallejo's poetry, José María Arguedas's novels of Andean life and the work of Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa lead its literature. Music ranges from Andean huayno and the scissors dance to Afro-Peruvian festejo and landó, carried to the world by Chabuca Granda and Susana Baca.
summary.monuments: Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel above the Urubamba River, is the most celebrated of Peru's UNESCO World Heritage sites, with the historic centre of Cusco built on Inca foundations close by. On the coast, the adobe city of Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú, and the sacred city of Caral reveal civilisations far older than the Inca. The Nazca Lines etched into the desert and the colonial centres of Lima and Arequipa are also inscribed by UNESCO.

highlights.title: Machu Picchu
highlights.line: The Inca citadel among cloud-forest peaks is breathtaking at any hour; tickets are timed and limited, so book well ahead and consider Huayna Picchu.

highlights.title: The Inca Trail
highlights.line: Four days on stone paths through ruins and cloud forest end at the Sun Gate; permits sell out months ahead and the trail closes each February.

highlights.title: Cusco
highlights.line: The old Inca capital mixes colonial churches with perfect Inca walls; take it slow for the first day at 3,400 metres and explore the San Blas quarter.

highlights.title: Sacred Valley
highlights.line: Pisac's terraces and market and Ollantaytambo's living Inca town are lower than Cusco, making them a gentle place to acclimatise.

highlights.title: Moray and Maras
highlights.line: Circular Inca terraces at Moray sit near thousands of salt pans at Maras still worked by local families; buy salt directly from them.

highlights.title: Rainbow Mountain (Vinicunca)
highlights.line: Mineral-striped slopes above 5,000 metres reward a tough dawn hike; acclimatise first and consider nearby Palccoyo for fewer crowds.

highlights.title: Lake Titicaca
highlights.line: Visit the Uros reed islands and stay with a family on Amantaní or Taquile, whose textile art is recognised by UNESCO.

highlights.title: Fiesta de la Candelaria, Puno
highlights.line: Every February tens of thousands of dancers and musicians honour the Virgin of Candelaria in a UNESCO-listed festival.

highlights.title: Colca Canyon
highlights.line: Watch Andean condors ride the morning thermals at Cruz del Cóndor and soak in hot springs at Chivay.

highlights.title: Arequipa
highlights.line: The 'White City' is built of pale volcanic sillar under El Misti; lose an afternoon in the colourful Santa Catalina Monastery.

highlights.title: Nazca Lines
highlights.line: Giant desert drawings of a hummingbird, monkey and spider are best seen on a small-plane flight; the roadside viewing tower is a cheaper option.

highlights.title: Paracas and the Ballestas Islands
highlights.line: Boat trips pass sea lions, Humboldt penguins and huge seabird colonies; go early when the sea is calmer.

highlights.title: Huacachina
highlights.line: A palm-ringed oasis among towering dunes near Ica; try sandboarding at sunset and visit a pisco bodega.

highlights.title: Ceviche in Lima
highlights.line: Fresh fish cured in lime with chilli and red onion is a lunchtime dish, so go before mid-afternoon when cevicherías close.

highlights.title: Barranco and Miraflores
highlights.line: Lima's clifftop districts offer ocean views, street art and galleries; walk the Puente de los Suspiros at dusk.

highlights.title: Historic centre of Lima
highlights.line: Baroque balconies line the Plaza Mayor; tour the catacombs and library of the San Francisco monastery.

highlights.title: Museo Larco
highlights.line: Thousands of pre-Columbian ceramics, especially Moche, fill a colonial mansion with a lovely garden café.

highlights.title: Huaca Pucllana
highlights.line: A 1,500-year-old adobe pyramid stands in the middle of Miraflores; evening tours show it lit up.

highlights.title: Cordillera Blanca and Huaraz
highlights.line: The world's highest tropical range offers glacier lakes like Laguna 69; spend a few days acclimatising before big hikes.

highlights.title: Chan Chan and Huanchaco
highlights.line: Explore the vast adobe Chimú capital, then watch fishermen ride caballitos de totora reed boats on Huanchaco's waves.

highlights.title: Kuélap and Gocta
highlights.line: The cloud-forest fortress of the Chachapoyas rivals Machu Picchu with far fewer visitors, and Gocta Falls is one of the world's tallest.

highlights.title: Caral
highlights.line: The oldest known city in the Americas, about 5,000 years old, lies a few hours north of Lima; guided visits explain its pyramids.

highlights.title: Manu National Park
highlights.line: One of the most biodiverse places on Earth, from cloud forest to lowland jungle; access is by multi-day guided trips.

highlights.title: Tambopata
highlights.line: Easy-to-reach Amazon lodges near Puerto Maldonado offer dawn visits to clay licks where hundreds of macaws gather.

highlights.title: Iquitos and the Amazon River
highlights.line: Reach this jungle city by plane or riverboat, visit the Belén market and spot pink river dolphins in the Pacaya-Samiria reserve.

highlights.title: Señor de los Milagros, Lima
highlights.line: Each October, purple-clad faithful accompany the image of the Lord of Miracles in one of the largest Catholic processions in the Americas.

highlights.title: Inti Raymi
highlights.line: On 24 June Cusco re-enacts the Inca Festival of the Sun at Sacsayhuamán; book seats early or watch the free town-square segments.

highlights.title: San Pedro Market, Cusco
highlights.line: Fresh juices, soups, bread and Andean produce fill this lively market; bring small change and an appetite.

highlights.title: Lomo saltado and chifa
highlights.line: Stir-fried beef with fries reflects Peru's Chinese heritage; try a chifa restaurant in Lima's Barrio Chino.

highlights.title: Pachamanca
highlights.line: Meats, potatoes and beans cooked under hot stones in an earth oven are a festive Andean feast, often served on weekends in the countryside.

highlights.title: Pisco sour
highlights.line: Peru's signature cocktail of grape brandy, lime and egg white is best sipped slowly, especially at altitude.

highlights.title: Northern beaches
highlights.line: Máncora offers sun and surf, and Chicama is famous for one of the world's longest left-breaking waves.

highlights.title: Afro-Peruvian music in El Carmen
highlights.line: This village near Chincha is a heartland of festejo and cajón drumming, especially around Christmas and Holy Week.

funFacts: The potato was first domesticated in the Andes of southern Peru thousands of years ago, and Peru grows thousands of native varieties.
The sacred city of Caral is about 5,000 years old, making it roughly as old as Egypt's first pyramids.
Machu Picchu was built in the mid-1400s, probably as an estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.
Local farmers knew Machu Picchu long before Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.
The Inca kept records with quipu, knotted cords whose colours and positions encoded numbers and information.
The Inca road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, stretched some 30,000 kilometres and is a UNESCO site shared by six countries.
Every year communities near Cusco rebuild the Q'eswachaka rope bridge by hand from woven grass, a tradition recognised by UNESCO.
Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, sits at about 3,800 metres and is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.
The Uros people live on islands they build themselves from totora reeds, adding fresh layers as the bottom rots.
Colca Canyon is roughly twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.
Peru holds most of the world's tropical glaciers, concentrated in the Cordillera Blanca.
Huascarán, at about 6,768 metres, is Peru's highest mountain and the highest peak in the tropics.
The most distant source of the Amazon River lies high in the Peruvian Andes.
Iquitos is often called the largest city in the world that cannot be reached by road.
Much of Lima almost never sees real rain; instead a fine winter mist called garúa drifts in from the cold Pacific.
The cold Humboldt Current makes Peru's sea one of the most productive fisheries on Earth.
Peru is the world's second-largest producer of copper.
In recent years Peru has become the world's leading exporter of blueberries.
The vicuña, a wild relative of the llama with exceptionally fine wool, appears on Peru's coat of arms.
In Cusco Cathedral, Marcos Zapata's painting of the Last Supper shows Christ and the apostles about to eat guinea pig.
Chifa cuisine was born from Chinese immigrants who arrived in the nineteenth century, and Nikkei cuisine from Japanese immigrants who came from 1899.
In 2023 UNESCO recognised the practices and meanings associated with ceviche as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
Chicha morada is a sweet, non-alcoholic drink made by boiling purple corn with pineapple, cinnamon and cloves.
Lúcuma, an Andean fruit with a maple-like flavour, is one of Peru's favourite ice-cream flavours.
Pisco takes its name from the port of Pisco, and both Peru and Chile claim the grape brandy as their own.
Lima was founded in 1535 by Francisco Pizarro and was first called the City of Kings.
The National University of San Marcos in Lima, founded in 1551, is the oldest officially established university in the Americas.
Quechua was made an official language of Peru in 1975 and is spoken by millions of people today.
The Nazca Lines were made by removing reddish surface stones to reveal the paler ground beneath.
Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, son of a Spanish captain and an Inca noblewoman, published his celebrated chronicle of Inca history in 1609.
Mario Vargas Llosa won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010.
The Peruvian Paso horse is famous for an exceptionally smooth natural gait that makes it comfortable to ride for long distances.
Manu National Park has recorded more than 1,000 bird species, about a tenth of all the world's birds.

languageGuide.intro: Peruvian Spanish is clear and fairly slow, with a gentle courtesy: use 'usted' with elders and strangers, and greet with 'buenos días' before asking anything. Many Andean people speak Quechua or Aymara as their first language, so a Quechua 'sulpayki' (thank you) brings smiles, and English is common only in tourist hubs like Cusco and Miraflores.

phrases.local: Un pasaje a Cusco, por favor
phrases.say: oon pah-SAH-heh ah KOOS-koh, por fah-VOR

phrases.local: A la izquierda / a la derecha
phrases.say: ah lah ees-KYEHR-dah / ah lah deh-REH-chah

phrases.en: Could you give me a little discount?

culture.history: Peru cradled some of the Americas' oldest civilisations, from Caral to the Nazca, Moche and Chimú, culminating in the Inca Empire ruled from Cusco. Spanish conquest from 1532 brought devastation through war, disease and forced labour, and Lima became the seat of a vast viceroyalty. Independence was declared in 1821 and secured in 1824. Between 1980 and 2000, armed conflict involving the Shining Path and state forces killed tens of thousands, most of them Quechua-speaking rural people, as documented by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
culture.politics: Peru is a unitary presidential republic in which an elected president governs alongside Congress, which holds strong powers, including to remove a president for 'moral incapacity'. Frequent clashes between the executive and legislature have made political stability a pressing concern. The inclusion of Andean and Amazonian communities in national life remains a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Andean textiles, among the finest in the world, carry millennia of technique and symbolism, and the Cusco School fused Indigenous and European painting. Machu Picchu and colonial Cusco embody Inca and Spanish architecture side by side. César Vallejo's poetry and the novels of Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa lead its literature, while huayno and Afro-Peruvian music like the festejo fill its festivals.

love.expression: Family is the centre of affection, and love is shown through shared meals, care for elders and generous hospitality. Greetings are warm, with a cheek kiss common in cities, while Andean communities often express care through reciprocity and collective work.

etiquette: Greet with a handshake or, among acquaintances in cities, a cheek kiss.
Ask before photographing people, especially in Andean communities.
Allow time to adjust to altitude in Cusco and Puno, and accept coca tea if offered.

name: Colombia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. some 65 Indigenous languages, the creoles of San Basilio de Palenque and San Andrés, and Romani

people: Most Colombians are of mixed Indigenous, European and African heritage, with Afro-Colombians (about one in ten, concentrated on the Pacific and Caribbean coasts), more than 100 Indigenous peoples such as the Wayuu, Nasa, Zenú, Emberá and the Kogi and Arhuaco of the Sierra Nevada, the Raizal islanders of San Andrés and a small Rom community. Roughly two-thirds or more are Catholic, with a fast-growing Evangelical and Protestant presence. About four in five live in cities, mainly in the Andean highlands and along the Caribbean, and the country has welcomed nearly three million Venezuelan migrants while its own diaspora lives largely in the United States and Spain.

plug.note: Same flat-pin plugs as the US; UK and EU travellers need an adapter, and devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Exceptional biodiversity: the most bird species of any country and vast páramo wetlands
Coffee and a flourishing cut-flower industry
Oil, coal, gold and the world's finest emeralds
Abundant rivers, rainfall and hydropower
Music, dance and literature of global reach
A resilient, entrepreneurial and warm-hearted people
struggles: The unfinished work of peace, with armed groups still fighting over territory in rural regions
Threats and killings targeting social leaders and environmental defenders
Coca cultivation and drug trafficking that fuel violence
Unequal land ownership and deep gaps between cities and the countryside
Deforestation in the Amazon and Andean foothills
Integrating millions of Venezuelan migrants and Colombians internally displaced by conflict
prayFor: For lasting peace in the regions still shaped by armed groups, and for the courage of those who work for reconciliation
For social leaders, Indigenous guards and environmental defenders, that they may live and serve without fear
For the millions displaced by conflict and for Venezuelan families building new lives, that they find welcome and home
For farmers seeking fair livelihoods free from the drug economy, and for just land reform
For the forests, páramos and rivers that give Colombia its life, and for those who protect them

summary.history: Before Europeans arrived, the Muisca of the eastern highlands, the Tairona of the Sierra Nevada, the Zenú of the Caribbean plains and many other peoples built farming societies renowned for their goldwork. Spanish conquest from the early 1500s brought war and epidemics, and colonial wealth from gold, cattle and trade through Cartagena rested on the labour of Indigenous people and enslaved Africans. Independence was won after Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819, followed by a long nineteenth century of civil wars between Liberals and Conservatives. The assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948 unleashed La Violencia, and from the 1960s guerrillas, paramilitaries, state forces and drug cartels waged a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. A 2016 peace agreement with the FARC opened a new, still-fragile chapter of truth-telling and rebuilding.
summary.politicalHistory: Colombia first emerged as part of Gran Colombia, which also included today's Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, before breaking apart in 1830–31. The country swung between federal and centralist constitutions, and in 1903 Panama seceded with United States backing. After La Violencia and a brief military government in the 1950s, Liberals and Conservatives shared power under the National Front from 1958 to 1974, which ended partisan bloodshed but excluded other voices. The 1991 constitution recognised Colombia as a multi-ethnic, pluricultural nation and created a strong Constitutional Court, and the country remains a unitary presidential republic with a bicameral Congress.
summary.art: Gabriel García Márquez made magical realism a world literature with One Hundred Years of Solitude, and the painter and sculptor Fernando Botero gave the world his serene, rounded figures. Cumbia, vallenato, champeta and Cali's salsa carry rhythms woven from Indigenous, African and Spanish roots, celebrated by artists like Totó la Momposina. Crafts are as vivid as the music: Wayuu woven bags, the Zenú sombrero vueltiao, Mompox silver filigree and the pre-Hispanic gold treasures of the Museo del Oro.
summary.monuments: Cartagena's walled port, fortresses and the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas are a UNESCO World Heritage site recalling both Spanish power and the enslaved people who built it. The carved stone guardians of San Agustín and the painted tombs of Tierradentro preserve mysterious pre-Hispanic cultures, while Teyuna, the 'Lost City' of the Sierra Nevada, remains sacred to its Indigenous descendants. The Coffee Cultural Landscape and the riverside town of Mompox are UNESCO-listed, and the Las Lajas Sanctuary, rising from a canyon near Ipiales, draws pilgrims from across the Andes.

highlights.title: Cartagena's walled city
highlights.line: Bougainvillea balconies and plazas glow at dusk; walk the ramparts at sunset and explore lively Getsemaní just outside the walls.

highlights.title: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas
highlights.line: The largest Spanish fortress in the Americas guards Cartagena; go early before the heat and walk its tunnels.

highlights.title: Rosario Islands
highlights.line: Coral islands an hour by boat from Cartagena offer snorkelling; choose operators who respect the marine park.

highlights.title: Tayrona National Park
highlights.line: Jungle meets white beaches beneath the Sierra Nevada; the park closes for some weeks each year to let nature and Indigenous communities rest, so check dates.

highlights.title: Ciudad Perdida (Teyuna)
highlights.line: A four-to-five-day guided trek leads to stone terraces built centuries before Machu Picchu, sacred to the Kogi, Arhuaco and Wiwa peoples.

highlights.title: Minca
highlights.line: A cool mountain village above Santa Marta with coffee farms, waterfalls and superb birdwatching.

highlights.title: La Guajira
highlights.line: The desert peninsula of the Wayuu people offers Cabo de la Vela and dunes plunging into the sea at Punta Gallinas; travel with Wayuu-run tours.

highlights.title: Mompox
highlights.line: A timeless river town on the Magdalena, famous for silver filigree and solemn Holy Week processions.

highlights.title: San Basilio de Palenque
highlights.line: Founded by people who escaped slavery, this village keeps its own creole language and drum traditions; visit with a local guide.

highlights.title: Barranquilla Carnival
highlights.line: Four days of cumbia, masks and parades before Lent, proclaimed a Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage by UNESCO.

highlights.title: Museo del Oro, Bogotá
highlights.line: Tens of thousands of pre-Hispanic gold pieces, including the Muisca raft linked to the El Dorado legend; it is closed on Mondays.

highlights.title: La Candelaria and the Botero Museum
highlights.line: Bogotá's colonial quarter is full of murals and cafés, and the Botero Museum is free; try a hot chocolate with cheese.

highlights.title: Monserrate
highlights.line: Ride the cable car or funicular to the hilltop sanctuary above Bogotá, or join the Sunday pilgrims who climb on foot.

highlights.title: Bogotá's Ciclovía
highlights.line: On Sundays and holidays more than 100 kilometres of streets close to cars for cyclists, runners and families; rent a bike and join in.

highlights.title: Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá
highlights.line: An underground church carved inside a salt mine, with Stations of the Cross lit in shifting colours.

highlights.title: Villa de Leyva
highlights.line: A whitewashed colonial town with one of the largest cobbled squares in the Americas; nearby fossils and vineyards make a good weekend.

highlights.title: Comuna 13, Medellín
highlights.line: Once among the city's most violent neighbourhoods, it now tells its story through murals, hip-hop and outdoor escalators; take a resident-led tour.

highlights.title: Metrocable to Parque Arví
highlights.line: Medellín's cable cars glide over hillside neighbourhoods to forest trails, a ride that shows how transport changed the city.

highlights.title: Feria de las Flores, Medellín
highlights.line: In August, silleteros from Santa Elena parade with huge flower arrangements carried on their backs.

highlights.title: Guatapé and El Peñón
highlights.line: Climb about 700 steps up the giant rock for views of a sprawling reservoir, then wander Guatapé's brightly painted streets.

highlights.title: Valle de Cocora
highlights.line: Wax palms, Colombia's national tree, tower over green hills near Salento; start the loop hike early before the afternoon rain.

highlights.title: Coffee farm stay
highlights.line: In the Coffee Cultural Landscape, a finca visit walks you from bean to cup; buy beans directly from the growers.

highlights.title: Salsa in Cali
highlights.line: Colombia's salsa capital dances fast and footwork-heavy; take a class, then join a local club, especially during the Feria de Cali in December.

highlights.title: Pacific coast whales
highlights.line: Humpback whales arrive from the south to give birth off Nuquí and Bahía Solano, roughly July to October; stay in community-run lodges.

highlights.title: Caño Cristales
highlights.line: A river that turns red, yellow and green with aquatic plants, roughly June to November; access is only with authorised guides.

highlights.title: San Agustín
