highlights.line: Hundreds of ancient carved stone figures stand in green hills near the source of the Magdalena; hire a horse or jeep for outlying sites.

highlights.title: Tatacoa Desert
highlights.line: Red and grey eroded canyons under some of Colombia's clearest night skies; visit the small observatory after dark.

highlights.title: Las Lajas Sanctuary
highlights.line: A neo-Gothic basilica bridges a river canyon near the Ecuadorian border, built where many believe Mary appeared in the eighteenth century.

highlights.title: Amazon from Leticia
highlights.line: Look for pink river dolphins, visit Indigenous communities with respect and step between Colombia, Brazil and Peru at the Tres Fronteras.

highlights.title: San Andrés and Providencia
highlights.line: The 'sea of seven colours' surrounds islands of Raizal culture, where English-based Creole and Caribbean traditions endure.

highlights.title: Bandeja paisa
highlights.line: Antioquia's generous platter of beans, rice, meats, plantain, avocado, arepa and egg is meant for a long lunch.

highlights.title: Arepas and coastal street food
highlights.line: Try arepa de huevo and carimañola on the Caribbean coast, and a cheese-filled arepa almost anywhere.

highlights.title: Fruit markets and ajiaco
highlights.line: At Bogotá's Paloquemao market taste lulo, guanábana and granadilla, then warm up with ajiaco, the capital's chicken-and-potato soup.

funFacts: Colombia is the only country in South America with coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
Colombia is named after Christopher Columbus, although he never set foot on its mainland.
Colombia has recorded more bird species than any other country, around 1,900.
Colombia is the world's leading source of emeralds, prized for their deep green colour.
Colombia is the world's second-largest exporter of cut flowers, after the Netherlands.
Colombia is one of the world's largest producers of arabica coffee.
The fictional coffee farmer Juan Valdez and his mule Conchita were created in 1958 to represent Colombia's growers.
The Quindío wax palm, Colombia's national tree, is among the tallest palms in the world.
Colombia's national flower is an orchid, Cattleya trianae, and the country has thousands of orchid species.
Bogotá sits at about 2,640 metres above sea level, making it one of the highest major capitals in the world.
Bogotá's Sunday Ciclovía began in the 1970s and today opens more than 100 kilometres of streets to people on foot and bicycle.
Bogotá's TransMilenio, opened in 2000, became a model for bus rapid-transit systems around the world.
Medellín's Metrocable, opened in 2004, pioneered the use of cable cars as everyday public transport for hillside neighbourhoods.
The El Dorado legend grew from a Muisca ceremony at Lake Guatavita in which a new ruler, covered in gold dust, offered treasures to the waters.
Bogotá's Museo del Oro holds the largest collection of pre-Hispanic goldwork in the world.
Gabriel García Márquez received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.
San Basilio de Palenque is often described as the first free town in the Americas, founded by people who escaped slavery.
Palenquero, spoken in San Basilio de Palenque, is a Spanish-based creole with roots in Bantu languages from Central Africa.
The colours of Caño Cristales come from an aquatic plant, Macarenia clavigera, that turns red in the sun.
Colombia is home to roughly half of the world's páramos, high-altitude wetlands that supply water to millions.
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises from the Caribbean to almost 5,700 metres, making it the world's highest coastal mountain range.
In Colombia the Andes split into three ranges: the Western, Central and Eastern cordilleras.
Colombia's southern Amazon region lies just south of the equator.
Tejo, in which players throw metal discs at targets packed with small explosive charges, is Colombia's official national sport.
In much of Colombia people use the formal 'usted' even with close friends, children and partners.
A 'tinto' in Colombia is not red wine but a small cup of black coffee.
Panama was part of Colombia until it separated in 1903.
Gran Colombia, founded in 1819, united today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.
Colombia's 1991 constitution recognises the nation as multi-ethnic and pluricultural and protects Indigenous and Afro-Colombian territories.
Vallenato music, played with accordion, caja drum and guacharaca scraper, is on UNESCO's list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.
Barranquilla's Carnival was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2003.
The sombrero vueltiao, woven by Zenú artisans from caña flecha fibre, is officially a cultural symbol of the nation.
Humpback whales travel thousands of kilometres from Antarctic waters to give birth along Colombia's Pacific coast.

languageGuide.intro: Colombian Spanish is famously clear and courteous: many people use 'usted' even with friends, start requests with 'me regala…' ('would you give me…') and answer thanks with 'con mucho gusto'. Accents shift from crisp Bogotá to the fast, relaxed Caribbean coast, and English is limited outside tourist areas, so politeness and a few phrases matter.

phrases.local: A la izquierda / a la derecha
phrases.say: ah lah ees-KYEHR-dah / ah lah deh-REH-chah

phrases.en: Could I have a black coffee?
Can you do a better price?

culture.history: The Muisca, Tairona, Zenú and many other peoples inhabited the land before Spanish colonisation created the Viceroyalty of New Granada, built in part on enslaved African labour. Independence was secured after the Battle of Boyacá in 1819. The mid-twentieth-century period known as La Violencia gave way to decades of armed conflict among guerrillas, paramilitaries, state forces and drug cartels, displacing millions. A peace agreement with the FARC in 2016 opened a still-unfinished path toward reconciliation.
culture.politics: Colombia is a unitary presidential republic with a bicameral Congress, organised into departments and a capital district. The 1991 constitution expanded rights and created a Constitutional Court that plays a strong role in civic life. Peace-building, land rights and the inclusion of rural, Afro-Colombian and Indigenous communities are defining themes.
culture.arts: Gabriel García Márquez gave the world magical realism with One Hundred Years of Solitude. Cumbia and vallenato carry the rhythms of the Caribbean coast, and Fernando Botero's rounded figures are instantly recognisable. Pre-Columbian goldwork, preserved in Bogotá's Gold Museum, and colonial Cartagena's walled city reveal deep artistic layers.

love.expression: Colombians are known for warmth and courtesy: affectionate nicknames, attentive questions about family, and plenty of time for dancing and long conversations. Romance is often expressive and friends are treated like family, though manners differ between the more formal highlands and the easygoing coast.

etiquette: Greet people properly before any request; courtesy matters.
Use usted widely, as many Colombians do even with friends and family.
Avoid joking about drugs or the conflict, which caused deep pain.

name: United States

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. some 200 Native American, Alaska Native and Hawaiian languages and many immigrant languages

people: The United States is a nation of nations: about 58% of people identify as non-Hispanic white, around 19% as Hispanic or Latino, 12% as Black or African American and 6% as Asian American, alongside Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders and the 574 federally recognised American Indian and Alaska Native tribes. Roughly six in ten are Christian, Protestant and Catholic, while nearly three in ten are religiously unaffiliated, with Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist and Native spiritual traditions also part of the fabric. More than four in five live in urban areas, and the country is home to the largest immigrant population in the world.

plug.note: UK, EU and Australian travellers need an adapter, and devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter; most phone and laptop chargers are dual-voltage.

resources: Vast farmland, forests and fresh water, including the Great Lakes
Abundant energy: the world's largest producer of oil and natural gas, and growing wind and solar
World-leading universities, research and medical science
Technology, entrepreneurship and capital markets
Film, music and popular culture with global reach
Extraordinary public lands, from national parks to wilderness
struggles: Deep political polarisation and declining trust in institutions
Gun violence, including mass shootings and suicides
The opioid and fentanyl overdose crisis
High costs of housing and health care, and rising homelessness
Persistent racial and economic inequality
Climate-driven disasters such as wildfires, hurricanes, floods and drought
prayFor: For healing across political, racial and religious divides, and for neighbours who listen to one another
For families grieving loved ones lost to gun violence and overdose, and for communities working to prevent it
For people without stable homes or affordable care, and for those who serve them
For immigrants, refugees and Native nations, that their dignity be honoured and their gifts received
For those rebuilding after fires, storms and floods, and for wise care of the land

summary.history: For more than ten thousand years, hundreds of Native nations shaped the continent, from the mound-building city of Cahokia to the pueblos of the Southwest and the confederacies of the Northeast. From the sixteenth century, Spanish, French, Dutch and British colonisation brought epidemics, warfare and dispossession, while millions of Africans were enslaved on plantations. Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776, and the new republic expanded westward through purchase, war with Mexico and the forced removal of Native peoples such as the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears. The Civil War of 1861–1865 ended slavery, but segregation and racial terror endured until the civil rights movement won landmark laws in the 1960s. Waves of immigration, industrial growth and two world wars made the United States a global power whose story still holds both soaring ideals and unfinished justice.
summary.politicalHistory: The colonies declared independence in 1776 and, after the weak Articles of Confederation, adopted a federal Constitution in 1787, with George Washington taking office as the first president in 1789 and the Bill of Rights added in 1791. The Civil War preserved the Union, and the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments abolished slavery and promised citizenship and voting rights regardless of race. Women won the vote nationally in 1920, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 began to make equal rights real for Black Americans. Today the United States is a federal presidential republic of 50 states with a bicameral Congress, an independent judiciary and a long-dominant two-party system.
summary.art: Jazz, blues, gospel, country, rock and roll and hip-hop, many born in African American communities, transformed music worldwide through figures such as Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Mahalia Jackson and Johnny Cash. American literature runs from Emily Dickinson, Herman Melville and Mark Twain to Langston Hughes, William Faulkner and Toni Morrison, while Hollywood shaped the language of modern cinema. Quilting, Native pottery and beadwork, and painters such as Georgia O'Keeffe and Jackson Pollock show the range of its visual arts.
summary.monuments: The Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor, a gift from France, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and an enduring symbol of welcome to immigrants. Independence Hall in Philadelphia, where the Declaration of Independence and Constitution were adopted, is also UNESCO-listed, as are the ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, the great mounds of Cahokia and Taos Pueblo. Natural wonders such as Yellowstone, the world's first national park, and the Grand Canyon are as central to the national story as the Lincoln Memorial in Washington.

highlights.title: New York City
highlights.line: Walk Central Park, cross the Brooklyn Bridge and spend a morning at the Metropolitan Museum; a 7-day subway pass makes getting around easy.

highlights.title: Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island
highlights.line: Take the official ferry to see Lady Liberty and the museum where some 12 million immigrants were processed; book pedestal or crown tickets well ahead.

highlights.title: Washington, D.C.
highlights.line: The Smithsonian museums are free; reserve timed passes for the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

highlights.title: Independence Hall, Philadelphia
highlights.line: See where the Declaration and Constitution were signed, then the Liberty Bell nearby; free timed tickets are needed in busy seasons.

highlights.title: Boston's Freedom Trail
highlights.line: A red-brick line leads 4 kilometres past sixteen Revolutionary-era sites; finish with seafood chowder in the North End.

highlights.title: Grand Canyon
highlights.line: Watch sunrise from the South Rim and walk part of the Bright Angel Trail; an annual national parks pass pays off on a multi-park trip.

highlights.title: Yellowstone
highlights.line: Old Faithful, rainbow hot springs and roaming bison fill the first national park; stay on boardwalks and keep a wide distance from wildlife.

highlights.title: Yosemite
highlights.line: Granite walls, giant sequoias and waterfalls peak in spring; check whether entry reservations are required when you visit.

highlights.title: Zion and Bryce Canyon
highlights.line: Hike the river through the Narrows in Zion, then see Bryce's hoodoos glow at sunrise; Angels Landing needs a permit.

highlights.title: Monument Valley
highlights.line: Red sandstone buttes stand on Navajo Nation land; take a Navajo-guided tour to go beyond the scenic drive and learn the stories.

highlights.title: Powwows
highlights.line: Gatherings like the Gathering of Nations in Albuquerque celebrate Native dance, drumming and regalia; ask before taking photos.

highlights.title: Santa Fe and Taos Pueblo
highlights.line: Adobe streets, Native and Hispano art and green chile define northern New Mexico; Taos Pueblo has been lived in for about a thousand years.

highlights.title: Route 66
highlights.line: The old 'Mother Road' from Chicago to Santa Monica passes neon motels and small-town diners; drive a stretch through Arizona or New Mexico.

highlights.title: Chicago
highlights.line: Take an architecture river cruise past pioneering skyscrapers, then try deep-dish pizza and see the Art Institute's collection.

highlights.title: New Orleans
highlights.line: Hear live jazz on Frenchmen Street, eat beignets at dawn and gumbo at night, and visit the city's historic churches and cemeteries with a guide.

highlights.title: Memphis and the Mississippi Delta
highlights.line: Walk Beale Street for the blues and visit the National Civil Rights Museum at the Lorraine Motel, where Martin Luther King Jr. was killed.

highlights.title: Nashville
highlights.line: Catch a show at the Ryman Auditorium or the Grand Ole Opry; many honky-tonks on Broadway have free live music all day.

highlights.title: Civil rights trail in Alabama
highlights.line: In Montgomery visit the Legacy Museum and the National Memorial for Peace and Justice, then cross the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma.

highlights.title: Gospel Sunday in Harlem
highlights.line: Joining a historic Black church service is a moving experience; dress respectfully and stay for the whole service rather than leaving midway.

highlights.title: Texas barbecue
highlights.line: Central Texas smokes brisket low and slow; arrive early at famed pits in Austin or Lockhart before the meat sells out.

highlights.title: San Antonio Missions
highlights.line: Four Spanish colonial missions and the Alamo form a UNESCO site; cycle the river trail between them.

highlights.title: Pacific Coast Highway and Big Sur
highlights.line: Cliffs drop into the Pacific on one of the world's great drives; check for road closures from landslides before you go.

highlights.title: San Francisco
highlights.line: Ride a cable car, walk across the Golden Gate Bridge and eat your way through the Mission District; bring layers for the fog.

highlights.title: Redwood forests
highlights.line: Walk among the tallest trees on Earth in Redwood National and State Parks or Muir Woods, which requires parking reservations.

highlights.title: Hawaiʻi
highlights.line: See active volcanoes in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, learn a little ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi and treat sacred sites and reefs with care.

highlights.title: Alaska
highlights.line: Glaciers, Denali and brown bears await; travel in summer and consider the Inside Passage by ferry or ship.

highlights.title: Great Smoky Mountains
highlights.line: The most-visited national park offers misty ridges and wildflowers; entry is free but parked cars need a parking tag.

highlights.title: Blue Ridge Parkway
highlights.line: This slow, scenic road through the Appalachians is glorious in October foliage; stop for bluegrass and mountain crafts.

highlights.title: New England in autumn
highlights.line: Maple forests turn scarlet and gold from late September; stay in Vermont or New Hampshire villages and try fresh apple cider.

highlights.title: Everglades
highlights.line: Walk the Anhinga Trail to see alligators and wading birds at close range, best in the drier winter months.

highlights.title: Pacific Northwest
highlights.line: Visit Seattle's Pike Place Market, then the rainforests and wild beaches of Olympic National Park.

highlights.title: A baseball game
highlights.line: An afternoon at Fenway Park or Wrigley Field, with a hot dog and the seventh-inning stretch, is a beloved American ritual.

highlights.title: Thanksgiving and diner culture
highlights.line: If invited to a Thanksgiving meal, bring a dish or dessert; any time of year, a classic diner breakfast with pie and coffee is pure Americana.

funFacts: Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park.
The United States has 63 national parks, and California has more of them than any other state.
The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars.
Alaska has more coastline than all the other states combined.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaiʻi is taller than Mount Everest.
Death Valley holds the record for the highest air temperature officially recorded on Earth, 56.7 °C in 1913.
The General Sherman tree, a giant sequoia in California, is the largest known living tree by volume.
A coast redwood named Hyperion, about 116 metres tall, is the tallest known living tree.
The Great Lakes, shared with Canada, hold about a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.
The United States has more tornadoes than any other country, more than a thousand in a typical year.
Hawaiian is an official language of the state of Hawaiʻi alongside English.
More than 350 languages are spoken in American homes.
Spanish-founded St. Augustine, Florida, established in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the continental United States.
Around the year 1100, Cahokia near present-day St. Louis was a city of many thousands, larger than most European towns of the time.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France, dedicated in 1886, and its copper skin turned green as it weathered.
Ellis Island processed around 12 million immigrants between 1892 and 1954.
The US Constitution, drafted in 1787, is the oldest written national constitution still in use.
Wyoming became the first territory to grant women the right to vote, in 1869.
Navajo Code Talkers used their language to transmit military messages in the Second World War, and their code was never broken.
Juneteenth, a federal holiday since 2021, marks 19 June 1865, when news of freedom reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas.
Thanksgiving has been fixed on the fourth Thursday of November since 1941.
The Library of Congress is one of the largest libraries in the world, with well over 170 million items.
Most Smithsonian museums in Washington, D.C. are free to enter.
New York City's subway runs 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
The Golden Gate Bridge is painted a colour called International Orange, chosen partly to stand out in fog.
Jazz was born in New Orleans in the early twentieth century, blending blues, ragtime, brass bands and spirituals.
The chocolate chip cookie was invented in the 1930s by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts.
In 1969 Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon.
There are 574 federally recognised American Indian and Alaska Native tribes, each with its own government.
The Mississippi River drains all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces.
Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area.
The Grand Canyon is about 446 kilometres long and in places more than 1.8 kilometres deep.
Mesa Verde in Colorado preserves around 600 cliff dwellings built by Ancestral Puebloans.

languageGuide.intro: American English has no formal 'you', so politeness comes through 'please', 'thank you', a friendly tone and, especially in the South, 'sir' and 'ma'am'; 'How are you?' is often just a greeting, answered with 'Good, thanks, and you?'. Words differ from British English (check, restroom, elevator, to go), and Spanish is widely spoken in the Southwest, Florida and many big cities.

culture.history: Hundreds of Indigenous nations lived across the continent before European colonisation, which brought war, disease and dispossession. Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776 and founded a republic whose ideals of liberty coexisted with the enslavement of millions of Africans and their descendants. A civil war from 1861 to 1865 ended slavery, but segregation and racial violence persisted until the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s won landmark legislation. Waves of immigration and two world wars made the nation a global power.
culture.politics: The United States is a federal presidential republic of 50 states, with power divided among the president, a bicameral Congress and an independent Supreme Court. Its written constitution and Bill of Rights, among the oldest in force, emphasise checks and balances. The balance between federal and state power, and the reach of civil rights, are enduring civic themes.
culture.arts: Jazz, blues, gospel, country, rock and hip-hop, many rooted in African American creativity, transformed global music. Its literature runs from Melville, Dickinson and Twain to Faulkner and Toni Morrison, and Hollywood shaped modern cinema. In architecture, the skyscraper and Frank Lloyd Wright's organic designs left lasting marks.

love.expression: Affection is often spoken openly, with 'love you' said freely among family and close friends, and encouragement is generously given. Love is also shown through practical help and time together, with great variety across regions, faiths and the many cultures that make up the country.

etiquette: Tip around 15–20% at sit-down restaurants and for many services.
Be punctual; arriving on time is a sign of respect.
Small talk is friendly and expected, but personal space is valued.

name: Canada

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. some 70 Indigenous languages and many immigrant languages

people: Most Canadians live in cities within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, in a deeply multicultural society where nearly a quarter of people were born abroad; English- and French-speaking communities sit alongside First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples (about 5%). In the 2021 census about 53% identified as Christian (largely Catholic), about 35% reported no religion, and Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Jewish communities are well established, especially around Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal.

plug.note: Same plugs as the US; UK, EU and Australian travellers need an adapter, and devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Vast fresh water, forests and hydroelectric power
Energy and critical minerals (oil, uranium, potash, nickel)
Prairie farmland — wheat, canola and pulses
Indigenous knowledge, languages and land stewardship
A highly educated, multicultural workforce shaped by immigration
Wilderness and national parks of world renown
struggles: Housing that has become unaffordable for many, especially young people and newcomers
The unfinished work of reconciliation with Indigenous peoples, including the legacy of residential schools and unsafe drinking water on some reserves
A toxic-drug and opioid crisis that has taken tens of thousands of lives
Record wildfire seasons, melting permafrost and other climate pressures in the North
Long waits for family doctors and hospital care
Rising cost of living and food-bank use
prayFor: For survivors of residential schools and their families, and for honest, patient reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians
For young people and newcomers seeking an affordable home and a place to belong
For all who are caught in addiction, and for the families, outreach workers and nurses who keep showing up for them
For firefighters, northern communities and all whose land is changing under a warming climate
For doctors, nurses and caregivers stretched thin, and for patients waiting for care

summary.history: First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples have lived across these lands for thousands of years, in societies as varied as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the fishing nations of the Pacific coast and the Inuit of the Arctic, and Norse voyagers briefly settled at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000 CE. French and British colonisation from the 1500s was built on the fur trade and on treaties and alliances with Indigenous nations, and Britain took control of New France in 1763. Confederation in 1867 joined the colonies into a dominion that pushed westward with the railway, while the Indian Act, broken treaty promises and more than a century of residential schools inflicted deep harm on Indigenous peoples. Canadians fought in both World Wars, built a welfare state and, from the 1960s, welcomed immigrants from around the world, and the 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission has set much of the country's present moral agenda.
summary.politicalHistory: The British North America Act of 1867 created a federation of four provinces, which grew to ten provinces and three territories, the newest being Nunavut in 1999. Canada gained legislative independence with the Statute of Westminster in 1931 and patriated its constitution in 1982, adding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Quebec held sovereignty referendums in 1980 and 1995, the second rejected by a margin of about one percentage point. Today Canada is a federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with the Crown represented by a Governor General and government formed by whoever holds the confidence of the elected House of Commons.
summary.art: Inuit stone carving and printmaking, the totem poles and formline art of Northwest Coast nations, and Métis beadwork are among the country's most distinctive traditions. The Group of Seven, Tom Thomson and Emily Carr gave the northern and coastal landscape a painted voice, while writers such as Lucy Maud Montgomery, Gabrielle Roy, Margaret Atwood and Alice Munro are read worldwide. In music, Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell, Buffy Sainte-Marie and Quebec's chansonniers like Félix Leclerc shaped generations.
summary.monuments: Old Quebec, the only walled city north of Mexico, and the Rideau Canal in Ottawa are UNESCO World Heritage Sites that tell the story of colonial settlement and nation-building. L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland preserves the earliest known European settlement in the Americas, and SGang Gwaay on Haida Gwaii guards weathered Haida mortuary poles. Parliament Hill in Ottawa and Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, where Plains peoples hunted bison for millennia, round out a heritage that is both Indigenous and settler.

highlights.title: Banff & the Icefields Parkway
highlights.line: Turquoise lakes like Louise and Moraine sit beneath the Rockies; drive the Icefields Parkway to Jasper and book the Moraine Lake shuttle in summer, as private cars are no longer allowed.

highlights.title: Jasper Dark Sky Preserve
highlights.line: One of the world's largest dark-sky preserves; come for the October Dark Sky Festival and pack warm layers.

highlights.title: Stanley Park, Vancouver
highlights.line: Cycle the 9 km seawall past totem poles at Brockton Point, then eat your way through Granville Island Public Market.

highlights.title: Haida Gwaii
highlights.line: The 'islands of the people' hold living Haida culture and the UNESCO site SGang Gwaay; visits to Gwaii Haanas need a reservation and orientation.

highlights.title: Tofino & Pacific Rim
highlights.line: Wild surf beaches and old-growth rainforest on Vancouver Island; winter storm-watching is a local ritual.

highlights.title: Okanagan Valley
highlights.line: Lakeside vineyards and orchards in British Columbia's desert-like south; visit in late summer for peaches and the harvest.

highlights.title: Royal Tyrrell Museum, Drumheller
highlights.line: One of the world's great dinosaur museums, set in Alberta's eerie badlands among hoodoo rock pillars.

highlights.title: Calgary Stampede
highlights.line: Ten July days of rodeo, chuckwagon races and free pancake breakfasts; the Elbow River Camp shares First Nations culture.

highlights.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
highlights.line: A UNESCO site where Blackfoot peoples hunted bison for some 6,000 years; the interpretive centre is built into the cliff.

highlights.title: Polar bears in Churchill
highlights.line: In October and November bears gather on Hudson Bay's shore; in summer you can kayak among thousands of beluga whales.

highlights.title: Canadian Museum for Human Rights, Winnipeg
highlights.line: A striking building that tells hard stories honestly, including residential schools; allow at least three hours.

highlights.title: Qaumajuq, Winnipeg Art Gallery
highlights.line: Home to the world's largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art, shown in a luminous glass vault.

highlights.title: Northern lights in Yellowknife
highlights.line: Clear winter skies make this one of the best aurora spots on Earth; go between late November and early April.

highlights.title: Dawson City, Yukon
highlights.line: A Klondike Gold Rush town of boardwalks and false-front saloons; in June the sun barely sets.

highlights.title: Niagara Falls
highlights.line: Ride the boat into the mist of Horseshoe Falls, then escape the crowds in the wineries of Niagara-on-the-Lake.

highlights.title: St. Lawrence Market, Toronto
highlights.line: Try the classic peameal bacon sandwich, then explore Kensington Market and the Art Gallery of Ontario.

highlights.title: Algonquin Provincial Park
highlights.line: Paddle a canoe across glassy lakes and listen for loons; the maples blaze red in late September.

highlights.title: Parliament Hill & the Rideau Canal
highlights.line: Ottawa's UNESCO-listed canal becomes a 7.8 km skating rink in winter — buy a BeaverTail pastry on the ice.

highlights.title: Old Quebec
highlights.line: Walk the walls and cobbled lanes beneath Château Frontenac, and come in February for the Winter Carnival.

highlights.title: Montreal food & Mount Royal
highlights.line: Compare Fairmount and St-Viateur bagels, try smoked meat, then climb Mount Royal for the view.

highlights.title: Saint Joseph's Oratory, Montreal
highlights.line: Canada's largest church, founded by St André Bessette; pilgrims still climb the central stairs on their knees.

highlights.title: Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré
highlights.line: A great basilica and pilgrimage site east of Quebec City, beloved for centuries by French-Canadian and Mi'kmaq faithful.

highlights.title: Notre-Dame-du-Cap, Trois-Rivières
highlights.line: Canada's national Marian shrine, with a small 18th-century stone church beside a large modern basilica on the St Lawrence.

highlights.title: Cabane à sucre
highlights.line: In March and April, sugar shacks in Quebec serve feasts of pea soup, ham and maple taffy rolled on snow.

highlights.title: Whales at Tadoussac
highlights.line: Where the Saguenay Fjord meets the St Lawrence, minke, fin and beluga whales feed from June to October.

highlights.title: Bay of Fundy
highlights.line: Walk the ocean floor around the Hopewell Rocks at low tide, then watch the world's highest tides return.

highlights.title: Cabot Trail, Cape Breton
highlights.line: A coastal loop of highlands and fiddle music; catch a ceilidh and the Celtic Colours festival in October.

highlights.title: Lunenburg
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed, brightly painted fishing town in Nova Scotia and home port of the schooner Bluenose II.

highlights.title: Prince Edward Island
highlights.line: Red-sand beaches, Green Gables and summer lobster suppers in church halls.

highlights.title: Gros Morne National Park
highlights.line: Fjords and exposed Earth's mantle rock in western Newfoundland; hike or take a boat on Western Brook Pond.

highlights.title: L'Anse aux Meadows
highlights.line: Stand where Norse sailors built sod houses a thousand years ago, at the northern tip of Newfoundland.

highlights.title: Icebergs off St. John's
highlights.line: From May to June, icebergs drift past Signal Hill; end the night with music on George Street.

highlights.title: Poutine
highlights.line: Fries, squeaky cheese curds and gravy — born in rural Quebec, best eaten late at night from a casse-croûte.

funFacts: Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world, more than 240,000 km including its islands.
Canada is the second-largest country on Earth by area, after Russia.
The border between Canada and the United States, about 8,900 km long, is the longest international border in the world.
The Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, with a range that can exceed 15 m.
Canada is thought to contain more lakes than any other country.
Insulin was first isolated for treating diabetes in Toronto in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best.
Basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith, in 1891 — though he did it while teaching in Massachusetts.
Canada Post gives Santa Claus the postal code H0H 0H0, and volunteers answer letters sent to him.
Quebec produces roughly 70% of the world's maple syrup.
The name Canada is thought to come from the Huron-Iroquois word kanata, meaning village or settlement.
Nunavut, created in 1999, is Canada's largest territory and has Inuktut as one of its official languages.
Alert, Nunavut, is the northernmost permanently inhabited place in the world.
Mount Logan in the Yukon, at about 5,959 m, is Canada's highest peak.
Canada spans six time zones, including Newfoundland's, which is offset by half an hour.
Newfoundland only joined Canada in 1949.
The maple leaf flag was adopted in 1965.
The one-dollar coin is nicknamed the loonie after the loon on it, and the two-dollar coin became the toonie.
The Hawaiian pizza was invented in Chatham, Ontario, in 1962 by Greek-Canadian restaurateur Sam Panopoulos.
Toronto's CN Tower was the world's tallest freestanding structure for more than three decades.
Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron is the largest island in a freshwater lake anywhere in the world.
Wood Buffalo National Park is larger than Switzerland and contains what is believed to be the world's longest beaver dam.
By law, lacrosse is Canada's national summer sport and ice hockey its national winter sport.
Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857.
Canada's motto, A mari usque ad mare, means 'From sea to sea'.
The Canadarm robotic arm, built in Canada, flew on NASA's Space Shuttles for 30 years.
In the 2021 census, Canadians reported speaking more than 70 Indigenous languages.
Churchill, Manitoba, is often called the polar bear capital of the world.
Dinosaur Provincial Park in Alberta has yielded fossils of dozens of dinosaur species and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Quebec City's Hôtel de Glace is rebuilt from ice and snow every winter.
Canada holds about a fifth of the world's fresh water, though a much smaller share is renewable each year.
The Trans Canada Trail is one of the world's longest networks of recreational trails, at around 28,000 km.
Canada has two official languages, English and French, and New Brunswick is its only officially bilingual province.
The Rideau Canal, opened in 1832, is the oldest continuously operated canal system in North America.

languageGuide.intro: English is the everyday language across most of Canada, but in Quebec and parts of New Brunswick and Ontario, French comes first — opening with 'Bonjour' and using the polite 'vous' with strangers is warmly received, and many people will switch to English if you ask. Quebec French has its own sounds and words: 'tu' is often pronounced 'tsu', 'dîner' means lunch, 'souper' means dinner, and 'bienvenue' is the usual reply to 'merci'.
