culture.history: First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples have lived on the land for millennia, and French and British colonisation began in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with Britain gaining New France in 1763. Confederation in 1867 created the Dominion of Canada, which gained full control of its constitution in 1982. For over a century the state ran residential schools that separated Indigenous children from their families, a harm the Truth and Reconciliation Commission described in 2015 as cultural genocide. Large-scale immigration has made Canada one of the world's most multicultural societies.
culture.politics: Canada is a federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with ten provinces and three territories. Government is formed by the party with the confidence of the elected House of Commons, alongside an appointed Senate, and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects fundamental rights. Bilingualism, Quebec's distinct place and reconciliation with Indigenous peoples are defining civic themes.
culture.arts: Inuit sculpture and printmaking and the art of Northwest Coast nations are among its most distinctive traditions. The Group of Seven painters gave the northern landscape a national voice, and writers such as Margaret Atwood, Alice Munro and Michael Ondaatje are read worldwide. Leonard Cohen and Joni Mitchell shaped songwriting for generations.

love.expression: Affection tends to be friendly, considerate and unassuming, often expressed by helping a neighbour or showing up with food in hard times. Time outdoors, at the cottage or around a hockey rink, is a common shape for closeness, with distinct styles in Quebec, the Prairies, the Atlantic and Indigenous communities.

etiquette: In Quebec, start with bonjour; a little French is warmly received.
Tip around 15–20% at restaurants.
Use the names First Nations, Inuit and Métis respectfully and accurately.

name: Australia

languages.note: ≈ living languages, incl. some 120 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages (many endangered, a handful still learned by children), Kriol and many immigrant languages

people: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples — around 3.8% of the population — belong to hundreds of distinct nations with the oldest continuous cultures on Earth, while nearly a third of Australians were born overseas, especially in England, India, China, New Zealand and the Philippines. Most people live in a handful of coastal cities, above all Sydney and Melbourne; in the 2021 census about 44% identified as Christian, about 39% reported no religion, and Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and Jewish communities are growing.

plug.note: Angled two- or three-pin Type I sockets, often with a switch; UK, EU and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Iron ore, coal, lithium, gold and natural gas
Abundant sun and wind for a renewable-energy future
The living cultures and land knowledge of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
The Great Barrier Reef and other unique ecosystems
Agriculture — wheat, beef, wool and wine
World-class universities and a multicultural population
struggles: Deep gaps in health, life expectancy, incarceration and opportunity faced by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
Housing that is among the least affordable in the world
Bushfires, floods, drought and coral bleaching made more severe by a warming climate
Lingering division after the 2023 referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament
Limited access to health care and services in remote and rural communities
Cost-of-living pressure on families
prayFor: For healing, justice and self-determination for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, and for listening hearts on all sides
For farmers, firefighters and towns facing fire, flood and drought
For families struggling to find a secure, affordable home
For the protection of the reef, the bush and the creatures found nowhere else
For people in remote places to have the care, schools and connection they need

summary.history: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on this continent and its islands for at least 50,000 years, caring for Country through songlines, law and land management such as cultural burning. Dutch sailors charted parts of the coast from 1606, and in 1788 Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney Cove, claiming land it called empty. Colonisation brought disease, dispossession and frontier violence, and from the late 1800s into the 1970s many Aboriginal children were taken from their families — the Stolen Generations, for whom the nation formally apologised in 2008. Gold rushes, wool and later mass migration from Europe and Asia built a prosperous, diverse nation that continues to grapple with recognising its first peoples.
summary.politicalHistory: Six self-governing British colonies federated on 1 January 1901 to form the Commonwealth of Australia under a written constitution. Ties to Britain loosened through the Statute of Westminster (adopted in 1942) and the Australia Act of 1986, while a 1967 referendum allowed Aboriginal people to be counted in the census and covered by federal laws. Voters rejected becoming a republic in 1999 and rejected an Indigenous Voice to Parliament in 2023. Australia is a federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy with compulsory voting, six states and two self-governing mainland territories.
summary.art: Aboriginal rock art at sites like Ubirr and Murujuga is among the oldest art on Earth, and the Western Desert dot-painting movement, born at Papunya in 1971, brought artists such as Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri and Emily Kame Kngwarreye to the world. Painters of the Heidelberg School like Tom Roberts and Frederick McCubbin shaped a national image of the bush, and writers Henry Lawson, Miles Franklin, Patrick White and Oodgeroo Noonuccal gave it words. From didgeridoo (yidaki) and bush ballads to Yothu Yindi and Archie Roach, music has carried both celebration and lament.
summary.monuments: The Sydney Opera House, a UNESCO site since 2007, is the country's most recognisable building. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa and Kakadu national parks are listed for both their natural wonder and their living Aboriginal cultural landscapes, and Budj Bim in Victoria preserves eel traps the Gunditjmara built thousands of years ago. The Australian Convict Sites, including Port Arthur, and the Australian War Memorial in Canberra tell harder chapters of the national story.

highlights.title: Uluṟu
highlights.line: Walk the 10 km base loop at dawn with an Aṉangu-led tour; climbing has been banned since 2019 out of respect for the rock's sacred meaning.

highlights.title: Kata Tjuṯa
highlights.line: Thirty-six red domes near Uluṟu; hike the Valley of the Winds early before the heat closes the trail.

highlights.title: Sydney Opera House
highlights.line: Take a backstage tour or catch any performance, then sit on the steps as ferries cross the harbour.

highlights.title: Bondi to Coogee walk
highlights.line: A 6 km cliff-top coastal path past ocean pools and beaches; swim between the red-and-yellow flags.

highlights.title: Blue Mountains
highlights.line: Eucalyptus haze turns the valleys blue; see the Three Sisters at Echo Point and learn their Gundungurra story.

highlights.title: Great Barrier Reef
highlights.line: Snorkel or dive from Cairns or Port Douglas, choosing an eco-certified operator and reef-safe sunscreen.

highlights.title: Daintree Rainforest
highlights.line: Ancient rainforest meets the reef at Cape Tribulation; join a Kuku Yalanji guide at Mossman Gorge.

highlights.title: Kakadu National Park
highlights.line: See rock art at Ubirr and Nourlangie and cruise Yellow Water among crocodiles; best in the dry season, May to October.

highlights.title: Mindil Beach Sunset Market, Darwin
highlights.line: Dry-season Thursday and Sunday evenings of laksa, crafts and a tropical sunset over the Timor Sea.

highlights.title: Purnululu (Bungle Bungles)
highlights.line: Striped beehive domes in the Kimberley, best seen on a scenic flight; access is by 4WD only.

highlights.title: Ningaloo Reef
highlights.line: Swim with whale sharks from about March to July, a short reach from Exmouth's beaches.

highlights.title: Rottnest Island
highlights.line: Cycle car-free bays near Perth and meet the quokkas — but don't touch or feed them.

highlights.title: Kings Park, Perth
highlights.line: One of the world's largest inner-city parks, with spring wildflowers and views over the Swan River.

highlights.title: Margaret River
highlights.line: Surf breaks, limestone caves and some of the country's finest wineries in Western Australia's south-west.

highlights.title: Great Ocean Road
highlights.line: Drive past the Twelve Apostles sea stacks at sunset, and look for koalas in the trees at Kennett River.

highlights.title: Melbourne laneways & coffee
highlights.line: Hunt down street art in Hosier Lane and order a flat white — Melbourne takes its coffee seriously.

highlights.title: A footy game at the MCG
highlights.line: Watch Australian rules football with 90,000 fans at the Melbourne Cricket Ground; pie and sauce compulsory.

highlights.title: Phillip Island Penguin Parade
highlights.line: At dusk, little penguins waddle ashore to their burrows; photography is not allowed, so just watch.

highlights.title: Budj Bim
highlights.line: A UNESCO site where the Gunditjmara engineered stone eel traps thousands of years ago; book a guided tour.

highlights.title: Grampians (Gariwerd)
highlights.line: Sandstone peaks, waterfalls and rock-art shelters; start at the Brambuk cultural centre in Halls Gap.

highlights.title: Cradle Mountain
highlights.line: Walk the Dove Lake circuit in Tasmania's wilderness and look for wombats at dusk.

highlights.title: MONA, Hobart
highlights.line: A provocative underground art museum reached by ferry up the Derwent; pair it with Salamanca Market on Saturday.

highlights.title: Port Arthur Historic Site
highlights.line: A UNESCO convict site whose ruins tell of punishment and survival; the evening ghost tour is popular.

highlights.title: Barossa Valley
highlights.line: German-settled wine country near Adelaide famous for shiraz, bakeries and long lunches.

highlights.title: Kangaroo Island
highlights.line: Sea lions on the beach at Seal Bay and wildlife recovering after the 2019–20 fires.

highlights.title: Coober Pedy
highlights.line: An opal-mining town where many people live underground to escape the heat; stay in a dugout hotel.

highlights.title: K'gari (Fraser Island)
highlights.line: The world's largest sand island, with freshwater lakes like Lake McKenzie; drive the beach by 4WD.

highlights.title: Whitehaven Beach, Whitsundays
highlights.line: Silica sand so fine it squeaks; sail the islands and check for stinger season (roughly November to May).

highlights.title: Canberra
highlights.line: Visit the Australian War Memorial's Last Post ceremony at closing time and the National Gallery's Aboriginal art.

highlights.title: Cape Byron
highlights.line: Walk to the most easterly point of the mainland and watch humpback whales pass from June to November.

highlights.title: Mary MacKillop Place, North Sydney
highlights.line: Pray at the tomb of St Mary MacKillop, Australia's first canonised saint, who founded schools for poor children.

highlights.title: Sausage sizzle & meat pie
highlights.line: A sausage in bread with onions outside a hardware store or polling booth is a beloved Australian ritual.

highlights.title: Bush tucker
highlights.line: Taste native foods like wattleseed, lemon myrtle, finger lime and quandong, ideally on an Indigenous-led experience.

funFacts: Australia is the only country that occupies an entire continent on its own.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures are among the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth, stretching back at least 50,000 years.
The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching for about 2,300 km.
Australia has more than 10,000 beaches.
The Dingo Fence, at more than 5,500 km, is one of the longest fences in the world.
The platypus and echidnas, both found in Australia, are the only living mammals that lay eggs.
A group of kangaroos is called a mob.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings.
Koalas sleep for around 18 to 22 hours a day.
In 1894 South Australia gave women the vote and became the first place in the world to let women stand for parliament.
Voting in federal elections has been compulsory since 1924.
Canberra was purpose-built as the capital, designed by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin.
The Dutch navigator Willem Janszoon made the first recorded European landing on Australia in 1606.
Rottnest Island's name comes from Dutch for 'rat's nest', because explorer Willem de Vlamingh mistook quokkas for giant rats.
The flight 'black box' recorder was invented by Australian scientist David Warren.
Australian-born Howard Florey shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for turning penicillin into a usable medicine.
Australia issued the world's first polymer banknotes in 1988.
Australia has many more sheep than people.
Lake Hillier in Western Australia is naturally bubblegum pink.
Australia is the driest inhabited continent.
Mount Kosciuszko, at 2,228 m, is the highest peak on the Australian mainland.
Australia produces the vast majority of the world's precious opal.
When the British arrived there were more than 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, many with several dialects.
Nearly a third of people living in Australia were born overseas.
Uluṟu rises about 348 m above the surrounding plain, and much more of the rock lies underground.
Lord Howe Island limits the number of tourists on the island at any one time to around 400.
Anna Creek Station in South Australia is the largest working cattle station in the world.
Australia claims about 42% of Antarctica, the largest claim of any country.
The Melbourne Cup, first run in 1861, is known as 'the race that stops a nation' and is a public holiday in Melbourne.
The Royal Flying Doctor Service, founded in 1928, brings medical care by plane to remote Australia.
Children on remote stations have long studied through the School of the Air, first by radio and now online.
Scientists at Australia's CSIRO developed a key technology behind fast Wi-Fi.
K'gari (Fraser Island) is the largest sand island in the world.

languageGuide.language: Australian English (with Aboriginal words of welcome)
languageGuide.intro: Australians speak English with a relaxed, friendly tone, shortening words ('arvo' for afternoon, 'brekkie' for breakfast) and using first names almost immediately; 'mate' is used with everyone and irony is part of the fun. There are hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, each belonging to a particular Country, so a greeting in the local language of the place you are visiting is a lovely gesture of respect — but use it only there, and learn more from local communities.

phrases.en: Hello — Noongar language, Perth & south-west WA
Hello / good — Western Desert languages, e.g. around Uluṟu
It's your turn to buy the drinks

culture.history: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for the continent for tens of thousands of years, forming one of the oldest continuous cultures on earth. British colonisation began with a penal settlement in 1788, bringing dispossession, frontier violence and disease. The six colonies federated in 1901, and for decades policies removed Aboriginal children from their families, the Stolen Generations, for which the nation formally apologised in 2008. Post-war migration from Europe and later Asia transformed the country into a diverse society.
culture.politics: Australia is a federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy of six states and two territories. Government is formed in the elected House of Representatives, with a powerful elected Senate, and voting is compulsory. Recognition of First Nations peoples, including the defeated 2023 referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, remains a defining civic conversation.
culture.arts: Aboriginal art, from ancient rock painting to the acrylic dot painting movement begun at Papunya in the 1970s, is among the world's oldest living art traditions. Jørn Utzon's Sydney Opera House is a modern architectural icon. Patrick White won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and figures such as the painter Albert Namatjira and the singer Archie Roach carry Indigenous voices into the national story.

love.expression: Affection often comes wrapped in humour, gentle teasing and easygoing loyalty, with 'mateship' prizing reliability in good times and hard ones. Love is shown in shared barbecues, beach days and practical help, with diverse styles across a multicultural population and First Nations communities.

etiquette: A casual, first-name manner is normal; avoid seeming pretentious.
Shout your round at the pub when it is your turn.
Respect Acknowledgements of Country and sites of cultural significance, such as Uluṟu.

name: Philippines

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, Waray and many Indigenous languages

people: Filipinos belong to dozens of ethnolinguistic groups — Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, Bisaya, Bikolano, Moro peoples such as the Maranao and Tausug, and Indigenous peoples like the Ifugao and T'boli — with Chinese-Filipino and Spanish-descended families woven through the nation's history. About 80% are Catholic, with Muslims (around 6%, mostly in Mindanao), Iglesia ni Cristo, evangelical and other Christian communities making up most of the rest. Roughly half live in cities, above all Metro Manila, and some ten million Filipinos live or work abroad, sustaining families at home with their remittances.

plug.note: US flat-pin plugs usually fit, but US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter for 220 V; UK and European travellers need an adapter.

resources: Some of the richest marine biodiversity on Earth, at the heart of the Coral Triangle
A young, English-speaking workforce and a global community of nurses, seafarers and caregivers
Fertile volcanic soils for rice, coconuts, bananas and mangoes
Nickel, copper and gold
Geothermal energy, among the largest capacities in the world
Deep faith, family bonds and the spirit of bayanihan (communal help)
struggles: Persistent poverty and inequality between Metro Manila and rural provinces
Some twenty typhoons a year plus earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, intensified by climate change
Families separated for years by overseas work
Human-rights concerns, including thousands of killings linked to the anti-drug campaign
A fragile peace transition in Bangsamoro and lingering insurgency in some regions
Tensions in the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea) that endanger fishers' livelihoods
prayFor: For the families of overseas workers — for safe journeys, fair employers and joyful reunions
For communities rebuilding after typhoons and floods, and for those who live on the coasts and slopes most at risk
For the poor in city slums and farming villages to have dignified work, food and schooling
For grieving families seeking justice and healing, and for a culture that protects every life
For lasting peace in Mindanao between Muslims, Christians and Indigenous peoples

summary.history: Austronesian seafarers settled the islands thousands of years ago, forming barangay communities and sultanates that traded with China, Southeast Asia and the Islamic world, while Islam took root in Sulu and Mindanao from the 14th century. Ferdinand Magellan's 1521 arrival was followed from 1565 by more than three centuries of Spanish rule, which spread Catholicism but also brought forced labour and the exploitation of land. The 1896 revolution against Spain was overtaken by the 1898 Spanish–American War and a brutal Philippine–American War, then American colonial rule and a devastating Japanese occupation in World War II, in which Manila was largely destroyed. Since independence in 1946 the nation has endured dictatorship, poverty and conflict in Mindanao, but also the peaceful People Power uprising of 1986 and the vast outward migration that links Filipinos to every corner of the world.
summary.politicalHistory: Revolutionaries declared independence from Spain on 12 June 1898 and established the Malolos Republic, often called Asia's first constitutional republic, but the United States took control after the Philippine–American War. A self-governing Commonwealth was created in 1935 and full independence came on 4 July 1946. Ferdinand Marcos declared martial law in 1972 and ruled by decree until the nonviolent People Power Revolution of 1986 restored democracy, enshrined in the 1987 Constitution. The Philippines is now a presidential, unitary republic with a bicameral Congress and the autonomous Bangsamoro region in Mindanao.
summary.art: Indigenous weaving such as the T'boli t'nalak and Ifugao textiles, Maranao okir carving and the gong music of kulintang ensembles reflect pre-colonial artistry. Under Spain and after, painters Juan Luna and Fernando Amorsolo and the novelist-hero José Rizal, whose Noli Me Tángere stirred the revolution, shaped a national identity. Filipinos are famed singers, from kundiman love songs and Lucio San Pedro's lullabies to today's OPM (Original Pilipino Music) and the karaoke found in almost every home.
summary.monuments: The Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras, carved by Ifugao communities, are a UNESCO site still farmed today. Four Baroque churches — San Agustin in Manila, Paoay, Santa Maria and Miagao — are listed together for their earthquake-resistant 'fortress' style, and the Spanish colonial town of Vigan is remarkably intact. Intramuros, Manila's old walled city, and Rizal Park, where José Rizal was executed in 1896, are at the heart of national memory.

highlights.title: Intramuros & San Agustin Church, Manila
highlights.line: Cycle the old walled city on a bamboo bike, then step inside the country's oldest stone church, a UNESCO site.

highlights.title: Quiapo Church & the Black Nazarene
highlights.line: Join devotees at the Minor Basilica of the Black Nazarene; the 9 January Traslación draws millions — keep valuables close.

highlights.title: Binondo, Manila
highlights.line: Often called the world's oldest Chinatown; join a food walk for dumplings, hopia and Chinese-Filipino history.

highlights.title: Banaue & Batad rice terraces
highlights.line: Hike down to the amphitheatre of Batad's terraces; stay overnight in a homestay to see them at dawn.

highlights.title: Sagada
highlights.line: Mountain town of caves, pine forests and the hanging coffins of Echo Valley; hire a local guide, as required.

highlights.title: Vigan
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed Spanish colonial town of cobbled Calle Crisologo; ride a kalesa and eat empanada from a street stall.

highlights.title: Paoay Church
highlights.line: A massive coral-stone Baroque church with huge buttresses built to withstand earthquakes, in Ilocos Norte.

highlights.title: Batanes
highlights.line: Stone houses, rolling hills and wind-swept cliffs in the far north; flights are weather-dependent, so keep spare days.

highlights.title: El Nido, Palawan
highlights.line: Island-hop limestone lagoons by bangka; book tours that respect the park's visitor limits.

highlights.title: Coron
highlights.line: Swim in the clear Kayangan Lake and dive World War II Japanese shipwrecks in the bay.

highlights.title: Puerto Princesa Underground River
highlights.line: Paddle into one of the world's longest navigable underground rivers; permits are limited, so book ahead.

highlights.title: Tubbataha Reefs
highlights.line: A UNESCO marine park in the Sulu Sea reachable only by liveaboard, from about March to June.

highlights.title: Chocolate Hills, Bohol
highlights.line: More than a thousand grassy cones that turn brown in the dry season; climb the viewpoint at Carmen.

highlights.title: Philippine tarsiers, Bohol
highlights.line: See these tiny, wide-eyed primates at a sanctuary that keeps visitors quiet and flash-free.

highlights.title: Basilica del Santo Niño, Cebu
highlights.line: Home of the nation's oldest Christian relic; visit during the January Sinulog festival for drums and dancing.

highlights.title: Whale sharks in Donsol
highlights.line: Swim with butanding in the wild between roughly February and May, with trained local spotters.

highlights.title: Mayon Volcano, Albay
highlights.line: Admire the near-perfect cone from the Cagsawa ruins, where a church was buried by an 1814 eruption.

highlights.title: Siargao
highlights.line: The teardrop island of the Cloud 9 surf break, coconut forests and island-hopping.

highlights.title: Boracay's White Beach
highlights.line: Powder-white sand and famous sunsets; the island was cleaned up after a six-month closure in 2018.

highlights.title: Miagao Church, Iloilo
highlights.line: A UNESCO Baroque church whose facade is carved with a coconut tree and local life.

highlights.title: Ati-Atihan, Kalibo
highlights.line: In January, painted dancers fill the streets in honour of the Santo Niño, in one of the country's oldest festivals.

highlights.title: MassKara Festival, Bacolod
highlights.line: October's smiling-mask street party, plus the city's beloved chicken inasal.

highlights.title: Philippine Eagle Center, Davao
highlights.line: Meet the endangered national bird, then taste durian and pomelo at Davao's fruit stands.

highlights.title: Mount Apo
highlights.line: The country's highest peak, sacred to Indigenous communities; a multi-day climb with local guides.

highlights.title: Camiguin
highlights.line: A small island of volcanoes, hot springs, a sunken cemetery and sweet lanzones fruit.

highlights.title: Lake Sebu
highlights.line: Meet T'boli weavers of t'nalak cloth from abaca fibre, and zipline over seven waterfalls.

highlights.title: Fort Pilar, Zamboanga
highlights.line: A 17th-century Spanish fort whose outer wall is a shrine to Our Lady of the Pillar, honoured by Christians and many Muslims alike.

highlights.title: Tagaytay & Taal
highlights.line: Look out over Taal Lake and its volcano island while eating hot bulalo beef soup.

highlights.title: Ride a jeepney
highlights.line: Hop on the colourful 'king of the road', pass your fare forward and say 'Para po!' to stop.

highlights.title: Lechon & adobo
highlights.line: Try Cebu's crisp-skinned roast pig and the national stew of vinegar, soy and garlic.

highlights.title: Halo-halo
highlights.line: A tall glass of shaved ice, milk, beans, jellies, ube and leche flan — 'mix-mix' it before eating.

highlights.title: Simbang Gabi
highlights.line: Attend the nine dawn Masses before Christmas, then share bibingka and puto bumbong outside the church.

highlights.title: Videoke night
highlights.line: Join a family karaoke session; enthusiasm matters far more than pitch.

funFacts: The Philippines is made up of 7,641 islands, according to a 2017 government count.
The country is named after King Philip II of Spain.
The Philippines and Timor-Leste are the only predominantly Catholic countries in Asia.
Christmas songs and decorations often appear in September, making the Filipino Christmas season one of the longest in the world.
Simbang Gabi is a tradition of nine dawn Masses held from 16 to 24 December.
The eight rays of the sun on the flag stand for the first eight provinces that revolted against Spain.
By law, the Philippine flag is flown with the red stripe on top in times of war.
Independence from Spain was proclaimed on 12 June 1898 in Kawit, Cavite, where the national flag was first unfurled.
The Malolos Republic of 1899 is often called the first constitutional republic in Asia.
National hero José Rizal was an ophthalmologist, novelist, poet and polyglot.
Jeepneys grew out of US military jeeps left behind after World War II.
Basketball is by far the most popular sport in the Philippines.
The Philippine tarsier is one of the smallest primates in the world.
The Philippine eagle, the national bird, is one of the largest eagles in the world.
The Philippines lies within the Coral Triangle, the global centre of marine biodiversity.
Whale sharks are called butanding in the Philippines.
The Philippine Trench, east of the islands, reaches depths of more than 10,000 m.
Mount Apo in Mindanao, at around 2,950 m, is the country's highest mountain.
Around twenty tropical cyclones enter Philippine waters in an average year.
Taal Volcano sits on an island in a lake, and has its own crater lake.
Mayon Volcano is renowned for having one of the most perfectly symmetrical cones on Earth.
Bohol's Chocolate Hills number more than 1,200.
San Agustin Church in Manila, completed in 1607, is the oldest stone church in the country.
The Las Piñas Bamboo Organ, built in the early 1800s, has pipes made mostly of bamboo.
Binondo, founded in 1594, is often called the oldest Chinatown in the world.
Filipino immigrant Pedro Flores helped popularise the yo-yo in the United States in the 1920s.
The Philippines is one of the world's largest producers of coconuts.
Filipino nurses form one of the largest groups of foreign-trained nurses in the US and the UK.
Remittances from Filipinos abroad equal close to a tenth of the country's economy.
The Philippines has one of the largest English-speaking populations in the world.
Filipino, the national language, is based mainly on Tagalog and borrows heavily from Spanish and English.
Halo-halo, the famous dessert, literally means 'mix-mix'.
Filipinos add 'po' and 'opo' to sentences as a sign of respect to elders and strangers.

languageGuide.intro: Filipino (based on Tagalog) is spoken nationwide alongside English, which is an official language and widely used in cities, signs and business — many people mix the two in 'Taglish', and in the Visayas and Mindanao, Cebuano is often the everyday tongue. Add 'po' to sound respectful (especially with elders), and pronounce words as written: every vowel is sounded, and 'ng' is a single sound as in 'sing'.

culture.history: Before colonisation the islands were home to seafaring communities organised in barangays, trading across Southeast Asia, with Islamic sultanates in the south. Spain ruled from 1565 to 1898, bringing Catholicism and a long struggle for independence in which writer José Rizal was executed in 1896. American colonial rule followed, then a devastating Japanese occupation during the Second World War, with independence in 1946. Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos (1972–1981) brought repression and abuses, ended by the peaceful People Power Revolution of 1986.
culture.politics: The Philippines is a unitary presidential republic in which the president serves a single six-year term, alongside a bicameral Congress and an independent Supreme Court. The 1987 Constitution was written in the spirit of People Power, and the strength of political families and the defence of democratic institutions remain defining civic themes.
culture.arts: José Rizal's novels Noli Me Tángere and El Filibusterismo shaped national consciousness, while painters Juan Luna and Fernando Amorsolo captured history and rural light. The kundiman love song, rondalla string bands and the UNESCO-listed Baroque Churches of the Philippines reflect a layered Malay, Spanish and American heritage.

love.expression: Affection is woven through family life: elders are honoured, meals are shared generously, and care is shown by looking after one another in practical ways. Courtship traditionally involved patience and respect for the family, remembered in the harana serenade, and today ranges from shy and traditional to openly romantic.

etiquette: Add 'po' and 'opo' when speaking to elders and strangers as a sign of respect.
Younger people may greet elders with the mano, gently pressing the elder's hand to their forehead.
If invited to a home, accept at least a little food; a small gift or pasalubong is warmly appreciated.

name: Japan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa, Ainu (critically endangered) and Korean

people: Most people are ethnically Japanese, alongside the Indigenous Ainu of Hokkaido, the Ryukyuan peoples of Okinawa, long-settled Korean and Chinese communities, and a growing number of foreign residents (around 3%) from Vietnam, the Philippines, Brazil, Nepal and elsewhere. Faith is often a matter of practice rather than membership: many people visit Shinto shrines for births, festivals and New Year and turn to Buddhist rites for funerals, while Christians make up about 1%. More than 90% live in cities, and Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world.

plug.note: US two-pin plugs usually fit, though many outlets lack a grounding hole; European and UK travellers need an adapter. Most phone and laptop chargers handle 100 V fine.

basics.local: ありがとうございます

resources: A highly skilled workforce and world-leading manufacturing and robotics
Advanced research, technology and design
Rich fishing grounds and a refined food culture
Forests covering about two-thirds of the land
Geothermal hot springs and volcanic landscapes
Deep cultural heritage — from tea and crafts to anime — admired worldwide
struggles: A rapidly ageing and shrinking population with very low birth rates
Earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons and volcanic eruptions, including the 2011 disaster and the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake
Long working hours, loneliness and isolation, especially among the elderly and the young
Rural depopulation leaving villages and homes empty
Persistent gender gaps in pay and leadership
Questions of how to welcome and integrate foreign workers and their families
prayFor: For elderly people living alone, and for neighbours and carers who look in on them
For young families, that they may find the time, support and hope to flourish
For communities still recovering from earthquakes and tsunamis, including Fukushima and Noto
For overworked and lonely people to find rest, friendship and meaning
For migrant workers and newcomers to be met with fairness and welcome

summary.history: People have lived on the islands for tens of thousands of years, and the Jōmon culture created some of the world's earliest pottery before rice farming spread in the Yayoi era. From the 6th century Buddhism and Chinese learning arrived via Korea, imperial courts flourished in Nara and Kyoto, and from the 12th century warrior governments of shoguns held real power, culminating in the long, largely closed Tokugawa peace of 1603–1868. After the Meiji Restoration, Japan industrialised at astonishing speed and built an empire that colonised Korea and Taiwan and waged war across Asia, causing immense suffering, and itself endured firebombing and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. Rebuilt as a peaceful democracy, Japan became one of the world's largest economies, while still reckoning with wartime memory, a shrinking population and frequent natural disasters.
summary.politicalHistory: For centuries emperors reigned in Kyoto while shoguns ruled, until the 1868 Meiji Restoration returned power to the imperial court and created a centralised modern state with the 1889 Meiji Constitution. Party politics in the 1920s gave way to militarism in the 1930s and defeat in 1945, followed by US-led occupation. The 1947 Constitution made the emperor a symbol of the state, established parliamentary democracy and renounced war in Article 9. Japan is today a constitutional monarchy with a bicameral Diet and a prime minister chosen by parliament, while US administration of Okinawa continued until 1972.
summary.art: Japan's arts range from ink painting, ceramics and the tea ceremony to Noh, kabuki and bunraku puppet theatre. Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji and Matsuo Bashō's haiku are literary treasures, and the woodblock prints of Hokusai and Hiroshige deeply influenced European painters such as Van Gogh. Modern voices include novelists Natsume Sōseki and Yasunari Kawabata, filmmaker Akira Kurosawa, and the manga and anime traditions of Osamu Tezuka and Studio Ghibli.
summary.monuments: Kyoto's temples and shrines, including Kiyomizu-dera and Kinkaku-ji, and Nara's Tōdai-ji with its giant bronze Buddha are UNESCO sites at the heart of Japanese Buddhist heritage. Himeji Castle is the finest surviving original castle, and the floating torii of Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima is an iconic image of Shinto. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome) and the Hidden Christian sites of Nagasaki bear witness to suffering, endurance and faith.

highlights.title: Fushimi Inari Taisha, Kyoto
highlights.line: Thousands of vermilion torii gates climb the mountain; start before 8 am or hike past the halfway point to find quiet.

highlights.title: Kiyomizu-dera, Kyoto
highlights.line: A wooden temple stage over a forested hillside; walk up through the old lanes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka.

highlights.title: Kinkaku-ji & Arashiyama
highlights.line: See the gold-leaf Golden Pavilion, then walk the bamboo grove and Tenryū-ji garden early in the morning.

highlights.title: Tōdai-ji, Nara
highlights.line: One of the world's largest wooden buildings shelters a 15 m bronze Buddha; bow to the deer, which often bow back.

highlights.title: Sensō-ji, Asakusa
highlights.line: Tokyo's oldest temple; come in the evening when the lanterns glow and the crowds thin.

highlights.title: Meiji Jingū, Tokyo
highlights.line: A forested Shinto shrine beside Harajuku; on weekends you may see a traditional wedding procession.

highlights.title: Tsukiji Outer Market
highlights.line: Graze on tamagoyaki, fresh sushi and grilled scallops; go before lunchtime, as stalls close early.

highlights.title: Shibuya & Shinjuku
highlights.line: Cross the famous scramble, then find tiny bars in Golden Gai or yakitori stalls in Omoide Yokochō.

highlights.title: Mount Fuji
highlights.line: Climb in the official season from July to early September, or admire it from Lake Kawaguchi on a clear winter morning.

highlights.title: Hakone
highlights.line: Soak in an onsen, ride the ropeway over volcanic vents and stay in a ryokan with a multi-course kaiseki dinner.

highlights.title: Nikkō
highlights.line: The lavishly carved Tōshō-gū shrine in cedar forests; autumn colours peak around October.

highlights.title: Kanazawa
highlights.line: Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, plus samurai and geisha districts and gold-leaf crafts.

highlights.title: Shirakawa-gō
highlights.line: Steep thatched gasshō houses in a UNESCO mountain village; stay overnight in a farmhouse inn.

highlights.title: Takayama
highlights.line: Morning markets, sake breweries and an old town of dark wooden merchant houses in the Japanese Alps.

highlights.title: Kumano Kodō
highlights.line: Walk ancient pilgrimage trails through Kii Peninsula forests to the Kumano shrines, staying in family inns.

highlights.title: Kōyasan
highlights.line: Spend a night in a temple lodging, eat Buddhist vegetarian cuisine and join the dawn prayers.

highlights.title: Himeji Castle
highlights.line: The brilliant white 'White Heron Castle', Japan's finest original castle; climb all six floors.

highlights.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial
highlights.line: The Genbaku Dome and Peace Memorial Museum are deeply moving; leave time for quiet reflection.

highlights.title: Miyajima (Itsukushima)
highlights.line: See the great torii appear to float at high tide, and try grilled oysters and momiji manjū.

highlights.title: Naoshima
highlights.line: An island of contemporary art museums by Tadao Andō, including the Chichū Art Museum; book timed tickets.

highlights.title: Dōtonbori, Osaka
highlights.line: Neon canal-side street food — takoyaki, okonomiyaki and kushikatsu (no double-dipping the sauce).

highlights.title: Nagasaki's Christian heritage
highlights.line: Visit Ōura Cathedral, the 26 Martyrs Memorial and the UNESCO Hidden Christian sites, a story of faith kept in secret for 250 years.

highlights.title: Sapporo Snow Festival
highlights.line: Each February giant snow and ice sculptures fill Ōdōri Park; warm up with miso ramen.

highlights.title: Shiretoko
highlights.line: A UNESCO wilderness in Hokkaido with brown bears and, in winter, drift ice along the coast.

highlights.title: Okinawa
highlights.line: Subtropical beaches, Ryukyuan culture and Shuri Castle, being rebuilt after the 2019 fire; learn the island's wartime history at the Peace Memorial Park.

highlights.title: Yakushima
highlights.line: Hike moss-covered forests to the ancient Jōmon Sugi cedar; expect rain, as it is one of Japan's wettest places.

highlights.title: Sakurajima, Kagoshima
highlights.line: An active volcano across the bay; soak your feet in the free foot bath with steam on the horizon.

highlights.title: Aso caldera, Kumamoto
highlights.line: One of the world's largest volcanic calderas, with grazing horses and green highlands.

highlights.title: Hanami
highlights.line: Picnic under the cherry blossoms in late March to early April; check the official blossom forecast.

highlights.title: Onsen etiquette
highlights.line: Wash thoroughly before entering, keep your towel out of the water, and check the rules on tattoos.

highlights.title: Regional ramen
highlights.line: Taste rich tonkotsu in Fukuoka, miso in Sapporo and soy-based shōyu in Tokyo; slurping is fine.

highlights.title: Sumo tournament
highlights.line: Grand tournaments are held in Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya and Fukuoka; arrive early to watch the junior ranks.

highlights.title: Nebuta Matsuri, Aomori
highlights.line: In early August, enormous illuminated paper floats parade through the streets — join in as a haneto dancer.

funFacts: Japan has 14,125 islands, according to a 2023 recount by its mapping authority.
The name Nihon (or Nippon) means 'origin of the sun', which is why Japan is called the Land of the Rising Sun.
Japan writes with three scripts at once: hiragana, katakana and kanji.
The word emoji comes from Japanese e (picture) and moji (character).
Karaoke was invented in Japan; the word means 'empty orchestra'.
Instant noodles were invented by Momofuku Ando in 1958.
The first Shinkansen bullet train began running in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics.
Delays on the Tōkaidō Shinkansen are typically measured in seconds rather than minutes.
Greater Tokyo is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, with about 37 million people.
Japan has about 110 active volcanoes.
Mount Fuji is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707.
Japan has around 3,000 hot-spring areas.
Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, founded in 705, is recognised as the oldest hotel in the world.
Kongō Gumi, a temple-building firm founded in 578, is one of the oldest companies in the world.
Japan has more than 90,000 people aged 100 or over.
Japan has roughly four million vending machines.
There are around 80,000 Shinto shrines in Japan.
The Tale of Genji, written by Murasaki Shikibu over a thousand years ago, is often called one of the world's first novels.
Sushi began as a way of preserving fish in fermented rice.
During the Edo period the Dutch were the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan, from the small island of Dejima in Nagasaki.
Japanese still uses words borrowed from Dutch, such as biiru (beer) and kōhī (coffee).
In Nagasaki, Hidden Christians secretly kept their faith for about 250 years before revealing themselves to a French priest in 1865.
The Ainu were officially recognised by law as an Indigenous people of Japan in 2019.
Snow monkeys at Jigokudani in Nagano bathe in natural hot springs in winter.
The Seikan Tunnel linking Honshu and Hokkaido runs about 54 km, partly under the sea.
The Akashi Kaikyō Bridge held the record for the world's longest suspension-bridge span from 1998 to 2022.
Japan's school and fiscal years begin in April, in time with the cherry blossoms.
Japan's weather agency declares the start of cherry blossom season in Tokyo by watching an official sample tree at Yasukuni Shrine.
The Sapporo Snow Festival began in 1950 with six snow statues built by local high-school students.
Yakushima's Jōmon Sugi cedar is at least 2,000 years old.
Japan's population peaked around 2008 and has been shrinking since.
Eastern Japan's electricity runs at 50 Hz and western Japan's at 60 Hz, a legacy of generators bought from Germany and the US in the 1890s.
Japanese Kit Kats come in hundreds of flavours, from matcha to sake.

languageGuide.intro: Japanese has polite and casual forms; as a visitor, the polite '-masu' and 'desu' endings plus a small bow are always right, and 'sumimasen' works for excuse me, sorry and even thank you. Pronunciation is simple and even — every syllable gets equal weight, vowels are pure (a, i, u, e, o), and the 'u' is often almost silent, as in 'desu' (dess); English is on signs and transit everywhere but less spoken outside big cities.

phrases.local: どうもありがとうございます

phrases.en: Does this train go to Kyoto?
phrases.local: この電車は京都に行きますか？
phrases.roman: Kono densha wa Kyōto ni ikimasu ka?
phrases.say: koh-noh DEN-shah wah KYOH-toh nee ee-kee-MAHS kah

phrases.local: この住所までお願いします
オランダから来ました

phrases.en: Pleased to know you (I'm in your care)
phrases.local: よろしくお願いします
ありがとうございます

culture.history: Japan's culture grew from Jōmon and Yayoi roots into a refined imperial court in Heian-era Kyoto, followed by centuries of rule by samurai shogunates. Under the Tokugawa shogunate the country largely closed itself off until the Meiji Restoration of 1868 launched rapid modernisation. Imperial expansion brought colonial rule over Korea and Taiwan and wartime atrocities across Asia, and the war ended with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. Postwar Japan rebuilt itself as a peaceful democracy and one of the world's largest economies.
culture.politics: Japan is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system: the emperor is the symbol of the state with no political power, and the prime minister is chosen by the bicameral National Diet. Article 9 of the 1947 Constitution, which renounces war, remains a defining and much-debated civic theme.
culture.arts: Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji, Matsuo Bashō's haiku and the woodblock prints of Hokusai and Hiroshige are treasured worldwide. Noh, kabuki and bunraku puppet theatre, the tea ceremony and the aesthetics of wabi-sabi sit alongside the films of Akira Kurosawa and Yasujirō Ozu.

love.expression: Affection is often expressed quietly, through attentiveness, thoughtful gestures and reading what another person needs without being asked. Gifts carry real meaning, from omiyage souvenirs for colleagues to handmade chocolates on Valentine's Day, and younger couples may be more openly expressive than their parents.

etiquette: Remove your shoes at the entrance (genkan) of homes, many inns and some temples and restaurants.
Tipping is not customary and can cause confusion; excellent service is simply expected.
Never stand chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick to chopstick, as both recall funeral rites.

name: South Korea

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue): Korean, Jejueo and Korean Sign Language; English widely studied

people: South Koreans are one of the world's most ethnically and linguistically homogeneous peoples, though migrant workers, marriage migrants and international students are a fast-growing presence. Roughly half say they have no religion, about a quarter to three in ten are Christian (Protestant and Catholic) and around one in six Buddhist, with Confucian family ethics and shamanic traditions woven through daily life. More than four in five people live in cities, half of them in greater Seoul, and a large diaspora lives in the US, China, Japan and Central Asia.

plug.note: Continental European plugs fit; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Highly educated, hard-working population
Semiconductor and electronics industry
Shipbuilding, steel and automotive manufacturing
World-class digital infrastructure
Global cultural reach of film, music, drama and food (Hallyu)
Mountains, coasts and islands such as Jeju
struggles: The world's lowest birth rate and a rapidly ageing society
Intense academic and job competition, long working hours and high youth stress
High suicide rate, especially among older people
Elder poverty and loneliness
Housing costs and concentration of wealth and opportunity in greater Seoul
Unresolved division and military tension with North Korea
prayFor: For young people weighed down by exam and job pressure — that they would know their worth is not measured by rank or results
For older people living alone or in poverty, that they would be honoured, cared for and never forgotten
For couples and families longing for children or afraid to start a family, for homes and workplaces that make room for life
For those carrying despair in silence, that help, hope and listening friends would reach them in time
For the divided peninsula and separated families, for peace, reconciliation and freedom for all Koreans

summary.history: People have lived on the Korean peninsula for tens of thousands of years, and the kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla gave way to unified Silla, then Goryeo and the long Joseon dynasty (1392–1897), which shaped Confucian society and created the Hangul alphabet. Korea endured invasions from Japan and the Manchus and was annexed by Japan in 1910, a colonial period remembered for forced labour, suppression of language and the suffering of the so-called comfort women. Liberation in 1945 brought division between Soviet and American zones, and the Korean War (1950–53) killed millions and left families separated across a line that still holds. From deep poverty, South Korea industrialised at extraordinary speed — the ‘Miracle on the Han River’ — and today is a wealthy, technologically advanced society with a worldwide cultural influence.
summary.politicalHistory: The Republic of Korea was proclaimed in 1948 under Syngman Rhee, whose increasingly authoritarian rule ended with the April Revolution of 1960. Park Chung-hee took power in a 1961 coup and led a developmental dictatorship until his assassination in 1979, followed by Chun Doo-hwan's military regime and the violent suppression of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising. Mass protests in June 1987 won direct presidential elections and a new constitution, creating today's democratic presidential republic with a single five-year presidential term and a unicameral National Assembly. Peaceful transfers of power and a strong civil society have since become hallmarks of Korean democracy.
summary.art: Korea is famed for celadon and white porcelain, Buddhist painting, calligraphy and the restrained beauty of hanok architecture and hanbok dress. Its music ranges from court music and the solo storytelling of pansori to the gayageum zither and today's globally popular K-pop, while literature stretches from Joseon-era sijo poetry and the novels of Pak Wan-suh to Han Kang, Nobel laureate in literature. Korean cinema, from Im Kwon-taek to Bong Joon-ho, has become one of the most admired in the world.
summary.monuments: Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces and Jongmyo Shrine in Seoul preserve the royal world of the Joseon dynasty, with Changdeokgung and Jongmyo listed by UNESCO. Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa Temple in Gyeongju, and Haeinsa Temple with its 13th-century Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, are masterpieces of Buddhist art. Suwon's Hwaseong Fortress shows late-Joseon engineering, and the volcanic landscapes of Jeju, including Seongsan Ilchulbong, are a UNESCO natural site.

highlights.title: Gyeongbokgung Palace
highlights.line: Seoul's grandest Joseon palace, rebuilt after centuries of loss; arrive for the changing of the guard and enter free if you wear hanbok.

highlights.title: Changdeokgung & the Secret Garden
highlights.line: A UNESCO palace that bends to the hills rather than flattening them; book the guided Huwon garden tour ahead, especially in autumn.

highlights.title: Jongmyo Shrine
highlights.line: The austere royal ancestral shrine where Confucian rites with ancient court music are still performed each May; entry is mostly by guided tour.

highlights.title: Bukchon Hanok Village
highlights.line: Lanes of tiled-roof wooden houses between two palaces; people live here, so visit in daytime hours and keep your voice low.

highlights.title: Gwangjang Market
highlights.line: One of Seoul's oldest markets — sit at a stall for crispy mung-bean bindaetteok, mini gimbap and rice wine.

highlights.title: National Museum of Korea
highlights.line: A vast, free museum whose quiet room of two pensive Buddha statues is worth the trip on its own.

highlights.title: Namsan & N Seoul Tower
highlights.line: Walk up through the woods on Namsan's trails at dusk for the city lights, rather than queuing for the cable car.

highlights.title: Bukhansan National Park
highlights.line: Granite peaks on the edge of a megacity, reached by subway and bus; join the weekend hikers in their bright gear and share snacks at the top.

highlights.title: The DMZ
highlights.line: A sobering visit to the border that divides the peninsula; only go on an authorised tour, bring your passport and check for closures.

highlights.title: Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon
highlights.line: Walk the UNESCO-listed 5.7 km wall of King Jeongjo's 18th-century fortress, then eat Suwon's famous fried chicken.

highlights.title: Bulguksa & Seokguram, Gyeongju
highlights.line: Silla-era temple and granite grotto Buddha facing the eastern sea; go early to see the grotto in peace.

highlights.title: Gyeongju's royal tombs
highlights.line: Grassy burial mounds rise between houses in this ‘museum without walls’; rent a bike and include the Cheomseongdae observatory and Woljeong Bridge at night.

highlights.title: Andong Hahoe Folk Village
highlights.line: A living clan village in a river bend, UNESCO-listed, where you can see the masked Hahoe byeolsingut talnori dance.

highlights.title: Haeinsa Temple
highlights.line: Home to the 80,000-plus woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana, stored for centuries in ingeniously ventilated halls in the Gaya mountains.

highlights.title: A temple stay
highlights.line: Spend a night at a mountain monastery for dawn chanting, a silent bowl meal and tea with a monk; book through the official Templestay programme.

highlights.title: Busan's Gamcheon Culture Village
highlights.line: A hillside of pastel houses built by refugees of the Korean War, now full of murals; follow the fish-shaped signs.

highlights.title: Jagalchi Fish Market
highlights.line: Korea's largest seafood market, run largely by tough, warm ‘Jagalchi ajummas’; pick your fish downstairs and have it cooked upstairs.

highlights.title: Haedong Yonggungsa
highlights.line: A rare Buddhist temple perched on sea rocks at Busan's edge, beautiful at sunrise before the crowds arrive.

highlights.title: Seongsan Ilchulbong, Jeju
highlights.line: Climb the UNESCO-listed tuff cone for sunrise over the ocean, then watch the haenyeo divers at the beach below.

highlights.title: Hallasan
highlights.line: South Korea's highest peak, a shield volcano at the heart of Jeju; summit trails need an online reservation and an early start.

highlights.title: Jeju Olle Trails
highlights.line: A network of walking routes around the island's coast and villages; pick one section and walk it slowly, stopping for tangerines.

highlights.title: Haenyeo Museum & the sea women
highlights.line: Learn the story of Jeju's breath-hold divers, a UNESCO-recognised culture of women who still harvest the sea without tanks.

highlights.title: Jeonju Hanok Village
highlights.line: Over 700 traditional houses in the city famed for bibimbap and makgeolli; stay in a hanok guesthouse with heated floors.

highlights.title: Seoraksan National Park
highlights.line: Dramatic granite ridges in the northeast, spectacular in October colours; the Ulsanbawi climb is steep but unforgettable.

highlights.title: Boseong green tea fields
highlights.line: Terraced tea plantations rolling down southern hillsides; try green-tea ice cream and walk among the rows in morning mist.

highlights.title: Suncheon Bay wetlands
highlights.line: Golden reed beds and tidal flats visited by hooded cranes in winter; time your visit for sunset from the viewpoint.

highlights.title: Jjimjilbang bathhouse
highlights.line: Soak, scrub and sleep in a 24-hour bathhouse like a local; bathing areas are nude and gender-separated, the common halls are not.

highlights.title: Korean barbecue
highlights.line: Grill samgyeopsal at your table, wrap it in lettuce with garlic and ssamjang, and let elders or hosts pour your drink first.

highlights.title: Kimchi-making class
highlights.line: Kimjang, the communal autumn kimchi making, is UNESCO-listed; join a class or visit Seoul's Museum Kimchikan to taste the varieties.

highlights.title: Street food & pojangmacha
highlights.line: Tteokbokki, hotteok and fish-cake skewers from steaming tent bars are part of evening life; pay in cash at small stalls.

highlights.title: Noraebang night
highlights.line: Rent a private karaoke room with friends — singing together, badly or well, is a beloved Korean way to bond.

highlights.title: Myeongdong Cathedral
highlights.line: The 1898 Gothic-revival heart of Korean Catholicism and a refuge for pro-democracy protesters in 1987; quiet visitors are welcome at Mass.

highlights.title: A KBO baseball game
highlights.line: Join the cheering chants, snack on fried chicken and beer, and experience one of the most joyful crowds in Korean life.

funFacts: The Hangul alphabet was created under King Sejong in 1443 and promulgated in 1446, and Korea celebrates Hangul Day every 9 October.
In June 2023 South Korea officially dropped its traditional ‘Korean age’ count for legal and administrative purposes.
Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type — older than the Gutenberg Bible.
The Tripitaka Koreana at Haeinsa consists of more than 80,000 carved woodblocks made in the 13th century.
Cheomseongdae in Gyeongju, built in the 7th century, is one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia.
Many buildings label the fourth floor ‘F’ because the word for four sounds like the word for death.
Writing a living person's name in red ink is traditionally avoided, because red was used for the names of the dead.
Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics and PyeongChang hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics.
Korean uses two sets of numbers: native Korean for counting things and ages, Sino-Korean for dates, money and phone numbers.
The national flag, the Taegukgi, shows a red-and-blue taeguk circle surrounded by four trigrams from the I Ching.
The national flower is the mugunghwa, the rose of Sharon, whose name evokes ‘eternal blossoming’.
Taekwondo developed in Korea and has been an Olympic sport since the 2000 Sydney Games.
In 2018 North and South Korea jointly inscribed ssireum, traditional Korean wrestling, on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Jeju has its own language, Jejueo, which UNESCO classifies as critically endangered.
Ondol underfloor heating, which warms homes through the floor, has roots going back well over a thousand years.
Kimchi comes in hundreds of varieties, and the communal making of it, kimjang, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
On Lunar New Year, eating a bowl of tteokguk rice-cake soup is said to make you a year older.
At Seollal, children perform a deep New Year's bow called sebae to elders and receive gifts of money.
Chuseok, the autumn harvest festival, is celebrated with half-moon rice cakes called songpyeon.
Kim, Lee and Park are so common that together they cover nearly half of all South Koreans.
Seoul's Cheonggyecheon stream was uncovered and restored in 2005 after decades buried under a road and an elevated highway.
After the devastation of war, South Korea carried out one of the world's most successful reforestation efforts, and forests now cover about 60% of its land.
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for close to a thousand years.
Bong Joon-ho's ‘Parasite’ became the first non-English-language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture, in 2020.
Han Kang became the first Korean writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 2024.
The word ‘Hallyu’ — the Korean Wave — was popularised by Chinese media in the late 1990s.
South Korea was one of the first countries to launch a nationwide commercial 5G mobile network, in April 2019.
The haenyeo of Jeju dive without breathing equipment, and many of them are over sixty.
Busan's port ranks among the busiest container ports in the world.
When receiving something from an elder, Koreans use both hands, or support the giving arm with the other hand, as a sign of respect.
Pepero Day on 11 November is named after a stick-shaped biscuit, because the date 11.11 resembles four sticks.
Hanbok wearers get free entry to Seoul's royal palaces.
Korea's Seoraksan and Jirisan were among the earliest areas to be designated national parks, with Jirisan becoming the first in 1967.

languageGuide.intro: Korean has polite speech levels, and the ‘-yo’ and ‘-nida’ endings used here are safe with anyone you meet; Hangul can be learned in an afternoon and makes signs much easier. English appears on transport signs and in tourist areas, but less so in conversation, especially outside Seoul and Busan.

phrases.en: Could you give me a discount?
Shall we take a photo together?

culture.history: The Korean peninsula was shaped by the Three Kingdoms, unified Silla, Goryeo and the long Joseon dynasty, under which King Sejong introduced the Hangul alphabet in the 15th century. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled harshly until 1945, after which the peninsula was divided and devastated by the Korean War of 1950–1953. The South endured decades of authoritarian and military rule, including the violent suppression of the Gwangju Uprising in 1980, before mass protests won democratic reforms in 1987. Rapid industrialisation transformed one of the world's poorest countries into a high-tech economy within two generations.
culture.politics: South Korea is a presidential republic in which the president serves a single five-year term, alongside a unicameral National Assembly and a Constitutional Court. Democracy won through citizen protest, and the unresolved division with North Korea, remain defining civic themes.
culture.arts: Goryeo celadon, hanok architecture and the elegance of Hangul itself are national treasures, as are the landscape paintings of Jeong Seon and the genre scenes of Kim Hong-do. The sung storytelling of pansori, the poetry of Yun Dong-ju and the novels of Han Kang sit alongside a globally loved film and pop culture.

love.expression: Friendship and romance are bound up with jeong, a deep, accumulated affection and loyalty that grows through shared time. Couples often mark 100-day anniversaries and may wear matching outfits, while friends and family show care by feeding one another, paying for meals and checking in often.

etiquette: Give and receive things, including drinks, with both hands or with your left hand supporting your right, especially with elders.
Pour drinks for others rather than yourself, and younger people turn slightly away from elders when drinking.
Avoid writing someone's name in red ink, which is associated with the deceased.

name: India

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); 22 languages are listed in the Constitution's Eighth Schedule

people: India is home to more people than any other country, an immense mosaic of Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman and Austroasiatic peoples, including over a hundred million Adivasi (tribal) people. About four in five Indians are Hindu, around 14% Muslim — one of the world's largest Muslim populations — with Christians (about 2%), Sikhs (about 2%), Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Jews also rooted here for centuries. Roughly two-thirds live in villages, though cities are growing fast, and a diaspora of tens of millions lives in the Gulf, the UK, North America, Africa and beyond.

plug.note: Two-pin European plugs often fit, but older three-round-pin D and large M sockets are common, so a universal adapter is wise; US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: A young, entrepreneurial population of over a billion
World-leading IT, software and pharmaceutical industries
Fertile river plains of the Ganges, Indus tributaries and Deccan
Coal, iron ore, bauxite and growing solar power
Spices, tea, cotton and an extraordinary food heritage
Ancient spiritual, philosophical and artistic traditions
struggles: Severe air pollution and water stress in many cities and regions
Poverty, informal work and not enough good jobs for young people
Caste discrimination and inequality that persist despite legal protections
Violence against women and low female workforce participation
Communal tensions between religious communities and pressure on minorities
Climate extremes: heatwaves, floods and failing monsoons for farmers
prayFor: For farmers and labourers living season to season, for fair prices, good rains and dignity in their work
For girls and women, for safety in streets and homes and room to learn, work and lead
For Dalit and Adivasi communities, that the dignity of every person would be honoured in law and in daily life
For peace between Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs and all faiths, and for freedom of conscience for everyone
For children breathing polluted air and families without clean water, for wise care of land, rivers and sky

summary.history: The Indus Valley civilisation flourished in the northwest some 4,500 years ago, and in the millennia that followed the Vedic traditions, Buddhism and Jainism arose and empires such as the Mauryas, Guptas, Cholas and Vijayanagara left deep marks on Asia. From the 12th century Islamic sultanates and then the Mughal Empire built a rich Indo-Islamic culture, while European traders arrived by sea. The British East India Company and then the British Crown ruled much of the subcontinent until 1947, a period of economic extraction and devastating famines as well as railways and new institutions. Independence came with Partition, when perhaps a million people died and some fifteen million were displaced, and India has since grown into the world's most populous democracy and a rising economic power.
summary.politicalHistory: A non-violent freedom movement led by figures such as Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and B. R. Ambedkar won independence from Britain on 15 August 1947. The Constitution, drafted under Ambedkar's leadership, came into force on 26 January 1950, making India a federal parliamentary republic with universal adult suffrage. Democracy was suspended during the Emergency of 1975–77 under Indira Gandhi but restored at the ballot box, and economic liberalisation from 1991 reshaped the country. Today power alternates through regular elections at national and state level, with a President as head of state and a Prime Minister leading the government.
summary.art: India's classical dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi, and its Hindustani and Carnatic music traditions, carry centuries of devotion and refinement. Literature spans the Sanskrit epics, the Tamil Sangam poems, Kabir and Mirabai, Rabindranath Tagore, Premchand and countless writers in dozens of languages. Its crafts — Mughal miniatures, Madhubani painting, block-printed and handwoven textiles, and stone and bronze sculpture — are matched today by the world's most prolific film industries.
summary.monuments: The Taj Mahal in Agra, built by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal, is perhaps the world's best-known monument of love and Mughal art. The painted Buddhist caves of Ajanta and the rock-cut temples of Ellora, the Sun Temple at Konark and the great Chola temples of Thanjavur are UNESCO World Heritage Sites of extraordinary craftsmanship. The ruins of Hampi recall the Vijayanagara Empire, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar is the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith, open to all.

highlights.title: Taj Mahal, Agra
highlights.line: The marble mausoleum glows differently at every hour; go at sunrise, and note it is closed on Fridays.

highlights.title: Agra Fort & Fatehpur Sikri
highlights.line: Red-sandstone Mughal power: see the fort's view to the Taj, then the abandoned royal city of Akbar nearby.

highlights.title: Varanasi's ghats
highlights.line: Take a dawn boat on the Ganges past bathing pilgrims and cremation ghats, and join the evening Ganga aarti; photograph the cremations only with great respect, or not at all.

highlights.title: Golden Temple, Amritsar
highlights.line: Cover your head, wash your feet and sit on the floor for the langar, a free community meal served to tens of thousands every day.

highlights.title: Old Delhi
highlights.line: Climb the minaret of the Jama Masjid, then wander Chandni Chowk's spice lanes and eat parathas in Paranthe Wali Gali.

highlights.title: Humayun's Tomb & Qutub Minar
highlights.line: Two UNESCO sites in Delhi: the garden tomb that inspired the Taj, and a soaring 13th-century victory tower.

highlights.title: Amber Fort, Jaipur
highlights.line: A hilltop palace of mirrors and courtyards above the Pink City; walk up rather than riding an elephant.

highlights.title: Udaipur & Lake Pichola
highlights.line: The City Palace rises from the lake; take a sunset boat and stay in a haveli with a rooftop view.

highlights.title: Jaisalmer
highlights.line: A living sandstone fort in the Thar Desert; spend a night on the dunes with a camel safari and folk musicians.

highlights.title: Ranthambore National Park
highlights.line: Tigers among ruined forts and lakes; book safaris well ahead and go with patience — sightings are never guaranteed.

highlights.title: Rishikesh
highlights.line: Join a yoga class and the evening aarti by the Ganges where it leaves the Himalayan foothills; the town is vegetarian and alcohol-free.

highlights.title: Ladakh
highlights.line: High-desert monasteries such as Thiksey and Hemis under vast skies; rest two days on arrival in Leh to acclimatise to the altitude.

highlights.title: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
highlights.line: Ride the UNESCO-listed ‘toy train’ through tea gardens and, on clear mornings, see Kangchenjunga from Tiger Hill.

highlights.title: Kolkata & Durga Puja
highlights.line: During the autumn festival the city fills with artful pandals; any time of year, visit the Victoria Memorial and drink chai from clay cups.

highlights.title: Sundarbans
highlights.line: Boat through the world's largest mangrove forest, home of the Bengal tiger, with a licensed local guide.

highlights.title: Kaziranga National Park, Assam
highlights.line: Home to most of the world's greater one-horned rhinos; go between November and April.

highlights.title: Meghalaya's living root bridges
highlights.line: Khasi communities have trained rubber-fig roots into bridges for generations; the walk down to Nongriat's double-decker bridge is steep but magical.

highlights.title: Bodh Gaya
highlights.line: Sit quietly under the Bodhi tree at the Mahabodhi Temple, where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment.

highlights.title: Khajuraho
highlights.line: Exquisitely carved 10th–11th-century Hindu and Jain temples in Madhya Pradesh, best seen in soft morning light.

highlights.title: Konark Sun Temple
highlights.line: A 13th-century temple built as the chariot of the sun god, with giant carved stone wheels that act as sundials.

highlights.title: Ajanta & Ellora Caves
highlights.line: Buddhist murals at Ajanta and the colossal rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora; Ajanta is closed Mondays and Ellora Tuesdays.

highlights.title: Mumbai
highlights.line: Admire the Gothic Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, walk Marine Drive at dusk and eat vada pav from a street stall.

highlights.title: Old Goa's churches
highlights.line: The Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the relics of St Francis Xavier; combine with Goa's Portuguese-era Latin quarter, Fontainhas.

highlights.title: Hampi
highlights.line: Boulder-strewn ruins of the Vijayanagara capital; rent a bicycle and watch sunset from Hemakuta Hill.

highlights.title: Mysore Palace
highlights.line: Illuminated by nearly 100,000 bulbs on Sunday evenings and during the Dasara festival; also try Mysore pak sweets.

highlights.title: Meenakshi Amman Temple, Madurai
highlights.line: Towering gopurams covered in painted deities; stay for the nightly ceremony carrying Shiva to Meenakshi's chamber.

highlights.title: Mahabalipuram
highlights.line: Seventh- and eighth-century Pallava shore temples and rock reliefs on the Bay of Bengal, an easy trip from Chennai.

highlights.title: Kerala backwaters
highlights.line: Drift through palm-lined canals on a kettuvallam houseboat from Alappuzha, eating fish curry cooked on board.

highlights.title: Munnar tea hills
highlights.line: Walk through emerald tea estates in the Western Ghats and visit a tea museum; nights are cool, so pack a layer.

highlights.title: Fort Kochi
highlights.line: Chinese fishing nets, a 16th-century synagogue, St Francis Church and a Kathakali performance in one walkable old town.

highlights.title: A thali meal
highlights.line: A round plate of rice, breads, dals, vegetables, pickles and sweets, refilled until you say stop; eat with your right hand.

highlights.title: A long-distance train
highlights.line: Share snacks and conversation in sleeper or AC class — India's railways are a journey into everyday life; book early on the official IRCTC site.

highlights.title: Holi and Diwali
highlights.line: Throw colours in spring at Holi and see homes glow with oil lamps at Diwali in autumn; join in as a guest of local families if invited.

funFacts: In 2023 India overtook China to become the world's most populous country, according to UN estimates.
The mathematician Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in the year 628.
Chess is believed to have originated in India as the game chaturanga around the 6th century.
Snakes and ladders comes from an Indian game called Moksha Patam, designed to teach about virtue and vice.
The English word ‘shampoo’ comes from the Hindi ‘champo’, meaning to press or massage.
India has a single time zone, Indian Standard Time, set at UTC+5:30.
Rupee banknotes show their value in 17 languages: Hindi and English on the front and 15 more on the back.
India's Constitution is the longest written national constitution in the world.
In August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 made India the first country to land a spacecraft near the Moon's south pole.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya are among the rainiest places on Earth.
The Golden Temple's community kitchen serves free meals to tens of thousands of people each day, regardless of faith.
India has one of the largest postal networks in the world, with more than 150,000 post offices.
Srinagar has a floating post office on a houseboat on Dal Lake.
Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver around 200,000 home-cooked lunches a day with a famous colour-coded system.
India is the world's largest producer of milk.
India grows more varieties of spices than any other country and is the world's largest spice producer.
The Kumbh Mela, a Hindu pilgrimage that draws tens of millions, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Rabindranath Tagore, who wrote India's national anthem, also wrote Bangladesh's, and in 1913 became the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature.
The national animal is the Bengal tiger, the national bird the peacock and the national aquatic animal the Ganges river dolphin.
The International Day of Yoga on 21 June was adopted by the UN in 2014 after a proposal from India.
For decades, election officials set up a polling station in Gujarat's Gir forest for a single voter, a temple priest.
The Indus Valley city of Dholavira in Gujarat had sophisticated water reservoirs more than 4,000 years ago.
Diamonds were mined in India long before anywhere else, and the Koh-i-Noor is believed to come from the Golconda region.
India's film industries in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Bengali and more together produce more films than any other country.
The Sundarbans, shared with Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest.
The mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan, largely self-taught, produced nearly 4,000 results, many still being studied today.
Kerala has long had one of the highest literacy rates of any Indian state, above 90%.
The Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya is believed to descend from the tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment.
Kabaddi, a tag-and-breath-holding team sport, has ancient roots in India and now has a popular professional league.
Cotton was spun and woven in the Indian subcontinent thousands of years ago, and words like ‘calico’ and ‘chintz’ come from Indian origins.
Over 640 million people voted in the 2024 general election, the largest democratic exercise in history.
The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved downwards out of a single mass of rock.
Mango is the national fruit, and India grows more mangoes than any other country.

languageGuide.intro: Hindi uses polite ‘aap’ (you) and verb forms ending in ‘-iye’, and adding ‘ji’ after a name or ‘haan ji’ (yes) sounds warm and respectful; some words change with your gender, shown here as male/female. Hindi is widely understood in the north and centre, while English is common in cities and tourism — in the south and northeast, local languages such as Tamil or Bengali come first, so start with English there.

phrases.en: Please take me to this address

culture.history: From the cities of the Indus Valley through the Vedic age, the Maurya empire of Ashoka and the Gupta era, the subcontinent nurtured Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and later Sikhism, and absorbed Islam through centuries of sultanates and the Mughal empire. The British East India Company and then the British Raj ruled for nearly two centuries, an era marked by economic extraction and catastrophic famines. A mass independence movement, shaped by Mahatma Gandhi's nonviolence, won freedom in 1947, but Partition into India and Pakistan brought communal violence and the displacement of millions.
culture.politics: India is a federal parliamentary republic and the world's most populous democracy: a largely ceremonial president is head of state, while the prime minister leads a government answerable to the bicameral Parliament of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The 1950 Constitution, whose drafting committee was chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, enshrines secularism and pluralism, and holding together an immensely diverse union remains its defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Classical dance forms such as Bharatanatyam and Kathak, and the Hindustani and Carnatic music traditions carried worldwide by Ravi Shankar, are among the oldest living art forms on earth. Literature runs from Kalidasa's Sanskrit poetry to the Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore, architecture from the rock-cut caves of Ajanta to the Taj Mahal, and film from Satyajit Ray to today's vast industries.

love.expression: Love is often expressed through family: cooking for someone, remembering their needs and showing up for festivals and milestones. Both arranged and love marriages are common, public displays of affection tend to be restrained, and customs vary enormously across regions, faiths and generations.
