etiquette: Use your right hand for eating, giving and receiving.
Remove your shoes before entering homes and places of worship, and dress modestly at religious sites.
A namaste with palms pressed together is a respectful greeting, especially with elders or women who may prefer not to shake hands.

name: Thailand
nativeName: ประเทศไทย (Prathet Thai)

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Malay, Khmer, Karen, Hmong and Chinese varieties

people: Most people are Thai, speaking Central Thai alongside regional languages such as Isan (close to Lao), Northern and Southern Thai, with large communities of Thai-Chinese descent and Malay Muslims in the deep south, plus Karen, Hmong, Akha and other hill peoples and millions of migrant workers from Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos. Around 93–95% are Theravada Buddhist, about 5% Muslim and roughly 1% Christian, with spirit houses and merit-making woven into daily life. Just over half the population lives in urban areas, with Greater Bangkok by far the largest city.

plug.note: Many outlets accept both US flat-pin and European round-pin plugs; UK travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

basics.local: สวัสดีครับ / ค่ะ
ขอบคุณครับ / ค่ะ
ขอโทษครับ / ค่ะ

resources: Fertile rice lands and a world-leading role in rice, rubber and sugar exports
A vibrant tourism industry and renowned hospitality
Automotive and electronics manufacturing hub of Southeast Asia
Rich seas, coral reefs, islands and tropical forests
One of the world's great cuisines
Deep Buddhist and artisan traditions
struggles: Wide gaps between Bangkok and rural regions, especially the northeast
High household debt among families and farmers
A rapidly ageing society
Political polarisation and recurring cycles of protest and military intervention
Long-running insurgency in the Muslim-majority far south
Air pollution from burning, floods, coastal erosion and pressure on reefs and wildlife
prayFor: For farming families in Isan and the north, for fair incomes, freedom from crushing debt and hope for their children
For migrant workers from neighbouring countries, for safety, fair treatment and protection from trafficking
For peace and mutual trust in the deep south, and comfort for all who have lost loved ones there
For a society able to disagree without fear, and for leaders who listen and serve the common good
For clean air in the north, healthy seas and forests, and wise care for the land

summary.history: Mainland Southeast Asia has long been home to rice-growing communities, and Ban Chiang in the northeast shows Bronze Age culture thousands of years old. Mon and Khmer realms shaped the region before Thai-speaking peoples founded Sukhothai in the 13th century, followed by the powerful kingdom of Ayutthaya, a cosmopolitan trading hub until Burmese armies destroyed it in 1767. Kings of the Chakri dynasty moved the capital to Bangkok in 1782, and through diplomacy and reform under kings such as Mongkut and Chulalongkorn, Siam avoided European colonisation, though it ceded territory to Britain and France. The 20th century brought the end of absolute monarchy, Japanese occupation in the Second World War, rapid economic growth, and both remarkable development and recurring political turmoil.
summary.politicalHistory: A bloodless revolution in 1932 turned Siam, renamed Thailand in 1939, from an absolute into a constitutional monarchy. Since then the country has seen a long series of military coups — around a dozen successful ones — and numerous constitutions, with civilian governments repeatedly displaced, as well as violent crackdowns on protest in 1973, 1976, 1992 and 2010. King Bhumibol Adulyadej's 70-year reign (1946–2016) made the monarchy a central and revered institution protected by strict laws. Today Thailand is a constitutional monarchy with an elected House of Representatives, a Senate chosen through an indirect selection process, and a political life still shaped by tensions between elected parties, the military and the courts.
summary.art: Thai art is rooted in Buddhist devotion: gilded temple murals, graceful bronze Buddha images of the Sukhothai style, and intricate lacquer, mother-of-pearl and gold-leaf work. Classical masked dance-drama (khon), the piphat ensemble and the folk music of mor lam from Isan live alongside luk thung country songs. Literature includes the Ramakien, a Thai version of the Ramayana, and the poetry of Sunthorn Phu, and Thai silk, made famous internationally by Jim Thompson, remains a celebrated craft.
summary.monuments: The Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok, home of the revered Emerald Buddha, are the spiritual and ceremonial heart of the kingdom. The UNESCO-listed historic cities of Ayutthaya and Sukhothai preserve the ruins of earlier Thai capitals, with their stupas, prangs and serene Buddha images. Phanom Rung and Phimai in Isan are magnificent Khmer-era temples, and Wat Arun and Wat Pho, with its giant reclining Buddha, line Bangkok's Chao Phraya River.

highlights.title: Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew
highlights.line: Bangkok's dazzling royal complex and the Emerald Buddha; cover shoulders and knees, and ignore anyone outside claiming it is closed.

highlights.title: Wat Pho
highlights.line: See the 46-metre gilded reclining Buddha, then get a traditional massage at the temple's renowned school.

highlights.title: Wat Arun
highlights.line: The porcelain-studded ‘Temple of Dawn’ across the river; cross by the cheap ferry and return at sunset for the silhouette.

highlights.title: Chao Phraya Express Boat
highlights.line: Bangkok's river is its old highway; the orange-flag boat is a cheap, breezy way between temples and markets.

highlights.title: Yaowarat, Bangkok's Chinatown
highlights.line: After dark the street becomes one long kitchen: try oyster omelette, noodles and mango sticky rice.

highlights.title: Chatuchak Weekend Market
highlights.line: Thousands of stalls of crafts, clothes and food; go early before the heat and bring cash.

highlights.title: Ayutthaya
highlights.line: Explore the ruins of the old capital by bicycle, including the Buddha head entwined in tree roots at Wat Mahathat.

highlights.title: Sukhothai Historical Park
highlights.line: Lotus ponds and serene Buddhas of the first Thai kingdom; magical during Loy Krathong in November.

highlights.title: Kanchanaburi
highlights.line: Walk the Bridge on the River Kwai and visit the war cemetery and Hellfire Pass, honouring the prisoners and Asian labourers who died on the Death Railway.

highlights.title: Erawan Falls
highlights.line: Seven turquoise tiers in a jungle national park; arrive early and swim in the lower pools with the nibbling fish.

highlights.title: Khao Yai National Park
highlights.line: Wild elephants, gibbons and hornbills a few hours from Bangkok; a guided night drive can reveal civets and deer.

highlights.title: Chiang Mai Old City
highlights.line: More than thirty temples inside the moat walls; chat with monks at Wat Chedi Luang's ‘monk chat’.

highlights.title: Doi Suthep
highlights.line: Climb the 300-plus naga-lined steps to Chiang Mai's mountain temple for views over the valley.

highlights.title: Chiang Mai Sunday Walking Street
highlights.line: Ratchadamnoen Road fills with handicrafts, music and food; buy directly from the makers.

highlights.title: Yi Peng & Loy Krathong
highlights.line: Float a candle-lit krathong on the water at the November full moon; choose a banana-leaf one, not foam.

highlights.title: An ethical elephant sanctuary
highlights.line: Choose a sanctuary that does not offer riding or performances, where you watch and feed rescued elephants.

highlights.title: Wat Rong Khun, Chiang Rai
highlights.line: The White Temple is a contemporary artist's vision of heaven and hell; go early to beat the crowds.

highlights.title: Mae Hong Son & Pai
highlights.line: A winding mountain road through misty valleys, hot springs and Shan and Karen villages; drive carefully or take the minibus.

highlights.title: Doi Inthanon
highlights.line: Thailand's highest peak, with twin royal pagodas, cloud forest trails and cool mornings.

highlights.title: Phanom Rung
highlights.line: A Khmer temple on an extinct volcano in Isan; on a few days each year the sun shines through all fifteen doorways.

highlights.title: Mekong at Nong Khai
highlights.line: Slow riverside life facing Laos, with Sala Kaew Ku's giant surreal sculptures nearby.

highlights.title: Isan food
highlights.line: Som tam papaya salad, grilled chicken and sticky rice eaten with your fingers — fiery, sour and unforgettable.

highlights.title: Phang Nga Bay
highlights.line: Kayak through limestone sea caves into hidden lagoons; go early or at high tide with a responsible operator.

highlights.title: Railay, Krabi
highlights.line: Beaches reachable only by boat, framed by limestone cliffs loved by climbers.

highlights.title: Khao Sok National Park
highlights.line: Ancient rainforest and floating raft houses on Cheow Lan Lake; listen for gibbons at dawn.

highlights.title: Similan Islands
highlights.line: Some of Thailand's best diving and snorkelling; the park closes from mid-May to mid-October to let reefs recover.

highlights.title: Ko Lanta
highlights.line: A relaxed island with long beaches, Muslim fishing villages and an old town on stilts.

highlights.title: Ang Thong Marine Park
highlights.line: A day trip from Ko Samui to 42 jungle-clad islands, with a climb to a viewpoint over an emerald lake.

highlights.title: Phuket Old Town
highlights.line: Sino-Portuguese shophouses, Peranakan food and Sunday night market — a different face of the island.

highlights.title: Morning alms round
highlights.line: Watch monks collect food at dawn in reverent quiet; if you offer, kneel, stay silent and don't use flash.

highlights.title: Muay Thai night
highlights.line: Watch a bout at Bangkok's Rajadamnern or Lumpinee stadium, from the ritual wai kru dance to the final round.

highlights.title: Songkran
highlights.line: Thai New Year in mid-April, UNESCO-listed, mixes water fights with gentle rituals of pouring water on elders' hands.

highlights.title: Thai cooking class
highlights.line: Shop at a market, then pound your own curry paste — a favourite in Chiang Mai and Bangkok.

funFacts: Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a European power.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is so long that it is recognised by Guinness as the world's longest place name; Thais call it Krung Thep, ‘City of Angels’.
Siam was officially renamed Thailand in 1939.
Thailand counts years in the Buddhist Era, which is 543 years ahead of the Gregorian calendar.
The Thai alphabet has 44 consonant letters, and spoken Thai has five tones.
The national anthem is played in public spaces and on radio and television at 8 am and 6 pm every day, and many people stand still.
Each day of the week has its own colour in Thai tradition — Monday is yellow, Tuesday pink, Wednesday green.
Kitti's hog-nosed bat, or bumblebee bat, found in western Thailand, is one of the smallest mammals in the world.
Thailand is consistently one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Red Bull grew out of a Thai energy drink called Krating Daeng.
Nuad Thai, traditional Thai massage, was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.
Songkran, the Thai New Year water festival, joined UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2023.
Tom yum kung soup was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2024.
Muay Thai is called ‘the art of eight limbs’ because it uses fists, elbows, knees and shins.
The wai greeting — palms together with a slight bow — changes in height depending on whom you greet.
The head is considered the most sacred part of the body, so touching someone's head is avoided.
Pointing your feet at people or at Buddha images is considered rude.
The Emerald Buddha is carved from green stone, probably jade or jasper, and its robes are changed three times a year with the seasons.
Almost every Thai person has a short nickname, often playful, used far more than their formal name.
Many Thai homes and businesses have a spirit house where offerings are left for the guardian spirits of the land.
Lopburi holds an annual monkey buffet festival in honour of its resident macaques.
At the Phi Ta Khon festival in Dan Sai, villagers dance in colourful ghost masks made from coconut-tree parts and rice steamers.
Chang and Eng Bunker, the famous conjoined twins who gave rise to the term ‘Siamese twins’, were born in Siam in 1811.
The Siamese cat originated in Thailand, where it appears in an old manuscript of cat poems.
Ayutthaya was one of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities in the world around 1700.
Doi Inthanon, at about 2,565 metres, is Thailand's highest mountain.
Thailand's national flower is the ratchaphruek, the golden shower tree, and its national animal is the elephant.
In 2024 Thailand passed a law recognising same-sex marriage, the first country in Southeast Asia to do so.
Thai and Lao are closely related, and many people in Isan speak a language close to Lao at home.
Many Thai men traditionally spend a period as Buddhist monks, sometimes only a few weeks, as an act of merit for their parents.
Thailand's crystal-clear Similan Islands national park closes for about five months each year to protect its reefs.
Durian is so pungent that many Thai hotels and public transport ban it.
Thai students and civil servants wear uniforms, and university students do too.

languageGuide.intro: Thai is tonal, so pitch changes meaning, but a smile and polite end particles go a long way: men end sentences with ‘khrap’, women with ‘kha’. English is common in tourist areas, hotels and Bangkok, but much less so in the countryside, where a few Thai words bring delight.

culture.history: Thai kingdoms rose at Sukhothai in the 13th century and flourished at Ayutthaya until its destruction by Burmese forces in 1767, after which the Chakri dynasty founded Bangkok in 1782. Skilful diplomacy kept Siam from formal colonisation, though it ceded territory to Britain and France. A 1932 revolution ended absolute monarchy, but the decades since have been shaped by repeated military coups and periods of violent crackdown on protest alongside rapid economic growth.
culture.politics: Thailand is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system and a bicameral National Assembly, in which the monarchy is deeply revered and protected by strict lèse-majesté laws. The military has repeatedly intervened in politics, and the balance between elected government, the armed forces and royal institutions is a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Gilded temple architecture such as Wat Arun and Wat Phra Kaew, the masked khon dance drama based on the Ramakien epic, and the piphat percussion ensemble are signature traditions. The 19th-century poet Sunthorn Phu remains beloved, and Thai silk, mural painting and contemporary cinema carry the tradition forward.

love.expression: Affection is often shown gently and indirectly, guided by kreng jai, a considerate wish not to burden or embarrass others. Care tends to appear in small daily acts such as sharing food and spending relaxed time together, and public displays of affection are usually discreet, especially outside big cities.

etiquette: Never touch someone's head or point your feet at people or Buddha images.
Cover shoulders and knees and remove shoes when visiting temples.
Speak respectfully about the royal family; criticism is a serious criminal offence.

name: Morocco

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Tachelhit, Central Atlas Tamazight, Tarifit, Hassaniya and Spanish in the north

people: Moroccans share a blended Arab and Amazigh (Berber) heritage, with many speaking Tachelhit, Central Atlas Tamazight or Tarifit at home, Hassaniya-speaking Sahrawi communities in the south, and Andalusian, Jewish and sub-Saharan African threads woven through the culture. Nearly everyone is Sunni Muslim of the Maliki tradition, with Sufi brotherhoods long important; a small, ancient Jewish community remains and a few Christians, mostly migrants. About two-thirds live in cities such as Casablanca, Rabat, Fes and Marrakesh, and a large diaspora lives in France, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands and Italy.

plug.note: European plugs fit; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: The world's largest phosphate reserves
Sun and wind for a fast-growing renewable energy sector, including the Noor Ouarzazate solar complex
Atlantic and Mediterranean fisheries and ports such as Tanger Med
Agriculture: citrus, olives, tomatoes and the unique argan tree
A young, multilingual population
World-famous crafts, medinas and hospitality
struggles: High youth unemployment and many young people seeking to emigrate
Severe drought and water scarcity affecting farmers and cities
Inequality between cities and rural mountain regions, and recovery after the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake
Female illiteracy and limited work opportunities for women in rural areas
Limits on press freedom and space for dissent
The unresolved dispute over Western Sahara and the long displacement of Sahrawi refugees
prayFor: For families in the Atlas villages still rebuilding homes and lives after the 2023 earthquake
For young Moroccans, for meaningful work at home and for safety for those who risk the sea journey north
For rain on dry fields and wisdom in caring for scarce water
For girls and women in rural areas, for schooling, health care and opportunity
For a just and peaceful resolution in Western Sahara, and comfort for all families divided or displaced by the conflict

summary.history: Some of the oldest known remains of Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years old, were found at Jebel Irhoud, and Amazigh peoples have lived across the land for millennia, trading with Phoenicians and later ruled as part of Roman Mauretania. Arab armies brought Islam in the 7th–8th centuries, and dynasties such as the Idrisids, Almoravids, Almohads, Marinids, Saadians and the Alaouites — ruling since the 17th century — built empires stretching at times into Spain and West Africa. In 1912 Morocco was divided into French and Spanish protectorates, resisted notably in the Rif War of the 1920s. Independence in 1956 was followed by decades of development and hardship, including the repression of the ‘Years of Lead’, and today Morocco is a fast-modernising country bridging Africa, Europe and the Arab world.
summary.politicalHistory: Morocco regained independence from France and Spain in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V, who took the title of king, and his son Hassan II ruled from 1961 to 1999 through a period of coup attempts and political repression known as the Years of Lead. Since 1975 Morocco has administered most of Western Sahara, whose sovereignty is contested by the Polisario Front, which fought a war with Morocco until a 1991 UN ceasefire; many Sahrawis have lived for decades in refugee camps in Algeria. In 2004 a truth commission examined past abuses, and after the 2011 protests a new constitution recognised Tamazight as an official language and gave more powers to the elected government. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in which the king retains strong executive and religious authority as Commander of the Faithful, alongside an elected parliament and a prime minister drawn from the largest party.
summary.art: Morocco's craft traditions are dazzling: zellij mosaic tilework, carved cedar and stucco, Fes blue pottery, Amazigh carpets and silver jewellery, and leather from the old tanneries. Music spans Andalusian classical nuba, Amazigh ahwash and ahidous, the trance music of the Gnawa and the chaabi popular songs, while writers such as Ibn Battuta, Driss Chraïbi, Mohamed Choukri, Fatima Mernissi and Tahar Ben Jelloun have shaped its literature. Calligraphy and the architecture of madrasas and riads show a refined Islamic aesthetic of pattern and light.
summary.monuments: The medinas of Fes, Marrakesh, Meknes, Tétouan and Essaouira are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, living cities of souks, mosques and madrasas such as Fes's Bou Inania and the University of al-Qarawiyyin. The Roman ruins of Volubilis recall the ancient province, and the earthen ksar of Aït Benhaddou embodies the caravan architecture of the south. Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque, with one of the world's tallest minarets, and Rabat's Hassan Tower and Kasbah of the Udayas show Morocco's grandeur old and new.

highlights.title: Jemaa el-Fna, Marrakesh
highlights.line: The great square becomes an open-air theatre of storytellers, musicians and food stalls at dusk; agree prices before photos with performers.

highlights.title: Majorelle Garden
highlights.line: Cobalt-blue villa, cacti and bamboo restored by Yves Saint Laurent; book a timed ticket and include the Berber Museum inside.

highlights.title: Bahia Palace & Ben Youssef Madrasa
highlights.line: Marrakesh's finest carved cedar, stucco and zellij; go at opening time for quiet courtyards.

highlights.title: Fes el-Bali
highlights.line: One of the world's largest car-free medinas; hire a licensed guide for your first day in the maze.

highlights.title: Chouara Tannery, Fes
highlights.line: Watch leather dyed in stone vats as it has been for centuries, from a leather shop's terrace — take the offered sprig of mint.

highlights.title: Al-Qarawiyyin & Bou Inania, Fes
highlights.line: Glimpse the ancient mosque-university through its doors, then enter the Marinid madrasa of Bou Inania, open to non-Muslims.

highlights.title: Chefchaouen
highlights.line: A blue-washed town in the Rif mountains; climb to the Spanish Mosque at sunset and hike to Akchour waterfalls.

highlights.title: Volubilis
highlights.line: Roman mosaics and columns in olive country; visit in the morning and combine with the holy town of Moulay Idriss.

highlights.title: Meknes
highlights.line: The imperial city of Moulay Ismail, with the monumental Bab Mansour gate and vast royal granaries.

highlights.title: Hassan II Mosque, Casablanca
highlights.line: A vast mosque partly over the Atlantic; non-Muslims can join guided tours outside prayer times.

highlights.title: Rabat's Kasbah of the Udayas
highlights.line: White-and-blue lanes and an Andalusian garden above the river mouth; pair with the Hassan Tower and Mohammed V Mausoleum.

highlights.title: Tangier
highlights.line: Where Africa looks at Europe: wander the Kasbah, the American Legation museum and Café Hafa's terraces over the strait.

highlights.title: Tétouan medina
highlights.line: A UNESCO-listed medina with strong Andalusian influence and excellent crafts school, far calmer than Fes or Marrakesh.

highlights.title: Asilah
highlights.line: A whitewashed seaside town whose walls are repainted with murals each year during its arts festival.

highlights.title: Aït Benhaddou
highlights.line: A fortified earthen village on the old caravan route, seen in many films; cross the river at golden hour.

highlights.title: Ouarzazate & the Draa Valley
highlights.line: Kasbahs and palm groves leading toward the Sahara; visit Taourirt Kasbah and the film studios.

highlights.title: Todra & Dades Gorges
highlights.line: Sheer red canyons and switchback roads; walk the floor of Todra early, when the light pours in.

highlights.title: Erg Chebbi, Merzouga
highlights.line: Ride into the dunes for a night in a desert camp, music by the fire and a sky crowded with stars.

highlights.title: Erg Chigaga
highlights.line: Wilder, remoter dunes beyond M'Hamid reached by 4x4 — quieter than Merzouga for those with time.

highlights.title: Imlil & Toubkal
highlights.line: Trek through Amazigh villages to North Africa's highest peak (4,167 m); a local guide is required and supports the communities rebuilding after the earthquake.

highlights.title: Ourika Valley
highlights.line: An easy escape from Marrakesh to riverside cafés and waterfalls at Setti Fatma.

highlights.title: Ouzoud Waterfalls
highlights.line: Morocco's highest falls tumble 110 metres among olive trees, with Barbary macaques nearby — don't feed them.

highlights.title: Ifrane & the cedar forests
highlights.line: The ‘Switzerland of Morocco’ in the Middle Atlas, where ancient cedars shelter wild Barbary macaques.

highlights.title: Essaouira
highlights.line: A windswept Atlantic port with UNESCO-listed ramparts; eat grilled sardines by the harbour and visit in June for the Gnaoua festival.

highlights.title: Taghazout
highlights.line: A surf village north of Agadir with gentle lessons for beginners and world-class breaks for the experienced.

highlights.title: Legzira & Sidi Ifni
highlights.line: Red cliffs and rock arches on a wild Atlantic beach, best at low tide and sunset.

highlights.title: Dakhla
highlights.line: A lagoon on the Atlantic coast of the far south famous for kitesurfing, oysters and desert-meets-ocean landscapes.

highlights.title: Argan cooperatives
highlights.line: Women's cooperatives in the Souss region crack argan nuts by hand; buy directly so more money reaches them.

highlights.title: A traditional hammam
highlights.line: Steam, black soap and a vigorous scrub with a kessa glove; bring a change of underwear and go to the local, not only the spa version.

highlights.title: Mint tea
highlights.line: Poured from height for foam and offered as a sign of welcome; accepting a glass is part of every conversation.

highlights.title: Friday couscous
highlights.line: Couscous is traditionally the Friday family meal; try it at a home or small restaurant after midday prayers.

highlights.title: Tagine & a cooking class
highlights.line: Slow-cooked tagines with preserved lemon, olives or prunes; learn to make one in a riad kitchen.

highlights.title: Ramadan iftar
highlights.line: If you visit during Ramadan, share the sunset meal of harira soup, dates and chebakia, and be discreet eating in public by day.

funFacts: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fes, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, is recognised by UNESCO and Guinness as the oldest existing, continually operating educational institution in the world.
Morocco was one of the first countries to recognise the independence of the United States, in 1777.
The American Legation in Tangier is the oldest building owned by the US government abroad.
Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, about 300,000 years old, are among the oldest known remains of Homo sapiens.
The minaret of Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque rises about 210 metres, one of the tallest in the world.
Morocco holds around 70% of the world's known phosphate reserves.
At the 2022 World Cup, Morocco became the first African and Arab team to reach the semi-finals.
Morocco will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal.
The 2011 constitution made Tamazight an official language alongside Arabic.
Tamazight is often written in Tifinagh, an ancient script that can be seen on road signs and public buildings.
The argan tree grows naturally almost nowhere else in the world but southwestern Morocco.
Goats sometimes climb argan trees to eat the fruit.
Couscous was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020 in a joint bid by Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania.
Gnawa music and culture was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.
Tbourida, the equestrian display in which riders fire muskets in unison, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
Mount Toubkal, at 4,167 metres, is the highest peak in North Africa.
At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco from Spain by only about 14 kilometres.
The name ‘Morocco’ comes from the city of Marrakesh.
The film ‘Casablanca’ (1942) was shot entirely in California.
Aït Benhaddou and the studios of Ouarzazate have appeared in films such as ‘Lawrence of Arabia’ and ‘Gladiator’.
The Noor Ouarzazate complex is one of the largest concentrated solar power plants in the world.
The great traveller Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier in 1304 and journeyed for nearly thirty years across Africa and Asia.
The Barbary macaque, found in Morocco's Atlas forests, is the only macaque species native to Africa.
Morocco is the world's largest exporter of canned sardines.
Taliouine in the Anti-Atlas is famous for producing some of the world's finest saffron.
The Alaouite dynasty has ruled Morocco since the 17th century, making it one of the world's oldest reigning dynasties.
The traditional Jewish quarters of Moroccan cities are called mellahs.
Each May, Kelaat M'Gouna in the Dades valley celebrates the rose harvest with a festival.
Chefchaouen's houses are painted in shades of blue, a tradition often linked to the Jewish refugees who settled there.
Moroccan Darija mixes Arabic with Amazigh, French and Spanish words — for example, ‘train station’ is ‘lagar’, from French.
The Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira brings Gnawa masters together with jazz and world musicians every year.
Fes's al-Attarine and Bou Inania madrasas date from the 14th century under the Marinid dynasty.
The Tanger Med port is one of the largest container ports in Africa and the Mediterranean.

languageGuide.intro: Darija is a spoken Moroccan Arabic, rich in Amazigh, French and Spanish words, and ‘afak’ (please) and ‘shukran’ open every door; ‘kh’ is a throaty sound as in Scottish ‘loch’, and some words change for men and women (shown as m/f). French is widely spoken in cities, business and tourism, Spanish in the north, and English increasingly among young people, while many rural people speak Tamazight first.

phrases.en: Reply: and peace be upon you
How are you? / Fine, thank God

phraseLanguage: Moroccan Arabic (Darija); French is also widely used in cities, business and administration

culture.history: Amazigh (Berber) peoples have lived here for millennia, meeting Phoenician traders and Roman rule before Arab armies brought Islam in the 7th century. Great dynasties such as the Idrisids, Almoravids and Almohads ruled empires reaching into Al-Andalus, and the Alaouite dynasty has reigned since the 17th century. France and Spain imposed protectorates in 1912, and independence came in 1956. The decades that followed included the repression of the 'Years of Lead', later examined by a national truth commission, and the long-unresolved dispute over Western Sahara.
culture.politics: Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in which the king holds substantial executive and religious authority as Commander of the Faithful, alongside an elected bicameral parliament and a prime minister drawn from the largest party. The 2011 constitution expanded parliamentary powers and recognised Tamazight as an official language, making Amazigh identity a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Zellige tilework, carved cedar and stucco fill riads and madrasas such as Fez's Bou Inania, and the University of al-Qarawiyyin was founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri. Gnawa trance music, Andalusian classical music and Amazigh song thrive, and literature runs from the travels of Ibn Battuta to Fatema Mernissi and Tahar Ben Jelloun.

love.expression: Love is often shown through hospitality and family loyalty: pouring mint tea, cooking a shared tagine, and being present for weddings and feasts that can last for days. Public displays of romance are generally modest, while affection between friends and relatives is warm and demonstrative, with customs varying between city and countryside.

etiquette: Use your right hand for eating, especially when sharing from a common dish, and accept offered mint tea.
Dress modestly, particularly outside tourist areas and during Ramadan, when eating in public by day is best avoided.
Ask before photographing people; French is a helpful second language in cities and shops.

name: Egypt

main: English and French in business and tourism
languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Nubian languages, Siwi (Amazigh) and Bedouin Arabic varieties

people: Around 116 million people live in Egypt, the great majority in the narrow Nile Valley and Delta, which make up only about 5% of the land; Greater Cairo alone is home to over 20 million. Roughly 90% are Sunni Muslim and around 10% Christian, mostly Coptic Orthodox — one of the world's oldest churches — alongside Nubians in the south, Bedouin communities in Sinai and the deserts, and Siwi-speaking Amazigh people at Siwa Oasis. It is a young, family-centred society, and millions of Egyptians work abroad, especially in the Gulf, sending home vital remittances.

plug.note: European plugs fit; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

basics.en: Please (to a man / to a woman)

resources: The Nile River and the fertile Delta
The Suez Canal
Offshore natural gas (such as the Zohr field)
Unrivalled ancient heritage and tourism
A large, young workforce and diaspora remittances
Cultural influence in the Arab world — Al-Azhar, film, music and media
struggles: Severe inflation and repeated devaluations of the pound since 2022 have squeezed household budgets and food prices
Water scarcity: Egypt depends almost entirely on the Nile, and the dispute over Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam remains unresolved
Rapid population growth, crowded cities and high youth unemployment
Tight restrictions on political opposition, civil society and press freedom, with many people held in pre-trial detention
Climate risk to the low-lying Delta from sea-level rise and soil salinisation
Regional shocks — the wars in Gaza and Sudan, refugees arriving from Sudan, and Red Sea shipping attacks cutting Suez Canal revenue
prayFor: For families stretched by rising prices — that bread, rent and school fees stay within reach, and that work brings dignity to Egypt's young people
For the Nile and all who depend on it — wise, peaceful agreements over water between Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia
For Muslims and Christians to keep living as neighbours in mutual respect, and for the protection of Coptic communities and their churches
For freedom of conscience and speech, and for prisoners and their families waiting for news
For Sudanese and other refugees finding shelter in Egypt, and for Egyptians who open their homes to them

summary.history: Along the Nile one of the world's first states arose around 3100 BCE, and for nearly three thousand years pharaonic Egypt built pyramids, temples and a written civilisation of astonishing continuity. Persians, Alexander the Great, the Ptolemies and Rome followed; Christianity took deep root, and after the Arab conquest of 639–642 CE Egypt gradually became Arabic-speaking and majority Muslim. Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman rulers shaped medieval Cairo, until Napoleon's invasion in 1798 and the modernising dynasty of Muhammad Ali, whose forced-labour projects and debts paved the way for the Suez Canal (1869) and British occupation in 1882. The twentieth century brought a long struggle for full independence, wars with Israel between 1948 and 1973, peace in 1979, and in 2011 a popular uprising whose hopes for freedom remain only partly fulfilled.
summary.politicalHistory: Britain declared Egypt nominally independent as a kingdom in 1922 but kept troops there until 1956. The Free Officers' coup of 1952 ended the monarchy; Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal and led pan-Arab politics, Anwar Sadat made peace with Israel and was assassinated in 1981, and Hosni Mubarak then ruled for three decades. Mass protests toppled Mubarak in 2011, and Mohamed Morsi became the first freely elected president in 2012, before the military removed him in 2013 amid huge demonstrations and a deadly crackdown on his supporters. Egypt is today a presidential republic under the 2014 constitution (amended in 2019), in which the armed forces play a powerful role and political opposition is tightly limited.
summary.art: Pharaonic reliefs, statues, painted tombs and hieroglyphs set a visual language that endured for three millennia, later joined by Coptic textiles and icons and the Islamic arts of Cairo — calligraphy, mashrabiya lattice, inlaid wood and Mamluk metalwork. In the twentieth century Cairo became the Arab world's capital of film and song, with Umm Kulthum, Mohamed Abdel Wahab and Abdel Halim Hafez, while Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. Living crafts include the appliqué tent-making (khayamiya) of Cairo, Nubian painted houses, Fayoum pottery and Siwan embroidery.
summary.monuments: The Pyramids of Giza, Saqqara and Dahshur and Ancient Thebes — Karnak, Luxor Temple and the Valley of the Kings — are UNESCO World Heritage Sites at the heart of pharaonic history. The Nubian monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae were cut apart and moved to higher ground in a famous UNESCO rescue campaign when Lake Nasser rose in the 1960s. Historic Cairo, with the mosques of Ibn Tulun and Sultan Hassan and the churches of Coptic Cairo, and Saint Catherine's Monastery beneath Mount Sinai bear witness to Egypt's long Islamic and Christian story.

highlights.title: Pyramids of Giza & the Great Sphinx
highlights.line: The last standing Wonder of the Ancient World; arrive at opening time to beat heat and crowds, and walk to the panorama point for the classic view of all the pyramids.

highlights.title: Grand Egyptian Museum
highlights.line: A vast new museum beside the Giza plateau built to hold the treasures of Tutankhamun together; give it at least half a day and book tickets online.

highlights.title: National Museum of Egyptian Civilization
highlights.line: In Fustat, the Royal Mummies Hall lets you stand quietly before pharaohs such as Ramesses II; photography is not allowed in the hall.

highlights.title: Saqqara & the Step Pyramid of Djoser
highlights.line: The world's oldest monumental stone building, with beautifully carved private tombs nearby; combine it with Memphis and Dahshur in one day.

highlights.title: Dahshur's Bent & Red Pyramids
highlights.line: Quiet, uncrowded pyramids where you can climb down into the Red Pyramid's chambers — bring a scarf against the dust and a sense of adventure.

highlights.title: Al-Muizz Street, Islamic Cairo
highlights.line: A living open-air museum of Fatimid and Mamluk mosques, madrasas and fountains; come in the late afternoon when the lamps come on.

highlights.title: Khan el-Khalili bazaar
highlights.line: Cairo's medieval market for brass lanterns, spices and silver; rest with mint tea at the historic El Fishawy café and bargain with a smile.

highlights.title: Coptic Cairo
highlights.line: The Hanging Church, the Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus — remembered as a resting place of the Holy Family — and the Ben Ezra Synagogue sit within a few steps of each other.

highlights.title: Cairo Citadel
highlights.line: Saladin's fortress crowned by the Ottoman-style Mosque of Muhammad Ali offers a sweeping view over the city's minarets on clear days.

highlights.title: Al-Azhar Mosque & Al-Azhar Park
highlights.line: Pray or reflect in the thousand-year-old mosque, then watch sunset over the old city from the gardens built on a former rubbish mound.

highlights.title: Felucca sail in Aswan
highlights.line: Drift between granite boulders and Elephantine Island in a wooden sailboat at golden hour — the gentlest way to meet the Nile.

highlights.title: Karnak Temple, Luxor
highlights.line: Walk among the 134 colossal columns of the Great Hypostyle Hall; go early morning and return for the evening sound-and-light show if you like.

highlights.title: Luxor Temple by night
highlights.line: Floodlit statues of Ramesses II and an ancient avenue of sphinxes glow after dark — and a mosque still sits atop the temple's columns.

highlights.title: Valley of the Kings
highlights.line: Royal tombs painted with the journey of the sun through the underworld; your ticket covers three tombs, with extra tickets for gems such as Seti I.

highlights.title: Hot-air balloon over Luxor's West Bank
highlights.line: Rise at dawn above temples, sugarcane fields and the Theban hills; choose a licensed operator with a good safety record.

highlights.title: Temple of Hatshepsut
highlights.line: The terraced temple of Egypt's great female pharaoh at Deir el-Bahari, set dramatically against sheer cliffs.

highlights.title: Nile cruise or dahabiya
highlights.line: Sail between Luxor and Aswan stopping at Edfu and Kom Ombo; a small sailing dahabiya offers a slower, more intimate trip than the big boats.

highlights.title: Abu Simbel
highlights.line: Ramesses II's temples, moved stone by stone in the 1960s; join the early convoy or fly from Aswan, and visit around 22 February or 22 October for the solar alignment.

highlights.title: Philae Temple
highlights.line: The island temple of Isis reached by small boat, one of the last places where the old Egyptian religion was practised.

highlights.title: Nubian village of Gharb Soheil
highlights.line: Brightly painted houses, Nubian music and hospitality on the west bank near Aswan; ask before photographing people.

highlights.title: Alexandria
highlights.line: Stroll the Mediterranean corniche, visit the Bibliotheca Alexandrina and Qaitbay Citadel, and eat fresh fish chosen by weight in a seafront restaurant.

highlights.title: Siwa Oasis
highlights.line: Palm groves, salt lakes you can float in, mud-brick Shali fortress and Amazigh culture near the Libyan border — a long but rewarding journey.

highlights.title: White Desert
highlights.line: Chalk formations shaped like mushrooms and birds near Farafra; camp under brilliant stars with a licensed desert guide.

highlights.title: Mount Sinai & Saint Catherine's Monastery
highlights.line: Climb through the night to watch sunrise from the summit with Bedouin guides, then visit one of the oldest working Christian monasteries in the world.

highlights.title: Red Sea diving and snorkelling
highlights.line: Ras Mohammed and Dahab offer coral reefs teeming with fish; check current travel advice for Sinai and respect reef rules.

highlights.title: Wadi al-Hitan (Whale Valley)
highlights.line: A UNESCO desert valley in Fayoum where fossil whales with tiny hind legs lie in the sand — a startling lesson in deep time.

highlights.title: Koshary
highlights.line: Egypt's beloved street dish of rice, lentils, pasta and crispy onions under spicy tomato sauce; order it at a busy specialist shop.

highlights.title: Ful and ta'meya breakfast
highlights.line: Slow-cooked fava beans and Egyptian falafel made with fava rather than chickpeas, scooped up with baladi bread.

highlights.title: Fresh juices and karkadeh
highlights.line: Sip sugarcane juice from a street stall or chilled hibiscus karkadeh — sweet, cooling and very Egyptian.

highlights.title: Ramadan nights in Cairo
highlights.line: Streets glow with fanous lanterns and fill with shared iftar tables after sunset; join respectfully and avoid eating in public during fasting hours.

highlights.title: Temple of Seti I at Abydos
highlights.line: Some of the finest reliefs in Egypt, with paint still bright, and far fewer visitors than Luxor.

highlights.title: Dendera Temple of Hathor
highlights.line: Restored ceilings of deep blue and gold and a famous zodiac relief; an easy day trip north of Luxor.

highlights.title: Tanoura and Sufi music in Cairo
highlights.line: Watch whirling dancers in swirling coloured skirts at an evening performance in a historic Mamluk building such as Wekalet El Ghouri.

funFacts: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for around 3,800 years.
Cleopatra VII lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
Egyptians call their country Masr — and in everyday speech often use the same word for Cairo.
Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira, means 'the Victorious'.
Al-Azhar in Cairo has been a centre of learning since the 10th century and is one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, has no locks, because the Mediterranean and the Red Sea are at nearly the same level.
Roughly 95% of Egyptians live on only about 5% of the country's land, along the Nile and in the Delta.
The Nile flows from south to north, so 'Upper Egypt' is in the south and 'Lower Egypt' is the Delta in the north.
The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799 near the town of Rashid, carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
The English word 'paper' comes from papyrus, the Nile reed Egyptians used as a writing surface for thousands of years.
Archaeologists have found the town where pyramid builders lived, with bakeries and breweries, pointing to an organised workforce rather than the slaves of popular legend.
Ancient Egypt used a civil calendar of 365 days: twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days.
The temples of Abu Simbel were cut into more than a thousand blocks and reassembled about 65 metres higher to save them from Lake Nasser.
Twice a year, around 22 February and 22 October, sunlight reaches deep into Abu Simbel's sanctuary to light up statues of the gods and Ramesses II.
Lake Nasser, created by the Aswan High Dam, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
The Coptic language, the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language, is still used in the liturgy of the Coptic Orthodox Church.
Egypt's Copts form the largest Christian community in the Middle East.
Christian tradition says the Holy Family fled to Egypt, and churches along a route from Sinai to Upper Egypt remember their journey.
Sham el-Nessim, a spring holiday with roots in pharaonic times, is celebrated by Egyptians of all faiths with picnics, coloured eggs and salted fish.
Egyptian ta'meya (falafel) is made from fava beans rather than chickpeas, giving it a green centre.
Molokhia, a silky green soup of jute leaves, has been eaten in Egypt for centuries and inspires fierce family loyalty about how to cook it.
The Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002, was built to revive the spirit of Alexandria's ancient Great Library.
Alexandria's Qaitbay Citadel stands on the site of the ancient Pharos lighthouse, another of the Seven Wonders, and was likely built partly from its stones.
Naguib Mahfouz, a Cairo novelist, was the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1988.
Umm Kulthum's monthly Thursday-night concerts were broadcast across the Arab world, and a single song could last more than an hour.
Wadi al-Hitan holds fossils of ancient whales that still had small hind legs, showing how whales evolved from land mammals.
Cairo's metro, opened in 1987, was the first full metro system in Africa.
Egypt spans two continents: the Sinai Peninsula lies in Asia.
Egypt's highest peak is Mount Catherine in Sinai, about 2,629 metres high.
Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai holds one of the oldest continually used libraries in the world.
Ancient Egyptians honoured cats as sacred to the goddess Bastet, and vast numbers of mummified cats have been found at temple sites.
Aswan is one of the driest inhabited places on Earth, with almost no rain in most years.

languageGuide.intro: Egyptian Arabic (Masri) is the most widely understood Arabic dialect thanks to Egyptian film and TV; many words change slightly when speaking to a man or a woman, and the hard 'g' (as in 'go') replaces the 'j' of other dialects. English is common in hotels and tourist sites, and a few words of Arabic — especially 'shukran' and 'law samaht' — open hearts quickly.

phrases.en: How are you? (to a man / to a woman)
Can you lower the price a little?
What's your name? (to a man / to a woman)
Where are you from? (to a man / to a woman)
I need a doctor (man / woman speaking)
Please (to a man / to a woman)

culture.history: Along the Nile one of the world's earliest civilisations built pyramids, temples and a written culture spanning three millennia of pharaonic rule. Egypt then passed through Persian, Ptolemaic and Roman hands, became an early heartland of Christianity whose Coptic church endures, and after the Arab conquest of the 7th century became a centre of Islamic learning under the Fatimids and Mamluks. Ottoman rule was followed by British occupation from 1882, and the 1952 Free Officers' revolution ended the monarchy. Mass protests in 2011 voiced a deep longing for dignity and reform, followed by years of political upheaval.
culture.politics: Egypt is a presidential republic with a powerful executive, a bicameral parliament of the House of Representatives and the Senate, and a long-standing central role for the armed forces. The relationship between state security, the military and civil liberties has been a defining civic theme since 1952.
culture.arts: The monuments of Giza, Luxor and Abu Simbel, Coptic icons and the mosques and madrasas of Islamic Cairo make Egypt a living museum of architecture. Umm Kulthum's voice defined Arabic music for generations, Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, and Cairo has long been the heart of Arabic-language cinema.

love.expression: Affection is expressed warmly and often with words: compliments, blessings and the poetic language of classic love songs by singers like Abdel Halim Hafez. Family and friendship are central, with generous hospitality and long evenings together, while public romance is usually modest and customs differ between Muslim and Christian families, city and village.

iLoveYou.roman: Bahebbak (to a man) / Bahebbik (to a woman)

etiquette: Use your right hand for eating and handing things over.
Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, and women should bring a scarf for mosque visits.
Small tips (baksheesh) are customary for many services, so carry small notes.

name: Kenya

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Gikuyu, Dholuo, Luhya, Kalenjin, Kamba, Maa, Somali and Sheng street slang

people: Kenya is home to more than 40 ethnic communities — among the largest the Kikuyu, Luhya, Kalenjin, Luo and Kamba, alongside the Kisii, Meru, Mijikenda, Maasai, Samburu, Turkana, Somali and Swahili peoples — as well as Kenyans of Indian, Arab and European heritage. Around 85% are Christian, Protestant and Catholic with many independent African churches, and roughly 11% Muslim, mainly on the coast and in the north-east. The population is very young and still mostly rural, though Nairobi and other towns are growing fast, and Kenya also hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees, many from Somalia and South Sudan.

plug.note: UK plugs fit; European and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: Iconic wildlife and national parks such as the Maasai Mara
Tea, coffee and cut flowers
Geothermal and other renewable power from the Rift Valley
Mobile-money and tech innovation (M-Pesa, 'Silicon Savannah')
World-class distance runners and a young, entrepreneurial population
The Port of Mombasa, gateway to East Africa
struggles: High living costs, heavy public debt and tax rises — which sparked large youth-led protests in 2024, met with deadly force
Youth unemployment and a large informal economy, with many young graduates struggling to find work
Recurring droughts and floods hitting pastoralist communities in the arid north and east
Corruption and unequal access to land, healthcare and services
Insecurity in border areas, including al-Shabaab attacks near Somalia and deadly cattle raiding in the north-west
prayFor: For Kenya's young people — work that honours their gifts, and leaders who listen to their voices
For pastoralist families facing drought and flood, that rain and water come in season and herds and children are kept safe
For integrity in public life, and for the courage of those who resist corruption
For peace between communities, healing for those bereaved in protests and conflict, and safety along the northern borders
For refugees in Kakuma and Dadaab, and for the Kenyans who welcome them

summary.history: The shores of Lake Turkana hold some of humanity's oldest fossils and stone tools, and over thousands of years Cushitic, Nilotic and Bantu-speaking peoples settled the highlands, plains and coast. From around the 8th century, Swahili city-states such as Lamu, Malindi and Mombasa grew rich on Indian Ocean trade, later fought over by the Portuguese and the Omani Arabs, and the coast was also scarred by the slave trade. Britain took control in the 1890s, built the Uganda Railway and gave fertile highlands to white settlers, provoking the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s, which was crushed with mass detention camps and brutality. Independent since 1963, Kenya has become East Africa's largest economy while wrestling with inequality, ethnic tensions and the deep wounds of the 2007–08 post-election violence.
summary.politicalHistory: Kenya won independence from Britain on 12 December 1963 and became a republic in 1964 under Jomo Kenyatta, with the KANU party soon dominant. Under Daniel arap Moi Kenya became a one-party state by law in 1982, until domestic and international pressure restored multiparty politics in 1991; the opposition victory of Mwai Kibaki in 2002 ended KANU's long rule. The disputed 2007 election triggered violence that killed over 1,100 people, leading to a power-sharing deal and a new constitution in 2010 with a strong bill of rights and 47 devolved counties. Kenya is today a presidential republic with a bicameral parliament and an independent judiciary, whose Supreme Court in 2017 became the first in Africa to annul a presidential election.
summary.art: Oral storytelling, proverbs and praise poetry live on across Kenya's communities, while Swahili literature reaches back centuries to epic poems written in Arabic script; modern voices include Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Grace Ogot, Margaret Ogola and Binyavanga Wainaina. Music ranges from Luo benga and Swahili taarab to Congolese-influenced rhumba, gospel and today's Gengetone and Afro-pop. Crafts include Maasai and Samburu beadwork, Kamba wood carving, Kisii soapstone, carved Swahili doors in Lamu and the bright kanga cloths printed with proverbs.
summary.monuments: Lamu Old Town, Fort Jesus in Mombasa and the Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests are UNESCO World Heritage Sites that tell the coast's Swahili, Portuguese and Mijikenda story. The Thimlich Ohinga stone enclosures near Lake Victoria and the Lake Turkana National Parks hold deep human history, and the medieval Swahili town of Gedi lies in the forest near Malindi. Mount Kenya and the lakes of the Great Rift Valley are protected as natural World Heritage for their beauty and wildlife.

highlights.title: Maasai Mara National Reserve
highlights.line: Big cats, elephants and, from about July to October, the Great Migration's dramatic river crossings; conservancies bordering the reserve offer quieter game drives and support Maasai landowners.

highlights.title: Amboseli National Park
highlights.line: Large elephant herds against the snows of Kilimanjaro; the mountain is clearest at dawn.

highlights.title: Nairobi National Park
highlights.line: Lions, rhinos and giraffes with the city skyline behind them, just a short drive from downtown — go early in the morning.

highlights.title: Sheldrick Wildlife Trust elephant orphanage
highlights.line: Watch rescued baby elephants at their late-morning mud bath in Nairobi; booking ahead is required.

highlights.title: Giraffe Centre, Nairobi
highlights.line: Meet endangered Rothschild's giraffes eye to eye from a raised platform and learn about their conservation.

highlights.title: Nairobi National Museum
highlights.line: Kenya's history, art and the fossil story of human origins, with a botanic garden and snake park next door.

highlights.title: Lake Nakuru National Park
highlights.line: A Rift Valley soda lake with rhinos, tree-climbing lions on lucky days, and flamingos when water levels allow.

highlights.title: Hell's Gate & Lake Naivasha
highlights.line: Cycle past zebras and giraffes through a dramatic gorge, then take a boat among hippos on the lake.

highlights.title: Mount Longonot
highlights.line: A rewarding half-day hike to a volcanic crater rim with views across the Rift Valley floor.

highlights.title: Mount Kenya
highlights.line: Africa's second-highest mountain; trek to Point Lenana (4,985 m) over several days with a licensed guide and allow time to acclimatise.

highlights.title: Samburu National Reserve
highlights.line: Arid northern landscapes and the 'Samburu special five' — Grevy's zebra, reticulated giraffe, Beisa oryx, gerenuk and Somali ostrich.

highlights.title: Ol Pejeta Conservancy
highlights.line: Home to the world's last two northern white rhinos and a chimpanzee sanctuary, straddling the equator near Nanyuki.

highlights.title: Tsavo East & West
highlights.line: Red-dusted elephants, lava flows and the clear Mzima Springs in one of Kenya's largest protected areas.

highlights.title: Lamu Old Town
highlights.line: A car-free Swahili town of carved doors, narrow lanes and donkeys; sail on a dhow at sunset and dress modestly in town.

highlights.title: Fort Jesus & Mombasa Old Town
highlights.line: A 16th-century Portuguese fort and the coral-stone lanes around it; try Swahili street snacks as the call to prayer drifts over the harbour.

highlights.title: Diani Beach
highlights.line: Long white sands, coral reefs and colobus monkeys in the coastal forest south of Mombasa.

highlights.title: Watamu & Mida Creek
highlights.line: Turtle conservation, marine-park snorkelling and a creek boardwalk through mangroves for birdwatching.

highlights.title: Gedi Ruins
highlights.line: The haunting remains of a medieval Swahili town hidden in forest near Malindi, with mosques and palace walls.

highlights.title: Lake Turkana
highlights.line: The 'Jade Sea' of the remote north, where fossil sites and Turkana, El Molo and Dassanech communities await the adventurous traveller.

highlights.title: Kakamega Forest
highlights.line: Kenya's last remnant of Guineo-Congolian rainforest, alive with birds, butterflies and monkeys; walk with a local guide.

highlights.title: Kisumu & Lake Victoria
highlights.line: Sunsets over Africa's largest lake and fresh tilapia fried by the shore at Dunga Beach.

highlights.title: Thimlich Ohinga
highlights.line: Dry-stone enclosures built centuries ago near Lake Victoria, a UNESCO site that few travellers reach.

highlights.title: Iten, 'Home of Champions'
highlights.line: Run at altitude alongside world-class athletes in the highland town that has produced generations of champions.

highlights.title: Lake Bogoria
highlights.line: Hot springs and spouting geysers on a lakeshore that is sometimes pink with flamingos.

highlights.title: Nyama choma
highlights.line: Slow-roasted goat or beef shared with friends, best with kachumbari salad and ugali on a Saturday afternoon.

highlights.title: Ugali and sukuma wiki
highlights.line: The everyday Kenyan plate: firm maize-meal ugali with sautéed collard greens, eaten by hand.

highlights.title: Kenyan chai
highlights.line: Tea boiled with milk, sugar and sometimes ginger or spices — the rhythm of every Kenyan day.

highlights.title: Swahili coastal cuisine
highlights.line: Coconut fish curry, pilau and fluffy mahamri doughnuts in Mombasa or Lamu.

highlights.title: Riding a matatu
highlights.line: Graffiti-painted minibuses with booming music are Nairobi's beating heart; hold your bag close and enjoy the ride.

highlights.title: Sunday church service
highlights.line: Join a joyful service with choirs and dancing in a Nairobi or village church — visitors are warmly welcomed.

highlights.title: Maasai Market
highlights.line: A rotating Nairobi craft market for beadwork, kikoi cloths and carvings; bargain kindly and buy direct from artisans.

highlights.title: Kiambu coffee farm tour
highlights.line: Follow Kenya's prized coffee from red cherry to cup on a farm just outside Nairobi.

highlights.title: Lamu Cultural Festival
highlights.line: Dhow races, donkey races, Swahili poetry and music celebrate the island's heritage; dates vary each year.

funFacts: Kenya takes its name from Mount Kenya, known in Gikuyu as Kirinyaga.
The equator runs through Kenya, and towns like Nanyuki have signs marking the exact line.
Mount Kenya, at 5,199 metres, is the second-highest mountain in Africa after Kilimanjaro.
M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007, pioneered sending money by mobile phone and is now used by the large majority of Kenyan adults.
Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004; her Green Belt Movement has planted tens of millions of trees.
'Turkana Boy', found near Lake Turkana in 1984, is one of the most complete early human skeletons ever discovered, about 1.5 million years old.
Lake Turkana is the world's largest permanent desert lake.
Kenya is one of the world's biggest exporters of black tea.
Many of the roses sold in European flower shops were grown on farms around Lake Naivasha.
Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019.
'Hakuna matata' really is Swahili, meaning 'there are no worries'.
Swahili is a Bantu language enriched by centuries of contact with Arabic, Persian, Portuguese and English.
Lamu Old Town has almost no cars; donkeys and boats are the main way to get around.
Most of Kenya's electricity comes from renewable sources, and it is among the world's top ten producers of geothermal power.
Kenya banned plastic carrier bags in 2017, with some of the strictest penalties in the world.
Nairobi National Park lies so close to the city that giraffes can be photographed in front of skyscrapers.
Sudan, the last male northern white rhino, died at Ol Pejeta in 2018; scientists are working to save the subspecies through IVF.
Nairobi's name comes from the Maasai phrase 'Enkare Nyrobi', meaning 'cool water'.
The Maasai shield and spears on Kenya's flag symbolise the defence of freedom.
Kenya's national anthem was set to the melody of a traditional Pokomo lullaby.
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o wrote his first Gikuyu-language novel on prison toilet paper while detained without trial in 1978.
Sheng, a lively mix of Swahili, English and other languages, was born on the streets of Nairobi.
Matatus are often painted with murals of musicians and footballers, and fitted with booming sound systems.
Fort Jesus in Mombasa was built by the Portuguese in the 1590s.
The East African Rift is slowly pulling the continent apart by a few millimetres a year.
Lake Victoria, shared by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, is the largest lake in Africa.
Kenya celebrates Mashujaa (Heroes') Day on 20 October and Jamhuri (Republic) Day on 12 December.
The Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests were once fortified villages and are still guarded by elders as holy places.
Hell's Gate is one of the few Kenyan parks where visitors are allowed to cycle or walk among wildlife.
Ugali, a stiff porridge of maize flour, is so central that many Kenyans feel a meal without it is not quite a meal.
Each year more than a million wildebeest, with zebras and gazelles, migrate between Tanzania's Serengeti and Kenya's Maasai Mara.
Kenya was the first country in Africa to have its Supreme Court annul a presidential election, in 2017.
Lesser flamingos on Rift Valley lakes get their pink colour from the algae they eat.

languageGuide.intro: Swahili (Kiswahili) is pronounced almost exactly as written, with the stress nearly always on the second-to-last syllable, and greetings matter — Kenyans usually ask how you are before getting to business. English is widely spoken in towns and tourist areas, but a warm 'Habari!' or 'Asante sana' is always appreciated.

phrases.en: Hello, how are you? (reply: Sijambo — I'm fine)
Good morning (lit. news of the morning?)
Respectful greeting to an elder (reply: Marahaba)

culture.history: Kenya's land is among the oldest homes of humankind, and its coast gave rise to Swahili city-states such as Lamu and Mombasa, trading across the Indian Ocean and later contested by the Portuguese and Omani Arabs. Britain declared a protectorate in 1895 and a colony in 1920, seizing fertile highlands for settlers. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was met with mass detention and brutal abuses, and independence came in 1963. Later decades brought one-party rule, multiparty reform and, after the deadly violence following the 2007 election, a new constitution in 2010.
culture.politics: Kenya is a presidential republic with a bicameral Parliament of the National Assembly and Senate and an independent judiciary. The 2010 Constitution devolved significant power to 47 elected county governments, and building an inclusive nation across more than forty ethnic communities remains a defining civic theme.
culture.arts: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, who chose to write in Gikuyu, and Margaret Ogola are towering literary figures, and the UNESCO-listed Lamu Old Town preserves classic Swahili architecture. Benga guitar music, coastal taarab and the intricate beadwork of Maasai and Samburu communities carry rich living traditions.

love.expression: Love is deeply communal: weddings, dowry ceremonies such as the Kikuyu ruracio and family gatherings bring whole extended families together. Care is shown by showing up, sharing food and supporting one another through harambee, the spirit of pulling together, with expressions varying across Kenya's many communities and between city and countryside.

etiquette: Greet people and ask how they are before getting to business; rushing a greeting can seem rude.
Shake hands with your right hand, and show particular respect to elders.
Always ask before photographing people, including in Maasai communities.

name: South Africa

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); 12 official languages, including South African Sign Language since 2023

people: About 63 million people live in South Africa: roughly 81% Black African — Zulu, Xhosa, Pedi, Tswana, Sotho, Tsonga, Swazi, Venda, Ndebele and others — with Coloured (about 8%), White (about 7%) and Indian or Asian (under 3%) South Africans, while the San and Khoikhoi carry the land's most ancient roots. Around four in five identify as Christian, including large African-initiated churches such as the Zion Christian Church, alongside Muslim, Hindu, Jewish and African traditional faith communities. Roughly two-thirds live in towns and cities, with Gauteng — Johannesburg and Pretoria — as the economic heart, and the country is also home to many migrants from across Africa.

plug.note: The large three-round-pin type M is most common, so most visitors need a local adapter; two-pin European plugs fit some sockets. US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

basics.say: ngee-(click)EH-lah — 'c' is a soft tut-tut click

basics.en: Goodbye (said by the one leaving / the one staying)
basics.say: SAH-lah KAH-hleh / HAHM-bah KAH-hleh — 'hl' like Welsh 'll'
oo-(click)OH-loh — 'x' is a side click, like urging on a horse

resources: Platinum, gold, manganese, chrome and coal
Extraordinary biodiversity — the Cape Floral Kingdom, Kruger and two oceans
A celebrated Constitution, independent courts and a free press
Africa's most sophisticated financial sector and infrastructure
Wine, fruit and a strong agricultural export sector
Cultural creativity — music, sport, storytelling and the spirit of ubuntu
struggles: One of the world's highest unemployment rates — around a third of the workforce, and far higher among young people
Deep inequality rooted in apartheid's legacy, with wealth and land still unevenly shared
High rates of violent crime, including gender-based violence
Years of electricity cuts (load-shedding) and failing water and municipal services
Corruption and the costly legacy of 'state capture'
Outbreaks of xenophobic violence against migrants from other African countries
prayFor: For work and hope for millions of young South Africans, and for fair opportunity regardless of where they were born
For safety in homes and streets, and especially for women and children facing violence
For honest, capable leadership in government and towns, so that water, power and schools serve everyone
For continued healing of the wounds of apartheid, and for reconciliation that walks hand in hand with justice
For migrants and refugees, that they are received with ubuntu — the humanity that knows 'I am because we are'

summary.history: Southern Africa holds some of humanity's deepest roots — from the fossil hominids of the Cradle of Humankind to the engraved ochre of Blombos Cave — and San hunter-gatherers and Khoikhoi herders lived here long before Bantu-speaking farmers arrived in the first millennium CE and built kingdoms such as Mapungubwe. Dutch settlers founded Cape Town in 1652 and brought enslaved people from Asia and Africa, while colonial expansion dispossessed the Khoikhoi and San. British rule, frontier wars, the rise of the Zulu kingdom and the discovery of diamonds and gold in 1867–86 reshaped the land, leading to the South African War of 1899–1902 with its concentration camps for Boer and Black civilians. From 1948 white-minority rule hardened into apartheid — pass laws, forced removals and violent repression, from Sharpeville in 1960 to Soweto in 1976 — until mass resistance, international pressure and negotiation brought the first democratic elections in 1994, followed by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and an ongoing struggle to overcome poverty and inequality.
summary.politicalHistory: The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910 as a British dominion governed by the white minority; it became a republic in 1961 and left the Commonwealth. From 1948 the National Party built apartheid into law, banning the ANC and PAC in 1960 and imprisoning leaders such as Nelson Mandela for 27 years. Negotiations after 1990 led to the 1994 election, Mandela's presidency and the 1996 Constitution, admired worldwide for its Bill of Rights and Constitutional Court. South Africa is today a parliamentary republic in which the National Assembly elects the president; after the ANC lost its majority in the May 2024 election, a multi-party Government of National Unity was formed.
summary.art: San rock paintings, some thousands of years old, survive in the Drakensberg and Cederberg, while Zulu beadwork and basketry, Ndebele mural painting and Venda wood carving carry rich meaning. Music is a national treasure — the isicathamiya of Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Miriam Makeba and Hugh Masekela, mbaqanga, kwaito, jazz and today's globe-conquering amapiano — and choirs fill churches and stadiums alike. Writers from Sol Plaatje and Alan Paton to Zakes Mda and Nobel laureates Nadine Gordimer and J. M. Coetzee, and artists such as Gerard Sekoto, Esther Mahlangu and William Kentridge, have wrestled beautifully with the nation's story.
summary.monuments: Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela and many other political prisoners were held, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a place of remembrance, as are the Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape and the fossil sites of the Cradle of Humankind. Constitution Hill and the Apartheid Museum in Johannesburg, the Hector Pieterson Memorial in Soweto and the Union Buildings in Pretoria tell the story of oppression, resistance and democracy. Natural treasures include Table Mountain, the uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park and the iSimangaliso Wetland Park.

highlights.title: Table Mountain
highlights.line: Ride the rotating cableway or hike up Platteklip Gorge for views over Cape Town and two oceans; check the wind and the 'tablecloth' cloud before you go.

highlights.title: Robben Island
highlights.line: Former political prisoners often guide tours of the prison where Nelson Mandela spent 18 years; book ferries well ahead from the V&A Waterfront.

highlights.title: Bo-Kaap
highlights.line: Brightly painted houses and Cape Malay heritage on the slopes of Signal Hill; join a cooking class to learn to fold samoosas.

highlights.title: Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden
highlights.line: Fynbos and proteas beneath Table Mountain, with a treetop canopy walkway and summer Sunday concerts.

highlights.title: Cape Point & the Cape of Good Hope
highlights.line: Wild cliffs, baboons and ostriches at the tip of the peninsula; keep food out of sight from the baboons.

highlights.title: Boulders Beach penguins
highlights.line: Walk the boardwalks among endangered African penguins near Simon's Town — and swim with them at the sheltered beach.

highlights.title: Chapman's Peak Drive
highlights.line: One of the world's great coastal roads, carved into the cliffs between Hout Bay and Noordhoek.

highlights.title: Cape Winelands
highlights.line: Stellenbosch, Franschhoek and Paarl offer gabled Cape Dutch estates and Pinotage; learn too about the farm workers' history and visit worker-owned labels.

highlights.title: Hermanus whale watching
highlights.line: Southern right whales come close to the shore cliffs from about June to November.

highlights.title: Garden Route & Tsitsikamma
highlights.line: Forests, lagoons and the Storms River suspension bridge along a classic road trip.

highlights.title: Addo Elephant National Park
highlights.line: Hundreds of elephants in the Eastern Cape, in a malaria-free park easy to self-drive.

highlights.title: Kruger National Park
highlights.line: One of Africa's great wildlife reserves, roughly the size of Wales; drive yourself on good roads and stay in rest camps for good value.

highlights.title: Panorama Route & Blyde River Canyon
highlights.line: Huge green canyon views, the Three Rondavels and God's Window in Mpumalanga.

highlights.title: Vilakazi Street, Soweto
highlights.line: The street where Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu both lived; go with a local guide and eat at a family-run shisanyama.

highlights.title: Hector Pieterson Memorial
highlights.line: Honours the schoolchildren killed in the 1976 Soweto uprising — a quiet, essential visit.

highlights.title: Apartheid Museum, Johannesburg
highlights.line: A powerful, carefully curated journey through segregation and resistance; allow at least two to three hours.

highlights.title: Constitution Hill
highlights.line: A former prison where Gandhi and Mandela were held, now home to the Constitutional Court and its moving public art.

highlights.title: Cradle of Humankind
highlights.line: Explore the Sterkfontein Caves and the Maropeng visitor centre, where some of our species' oldest relatives were found.

highlights.title: Union Buildings, Pretoria
highlights.line: Gardens with a giant statue of Mandela, especially lovely when the jacarandas bloom purple in October and November.

highlights.title: Durban's Golden Mile
highlights.line: Warm Indian Ocean beaches, surfing and a seafront promenade; visit the Victoria Street Market for spices.

highlights.title: Bunny chow
highlights.line: Durban's famous hollowed-out loaf filled with curry — eat it with your hands, starting with the bread 'lid'.

highlights.title: iSimangaliso Wetland Park
highlights.line: Hippos and crocodiles in St Lucia's estuary, nesting turtles and wild coastline in a UNESCO site.

highlights.title: Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park
highlights.line: The park where conservation work helped save the southern white rhino from near-extinction.

highlights.title: Drakensberg mountains
highlights.line: Hike to the Amphitheatre and Tugela Falls and seek out ancient San rock art with a guide.

highlights.title: Wild Coast
highlights.line: Rolling green hills, Xhosa villages and the Hole in the Wall rock arch; stay at community-run lodges near Coffee Bay.

highlights.title: Karoo stargazing at Sutherland
highlights.line: Visit the Southern African Large Telescope and see the Milky Way under some of the darkest skies on Earth.

highlights.title: Namaqualand flower season
highlights.line: From about August to September the semi-desert bursts into carpets of wildflowers, best on sunny afternoons.

highlights.title: Mapungubwe National Park
highlights.line: The site of a 13th-century African kingdom famous for its golden rhinoceros, where three countries meet.

highlights.title: A braai
highlights.line: Wood-fire grilling of boerewors, lamb chops and pap with friends is a ritual that crosses all communities.

highlights.title: Cape Malay cuisine
highlights.line: Fragrant bobotie, bredie stews and koeksisters show the Cape's Asian and African heritage.

highlights.title: Rooibos in the Cederberg
highlights.line: Visit the only region where rooibos grows commercially, among sandstone rock formations and San art.

highlights.title: Live music night
highlights.line: Catch jazz, amapiano or maskandi in Johannesburg or Cape Town — South Africa's soul is in its music.

highlights.title: A township church choir
highlights.line: Sunday services with soaring harmonies are among the most moving experiences in the country; go with a local host.

funFacts: South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
South Africa has 12 official languages; South African Sign Language became the 12th in 2023.
South Africa is the only country to have built nuclear weapons and then voluntarily dismantled them all.
Vilakazi Street in Soweto was home to two Nobel Peace Prize laureates, Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu.
The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms yet has around 9,000 plant species, most found nowhere else.
The world's first human-to-human heart transplant was performed in Cape Town in 1967 by Christiaan Barnard.
Rooibos tea grows commercially only in the Cederberg region of the Western Cape.
A small cross-hatched drawing on stone from Blombos Cave, about 73,000 years old, is among the oldest known drawings in the world.
Homo naledi, a previously unknown human relative, was discovered in the Rising Star cave system in 2013.
Kruger National Park covers nearly 20,000 square kilometres — about the size of Wales.
Tugela Falls in the Drakensberg is often ranked as the second-highest waterfall in the world.
On Mandela Day, 18 July, people are invited to give 67 minutes of service — one for each year Mandela devoted to public life.
The Springboks have won the Rugby World Cup four times, more than any other nation.
Afrikaans developed from Dutch in the Cape with influences from Malay, Portuguese, Khoikhoi and Bantu languages, and was first written by Cape Muslims in Arabic script.
The click sounds of isiXhosa and isiZulu were borrowed from the Khoisan languages.
The Pinotage grape was created in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut.
South African-born physicist Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize for the theory behind the CT scan.
South Africa holds most of the world's known reserves of platinum.
The Southern African Large Telescope at Sutherland is the largest single optical telescope in the southern hemisphere.
The MeerKAT radio telescope in the Karoo is part of the international Square Kilometre Array project.
Mahatma Gandhi first developed his philosophy of non-violent resistance during 21 years in South Africa.
Durban is home to one of the largest communities of Indian heritage outside Asia, descended largely from indentured labourers who arrived from 1860.
Bunny chow was invented in Durban, and despite its name contains no rabbit.
The isiZulu saying 'umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu' — a person is a person through other people — expresses the philosophy of ubuntu.
Africa's southernmost point is Cape Agulhas, not the more famous Cape of Good Hope.
South Africa's national anthem combines five languages: isiXhosa, isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans and English.
The opening hymn of the anthem, 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika', was composed in 1897 by Enoch Sontonga, a Methodist school teacher.
