The Constitutional Court was built on the site of an old prison, using bricks from the demolished awaiting-trial block.
Kimberley's 'Big Hole' is one of the largest holes ever dug by hand, by diamond miners between 1871 and 1914.
Johannesburg grew from nothing after gold was discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu popularised the phrase 'Rainbow Nation' to describe post-apartheid South Africa.
Amapiano, a style of house music with log-drum basslines, was born in South Africa's townships in the 2010s and spread worldwide.
The African penguins of Boulders Beach are an endangered species that brays like a donkey.

languageGuide.intro: isiZulu is South Africa's most widely spoken home language; it is written phonetically, but includes three click sounds — 'c' (a soft tut-tut), 'q' (a hollow pop) and 'x' (a side click like urging on a horse) — and greetings change for one person or several. English is used everywhere in cities and business, and even a simple 'Sawubona' is received with real warmth.

phrases.en: Hello (lit. I see you) — to one person

phraseLanguage: isiZulu (one of 12 official languages; English is widely understood)

culture.history: San and Khoikhoi peoples lived here for tens of thousands of years, joined over many centuries by Bantu-speaking farming communities who built kingdoms such as Mapungubwe and, later, the Zulu kingdom. Dutch settlement at the Cape from 1652 brought slavery and dispossession, followed by British rule, frontier wars and a mineral rush that entrenched migrant labour. From 1948 the apartheid state enforced racial segregation and brutal repression, resisted for decades by movements at home and in exile. In 1994 the first democratic elections made Nelson Mandela president, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission sought to confront the past.
culture.politics: South Africa is a parliamentary republic in which the National Assembly elects the president, who is both head of state and government, alongside a National Council of Provinces and a strong Constitutional Court. The 1996 Constitution, with one of the world's most expansive Bills of Rights, frames the defining civic theme: building a shared, just society while confronting deep inequality.
culture.arts: Ancient San rock art, bold Ndebele house painting and Zulu beadwork sit alongside the isicathamiya harmonies of Ladysmith Black Mambazo and the music of Miriam Makeba and Hugh Masekela. Nobel laureates Nadine Gordimer and J. M. Coetzee, and writers such as Es'kia Mphahlele and Zakes Mda, gave voice to the country's struggles and hopes.

love.expression: The spirit of ubuntu, 'I am because we are', shapes how love is shown: through presence, community and caring for one another's families. Marriage customs such as lobola negotiations bring families together, and expression varies widely across the country's many cultures, languages and communities.

etiquette: Take time over greetings; asking how someone is before making a request is expected.
Receive gifts or items with both hands, or with your right hand while your left touches your forearm, as a sign of respect.
Learning a greeting in the local language, such as Sawubona or Molo, is warmly received.

name: Israel
capital: Jerusalem (proclaimed; its status is internationally disputed and most embassies are in Tel Aviv)

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Russian, Amharic, Yiddish, English, French and Ladino; Arabic has 'special status' since 2018

people: Israel's roughly 10 million people are about 73% Jewish — with family roots in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, Ethiopia, the former Soviet Union and beyond, and ranging from secular to Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) — and about 21% Arab citizens, most of them Muslim, with Christian, Druze and Bedouin communities. The country is highly urban, centred on Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa, and its figures include Israelis living in East Jerusalem and in settlements in the occupied West Bank. Alongside them, around five million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza live under Israeli occupation or blockade without Israeli citizenship, a reality at the heart of the region's conflict.

plug.note: Two-pin European (type C) plugs fit most sockets; UK and US travellers need an adapter, and US devices that are not dual-voltage need a converter.

resources: A world-leading technology and innovation sector
Water know-how — drip irrigation, desalination and wastewater recycling
Universities, research institutes and a highly educated workforce
Holy sites and heritage sacred to Jews, Christians, Muslims, Druze and Bahá'ís
Offshore natural gas fields in the Mediterranean
Dead Sea minerals and Negev desert landscapes
struggles: The trauma of the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and some 250 taken hostage, and the anguish of hostage families
The war in Gaza that followed, in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed and most of Gaza's people displaced amid a grave humanitarian crisis, with many Israeli soldiers also killed
The unresolved occupation of the West Bank, settlement expansion and violence affecting Palestinian and Israeli civilians alike
Rocket and drone fire that has displaced communities in the north and south
Deep political and religious polarisation, seen in the 2023 mass protests over judicial reform and debates over military service
A high cost of living and housing, and gaps in opportunity and safety for Arab citizens of Israel
prayFor: For every hostage and every grieving family — Israeli and Palestinian — that they may know comfort, return and peace
For an end to the killing, protection for all civilians, and food, water and medicine for the people of Gaza
For healing of trauma in children, soldiers, the displaced and the bereaved on every side
For courageous peacemakers, Jewish and Arab, who build friendship, justice and security across the divide
For Jews, Christians, Muslims, Druze and all who pray in this land, that holy places become places of reverence rather than conflict

summary.history: This small land between the Mediterranean and the Jordan River is the setting of the Hebrew Bible and the life of Jesus, and holds places of deep Islamic devotion; ancient Israelite kingdoms rose here, and after Rome destroyed the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE most Jews lived in diaspora while the land passed through Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman rule, home throughout to Arab Muslims and Christians and smaller Jewish communities. From the late 19th century Zionist immigration grew, and under the British Mandate (1920–48) Jewish and Arab national movements came into conflict. After the Holocaust, in which six million Jews were murdered, the UN proposed partition in 1947; Israel declared independence in 1948, and in the war that followed some 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled — the Nakba — while in the following years hundreds of thousands of Jews left or were driven from Arab countries and came to Israel. The 1967 war brought the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan Heights under Israeli control; peace treaties with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994) and the Oslo Accords raised hopes, but occupation, intifadas, terror attacks and wars — above all the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 and the devastating war in Gaza that followed — have brought immense suffering to Israelis and Palestinians alike.
summary.politicalHistory: David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel on 14 May 1948 as the British Mandate ended. Israel is a parliamentary democracy with a 120-seat Knesset elected by nationwide proportional representation and a largely ceremonial president; it has no single written constitution, but a series of Basic Laws, including the contested 2018 Nation-State Law. Labour-led governments dominated until Menachem Begin's Likud won in 1977 and made peace with Egypt; Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who signed the Oslo Accords, was assassinated by a Jewish extremist in 1995. Coalition politics remain fragile: five elections were held between 2019 and 2022, and a 2023 plan to overhaul the judiciary sparked some of the largest protests in the country's history before war broke out that October.
summary.art: Ancient synagogue and church mosaics, the Dead Sea Scrolls and illuminated Hebrew manuscripts stand beside a modern art scene that began with Jerusalem's Bezalel school in 1906. The revival of Hebrew fed a rich literature — S. Y. Agnon (Nobel 1966), the poet Yehuda Amichai, Amos Oz and David Grossman — alongside Arab writers such as Emile Habibi and Sayed Kashua. Music weaves Ashkenazi, Mizrahi, Yemenite, Arab and Ethiopian traditions, from Ofra Haza and Arik Einstein to the Israel Philharmonic and the Batsheva Dance Company.
summary.monuments: The Old City of Jerusalem, with the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Haram al-Sharif/Temple Mount with the Dome of the Rock, is sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims; it lies in East Jerusalem, which Israel annexed but most of the world regards as occupied. Masada, the White City of Tel Aviv, the Bahá'í Gardens of Haifa and Acre's Crusader and Ottoman Old City are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Yad Vashem in Jerusalem, the World Holocaust Remembrance Center, honours the six million Jews murdered in the Shoah and the Righteous Among the Nations who saved them.

highlights.title: Jerusalem's Old City
highlights.line: Four quarters, three faiths and thousands of years within a single square kilometre; it lies in East Jerusalem, whose status is disputed, so check current advice and dress modestly.

highlights.title: Western Wall (Kotel)
highlights.line: Judaism's holiest place of prayer; visit at the start of Shabbat on Friday evening, but don't photograph worshippers on Shabbat itself.

highlights.title: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
highlights.line: Honoured as the site of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection, shared by several churches; come very early for a quieter visit to the tomb.

highlights.title: Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount
highlights.line: The esplanade of Al-Aqsa Mosque and the golden Dome of the Rock; non-Muslims may visit only in limited morning hours, and access can change at short notice.

highlights.title: Via Dolorosa
highlights.line: Follow the Stations of the Cross through the Old City's lanes; Franciscans lead a procession on Friday afternoons.

highlights.title: Yad Vashem
highlights.line: The World Holocaust Remembrance Center, a profound and sombre visit; allow at least three hours and note that children under ten are not admitted to the history museum.

highlights.title: Israel Museum
highlights.line: The Shrine of the Book holds the Dead Sea Scrolls, and a large model shows Jerusalem in the Second Temple period.

highlights.title: Mahane Yehuda Market
highlights.line: Jerusalem's market of halva, spices and fresh produce by day, with bars and music by night; it is busiest and most fun on Thursday and Friday before Shabbat.

highlights.title: Tel Aviv beaches & promenade
highlights.line: Kilometres of sand, matkot paddle games and sunset runs along the Mediterranean seafront.

highlights.title: White City, Tel Aviv
highlights.line: Over 4,000 Bauhaus-style buildings; take a guided walk along Rothschild Boulevard and visit the Bauhaus Center.

highlights.title: Old Jaffa
highlights.line: An ancient Arab-Jewish port city of stone lanes, a flea market, galleries and the fishing harbour — try the bakeries and hummus spots.

highlights.title: Bahá'í Gardens, Haifa
highlights.line: Nineteen immaculate terraces cascade down Mount Carmel to the golden-domed Shrine of the Báb; free guided tours run most days.

highlights.title: Acre (Akko) Old City
highlights.line: Crusader halls beneath an Ottoman walled town, a lively market and seafront ramparts; eat fresh fish and hummus by the harbour.

highlights.title: Caesarea
highlights.line: Herod's Roman harbour city with a seaside theatre and hippodrome; finish with a swim at the aqueduct beach.

highlights.title: Rosh HaNikra grottoes
highlights.line: Sea caves of white chalk at the northern border, reached by cable car — check whether the site is open given the security situation.

highlights.title: Nazareth
highlights.line: The Basilica of the Annunciation, Mary's Well and the old market of Israel's largest Arab city; stay in a guesthouse in the historic centre.

highlights.title: Sea of Galilee
highlights.line: Visit Capernaum, Tabgha and the Mount of Beatitudes where Jesus taught, and take a boat across the lake at dawn.

highlights.title: The Jesus Trail
highlights.line: A multi-day walk from Nazareth to Capernaum through villages, olive groves and Galilee hills.

highlights.title: Tzfat (Safed)
highlights.line: A hilltop city of Jewish mysticism, blue-painted lanes, ancient synagogues and artists' galleries.

highlights.title: Masada
highlights.line: Herod's desert fortress; climb the Snake Path before sunrise or take the cable car, and watch the light rise over the Dead Sea.

highlights.title: Floating in the Dead Sea
highlights.line: Bob effortlessly at the lowest place on Earth at Ein Bokek; don't shave beforehand and keep the water out of your eyes.

highlights.title: Ein Gedi Nature Reserve
highlights.line: Waterfalls, pools and Nubian ibex in a desert oasis beside the Dead Sea; start early before it gets hot.

highlights.title: Makhtesh Ramon
highlights.line: A vast erosion crater in the Negev; stargaze from Mitzpe Ramon, a dark-sky town on its rim.

highlights.title: Timna Park
highlights.line: Red sandstone pillars, ancient copper mines and rock art in the far south near Eilat.

highlights.title: Eilat coral reefs
highlights.line: Snorkel among colourful fish at the Coral Beach Nature Reserve on Israel's short Red Sea coast.

highlights.title: Beit She'an
highlights.line: One of the best-preserved Roman-Byzantine cities in the region, with columned streets toppled by a 749 CE earthquake.

highlights.title: Hula Valley
highlights.line: Watch huge flocks of cranes and other migrating birds in autumn and winter at the Agamon Hula reserve.

highlights.title: Druze hospitality on Mount Carmel
highlights.line: Visit Daliyat al-Karmel for Druze food, coffee and stories of a distinctive community.

highlights.title: Hummus at Abu Ghosh
highlights.line: An Arab village outside Jerusalem famed for hummus and for its Crusader-era church with Gregorian chant.

highlights.title: Shabbat dinner
highlights.line: If invited to a Friday-night Shabbat meal with candles, blessings, challah bread and long conversation, say yes.

highlights.title: Sabich & shakshuka
highlights.line: Try sabich — pita with fried aubergine, egg and tahini, brought by Iraqi Jews — and shakshuka, eggs in spiced tomato sauce from North Africa.

highlights.title: Tel Megiddo
highlights.line: The layered biblical mound known in Greek as Armageddon, with ancient gates and a water system.

highlights.title: Beit Guvrin caves
highlights.line: Hundreds of hand-carved bell caves and columbaria in the lowlands, a UNESCO site full of echoes.

funFacts: Hebrew is widely regarded as the only language to be fully revived as an everyday spoken mother tongue after centuries as mainly a written and liturgical language.
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, a key figure in reviving Hebrew, raised his son as the first native Hebrew speaker in modern times.
The Dead Sea shore, at around 430 metres below sea level, is the lowest point on land on Earth.
The Dead Sea is roughly ten times saltier than the ocean, which is why you float so easily.
The Dead Sea's level has been falling by about a metre a year.
The Sea of Galilee is the lowest freshwater lake on Earth, about 210 metres below sea level.
Israel reuses around 85–90% of its wastewater for agriculture, the highest share in the world.
Modern drip irrigation was developed in Israel by Simcha Blass and the kibbutz company Netafim in the 1960s.
Desalination plants supply a large share of Israel's household drinking water.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, were found from 1947 onwards in caves near Qumran, starting with a Bedouin shepherd's discovery.
Hundreds of millions of migrating birds fly over Israel every spring and autumn, along one of the world's great flyways between Africa and Eurasia.
Makhtesh Ramon is the world's largest erosion crater of its kind, and the Hebrew word 'makhtesh' is now used by geologists worldwide.
Tel Aviv's White City has more than 4,000 buildings in the Bauhaus and International Style, many built by architects fleeing 1930s Europe.
Israel's working week runs from Sunday to Thursday, with the weekend on Friday and Saturday.
Many Israeli buildings have a 'Shabbat elevator' that stops automatically at every floor so observant Jews need not press buttons.
Jerusalem's Old City is traditionally divided into four quarters: Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian.
The key to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has for centuries been held by a Muslim family, an arrangement that helps keep peace among the Christian denominations.
Haifa is the world centre of the Bahá'í Faith, though there is no local Bahá'í community in Israel by the faith's own choice.
On Yom Kippur almost all traffic stops, and children cycle freely down empty highways.
The navigation app Waze was created in Israel.
In Operation Solomon in 1991, about 14,000 Ethiopian Jews were airlifted to Israel in around 36 hours; one plane carried a record 1,088 passengers.
Sabich, a beloved pita sandwich, comes from the Saturday-morning breakfast of Iraqi Jews.
Israel has won the Eurovision Song Contest four times: 1978, 1979, 1998 and 2018.
Naomi Shemer's song 'Jerusalem of Gold', written in 1967, is one of the most beloved Hebrew songs.
Acre (Akko) is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Degania, founded in 1910 by the Sea of Galilee, was the first kibbutz.
Israel's national bird is the hoopoe, chosen in a public vote in 2008.
Ada Yonath became the first Israeli woman to win a Nobel Prize, in Chemistry in 2009, for mapping the structure of the ribosome.
S. Y. Agnon, who won the 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature, appeared on Israel's 50-shekel banknote.
Israel's coast on the Red Sea at Eilat is only about 12 kilometres long.
Copper was mined at Timna thousands of years ago, making it one of the oldest copper-mining sites in the world.
Nubian ibex wander so freely at Ein Gedi and Mitzpe Ramon that they often stroll past visitors.
Jaffa oranges, grown by Arab and Jewish farmers, became a world-famous export brand in the 19th and 20th centuries.

languageGuide.intro: Hebrew is written right to left without most vowels, and many phrases change depending on whether you speak to — or are — a man or a woman; the 'ch' is a throaty sound as in Scottish 'loch'. English is very widely spoken, and Arabic is the first language of about a fifth of citizens, so 'shalom' and 'shukran' are both useful.

phrases.en: How are you? (to a man / to a woman)
What's your name? (to a man / to a woman)
Where are you from? (to a man / to a woman)

culture.history: This land holds the memory of the ancient Israelite kingdoms and the Jerusalem Temple, destroyed by Rome in 70 CE, after which most Jews lived in a centuries-long diaspora while the region passed through Byzantine, Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman rule. Under the British Mandate, Zionist immigration grew, and after the Holocaust the State of Israel was declared in 1948. The war that followed saw the flight or expulsion of some 700,000 Palestinians, remembered as the Nakba, and since 1967 Israel has occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem and controlled Gaza. The unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict continues to bring deep grief to both peoples.
culture.politics: Israel is a parliamentary democracy without a single written constitution, governed by Basic Laws, in which a 120-member Knesset elected by proportional representation forms coalition governments and a largely ceremonial president serves as head of state. Defining civic themes include the balance between Israel's Jewish and democratic character, the role of the judiciary, and the unresolved occupation and conflict with the Palestinians.
culture.arts: The revival of Hebrew as a spoken language fed a rich literature, from Nobel laureate S. Y. Agnon to the poet Yehuda Amichai, alongside Arabic-language writers such as Emile Habibi. Tel Aviv's 'White City' of Bauhaus buildings is UNESCO-listed, and music blends Ashkenazi, Mizrahi, Arab and Ethiopian traditions, carried worldwide by singers like Ofra Haza.

love.expression: Affection tends to be direct, warm and talkative, with long Friday-night Shabbat dinners and lively family gatherings at the heart of life. Friendships are often intensely loyal, and expression ranges widely between secular, religious, Jewish, Arab and Druze communities.

iLoveYou.local: אני אוהב אותך / אני אוהבת אותך
iLoveYou.roman: Ani ohev otakh (male to female) / Ani ohevet otkha (female to male)
iLoveYou.say: ah-NEE oh-HEV oh-TAKH / ah-NEE oh-HEH-vet ot-KHA

etiquette: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; public transport and many shops close, especially in Jerusalem.
Dress modestly at holy sites of every faith, covering shoulders and knees.
Directness in conversation is normal and not meant as rudeness.

name: Albania

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Greek, Aromanian and Romani spoken by minorities

people: Albanians (Shqiptarë) make up the great majority, with Greek, Aromanian (Vlach), Macedonian, Roma and Balkan Egyptian communities. Faith is worn lightly and shared across lines: roughly half identify as Muslim (Sunni and Bektashi), with Catholic and Orthodox Christian minorities of under a tenth each and many who believe without a denomination. Tirana and the coast are growing fast while mountain villages empty, and a diaspora about as large as the resident population lives in Italy, Greece and beyond.
resources: Adriatic and Ionian coastline
Hydropower from mountain rivers
Chromium and other minerals
Oil and bitumen deposits
Olive, wine and Mediterranean agriculture
A tradition of hospitality (besa) and a young, multilingual diaspora
struggles: Large-scale emigration of young and skilled people
Corruption and organised crime weakening trust in institutions
Low wages and informal work outside Tirana
Over-tourism and unregulated construction on the coast
Long, demanding path toward EU membership
prayFor: For young Albanians to find meaningful work and a future at home, and for families separated by emigration
For honest, just institutions and courage for those who fight corruption
For the coast, rivers and mountains to be protected as tourism grows
For the continued gift of peace between Muslims, Catholics and Orthodox
For healing of memories left by decades of isolation and persecution

summary.history: The land was home to the ancient Illyrians, then passed under Greek colonies, Rome and Byzantium. In the 15th century Skanderbeg led decades of resistance to the Ottomans, who ruled for over four centuries and under whom much of the population became Muslim. Independence came in 1912, followed by instability, Italian occupation and war. From 1944 a communist regime sealed the country off, banned religion in 1967, and imprisoned or sent to labour camps many thousands. Since 1991 Albania has lived through the shock of opening, the 1997 pyramid-scheme collapse, mass emigration, and steady rebuilding.
summary.politicalHistory: Albania declared independence in Vlorë in 1912 and became a principality, then a republic and in 1928 a monarchy under King Zog. After Italian and German occupation, Enver Hoxha's communist party ruled from 1944 in one of the most isolated dictatorships in the world. Multi-party elections came in 1991, and the 1998 constitution established a parliamentary republic. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and opened EU accession negotiations in 2022.
summary.art: Iso-polyphony, the layered folk singing of the south, is recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage, alongside epic songs sung to the lahuta in the northern highlands. Ismail Kadare carried Albanian literature to the world, following the national-awakening poet Naim Frashëri and the priest-poet Gjergj Fishta. Filigree silverwork, carpet weaving and the 16th-century icon painter Onufri, famed for his deep red, remain treasured crafts.
summary.monuments: Butrint, a UNESCO site, holds Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Venetian layers in a lagoon landscape. The 'cities of a thousand windows', Berat and Gjirokastër, preserve Ottoman-era towns on hillsides. Krujë Castle recalls Skanderbeg's resistance, and the Et'hem Bey Mosque in Tirana survived the years of enforced atheism. The thousands of concrete bunkers and the Bunk'Art museums now tell the story of the dictatorship.

name: Andorra

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Spanish, Portuguese and French widely spoken

people: Andorran citizens are a minority of residents; most people living here are Spanish, Portuguese or French, along with growing communities from Latin America and elsewhere. Catholic tradition shapes the calendar and the Romanesque village churches, though practice is modest. Life is concentrated in the narrow valleys around Andorra la Vella and Escaldes-Engordany, with millions of visitors passing through each year.
resources: High Pyrenean mountains and valleys
Ski resorts and year-round tourism
Retail and duty-advantaged commerce
Banking and services
Hydropower and clean mountain water
Romanesque churches and a living Catalan culture
struggles: Housing so expensive that workers and young Andorrans struggle to stay
Heavy dependence on tourism and seasonal work
Traffic, construction and pressure on fragile mountain landscapes
Climate change shortening the snow season
Integration and political voice for a largely non-citizen population
prayFor: For affordable homes so that families and seasonal workers can put down roots
For wise care of the mountains, snow and water in a warming climate
For belonging and fair treatment for the many residents who are not citizens
For rest and dignity for those who work long hours in tourism and retail
For the little Romanesque churches to remain places of prayer, not only of sightseeing

summary.history: People have lived in these Pyrenean valleys since prehistoric times, and tradition credits Charlemagne with granting the Andorrans a charter. In 1278 the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix agreed to share sovereignty, the origin of the co-principality; the Count's rights later passed to the French crown and then the French head of state. For centuries Andorra was a poor, isolated land of shepherds and smugglers, kept neutral and largely untouched by Europe's wars. From the mid-20th century roads, tourism, skiing and commerce transformed it into one of Europe's wealthiest microstates.
summary.politicalHistory: Andorra's paréage agreements of 1278 and 1288 created a co-principality shared by the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix. The General Council (Consell de la Terra), founded in 1419, is among the oldest parliaments in Europe. The 1993 constitution, approved by referendum, made Andorra a fully sovereign parliamentary democracy with the two co-princes as constitutional heads of state. It joined the United Nations that same year and has negotiated an association agreement with the EU.
summary.art: Andorra's treasure is Romanesque art: stone churches with slender bell towers and once-vivid wall paintings, such as those of Sant Joan de Caselles. Catalan folk traditions live on in sardana dancing, the contrapàs and the Ball de Marratxa, and the Pyrenean summer solstice fire festivals are UNESCO intangible heritage. Ironwork from the old forges and the Andorran National Classical Orchestra reflect older crafts and a newer cultural life.
summary.monuments: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, preserves shepherds' huts, terraces and paths of high-mountain life. Sant Joan de Caselles and Santa Coloma, with its rare round bell tower, are among the finest Romanesque churches. Casa de la Vall in Andorra la Vella was for centuries the seat of the General Council. The Sanctuary of Meritxell honours the country's patron saint and was rebuilt by Ricardo Bofill after a fire in 1972.

name: Belarus

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Russian dominates daily life, many speak trasianka (mixed speech)

people: Most people are Belarusian, with Russian, Polish and Ukrainian minorities and a historic Jewish presence almost destroyed in the Holocaust. Orthodox Christianity is the largest faith, with a significant Catholic community, especially in the west, and smaller Protestant, Muslim (Tatar) and Jewish communities. Around four in five people live in cities, and since 2020 hundreds of thousands have left, forming a large diaspora in Poland, Lithuania and beyond.
resources: Potash, among the world's largest reserves
Fertile farmland, forests and peat bogs
Białowieża Forest and the Pripyat wetlands
Machine-building, tractors and heavy trucks
Strong IT and engineering talent
A highly educated population
struggles: Severe restrictions on free expression and independent media, with many political prisoners
Emigration of young and skilled people since 2020
International isolation and sanctions tied to the war in Ukraine
Heavy economic dependence on Russia
Lasting health and land effects of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in the south-east
Demographic decline and an ageing countryside
prayFor: For all who are imprisoned for their convictions and for their families who wait
For freedom of conscience, speech and worship for every Belarusian
For families divided by emigration, and for those abroad longing for home
For an end to the war in Ukraine and protection for all caught up in it
For healing of the land and people still bearing the wounds of Chernobyl and of World War II

summary.history: Slavic tribes settled these forests and marshes, and the principality of Polotsk was an early centre of Kievan Rus'. From the 13th century the lands formed the heart of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, later joined with Poland in a multi-faith commonwealth where Jews, Tatars, Catholics and Orthodox lived side by side. The partitions of Poland brought the region under the Russian Empire in the late 18th century. World War II was catastrophic: about a quarter or more of the population died, hundreds of villages like Khatyn were burned, and Belarusian Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. The 1986 Chernobyl disaster contaminated much of the south-east, and independence came with the Soviet collapse in 1991.
summary.politicalHistory: A short-lived Belarusian People's Republic was declared in 1918, but the territory became the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, a founding member of the USSR and of the UN. Belarus declared independence in 1991 and adopted a constitution in 1994, creating a presidential republic. Constitutional changes from the mid-1990s concentrated power in the presidency, and elections have since been judged by international observers as neither free nor fair. Mass peaceful protests after the disputed 2020 election were met with arrests and repression, and the country remains closely aligned with Russia through the Union State.
summary.art: Belarusian culture treasures the 16th-century humanist Francysk Skaryna, one of the first printers of the Bible in an East Slavic language, and the national poets Yanka Kupala and Yakub Kolas. Marc Chagall was born in Vitebsk and painted its streets throughout his life, and Svetlana Alexievich, Nobel laureate in 2015, gave voice to ordinary people's testimony. Straw weaving, rushnyk embroidery, Slutsk sashes and polyphonic village singing remain loved crafts and traditions.
summary.monuments: Białowieża Forest, shared with Poland, is a UNESCO site sheltering the European bison in one of Europe's last primeval forests. The Mir Castle Complex and Nesvizh Palace, both UNESCO sites, reflect the Radziwiłł magnates' power and Renaissance-Baroque grandeur. The Brest Fortress memorial and the Khatyn memorial mark the sacrifices and atrocities of World War II. Points of the Struve Geodetic Arc also cross the country.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); three standard forms of one mutually intelligible language, Latin and Cyrillic scripts

people: Three constituent peoples share the country: Bosniaks (about half), Serbs (about a third) and Croats (about a sixth), alongside Roma, Jews and other smaller communities. Faith largely follows these lines, with Islam, Serbian Orthodoxy and Catholicism each deeply rooted, and mosques, churches and synagogues standing within sight of each other in Sarajevo and Mostar. The population has fallen sharply since the war and through emigration, and a large diaspora lives in Germany, Austria, Croatia, Serbia, Scandinavia and North America.
resources: Forests, rivers and some of Europe's last wild waterways
Hydropower and coal
Fertile valleys and fruit growing
Metal, wood and furniture industries
A layered heritage where East and West meet
Resilient, warm hospitality and a gifted diaspora
struggles: Deep political division along ethnic lines within a complex post-war constitutional system
Emigration of young people and population decline
Unemployment, low wages and corruption
Unhealed memories of the 1992–1995 war, missing persons still being identified, and genocide denial
Severe winter air pollution in cities
Landmines that still remain in parts of the countryside
prayFor: For healing and truthful remembrance among Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats and all who suffered in the war
For families still searching for the remains of missing loved ones
For young people to see a hopeful future and choose to stay
For leaders willing to build trust and serve all citizens equally
For clean air, safe land free of mines, and protection of wild rivers

summary.history: Illyrians and then Romans lived here before Slavs settled in the early Middle Ages; a medieval Bosnian kingdom flourished, with its own Bosnian Church and the distinctive stećak tombstones. The Ottomans conquered Bosnia in 1463 and Herzegovina soon after, and over four centuries many people embraced Islam while Orthodox, Catholic and Sephardic Jewish communities also grew. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878 and annexed it in 1908; the assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 sparked World War I. After the horrors of World War II and decades within socialist Yugoslavia, the 1992–1995 war brought the siege of Sarajevo, mass displacement and ethnic cleansing; around 100,000 people were killed, and the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica was ruled genocide by international courts.
summary.politicalHistory: Bosnia became a republic within socialist Yugoslavia after 1945. It declared independence in 1992 after a referendum largely boycotted by Bosnian Serbs, and war followed. The 1995 Dayton Agreement ended the fighting and created a state of two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, plus the Brčko District, with a rotating three-member presidency and an international High Representative. The country was granted EU candidate status in 2022, while constitutional reform remains contested.
summary.art: Sevdalinka, the yearning urban love song, is the soul of Bosnian music, and ganga singing echoes in the highlands. Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize in 1961 for novels such as 'The Bridge on the Drina', and Meša Selimović explored conscience and faith; the Sarajevo Haggadah, a medieval illuminated manuscript, survived wars thanks to protectors of several faiths. Copper engraving in Baščaršija, carpet weaving and Konjic woodcarving, recognised by UNESCO, continue old crafts.
summary.monuments: Mostar's Old Bridge, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004, is a UNESCO site and symbol of reconciliation. The Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge in Višegrad and the medieval stećci tombstones are also UNESCO-listed. Sarajevo's Baščaršija, the Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque and nearby cathedrals and synagogue show the city's interwoven faiths. The Srebrenica-Potočari Memorial honours the victims of the 1995 genocide.

name: Bulgaria

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Romani also widely spoken

people: Bulgarians form the large majority, with sizeable Turkish and Roma minorities and smaller Pomak (Bulgarian-speaking Muslim), Armenian and Aromanian communities. Most people belong to the Bulgarian Orthodox tradition, around a tenth are Muslim, and there are Catholic, Protestant and Jewish minorities. Sofia and the cities grow while many villages age and empty, and a large diaspora lives in Germany, Spain, the UK and elsewhere.
resources: Black Sea coast and the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope mountains
Fertile Thracian plain, rose oil, wine and sunflowers
Copper, coal and other minerals
Growing IT and outsourcing sector
Mineral springs and spa traditions
Ancient Thracian, Roman and Orthodox heritage
struggles: One of the fastest-shrinking populations in the world through emigration and low birth rates
Corruption and repeated political instability with many snap elections
Poverty in rural areas and among many Roma communities
Strain on healthcare as doctors and nurses emigrate
Energy dependence and the transition away from coal
prayFor: For villages and elderly people left behind as young people emigrate
For honest leadership and stable, trustworthy institutions
For dignity, education and opportunity for Roma children and families
For good doctors and nurses to stay and for care that reaches all
For unity and mutual respect among Bulgarians, Turks, Roma and all communities

summary.history: Thracians crafted gold and built tombs here long before Greeks and Romans arrived. In 681 Bulgars and Slavs founded the First Bulgarian Empire, which adopted Christianity in 864 and became a cradle of Slavic literacy and the Cyrillic script. After the Second Bulgarian Empire fell to the Ottomans in 1396, nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule followed, with churches and monasteries keeping language and faith alive. Liberation came in 1878 after the April Uprising and Russo-Turkish war, followed by Balkan Wars and two World Wars in which Bulgaria sided with the Central Powers and the Axis; yet in 1943 church leaders, politicians and citizens prevented the deportation of Bulgaria's own Jews, even as Jews from occupied Thrace and Macedonia were deported and murdered. Communist rule, including the forced renaming and expulsion of Turks in the 1980s, ended in 1989.
summary.politicalHistory: The Principality of Bulgaria was created in 1878 under the Tărnovo Constitution and declared full independence as a tsardom in 1908. A communist People's Republic was established in 1946 after a Soviet-backed takeover, and the one-party state ruled until 1989. The 1991 constitution created a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president. Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007, and entered the Schengen area in stages from 2024.
summary.art: Bulgaria gave the world the Cyrillic alphabet through the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and Orthodox icon painting and woodcarving flourished in monastery schools such as Tryavna and Samokov. Haunting polyphonic women's choirs, the bagpipe (gaida) and the dancing rituals of the Nestinari are cherished traditions, alongside Martenitsa and Surova, recognised by UNESCO. Writers Ivan Vazov and Hristo Botev and painters Vladimir Dimitrov and Zlatyu Boyadzhiev shaped modern Bulgarian art.
summary.monuments: Rila Monastery, a UNESCO site, has preserved faith and learning since the 10th century. The Boyana Church's 13th-century frescoes and the Thracian tomb of Kazanlak are also UNESCO-listed treasures. The rock-hewn churches of Ivanovo and the Madara Rider carving show medieval and early Bulgarian art. Sofia's Alexander Nevsky Cathedral honours those who fell in the war of liberation, and Plovdiv's Roman theatre speaks of an even older past.

name: Cyprus

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English widely spoken, plus Armenian and Cypriot Maronite Arabic

people: Greek Cypriots, mostly Orthodox Christian, form the majority in the south, while Turkish Cypriots, mostly Sunni Muslim, live largely in the north, together with settlers from Turkey. Small Maronite, Armenian and Latin Catholic communities have deep roots, and many Europeans, Russians, Ukrainians, South Asians and others now live and work on the island. Families on both sides still carry memories of displacement, and large Cypriot diasporas live in the UK and Australia.
resources: Strategic location in the eastern Mediterranean
Sun, sea and tourism
Shipping and ship management
Financial and professional services
Offshore natural gas discoveries
Halloumi, wine, citrus and a rich food culture
struggles: Division of the island since 1974, with displaced families on both sides and missing persons still being sought
Water scarcity, drought and wildfires in a warming climate
Housing costs rising beyond many young Cypriots
Fair treatment of migrant workers and asylum seekers
Reputational and regulatory pressures in the financial sector
prayFor: For reconciliation and a just, lasting peace between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots
For families still seeking their missing and longing for homes they lost
For rain, healthy forests and wise use of water
For welcome and dignity for migrant workers and refugees on the island
For young Cypriots to find homes, work and hope on the island they love

summary.history: Cyprus has been settled since the Neolithic and became famed for its copper, from which its name may come. Mycenaean Greeks, Phoenicians, Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians and Romans followed, and the apostles Paul and Barnabas brought Christianity early. After Byzantine rule came Crusaders, the Lusignan kings, Venice and, from 1571, the Ottomans, under whom Greek and Turkish communities lived intertwined. British administration began in 1878, and independence in 1960 was followed by intercommunal violence in 1963–64. In 1974 a coup backed by the Greek military junta was followed by a Turkish military intervention, dividing the island and displacing roughly a third of Greek Cypriots and many Turkish Cypriots.
summary.politicalHistory: Cyprus became an independent republic in 1960 under a power-sharing constitution guaranteed by Britain, Greece and Turkey, with Britain retaining two sovereign base areas. The power-sharing system broke down in 1963–64, and since 1974 the island has been divided by a UN-patrolled buffer zone. In 1983 the north declared the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus', recognised only by Turkey. The Republic of Cyprus is a presidential democracy and joined the EU in 2004, though EU law is suspended in the north; the 2004 Annan reunification plan was approved by Turkish Cypriots and rejected by Greek Cypriots.
summary.art: Byzantine icon painting and church frescoes reach a high point in the Troodos mountain churches, while Lefkara lace and embroidery, said to have charmed Leonardo da Vinci, remain living crafts. Cypriot folk music, the poetic duelling of tsiattista and Turkish Cypriot folk songs carry island humour and longing. Poets such as Vasilis Michaelides and Kostas Montis wrote of Cypriot identity, loss and hope.
summary.monuments: The painted churches of the Troodos region are a UNESCO site, famed for their Byzantine frescoes. Paphos, also UNESCO-listed, holds superb Roman mosaics and the Tombs of the Kings, and the Neolithic village of Choirokoitia is one of the best-preserved prehistoric settlements in the eastern Mediterranean. Kourion's theatre overlooks the sea, and in the north, Salamis and the Gothic cathedral-turned-mosque in Famagusta tell of many civilisations.

name: Czechia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Slovak widely understood

people: Most people identify as Czech or Moravian, with Slovak, Ukrainian, Vietnamese, Polish, Roma and German communities; several hundred thousand Ukrainian refugees have arrived since 2022. Czechia is one of the least religiously affiliated societies in Europe: most people declare no religion, while Catholics are the largest faith group and Protestant traditions recall Jan Hus and the Bohemian Reformation. Around three-quarters of people live in towns and cities.
resources: Strong manufacturing and automotive industry
Engineering and technical education
Forests, rivers and fertile Bohemian and Moravian land
Glassmaking, brewing and wine traditions
Spa towns and mineral springs
Rich architectural and musical heritage
struggles: Housing affordability, especially in Prague and Brno
Energy transition away from coal and dependence on imported gas
Exclusion and discrimination faced by many Roma communities
Regional inequality and over-indebted households
Drought and bark-beetle damage to forests
Political polarisation and disinformation
prayFor: For a society that, whether believing or not, keeps searching for truth and meaning
For Roma families to live free of prejudice, with good schools and work
For Ukrainian refugees to find welcome, safety and a home
For healthy forests, rivers and land in a drying climate
For families burdened by debt and rising costs

summary.history: Celtic Boii, from whom Bohemia takes its name, and later Slavic peoples settled the land, and Great Moravia welcomed the missionaries Cyril and Methodius in the 9th century. The Přemyslid dynasty built the Kingdom of Bohemia, which reached a golden age under Charles IV, who made Prague an imperial capital. The reformer Jan Hus was burned in 1415, sparking the Hussite movement; after defeat at the White Mountain in 1620, Habsburg rule brought forced re-Catholicisation and centuries of Germanisation. Czechoslovakia was born in 1918, betrayed at Munich in 1938 and occupied by Nazi Germany, which murdered most of its Jews and many Roma; after the war some three million Germans were expelled, often brutally. Communist rule followed in 1948, the Prague Spring was crushed in 1968, and the Velvet Revolution brought freedom in 1989.
summary.politicalHistory: Czechoslovakia was declared in 1918 under Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and remained a parliamentary democracy until 1938. After Nazi occupation, the Communist Party seized power in 1948, and the 1968 reforms of the Prague Spring were ended by a Warsaw Pact invasion. The nonviolent Velvet Revolution of 1989 led to free elections, with Václav Havel as president. Czechoslovakia separated peacefully on 1 January 1993, and the Czech Republic, a parliamentary democracy, joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
summary.art: Czech music is world-renowned through Smetana, Dvořák, Janáček and Martinů. Literature runs from Karel Čapek, who coined the word 'robot', to Franz Kafka, Jaroslav Hašek, Bohumil Hrabal, Milan Kundera and Václav Havel, while Alfons Mucha shaped Art Nouveau. Bohemian crystal, marionette theatre, blueprint (modrotisk) textiles and the animated films of Jiří Trnka and Jan Švankmajer are cherished arts.
summary.monuments: The historic centre of Prague, a UNESCO site, gathers Prague Castle, St Vitus Cathedral, the Charles Bridge and the Old Town astronomical clock. Český Krumlov and Telč are beautifully preserved UNESCO towns, and Kutná Hora's St Barbara's Church recalls medieval silver wealth. The Villa Tugendhat in Brno is a modernist landmark, and the Terezín memorial remembers the victims of the Nazi ghetto and camp.

name: Denmark

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; German minority in the south, Faroese and Greenlandic in the wider realm

people: Most people are Danes, and around one in six are immigrants or their descendants, with roots in Poland, Syria, Turkey, Ukraine, Romania and many other countries; a German-speaking minority lives in South Jutland. Around seven in ten belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Denmark, though weekly attendance is low, and Muslims form the second-largest faith community. The Kingdom also includes the Faroe Islands and Greenland, home to the Kalaallit (Inuit) people, each with self-government.
resources: Wind energy and green technology
Pharmaceuticals and life sciences
Shipping and logistics
Agriculture, dairy and pork exports
High social trust and strong welfare institutions
Design, architecture and a culture of cooperation
struggles: Polarised debates over immigration, integration and asylum policy
Agricultural nutrient pollution harming seas and fjords
Loneliness and rising mental-health strain among young people
Sea-level rise and storm surges along low coasts
Reckoning with the colonial past and present relationship with Greenland
prayFor: For newcomers to find genuine belonging and for neighbourhoods to grow in trust
For young people struggling with loneliness, anxiety and pressure
For healing of the waters of the Baltic and the fjords
For respectful, honest relationships with the peoples of Greenland and the Faroe Islands
For the comfort of hygge to reach the lonely, the elderly and the forgotten

summary.history: Hunter-gatherers and early farmers left bog bodies, burial mounds and the Sun Chariot, and by the Viking Age Danes raided, traded and settled across England, Normandy and the Baltic. Harald Bluetooth unified Denmark and turned it toward Christianity around 965, and the Kalmar Union (1397) briefly joined all of Scandinavia under Danish rule. The Lutheran Reformation came in 1536; Denmark later took part in the transatlantic slave trade and held colonies in the Caribbean, West Africa and India, alongside Iceland, Greenland and the Faroes. Wars cost Denmark Skåne, Norway and Schleswig-Holstein, and during the Nazi occupation (1940–45) ordinary Danes helped almost all of the country's Jews escape to Sweden in 1943.
summary.politicalHistory: Denmark was a monarchy for over a thousand years and an absolute monarchy from 1660. The June Constitution of 1849 created a constitutional monarchy, and parliamentary rule was established in 1901. The 1953 constitution created a single-chamber Folketing and allowed female succession to the throne. Denmark was a founding member of NATO in 1949 and joined the European Community in 1973, while home rule was granted to the Faroe Islands (1948) and Greenland (1979, extended in 2009).
summary.art: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales and Søren Kierkegaard's philosophy are among Denmark's great gifts, along with Karen Blixen's stories. The Skagen painters and Vilhelm Hammershøi captured northern light, and Carl Nielsen shaped Danish music. Danish design and architecture, from Arne Jacobsen and Kaare Klint to Jørn Utzon's Sydney Opera House, unite simplicity, craft and everyday beauty.
summary.monuments: The Jelling mounds and runic stones, a UNESCO site, mark Denmark's turn to Christianity. Kronborg Castle in Helsingør, setting of Hamlet, and Roskilde Cathedral, burial place of Danish monarchs, are also UNESCO-listed. The Wadden Sea and Stevns Klint protect remarkable natural heritage. Copenhagen's Nyhavn, the Round Tower and the Christiansborg Palace, seat of parliament, tell the story of the capital.

name: Estonia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Võro and Seto varieties

people: About two-thirds of people are Estonian, a Finnic people, and around a quarter are Russian-speaking, concentrated in Tallinn and the north-east around Narva; Ukrainians, Belarusians and Finns are also present. Estonia is among the least religious countries in the world, with Orthodox and Lutheran Christians the largest faith groups, while folk traditions tied to forests and seasons remain beloved. Nearly half the population lives in the Tallinn region.
resources: World-leading digital government and tech start-up culture
Forests covering about half the land
Oil shale (being phased down)
Islands, bogs and Baltic coastline
Choral song tradition binding the nation
Highly educated, innovative people
struggles: Integration and mutual trust between Estonian- and Russian-speaking communities
Security anxieties stemming from the war in Ukraine
Energy transition away from oil shale in Ida-Virumaa
Ageing and shrinking population
Regional gaps between Tallinn and rural areas
prayFor: For trust, friendship and fair opportunity between Estonian and Russian speakers
For peace and security in the Baltic region
For workers and families in Ida-Virumaa as the oil-shale industry winds down
For a spiritually searching people to find deep meaning and hope
For the care of forests and bogs that shape the nation's soul

summary.history: Finnic peoples have lived here for millennia, farming, fishing and keeping nature-centred beliefs. In the 13th century German and Danish crusaders conquered the land, and a Baltic German nobility dominated Estonian peasants for centuries under Danish, Swedish and then Russian rule. A national awakening in the 19th century revived language and song, and independence was won in the 1918–20 War of Independence. Soviet occupation in 1940, Nazi occupation and Soviet return brought mass deportations to Siberia, executions, the murder of Estonia's Jews and an exodus to the West, followed by decades of Russification. The 'Singing Revolution' of 1987–91 restored independence peacefully.
summary.politicalHistory: The Republic of Estonia was declared on 24 February 1918 and became a parliamentary democracy before an authoritarian period from 1934. It was annexed by the USSR in 1940, an occupation never recognised by many Western countries. Independence was restored in August 1991, and the 1992 constitution created a parliamentary republic with an indirectly elected president. Estonia joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the eurozone in 2011, pioneering e-government and online voting.
summary.art: The Song Festival tradition, with tens of thousands singing together, is recognised by UNESCO and carried the nation through occupation. Arvo Pärt's spiritual minimalism and Veljo Tormis's choral music are known worldwide, and the epic 'Kalevipoeg' and the writers Jaan Kross and A. H. Tammsaare shaped literature. Kihnu Island's cultural space, Seto leelo singing and smoke-sauna traditions are living UNESCO heritage.
summary.monuments: Tallinn's Old Town, a UNESCO site, is one of the best-preserved medieval Hanseatic towns. The Song Festival Grounds in Tallinn are the heart of the Singing Revolution. Kuressaare Castle on Saaremaa and Toompea Castle show medieval power, while Soomaa and Lahemaa national parks protect wild bogs and coast. Points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a UNESCO site, also run through Estonia.

name: Finland

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. three Sámi languages and immigrant languages

people: Most people are Finnish speakers, with a Swedish-speaking minority of about five percent, the Indigenous Sámi in Lapland, Finnish Kale Roma, and growing communities from Russia, Estonia, Ukraine, Iraq, Somalia and elsewhere. Around two-thirds belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland, a share that is gradually falling, with a smaller Orthodox Church and growing numbers who are unaffiliated. Most people live in the south, especially the Helsinki region, while the north is sparsely populated.
resources: Vast forests and a sustainable forestry industry
Tens of thousands of lakes and clean water
World-renowned education system
Technology, telecoms and gaming
Nuclear and renewable energy
High social trust and sauna culture
struggles: An ageing population and a falling birth rate
Unemployment and regional decline outside the growth centres
Mental-health strain, loneliness and alcohol harm
Security concerns along the long border with Russia
Balancing forestry with biodiversity and climate goals
Recognition of Sámi rights and land
prayFor: For the lonely, the depressed and those quietly struggling through long winters
For Sámi people to see their rights, language and lands honoured
For peace on Finland's eastern border and among the nations of the region
For young families, and for the elderly to be cared for with dignity
For forests and lakes to be stewarded for generations to come

summary.history: People arrived as the ice retreated, and Finnic and Sámi peoples lived by hunting, fishing and farming. From the 12th–13th centuries Finland became part of the Swedish realm, receiving Christianity and later the Lutheran Reformation, with Mikael Agricola creating written Finnish. In 1809 Russia took Finland as an autonomous Grand Duchy, where a national awakening grew around the Kalevala and the Finnish language. Independence in 1917 was followed by a painful civil war in 1918, and in the Winter War and Continuation War against the Soviet Union Finland kept its independence but lost Karelia, with over 400,000 people resettled. Post-war Finland rebuilt from a poor agrarian country into a prosperous welfare state.
summary.politicalHistory: Finland declared independence from Russia on 6 December 1917 and adopted a republican constitution in 1919. After World War II it maintained neutrality and careful relations with the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Finland joined the EU in 1995 and the eurozone in 1999, and a new constitution in 2000 strengthened parliament's role. In 2023, after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland joined NATO.
summary.art: The Kalevala, compiled by Elias Lönnrot, inspired painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela and composer Jean Sibelius, whose 'Finlandia' became a song of national hope. Tove Jansson's Moomins, Aleksis Kivi's 'Seven Brothers' and Väinö Linna's war novels are much-loved literature. Finnish design, from Alvar Aalto's architecture to Marimekko and iittala glass, and the smoke sauna tradition, recognised by UNESCO, express a closeness to nature.
summary.monuments: Suomenlinna, a UNESCO-listed sea fortress, guards the approach to Helsinki. Old Rauma, the Petäjävesi Old Church and the Bronze Age burial cairns of Sammallahdenmäki are also UNESCO sites. Helsinki Cathedral, the Uspenski Orthodox Cathedral and the rock-hewn Temppeliaukio Church show the capital's faith traditions. In Lapland, Sámi heritage is presented at the Siida museum in Inari.

name: Hungary

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Romani, German and other minority languages also spoken

people: Most people are Hungarian (Magyar), with Roma the largest minority and smaller German, Slovak, Romanian, Croatian and Serbian communities; large Hungarian minorities also live in neighbouring Romania, Slovakia, Serbia and Ukraine. Catholics are the largest faith group, followed by Reformed (Calvinist) and Lutheran Christians, with a Jewish community, centred in Budapest, that is among the largest in Central Europe, and many who declare no religion. Around a fifth of the population lives in Budapest.
resources: Fertile Great Plain and strong agriculture
Thermal springs and spa culture
Automotive and electronics manufacturing
The Danube and Lake Balaton
Strong mathematical and scientific tradition
Wine regions such as Tokaj
struggles: Deep political polarisation and EU concerns over rule of law and media pluralism
High inflation and cost-of-living pressures in recent years
Poverty and segregation affecting many Roma communities
Strain on healthcare and education with staff shortages
Ageing population and emigration of young professionals
Drought on the Great Plain
prayFor: For healing across political divides and space for honest, respectful public life
For Roma children to learn and grow in schools free of segregation
For nurses, doctors and teachers who carry heavy loads
For families stretched by rising prices
For rain and fruitful land on the Great Plain

summary.history: Celts, Romans (in the province of Pannonia), Huns and Avars passed through before Magyar tribes settled the Carpathian Basin around 895. King Stephen I was crowned in 1000, establishing a Christian kingdom. The Mongol invasion of 1241 and the defeat at Mohács in 1526 led to Ottoman occupation of central Hungary for 150 years, followed by Habsburg rule; the 1848 revolution was crushed but led to the Dual Monarchy of 1867. The Treaty of Trianon (1920) cost Hungary about two-thirds of its territory, a lasting wound. In 1944 some 430,000 Jews were deported, most murdered at Auschwitz; Soviet troops crushed the 1956 revolution, and communism ended peacefully in 1989.
summary.politicalHistory: The medieval Kingdom of Hungary lasted for centuries, joining the Habsburg lands and becoming a co-equal partner in Austria-Hungary in 1867. After World War I a brief republic and a short-lived Soviet republic were followed by the Regency of Miklós Horthy. After World War II Hungary became a communist People's Republic; the 1956 uprising was suppressed by Soviet forces. A negotiated transition in 1989 created a parliamentary republic, a new Fundamental Law took effect in 2012, and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
summary.art: Franz Liszt, Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály brought Hungarian music to the world, Bartók and Kodály drawing deeply on village folk songs. Poets Sándor Petőfi and Attila József and Nobel laureate Imre Kertész are central to its literature. Herend and Zsolnay porcelain, Matyó embroidery, and the táncház folk-dance movement, recognised by UNESCO, are treasured living arts.
summary.monuments: Budapest's Danube banks, Buda Castle and Andrássy Avenue form a UNESCO World Heritage site, crowned by the Hungarian Parliament Building. The Benedictine Archabbey of Pannonhalma, the Early Christian necropolis of Pécs and the village of Hollókő are also UNESCO-listed. The Dohány Street Synagogue, one of the largest in the world, and the 'Shoes on the Danube Bank' memorial honour Hungarian Jewry and the victims of 1944–45.

name: Iceland

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English widely spoken, Polish is the largest immigrant language

people: Icelanders, descended from Norse and Gaelic settlers, form the majority, and around a sixth of residents are immigrants, with Poles the largest group. Most people are members of the Evangelical Lutheran National Church, though the share is falling and many are secular; there are small Catholic communities (largely immigrant) and a revived Norse-pagan Ásatrú fellowship. About two-thirds of people live in the capital region around Reykjavík.
resources: Geothermal energy and hydropower
Rich North Atlantic fishing grounds
Dramatic volcanic and glacial landscapes
Tourism
Aluminium smelting powered by renewable energy
A highly literate society with a medieval saga heritage
struggles: Volcanic eruptions on the Reykjanes peninsula, which forced the evacuation of Grindavík
Housing shortage and high cost of living
Heavy reliance on tourism and its pressure on fragile nature
Shrinking glaciers in a warming climate
Integration and fair treatment of immigrant workers
prayFor: For the people of Grindavík and all who have lost homes to eruptions
For safety and wisdom for those who watch and respond to the volcanoes
For affordable homes and a fair welcome for immigrant families
For care of glaciers, seas and fragile land in a changing climate
For fishing communities living with the sea's dangers and uncertainties

summary.history: Irish monks may have visited before Norse settlers, often with Gaelic slaves and wives, arrived from about 874. The settlers founded the Althing in 930 and accepted Christianity by consensus around 1000. Civil strife ended in submission to the Norwegian crown in 1262–64, and Iceland later came under Danish rule. Centuries of hardship followed: plague, a restrictive trade monopoly and the Laki eruption of 1783–84, which caused a famine that killed around a fifth of the population. A 19th-century independence movement led to sovereignty and later full independence, and Iceland went from one of Europe's poorest countries to one of its richest, weathering the 2008 banking collapse.
summary.politicalHistory: The Althing, founded in 930, is often called one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland lost its independence to Norway in the 13th century and then lived under Danish rule. It gained home rule in 1904 and sovereignty as the Kingdom of Iceland, in personal union with Denmark, in 1918. The Republic of Iceland was proclaimed at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944, and it is a parliamentary democracy and founding NATO member with no standing army.
summary.art: The medieval Sagas of Icelanders and the Eddas, preserving Norse myth, are among the treasures of world literature. Halldór Laxness won the Nobel Prize in 1955, and the tradition of 'jólabókaflóð', giving books at Christmas, shows a living love of reading. Rímur chanting, knitted lopapeysa sweaters and modern music from Björk and Sigur Rós to film composers carry Icelandic creativity forward.
summary.monuments: Þingvellir National Park, a UNESCO site, is where the Althing met in the rift between continental plates. Vatnajökull National Park and Surtsey island, both UNESCO-listed, show the island's living geology. Hallgrímskirkja in Reykjavík and the turf houses such as Glaumbær recall faith and older ways of life. Skálholt and Hólar were the historic bishoprics and centres of learning.

name: Kosovo

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Turkish, Bosnian and Romani have official status in some municipalities

people: Albanians form the great majority, alongside Serbs, Bosniaks, Turks, Gorani, Roma, Ashkali and Egyptian communities. Most people are Muslim, Serbs are Serbian Orthodox, and there is a small Catholic Albanian community. Kosovo has one of the youngest populations in Europe, and a very large diaspora, especially in Germany and Switzerland, supports families at home.
resources: One of Europe's youngest, most energetic populations
Lignite reserves and minerals such as lead and zinc
Fertile plains and fruit growing
Remittances and a globally connected diaspora
Šar and Accursed Mountains (Bjeshkët e Nemuna)
Medieval Serbian Orthodox and Ottoman heritage
