Limited international recognition and visa and trade barriers
High youth unemployment and emigration
Severe air pollution from lignite power plants
Families still searching for people missing since the 1998–1999 war
Corruption and weak rule of law
prayFor: For peace, safety and mutual respect between Albanians, Serbs and all communities
For the families of the missing to find answers and rest
For young people to find good work and a future at home
For clean air and healthy land
For protection of holy places of every faith and for those who pray in them

summary.history: Dardanians and Illyrians lived here in antiquity before Roman and Byzantine rule, and Slavs settled from the 6th–7th centuries. In the Middle Ages Kosovo became a heartland of the Serbian state and its Orthodox Church, and the 1389 Battle of Kosovo became a powerful symbol in Serbian memory. Under five centuries of Ottoman rule many Albanians embraced Islam, and Albanians gradually became the majority; in 1878 the League of Prizren began the Albanian national movement. In the 20th century Kosovo passed to Serbia and Yugoslavia, and after its autonomy was revoked in 1989 Albanians faced repression. In the 1998–1999 war some 13,000 people died, around 800,000 Albanians were expelled or fled, and after NATO's intervention many Serbs and Roma fled reprisals; churches, mosques and homes on both sides were destroyed.
summary.politicalHistory: Kosovo was an autonomous province within Serbia in socialist Yugoslavia, gaining broad self-rule under the 1974 constitution, which was revoked in 1989. After the 1999 war it was placed under UN administration under Security Council Resolution 1244, with NATO-led KFOR peacekeepers. Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and adopted a constitution creating a parliamentary republic. It is recognised by around half of UN member states but not by Serbia, which considers it part of its territory, and EU-facilitated dialogue between the two continues.
summary.art: Kosovo's Albanian tradition holds epic songs of the highlands sung with the çifteli and lahuta, and the white plis felt cap remains a symbol of identity. Medieval Serbian Orthodox frescoes in Kosovo's monasteries are masterpieces of Byzantine art. Poet Ali Podrimja and novelist Rexhep Qosja, the Prizren filigree tradition and a young contemporary art and film scene, including the DokuFest festival in Prizren, show a creative spirit.
summary.monuments: The Medieval Monuments in Kosovo, a UNESCO site, include the monasteries of Visoki Dečani and Gračanica and the Patriarchate of Peć. Prizren's Ottoman-era old town, the Sinan Pasha Mosque and the League of Prizren complex recall Albanian history. Pristina's Newborn monument celebrates independence, while the Jashari memorial in Prekaz is significant for Kosovo Albanians. Archaeological Ulpiana shows the Roman past.

name: Latvia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Latgalian and the endangered Livonian

people: About two-thirds of residents are Latvian, a Baltic people, and around a quarter are Russian, with Belarusian, Ukrainian, Polish and Lithuanian minorities and the small Indigenous Livonian community. Lutheran, Catholic (especially in eastern Latgale) and Orthodox Christians are the main faith traditions, alongside many with no affiliation and a revived Dievturība folk religion. Around a third of people live in Riga, and emigration since 2004 has created a large diaspora in the UK, Ireland and Germany.
resources: Forests covering about half the land, timber and wood products
Baltic Sea ports and transit routes
Rivers, lakes and long sandy coastline
IT, logistics and services sector
Rich song and dance traditions
Art Nouveau architecture in Riga
struggles: Population decline through emigration and low birth rates
Social and linguistic divides between Latvian and Russian speakers
Regional inequality, especially in Latgale
Security fears in the shadow of the war in Ukraine
Income inequality and pressure on healthcare
prayFor: For trust, understanding and shared belonging among Latvian and Russian speakers
For families separated by emigration, and for those who long to return
For hope and opportunity in Latgale and rural areas
For peace and security in the Baltic region
For the elderly and the sick to receive good care

summary.history: Baltic tribes such as the Curonians, Semigallians, Latgalians and Selonians, along with the Finnic Livonians, lived here for millennia. In the 13th century German crusaders conquered the land, founding Riga as a Hanseatic city and imposing a German landholding nobility. Polish-Lithuanian, Swedish and, from the 18th century, Russian rule followed, with serfdom abolished in the 19th century as a national awakening grew. Independence was won in 1918–20, then lost to Soviet occupation in 1940; deportations, Nazi occupation, the murder of most of Latvia's Jews and renewed Soviet rule brought immense suffering and large-scale Russian-speaking settlement. The nonviolent Singing Revolution and the Baltic Way human chain of 1989 led to restored independence in 1991.
summary.politicalHistory: The Republic of Latvia was proclaimed on 18 November 1918, and its 1922 constitution (Satversme) created a parliamentary democracy, interrupted by authoritarian rule from 1934. The country was occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940. Independence was restored in 1991 and the 1922 constitution reinstated, with a parliament (Saeima) electing the president. Latvia joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the eurozone in 2014.
summary.art: The Song and Dance Festival, recognised by UNESCO together with those of Estonia and Lithuania, gathers tens of thousands of singers and dancers. The dainas, short folk songs collected by Krišjānis Barons, number in the hundreds of thousands, and poets Rainis and Aspazija shaped modern literature. Painter Mark Rothko was born in Daugavpils, and amber jewellery, woven belts and choral composers such as Pēteris Vasks continue rich traditions.
summary.monuments: The historic centre of Riga, a UNESCO site, is famed for its medieval core and Europe's richest collection of Art Nouveau buildings. Rundāle Palace, designed by Rastrelli, and Turaida Castle in the Gauja valley are beloved landmarks. The Freedom Monument in Riga symbolises independence, and the Salaspils and Rumbula memorials honour victims of Nazi atrocities. Points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a UNESCO site, also cross Latvia.

name: Liechtenstein

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); everyday speech is an Alemannic dialect

people: About two-thirds of residents are Liechtenstein citizens, and the rest are mostly Swiss, Austrian, German and Italian. The great majority are Catholic, with Protestant and Muslim minorities. It is a small, tightly knit country of villages along the Rhine valley and slopes, where more people work than live, as thousands commute daily from Switzerland and Austria.
resources: Highly specialised precision manufacturing and dental technology
Financial services
Alpine landscapes and the Rhine valley
Political stability and close ties with Switzerland and the EU (EEA)
The princely art collections
A skilled cross-border workforce
struggles: High housing costs and limited land
Dependence on cross-border commuters and foreign labour
Past reputation as a tax haven and ongoing financial-transparency reforms
Traffic congestion in the Rhine valley
Integration and political participation for non-citizen residents
prayFor: For the many commuters and foreign residents who keep the country running, that they may be valued and included
For integrity and wisdom in finance and business
For affordable homes for young families
For care of the Alpine environment and the Rhine
For a small nation to use its prosperity generously for the good of others

summary.history: The Rhine valley was settled by Celtic Raeti and became part of the Roman province of Raetia, later passing to the Alemanni and Frankish rule. In the Middle Ages the lordships of Schellenberg and Vaduz were held by various noble families. The Liechtenstein family, wealthy Austrian nobles, bought them in 1699 and 1712, and in 1719 the Holy Roman Emperor united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein. For much of its history it was poor and agricultural, with emigration to America, before transforming after World War II into a prosperous industrial and financial centre.
summary.politicalHistory: Liechtenstein became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719 and gained sovereignty in 1806. It was in the German Confederation until 1866, abolished its army in 1868, and stayed neutral in both World Wars. The 1921 constitution created a constitutional monarchy with democratic and parliamentary elements, and a customs union with Switzerland followed in 1923. Women gained the vote in 1984; Liechtenstein joined the UN in 1990 and the European Economic Area in 1995, and a 2003 referendum expanded the prince's powers.
summary.art: The Princely Collections, among the finest private art collections in the world, include works by Rubens, Van Dyck and Raphael, shown largely in Vienna. The Kunstmuseum Liechtenstein in Vaduz presents modern and contemporary art. Composer Josef Rheinberger, born in Vaduz, wrote organ and sacred choral music still performed today, and folk traditions such as Funkensonntag bonfires continue.
summary.monuments: Vaduz Castle, the residence of the princely family, overlooks the capital. Gutenberg Castle in Balzers and the ruins of Schellenberg's upper and lower castles recall the medieval past. Vaduz Cathedral of St Florin and the Liechtenstein National Museum tell the country's story. The Eschnerberg historical trail links prehistoric and medieval sites.

name: Lithuania

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Polish and Russian spoken by minorities

people: Most people are Lithuanian, with Polish (around 6%), Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian minorities, and small Tatar and Karaim communities with centuries-old roots. Lithuania is predominantly Catholic, with Orthodox, Old Believer, Lutheran, Muslim and Jewish minorities; before the Holocaust, Vilnius was a world centre of Jewish learning. About two-thirds of people live in towns and cities, and emigration has created a large diaspora.
resources: Fertile farmland and forests
Baltic coast and the Curonian Spit
Klaipėda, an ice-free seaport
Fintech, lasers and life sciences
An ancient language, close to early Indo-European
Amber and rich folk traditions
struggles: Population decline through emigration and low birth rates
Security concerns in the shadow of the war in Ukraine and on the Belarus border
Regional and income inequality
High rates of suicide and alcohol harm, though both have declined
Reckoning honestly with the Holocaust and difficult chapters of the past
prayFor: For those who struggle with despair and addiction, and for all who care for them
For peace and security for Lithuania and its neighbours
For families separated by emigration and for villages left behind
For honest remembrance and healing of the wounds of the Holocaust and Soviet repression
For friendship among Lithuanians, Poles, Russians and all who call Lithuania home

summary.history: Baltic tribes lived here for thousands of years and were the last in Europe to accept Christianity, officially in 1387. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania became one of Europe's largest states in the 14th–15th centuries, joined with Poland in 1569 in a commonwealth home to many faiths and peoples. The partitions of 1795 brought Russian rule, with bans on Lithuanian printing resisted by book smugglers. Independence came in 1918, but Soviet occupation in 1940 and Nazi occupation followed: around 90% of Lithuania's Jews were murdered, some with local collaboration, and Soviet deportations sent tens of thousands to Siberia while partisans resisted into the 1950s. Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in 1990.
summary.politicalHistory: The Kingdom of Lithuania was briefly established under Mindaugas in 1253, and the Grand Duchy later united with Poland in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The modern state declared independence on 16 February 1918, with Vilnius contested by Poland between the wars and an authoritarian government from 1926. Annexed by the USSR in 1940, Lithuania restored independence on 11 March 1990, and Soviet troops killed 14 civilians defending the Vilnius TV tower in January 1991. The 1992 constitution created a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president, and Lithuania joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the eurozone in 2015.
summary.art: Lithuanian polyphonic sutartinės songs and cross-crafting are UNESCO intangible heritage, and the Song and Dance Festival is shared with Latvia and Estonia. M. K. Čiurlionis was both painter and composer, and poets Kristijonas Donelaitis and Czesław Miłosz, who grew up in Lithuania, shaped its literature. Amber jewellery, woven sashes and wooden folk sculpture of the Pensive Christ (Rūpintojėlis) remain much-loved crafts.
summary.monuments: Vilnius Old Town, a UNESCO site, is one of the largest Baroque old towns in Central and Eastern Europe. The Curonian Spit's dunes, Kernavė's hill forts and Kaunas's modernist architecture are also UNESCO-listed. The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai is a pilgrimage site of faith and resistance, and Trakai Island Castle recalls the Grand Duchy. The Paneriai memorial honours tens of thousands of Jews and others murdered there.

name: Luxembourg

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; Portuguese is widely spoken

people: Nearly half of residents are foreign nationals — especially Portuguese, French, Italian and Belgian — and around 200,000 cross-border commuters arrive daily from France, Belgium and Germany. Most people identify as Catholic by tradition, with a growing secular share and smaller Protestant, Orthodox and Muslim communities. Daily life moves fluidly between Luxembourgish, French and German, and most residents live in and around the capital and the southern former steel towns.
resources: Financial services and investment-fund industry
Multilingual, highly international workforce
EU institutions (Court of Justice, European Investment Bank)
Steel heritage (ArcelorMittal) and industrial know-how
Satellite and space industry (SES)
Moselle vineyards and Ardennes forests
struggles: Severe housing costs that push workers across the border
Economic dependence on the financial sector
Traffic and commuter strain from cross-border workers
Social cohesion between residents with and without citizenship
Rising inequality and child poverty in a wealthy country
prayFor: For families squeezed by housing costs to find secure, affordable homes
For newcomers and cross-border workers to be truly welcomed and belong
For integrity and care for the common good in finance and public life
For children growing up in poverty amid plenty
For a generous Luxembourg that uses its wealth to bless neighbours near and far

summary.history: Celtic Treveri and later Romans lived in this land before Count Siegfried built a castle on the Bock rock in 963. The Luxembourg dynasty gave the Holy Roman Empire several emperors, and afterwards the fortress city passed among Burgundian, Spanish, French, Austrian and Prussian hands as the 'Gibraltar of the North'. In the 19th and 20th centuries iron ore and steel brought prosperity and immigration, especially from Italy and later Portugal. German occupation in both world wars was deeply painful; in WWII the country was annexed, young men were forcibly conscripted and the Jewish community was deported and murdered. After 1945 Luxembourg became a founding member of Benelux, NATO and the European Communities, and turned itself into a financial centre.
summary.politicalHistory: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 made Luxembourg a Grand Duchy in personal union with the Netherlands, and the 1839 Treaty of London fixed its present borders. The 1867 Treaty of London declared it perpetually neutral and demolished the fortress, and in 1890 the personal union ended and a separate Nassau-Weilburg line took the throne. Grand Duchess Charlotte led the government-in-exile during WWII, and neutrality was abandoned for NATO in 1949. Today it is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy with a unicameral Chamber of Deputies.
summary.art: Luxembourg's culture blends Germanic and Romance influences, seen in its trilingual literature, from the national poet Michel Rodange's epic 'Renert' to modern writers in all three languages. Photographer Edward Steichen, born in Luxembourg, created 'The Family of Man' exhibition, now permanently shown at Clervaux Castle. Folk traditions include the Echternach dancing procession, sacred choral music, and Villeroy & Boch ceramics from Septfontaines.
summary.monuments: The old quarters and fortifications of Luxembourg City, including the Bock casemates, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site that tells the story of a millennium of sieges. Vianden Castle rises dramatically over the Our valley, and Clervaux Castle houses 'The Family of Man', inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World. The Hopping Procession of Echternach, held each Whit Tuesday around the abbey basilica, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, and the Grand Ducal Palace marks the heart of the capital.

name: Malta

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages

people: Maltese people have a distinct identity shaped by Mediterranean crossroads, speaking a Semitic language written in Latin script alongside English. Roman Catholicism remains central to culture and village life, with parish feasts (festi) shaping the calendar, though practice is declining; recent growth has brought large communities of workers from elsewhere in the EU, Asia and Africa. It is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, almost entirely urban, with Gozo offering a slower island rhythm.
resources: Strategic Mediterranean location and Freeport
Tourism and 7,000 years of layered heritage
Bilingual, service-oriented workforce
Financial services, iGaming and maritime registry
Deep natural harbours
Strong family and parish community life
struggles: Overdevelopment, construction strain and loss of open space
Concerns about corruption and rule of law
Treatment and integration of migrants and foreign workers
Water scarcity and traffic congestion
Housing affordability for young Maltese
prayFor: For honesty, justice and courage in public institutions
For migrants and foreign workers to be treated with dignity
For wise stewardship of the islands' limited land, sea and water
For young families seeking affordable homes
For faith communities to remain living sources of hope, not only tradition

summary.history: Neolithic farmers built some of the world's oldest free-standing temples on Malta and Gozo over 5,000 years ago. Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Byzantines and Arabs followed; tradition holds that St Paul was shipwrecked here around AD 60, and Arab rule left its mark on the Maltese language. Normans and successive European powers ruled until Charles V granted the islands to the Knights of St John in 1530, who withstood the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565 and built Valletta. Napoleon seized Malta in 1798, the British took it in 1800, and it became a vital naval base whose people endured devastating bombing in WWII and received the George Cross collectively.
summary.politicalHistory: Malta gained independence from Britain in 1964 as a Commonwealth realm and became a republic in 1974. The last British forces left in 1979, an anniversary marked as Freedom Day. Politics has been dominated by two parties, the Nationalist and Labour parties, with sharp rivalries over relations with Europe. Malta joined the EU in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008, and it remains a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state.
summary.art: Caravaggio painted 'The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist' in Valletta, and Mattia Preti's paintings fill the island's Baroque churches. Maltese traditions include the għana folk singing, brass band marches for village feasts, lace-making in Gozo, and Mdina glass. Literature in Maltese flowered from the 19th century with national poet Dun Karm Psaila, who wrote the national anthem.
summary.monuments: The Megalithic Temples of Malta, including Ġgantija on Gozo and Ħaġar Qim, are UNESCO sites older than Stonehenge and the pyramids. The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is a unique underground prehistoric burial complex, and the city of Valletta itself is a UNESCO-listed Baroque fortress capital. St John's Co-Cathedral, built by the Knights, and the silent walled city of Mdina speak of the islands' long religious and military history.

name: Moldova

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages

people: Most people are ethnic Moldovans/Romanians, with Ukrainian, Russian, Gagauz (a Turkic-speaking Orthodox people) and Bulgarian minorities; Transnistria, east of the Dniester, has a large Russian-speaking population. Over 90% are Eastern Orthodox Christians, and village life remains strong although Chișinău draws many young people. A large share of Moldovans work abroad, and remittances and divided families are part of everyday reality.
resources: Fertile black-earth (chernozem) soils
Ancient wine culture and vast cellars
Fruit, walnuts and sunflower agriculture
Multilingual, hardworking people and diaspora
Monastic heritage and rural traditions
Growing IT sector
struggles: Emigration and depopulation, with children raised by grandparents
Poverty, especially in rural areas and among the elderly
Unresolved Transnistria conflict
Energy dependence and price shocks
Corruption and the legacy of the 2014 bank fraud
Pressures from the war in neighbouring Ukraine
prayFor: For families separated by migration to be held together in love
For elderly people and rural villages facing poverty and loneliness
For peaceful, just resolution in Transnistria and security amid the war next door
For honest institutions and hope for young people to build a future at home
For the generosity Moldovans showed Ukrainian refugees to be returned to them in blessing

summary.history: The land between the Prut and the Dniester was home to Dacian and other peoples before Slavic and nomadic waves passed through. The medieval Principality of Moldavia, founded in the 14th century, flourished under Stephen the Great before becoming an Ottoman tributary. In 1812 Russia annexed its eastern half as Bessarabia; it united with Romania in 1918, was annexed by the USSR in 1940, and suffered war, Holocaust killings of its large Jewish population, deportations and a famine in 1946–47. Soviet rule brought Russification and industrialisation, and independence in 1991 was followed by a short war over Transnistria.
summary.politicalHistory: Moldova declared independence from the USSR in August 1991. Fighting in 1992 left Transnistria as a breakaway region with Russian troops, while Gagauzia gained autonomy in 1994. A 1994 constitution established a republic that became parliamentary in 2000, with presidents chosen by parliament until direct elections resumed in 2016. Politics has swung between pro-European and pro-Russian orientations; Moldova received EU candidate status in 2022.
summary.art: Moldovan culture shares much with Romania: doina laments, lively hora circle dances and folk ensembles with the nai (panpipe) and cimbalom. Woven carpets, embroidered shirts and painted Easter eggs are treasured crafts, and Martisor in March greets spring. Writers include poet Grigore Vieru and novelist Ion Druță, while the Romanian classic Mihai Eminescu is honoured as a shared national poet, and composer Eugen Doga is beloved for his film waltzes.
summary.monuments: The cave monastery of Orheiul Vechi, carved into limestone cliffs above the Răut river, is the country's most iconic site. Soroca Fortress, built under Stephen the Great, guarded the Dniester, and Căpriana and Saharna monasteries are spiritual centres. The vast wine cellars of Mileștii Mici and Cricova, with hundreds of kilometres of tunnels, are a point of national pride, and the Struve Geodetic Arc points in Moldova are part of a UNESCO site.

name: Monaco

languages.note: ≈ languages in common use; French is official

people: Only around a fifth of residents are Monégasque citizens; most are French, Italian and other foreign nationals, and tens of thousands commute in daily from France and Italy. Roman Catholicism is the state religion and the majority faith, alongside other Christian and Jewish communities. It is entirely urban and one of the most densely populated places on earth.
resources: Tourism, events and the Grand Prix
Banking and wealth management
Mediterranean coastline and port
Oceanographic research tradition
Cultural institutions (opera, ballet, philharmonic)
Political stability
struggles: Extreme cost of living and scarcity of land
Dependence on wealthy residents and a narrow economy
Pressure to meet international financial transparency standards
Coastal construction and marine-environment pressures
Gap between residents and workers who cannot afford to live there
prayFor: For wealth to be held with generosity and humility
For the many workers who serve Monaco but live beyond it
For care of the Mediterranean sea and its creatures
For integrity in finance and governance
For lonely and isolated people hidden behind affluence

summary.history: Ligurians and later Greek traders knew the rock of Monaco, named after a temple to Hercules Monoikos. In 1297 François Grimaldi, disguised as a monk, seized the fortress, and the Grimaldi family has ruled ever since, though under Spanish, French and Sardinian protection at various times. In 1848 Menton and Roquebrune broke away, costing Monaco most of its territory, and Prince Charles III answered by founding the Monte-Carlo casino in 1863. During WWII Monaco was occupied by Italy and then Germany, and Jewish refugees were rounded up and deported. After the war it grew into a centre of tourism, finance and glamour, expanding by land reclamation.
summary.politicalHistory: Monaco's sovereignty was confirmed by the 1861 Franco-Monégasque Treaty, and a 1918 treaty tied its independence closely to France. Its first constitution came in 1911, ending absolute rule, and the 1962 constitution established a constitutional monarchy with an elected National Council. Monaco joined the UN in 1993 and the Council of Europe in 2004, and remains a principality where the Prince holds substantial executive power.
summary.art: The Opéra de Monte-Carlo, designed by Charles Garnier, premiered works by Massenet, Puccini and Ravel, and Diaghilev's Ballets Russes made Monte Carlo its base in the 1920s. Today the Monte-Carlo Philharmonic, Les Ballets de Monte-Carlo and the circus festival continue this heritage. The Monégasque language survives in schools, street signs and traditional songs.
summary.monuments: The Prince's Palace on the Rock has been the Grimaldi seat since the 13th century. The Oceanographic Museum, founded by Prince Albert I, perches on a cliff and reflects a century of marine science. Monte-Carlo Casino and Opera, the Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate, and the Exotic Garden show Monaco's mix of faith, culture and spectacle.

name: Montenegro

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); the South Slavic varieties are mutually intelligible

people: Montenegro is a mosaic: people identify as Montenegrins (about 41%) and Serbs (about a third), with Bosniak, Albanian, Muslim-identifying, Croat and Roma communities. Around 70% are Orthodox Christians, about a fifth Muslim and a few percent Catholic, and questions of identity and church allegiance run deep. Most people live in Podgorica, Nikšić and along the coast, while mountain villages are emptying.
resources: Dramatic Adriatic coastline and the Bay of Kotor
Mountains, canyons and national parks (Durmitor, Lovćen, Biogradska Gora)
Tourism
Hydropower potential and the Tara river
Bauxite and aluminium heritage
Rich tradition of hospitality and oral poetry
struggles: Deep political polarisation over identity, church and alignment
Organised crime and corruption
Seasonal, tourism-dependent economy and youth unemployment
Unregulated coastal construction and environmental damage
Depopulation of the north
prayFor: For reconciliation across divisions of identity and faith
For justice and integrity against corruption and organised crime
For young people to find meaningful work and stay
For protection of the coast, rivers and mountains
For peace and respect between Orthodox, Muslim and Catholic neighbours

summary.history: Illyrian tribes inhabited the area before Roman rule, and Slavs settled from the 7th century, forming the medieval state of Duklja and later Zeta. As the Ottomans conquered the Balkans, the mountain stronghold around Cetinje kept a precarious autonomy, led from 1516 by prince-bishops, an office held by the Petrović-Njegoš family from 1696. Recognised as independent in 1878 at the Congress of Berlin, Montenegro became a kingdom in 1910 but was absorbed into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918. Within Yugoslavia it endured WWII occupation and civil war, and during the 1990s wars its forces took part in the siege of Dubrovnik while Montenegro also sheltered refugees.
summary.politicalHistory: After centuries of theocratic rule by prince-bishops, Danilo I secularised the state in 1852 and Nikola I proclaimed a kingdom in 1910. In 1918 a contested assembly in Podgorica deposed the dynasty and joined Serbia, a decision still debated. Montenegro was a republic of socialist Yugoslavia, then in union with Serbia until a 2006 referendum restored independence by a narrow majority. It is now a parliamentary republic, joined NATO in 2017 and is a candidate for EU membership.
summary.art: Montenegro's epic tradition includes guslar singers performing heroic ballads on the one-stringed gusle. Prince-Bishop Petar II Petrović-Njegoš wrote 'The Mountain Wreath', a foundational South Slavic epic poem, and the Cetinje printing house of 1494 produced one of the first books in Cyrillic, the Oktoih. Painters such as Petar Lubarda and Dado (Miodrag Đurić) and the stone-carving and maritime traditions of Kotor round out a rich heritage.
summary.monuments: The Natural and Culturo-Historical Region of Kotor, with its walled town and fjord-like bay, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as is Durmitor National Park with the Tara River Canyon. Ostrog Monastery, built into a cliff, draws Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim pilgrims alike. Njegoš's Mausoleum on Mount Lovćen and the old royal capital of Cetinje embody national memory, and Stari Bar is a haunting ruined medieval town.

name: North Macedonia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Albanian is co-official

people: About 58% of residents are ethnic Macedonians and about a quarter Albanians, with Turkish, Roma, Serb, Bosniak and Aromanian (Vlach) communities. Roughly 60% are Orthodox Christians and about a third Muslims, and the two main communities often live somewhat parallel lives. Many people have emigrated, and Skopje is home to over a quarter of the population.
resources: Lake Ohrid, one of Europe's oldest lakes
Mountains and national parks (Mavrovo, Galičica, Pelister)
Wine, tobacco and early fruit and vegetables
Byzantine and Ottoman heritage
Young, multilingual people and diaspora
Lead, zinc and chromium deposits
struggles: Emigration of young people
Severe winter air pollution in Skopje and Tetovo
Ethnic tensions between Macedonian and Albanian communities
Stalled EU accession and disputes with neighbours over identity
Corruption and weak rule of law
Low wages and unemployment
prayFor: For trust and friendship between Macedonian, Albanian, Roma and Turkish neighbours
For young people to see a future at home
For clean air and healthy cities
For honest leadership and fair institutions
For dignity and peace in questions of identity and history

summary.history: The region was part of ancient Paeonia and Macedon, then Roman and Byzantine provinces, and Ohrid became a great centre of Slavic Christianity through the disciples of Cyril and Methodius, Clement and Naum. Medieval Bulgarian and Serbian empires ruled before more than five centuries of Ottoman rule from the late 14th century. The 1903 Ilinden Uprising against the Ottomans was brutally crushed, and after the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 the region was divided between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria. During WWII Bulgarian occupation saw the Jews of Skopje, Bitola and Štip deported to Treblinka, and the 1963 Skopje earthquake killed over a thousand people.
summary.politicalHistory: A Macedonian republic was proclaimed within socialist Yugoslavia in 1944, and the country peacefully declared independence in 1991. A 2001 armed conflict with ethnic Albanian insurgents ended with the Ohrid Framework Agreement, which expanded minority rights. A long naming dispute with Greece was resolved by the 2018 Prespa Agreement, and the country became 'North Macedonia' in 2019. It is a parliamentary republic and joined NATO in 2020.
summary.art: Byzantine fresco painting reached a high point in the churches of Ohrid and Nerezi, whose 12th-century 'Lamentation' anticipates later European art. Intricately carved wooden iconostases by the Mijački carvers, colourful embroidered costumes, and asymmetric folk rhythms such as the 'teškoto' dance are cherished heritage. Poets Kočo Racin and Blaže Koneski shaped modern Macedonian literature, and Struga Poetry Evenings is an internationally known festival.
summary.monuments: The Natural and Cultural Heritage of the Ohrid Region, including the town's churches and the lake, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. St Panteleimon at Nerezi, the Monastery of St Naum, and St John at Kaneo on its cliff are treasured religious sites. Skopje's Stone Bridge and Old Bazaar, the ancient city of Heraclea Lyncestis near Bitola, and the Kokino megalithic observatory reveal layers of history.

name: Norway

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Sámi languages, Kven and immigrant languages

people: Most people are ethnic Norwegians, with the Indigenous Sámi in the north and national minorities such as Kvens, Forest Finns, Roma, Romani/Tater and Jews; about one in five residents are immigrants or children of immigrants. The Lutheran Church of Norway counts around 60% as members, though regular practice is low, and there are growing Muslim and Catholic communities. People are concentrated in the south and along the coast, with strong traditions of outdoor life (friluftsliv).

Hydropower supplying nearly all electricity
Fisheries and aquaculture
Fjords, mountains and Arctic landscapes
High-trust society and strong welfare state
Maritime and energy expertise
struggles: Economic dependence on fossil fuels amid climate goals
Conflicts over land use, wind power and Sámi rights
Integration and inequality affecting immigrant communities
Rural depopulation and the costs of remote services
Mental-health pressures among young people

For the Sámi people's rights, land and languages to be honoured
For newcomers to find belonging and opportunity
For young people to experience hope, purpose and community
For Norway's wealth to keep serving peace and the vulnerable worldwide

summary.history: After the Ice Age, hunters and fishers settled the coast, and the ancestors of the Sámi lived in the north for millennia. Norse chieftains and Viking voyagers ranged from Ireland to Greenland, and Olaf II (St Olaf) helped Christianise the realm in the 11th century. The Black Death devastated Norway, and it entered unions with Denmark (from 1380, for over four centuries) and then Sweden (1814–1905), while Sámi people endured long policies of forced assimilation. German occupation in 1940–45 brought resistance and suffering, including deportation of Norway's Jews, and after 1969 North Sea oil transformed the country's wealth.
summary.politicalHistory: Norway adopted its liberal Eidsvoll Constitution on 17 May 1814, one of the oldest still in force, before being forced into union with Sweden. The union was peacefully dissolved in 1905 and Prince Carl of Denmark became King Haakon VII. Parliamentary government, universal suffrage (women from 1913) and a strong labour movement shaped a social democracy. Norway is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system; it joined NATO in 1949 but voters rejected EU membership in 1972 and 1994.
summary.art: Edvard Munch's 'The Scream' and Henrik Ibsen's plays such as 'A Doll's House' are world-famous, as are Edvard Grieg's 'Peer Gynt' and Sigrid Undset's Nobel-winning novels. Sámi joik singing, Hardanger fiddle music, rosemaling decorative painting and woodcarving are living traditions. Stave-church carvings and the Oseberg Viking ship show artistry stretching back over a thousand years.
summary.monuments: Urnes Stave Church, the West Norwegian Fjords (Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord), Bryggen in Bergen and the mining town of Røros are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Rock Art of Alta preserves thousands of prehistoric carvings. In Oslo, the Viking ship finds, Akershus Fortress and Vigeland's sculpture park tell the nation's story from Viking sea-kings to modern humanism.

name: Romania

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. minority and immigrant languages

people: Most people are ethnic Romanians, with a large Hungarian community (about 6%, concentrated in Transylvania), Roma (officially around 3%, likely more) and smaller German, Ukrainian, Turkish, Tatar and Lipovan communities. About 85% are Romanian Orthodox, with Catholic, Reformed, Pentecostal and other churches. Roughly half live in rural areas, and several million Romanians live and work abroad.

Danube Delta wetlands
Fertile farmland and natural gas
Strong IT and engineering talent
Black Sea port of Constanța
Rich rural traditions and monastic heritage

Rural poverty and gaps in health and education
Discrimination against Roma communities
Corruption and trust in institutions
Illegal logging and threats to old-growth forests
Political polarisation
prayFor: For families split by labour migration and for children left behind
For Roma families to be met with dignity, justice and opportunity
For villages and rural communities to have good schools and care
For honesty and courage in public life
For protection of forests, rivers and the Danube Delta

summary.history: Dacian kingdoms flourished here before Rome conquered Dacia in AD 106, leaving a lasting Latin linguistic legacy. Through centuries of migrations, Wallachia and Moldavia emerged as principalities while Transylvania came under Hungarian and later Habsburg rule; leaders such as Stephen the Great and Michael the Brave resisted Ottoman dominance. Roma were held in slavery in Wallachia and Moldavia until abolition in the 1850s. Romania gained Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina in 1918, and in WWII the Antonescu regime allied with Nazi Germany and took part in the murder of hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma. Communist rule followed, culminating in Nicolae Ceaușescu's repressive dictatorship.
summary.politicalHistory: Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859 under Alexandru Ioan Cuza, independence from the Ottomans was won in 1877–78, and a kingdom was proclaimed in 1881. Interwar democracy gave way to royal dictatorship and the fascist-aligned Antonescu regime, and a communist people's republic was imposed in 1947. The December 1989 revolution overthrew Ceaușescu, and a 1991 constitution established a semi-presidential republic. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007.
summary.art: Painted monasteries, carved wooden churches, embroidered blouses (ia) and the Horezu pottery are treasured crafts, and doina laments and călușari ritual dance are recognised by UNESCO. Sculptor Constantin Brâncuși reshaped modern art, composer George Enescu wrote the Romanian Rhapsodies, and poet Mihai Eminescu is the national poet. Writers such as Mircea Eliade, Emil Cioran and Herta Müller, and the Romanian New Wave in cinema, have shaped wider European culture.
summary.monuments: The painted monasteries of northern Moldavia such as Voroneț, the wooden churches of Maramureș, and the fortified Saxon churches of Transylvania are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Sighișoara's medieval citadel, Horezu Monastery and the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains reflect different chapters of the nation's story. Bran and Peleș castles and Bucharest's vast Palace of the Parliament, built under Ceaușescu, are among the most visited sites.

name: Russia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. many Indigenous and immigrant languages; Russian is the shared language

people: Russia is home to over 190 peoples: ethnic Russians are about 80%, with Tatars, Bashkirs, Chechens, Chuvash, Avars, Yakuts (Sakha), Buryats and many small Indigenous peoples of the North and Siberia. Orthodox Christianity is the largest faith tradition, Islam is historic and widespread (especially in the Volga region and North Caucasus), and there are Buddhist, Jewish, Protestant and shamanic communities alongside many non-religious people. About three-quarters live in cities, mostly in the European west, while vast Siberian and Far Eastern regions are sparsely populated.
resources: Oil, natural gas, coal and metals
Vast forests, rivers and Lake Baikal's fresh water
Wheat and fertile black-earth farmland
Scientific, mathematical and engineering tradition
World-renowned literature, music and ballet
Diverse peoples and languages

Restrictions on independent media, civil society and dissent
Sanctions, isolation and an economy dependent on hydrocarbons
Demographic decline and emigration of young professionals
Regional inequality and poverty in rural areas and small towns
Alcoholism, HIV and lower life expectancy, especially for men
prayFor: For an end to the war and for a just peace, and comfort for all who grieve
For freedom of conscience, truth-telling and courage for ordinary people
For families in struggling towns and villages, and for the elderly and the sick
For the many peoples and languages of Russia to be honoured and flourish
For churches and faith communities to be places of mercy and reconciliation

summary.history: Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Turkic and many Siberian peoples shared these lands, and in the 9th–10th centuries Kievan Rus' emerged and adopted Orthodox Christianity in 988. After the Mongol conquest of the 13th century, Muscovy rose to dominance and expanded into an empire stretching across Siberia to the Pacific, conquering and colonising many peoples, while serfdom bound most peasants until 1861. The 1917 revolutions and civil war brought the Bolsheviks to power, and the Soviet era combined rapid industrialisation with famine, the Gulag and mass repression. The USSR lost some 27 million people in WWII, became a superpower and then dissolved in 1991; since then Russia has fought wars in Chechnya, Georgia and, since 2014 and at full scale from 2022, in Ukraine, causing immense suffering on all sides.
summary.politicalHistory: Muscovite grand princes became tsars from 1547, and Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721, an autocracy that permitted a limited parliament (Duma) only after the 1905 revolution. In 1917 the monarchy fell and the Bolsheviks under Lenin created a one-party state, formalised as the Soviet Union in 1922. After Gorbachev's reforms and the USSR's dissolution in 1991, the Russian Federation adopted a 1993 constitution establishing a strong presidential system. Since the 2000s power has become increasingly centralised, with constitutional amendments in 2020 extending presidential term options.
summary.art: Russian literature, from Pushkin, Gogol, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky and Chekhov to Akhmatova and Solzhenitsyn, is among the world's richest. Composers Tchaikovsky, Mussorgsky, Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky and Shostakovich, and the Bolshoi and Mariinsky ballets, shaped global music and dance. Icon painting reached its height with Andrei Rublev, and folk crafts include Khokhloma and Gzhel ware, Palekh lacquer miniatures and wooden matryoshka dolls.
summary.monuments: The Kremlin and Red Square in Moscow, the historic centre of St Petersburg with the Hermitage, and the Kizhi Pogost wooden churches are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Trinity Lavra of St Sergius and the White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal reflect the depth of Orthodox heritage, and the Kazan Kremlin unites Tatar and Russian history. Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake, and the volcanoes of Kamchatka are natural wonders of global importance.

name: San Marino

languages.note: ≈ languages in use; Italian is official

people: Sammarinese citizens share language and culture with the surrounding Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, and many residents are Italian nationals; a large diaspora lives in Italy, France, the US and Argentina. The great majority are Roman Catholic by tradition. Life centres on nine small municipalities (castelli), with many people commuting to and from Italy.
resources: Tourism to Mount Titano and the historic centre
Long tradition of liberty and stable institutions
Banking and small manufacturing
Postage stamps and coins for collectors
Close economic ties with Italy
Strong civic and community life
struggles: Small, narrow economy dependent on Italy
Restructuring of the banking sector after past crises
Ageing population
Negotiating a new association with the European Union
Limited land and housing for young families
prayFor: For wisdom in shaping San Marino's future with Europe
For young people to find meaningful work and purpose
For care and companionship for the elderly
For integrity in finance and public service
For this ancient republic to keep being a place of welcome and freedom

summary.history: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in 301 by Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab who took refuge on Mount Titano. A monastic community grew into a self-governing commune, which kept its independence through the medieval and Renaissance struggles of Italian city-states, briefly occupied by Cesare Borgia in 1503 and by Cardinal Alberoni in 1739–40. Napoleon respected its independence, and in the 19th century it gave refuge to Garibaldi and others during Italian unification. In WWII it remained neutral and sheltered tens of thousands of refugees, though it was bombed in 1944.
summary.politicalHistory: San Marino considers itself the world's oldest surviving republic, with statutes dating from the 1600s still forming part of its constitutional framework. Its sovereignty was recognised by Italy through treaties in 1862 and later. It is governed by a Grand and General Council, and two Captains Regent serve jointly as heads of state for six-month terms, a tradition centuries old. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the UN in 1992.
summary.art: Sammarinese culture draws on Italian and Romagnol traditions, with sacred art, stone carving and ceramics. Crossbow tournaments by the Federation of Crossbowmen in medieval dress keep alive a centuries-old tradition, and the Medieval Days festival fills the streets each summer. San Marino is also known for beautifully designed postage stamps and coins.
summary.monuments: The Historic Centre of San Marino and Mount Titano are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a living example of a medieval city-republic. The Three Towers — Guaita, Cesta and Montale — crown the ridge and appear on the flag. The neo-Gothic Palazzo Pubblico and the Basilica of San Marino, which holds the relics of the founding saint, are the civic and spiritual heart of the republic.

name: Serbia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. minority and immigrant languages; figures exclude Kosovo

people: About 80% are ethnic Serbs, with Hungarians (mainly in Vojvodina), Bosniaks (in Sandžak), Roma, Croats, Slovaks, Romanians and other communities, especially in multiethnic Vojvodina. Around 80% are Serbian Orthodox, with Catholic, Muslim and Protestant minorities. Many young people have emigrated, and Belgrade and Novi Sad are growing while rural areas age.
resources: Fertile Pannonian farmland in Vojvodina
The Danube and Sava rivers
Raspberries and fruit growing
Copper, gold and lithium deposits
IT sector and engineering talent
Medieval Orthodox monasteries and strong hospitality
struggles: Emigration and an ageing population
Unresolved dispute and tensions over Kosovo
Corruption and concerns about media freedom
Air pollution and debate over mining
Legacy and memory of the 1990s wars
Poverty and discrimination affecting Roma
prayFor: For healing of memories and reconciliation with neighbours
For peace and safety for Serbs, Albanians and all communities in the region
For honesty, freedom and justice in public life
For young people to find hope and work at home
For clean air, rivers and land

summary.history: Ancient Illyrian, Thracian and Celtic peoples lived here before the Romans; Slavs settled from the 6th–7th centuries. Under the Nemanjić dynasty a medieval Serbian kingdom and later empire flourished, and St Sava founded an autocephalous Serbian Church in 1219. The 1389 Battle of Kosovo became a defining memory, and by 1459 Serbia fell under Ottoman rule for some four centuries. Uprisings in 1804 and 1815 began a struggle for statehood; Serbia suffered enormous losses in WWI, and in WWII occupation, the Ustaše genocide of Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia and the murder of Serbia's Jews and Roma left deep wounds. In the 1990s wars of Yugoslavia's breakup brought atrocities committed by various forces, including Serbian forces, and suffering for all communities, followed by the 1999 NATO bombing.
summary.politicalHistory: Serbia won autonomy in 1830 and full independence at the 1878 Congress of Berlin, becoming a kingdom in 1882. In 1918 it led the creation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia), which became Tito's socialist federation after 1945. Under Slobodan Milošević in the 1990s Serbia was at the centre of the wars of dissolution, until mass protests ousted him in 2000. After the union with Montenegro ended in 2006, Serbia became an independent parliamentary republic; Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise, and Serbia is an EU candidate.
summary.art: Medieval Serbian frescoes, such as the 'White Angel' at Mileševa, are masterpieces of Byzantine-era art. Epic poetry sung to the gusle, kolo circle dances and brass bands (celebrated at the Guča festival) are vital traditions. Writers Ivo Andrić (Nobel Prize, 1961), Danilo Kiš and Miloš Crnjanski, inventor-scientist Nikola Tesla's legacy and painter Paja Jovanović are national touchstones.
summary.monuments: Studenica Monastery, Stari Ras with Sopoćani, and the Gamzigrad-Romuliana palace of Emperor Galerius are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and Serbia also regards the medieval monuments in Kosovo as central to its heritage. Belgrade's Kalemegdan fortress overlooks the meeting of the Sava and Danube, and the Church of St Sava is one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world. Petrovaradin Fortress in Novi Sad and Đerdap Gorge with the prehistoric site Lepenski Vir are other treasures.

name: Slovakia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. minority and immigrant languages

people: Most people are ethnic Slovaks, with a large Hungarian minority in the south (about 8%), Roma communities (estimated around 7–9%, many in segregated settlements in the east) and Rusyns and Ukrainians in the northeast. About 56% are Roman Catholic, with Lutheran, Greek Catholic and Reformed churches and a growing non-religious share. Just over half live in towns and cities, and the country is known for close-knit villages in its mountain valleys.
resources: Car manufacturing (one of the world's highest per capita)
Tatra mountains and forests
Mineral and thermal springs
Danube access and central European location
Skilled industrial workforce
Castles, wooden churches and folk traditions
struggles: Deep exclusion and poverty in many Roma settlements
Regional inequality between west and east
Political polarisation and declining trust in institutions
Emigration of young and skilled people
Economic dependence on the automotive industry
prayFor: For Roma families to have housing, education and real belonging
For eastern regions and struggling towns to find new opportunity
For trust, dialogue and peace in public life
For young people to find a future at home
For churches to be sources of compassion and unity

summary.history: Celts and then Slavs settled the land, and in the 9th century it lay at the heart of Great Moravia, where Saints Cyril and Methodius brought Christianity and Slavonic letters. For nearly a thousand years the region was part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and Bratislava (Pressburg) served as the Hungarian coronation city during the Ottoman period. A Slovak national revival in the 19th century, led by figures like Ľudovít Štúr, faced Magyarisation pressures. In 1918 Slovaks joined Czechs in Czechoslovakia; from 1939 to 1945 a Nazi-aligned Slovak State deported most of its Jews to their deaths, and the 1944 Slovak National Uprising rose against it.
summary.politicalHistory: Czechoslovakia was founded in 1918 as a democratic republic, broken up under Nazi pressure in 1939, and restored in 1945. Communists took power in 1948, the 1968 Prague Spring led by Slovak Alexander Dubček was crushed by Warsaw Pact troops, and the 1989 Velvet Revolution ended one-party rule. Slovakia became independent through the peaceful 'Velvet Divorce' on 1 January 1993. It is a parliamentary republic, and joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the eurozone in 2009.
summary.art: Slovak folk culture is vivid: fujara shepherd's flutes (UNESCO-listed), polyphonic singing, embroidered costumes and the painted houses of Čičmany. The wood-carved altar of Master Paul of Levoča is the tallest Gothic wooden altar in the world. Poets Pavol Országh Hviezdoslav and Andrej Sládkovič and painter Martin Benka shaped modern Slovak identity, and Andy Warhol's Rusyn family roots are honoured in a museum in Medzilaborce.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Levoča with Spiš Castle, Banská Štiavnica's mining town, Bardejov's historic centre, Vlkolínec village and the wooden churches of the Carpathian region. Bratislava Castle and St Martin's Cathedral, where Hungarian monarchs were crowned, stand above the Danube. The caves of the Slovak Karst, such as Dobšiná Ice Cave, are also UNESCO-listed natural wonders.

name: Slovenia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Hungarian and Italian are co-official in their regions

people: Most people are Slovenes, with Croats, Serbs, Bosniaks and others who came during the Yugoslav era, small autochthonous Italian and Hungarian communities, and Roma. Roughly half to three-fifths identify as Catholic, with Orthodox, Muslim and Protestant minorities and many non-religious people. About half live in rural areas and small towns, and a love of mountains, beekeeping and outdoor life runs deep.
resources: Forests covering about 60% of the land
Alps, karst caves and a short Adriatic coast
Port of Koper
Skilled manufacturing (pharmaceuticals, appliances, vehicles)
Rich biodiversity and clean water
Beekeeping tradition and the Carniolan honeybee
struggles: Ageing population and pressure on pensions and healthcare
Long healthcare waiting times
Increasing floods and extreme weather (notably 2023)
Housing affordability for young people
Political polarisation
prayFor: For families and communities recovering from floods and storms
For care and dignity for the elderly and sick
For young people to afford homes and build families
For respectful dialogue across political divides
For faithful stewardship of forests, rivers and mountains

summary.history: The area hosted prehistoric pile-dwellers and later the Roman town of Emona, and Slavic ancestors of the Slovenes formed the principality of Carantania in the 7th century. For over a thousand years the lands were ruled by Frankish, Bavarian and Habsburg powers, and the Reformation gave Slovenes their first printed books through Primož Trubar in the 1550s. The Isonzo (Soča) front of WWI saw some of the war's bloodiest fighting, and WWII brought division among German, Italian and Hungarian occupiers, partisan resistance and bitter civil conflict, followed by post-war mass killings by the new regime. Within Yugoslavia Slovenia became its most prosperous republic.
summary.politicalHistory: After the Habsburg collapse in 1918 Slovenia joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and after 1945 became a republic of socialist Yugoslavia. Democratic elections in 1990 and a referendum led to independence on 25 June 1991, followed by a ten-day war. A 1991 constitution established a parliamentary republic. Slovenia joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2007.
summary.art: France Prešeren, the national Romantic poet, wrote the verses of today's anthem, and Ivan Cankar is the great modern prose writer. Architect Jože Plečnik reshaped Ljubljana with bridges, markets and the National Library. Painted beehive panels, Idrija lace, polka-style folk music and contemporary groups such as Laibach reflect a lively cultural scene.
summary.monuments: The Škocjan Caves are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the works of Plečnik in Ljubljana and the mercury mining town of Idrija. Lake Bled with its island church and clifftop castle, and Triglav National Park around the country's highest peak, are national symbols. Postojna Cave and Predjama Castle built into a cliff are among Europe's most remarkable sites.

name: Sweden

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. national minority (Finnish, Meänkieli, Sámi, Romani, Yiddish) and immigrant languages

people: Most people are ethnic Swedes, with the Indigenous Sámi in the north, Sweden Finns and Tornedalians, Roma and Jews as national minorities; about one in five residents was born abroad, including large Syrian, Iraqi, Finnish, Polish and Somali communities. Around half belong to the Church of Sweden, though practice is low, alongside growing Muslim, Catholic, Orthodox and free-church communities. Most people live in the urbanised south, while the north is sparsely populated forest and mountain land.
resources: Forests, timber and paper
Iron ore and hydropower
Innovation and global companies in engineering, tech and design
Strong welfare state and high-trust institutions
Archipelagos, lakes and the right of public access (allemansrätten)
Cultural exports in music and literature
struggles: Gang violence and shootings in some urban areas
Segregation and integration challenges
Loneliness, especially among the elderly and young
Housing shortages in big cities
Tensions between mining, forestry, green industry and Sámi reindeer herding
prayFor: For safety and peace in neighbourhoods affected by violence, and for young people drawn into gangs
For newcomers and long-time residents to build trust and community together
For the lonely to find friendship and belonging
For the Sámi people's land, livelihoods and voice
For wise stewardship of forests, waters and northern landscapes

summary.history: After the Ice Age, hunter-gatherers moved north, the Sámi lived across the northern lands, and Norse peoples built farms, trade towns such as Birka, and Viking routes reaching Russia and Byzantium. Christianity spread slowly from the 9th to 12th centuries, and in 1397 Sweden joined the Kalmar Union, which it left under Gustav Vasa in 1523, adopting Lutheranism. In the 17th century Sweden became a great European power through the Thirty Years' War, but defeat in the Great Northern War (1700–21) ended its empire and Finland was lost to Russia in 1809. Poverty drove over a million Swedes to emigrate to America in the 19th and early 20th centuries, while Sámi people faced assimilation and racial-biological research; neutrality kept Sweden out of the world wars.
summary.politicalHistory: Gustav Vasa founded the modern Swedish state in 1523, and royal absolutism alternated with periods of parliamentary 'liberty'. The 1809 Instrument of Government introduced separation of powers, and Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte founded the current dynasty in 1818. Universal suffrage came in 1921, and Social Democratic governments built the 'folkhem' welfare state for much of the 20th century. The 1974 constitution made the monarch purely ceremonial; Sweden joined the EU in 1995 and, ending long military non-alignment, NATO in 2024.
summary.art: Writers August Strindberg, Selma Lagerlöf and Astrid Lindgren, and film-maker Ingmar Bergman, shaped world culture. Painters Carl Larsson and Anders Zorn captured Swedish light and home life, and Swedish design is known for simplicity and craft, from Dala horses to glassware from Småland. Folk fiddle music, the nyckelharpa, choral singing and pop from ABBA onwards make music central to national life.
summary.monuments: The Royal Domain of Drottningholm, the Hanseatic town of Visby, and Birka with Hovgården are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, as is the Laponian Area, a Sámi cultural and natural landscape. The Vasa Museum in Stockholm displays a 17th-century warship that sank on its maiden voyage. Uppsala Cathedral and Gamla Uppsala's royal mounds, and Stockholm's Gamla Stan, are anchors of national memory.

name: Switzerland

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages; four national languages

people: Switzerland is a nation of four language communities — about 62% German-speaking, 23% French, 8% Italian and under 1% Romansh — and about a quarter of residents are foreign nationals, especially Italians, Germans, Portuguese and French. Roughly a third are Catholic, about a fifth Reformed Protestant, around 6% Muslim, and a growing third non-religious. Most people live on the central plateau between Geneva and Lake Constance, while Alpine valleys preserve strong local identities.
resources: The Alps, glaciers and fresh water (the 'water tower of Europe')
Hydropower
Pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watchmaking
Banking and international organisations in Geneva
Direct democracy and multilingual federalism
World-class universities and research
struggles: Melting glaciers and growing risk of rockfalls and landslides
High cost of living, rents and health-insurance premiums
Debates over immigration and relations with the EU
Pressure on banking reputation and secrecy legacy
Loneliness and mental-health strain amid a demanding work culture
prayFor: For mountain communities facing glacier loss, landslides and changing climate
For families struggling with rents and health costs
For welcome and respect toward migrants and refugees
For Geneva's humanitarian work to bring real peace to suffering places
For integrity in finance and generosity with abundance

summary.history: Celtic Helvetii lived here when Rome conquered the region, and Germanic Alemanni and Burgundians later settled, shaping today's language divide. In 1291, by tradition, the forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore an alliance that grew into the Old Swiss Confederacy, which won independence from Habsburg control and fielded famed mercenary armies. The Reformation of Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva led to religious wars between cantons, and Napoleon briefly imposed a centralised republic. Neutrality was recognised in 1815; in WWII Switzerland stayed neutral but turned back many Jewish refugees and traded with Nazi Germany, which it later confronted in official inquiries.
summary.politicalHistory: The Peace of Westphalia formally recognised Swiss independence in 1648, and the Congress of Vienna fixed neutrality and borders in 1815. After the brief Sonderbund civil war of 1847, the 1848 federal constitution created a modern federal state, revised in 1874 and 1999. Direct democracy through referendums and initiatives became central, though women gained the federal vote only in 1971. Switzerland is governed by a seven-member Federal Council, joined the UN only in 2002 and remains outside the EU.
summary.art: Painters Ferdinand Hodler and Paul Klee, sculptor Alberto Giacometti and architect Le Corbusier are major figures, and Dada was born in Zurich's Cabaret Voltaire in 1916. Writers include Jean-Jacques Rousseau of Geneva, Gottfried Keller, Johanna Spyri ('Heidi') and Friedrich Dürrenmatt. Alpine yodelling, the alphorn, Basel Fasnacht carnival and Swiss watchmaking craftsmanship (on UNESCO's intangible heritage list) are living traditions.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Old City of Bern, the Abbey of St Gall with its library, the Benedictine Convent of Müstair, and the Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch with Europe's largest glacier. The Rhaetian Railway through the Albula and Bernina landscapes is a UNESCO-listed engineering marvel. Chillon Castle on Lake Geneva and the Matterhorn are iconic, and Geneva hosts the Red Cross museum and the UN's European headquarters.

name: Ukraine

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. minority languages; population figures are highly uncertain because of war and displacement

people: Most people are Ukrainians, with Russian, Crimean Tatar, Hungarian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Polish, Jewish and Roma communities; many families are bilingual in Ukrainian and Russian. Most are Orthodox Christians, divided between different Orthodox churches, with a large Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church in the west, and Protestant, Roman Catholic, Muslim and Jewish communities. Since 2022 millions have been displaced inside the country or have fled abroad, and many families are separated by war.
resources: Vast black-earth farmland — a breadbasket for the world
Black Sea ports and the Dnipro river
Iron ore, coal and other minerals
Strong IT and engineering talent
Resilient civil society and volunteer networks
Rich folk, sacred and literary culture
struggles: Full-scale war since 2022, with civilians and soldiers killed and wounded and towns destroyed
Millions displaced, refugees abroad and separated families
Attacks on energy infrastructure and hardship in winter
Landmines and unexploded ordnance across farmland
Trauma, grief and disability on a vast scale
Corruption and the immense task of reconstruction
prayFor: For an end to the war and a just and lasting peace, and comfort for all who grieve
For safety, warmth and light for civilians, children and the elderly
For displaced people and refugees to find shelter and a way home
For healing of bodies, minds and memories, and care for the wounded
For honest leadership and hope as communities rebuild

summary.history: The steppes and forests of Ukraine have hosted Trypillian farmers, Scythians, Greek colonies on the Black Sea and many nomadic peoples. Kyivan Rus' flourished from the 9th century and adopted Christianity under Volodymyr in 988, before the Mongol invasion of 1240; later the lands were divided among Lithuania, Poland, the Crimean Khanate and Muscovy, and the Cossack Hetmanate emerged in the 17th century. Under the Russian Empire and later Soviet rule, Ukrainian language and identity were suppressed, and the 1932–33 famine (Holodomor) killed millions. WWII devastated the country, including the Holocaust — at Babyn Yar and elsewhere — and fighting that killed millions, followed in 1944 by the deportation of the Crimean Tatars; the 1986 Chornobyl disaster scarred the north.
summary.politicalHistory: A Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence in 1918 but was absorbed into the Soviet Union, becoming the Ukrainian SSR. After a 1991 referendum Ukraine became independent, adopting a constitution in 1996 and a semi-presidential system. Mass protests in 2004 (the Orange Revolution) and 2013–14 (the Revolution of Dignity) reshaped politics; in 2014 Russia annexed Crimea and war began in the Donbas, escalating into a full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022. Ukraine received EU candidate status in 2022.
summary.art: Ukrainian culture is renowned for pysanky decorated eggs, vyshyvanka embroidery, Petrykivka decorative painting and polyphonic folk song, as well as the bandura and kobzar tradition. Taras Shevchenko, Ivan Franko and Lesya Ukrainka are the great literary voices, and Mykola Leontovych's 'Shchedryk' became the worldwide 'Carol of the Bells'. Painter Kazimir Malevich, born in Kyiv, and folk artist Maria Prymachenko are celebrated far beyond Ukraine.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Kyiv's St Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the historic centre of Lviv, and the historic centre of Odesa. The ancient city of Tauric Chersonese and the wooden tserkvas of the Carpathians show the land's deep layers of faith and history. Kamianets-Podilskyi fortress and the Khotyn fortress are also beloved symbols, and many sites have been damaged in the war.

name: Antigua and Barbuda

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages

people: Most Antiguans and Barbudans are of African descent, with smaller communities of European, Lebanese/Syrian, Indian, Chinese and mixed heritage, and many newer arrivals from Guyana, Jamaica and the Dominican Republic. Christianity predominates — Anglican, Moravian, Methodist, Adventist, Pentecostal and Catholic churches all have deep roots. Most people live on Antigua, around St. John's; Barbuda is home to under 2,000 people, and a large diaspora lives in the US, UK and Canada.
resources: Beaches and coral-fringed coastline (traditionally '365 beaches')
Tourism and yachting (Antigua Sailing Week, English Harbour)
Sheltered natural harbours
Barbuda's lagoons and frigate-bird colony
Cricket heritage and a strong sporting culture
A close-knit, welcoming island community
struggles: Heavy dependence on tourism, exposed to global shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic
Hurricane risk — Hurricane Irma (2017) devastated Barbuda and forced its entire evacuation
Contested land-tenure changes on Barbuda after Irma, straining trust between islands
High public debt and cost of living
Water scarcity and climate-driven coastal erosion
prayFor: For Barbudans still rebuilding homes, livelihoods and a sense of security since Hurricane Irma
For fair, peaceful resolution of land questions that honours Barbuda's communal heritage
For tourism workers and small businesses facing uncertain seasons, that work may be stable and dignified
For wise care of water, reefs and coastline in a warming climate
For young people, that they may find meaningful futures at home as well as abroad

summary.history: Arawak-speaking and later Kalinago (Carib) peoples lived on the islands long before Columbus sighted Antigua in 1493. English settlers arrived in 1632, and Antigua became a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans, with Barbuda leased to the Codrington family to supply food and labour. A planned uprising of the enslaved in 1736 was brutally suppressed, and slavery ended under British emancipation in 1834. After a long era of plantation poverty, labour movements in the 20th century paved the way for self-government, and tourism replaced sugar as the economic mainstay.
summary.politicalHistory: Antigua and Barbuda became an Associated State of the United Kingdom in 1967 and fully independent on 1 November 1981. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with the British monarch as head of state represented by a Governor-General. Politics was long dominated by the Antigua Labour Party and the Bird family, with V. C. Bird Sr. as the first prime minister; Barbuda has its own elected council and a distinct communal land tradition.
summary.art: Calypso, soca and steelpan flourish around Antigua Carnival, held each summer to mark emancipation. Literature includes Jamaica Kincaid, whose books such as 'A Small Place' and 'Annie John' explore colonial legacy and island life. Local crafts include pottery from the Sea View Farm tradition, basketry and vivid painting of island scenes.
summary.monuments: Antigua Naval Dockyard and Related Archaeological Sites (Nelson's Dockyard), a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the best-preserved Georgian naval dockyard in the world, built partly by enslaved labour. Shirley Heights and Fort James recall the islands' role in colonial warfare. Betty's Hope, a restored sugar plantation, tells the story of slavery and sugar, while Barbuda's Codrington Lagoon shelters one of the largest frigate-bird colonies in the world.

name: Bahamas

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages such as Haitian Creole

people: Around nine in ten Bahamians are of African descent, alongside people of European (including Loyalist) heritage and a sizeable Haitian and Haitian-Bahamian community. The country is strongly Christian — Baptist, Anglican, Catholic, Pentecostal and Methodist congregations are central to community life. About three-quarters of people live on New Providence (Nassau) and Grand Bahama, while many 'Family Islands' are thinly populated.
resources: Clear shallow seas, reefs and blue holes across some 700 islands
Tourism and cruise industry
International financial services
Andros Barrier Reef and rich fisheries (conch, spiny lobster)
Proximity to the United States
Junkanoo culture and a vibrant musical heritage
struggles: Extreme hurricane exposure — Hurricane Dorian (2019) devastated Abaco and Grand Bahama
Low elevation leaves much of the land vulnerable to sea-level rise
High cost of living and dependence on imports and tourism
Gun violence and crime concentrated in parts of Nassau
Precarious conditions and statelessness concerns for many people of Haitian descent
prayFor: For families on Abaco and Grand Bahama still grieving loss and rebuilding after Hurricane Dorian
For safety and hope in neighbourhoods affected by violence, and for young people seeking a way forward
For Haitian-Bahamian families, that they may live with dignity, belonging and secure legal status
For protection of reefs, mangroves and low-lying communities as seas rise
For a fairer economy where island prosperity reaches every household

summary.history: The Lucayan people, a Taíno group, were living on the islands when Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492; within a generation they had been enslaved and taken away to Hispaniola and Cuba, and their society destroyed. English Puritan settlers (the Eleutheran Adventurers) arrived in 1648, and the islands later became a haven for pirates before British rule was firmly established in 1718. American Loyalists arrived after 1783 with enslaved Africans, and slavery ended in 1834. Blockade-running during the US Civil War, rum-running during Prohibition and, from the mid-20th century, tourism and finance shaped the modern economy.
summary.politicalHistory: The Bahamas gained internal self-government in 1964, and the 'Quiet Revolution' of 1967 brought the first majority-Black government under the Progressive Liberal Party. Independence followed on 10 July 1973, with Sir Lynden Pindling as the first prime minister. The country is a stable parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with power alternating between the Progressive Liberal Party and the Free National Movement.
summary.art: Junkanoo — a dazzling street parade of crêpe-paper costumes, cowbells, goatskin drums and horns on Boxing Day and New Year's Day — is the heart of Bahamian culture. Rake-and-scrape music, played with a carpenter's saw, accordion and goatskin drum, is a distinctive folk tradition, as is straw plaiting sold in markets. Painter Amos Ferguson and the actor Sidney Poitier, who grew up on Cat Island, are among the best-known Bahamian artists.
summary.monuments: Fort Charlotte and Fort Fincastle, with the nearby Queen's Staircase cut from limestone by enslaved people, recall Nassau's colonial past. The Pompey Museum of Slavery and Emancipation, in Nassau's old Vendue House, tells the story of enslavement and freedom. Inagua National Park protects one of the largest breeding colonies of Caribbean flamingos, and Andros's blue holes and barrier reef are among the region's great natural wonders.

name: Barbados

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages

people: Most Barbadians (Bajans) are of African descent, with smaller communities of European, Indian, Middle Eastern and mixed heritage. Christianity is central to life — Anglican, Pentecostal, Adventist, Methodist and Catholic churches — with small Muslim, Hindu and Rastafarian communities. The island is densely populated and largely urbanised along the west and south coasts, and a sizeable diaspora lives in the UK, US and Canada.
resources: Beaches and coral reefs
Tourism
High literacy and strong education tradition
Rum distilling heritage
International business and financial services
Diplomatic voice on climate finance for small island states
struggles: Climate vulnerability — hurricanes, coastal erosion and Sargassum seaweed influxes
High public debt following years of slow growth
Dependence on imported food and fuel
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension
Rising gun-related violence among young men
prayFor: For families coping with the high cost of food and living
For good health and care for those living with diabetes and heart disease
For young men drawn into violence, that they may find purpose, mentors and peace
For Barbados' voice for climate justice to bear fruit for small island nations
For honest, healing conversation about the legacy of slavery and reparatory justice

summary.history: Amerindian peoples lived on Barbados for centuries but the island appears to have been largely uninhabited when English settlers arrived in 1627. In the 1640s it became the laboratory of the Caribbean 'sugar revolution', with large plantations worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans under harsh slave codes that were copied across English colonies. Bussa's Rebellion in 1816 was the largest uprising of the enslaved on the island, and slavery was abolished in 1834, followed by apprenticeship until 1838. Labour riots in 1937 sparked the modern trade-union and political movement that led to self-government.
summary.politicalHistory: Barbados has one of the oldest parliaments in the Americas, dating from 1639. It gained independence from Britain on 30 November 1966 under Errol Barrow, its first prime minister. On 30 November 2021 it became a parliamentary republic within the Commonwealth, replacing the British monarch with a President as head of state, while retaining a Westminster-style parliamentary system with power alternating between the Barbados Labour Party and the Democratic Labour Party.
summary.art: Calypso and soca flourish around Crop Over, a festival with roots in the end of the sugar harvest, and Tuk bands blend drums and penny whistle in a uniquely Bajan sound. Writers George Lamming ('In the Castle of My Skin') and poet Kamau Brathwaite are giants of Caribbean literature. Pottery from Chalky Mount and mahogany woodwork are traditional crafts, and Rihanna is the island's most famous modern musician.
summary.monuments: Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserves colonial-era street patterns and military buildings. St Nicholas Abbey and Sunbury Plantation House recall the plantation era, while the Emancipation Statue (Bussa) commemorates resistance to slavery. Harrison's Cave and the Animal Flower Cave showcase the island's limestone landscape, and the Nidhe Israel Synagogue is among the oldest in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Belize
