languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Mayan languages, Garifuna and Plautdietsch

people: Belize is one of the most diverse small countries in the world: Mestizo people are now the largest group, alongside Creole, Maya (Q'eqchi', Mopan and Yucatec), Garifuna, East Indian, Mennonite, Chinese and Middle Eastern communities. Most people are Christian — Catholic and a growing range of Protestant and evangelical churches, with Mennonite colonies keeping their own traditions. About half live in rural areas, and many Belizeans live abroad, especially in the US.
resources: Belize Barrier Reef, the largest in the Western Hemisphere
Rainforests and protected areas covering much of the land
Maya archaeological heritage
Agriculture — sugar, citrus, bananas and marine products
Ecotourism
Remarkable cultural and linguistic diversity
struggles: Gang violence and high homicide rates, especially in Belize City
Poverty, particularly in rural and southern Maya communities
Hurricane and flood exposure
Deforestation and pressure on reefs and fisheries
The long-running territorial claim by Guatemala, referred to the International Court of Justice
prayFor: For peace in Belize City's neighbourhoods and second chances for young people caught in gang life
For Maya communities in the south, that their land rights and ways of life be respected
For protection of the reef and forests and the families who depend on them
For a just and peaceful resolution of the border question with Guatemala
For unity and mutual respect among Belize's many peoples

summary.history: The Maya civilisation flourished here for millennia, building cities such as Caracol, Lamanai and Xunantunich; Maya peoples remain part of Belize today. From the 17th century British buccaneers and loggers (Baymen) settled the coast to cut logwood and later mahogany, using enslaved Africans; the Battle of St George's Caye in 1798 secured the settlement against Spain. Garifuna people arrived from Honduras in the early 19th century, and refugees of Yucatán's Caste War, Mennonites and others followed. The colony of British Honduras was formally declared in 1862, and slavery had ended under British law in 1834.
summary.politicalHistory: British Honduras achieved self-government in 1964 and was renamed Belize in 1973. Independence was delayed by Guatemala's territorial claim and came on 21 September 1981, with a British garrison remaining for some years for defence. George Price, leader of the People's United Party, is honoured as the father of the nation. Belize is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with power alternating between the People's United Party and the United Democratic Party.
summary.art: Punta rock, born from Garifuna drumming and pioneered by Pen Cayetano and Andy Palacio, is Belize's signature sound, alongside Kriol brukdown music. Garifuna language, dance and music are recognised by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Maya embroidery, basketry and slate carving, and Mennonite furniture-making, enrich the country's crafts.
summary.monuments: The Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, including the Great Blue Hole, a vast marine sinkhole. Caracol, Lamanai, Xunantunich and Altun Ha reveal the grandeur of Classic Maya cities. Actun Tunichil Muknal cave preserves Maya ceremonial remains, and the Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary was established as a jaguar reserve.

name: Bolivia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); the constitution recognises 36 Indigenous languages

people: Bolivia has one of the largest Indigenous populations in the Americas — Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní and dozens of smaller lowland peoples — alongside a large mestizo population and smaller European, Afro-Bolivian and other communities. Most people are Catholic, with a strong and growing evangelical presence, and Andean spirituality (honouring Pachamama) is woven into Christian practice. About seven in ten live in cities such as Santa Cruz, El Alto, La Paz and Cochabamba, and many Bolivians work in Argentina, Spain, Chile and the US.
resources: Lithium reserves in the Uyuni salt flats, among the largest in the world
Natural gas
Silver, tin and zinc mining
Amazon rainforest, Andean highlands and great biodiversity
Quinoa, soy and agricultural lowlands
Living Indigenous cultures and languages
struggles: Economic strain — falling gas output, shortages of US dollars and fuel, and rising prices
Deep political polarisation, including the disputed 2019 election crisis and deadly unrest
Deforestation and wildfires in the Amazon and Chiquitania
Poverty and inequality, especially in rural highland and lowland areas
Water stress from shrinking glaciers in the Andes
Weak judicial institutions and public trust
prayFor: For families struggling with rising prices and shortages, that daily bread and fuel be within reach
For reconciliation across political, regional and ethnic divides, and justice for victims of past violence
For forests, glaciers and rivers, and the communities who depend on them
For Indigenous peoples to flourish in dignity, voice and language
For honest, fair institutions that serve every Bolivian

summary.history: The Andean highlands were home to the Tiwanaku civilisation around Lake Titicaca and later to Aymara kingdoms incorporated into the Inca Empire. Spanish conquest in the 1530s turned the region into Upper Peru, and the silver mountain of Potosí became one of the richest places on earth, mined through forced Indigenous labour (the mita) at an immense human cost. The uprising of Túpac Katari in 1781 and early independence revolts in 1809 marked long resistance. Since independence Bolivia has lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–84) and territory in the Chaco War with Paraguay (1932–35), and has lived through cycles of mining booms, revolution and reform.
summary.politicalHistory: Bolivia declared independence in 1825 and was named after Simón Bolívar, with Antonio José de Sucre as its first president. The 1952 National Revolution brought universal suffrage, land reform and nationalisation of the tin mines, but was followed by a long period of military rule until a return to democracy in 1982. A new constitution in 2009 re-founded the country as the Plurinational State of Bolivia, recognising Indigenous nations; the disputed 2019 election led to a political crisis, an interim government and fresh elections in 2020. Bolivia is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Andean music — charango, panpipes (zampoña) and quena — and dances such as the diablada, morenada and caporales come alive at the Carnival of Oruro, a UNESCO Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage. Colonial 'Andean baroque' art from Potosí and the Jesuit mission baroque music of Chiquitos are celebrated traditions, and painter Melchor Pérez de Holguín is a master of the colonial era. Textile weaving, especially from Jalq'a and Tarabuco communities, carries ancient symbolism.
summary.monuments: UNESCO sites include the City of Potosí and its Cerro Rico, the historic city of Sucre, the Jesuit Missions of the Chiquitos, Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata and Noel Kempff Mercado National Park. The Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, is one of South America's most striking landscapes. Lake Titicaca's Isla del Sol is sacred in Andean tradition as a birthplace of the Inca origin story.

name: Chile

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Indigenous and immigrant languages

people: Most Chileans are of mixed European and Indigenous descent; Mapuche people are the largest Indigenous nation, alongside Aymara, Rapa Nui, Diaguita and others, and recent years have brought many immigrants from Venezuela, Peru, Haiti and Colombia. Catholicism remains the largest faith, though it has declined sharply, with a strong evangelical minority and a growing number of non-religious people. Nearly nine in ten people live in cities, with around 40% in greater Santiago.
resources: Copper — the world's largest producer
Lithium from the Atacama salt flats
Wine, fruit and salmon exports
Pacific fisheries and a 4,000 km coastline
Atacama skies hosting major astronomical observatories
Patagonian wilderness and a strong outdoor tourism sector
struggles: High inequality, which fuelled the mass protests of 2019
Unresolved Mapuche land claims and conflict in Araucanía
Drought and water scarcity, worsened by a decade-long 'megadrought'
Wildfires, including the deadly 2024 fires around Viña del Mar
Rising concerns about crime and the integration of recent migrants
Earthquake and tsunami risk
prayFor: For Mapuche communities and their neighbours, that dialogue, justice and peace may replace mistrust and violence
For families who lost loved ones and homes in the 2024 Valparaíso region fires
For a fairer society where pensions, health and education serve every Chilean
For migrants arriving in the north, that they meet welcome, dignity and safety
For rain, wise water use and care for the land

summary.history: Before the Spanish arrived, the Inca Empire reached into central Chile, while the Mapuche in the south resisted both Inca and Spanish conquest for centuries; Rapa Nui (Easter Island) developed its own Polynesian culture. Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541, and the colony grew on agriculture while the Arauco War with the Mapuche continued. After independence, Chile won the War of the Pacific (1879–84), gaining nitrate-rich northern lands, and later occupied Mapuche territory in the 'Pacification of Araucanía'. The 20th century brought nitrate and copper economies, social reform and deep political division.
summary.politicalHistory: Chile declared independence in 1818 under Bernardo O'Higgins and developed one of Latin America's more stable constitutional republics. Socialist president Salvador Allende was overthrown in a military coup on 11 September 1973, beginning the dictatorship of General Augusto Pinochet, during which thousands were killed or disappeared and many more tortured or exiled. A 1988 plebiscite ended military rule, and democracy returned in 1990. After the 2019 protests, two proposed new constitutions were rejected by voters in 2022 and 2023, and Chile remains a presidential republic under its amended 1980 constitution.
summary.art: Chile is a land of poets: Gabriela Mistral (1945) and Pablo Neruda (1971) both won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and Isabel Allende and Roberto Bolaño are internationally read novelists. Violeta Parra and Víctor Jara led the Nueva Canción movement, and the cueca is the national dance. Mapuche silverwork and weaving, and the moai of Rapa Nui, are treasured artistic traditions.
summary.monuments: Rapa Nui National Park, with its moai statues, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the Historic Quarter of Valparaíso, the wooden Churches of Chiloé, the Humberstone and Santa Laura saltpetre works and the Chinchorro mummies, the oldest artificially mummified human remains known. Torres del Paine National Park is an emblem of Patagonia. Santiago's Museum of Memory and Human Rights honours the victims of the dictatorship.

name: Costa Rica

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Bribri, Cabécar, Limón Creole English and immigrant languages

people: Most Costa Ricans ('Ticos') are of mixed Spanish and Indigenous heritage, with an Afro-Caribbean community concentrated in Limón, eight Indigenous peoples such as the Bribri and Cabécar, and a large Nicaraguan-born population. Catholicism is the official religion and the largest faith, with a substantial evangelical minority and many non-religious people. Most people live in the Central Valley around San José, Heredia, Alajuela and Cartago.
resources: Extraordinary biodiversity — around 5% of the world's species
Nearly all electricity from renewable sources
Ecotourism and protected areas covering about a quarter of the land
Coffee, bananas and pineapples
Medical-device manufacturing and services
Strong public education and health systems
struggles: A sharp rise in drug-trafficking-related violence and homicides
Growing inequality and pressure on public finances
Housing costs and urban congestion in the Central Valley
Environmental strain from agrochemicals and plantation expansion
Integration of Nicaraguan migrants and asylum seekers
prayFor: For peace in communities affected by drug-related violence, and protection for young people
For Nicaraguan refugees and migrants, that they find safety, welcome and work
For the strength of public schools and health care that have long served all Ticos
For wise stewardship of forests, rivers and oceans
For Indigenous and Afro-Caribbean communities to be heard and honoured

summary.history: Before Spanish contact the land was home to Chibchan and Mesoamerican-influenced peoples, who left the mysterious stone spheres of the Diquís delta. Spain colonised the area from the 1560s, but it remained a poor and remote province with a small population of smallholders. Independence from Spain came in 1821; coffee exports from the 1840s and banana plantations on the Caribbean coast, worked partly by Jamaican migrants, transformed the economy. In 1856 Costa Ricans fought off the filibuster William Walker, a defining national moment.
summary.politicalHistory: After independence Costa Rica was briefly part of the Mexican Empire and the Federal Republic of Central America, becoming a sovereign republic in 1848. Following a short civil war in 1948, José Figueres Ferrer's junta abolished the army, a decision written into the 1949 constitution that still governs the country. Since then Costa Rica has been one of Latin America's most stable democracies, a presidential republic with regular peaceful transfers of power; former president Óscar Arias received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for his Central American peace plan.
summary.art: Painted ox-carts (carretas) from Sarchí are a national symbol recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage. Music includes Guanacaste folk dance tunes and the marimba, while Limón's calypso tradition, led by Walter Ferguson, reflects Afro-Caribbean heritage. Literature includes Carmen Lyra and the poet Eunice Odio, and the Boruca people are known for their carved and painted masks.
summary.monuments: UNESCO sites include the Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís, Cocos Island National Park, the Guanacaste Conservation Area and the Talamanca Range–La Amistad reserves. San José's National Theatre, built with coffee wealth in the 1890s, is the country's cultural jewel. The Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims each August, and Arenal and Poás volcanoes are iconic natural sites.

name: Cuba

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Haitian Creole and Cuban Sign Language

people: Cubans are of mixed Spanish and African heritage in many shades, with smaller Chinese-descended and other communities; Indigenous Taíno ancestry survives in family lines, especially in the east. Religious life blends Catholicism, a growing Protestant and evangelical presence, and Afro-Cuban traditions such as Santería (Regla de Ocha), while many people are non-religious. About three-quarters live in cities, and recent years have seen one of the largest emigrations in Cuba's history, adding to a large diaspora in the US and Spain.
resources: Highly educated population and strong tradition of doctors and medical training
Nickel and cobalt deposits
Tobacco, rum and sugar heritage
Beaches, reefs and colonial cities attracting tourism
Rich musical and artistic culture
Biotechnology and vaccine research
struggles: Severe economic crisis — shortages of food, medicine and fuel, and high inflation
Repeated nationwide power blackouts
Mass emigration, especially of young people, separating families
Restrictions on political freedoms and the arrests that followed the July 2021 protests
Impact of the long-standing US embargo and economic isolation
Ageing population and deteriorating housing
prayFor: For families facing empty shelves, blackouts and long queues, that they have enough each day
For families separated by migration, and for those making dangerous journeys
For the sick and elderly, that medicines and care reach them
For freedom of conscience and expression, and for those imprisoned for speaking out
For a peaceful, hopeful future shaped by Cubans on the island and abroad together

summary.history: Taíno, Ciboney and Guanahatabey peoples lived on Cuba when Columbus arrived in 1492; Spanish conquest from 1511, forced labour and disease devastated them. Cuba became a key Spanish colony, and from the late 18th century a booming sugar economy imported hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans; slavery was abolished only in 1886. Long independence wars (1868–78 and 1895–98), led by figures such as Carlos Manuel de Céspedes, Antonio Maceo and José Martí, ended with US intervention in 1898. The 20th century brought heavy US economic influence, dictatorship, revolution and Cold War confrontation, including the 1962 Missile Crisis.
summary.politicalHistory: Cuba became formally independent in 1902 under a constitution that allowed US intervention (the Platt Amendment), and the US still holds Guantánamo Bay. Fulgencio Batista ruled in various forms until the 1959 revolution led by Fidel Castro brought a socialist one-party state allied with the Soviet Union. Power passed to Raúl Castro in 2008 and then to a new generation of leaders, and a new constitution in 2019 confirmed the Communist Party as the leading force of state and society.
summary.art: Cuban music — son, danzón, mambo, cha-cha-chá, rumba and bolero — has shaped popular music worldwide, from Benny Moré and Celia Cruz to the Buena Vista Social Club. Literature includes José Martí, Alejo Carpentier, Nicolás Guillén and Dulce María Loynaz, and Wifredo Lam fused Afro-Cuban and modernist painting. Ballet, cinema and cigar-making are also celebrated, and rumba is UNESCO-listed intangible heritage.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Old Havana and its fortifications, Trinidad and the Valley de los Ingenios of sugar mills, the historic centres of Cienfuegos and Camagüey, the Viñales Valley and the San Pedro de la Roca Castle in Santiago de Cuba. The Archaeological Landscape of the First Coffee Plantations in south-east Cuba recalls enslaved labour in the coffee economy. The Basilica of El Cobre, home of the Virgin of Charity, Cuba's patroness, is a beloved pilgrimage site.

name: Dominica

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Kokoy creole English

people: Most Dominicans are of African descent, and the Kalinago Territory on the east coast is home to around 3,000 Kalinago people, the largest surviving Indigenous community in the eastern Caribbean. Catholicism is the majority faith, alongside Adventist, Pentecostal, Methodist and other churches. Many people live in small villages along the coast, and the diaspora in the UK, US and neighbouring islands is large compared with the population at home.
resources: Lush rainforest, rivers and waterfalls — the 'Nature Island'
Geothermal energy potential
Fertile volcanic soils for bananas and root crops
Whale-watching and dive sites
Kalinago heritage
Citizenship-by-investment revenues funding reconstruction
struggles: Extreme hurricane exposure — Tropical Storm Erika (2015) and Hurricane Maria (2017) caused deadly destruction
Small, vulnerable economy and high reconstruction debt
Youth emigration and an ageing population
Questions over governance of the citizenship-by-investment programme
Kalinago community poverty and land concerns
prayFor: For communities still recovering from hurricanes, that homes and livelihoods be rebuilt stronger
For the Kalinago people, that their culture, land and dignity be honoured
For young Dominicans, that they find good work and hope at home
For transparent, wise stewardship of public resources
For protection of forests, rivers and reefs

summary.history: Dominica was settled by Arawak-speaking peoples and later the Kalinago, who called it Wai'tu kubuli ('tall is her body') and resisted European colonisation longer than on most islands. French and British powers contested the island through the 18th century before it passed to Britain in 1763 (confirmed in 1805). Plantations of coffee and later limes and bananas used enslaved African labour, while maroon communities resisted from the mountainous interior. Slavery ended in 1834, and in 1903 the Carib (now Kalinago) Territory was established.
summary.politicalHistory: Dominica became an Associated State of the United Kingdom in 1967 and gained independence on 3 November 1978 as a republic within the Commonwealth. Eugenia Charles, prime minister from 1980 to 1995, was the Caribbean's first female head of government. Dominica is a parliamentary republic with a President elected by parliament and a Prime Minister as head of government.
summary.art: Bouyon, a high-energy music born in the 1980s, and jing ping folk bands with accordion and boom-boom, are distinctly Dominican, and the World Creole Music Festival celebrates the island's sound. Writers Jean Rhys ('Wide Sargasso Sea') and Phyllis Shand Allfrey were born here. Kalinago basketry, woven from larouma reeds, is a living craft passed between generations.
summary.monuments: Morne Trois Pitons National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, includes the Boiling Lake, the Emerald Pool and volcanic landscapes of rainforest. The Kalinago Barana Autê heritage village shares Kalinago history and culture. Cabrits National Park preserves the 18th-century Fort Shirley, and the Waitukubuli National Trail crosses the island end to end.

name: Dominican Republic

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Haitian Creole and Samaná English

people: Most Dominicans are of mixed African and European heritage, with a significant population of Haitian origin and smaller Middle Eastern, Asian and other communities. Catholicism is the largest faith, with a fast-growing evangelical population and many people combining faith with folk traditions. Around 80% of people live in cities, especially Santo Domingo and Santiago, and the diaspora in the US — above all New York — is large and closely tied to home.
resources: Tourism — the Caribbean's most visited country
Gold mining (Pueblo Viejo)
Agriculture — cocoa, tobacco, bananas and sugar
Remittances and a dynamic diaspora
Free-trade-zone manufacturing
Baseball talent and a vibrant musical culture
struggles: Inequality despite years of fast growth
Treatment and legal status of Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian descent, including mass deportations
Unreliable electricity and water services
Hurricane and flood risk
Corruption and uneven access to quality education and health care
prayFor: For Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent, that they be treated with dignity and secure belonging
For peace and mutual respect between Dominicans and Haitians who share one island
For children and youth, that schools and health care give every one a fair start
For families in poor barrios and bateyes, that growth reaches their tables
For honest leadership and protection from storms

summary.history: The island of Hispaniola was home to the Taíno when Columbus arrived in 1492, and Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, became the first permanent European city in the Americas. The Taíno population collapsed under forced labour and disease, and enslaved Africans were brought to work sugar plantations. Spain later ceded the western third (Saint-Domingue, now Haiti) to France, and Haiti governed the whole island from 1822 to 1844. The 20th century included a US occupation (1916–24) and the brutal dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo, whose regime massacred thousands of Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian descent in the Parsley Massacre of 1937.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence was declared on 27 February 1844 under Juan Pablo Duarte and others, followed by a brief return to Spanish rule (1861–65) and a Restoration War. Trujillo ruled from 1930 until his assassination in 1961; Juan Bosch was elected and then overthrown in 1963, and a civil war in 1965 brought US intervention. Joaquín Balaguer governed for much of 1966–96, and since then the country has become a more stable presidential democracy with regular elections.
summary.art: Merengue and bachata — the latter once scorned as music of the poor — are now UNESCO-recognised intangible heritage and global dance music, with stars such as Juan Luis Guerra. Writers include Pedro Henríquez Ureña, Julia Álvarez and Junot Díaz from the diaspora. Carnival masks such as the diablo cojuelo, larimar jewellery and amber crafts are distinctive arts.
summary.monuments: The Colonial City of Santo Domingo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, holds the first cathedral, hospital and university buildings of the Americas. The Alcázar de Colón recalls the early colonial era, and the Basilica of Our Lady of Altagracia in Higüey is the country's great pilgrimage church. Los Haitises National Park and its Taíno cave art, and Pico Duarte, the highest peak in the Caribbean, are natural treasures.

name: Ecuador

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Amazonian Indigenous languages

people: Most Ecuadorians are mestizo, alongside Kichwa and other Indigenous nationalities of the Andes and Amazon, Afro-Ecuadorians centred in Esmeraldas and the Chota Valley, and Montubio coastal communities. Catholicism is the main faith, with a growing evangelical population. About two-thirds live in cities, especially Guayaquil and Quito, and large communities live in Spain, the US and Italy.
resources: The Galápagos Islands and their unique wildlife
Oil
Bananas (the world's largest exporter), shrimp, cocoa and flowers
Amazon rainforest and Andean volcanoes
Hydropower
Strong Indigenous organisations and living cultures
struggles: A surge in organised-crime violence and prison massacres, leading to a declared 'internal armed conflict' in January 2024
Drought-driven power cuts due to dependence on hydropower
Oil spills and deforestation in the Amazon
Poverty and job insecurity, driving emigration
Fragile public finances and political instability
prayFor: For peace in Guayaquil, Esmeraldas and other communities living under the shadow of gang violence
For those in prisons, their families and those who work there
For Amazonian peoples and the forests and rivers that sustain them
For young people, that they find honest work and hope without leaving home
For wise, trustworthy leadership and justice for all

summary.history: Ecuador's coast was home to some of the oldest pottery-making cultures in the Americas (Valdivia), and the highlands were later conquered by the Inca, with Quito becoming a northern capital. Spanish conquest in the 1530s brought colonial rule, the hacienda system and forced Indigenous labour, while Quito became a renowned centre of religious art. After independence, power shifted between conservative Quito and liberal, commercial Guayaquil. The 20th century brought cocoa and banana booms, an oil boom from the 1970s, a border war with Peru settled in 1998, and a severe financial crisis that led to dollarisation in 2000.
summary.politicalHistory: Ecuador was liberated from Spain in 1822 by forces led by Antonio José de Sucre, joined Gran Colombia, and became a separate republic in 1830. Its history includes frequent changes of government and military rule (1972–79) before a return to democracy in 1979. Between 1997 and 2005 three elected presidents were removed amid protests; a new constitution in 2008 recognised the rights of nature. Ecuador is a presidential republic.
summary.art: The colonial Quito School of painting and sculpture, including the sculptor Bernardo de Legarda and painter Miguel de Santiago, produced some of Latin America's finest religious art. Oswaldo Guayasamín's expressive paintings speak of Indigenous suffering and dignity, and the pasillo is the country's beloved musical genre. Toquilla straw hats (the 'Panama hat'), Otavalo textiles and Tigua painting are celebrated crafts.
summary.monuments: The Galápagos Islands and the City of Quito were among the very first UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1978; Sangay National Park, the historic centre of Cuenca and the Qhapaq Ñan Andean road system are also listed. Quito's La Compañía church glows with gold-leaf baroque interiors. Ingapirca is the country's largest Inca-Cañari site, and Cotopaxi volcano rises over the Avenue of the Volcanoes.

name: El Salvador

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Nawat (Pipil), critically endangered

people: Most Salvadorans are mestizo, with Indigenous Nahua-Pipil, Lenca and Cacaopera heritage that was long suppressed after the 1932 massacre. Catholicism and evangelical Protestantism are both strong, and faith shapes much of community life. It is Central America's most densely populated country, mostly urban, and around a quarter of Salvadorans live abroad, mainly in the US.
resources: Hard-working, resilient people and a large diaspora sending remittances
Geothermal energy from volcanic terrain
Coffee and sugar
Pacific surf coast
Textile and apparel manufacturing
Maya archaeological heritage
struggles: Decades of gang violence, followed since 2022 by a state of exception with mass arrests and serious human-rights concerns
Poverty and limited economic opportunity
Emigration and family separation
Deforestation, drought and vulnerability to earthquakes and storms
Concerns about checks and balances and judicial independence
prayFor: For communities that suffered from gang violence, that peace may be lasting and just
For people detained, their families, and for due process and humane treatment
For families separated by migration, and for those returned or deported
For the poor, that work and dignity be within reach
For healing from the memory of civil war and the 1932 massacre

summary.history: The land was home to Maya peoples in the west and later to the Nahua-speaking Pipil, who called it Cuzcatlán; the Spanish conquered it in the 1520s and 1530s. Colonial indigo and later coffee economies concentrated land in the hands of a small elite. In 1932 a peasant uprising was crushed in La Matanza, in which thousands of mostly Indigenous people were killed. Social exclusion and repression led to a civil war (1980–92) in which around 75,000 people died, including Archbishop Óscar Romero, murdered at Mass in 1980, and the victims of the El Mozote massacre.
summary.politicalHistory: El Salvador gained independence from Spain in 1821, belonged to the Federal Republic of Central America, and became a separate republic in 1841. For much of the 20th century it was governed by military regimes allied with landowning elites. The 1992 Chapultepec Peace Accords ended the civil war, turned the FMLN guerrillas into a political party and reformed the military and police. El Salvador is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Pupusas and handicrafts like the brightly painted wood of La Palma, inspired by Fernando Llort, are national symbols. Poet Roque Dalton and novelist Claribel Alegría are leading literary voices, and Salarrué wrote classic tales of rural life. Folk dance, marimba music and religious processions enliven town festivals.
summary.monuments: Joya de Cerén, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a Maya farming village buried by volcanic ash around 600 AD — the 'Pompeii of the Americas'. Tazumal and San Andrés are important Maya ceremonial centres. The tomb of Saint Óscar Romero in the Metropolitan Cathedral of San Salvador and the memorial at El Mozote honour victims of the war, and the Ruta de las Flores links colonial towns through coffee country.

name: Grenada

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); some older people speak French-based Patois

people: Most Grenadians are of African descent, with communities of mixed, Indian and European heritage across Grenada, Carriacou and Petite Martinique. Catholicism is the largest faith, followed by Anglican, Pentecostal, Adventist and other churches. Life is centred on St. George's and the parishes, and many families have relatives in the UK, US, Canada and Trinidad.
resources: Nutmeg, mace and cocoa — the 'Spice Isle'
Beaches, reefs and sailing waters
Tourism and yachting
St George's University, an international medical school
Fertile volcanic soils
Strong community and festival traditions
struggles: Hurricane exposure — Ivan (2004) devastated Grenada and Beryl (2024) destroyed most of Carriacou and Petite Martinique
Youth unemployment
Dependence on tourism and imports
Climate impacts on coasts and agriculture
Lingering pain from the 1983 crisis and invasion
prayFor: For the people of Carriacou and Petite Martinique rebuilding after Hurricane Beryl
For farmers of nutmeg and cocoa, that their land and harvests recover and flourish
For young Grenadians, that they find meaningful work and a future at home
For continued healing and reconciliation after the events of 1983
For resilience against storms and rising seas

summary.history: The Kalinago (Island Caribs) resisted European settlement for over a century; when the French took the island in the 1650s, tradition holds that Kalinago people leapt to their deaths at Sauteurs rather than surrender. Grenada passed between France and Britain and from 1783 was firmly British, with sugar and later cocoa and nutmeg plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Julien Fédon led a major rebellion against British rule in 1795–96, and slavery ended in 1834. In the 20th century labour leader Eric Gairy rose to prominence through the 1951 strikes.
summary.politicalHistory: Grenada became independent on 7 February 1974 under Eric Gairy. In 1979 the New Jewel Movement led by Maurice Bishop seized power and established a People's Revolutionary Government; in October 1983 an internal split led to Bishop's execution, followed days later by a US-led invasion. Parliamentary democracy was restored in 1984, and Grenada is today a Commonwealth realm with a Westminster-style system.
summary.art: Calypso, soca and steelpan peak at Spicemas, Grenada's carnival, with the J'ouvert 'jab jab' masqueraders covered in oil. The Big Drum dance of Carriacou preserves African nation dances and is a precious living tradition, alongside Carriacou's boat-building heritage. Grenadian writers include Merle Collins and Jacob Ross.
summary.monuments: Fort George and Fort Frederick overlook St. George's, one of the Caribbean's most picturesque harbour towns. Grand Étang National Park protects a crater lake and rainforest, and the Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park blends art and reef restoration. Leapers' Hill at Sauteurs remembers the Kalinago, while the Belmont and River Antoine estates recall cocoa and sugar history.

name: Guatemala

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); 22 Mayan languages plus Garifuna and Xinka are officially recognised

people: Over 40% of Guatemalans identify as Maya, belonging to some 22 linguistic communities, alongside Ladino (mestizo) people, Garifuna on the Caribbean coast and Xinka in the south-east. Catholicism and evangelical Protestantism are both very strong, often intertwined with Maya spirituality. Around half live in rural areas, and a large diaspora in the US sends remittances that sustain many families.
resources: Living Maya cultures, languages and weaving traditions
Coffee, cardamom (world's largest exporter), bananas and sugar
Volcanoes, highland lakes and cloud forests
Maya archaeological heritage
Remittances from a hard-working diaspora
Biodiversity of the Petén rainforest
struggles: Chronic child malnutrition — among the highest rates in the world
Deep inequality and exclusion of Indigenous communities
Corruption and pressure on judges, prosecutors and journalists
Gang violence and extortion
Climate shocks — droughts, storms and landslides — driving emigration
prayFor: For children who go hungry, that every child may grow well-nourished
For Maya communities, that their land, language and voice be respected
For justice-seekers, journalists and honest public servants who face pressure
For families of migrants on the dangerous road north
For healing for survivors and families of the disappeared from the armed conflict

summary.history: Guatemala was a heartland of Maya civilisation, from great Classic cities like Tikal to the highland kingdoms of the K'iche' and Kaqchikel. Spanish conquest under Pedro de Alvarado began in 1524, and colonial rule imposed forced labour and land seizures; Antigua Guatemala served as capital of Central America. After independence, coffee and later the United Fruit Company's banana plantations shaped an economy built on Indigenous labour. A 36-year internal armed conflict (1960–96) killed some 200,000 people, most of them Maya, and a UN-backed truth commission found acts of genocide against Maya communities in the early 1980s.
summary.politicalHistory: Guatemala gained independence from Spain in 1821, was part of the Central American Federation, and became a separate republic in 1839. A democratic 'Ten Years of Spring' (1944–54) ended in a CIA-backed coup, followed by decades of military rule and armed conflict. A new constitution in 1985 restored civilian rule, and peace accords were signed in 1996. Guatemala is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Maya weaving — huipiles whose patterns identify each town — is one of the world's great textile traditions. Literature includes the K'iche' sacred book Popol Vuh, Nobel laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias and Rigoberta Menchú, Nobel Peace laureate, whose testimony told of Maya suffering. Marimba is the national instrument, and the Holy Week carpets (alfombras) of Antigua are breathtaking works of devotion.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Tikal National Park, Antigua Guatemala and the Archaeological Park and Ruins of Quiriguá with its towering stelae; the Maya Biosphere Reserve protects El Mirador and other ancient sites. Lake Atitlán, ringed by volcanoes and Maya towns, is one of the world's most beautiful lakes. Chichicastenango's market and church of Santo Tomás are centres of Maya life and ritual.

name: Guyana

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Indigenous languages such as Makushi, Wapishana and Arawak

people: Guyanese of Indian descent form the largest group, followed by Afro-Guyanese, people of mixed heritage, and nine Indigenous (Amerindian) nations, with smaller Chinese and Portuguese-descended communities. Christianity is the majority faith, with Hindus around a quarter and Muslims under a tenth of the population, and religious festivals such as Diwali, Phagwah and Eid are national holidays. Most people live on the narrow coastal strip, much of it below sea level, while the vast interior is sparsely settled.
resources: Large offshore oil reserves, producing since 2019
Rainforest covering most of the country
Gold, bauxite and diamonds
Rice and sugar agriculture
Kaieteur Falls and rich biodiversity
Multicultural, multi-faith society
struggles: Managing sudden oil wealth fairly and transparently
Ethnic-political polarisation between Indo- and Afro-Guyanese communities
Coastal flooding risk as sea levels rise
Venezuela's renewed claim to the Essequibo region
Poverty and limited services in the interior and Indigenous villages
Mining-related deforestation and mercury pollution
prayFor: For oil wealth to lift every household and protect the land for future generations
For trust and unity across ethnic and political lines
For a peaceful, lawful resolution of the Essequibo dispute
For Indigenous communities, their land rights and wellbeing
For protection of the coast and the forests that breathe for the world

summary.history: Arawak, Carib and Warao peoples lived in the region for thousands of years. The Dutch established plantations from the early 17th century, and the British took control in the early 19th century, forming British Guiana in 1831. Sugar plantations depended on enslaved Africans; the Berbice Rebellion of 1763, led by Cuffy, and the Demerara Rebellion of 1823 were major uprisings. After emancipation in 1834–38, planters brought indentured labourers mainly from India, as well as from Portugal (Madeira) and China, shaping Guyana's diverse society.
summary.politicalHistory: British Guiana elected Cheddi Jagan's People's Progressive Party in 1953, but Britain suspended the constitution, and the independence movement later divided along ethnic lines. Guyana became independent on 26 May 1966 under Forbes Burnham and a 'Co-operative Republic' in 1970, with increasingly authoritarian rule until free elections in 1992. It is a republic with an executive president elected through parliamentary elections, and power has alternated between the PPP/C and the APNU coalition.
summary.art: Guyanese music blends calypso, chutney, soca and reggae, and Mashramani ('Mash') is the national republic-day festival. Writers include Wilson Harris, Edgar Mittelholzer, Martin Carter ('Poems of Resistance') and E. R. Braithwaite ('To Sir, With Love'). Painter Aubrey Williams and Indigenous crafts such as Wai Wai and Makushi basketry and hammock weaving are cultural treasures.
summary.monuments: Kaieteur Falls is one of the world's highest single-drop waterfalls, set in a vast rainforest. Georgetown's wooden St. George's Cathedral, Stabroek Market and the 1763 Monument honouring Cuffy are historic landmarks. Fort Zeelandia on Fort Island recalls the Dutch era, and the Rupununi savannahs and Iwokrama forest show the beauty of the interior.

name: Haiti

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Haitian Creole is spoken by virtually everyone

people: Most Haitians are of African descent, with a small mixed-heritage and Middle Eastern-descended minority. Catholicism and Protestantism are both widespread, and Vodou — a spiritual tradition rooted in West and Central African religions — is practised by many alongside Christianity. Around 60% now live in cities, especially Port-au-Prince, and a large diaspora in the US, Dominican Republic, Canada, France and Chile sends remittances crucial to families.
resources: The first free Black republic — a profound legacy of liberation
Creative, resilient people and a vibrant diaspora
Rich art, music and literary culture
Agriculture — coffee, mangoes, cocoa, vetiver
Mountains, beaches and coastline
Strong church and community networks
struggles: Armed gangs controlling much of Port-au-Prince, causing killings, kidnappings and mass displacement
Acute hunger affecting around half the population
Political vacuum and fragile institutions after the 2021 assassination of the president
Collapse of health and education services in many areas
Repeated disasters — the 2010 and 2021 earthquakes and hurricanes
Deforestation and soil erosion
prayFor: For safety and an end to violence for families in Port-au-Prince and the Artibonite
For the hundreds of thousands displaced from their homes, that they find shelter, food and return
For children, that schools reopen and they can learn and play in peace
For honest, courageous leaders and a path to legitimate, stable government
For doctors, nurses, teachers, pastors and neighbours who keep caring amid crisis

summary.history: Hispaniola was home to the Taíno, who were nearly annihilated after Spanish arrival in 1492. The western part became the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the richest colony in the world by the 18th century, built on the brutal enslavement of hundreds of thousands of Africans in sugar and coffee. In 1791 the enslaved rose up in the Haitian Revolution, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeating French, Spanish and British forces. Independence came at a heavy price: France demanded a huge indemnity in 1825 that burdened Haiti for generations, and the country later endured a US occupation (1915–34), dictatorship and natural disasters, including the 2010 earthquake that killed over 200,000 people.
summary.politicalHistory: Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804, the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people. The 19th century saw division and frequent changes of ruler; in the 20th century François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier and his son Jean-Claude ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986. A 1987 constitution established a semi-presidential system, and Jean-Bertrand Aristide was elected in 1990, overthrown, restored, and later ousted again in 2004, followed by a UN peacekeeping mission. After the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021 and the lapse of elected offices, a transitional council was established in 2024 and a Kenyan-led multinational security mission began to deploy.
summary.art: Haitian painting gained world fame from the 1940s through the Centre d'Art, with artists such as Hector Hyppolite and Philomé Obin, and metal sculpture from Croix-des-Bouquets is distinctive. Music includes konpa, rara and mizik rasin, and Haitian soup joumou — eaten on Independence Day — is UNESCO-recognised heritage. Writers such as Jacques Roumain, Frankétienne, Edwidge Danticat and Dany Laferrière have given Haiti a powerful literary voice.
summary.monuments: The National History Park — Citadelle, Sans Souci, Ramiers — a UNESCO World Heritage Site, includes the vast mountaintop Citadelle Laferrière built after independence to defend the nation. Jacmel's historic centre is known for its iron-balconied houses and carnival. The Bassin Bleu pools, Saut-d'Eau waterfall (a site of Catholic and Vodou pilgrimage) and the Musée du Panthéon National in Port-au-Prince are treasured places.

name: Honduras

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Bay Islands Creole English and Indigenous languages

people: Most Hondurans are mestizo, with Indigenous Lenca, Miskito, Tolupan, Pech, Tawahka and Maya Chortí peoples, Garifuna and English-speaking Afro-descendant communities on the Caribbean coast and Bay Islands. Christianity is central — the country is roughly split between Catholics and evangelical Protestants. About 60% live in cities, mainly Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula, and many Hondurans live and work in the US and Spain.
resources: Coffee (among the region's largest producers), bananas and palm oil
Bay Islands reefs on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef
Cloud forests and the Río Plátano rainforest
Maya heritage at Copán
Apparel manufacturing
Remittances and strong family ties
struggles: Very high levels of violence and extortion by gangs, driving displacement
Poverty affecting over half the population
Corruption and weak rule of law
Attacks on environmental and land defenders, including the 2016 murder of Berta Cáceres
Hurricane, drought and climate vulnerability (Mitch 1998; Eta and Iota 2020)
prayFor: For families living under extortion and threat, that they may find safety and peace
For land and water defenders, especially Lenca and Garifuna communities
For young people, that education and work offer them a future at home
For honest leadership and an end to impunity
For farmers facing drought and storms, that harvests may be abundant

summary.history: Western Honduras was part of the Maya world, with Copán one of its greatest Classic cities, while Lenca and other peoples lived in the highlands. Spain conquered the region in the 1520s–30s against fierce resistance, including the Lenca leader Lempira, after whom the currency is named. Silver mining and cattle ranching shaped the colony. In the late 19th and 20th centuries US banana companies gained such power that Honduras became the original 'banana republic', and in the 1980s it hosted US and Contra bases during the region's wars.
summary.politicalHistory: Honduras gained independence from Spain in 1821 and became a separate republic in 1838 after the Central American Federation dissolved. Its history includes frequent coups and long periods of military rule, with a return to civilian government under the 1982 constitution. In 2009 President Manuel Zelaya was removed in a coup, and the disputed 2017 election led to deadly protests. Honduras is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Garifuna music and dance — punta and paranda — are part of UNESCO-recognised Garifuna heritage. Painter José Antonio Velásquez is celebrated for primitivist scenes of village life, and writers include Froylán Turcios and Roberto Sosa. Lenca pottery, Copán stone carving and colourful mahogany crafts are cherished traditions.
summary.monuments: The Maya Site of Copán, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is famed for its hieroglyphic stairway and finely carved stelae. The Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, also UNESCO-listed, protects rainforest and Indigenous Miskito and Pech lands. The colonial Comayagua Cathedral holds one of the oldest clocks in the Americas, and the Fortress of San Fernando de Omoa guarded the Caribbean coast.

name: Jamaica

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Jamaican Sign Language

people: Over nine in ten Jamaicans are of African descent, with communities of Indian, Chinese, European, Middle Eastern and mixed heritage reflected in the motto 'Out of Many, One People'. Jamaica is strongly Christian — Pentecostal, Adventist, Baptist, Anglican and many other churches — and Rastafari, born here in the 1930s, is an influential spiritual movement. More than half live in towns and cities, and the diaspora in the UK, US and Canada is roughly as large as the population at home.
resources: Global cultural influence — reggae, ska, dancehall
World-class athletes
Bauxite and alumina
Tourism, beaches and the Blue Mountains
Blue Mountain coffee, rum and agriculture
A large, engaged diaspora
struggles: One of the highest homicide rates in the world, linked to gangs and guns
Hurricane exposure — Hurricane Beryl struck in July 2024
Public debt, though greatly reduced through long reform
Inequality and informal 'garrison' communities
Youth unemployment and emigration of nurses, teachers and skilled workers
prayFor: For peace in communities affected by violence, and protection for children and young men
For mothers and families grieving loved ones lost to violence
For farmers and fishers recovering from storms
For nurses, teachers and health workers, that they be supported and valued
For opportunity and hope that keeps talent flourishing at home

summary.history: The Taíno, who called the island Xaymaca ('land of wood and water'), were devastated after Spanish arrival in 1494. England seized Jamaica in 1655, and it became one of the most profitable sugar colonies, worked by enslaved Africans under horrific conditions. Maroon communities in the mountains fought the British to treaties in 1739, and the Christmas Rebellion of 1831–32, led by Samuel Sharpe, hastened emancipation in 1834–38. The Morant Bay Rebellion of 1865, led by Paul Bogle, was violently suppressed, and the labour uprisings of 1938 gave rise to modern political parties.
summary.politicalHistory: Jamaica gained universal adult suffrage in 1944 and independence on 6 August 1962, after briefly joining the West Indies Federation. Alexander Bustamante (Jamaica Labour Party) and Norman Manley (People's National Party) are national heroes who founded the two main parties. Politics was marked by violent rivalry in the 1970s and 1980s, but Jamaica has remained a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with regular changes of government.
summary.art: Jamaica gave the world ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall; Bob Marley, Toots Hibbert and Jimmy Cliff are global icons, and reggae is UNESCO-listed intangible heritage. Writers include Claude McKay, Louise Bennett-Coverley ('Miss Lou'), and Marlon James, winner of the Booker Prize. Edna Manley's sculpture and the intuitive painting of Kapo (Mallica Reynolds) are celebrated in the National Gallery.
summary.monuments: The Blue and John Crow Mountains, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, protect forests and the heritage of the Windward Maroons. Port Royal, once a notorious buccaneer haven, was largely sunk by a 1692 earthquake. The Bob Marley Museum in Kingston, Rose Hall Great House, and the Sam Sharpe Square in Montego Bay recall music, plantation history and the struggle for freedom.

name: Nicaragua

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Mayangna, Garifuna and Rama

people: Most Nicaraguans are mestizo, with Indigenous Miskito, Mayangna and Rama peoples and Afro-descendant Creole and Garifuna communities on the Caribbean coast, which has its own autonomous regions. Catholicism and evangelical Protestantism are both strong. About 60% live in cities, mostly on the Pacific side, and large communities live in Costa Rica, the US and Spain.
resources: Lakes Nicaragua and Managua and many volcanoes
Coffee, beef, gold and sugar
Renewable energy potential (geothermal and wind)
Bosawás rainforest biosphere
Pacific surf beaches and colonial cities
A strong poetic and literary tradition
struggles: Severe restrictions on civil society, independent media, universities and churches since 2018
The 2018 protest crackdown, with hundreds killed and many imprisoned or exiled
Poverty and large-scale emigration
Deforestation and settler violence against Indigenous communities in the Caribbean region
Hurricane and earthquake vulnerability
prayFor: For those imprisoned, exiled or stripped of nationality, and the families who miss them
For freedom of faith, conscience and expression, and for clergy and church communities under pressure
For Miskito and Mayangna communities, that their lands and lives be protected
For families divided by migration
For healing, truth and peaceful reconciliation in Nicaraguan society

summary.history: Nahua-speaking Nicarao and Chorotega peoples lived on the Pacific side, and Chibchan peoples in the east, when Spanish conquistadors arrived in the 1520s; many Indigenous people were enslaved and shipped to Peru. Granada and León, founded in 1524, became rival colonial cities, while the Caribbean coast fell under British influence with the Miskito Kingdom. In 1856 the American filibuster William Walker seized power until he was expelled by a Central American coalition. The 20th century brought repeated US interventions, the resistance of Augusto César Sandino, the Somoza dictatorship, the devastating 1972 Managua earthquake, and war in the 1980s.
summary.politicalHistory: Nicaragua became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic in 1838. The Somoza family ruled from 1937 until the Sandinista revolution of 1979, after which the Sandinista government fought US-backed Contra rebels in a war that cost tens of thousands of lives. Violeta Chamorro's 1990 election victory ended the war and brought a peaceful transfer of power. The Sandinista leader of the 1980s returned to the presidency in 2007, and since the 2018 crisis power has become increasingly concentrated, with opposition figures jailed or exiled; Nicaragua is formally a presidential republic.
summary.art: Rubén Darío, father of Spanish-language Modernismo, is Nicaragua's national poet, and Ernesto Cardenal, Gioconda Belli and Sergio Ramírez are major writers. El Güegüense, a satirical colonial-era street theatre, is UNESCO-listed intangible heritage. The primitivist painting of Solentiname, pottery of San Juan de Oriente and the marimba de arco enrich the arts.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the ruins of León Viejo, one of the oldest Spanish colonial settlements, and León Cathedral, the largest in Central America. Colonial Granada on Lake Nicaragua and the twin volcanoes of Ometepe Island are iconic. Masaya Volcano's glowing crater and the Bosawás Biosphere Reserve showcase the country's natural power.

name: Panama

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Guna, Emberá, Panamanian Creole English and immigrant languages

people: Most Panamanians are mestizo, alongside Afro-Panamanians (including descendants of West Indian canal workers), seven Indigenous peoples such as the Ngäbe, Guna and Emberá, and Chinese, Middle Eastern, Indian and other communities. Catholicism is the majority faith, with a large evangelical minority and small Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and Bahá'í communities. About 70% live in cities, especially around Panama City, while Indigenous comarcas are among the most rural and remote areas.

currency.name: US dollar (used alongside the Panamanian balboa, B/., in coins)

resources: The Panama Canal
Strategic position as a logistics, banking and trade hub
Copper deposits
Rainforests, two oceans and rich biodiversity
Tourism and the Darién wilderness
Diverse cultures, including Guna and Emberá heritage
struggles: Drought lowering Gatún Lake and restricting canal traffic in 2023–24
Social conflict over the Cobre Panamá copper mine, closed after mass protests in 2023
Deep inequality and poverty in Indigenous comarcas
Mass migration through the Darién Gap, with many deaths and abuses
Corruption and pension-system strain
prayFor: For migrants crossing the Darién, that they be protected from violence and danger
For Ngäbe, Guna and Emberá communities, that they share fully in the nation's wealth
For rain and water for the canal, and for the communities who depend on the same lakes
For just, peaceful dialogue over mining and the care of the land
For honest stewardship of public resources

summary.history: The isthmus was home to Cueva, Guna, Ngäbe and other peoples when Spanish explorers arrived in 1501; Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed it to the Pacific in 1513. Panama became a vital route for Spanish silver, with the Camino Real linking Portobelo and Panama City, and enslaved Africans and Cimarrón communities shaped its history. Part of Colombia after independence from Spain, it saw the Panama Railroad built in the 1850s and a failed French canal effort in the 1880s that killed thousands of workers. The US completed the canal in 1914, largely with West Indian labour.
summary.politicalHistory: Panama declared independence from Spain in 1821 and joined Gran Colombia, then separated from Colombia in 1903 with US support, granting the US control of the Canal Zone. Protests over sovereignty, including the 1964 Martyrs' Day riots, led to the 1977 Torrijos–Carter Treaties; military strongman Manuel Noriega was removed by a US invasion in December 1989. The canal passed fully to Panamanian control on 31 December 1999, and Panama is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Guna women's molas — layered, cut-through appliqué textiles — are among the Americas' most famous textile arts. The pollera dress, tamborito dance and Congo traditions of Portobelo, UNESCO-listed, are central to national culture. Rubén Blades and jazz pianist Danilo Pérez are internationally celebrated musicians.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Archaeological Site of Panamá Viejo and the Historic District of Panamá (Casco Viejo), the Fortifications of Portobelo and San Lorenzo, Darién National Park, Coiba National Park and the Talamanca Range–La Amistad reserves. The Panama Canal and its Miraflores Locks are a marvel of engineering. The Biomuseo, designed by Frank Gehry, celebrates the isthmus's role in uniting two continents.

name: Paraguay

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Indigenous languages, Plautdietsch and Portuguese

people: Paraguay is unusual in the Americas: most people are bilingual in Spanish and Guaraní, a language spoken by the majority including non-Indigenous Paraguayans. The population is largely mestizo, with around 19 Indigenous peoples, Mennonite colonies in the Chaco, and Brazilian, Japanese, Korean and Arab-descended communities. Catholicism is the main faith, with growing evangelical churches; around 60% live in cities, especially greater Asunción, and many work in Argentina, Spain and Brazil.
resources: Hydroelectric power — Itaipú and Yacyretá dams make it a major clean-energy exporter
Soy, beef and agricultural exports
The Paraná and Paraguay rivers
Guaraní language and culture
The Chaco and Pantanal ecosystems
A young population
struggles: Rapid deforestation of the Chaco and Atlantic Forest
Highly unequal land ownership and conflicts with small farmers and Indigenous peoples
Poverty and informal work
Corruption and the influence of organised crime
Drought affecting rivers, shipping and harvests
prayFor: For Indigenous communities and small farmers, that they may live securely on their land
For protection of forests in the Chaco and the life they hold
For young Paraguayans, that education and work open good paths at home
For honest institutions and freedom from the grip of organised crime
For rain in season and flourishing rivers

summary.history: Guaraní peoples lived across the region when the Spanish founded Asunción in 1537, which became a base for colonising much of southern South America. From the early 17th century Jesuit missions (reducciones) gathered Guaraní communities into towns that protected them from slave raiders until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767. After independence, Paraguay fought the catastrophic War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, losing a large share of its population — by some estimates over half. The Chaco War with Bolivia (1932–35) brought further loss but secured most of the Chaco.
summary.politicalHistory: Paraguay declared independence in 1811, and was long ruled by strongmen such as José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia and the López family. General Alfredo Stroessner ruled as dictator from 1954 to 1989, a regime marked by repression, disappearances and corruption, documented later in the 'Archives of Terror'. A 1992 constitution restored democracy, and Paraguay is a presidential republic in which the Colorado Party has governed for most of the period since 1947.
summary.art: Ñandutí lace, whose name means 'spider web' in Guaraní, and ao po'i embroidery are delicate national crafts. The Paraguayan harp and polka and guarania music, created by José Asunción Flores, are beloved, and Agustín Barrios Mangoré was a master guitarist-composer. Augusto Roa Bastos's novel 'I, the Supreme' is a classic of Latin American literature.
summary.monuments: The Jesuit Missions of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, eloquent ruins of mission towns. Asunción's National Pantheon of Heroes honours the nation's war dead. The Itaipú Dam is one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants, and the Chaco's Defensores del Chaco National Park protects wild dry forest.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue)

people: Most Kittitians and Nevisians are of African descent, with smaller communities of European, Indian and mixed heritage. Christianity shapes daily life, with Anglican, Methodist, Moravian, Pentecostal, Adventist and Catholic churches. About three-quarters of people live on St Kitts, and many families have relatives in the US, UK, Canada and the US Virgin Islands.
resources: Tourism, beaches and cruise visitors
Citizenship-by-investment revenue
Volcanic landscapes and rainforest of Mount Liamuiga and Nevis Peak
Offshore medical and veterinary schools
Geothermal energy potential on Nevis
Strong sense of community
struggles: Heavy reliance on tourism and citizenship-by-investment income
Hurricane and climate vulnerability
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes
Youth crime and gun violence
Tensions over the federation between St Kitts and Nevis
prayFor: For a resilient economy that serves every family, not only visitors and investors
For young people, that they be kept safe and find purpose
For good health and care for those with chronic illness
For harmony and trust between St Kitts and Nevis
For protection from storms and wise care of the islands

summary.history: The Kalinago called St Kitts Liamuiga ('fertile land'); in 1626 English and French settlers jointly massacred many of them at Bloody Point. St Kitts became the first English colony in the Caribbean (1623), and both islands became sugar colonies worked by enslaved Africans, sometimes called the 'mother colony' of the British West Indies. Britain gained full control under the 1783 Treaty of Versailles, and slavery ended in 1834. Nevis was the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton, and sugar remained central until the state-run industry closed in 2005.
summary.politicalHistory: Labour struggles in the 1930s, led by figures such as Robert Bradshaw, gave rise to the Labour Party that dominated mid-century politics. The islands, together with Anguilla until it seceded, became an Associated State in 1967, and St Kitts and Nevis gained independence on 19 September 1983. It is a federal parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm; Nevis has its own island assembly and a constitutional right to secede, which a 1998 referendum narrowly failed to approve.
summary.art: Calypso, soca and steelpan fill Sugar Mas, the national carnival, and Nevis celebrates Culturama. Masquerade troupes, the Moko Jumbies on stilts, and the folk 'Bull' play preserve African and Caribbean traditions. Batik and pottery are local crafts, and Caryl Phillips, born on St Kitts, is a celebrated novelist.
summary.monuments: Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is an exceptionally well-preserved 18th-century British fortress built by enslaved Africans. The Circus and Independence Square in Basseterre, the Alexander Hamilton House on Nevis and the Bath Hotel ruins recall colonial history. The St Kitts Scenic Railway once carried sugar cane around the island.

name: Saint Lucia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Kwéyòl is spoken by most people

people: Most Saint Lucians are of African descent, with communities of mixed, Indian and European heritage. Catholicism is the majority faith, reflecting French influence, alongside Adventist, Pentecostal, Anglican and other churches. Life is centred on Castries and the north-west, with many rural villages and a diaspora in the UK, US and Canada.
resources: The Pitons and volcanic landscapes
Tourism and beaches
Bananas and cocoa
Kwéyòl language and Creole culture
Two Nobel laureates and a rich intellectual tradition
Rainforest and marine reserves
struggles: Rising gun violence and homicides
Youth unemployment
Dependence on tourism and imports
Hurricane and landslide risk
Non-communicable diseases
prayFor: For peace in communities affected by violence, and comfort for grieving families
For young people, that they find work, skills and hope
For farmers and fishers facing storms and changing seas
For good health and care for all
For the treasures of Kwéyòl language and culture to keep flourishing

summary.history: Arawak-speaking peoples and later the Kalinago lived on the island, which they called Iouanalao or Hewanorra, and resisted early European settlement. France and Britain fought over Saint Lucia so often that it changed hands around fourteen times, earning the nickname 'Helen of the West Indies'. Sugar plantations relied on enslaved Africans, and during the French Revolutionary wars the formerly enslaved and maroon 'Brigands' fought for freedom. Britain took final control in 1814, slavery ended in 1834, and Indian indentured labourers arrived later in the century.
summary.politicalHistory: Saint Lucia became an Associated State in 1967 and gained independence on 22 February 1979. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with power alternating between the Saint Lucia Labour Party and the United Workers Party. John Compton, the island's first prime minister, is regarded as a father of the nation.
summary.art: Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel laureates: the poet and playwright Derek Walcott (Literature, 1992) and the economist Sir Arthur Lewis (Economics, 1979). Jounen Kwéyòl (Creole Day) celebrates Creole language, music and food, and the flower festivals of La Rose and La Marguerite are rooted in old societies. Painter Dunstan St Omer, Kwéyòl folk songs and the Saint Lucia Jazz Festival enrich the island's culture.
summary.monuments: The Pitons Management Area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, includes the twin volcanic spires of Gros Piton and Petit Piton rising from the sea. Pigeon Island National Landmark preserves Fort Rodney and 18th-century military ruins. The Sulphur Springs near Soufrière, the Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception in Castries with Dunstan St Omer's murals, and Morne Fortune are treasured places.

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue)

people: Most Vincentians are of African descent, with Garifuna (Black Carib) heritage, small Kalinago, Indian, Portuguese and European-descended communities, and many of mixed ancestry. Anglican, Methodist, Pentecostal, Adventist, Catholic and Spiritual Baptist churches are central to community life. Most people live on mainland St Vincent, and the Grenadine islands are small, seafaring communities; many Vincentians live abroad.
resources: The Grenadines' sailing waters and reefs (Tobago Cays)
Fertile volcanic soils for bananas, arrowroot and root crops
Tourism, including the new Argyle International Airport
Fisheries and boat-building traditions
Garifuna heritage
Strong regional diplomacy
struggles: Volcanic risk — La Soufrière erupted in 2021, displacing about a fifth of the population
Hurricane damage, including Hurricane Beryl in July 2024, which devastated Union Island and other Grenadines
Unemployment and poverty
Dependence on imports and vulnerable agriculture
Youth emigration
prayFor: For families in the Grenadines rebuilding homes and livelihoods after Hurricane Beryl
For farmers near La Soufrière restoring land after the eruption
For young people, that they find meaningful work at home
For the Garifuna story and heritage to be honoured
For safety and resilience in the face of storms and eruptions

summary.history: Kalinago and later Garifuna (Black Carib) people — descendants of Kalinago and Africans — fiercely defended St Vincent, making it one of the last Caribbean islands colonised by Europeans. Britain took control in 1763, and the Second Carib War (1795–96), led by Garifuna chief Joseph Chatoyer, ended in defeat; around 5,000 Garifuna were deported to Baliceaux and then to Roatán in Honduras, where many died. Sugar and arrowroot plantations worked by enslaved Africans dominated the economy until emancipation in 1834. Portuguese and Indian indentured labourers arrived later in the 19th century.
summary.politicalHistory: St Vincent joined the West Indies Federation, became an Associated State in 1969 and gained independence on 27 October 1979. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm; a 2009 referendum to become a republic was rejected. Joseph Chatoyer is honoured as the first National Hero.
summary.art: Vincy Mas, the carnival, brings calypso, soca and steelpan to the streets, and the island is known for soca and the Nine Mornings festival before Christmas. Garifuna heritage, including drumming and language revival efforts, is increasingly celebrated. Boat-building on Bequia and model-boat making are distinctive crafts.
summary.monuments: Fort Charlotte overlooks Kingstown, and the St Vincent Botanic Gardens, founded in 1765, are among the oldest in the Western Hemisphere, with a breadfruit tree descended from Captain Bligh's voyage. La Soufrière volcano dominates the north. The Tobago Cays Marine Park and Bequia's harbour are jewels of the Grenadines.

name: Suriname

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Maroon and Indigenous languages

people: Suriname is one of the most diverse societies anywhere: Hindustani (Indian-descended), Maroon, Creole, Javanese, Indigenous, Chinese, mixed-heritage and other communities live side by side. Christianity, Hinduism and Islam are all major faiths — Paramaribo's synagogue and mosque famously stand next to each other — alongside Winti and Indigenous traditions. Most people live in Paramaribo and along the coast, while Maroon and Indigenous villages line the interior rivers, and a large diaspora lives in the Netherlands.
resources: Rainforest covering over 90% of the land
Gold and offshore oil reserves
Bauxite and aluminium heritage
Rivers and hydropower
Multicultural and multi-faith harmony
Rice, bananas and fisheries
struggles: Recovery from a severe debt and currency crisis with high inflation
Gold-mining pollution (mercury) and deforestation in the interior
Land rights of Maroon and Indigenous peoples not yet legally secured
Coastal flooding and sea-level rise
Emigration of skilled workers
prayFor: For families recovering from the economic crisis and rising prices
For Maroon and Indigenous communities, that their land rights be recognised
For clean rivers and protection of the forest
For continued peace and respect among Suriname's many cultures and faiths
For truth and healing over the wounds of the 1980s, including the December murders and the interior war

summary.history: Indigenous peoples such as the Kalinya, Lokono, Trio and Wayana lived in the region long before Europeans arrived. English settlers founded a colony in 1650, but it passed to the Dutch in 1667, and plantations of sugar and coffee were worked by enslaved Africans under notoriously harsh conditions. Many escaped into the rainforest and formed Maroon nations — Saramaka, Ndyuka and others — which won peace treaties in the 1760s. Slavery was abolished in 1863, followed by a decade of forced 'state supervision', after which indentured labourers came from India, Java and China.
summary.politicalHistory: Suriname gained autonomy within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 and independence on 25 November 1975. A military coup in 1980 brought Dési Bouterse to power; in the December murders of 1982 fifteen prominent critics were killed, and an interior war (1986–92) caused many deaths, including the Moiwana massacre of Maroon villagers. Democracy was restored in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and Suriname is a parliamentary republic with a president elected by the National Assembly.
summary.art: Kaseko music, Maroon drumming and the Winti spiritual songs mingle with Indian baithak gana and Javanese gamelan. Writers include Anton de Kom, whose 'We Slaves of Suriname' (1934) is a landmark, and the poet Trefossa, who championed Sranan. Maroon woodcarving and Indigenous pottery and basketry are prized crafts.
summary.monuments: The Historic Inner City of Paramaribo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserves Dutch colonial wooden architecture, including the Cathedral Basilica of St Peter and Paul. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, also UNESCO-listed, protects vast pristine rainforest. Fort Zeelandia, the Neveh Shalom Synagogue next to the Keizerstraat Mosque, and Jodensavanne, an early Jewish settlement, tell Suriname's layered story.

name: Trinidad and Tobago

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Tobagonian Creole and Trinidadian Bhojpuri

people: Trinidad and Tobago's people are roughly balanced between those of Indian descent and those of African descent, with a large mixed population and Chinese, Syrian-Lebanese, Venezuelan, European and Indigenous (Santa Rosa First Peoples) communities. Christianity (Catholic, Pentecostal, Anglican and Spiritual Baptist), Hinduism and Islam are all prominent, and Diwali, Eid and Emancipation Day are national holidays. Tobago is smaller and predominantly Afro-Tobagonian, and the country has received many Venezuelan migrants.
resources: Oil and natural gas, including LNG and petrochemicals
The Pitch Lake, the world's largest natural asphalt deposit
Carnival and the birthplace of steelpan
Tobago's reefs and rainforest reserve
An educated, multicultural workforce
Cocoa heritage (Trinitario cocoa)
struggles: Record levels of gun violence and gang-related killings
Over-dependence on declining oil and gas output
Ethnic-political tensions
Integration and protection of Venezuelan migrants and refugees
Flooding and oil-spill risks, such as the February 2024 spill off Tobago
prayFor: For an end to gun violence and comfort for grieving families
For young people, that they find purpose and opportunity beyond crime
For Venezuelan migrants, that they be welcomed with safety and dignity
For a just transition to a more diverse, sustainable economy
For unity and respect across communities and faiths

summary.history: Trinidad was home to Arawak and Carib peoples who called it Iere; Columbus arrived in 1498, and Spanish rule brought missions and forced labour that devastated them. Under the 1783 Cedula of Population, French planters and enslaved Africans arrived, and the British seized Trinidad in 1797; Tobago changed hands many times before becoming British. After emancipation in 1834–38, around 144,000 indentured labourers came from India between 1845 and 1917, along with Chinese and Portuguese workers. Oil was discovered in the early 20th century, and the 1937 labour riots led by Tubal Uriah 'Buzz' Butler shaped modern politics.
summary.politicalHistory: Trinidad and Tobago became independent on 31 August 1962 under Eric Williams of the People's National Movement, and became a republic within the Commonwealth in 1976. The country weathered the Black Power protests of 1970 and an attempted coup by the Jamaat al Muslimeen in 1990. It is a parliamentary republic, with power alternating between the PNM and the United National Congress, and Tobago has its own House of Assembly.
summary.art: Trinidad gave the world the steelpan, the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century, as well as calypso and soca; Lord Kitchener and the Mighty Sparrow are calypso legends, and Peter Minshall transformed carnival masquerade into art. Writers include V. S. Naipaul (Nobel 1971), Samuel Selvon and Earl Lovelace. Chutney music, tassa drumming and Hosay processions reflect Indian and Muslim heritage.
summary.monuments: The Magnificent Seven mansions by the Queen's Park Savannah, Fort George and the Red House parliament recall Port of Spain's history. The Pitch Lake at La Brea and the Temple in the Sea at Waterloo, built by Siewdass Sadhu, are remarkable sites. Tobago's Main Ridge Forest Reserve, protected since 1776, is among the oldest legally protected forests in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Uruguay

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Uruguayan Portuguese and Uruguayan Sign Language

people: Most Uruguayans are of European descent, especially Spanish and Italian, with an Afro-Uruguayan minority whose candombe tradition is central to national culture, and Indigenous Charrúa ancestry in many families. Uruguay is the most secular country in the Americas, with church and state strictly separated since 1918; Catholics are the largest faith group, alongside many non-religious people and smaller evangelical and Jewish communities. About 95% live in urban areas, and nearly half in greater Montevideo.
resources: Fertile grasslands for beef, dairy and wool
Near-100% renewable electricity (wind, hydro, biomass, solar)
Forestry and pulp industry
Stable democratic institutions
Software and IT services
Atlantic and River Plate coastline
struggles: Rising violent crime linked to drug trafficking
Child poverty, especially among young families
An ageing population and emigration of young people
Severe drought in 2023 that threatened Montevideo's drinking water
Persistent disparities affecting Afro-Uruguayans
prayFor: For children in poverty, that every child has what they need to flourish
For safety in neighbourhoods touched by drug-related violence
For families of the disappeared, still seeking truth from the years of dictatorship
For water security and care for rivers and land
For Afro-Uruguayan communities, that equal dignity become lived reality
