summary.history: The Charrúa, Guaraní and other peoples lived in the region when the Spanish and Portuguese began competing for the Banda Oriental in the 16th and 17th centuries. Montevideo was founded in 1724–26 as a Spanish stronghold, and enslaved Africans were brought through its port. In 1831 the new state's forces massacred many Charrúa at Salsipuedes. Waves of European immigration in the 19th and early 20th centuries, cattle ranching and progressive reforms made Uruguay the 'Switzerland of South America'.
summary.politicalHistory: Led by José Gervasio Artigas, the Banda Oriental fought for independence from Spain, then from Portuguese-Brazilian rule, becoming independent in 1828 with its first constitution in 1830. Early 20th-century president José Batlle y Ordóñez established a welfare state, secular education and other reforms. A civic-military dictatorship (1973–85) imprisoned and tortured thousands and disappeared nearly 200 people. Democracy returned in 1985, and Uruguay is today a highly regarded presidential republic.
summary.art: Candombe drumming, with roots in Afro-Uruguayan communities, is UNESCO-recognised intangible heritage, and the tango — shared with Argentina — is also UNESCO-listed. Writers include Juan Carlos Onetti, Mario Benedetti, Eduardo Galeano and Juana de Ibarbourou, and the painters Pedro Figari and Joaquín Torres García shaped Latin American art. Murga, a satirical carnival chorus theatre, makes Montevideo's carnival one of the longest in the world.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Historic Quarter of Colonia del Sacramento, the Fray Bentos industrial landscape and the work of engineer Eladio Dieste, including the Church of Atlántida. Montevideo's Palacio Salvo and Plaza Independencia with Artigas' mausoleum are national landmarks. Punta del Este, the Cabo Polonio dunes and the Museo de la Memoria are places of beauty and memory.

name: Venezuela

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Wayuu, Warao, Pemon, Yanomami and other Indigenous languages

people: Most Venezuelans are of mixed European, African and Indigenous descent, with significant Afro-Venezuelan communities on the coast, more than 40 Indigenous peoples including the Wayuu, Warao, Pemon and Yanomami, and descendants of Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Lebanese and Colombian immigrants. Catholicism is the main faith, with a growing evangelical population. Nearly nine in ten live in cities, and since 2015 more than seven million Venezuelans have left the country, one of the largest displacements in the world.

income.band: Not classified (World Bank has no recent data)

resources: The world's largest proven oil reserves
Natural gas, gold, iron ore and bauxite
Angel Falls, the Andes, the Llanos and the Orinoco
Caribbean coastline and islands
Rich musical culture, including El Sistema youth orchestras
A talented people at home and in the diaspora
struggles: Prolonged economic collapse with hyperinflation, poverty and shortages
Mass emigration separating millions of families
Political crisis and serious human-rights concerns, including arbitrary detention
Weakened health care, electricity and water services
Illegal mining in the south harming forests, rivers and Indigenous peoples
prayFor: For families separated by emigration, and for migrants on the road and in host countries
For the sick, the elderly and children, that food and medicine reach every home
For political prisoners and their families, and for truth, justice and freedom
For Indigenous peoples and the Amazon threatened by illegal mining
For peaceful reconciliation and a hopeful future chosen by Venezuelans together

summary.history: Carib, Arawak and other peoples, including the Timoto-Cuica in the Andes, lived in the region before Columbus reached the coast in 1498; the name 'Little Venice' came from stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo. Under Spanish rule, cocoa plantations worked by enslaved Africans enriched a colonial elite. Venezuela was the cradle of South American independence, led by Simón Bolívar and Francisco de Miranda, and suffered devastating losses in the wars of independence. The discovery of oil in the early 20th century transformed it into one of Latin America's wealthiest countries, but dependence on oil left it vulnerable to booms, busts and corruption.
summary.politicalHistory: Venezuela declared independence in 1811, was part of Gran Colombia, and became a separate republic in 1830. The 19th and early 20th centuries were dominated by caudillos and dictators such as Juan Vicente Gómez and Marcos Pérez Jiménez, until the 1958 Punto Fijo pact ushered in four decades of two-party democracy. Hugo Chávez, elected in 1998, introduced the 1999 constitution and the 'Bolivarian Revolution'; after his death in 2013 his chosen successor took office amid deepening economic and political crisis, contested elections and international sanctions. Venezuela is formally a federal presidential republic.
summary.art: Joropo, played on harp, cuatro and maracas, is the national music of the plains, and El Sistema, founded by José Antonio Abreu, has brought orchestral music to hundreds of thousands of young people and produced conductor Gustavo Dudamel. Writers include Andrés Bello, Rómulo Gallegos ('Doña Bárbara') and Teresa de la Parra. Kinetic artists Jesús Rafael Soto and Carlos Cruz-Diez were pioneers of op art, and the Dancing Devils of Corpus Christi are UNESCO-listed.
summary.monuments: UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Canaima National Park with Angel Falls (Kerepakupai Merú), the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall; Coro and its port; and the Ciudad Universitaria de Caracas, a modernist masterpiece by Carlos Raúl Villanueva. The National Pantheon in Caracas holds the remains of Simón Bolívar. Los Roques archipelago and the Andean city of Mérida showcase the country's natural beauty.

name: Afghanistan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Uzbek, Turkmen, Hazaragi, Balochi and Nuristani languages

people: Afghanistan is home to Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras, Uzbeks, Turkmen, Aimaq, Baloch, Nuristanis and others, with deep traditions of hospitality, poetry and extended family life. Nearly everyone is Muslim — mostly Sunni, with a Shia minority of roughly 10–15%, many of them Hazara — while small Sikh and Hindu communities have dwindled. About three in four people live in rural areas, and a large diaspora lives in Iran, Pakistan, Europe and North America.
resources: Untapped mineral wealth (copper, iron ore, lithium, rare earths)
Lapis lazuli and gemstones of Badakhshan and Panjshir
Mountain water sources of the Hindu Kush feeding the Amu Darya and Helmand
Orchards and dried fruit, saffron and carpets
A resilient, young population with deep oral and literary traditions
Crossroads location on historic Silk Road routes
struggles: One of the world's largest humanitarian crises, with widespread hunger and malnutrition
Bans on girls' secondary and university education and sweeping limits on women's work and public life
Deep poverty after the collapse of foreign aid and banking isolation since 2021
Drought, flash floods and deadly earthquakes such as Herat in 2023
Mass returns and deportations of Afghans from Iran and Pakistan into a fragile economy
Landmines, unexploded ordnance and the long trauma of four decades of war
prayFor: For girls and women longing to learn, work and walk freely — that doors closed to them would open again
For families facing hunger this winter, that food, medicine and work would reach every valley
For returnees and displaced people, that they would find shelter, welcome and a way to rebuild
For healing of grief carried through generations of war, and for safety for every ethnic and religious community
For wisdom, mercy and justice among all who hold power, and for peace that lets the land flourish

summary.history: The land of Afghanistan has been a crossroads for millennia, home to Bactrian cities, Buddhist kingdoms whose legacy includes the great Bamiyan statues, and later Islamic empires such as the Ghaznavids and Timurids, whose Herat was a jewel of Persian culture. In 1747 Ahmad Shah Durrani founded the empire from which the modern state grew, and in the 19th century the land became a buffer in the rivalry between the British and Russian empires, fighting three Anglo-Afghan wars. The Soviet invasion of 1979 began more than forty years of war — resistance, civil war, Taliban rule, the US-led intervention after 2001 and a long insurgency — claiming hundreds of thousands of lives and driving millions into exile. Through it all, Afghans have kept alive their poetry, music, crafts and fierce bonds of family and community.
summary.politicalHistory: Afghanistan gained full control of its foreign affairs from Britain in 1919 under King Amanullah, and was a monarchy until 1973, when Mohammad Daoud Khan declared a republic. A communist coup in 1978 and the Soviet invasion in 1979 led to war, the fall of the communist government in 1992 and a devastating civil war, after which the Taliban took Kabul in 1996. After the 2001 intervention an Islamic Republic was established with elected presidents and a parliament, but it collapsed in August 2021 when the Taliban returned to power. The Taliban now govern as the Islamic Emirate, a system without elections or a constitution, which most states have not formally recognised.
summary.art: Afghanistan is famous for its hand-knotted carpets, lapis-blue Herati glass and tile work, and the Timurid-era miniature painting school of Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād in Herat. Poetry is its heartbeat: Rumi was born in Balkh, and Pashto poets such as Rahman Baba and Khushal Khan Khattak are recited across generations, alongside the landay, a two-line folk poem often voiced by women. Music centres on the rubab, Afghanistan's national instrument, and was carried in the 20th century by singers such as Ahmad Zahir and master rubab player Ustad Mohammad Omar.
summary.monuments: The Minaret of Jam, a 12th-century Ghurid tower hidden in a remote valley, and the cultural landscape of the Bamiyan Valley, whose giant Buddhas were destroyed in 2001, are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Herat's Friday Mosque and Citadel recall the city's Timurid golden age, while the Blue Mosque of Mazar-i-Sharif draws pilgrims and the Nowruz celebrations every spring. In Kabul, the Gardens of Babur, restored after the wars, hold the tomb of the founder of the Mughal Empire.

name: Armenia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Russian widely spoken, Yazidi Kurmanji and Assyrian Neo-Aramaic among minorities

people: Armenia is one of the most ethnically homogeneous countries in the region, with about 98% ethnic Armenians alongside Yazidis, Russians, Assyrians and others. Most people belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church, which traces its roots to the adoption of Christianity as state religion in the early 4th century. Around two-thirds live in towns and cities, a third in Yerevan alone, and a diaspora larger than the home population lives in Russia, the United States, France, Lebanon and beyond.
resources: Copper, molybdenum and gold mining
Brandy, wine and apricots from the Ararat Valley
A fast-growing IT and tech sector
A worldwide diaspora with deep cultural and economic ties
Ancient monasteries, manuscripts and an alphabet of its own
Lake Sevan, one of the largest high-altitude freshwater lakes in the world
struggles: The mass flight of over 100,000 ethnic Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023 and the task of housing and integrating them
Unresolved border tensions and an unsigned peace with Azerbaijan
Closed borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan, limiting trade and connection
Emigration of young people and rural depopulation
Poverty and unemployment outside Yerevan
High earthquake risk, remembered from the 1988 Spitak disaster
prayFor: For families displaced from Nagorno-Karabakh, that they would find homes, work and comfort for all they have lost
For a just and lasting peace between Armenians and Azerbaijanis, and healing of memories on both sides
For young Armenians, that they would see a hopeful future and be able to build it at home
For villages along the borders, that they would live without fear
For the churches and communities of Armenia, that their ancient faith would be a source of mercy and reconciliation

summary.history: Armenians have lived in the highlands around Mount Ararat for well over two millennia, heirs to the kingdom of Urartu and later to an Armenian kingdom that under Tigranes the Great briefly stretched from the Caspian to the Mediterranean. In 301 Armenia became the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, and around 405 Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet. For centuries Armenians lived under Persian, Byzantine, Arab, Mongol, Ottoman and Russian rule, and in 1915–1923 the Ottoman authorities carried out the Armenian Genocide, in which an estimated one million or more Armenians were killed and survivors scattered across the world. The 20th century brought Soviet rule, the devastating 1988 earthquake and war with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, a conflict that caused deep loss and mass displacement for both Armenians and Azerbaijanis.
summary.politicalHistory: A short-lived First Republic of Armenia (1918–1920) was absorbed into the Soviet Union, and Armenia declared independence again in 1991 as the USSR dissolved. The 1988–1994 war over Nagorno-Karabakh ended with Armenian forces in control of the region and surrounding districts, but in 2020 Azerbaijan retook much of the territory, and in September 2023 it took full control, after which almost the entire Armenian population of the region fled to Armenia. The 2018 'Velvet Revolution' of peaceful mass protests brought a change of government, and a 2015 constitutional referendum turned Armenia into a parliamentary republic in which the prime minister leads the government.
summary.art: Armenian culture is known for its illuminated manuscripts, notably those of Toros Roslin, preserved in Yerevan's Matenadaran, and for khachkars — intricately carved stone crosses unique to Armenia. Its music ranges from the haunting duduk, an apricot-wood oboe inscribed by UNESCO, to the sacred chants of Komitas and the orchestral works of Aram Khachaturian. Literature runs from the medieval mystic Grigor Narekatsi to the poets Hovhannes Tumanyan and Yeghishe Charents, while painters such as Martiros Saryan captured the land's intense colours.
summary.monuments: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church, and the ruins of the 7th-century Zvartnots cathedral are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, together with the monasteries of Haghpat and Sanahin and the partly rock-carved monastery of Geghard. The pagan-era Temple of Garni and the monastery of Khor Virap, with its view of Mount Ararat, are among the most visited places in the country. In Yerevan, the Tsitsernakaberd memorial honours the victims of the Armenian Genocide.

name: Azerbaijan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Russian widely spoken, also Lezgian, Talysh, Avar and others

people: About nine in ten people are ethnic Azerbaijanis, with Lezgins, Talysh, Russians, Avars and other Caucasus peoples making up the rest. Most are Muslim — a majority Shia, with a significant Sunni minority — in a society that is largely secular in public life, and there are long-established Jewish communities such as the Mountain Jews of Quba. Just over half the population is urban, centred on Baku, and many Azerbaijanis live abroad in Russia, Turkey and Europe, while far more ethnic Azerbaijanis live across the border in Iran.
resources: Caspian Sea oil and natural gas
Pipelines linking the Caspian to Turkey and Europe
Fertile lowlands for fruit, vegetables, tea and silk
A rich mugham music and carpet-weaving heritage
Diverse landscapes from the Greater Caucasus to semi-desert and mud volcanoes
A strategic East–West and North–South transit corridor
struggles: Heavy dependence on oil and gas revenues
Landmines and destroyed towns in areas regained in 2020–2023, slowing the return of people displaced since the 1990s
Unresolved peace and border tensions with Armenia
Tight restrictions on independent media, opposition and civil society
Water scarcity and the shrinking, polluted Caspian shoreline
Inequality between Baku and rural regions
prayFor: For families displaced for three decades, that they would return safely and rebuild homes and communities
For deminers and for children in former frontline areas, that no more lives would be lost to landmines
For a just and lasting peace between Azerbaijanis and Armenians, and healing of memories on both sides
For journalists, students and all who speak their conscience, that they would be free and protected
For a future that shares the country's wealth fairly beyond oil, with work and dignity in every region

summary.history: The land between the Caucasus and the Caspian was home to ancient Caucasian Albania, whose churches and Zoroastrian fire temples gave way after the 7th century to Islam and centuries of Persian, Turkic and Mongol rule. The Shirvanshahs built their palace in Baku, and the region later fragmented into khanates before being divided between Russia and Persia in the early 19th century — leaving Azerbaijanis split on both sides of the Aras River to this day. Baku's oil boom in the late 1800s made it one of the world's chief oil producers and a cosmopolitan city. The late Soviet period and the war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh brought pogroms and massacres that struck both Armenians and Azerbaijanis, including the killing of Azerbaijani civilians at Khojaly in 1992, and left hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis displaced for decades.
summary.politicalHistory: In 1918 the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic became one of the first secular democratic republics in the Muslim world and granted women the vote, but it was taken over by the Bolsheviks in 1920. Azerbaijan regained independence in 1991, and after early turmoil and war Heydar Aliyev, a former Soviet-era leader, came to power in 1993, establishing a strong presidential system that has remained under the same family. Constitutional changes have removed presidential term limits and lengthened terms, and elections are generally judged by international observers to fall short of democratic standards. After the 2020 war and a 2023 offensive, Azerbaijan restored control over Nagorno-Karabakh and the surrounding districts.
summary.art: Azerbaijan is renowned for mugham, an improvised classical music tradition recognised by UNESCO, and for the ashiq bards who sing epic tales with the saz. Its carpets — from Quba, Shirvan, Ganja, Karabakh and Tabriz traditions — are celebrated worldwide, and the national poet Nizami Ganjavi wrote the 12th-century romances 'Layla and Majnun' and 'Khosrow and Shirin'. In the 20th century Uzeyir Hajibeyov wrote the first opera of the Muslim world, 'Leyli and Majnun' (1908), and jazz-mugham fusion flourished through Vagif Mustafazadeh.
summary.monuments: The walled Old City of Baku, with the Palace of the Shirvanshahs and the Maiden Tower, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as is Gobustan, where thousands of rock carvings record life over some 40,000 years. The historic centre of Sheki and its Khan's Palace, famed for its stained-glass shebeke windows, was inscribed in 2019. The Ateshgah fire temple near Baku recalls the region's ancient fire-worship and its role on trade routes to India.

name: Bahrain

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages such as Malayalam, Urdu, Hindi, Persian and Tagalog

people: Roughly half of Bahrain's residents are citizens and half are foreign workers, largely from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines. Most citizens are Muslim — a Shia majority alongside a Sunni community that includes the ruling family — and the island has long-standing Christian churches, a Hindu temple and a small native Jewish community. Almost everyone lives in towns, as the main island is densely built from Manama to Muharraq.
resources: Oil and gas, including the region's first oil discovery of 1932
A regional banking and Islamic-finance hub
Aluminium smelting
Pearling heritage and rich marine life of the Gulf
A well-educated citizen workforce
Causeway and port links across the Gulf
struggles: Declining oil reserves and high public debt
Sectarian and political tensions unresolved since the 2011 protests
Restrictions on opposition, free expression and assembly
Vulnerability of migrant workers under sponsorship-based labour systems
Severe freshwater scarcity and dependence on desalination
Coastal land reclamation and sea-level rise threatening low-lying land and reefs
prayFor: For trust and reconciliation between Shia and Sunni Bahrainis, and for justice that heals old wounds
For migrant workers far from home, that they would be paid fairly, protected and treated with dignity
For young Bahrainis seeking meaningful work as the oil age wanes
For wisdom in caring for water, sea and coastline for generations to come
For families of detainees and all who carry the grief of the past decade

summary.history: Bahrain was the heart of Dilmun, a Bronze Age trading civilisation linking Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley, and its thousands of burial mounds still dot the island. For centuries it was known for its pearls and its freshwater springs, coming under Persian, Arab and, in the 16th century, Portuguese rule. The Al Khalifa family took control in 1783, and in the 19th century Bahrain entered treaty relations with Britain that made it a British protectorate. The discovery of oil in 1932, the first on the Arab side of the Gulf, transformed a pearling and trading society into a modern state.
summary.politicalHistory: Bahrain became fully independent from Britain in 1971, and an elected National Assembly created in 1973 was dissolved in 1975. After unrest in the 1990s, a 2001 National Action Charter and 2002 constitution made Bahrain a constitutional monarchy with a partly elected parliament. In 2011 mass protests, largely but not only by Shia citizens, were suppressed with support from Gulf Cooperation Council forces, followed by arrests and the dissolution of major opposition groups. Today the king holds wide powers, alongside a bicameral parliament with an elected lower house and an appointed upper house.
summary.art: Bahrain's traditional arts include fijiri, the haunting sea songs of pearl divers, and Gulf music on the oud, as well as boat building, weaving and the decorated wooden doors of old Muharraq. Poetry in both classical and Gulf colloquial Arabic is cherished, and the 20th-century poet Ibrahim al-Arrayed is a national figure. Contemporary artists and calligraphers show their work in Manama's galleries and at the Bahrain National Museum.
summary.monuments: Qal'at al-Bahrain, an ancient harbour and capital of Dilmun later crowned by a Portuguese fort, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the Dilmun Burial Mounds. The Pearling Path in Muharraq, a UNESCO-listed trail of merchants' houses and oyster beds, tells the story of the island's pearl economy. The Al-Fateh Grand Mosque and the Tree of Life, a lone mesquite growing in the desert, are much-loved landmarks.

name: Georgia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Azerbaijani, Armenian, Russian, Mingrelian, Svan and Abkhaz

people: Georgians make up about 87% of the population, with Azerbaijani and Armenian communities, Ossetians, Abkhaz, Yazidis, Kists and others. Most people belong to the Georgian Orthodox Church, with Muslim communities (around 10%) in Adjara and among Azerbaijanis, plus Armenian Apostolic, Catholic and ancient Jewish traditions. Around 60% live in cities, a third in Tbilisi, and many Georgians work abroad in Europe, Russia and Turkey.
resources: Some 8,000 years of winemaking and over 500 native grape varieties
Hydropower from Caucasus rivers
Manganese from Chiatura and mineral waters such as Borjomi
Black Sea ports and transit routes between Europe and Asia
Mountains, coast and hospitality that draw growing tourism
A singular alphabet, polyphonic singing and feasting culture
struggles: About 20% of internationally recognised territory — Abkhazia and South Ossetia — outside government control, with Russian troops stationed there
Hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the conflicts of the 1990s and 2008, many still without a home to return to
Deep political polarisation and disputes over the country's European or Russian orientation
Unemployment, rural poverty and emigration
Landslides, floods and glacial hazards in mountain regions
prayFor: For people displaced from Abkhazia, South Ossetia and the villages along the boundary lines, that they would find safety and a lasting home
For healing between Georgians, Abkhaz and Ossetians, and an end to fear and division
For honest, peaceful public life in which every voice is heard and no one is silenced
For young Georgians and rural families, that they would find good work without leaving their land
For the churches and mosques of Georgia, that they would sow mercy and hospitality

summary.history: Georgia's story stretches back to some of the earliest humans outside Africa, found at Dmanisi, and to the ancient kingdoms of Colchis — the land of the Golden Fleece — and Iberia. Christianity became the state religion in the 330s through the preaching of St Nino, and a unified Georgian kingdom reached its golden age under King David the Builder and Queen Tamar in the 11th–13th centuries. Mongol invasions, Persian and Ottoman rivalry and fragmentation followed, until the Russian Empire annexed Georgian lands in the 19th century. In the Soviet era Georgia suffered Stalin-era purges, even though Stalin himself was Georgian, and the end of the USSR brought civil war and conflicts in Abkhazia and South Ossetia that left many dead on all sides and displaced hundreds of thousands, most of them ethnic Georgians.
summary.politicalHistory: A Democratic Republic of Georgia existed from 1918 until the Red Army invaded in 1921, and Georgia declared independence again in 1991. The early 1990s brought a coup, civil war and secessionist wars, and the peaceful 2003 Rose Revolution ushered in reforms and a westward course. A brief war with Russia in 2008 over South Ossetia ended with Russia recognising Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent, which most of the world does not. Constitutional reforms completed in 2018 made Georgia a parliamentary republic, and the country became an EU candidate in December 2023, even as disputes over a 2024 'foreign influence' law brought large protests.
summary.art: Georgian polyphonic singing, with its layered, ancient harmonies, is recognised by UNESCO, as are the traditional qvevri clay vessels in which wine is fermented underground. Its literature is crowned by Shota Rustaveli's 12th-century epic 'The Knight in the Panther's Skin', and later writers include Ilia Chavchavadze and Vazha-Pshavela. Painting was transformed by the self-taught Niko Pirosmani, while cloisonné enamel, filmmakers such as Tengiz Abuladze and Otar Iosseliani, and fierce national dances carry the culture onward.
summary.monuments: Gelati Monastery, a medieval academy near Kutaisi, and the historical monuments of Mtskheta — including Svetitskhoveli Cathedral and the hilltop Jvari Monastery — are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Upper Svaneti, with its medieval stone defence towers beneath glaciers, is also inscribed for its preserved mountain way of life. The rock-cut cave city of Vardzia and the Gergeti Trinity Church beneath Mount Kazbek are among the country's most moving places.

name: Iran

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Luri, Gilaki, Mazandarani, Arabic, Balochi, Turkmen and Armenian

people: Iran is a mosaic of peoples: Persians form the largest group, alongside Azerbaijanis, Kurds, Lurs, Arabs, Baloch, Turkmen, Gilakis, Mazandaranis, Armenians and Assyrians. Around nine in ten people are Shia Muslim, with Sunni Muslims (mainly Kurds, Baloch and Turkmen), and long-established Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian communities, while Baha'is face persecution. About three-quarters live in cities, and a large diaspora lives in North America, Europe, Turkey and the Gulf.
resources: Some of the world's largest oil and natural gas reserves
Copper, iron ore, zinc and other minerals
Pistachios, saffron, dates and carpets
A highly educated population, with many women among university graduates
One of the world's oldest continuous civilisations, with 25+ UNESCO World Heritage Sites
Varied landscapes from Caspian forests to deserts and the Zagros mountains
struggles: High inflation and a falling currency, worsened by international sanctions and economic mismanagement
A severe water crisis — drying lakes and rivers, depleted aquifers and land subsidence
Restrictions on personal freedoms, women's dress and political expression, and harsh crackdowns on protest such as in 2022
Discrimination faced by some ethnic and religious minorities
Emigration of young and skilled people
Air pollution in major cities and high earthquake risk
prayFor: For families struggling with rising prices, that they would have enough bread, medicine and work
For women and young people longing for dignity and freedom, and for all who grieve loved ones lost or imprisoned
For rain and wise stewardship of water, that lakes, rivers and farmland would be restored
For religious and ethnic minorities, that they would be safe and respected
For peace between Iran and its neighbours, and an end to fear of war for ordinary people across the region

summary.history: The Iranian plateau was home to Elam, one of the earliest civilisations, before Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire in the 6th century BC, once the largest the world had seen. Parthian and Sasanian empires followed, until the Arab conquest of the 7th century brought Islam, while the Persian language and culture flowered anew under dynasties from the Samanids to the Safavids, who made Shia Islam the state faith in the 1500s. In the modern era Iran lost territory to Russia, endured foreign interference — including the 1953 coup against the elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh supported by Britain and the United States — and suffered the Iran–Iraq War of 1980–88, which killed hundreds of thousands on both sides. Iranians have long combined deep pride in their heritage with a restless search for justice and self-rule.
summary.politicalHistory: The Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1911 created Iran's first parliament, and in 1925 Reza Khan founded the Pahlavi dynasty, whose modernising but authoritarian rule continued under his son Mohammad Reza Shah. The 1979 Revolution overthrew the monarchy and established the Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, combining elected bodies such as the president and parliament with unelected clerical institutions headed by a Supreme Leader. Candidates are vetted by the Guardian Council, and waves of protest — in 1999, 2009, 2019 and 2022 — have been met with forceful crackdowns.
summary.art: Persian poetry is the soul of Iranian culture, from Ferdowsi's epic 'Shahnameh' to the lyrics of Rumi, Saadi, Hafez and Omar Khayyam, whose verses Iranians still quote daily. Iran is renowned for its hand-knotted carpets, miniature painting, calligraphy, tile work and classical music built on the radif modal system and instruments such as the tar, setar and santur. In modern times its cinema, with directors such as Abbas Kiarostami and Asghar Farhadi, has earned worldwide acclaim.
summary.monuments: Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid kings, and nearby Pasargadae with the tomb of Cyrus the Great are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square, with its Shah and Sheikh Lotfollah mosques, shows the height of Safavid architecture. The ancient adobe city of Yazd with its windcatchers, the Armenian monastic ensembles of the northwest, and the tombs of Hafez and Saadi in Shiraz are also cherished.

name: Iraq

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Turkmen, Neo-Aramaic (Syriac), Armenian and Mandaic

people: Arabs make up roughly three-quarters of Iraqis and Kurds about a fifth, alongside Turkmen, Assyrians and other Christians, Yazidis, Shabaks, Mandaeans and Armenians. Around 95% are Muslim — Shia Muslims are the majority, with a large Sunni minority — and the ancient Christian, Yazidi and Mandaean communities have shrunk sharply through war and emigration. About 70% live in cities, and the population is very young, with a large diaspora in Europe, North America and neighbouring countries.
resources: Among the world's largest proven oil reserves
The Tigris and Euphrates and the fertile land between them
Dates — once the world's leading producer
The southern marshes, a unique wetland ecosystem
Heritage of Sumer, Akkad, Babylon and Assyria, and of Abbasid Baghdad
A young, resilient population and many religious and ethnic traditions
struggles: Water scarcity as the Tigris and Euphrates shrink from upstream dams, drought and extreme heat
Recovery from the war against ISIS, including destroyed cities such as Mosul and over a million people still displaced
Corruption, unreliable electricity and weak public services
Near-total dependence on oil revenue and high youth unemployment
The lasting trauma of genocide against Yazidis and the shrinking of Christian and other minority communities
Tensions between Baghdad and the Kurdistan Region, and the influence of armed groups
prayFor: For water to return to the rivers and marshes, and for farmers and fishers whose livelihoods depend on them
For Yazidis, Christians and all survivors of ISIS, especially women and children still missing, that they would be found, healed and able to return home
For honest leaders and fair public services, so that every family has power, clean water and work
For young Iraqis, that they would see a future of peace and dignity in their own land
For reconciliation between Shia and Sunni, Arab and Kurd, and every community of this ancient land

summary.history: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, is where writing, cities and law codes first emerged, through the civilisations of Sumer, Akkad, Babylon and Assyria. After the Islamic conquests Baghdad became the Abbasid capital and, for centuries, a world centre of learning, until the Mongol sack of 1258. Ottoman rule lasted until the First World War, after which Britain created the modern state from three Ottoman provinces. The decades since have brought dictatorship, the Iran–Iraq War, the 1991 Gulf War and sanctions, the 2003 US-led invasion, sectarian civil war and the rise and defeat of ISIS — costing hundreds of thousands of lives and leaving deep scars, alongside a stubborn will to rebuild.
summary.politicalHistory: Iraq became a British-mandated kingdom in 1921 and formally independent in 1932, until the monarchy was overthrown in a 1958 military revolution. A series of coups brought the Ba'ath Party to power in 1968, and Saddam Hussein ruled as dictator from 1979, waging war on Iran, invading Kuwait and carrying out mass atrocities including the Anfal campaign against the Kurds. After the 2003 invasion removed him, a 2005 constitution created a federal parliamentary republic with an autonomous Kurdistan Region, in which power has generally been shared among Shia, Sunni and Kurdish parties. Mass youth-led protests in 2019 demanded an end to corruption and the sectarian quota system.
summary.art: Iraq gave the world the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Code of Hammurabi and cuneiform writing, and under the Abbasids Baghdad was home to poets such as Abu Nuwas and the House of Wisdom. The Iraqi maqam, a classical vocal tradition accompanied by the santur and joza, is recognised by UNESCO, and the oud was carried to new heights by Munir Bashir and Naseer Shamma. In the 20th century, poets Badr Shakir al-Sayyab and Nazik al-Malaika pioneered free verse in Arabic, and the architect Zaha Hadid was born in Baghdad.
summary.monuments: Babylon, Ashur, the ancient city of Hatra and the Ahwar marshes with the remains of Ur, Uruk and Eridu are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, testifying to Mesopotamia's role as a cradle of civilisation. The Erbil Citadel, one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements on earth, is also inscribed, as is the Abbasid city of Samarra with its spiral minaret. The shrines of Imam Ali in Najaf and Imam Husayn in Karbala draw millions of pilgrims, and Mosul's al-Nuri Mosque has been rebuilt after its destruction in 2017.

name: Jordan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English widely used, also Circassian, Chechen and Armenian

people: Jordanians include East Bank families with tribal and Bedouin roots, a large population of Palestinian origin, and smaller Circassian, Chechen and Armenian communities, alongside refugees from Syria and Iraq and migrant workers. Over nine in ten people are Sunni Muslim, and Christian communities with roots in the earliest churches make up a small but long-standing minority. More than 90% of people live in cities, above all in Amman, Zarqa and Irbid.
resources: Phosphate and potash mining
World-famous heritage: Petra, Jerash and Wadi Rum
The Dead Sea and the Red Sea at Aqaba
A well-educated workforce and strong medical sector
Hospitality and a long tradition of sheltering refugees
A position of relative stability at the heart of the region
struggles: One of the most water-scarce countries in the world
Hosting one of the largest refugee populations per person, including Palestinian refugees since 1948 and Syrians since 2011
High unemployment, especially among young people and women
High public debt and rising cost of living
Economic shocks from regional wars, including falling tourism since the war in Gaza began in 2023
prayFor: For water — for rain, for wise sharing of scarce resources, and for every household to have enough
For refugees from Palestine, Syria, Iraq and beyond, and the communities who host them, that they would live with dignity and hope
For young Jordanians searching for work and a future
For peace and justice across the region, and comfort for those in Jordan who grieve family in Gaza, the West Bank and elsewhere
For Muslims and Christians of Jordan, that their long friendship would deepen and bless their neighbours

summary.history: The lands east of the Jordan River have been inhabited since prehistoric times and were home to the biblical kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom, before the Nabataeans carved their capital Petra from rose-red rock. Roman, Byzantine, Umayyad and later Mamluk and Ottoman rule followed, leaving cities, desert castles and churches with some of the oldest mosaics in the region. After the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans in 1916, Britain created the Emirate of Transjordan. Wars in 1948 and 1967 brought hundreds of thousands of Palestinian refugees, and later crises in Iraq and Syria brought many more, shaping the country's people and its strained resources.
summary.politicalHistory: Transjordan was established in 1921 under Emir Abdullah of the Hashemite family and became the independent Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in 1946. Jordan governed the West Bank and East Jerusalem from 1948 until Israel took them in the 1967 war, and in 1970–71 the state fought Palestinian armed groups in what became known as Black September. King Hussein, who reigned from 1952 to 1999, signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994. Jordan is a constitutional monarchy in which the king holds broad executive powers alongside an elected House of Representatives and an appointed Senate.
summary.art: Jordanian traditional arts include Bedouin weaving, the cross-stitch embroidery of women's dresses, sand bottle art and the mosaics of Madaba. Music ranges from Bedouin poetry sung with the rababa to dabke line dancing at weddings, and the tradition of Nabati oral poetry remains alive. Modern writers such as Mustafa Wahbi al-Tal ('Arar') and novelist Abdelrahman Munif, and filmmakers such as the makers of 'Theeb', have brought Jordanian voices to the wider world.
summary.monuments: Petra, the Nabataean city carved into sandstone cliffs, is Jordan's most famous UNESCO World Heritage Site, joined by the desert landscape of Wadi Rum and the Umayyad desert palace of Quseir Amra with its painted frescoes. The baptism site 'Bethany Beyond the Jordan' (Al-Maghtas) and the early Christian mosaics of Umm er-Rasas are also inscribed. The Roman city of Jerash and the Madaba mosaic map of the Holy Land are among the best-preserved treasures of their kind.

name: Kazakhstan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Uzbek, Uyghur, Ukrainian, German, Tatar and Korean

people: Kazakhs make up about 70% of the population, with large Russian, Uzbek, Ukrainian, Uyghur, German, Tatar and Korean communities, many descended from people deported to the steppe in the Soviet era. Roughly 70% are Muslim, mainly Sunni, and about a quarter Christian, mostly Russian Orthodox, in a society that is largely secular in daily life. Around 60% live in cities such as Almaty, Astana and Shymkent, while herding traditions continue on the vast steppe.
resources: Oil and gas from the Caspian fields of Tengiz and Kashagan
The world's largest uranium production
Coal, copper, zinc, chromium and other minerals
Vast wheat lands of the northern steppe
Mountains, steppe and lakes of immense beauty
A nomadic heritage of hospitality, horsemanship and oral epic
struggles: Dependence on oil and mineral exports and the price swings that follow
Inequality and frustration that erupted in the deadly January 2022 unrest
Limits on political competition, independent media and peaceful protest
Environmental legacies: the shrinking Aral Sea and Soviet nuclear testing around Semey
Water stress, desertification and severe floods such as those of spring 2024
prayFor: For families in the Aral Sea region and around Semey still living with the health and environmental scars of the past
For fair sharing of the land's great wealth, so that villages and small towns flourish too
For freedom and justice for all who speak, write and gather peacefully
For peaceful harmony among the many peoples and faiths who call Kazakhstan home
For communities rebuilding after floods, and for wise care of rivers, lakes and steppe

summary.history: The Kazakh steppe was home to the Scythians and Saka, whose 'Golden Man' burial treasure is a national emblem, and later to Turkic khaganates, Silk Road cities such as Otrar and Turkistan, and the Mongol Golden Horde. In the 15th century the Kazakh Khanate formed, its people organised in three zhuz (hordes) of nomadic herders. The Russian Empire gradually absorbed the steppe in the 18th–19th centuries, and under Soviet rule forced collectivisation caused the famine of 1930–33, the Asharshylyk, in which over a million Kazakhs — perhaps more than a third of the people — died. Stalin-era deportations, the Gulag, the Virgin Lands campaign and some 450 nuclear tests near Semipalatinsk deeply reshaped the land and its population.
summary.politicalHistory: Kazakhstan became a Soviet republic in 1936 and was the last to declare independence, in December 1991, under Nursultan Nazarbayev, who ruled for nearly three decades with strong presidential powers and moved the capital to Astana in 1997. He stepped down in 2019 while keeping considerable influence, until the January 2022 unrest, in which over 200 people died, led to his retreat from remaining posts. A 2022 referendum amended the constitution, limiting the president to a single seven-year term, though the political system remains dominated by the presidency and the ruling party.
summary.art: Kazakh culture is rooted in nomadic arts: the felt yurt with its decorated interiors, the oral epics of the akyn bards and the improvised sung duels called aitys, both recognised by UNESCO. The two-stringed dombra is the national instrument, and the kuy instrumental pieces of Kurmangazy remain beloved. The poet and philosopher Abai Qunanbaiuly is the founding figure of modern Kazakh literature, and Mukhtar Auezov wrote his life in the novel 'The Path of Abai'.
summary.monuments: The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkistan, a masterpiece of Timurid architecture, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the Tamgaly petroglyphs and stretches of the Silk Road through the Zhetysu region. Saryarka, the steppe and lakes of northern Kazakhstan, is inscribed as a refuge for migratory birds and the saiga antelope. The futuristic skyline of Astana and the Charyn Canyon near Almaty show the country's modern and natural faces.

name: Kuwait

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages such as Hindi, Urdu, Malayalam, Tagalog and Bengali

people: Kuwaiti citizens make up only about a third of residents; the rest are migrant workers and their families, mainly from India, Egypt, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Most citizens are Muslim — majority Sunni with a substantial Shia minority — and there are churches serving both a small group of Kuwaiti Christians and many expatriates. Nearly everyone lives in the urban area around Kuwait Bay, and tens of thousands of stateless Bidoon residents live without full citizenship rights.
resources: Vast oil reserves, including the Burgan field, one of the largest in the world
One of the world's oldest and largest sovereign wealth funds
A strategic deep-water position at the head of the Gulf
A seafaring and pearling heritage
A lively parliamentary and press tradition by regional standards
struggles: Almost total dependence on oil for exports and public revenue
Extreme summer heat, among the highest temperatures recorded on earth
Exploitation and abuse risks for migrant and domestic workers
The unresolved status of the stateless Bidoon
Repeated deadlock between government and parliament, slowing reform
Water scarcity and reliance on energy-intensive desalination
prayFor: For migrant and domestic workers, that they would be paid fairly, treated with kindness and protected from abuse
For the Bidoon, that they would receive recognition, documents and a secure future
For wise and cooperative leadership that prepares the country for life after oil
For relief and safety in the summer heat, especially for those who work outdoors
For families still remembering loved ones lost or missing from the 1990–91 occupation

summary.history: Failaka Island off Kuwait's coast was settled in the Bronze Age Dilmun era and later hosted a Hellenistic outpost. In the 18th century families from central Arabia settled on Kuwait Bay, and the Al Sabah family emerged as rulers of a trading and pearling port. In 1899 Kuwait came under British protection, and the discovery of oil in 1938 transformed it into one of the world's wealthiest states per person. In August 1990 Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait, causing deaths, detentions and widespread destruction until a US-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces in February 1991, leaving hundreds of oil wells burning.
summary.politicalHistory: Kuwait gained independence from Britain in 1961 and adopted a constitution in 1962 that created an elected National Assembly with real powers, unusual in the Gulf. The emir, from the Al Sabah family, appoints the prime minister and cabinet, and the elected assembly can question ministers and block legislation, leading to frequent dissolutions and standoffs. Women won the right to vote and stand for parliament in 2005. In May 2024 the emir suspended parliament and some constitutional articles for up to four years.
summary.art: Kuwait's heritage includes sawt, a Gulf song form with oud and drums, and the fijiri sea songs of pearl divers. Sadu weaving, the geometric Bedouin textile craft, is recognised by UNESCO, and Kuwait's theatre and television drama have long been influential across the Gulf. Writers such as the poet Fahd al-Askar and novelists including Saud Alsanousi, whose 'The Bamboo Stalk' explores migrant identity, have given voice to Kuwaiti society.
summary.monuments: The Kuwait Towers, with their blue-and-green-tiled spheres, are the city's emblem, while the Grand Mosque is the largest in the country. Sadu House preserves Bedouin weaving and the Seif Palace and old Souk al-Mubarakiya recall the old port city. Archaeological sites on Failaka Island span Dilmun, Hellenistic and early Christian eras.

name: Kyrgyzstan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Uzbek, Dungan, Uyghur and Tajik

people: Kyrgyz make up around three-quarters of the population, with large Uzbek communities in the south, Russians, Dungans, Uyghurs, Tajiks and others. About 90% are Muslim, mainly Sunni, often blended with older nomadic customs, and a minority is Russian Orthodox. Roughly two-thirds live in rural areas, many as herders and farmers, while hundreds of thousands work abroad, especially in Russia.
resources: Gold, especially the Kumtor mine
Glaciers and rivers feeding hydropower and the region's water
High mountain pastures for horses, sheep and yaks
Issyk-Kul, a vast high-altitude lake that never freezes
A living nomadic culture of yurts, epics and horse games
Remittances from workers abroad sustaining many families
struggles: Heavy dependence on remittances from labour migrants in Russia
Rural poverty and limited jobs at home
Melting glaciers threatening long-term water supplies
Deadly border clashes with Tajikistan in 2021 and 2022 that displaced civilians on both sides
Political instability, corruption and narrowing space for independent media
Violence against women, including bride kidnapping (ala kachuu), despite being illegal
prayFor: For families separated by labour migration, that parents and children would be held together in love
For peace and good neighbourliness along the border with Tajikistan, and comfort for families who lost homes or loved ones
For women and girls, that they would be safe and free to choose their own future
For wise care of glaciers, rivers and pastures that sustain life across Central Asia
For honest leaders and room for every voice to be heard

summary.history: The Tian Shan mountains have long been home to nomadic peoples, from the Saka and Wusun to the Turkic tribes from whom the Kyrgyz emerged, and Silk Road cities such as Balasagun and Uzgen flourished here. The Kyrgyz moved into the region from the Yenisei area of Siberia over centuries, keeping a herding life under Mongol, Dzungar and Kokand rule. In the 19th century the Russian Empire absorbed the region, and in 1916 a revolt against wartime conscription was brutally crushed, causing massacres and a mass flight to China known as the Urkun. Soviet rule brought forced settlement, collectivisation and purges, but also schooling and industry.
summary.politicalHistory: The Kyrgyz SSR was created in 1936 and declared independence in 1991. Kyrgyzstan has seen three uprisings that toppled presidents — the 2005 Tulip Revolution, the 2010 revolution followed by deadly ethnic violence in Osh and Jalal-Abad that mostly struck Uzbek communities, and the 2020 unrest after disputed elections. After 2010 it briefly became the region's only parliamentary republic, but a 2021 referendum restored a strong presidential system.
summary.art: The Epic of Manas, among the longest oral epics in the world, is recited by manaschy storytellers and recognised by UNESCO. Kyrgyz arts include felt-making — the shyrdak and ala-kiyiz carpets — yurt craftsmanship and the three-stringed komuz, the national instrument. The novelist Chinghiz Aitmatov, author of 'Jamilia' and 'The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years', is the country's best-known writer.
summary.monuments: Sulaiman-Too, a sacred mountain rising above the city of Osh, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are Silk Road sites of the Chuy Valley including the Burana Tower. Western Tien-Shan is inscribed for its biodiversity. The stone caravanserai of Tash Rabat and the alpine lake Song-Kul, where herders still summer in yurts, show the meeting of history and landscape.

name: Lebanon

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Armenian, Kurdish and immigrant languages

people: Lebanon is home to 18 officially recognised religious communities: Muslims — Sunni and Shia in roughly equal numbers — and Druze make up most of the population, while Christians, chiefly Maronite, Greek Orthodox and Greek Catholic, are around a third. It also hosts Palestinian refugees present since 1948 and well over a million Syrians who fled war, along with migrant domestic workers. Nearly 90% of people live in cities, and a Lebanese diaspora many times larger than the home population lives in the Americas, West Africa, Europe, the Gulf and Australia.
resources: A highly educated, multilingual population
A worldwide diaspora sending support home
Fertile Bekaa Valley farmland, vineyards and orchards
Mountains, springs and Mediterranean coast in a small space
World-renowned cuisine, hospitality and creative industries
Some of the oldest heritage of the Mediterranean, from Phoenician Byblos to Roman Baalbek
struggles: One of the world's worst economic collapses since 2019, wiping out savings and pushing most of the population into poverty
The trauma and unanswered questions of the August 2020 Beirut port explosion
A sectarian power-sharing system prone to paralysis and corruption
Strain on services and tensions around hosting Syrian and Palestinian refugees
Cross-border hostilities with Israel since October 2023, displacing tens of thousands of people on both sides of the border
Emigration of doctors, teachers and young people
prayFor: For families who lost their savings, homes or loved ones, that they would find provision and hope
For justice and healing for the victims of the Beirut port explosion
For peace on Lebanon's southern border, and safety for civilians in Lebanon and northern Israel alike
For refugees and host communities, that they would live side by side with dignity
For leaders of every community to serve the common good, and for young Lebanese to see a future at home

summary.history: The Lebanese coast was the heartland of the Phoenicians, whose cities of Byblos, Sidon and Tyre spread trade, colonies and the alphabet across the Mediterranean. Persian, Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine rule followed, and Mount Lebanon became a refuge for Maronite Christians, Druze and Shia communities through the Islamic and Ottoman eras. In 1860 communal violence between Druze and Maronites led to an autonomous Ottoman province, and after the First World War France created Greater Lebanon under its mandate. The country later suffered a 15-year civil war (1975–1990) that killed an estimated 150,000 people, Israeli invasions and occupation of the south, Syrian military presence until 2005, and the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah.
summary.politicalHistory: Lebanon became independent from France in 1943, and an unwritten National Pact divided top offices among communities: a Maronite president, a Sunni prime minister and a Shia speaker of parliament. Demographic and political tensions, the presence of armed Palestinian groups and regional interventions contributed to the civil war, which ended with the 1989 Taif Agreement that rebalanced power and set parliament seats equally between Christians and Muslims. Lebanon remains a parliamentary republic based on confessional power-sharing, in which Hezbollah, both a political party and an armed movement, plays a major role, and long vacancies in top offices and mass protests in 2019 reflect deep political strain.
summary.art: Lebanon's music is loved across the Arab world through singers such as Fairuz and composers such as the Rahbani brothers, and the oud, darbuka and dabke dance animate celebrations. Kahlil Gibran's 'The Prophet' is one of the most translated books of the 20th century, and writers such as Amin Maalouf and Etel Adnan have carried Lebanese voices further. Its crafts include Jezzine cutlery, glassblowing and silk, and its cuisine and contemporary cinema, such as the films of Nadine Labaki, are internationally celebrated.
summary.monuments: Baalbek, with some of the largest Roman temples ever built, and Byblos, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, as are Tyre and Anjar. The Qadisha Valley and the Forest of the Cedars of God protect monasteries carved into cliffs and the ancient cedars that are a national symbol. The Jeita Grotto and the Ottoman-era palace of Beiteddine are among the country's most visited places.

name: Oman

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Balochi, Swahili, Mehri, Jibbali (Shehri) and immigrant languages

people: About 60% of residents are Omani citizens — Arabs alongside communities of Baloch, Zanzibari, Lawati and South Arabian heritage — and the rest are migrant workers, mainly from South Asia. Most Omanis follow Ibadi Islam, a distinct tradition known for its moderation, with Sunni and Shia minorities, while migrants bring Hindu, Christian and other faiths. Around 85% live in towns and cities, especially along the Batinah coast and around Muscat.
resources: Oil and natural gas, including liquefied natural gas exports
Frankincense trees of Dhofar, traded for millennia
A long coastline, fisheries and ports such as Duqm and Salalah
Ancient falaj irrigation channels sustaining date oases
A reputation for tolerance, quiet diplomacy and mediation
Mountains, wadis, deserts and turtle beaches for tourism
struggles: Dependence on hydrocarbons and pressure on public finances
Youth unemployment and the challenge of creating jobs for citizens
Water scarcity and salt intrusion into coastal aquifers
Cyclones and flash floods, such as Cyclone Shaheen in 2021
Vulnerability of migrant workers, and limits on free expression
prayFor: For young Omanis seeking work, that they would find meaningful livelihoods in a changing economy
For rain in its season, healthy aquifers and the farmers who tend the date gardens
For safety from storms and floods for coastal and mountain communities
For migrant workers, that they would be treated justly and with kindness
For Oman's peacemaking role in the region to bear fruit for all its neighbours

summary.history: Oman's land has been settled for millennia, linked to the Bronze Age copper trade of Magan and the frankincense routes of Dhofar. Omanis embraced Islam in the 7th century, largely peacefully, and Ibadi imams long governed the interior. After driving out the Portuguese in the 1600s, Omanis built a maritime empire stretching to Zanzibar and the East African coast, trading in spices and, painfully, in enslaved people. In the 19th and 20th centuries Oman became isolated and divided between coastal sultans and interior imams, and it fought a long insurgency in Dhofar before rapid modernisation from 1970.
summary.politicalHistory: The Al Bu Said dynasty has ruled since the mid-18th century, and Oman was never formally colonised, though it had close treaty ties with Britain. In 1970 Sultan Qaboos bin Said took power from his father and led a modernisation programme of roads, schools and hospitals, ending the Dhofar rebellion by 1976. A 1996 Basic Law, revised in 2021, sets out an absolute monarchy with an advisory Council of Oman, including an elected Majlis al-Shura. Political parties are not permitted.
summary.art: Oman's traditions include silver khanjar daggers and jewellery, palm-frond weaving, pottery from Bahla and dhow building in Sur. Music and dance such as al-'azi poetry recitation, al-razha sword dance and Dhofari songs reflect Arab, African and South Asian influences. The novelist Jokha Alharthi, whose 'Celestial Bodies' won the International Booker Prize in 2019, brought Omani literature to a global readership.
summary.monuments: Bahla Fort, the archaeological sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn, the Land of Frankincense in Dhofar and the falaj irrigation systems are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, as is the ancient city of Qalhat. Nizwa Fort and the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque in Muscat are central landmarks of Omani identity. The Ras al-Jinz reserve, where green turtles nest, shows the country's natural heritage.

name: Palestine

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Hebrew and English widely understood as second languages

people: About 5.5 million Palestinians live in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, and a similar or larger number live in the diaspora — in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the Gulf, Latin America and beyond — while around two million are citizens of Israel. Most are Sunni Muslim, and Palestinian Christians, one of the oldest Christian communities in the world, number roughly 1–2%, alongside a small Samaritan community near Nablus. Many are descendants of refugees of 1948, and nearly half of Gaza's population is under 18.

currency.name: Israeli new shekel (Jordanian dinar also used)

resources: Olive groves and olive oil, central to livelihoods and identity
A highly educated population with strong universities
Holy places revered by Muslims, Christians and Jews, drawing pilgrims
Crafts such as embroidery, Hebron glass and pottery, and olive-wood carving
Agricultural land of the Jordan Valley and Gaza's coastal plain
A deep attachment to land, family and community resilience (sumud)
struggles: The war in Gaza since October 2023: tens of thousands killed, most of the population displaced, homes, hospitals and infrastructure largely destroyed, and acute hunger
Military occupation of the West Bank, settlement expansion, settler violence and restrictions on movement and access to land and water
Violence in which civilians on both sides have been killed, and the trauma it leaves in Palestinian and Israeli families alike
Economic collapse, very high unemployment and dependence on aid
Political division between the West Bank and Gaza since 2007, and no elections for many years
Severe water scarcity and polluted water in Gaza
prayFor: For the people of Gaza — for food, water, medicine, shelter and an end to the killing — and comfort for every grieving family
For the safe return of hostages and detainees to their families, and for all held unjustly
For an end to violence against civilians, Palestinian and Israeli alike, and for a just and lasting peace with security and dignity for both peoples
For children who have known only fear and loss, that they would be held, healed and able to learn and play again
For Palestinian Christians and Muslims, and all who work across divides for reconciliation, that their hope would not be extinguished

summary.history: The land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean has been inhabited since the earliest times and is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, its story shaped by Canaanites, Israelites, Philistines, empires from Assyria to Rome, and later Byzantine, Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman rule. After the First World War Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate, during which Arab and Jewish national movements came into growing conflict. The 1948 war that accompanied Israel's founding saw some 700,000 Palestinians flee or be expelled — remembered as the Nakba, the catastrophe — while Jordan and Egypt took control of the West Bank and Gaza. Israel occupied both in the 1967 war, and since then cycles of uprising, terror attacks, military operations and failed peace efforts have caused immense suffering to Palestinians and Israelis; on 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel killed around 1,200 people and took some 250 hostages, and the ensuing Israeli military campaign in Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and created a humanitarian catastrophe.
summary.politicalHistory: The Palestine Liberation Organization, founded in 1964, became recognised as the representative of the Palestinian people, and in 1988 the Palestinian National Council proclaimed a State of Palestine, which today is recognised by around 140 UN member states and holds observer-state status at the United Nations. The 1993–95 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority with limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza, with a president and legislative council first elected in 1996. After Hamas won the 2006 legislative elections, conflict with Fatah led in 2007 to Hamas controlling Gaza and the Palestinian Authority governing parts of the West Bank; no national elections have been held since, and final-status issues such as borders, Jerusalem, refugees and security remain unresolved.
summary.art: Palestinian tatreez cross-stitch embroidery, with patterns that once identified a woman's village, is recognised by UNESCO, as is the Hikaye tradition of women's storytelling. Mahmoud Darwish, the national poet, along with writers such as Ghassan Kanafani, Fadwa Tuqan and Edward Said, gave voice to exile, memory and longing. Music and dance such as dabke and oud playing, Hebron glass, Bethlehem olive-wood and mother-of-pearl carving, and the cinema of directors such as Elia Suleiman continue to flourish.
summary.monuments: The Church of the Nativity and the Pilgrimage Route in Bethlehem, the Old Town of Hebron/Al-Khalil with the Tomb of the Patriarchs, revered by both Muslims and Jews, and the ancient terraced landscape of Battir are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, along with ancient Jericho (Tell es-Sultan). The Old City of Jerusalem, with the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound and Dome of the Rock, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Western Wall, is listed by UNESCO as a site of shared significance whose status is disputed. Gaza's Great Omari Mosque and the Byzantine-era Saint Hilarion Monastery bear witness to a city inhabited for millennia, and much of Gaza's heritage has been damaged or destroyed in the war.

name: Qatar

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. immigrant languages such as Hindi, Malayalam, Urdu, Nepali, Bengali and Tagalog

people: Qatari citizens are only around one in ten residents; the great majority are migrant workers from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Pakistan, Egypt and elsewhere, and men far outnumber women because of the labour force. Citizens are almost all Muslim, mostly Sunni, while migrants bring Hindu, Christian, Buddhist and other faiths, served by a dedicated religious complex for churches. Nearly everyone lives in and around Doha.
resources: The North Field, part of the world's largest natural gas field
One of the world's largest exporters of liquefied natural gas
A large sovereign wealth fund
Investment in education, research and museums
A hub airline and airport connecting continents
A role as regional mediator and host of diplomacy
struggles: The rights and safety of migrant workers, including deaths and abuses that drew scrutiny before the 2022 World Cup, and only partial reform of the kafala system
Extreme heat and very high water and energy use per person
Dependence on gas exports and on foreign labour
Limits on free expression and political participation
Pressure from regional rivalries and conflicts, including the 2017–2021 blockade by neighbouring states
prayFor: For migrant workers and their families back home, that wages would be fair, workplaces safe and every life honoured
For the families of workers who died far from home, that they would be comforted and justly supported
For wisdom in caring for water, desert and sea in a warming world
For those who mediate between warring parties, that their efforts would bring release of captives and lasting peace
For Qataris and newcomers alike, that they would build a society of justice and genuine welcome

summary.history: The Qatar peninsula has been inhabited since the Stone Age, and for centuries its small population lived from pearling, fishing and herding, with towns such as Zubarah thriving in the 18th century. The Al Thani family rose to leadership in the 19th century, and Qatar came under Ottoman and then, from 1916, British protection. The collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s brought hardship until oil exports began after 1949. The discovery and development of the giant North Field gas reserves from the 1990s transformed Qatar into one of the richest countries in the world, built largely by migrant labour.
summary.politicalHistory: Qatar became independent from Britain in 1971 and is governed by the Al Thani dynasty as an emirate. A constitution approved by referendum in 2003 created an advisory Shura Council, some of whose members were elected for the first time in 2021, though political parties are not permitted. Qatar has pursued an active foreign policy, hosting mediators, international media and major sporting events, which brought it into a dispute with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt, who imposed a blockade from 2017 until 2021.
summary.art: Qatar's traditional arts include pearl-diving songs, the ardah sword dance, Nabati poetry, falconry and the weaving of Sadu textiles. In recent decades it has invested heavily in museums and public art, including the Museum of Islamic Art designed by I. M. Pei and large installations by international artists in the desert and city. Calligraphy, Gulf music on the oud and contemporary Qatari artists and filmmakers are increasingly prominent.
summary.monuments: Al Zubarah, a fortified 18th–19th-century pearling and trading town, is Qatar's UNESCO World Heritage Site. The National Museum of Qatar, shaped like a desert rose, and the Museum of Islamic Art on Doha's Corniche present the country's history and the wider Islamic world. Souq Waqif, rebuilt in traditional style, and the Inland Sea (Khor al-Adaid), where dunes meet the sea, are much-loved places.

name: Saudi Arabia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), plus many immigrant languages; English widely used in business

people: About 60% of residents are Saudi citizens, from Najdi, Hijazi, southern and eastern regional traditions and Bedouin tribal heritage, and around 40% are foreign workers, mainly from South Asia, Egypt, Yemen and the Philippines. Saudi citizens are Muslim — mostly Sunni, with a Shia minority of perhaps 10–15% concentrated in the Eastern Province — and the country is custodian of Islam's holiest cities, Mecca and Medina, while non-Muslim worship is confined to private settings. More than 80% live in cities, and the population is young.
resources: Among the world's largest oil reserves and production capacity
A large sovereign wealth fund driving diversification
Mecca and Medina, drawing millions of pilgrims for Hajj and Umrah
Vast solar potential and mineral deposits such as phosphate and gold
Red Sea coral reefs, deserts and ancient sites opening to tourism
A young population, with rapidly rising numbers of women in education and work
struggles: Dependence on oil revenues and the challenge of diversifying the economy
Severe water scarcity, extreme heat and reliance on desalination
Restrictions on free expression, dissent and religious freedom, with harsh sentences and frequent use of the death penalty
The vulnerability of migrant and domestic workers under sponsorship systems
The human toll of the war in Yemen, in which the Saudi-led coalition's airstrikes and blockade, as well as cross-border attacks on Saudi cities, cost civilian lives
prayFor: For pilgrims of every nation who come to Mecca and Medina, that they would travel in safety, and for those who serve them
For migrant and domestic workers, that they would be protected, paid fairly and treated with dignity
For all who are imprisoned for their words or beliefs, and for their families
For a lasting peace between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and healing for families on both sides of the border
For young Saudis — women and men — as they shape a rapidly changing society, that it would grow in justice and compassion

summary.history: The Arabian Peninsula was home to ancient caravan kingdoms such as Dedan, Lihyan and the Nabataeans, whose tombs at Hegra still stand. In the 7th century the Prophet Muhammad began preaching Islam in Mecca and established the first Muslim community in Medina, from where the faith spread across the world. For centuries the Hijaz was governed by local sharifs under successive caliphates and the Ottomans, while central Arabia was a land of tribes and oasis towns. In 1744 a pact between Muhammad ibn Saud and the religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab founded the first Saudi state, and after two earlier states rose and fell, Abdulaziz ibn Saud reunited most of the peninsula in the early 20th century; the discovery of oil in 1938 then transformed the country.
summary.politicalHistory: Abdulaziz ibn Saud captured Riyadh in 1902, conquered the Hijaz in 1925 and proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932, which has since been ruled by his sons and, more recently, grandsons. It is an absolute monarchy with no elected national legislature or political parties; the Basic Law of 1992 names the Qur'an and Sunnah as the constitution, and an appointed Consultative (Shura) Council advises the king. Since 2016 the Vision 2030 programme has brought major economic and social changes, including allowing women to drive in 2018 and opening entertainment and tourism, alongside a tightening of controls on dissent.
summary.art: Arabian poetry, from the pre-Islamic odes of the Mu'allaqat to Nabati poetry in colloquial Arabic, is the most treasured art form, and calligraphy reaches its height in the craft of the kiswa that covers the Kaaba. Traditions such as the ardah sword dance, Al-Qatt Al-Asiri wall painting by women of the southwest are recognised by UNESCO. Modern writers such as Abdelrahman Munif and Raja Alem, and contemporary artists and filmmakers such as Haifaa al-Mansour, have drawn international attention.
summary.monuments: Hegra (Mada'in Salih), with its monumental Nabataean tombs carved in sandstone, was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, joined by the At-Turaif district of Diriyah, birthplace of the first Saudi state, and historic Jeddah, the old gateway to Mecca. Rock art in the Ha'il region, the Al-Ahsa oasis and the Hima cultural area are also inscribed. The Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, around the Kaaba, and the Prophet's Mosque in Medina are the holiest sites of Islam, open only to Muslims.

name: Syria

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Armenian, Neo-Aramaic (incl. Western Aramaic of Maaloula), Turkmen and Circassian

people: Syrians are mostly Arab, with Kurds (around 10%), Turkmen, Armenians, Assyrians, Circassians and others. Sunni Muslims are the majority, alongside Alawites, Druze, Ismailis, Twelver Shia and ancient Christian churches — once about a tenth of the population but much reduced by war and emigration. More than half of all Syrians have been displaced since 2011, with millions living as refugees in Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Egypt and Europe.
resources: Fertile land of the Euphrates valley and the plains around Aleppo and Hama
Oil, gas and phosphates in the east
Some of the world's oldest cities and a vast archaeological heritage
Renowned crafts: Damascene brocade, inlaid woodwork and Aleppo soap
A rich, hospitable food culture
Resilient people and a large, skilled diaspora
struggles: The aftermath of a war since 2011 that has killed hundreds of thousands of people and left vast areas destroyed
One of the world's largest displacement crises, with millions internally displaced or living as refugees
Deep poverty, food insecurity and a collapsed currency
Tens of thousands of people detained or missing, with families still searching for answers
Division of the country among different authorities and armed forces, with foreign military presence
Damage from the February 2023 earthquakes in the north-west, compounded by war
prayFor: For families searching for the missing and the detained, that truth would be known and loved ones restored
For refugees and displaced people, that they would find safety, welcome and, when they choose, a way home
For children who have grown up amid war, that they would be healed, schooled and free to dream
For bread, electricity, medicine and work in every town and village
For justice, reconciliation and peace among Syria's many communities, Sunni and Alawite, Kurd and Arab, Christian and Druze alike

summary.history: Syria lies at the heart of the Fertile Crescent, where early farming emerged and cities such as Ebla, Mari and Ugarit — whose scribes wrote one of the earliest alphabets — flourished. Aramaeans, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Romans and Byzantines ruled in turn, and Damascus and Aleppo rank among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth; Christianity took early root here, as at Antioch and on the road to Damascus. In 661 Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, and later Ayyubid, Mamluk and four centuries of Ottoman rule followed, until France took control under a League of Nations mandate after the First World War. Since 2011 Syria has been torn by war, with immense suffering inflicted on civilians by many armed actors, including chemical attacks, sieges, barrel bombs, mass detention and the atrocities of ISIS.
summary.politicalHistory: Syria gained independence from France in 1946, followed by a series of military coups, a brief union with Egypt (1958–61) and the Ba'ath Party's seizure of power in 1963. Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970 and ruled through a strong one-party state and security apparatus, crushing an uprising in Hama in 1982 in which thousands were killed. After his death in 2000 his son succeeded him, and peaceful protests in 2011 were met with force, spiralling into a multi-sided war involving government forces, opposition groups, Kurdish-led forces, jihadist groups and foreign powers that left the country divided among rival authorities.
summary.art: Syria is famed for Damascene crafts — inlaid wood and mother-of-pearl, brocade silk, glass and the legendary Damascus steel — as well as Aleppo's olive-oil soap. Its music includes Aleppo's muwashshahat and qudud halabiyya songs, kept alive by singers such as Sabah Fakhri, and the shadow-puppet theatre and hakawati storytellers of the coffee houses. The poets Adonis and Nizar Qabbani are among the most celebrated Arab poets of the 20th century, and Syrian painters, novelists and filmmakers continue to work at home and in exile.
summary.monuments: The Ancient City of Damascus with its Umayyad Mosque, the Ancient City of Aleppo with its citadel, the ancient caravan city of Palmyra and the Crusader castle of Krak des Chevaliers are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, all now on the list of World Heritage in Danger. The Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, known as the 'Dead Cities', and the Roman theatre of Bosra are also inscribed. Many of these places, including Palmyra and Aleppo's historic souks, were heavily damaged during the war, and their restoration has become a symbol of hope.

name: Tajikistan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Pamiri languages such as Shughni and Wakhi, and Yaghnobi

people: Tajiks, a Persian-speaking people, make up around 80% of the population, with Uzbeks the largest minority, along with Kyrgyz, Russians and the Pamiri peoples of Gorno-Badakhshan. Most people are Sunni Muslim, while the Pamiris are mainly Ismaili Shia; religious practice is tightly regulated by the state. About three-quarters live in rural valleys, the population is very young, and a large share of working-age men labour abroad, mainly in Russia.
resources: Glaciers and rivers that give enormous hydropower potential
Aluminium smelting, gold, silver and antimony
Cotton, fruit and apricots from fertile valleys
