The Pamir mountains, among the highest ranges on earth
Persian literary heritage shared across the region
Remittances from workers abroad sustaining families
struggles: Among the world's highest dependence on remittances, leaving families vulnerable to events in Russia
Poverty and limited jobs, especially in rural areas
Severe restrictions on political opposition, independent media and religious expression
Melting glaciers, mudslides and earthquakes
Tensions and deadly border clashes with Kyrgyzstan in 2021 and 2022, affecting civilians on both sides
A long, porous border with Afghanistan and the risks that come with it
prayFor: For families separated by labour migration, and for migrant workers abroad, that they would be safe and treated justly
For freedom of conscience and speech for all, and comfort for those imprisoned and their families
For peace and friendship with Kyrgyz neighbours, and healing for border communities who lost homes and loved ones
For safety in the mountains from floods, landslides and earthquakes
For young Tajiks, that they would find education and work that let them flourish at home

summary.history: Tajikistan's lands were part of ancient Bactria and Sogdiana, home to Iranian-speaking peoples whose Sogdian merchants ran much of the Silk Road trade, and to Zoroastrian, Buddhist and later Islamic cultures. Under the Samanid dynasty of the 9th–10th centuries, centred in Bukhara and Samarkand, New Persian literature was born, and Tajiks see this era as their cultural golden age. Turkic, Mongol and Timurid rule followed, then the Emirate of Bukhara, until the Russian Empire extended its control in the 19th century. Soviet borders drawn in the 1920s left the historic Tajik cities of Bukhara and Samarkand in Uzbekistan, and independence was followed by a civil war in 1992–97 that killed tens of thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands.
summary.politicalHistory: The Tajik Autonomous SSR was created within Uzbekistan in 1924 and became a full Soviet republic in 1929; Tajikistan declared independence in 1991. Civil war broke out between the post-Soviet government and an alliance of Islamist and democratic opposition groups, ending with a UN-brokered peace agreement in 1997 that briefly brought the opposition into government. Since then power has been concentrated in a strong presidency, with constitutional amendments extending presidential terms, the main opposition party banned in 2015 and elections judged by observers to lack genuine competition.
summary.art: Tajik culture shares the classical Persian heritage of Rudaki, honoured as the father of Persian poetry, and of Ferdowsi, Avicenna and Omar Khayyam, while the 20th-century writer Sadriddin Ayni shaped modern Tajik literature. Shashmaqom, a classical music tradition shared with Uzbekistan, and the falak songs of the mountains are recognised by UNESCO, as are the chakan embroidery of the Kulob region. Suzani needlework, carved wooden pillars and Pamiri house architecture reflect a deep sense of beauty.
summary.monuments: The proto-urban site of Sarazm, among the oldest settlements in Central Asia, and the Tajik National Park in the Pamirs are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Hisor Fortress near Dushanbe, the ruins of the Sogdian town of Panjakent with its painted murals, and the Buddhist monastery site of Ajina Tepa reveal layers of history. The Wakhan Valley along the Pamir Highway, facing Afghanistan's Hindu Kush, holds Zoroastrian and Buddhist traces and ancient fortresses such as Yamchun.

name: Turkey

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Laz, Circassian, Armenian and immigrant languages

people: Turks form the majority, and Kurds — perhaps 15–20% of the population — are the largest minority, alongside Arabs, Zaza, Laz, Circassians, Georgians, Armenians, Greeks, Jews and Roma, and over three million Syrian refugees. Almost all people are Muslim, mostly Sunni, with a large Alevi community, while ancient Armenian, Greek Orthodox, Syriac and Jewish communities remain small. About three-quarters live in cities, Istanbul alone being home to over 15 million, and millions of people of Turkish origin live in Germany and across Europe.
resources: A diverse industrial base — cars, textiles, steel and defence
Fertile farmland producing hazelnuts, apricots, figs, cotton and wheat
Strategic position bridging Europe and Asia, with the Bosphorus and Dardanelles straits
One of the world's leading tourism destinations
Rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates headwaters for hydropower and irrigation
A young, entrepreneurial population and a vibrant cultural life
struggles: Recovery from the February 2023 earthquakes, which killed more than 50,000 people in Turkey and left millions homeless
High inflation and a cost-of-living crisis
The long conflict between the state and the PKK, which has claimed tens of thousands of lives, and unresolved Kurdish political demands
Polarisation and pressure on independent media, judiciary and opposition
Hosting the world's largest refugee population, and the social strains that come with it
The risk of a major earthquake striking Istanbul
prayFor: For survivors of the 2023 earthquakes, that homes, livelihoods and hearts would be rebuilt
For families struggling with rising prices, that they would have enough for each day
For peace and reconciliation between Turks and Kurds, and comfort for all who have lost loved ones in decades of violence
For refugees and host communities, that they would live together with dignity and kindness
For freedom, fairness and gentleness in public life, and protection for religious and ethnic minorities

summary.history: Anatolia is one of the cradles of civilisation: Göbekli Tepe, built some 11,000 years ago, and Çatalhöyük are among the oldest monumental and urban sites known, followed by the Hittites, Phrygians, Lydians, Greek cities and Troy. It became the heart of the Roman and Byzantine empires, with Constantinople as their capital and Anatolia home to many of the earliest Christian communities. Turkic Seljuks arrived from the 11th century, and the Ottoman Empire, which took Constantinople in 1453, ruled much of southeastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa for centuries. Its final decades brought war and mass atrocities, above all the destruction of the Armenian people in 1915, as well as the killing of Assyrians and Greeks and the suffering of Muslim refugees expelled from the Balkans and Caucasus, before a war of independence led to the modern republic.
summary.politicalHistory: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk led the war of independence and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923, introducing sweeping secular reforms, a new alphabet and legal codes. Multi-party politics began in 1946–1950, but the military intervened in 1960, 1971 and 1980, and in 1997 forced a government out; an attempted coup in July 2016 was defeated, followed by a state of emergency and mass dismissals and arrests. A 2017 referendum changed Turkey from a parliamentary to an executive presidential system, which concentrates considerable power in the presidency.
summary.art: Turkish arts include Iznik tilework, carpet and kilim weaving, the paper marbling called ebru, calligraphy and Ottoman miniature painting, with Mimar Sinan as the great architect of the classical Ottoman age. Music ranges from Ottoman classical and Sufi music with the ney, and the Mevlevi whirling ceremony inspired by Rumi, to the folk songs of wandering minstrels (aşık) such as Yunus Emre's mystic verse and Aşık Veysel. In modern times Nazım Hikmet, Yaşar Kemal and Nobel laureate Orhan Pamuk have shaped Turkish literature.
summary.monuments: The historic areas of Istanbul — with Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapı Palace and the Süleymaniye Mosque — are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are Göreme and the rock churches of Cappadocia and the Roman city of Ephesus. Göbekli Tepe, the oldest known monumental site, and the travertine terraces of Pamukkale with ancient Hierapolis are also inscribed. Nemrut Dağ's giant stone heads and Ani, the ruined medieval Armenian capital on the border, speak of the many peoples who have shaped Anatolia.

name: Turkmenistan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Kazakh and Balochi

people: Turkmen make up around 85% of the population, organised historically in tribes such as the Teke, Yomut and Ersari, with Uzbek, Russian, Kazakh and Baloch minorities. Most people are Sunni Muslim, with a small Russian Orthodox community, and religious life is closely controlled by the state. About half live in towns, while many others live in oases along the Amu Darya and the Karakum Canal; independent estimates suggest significant emigration, so the official population figure is uncertain.
resources: Some of the world's largest natural gas reserves, including the Galkynysh field
Cotton and wheat grown in irrigated oases
Akhal-Teke horses, a celebrated ancient breed
Hand-knotted carpets of world renown
Silk Road heritage at Merv, Nisa and Kunya-Urgench
A Caspian coastline and the Karakum Desert
struggles: One of the most closed political systems in the world, with almost no free media, opposition or civil society
Dependence on gas exports to a few buyers
Shortages and high prices of basic goods for many families, and emigration in search of work
Water scarcity, the legacy of the Aral Sea crisis and inefficient irrigation
Methane leaks and environmental strain from the gas industry
prayFor: For families who struggle to find affordable food and work, and for those who have left to work abroad
For freedom to speak, believe and gather without fear, and for the release of those imprisoned unjustly
For wise use of water and land, and healing for communities affected by the Aral Sea disaster
For young Turkmen, that their gifts would find room to grow
For openness and friendship between Turkmenistan and the wider world

summary.history: The oases of present-day Turkmenistan hosted some of Central Asia's earliest farming settlements and the Bronze Age culture of Margiana, later becoming part of the Persian, Parthian and Silk Road worlds, with Nisa an early Parthian capital. Merv grew into one of the largest cities on earth under the Seljuks in the 12th century, before being destroyed by the Mongols in 1221. Turkic Oghuz tribes, ancestors of the Turkmen, settled the region from the 10th century and lived for centuries as semi-nomadic herders and horsemen between the khanates of Khiva and Bukhara and Persia. The Russian Empire conquered the region in the 1880s, notably at the Battle of Geok Tepe in 1881, where thousands of Turkmen were killed, and Soviet rule later brought collectivisation and the cotton monoculture that drained the Aral Sea.
summary.politicalHistory: The Turkmen SSR was formed in 1924 and declared independence in 1991 under Saparmurat Niyazov, the former Communist Party leader, who established a one-party state and an extreme personality cult as 'Turkmenbashi', father of the Turkmen. After his death in 2006, power passed to a successor within the same system, and in 2022 to that successor's son, through elections that international observers did not consider free or competitive. Turkmenistan declares a policy of permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995.
summary.art: Turkmen carpets, with their deep red tones and distinctive gül medallions, are among the finest in the world, and carpet-weaving is a matter of national pride. The Turkmen bagshy tradition of epic song with the two-stringed dutar and the kushtdepdi ritual dance are recognised by UNESCO, as are the epic of Gorogly and the art of Akhal-Teke horse breeding. The 18th-century poet Magtymguly Pyragy is revered as the father of Turkmen literature.
summary.monuments: Ancient Merv, a vast site of successive oasis cities including the Mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the Parthian fortresses of Nisa and the medieval minarets and mausoleums of Kunya-Urgench. The Darvaza gas crater, burning in the Karakum Desert since the Soviet era, has become a striking landmark. Ashgabat, rebuilt after the 1948 earthquake that killed tens of thousands, is now known for its white marble buildings.

name: United Arab Emirates

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), mostly immigrant languages such as Hindi, Urdu, Malayalam, Bengali, Tagalog and Persian

people: Emirati citizens make up only around one in nine residents; the rest come from nearly 200 countries, above all India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Egypt and Europe. Emiratis are Muslim, mostly Sunni, while residents practise Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism and other faiths, with churches, temples and the Abrahamic Family House in Abu Dhabi. Nearly all live in cities, especially Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah.
resources: Large oil and gas reserves, chiefly in Abu Dhabi
Some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds
Global hubs for aviation, shipping, trade and finance in Dubai and Abu Dhabi
Major investment in solar and nuclear energy
A diverse, international workforce
Desert, mangroves, mountains and coast drawing tourism
struggles: Rights and conditions of migrant and domestic workers, who make up most of the workforce
Extreme heat, water scarcity and heavy reliance on desalination
One of the world's highest carbon footprints per person
Restrictions on free expression, peaceful dissent and independent civil society
Involvement in regional conflicts, including the war in Yemen, and the civilian harm they cause
Rare but severe flooding, such as the record rainfall of April 2024
prayFor: For migrant workers and their families far away, that they would be paid fairly, treated kindly and kept safe
For those detained for their words or beliefs, and for their families
For wisdom in caring for water, desert, sea and climate, for the sake of future generations
For peace in the conflicts in which the region is entangled, and for every civilian caught in them
For harmony and genuine friendship among the many nations and faiths living side by side

summary.history: The land of the Emirates was settled thousands of years ago, with Bronze Age tombs at Hafit and Umm an-Nar and oasis settlements at Al Ain sustained by falaj irrigation. Arab tribes adopted Islam in the 7th century, and coastal towns lived from pearling, fishing, seafaring and trade, while Bedouin herded in the desert. In the 19th century Britain signed truces with local sheikhdoms, which became known as the Trucial States, and controlled their foreign affairs. After the pearl trade collapsed in the 1930s came hardship, until oil was discovered in Abu Dhabi in 1958, transforming the region within a generation.
summary.politicalHistory: When Britain withdrew in 1971, six emirates formed the United Arab Emirates under Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, and Ras al-Khaimah joined in 1972. The UAE is a federation of seven hereditary monarchies, in which the rulers form the Federal Supreme Council that elects the president and vice-president. The Federal National Council is an advisory body, half of whose members are chosen by a limited electorate, and political parties are not permitted.
summary.art: Emirati heritage includes Al Sadu weaving, Al Talli embroidery, falconry and the Al Ayyala and Al Razfa performances of chanting and swaying lines of men, all recognised by UNESCO. Nabati poetry, recited and composed widely, holds a central place in national culture. In recent decades the UAE has become a regional art hub, with Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Sharjah Biennial and Art Dubai showing artists from across the Arab world and beyond.
summary.monuments: The cultural sites of Al Ain — the oases, Hili, Bidaa Bint Saud and the Hafit tombs — are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi and the historic Al Fahidi district and creek of Dubai preserve religious and trading heritage, while the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, symbolises the country's rapid growth. Louvre Abu Dhabi, under its great latticed dome, presents art from many civilisations side by side.

name: Uzbekistan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Kazakh, Tatar and Korean

people: Uzbeks make up over 80% of the population, with Tajiks, Kazakhs, Karakalpaks, Russians, Tatars, Koreans and others; Karakalpakstan in the northwest is an autonomous republic. Around nine in ten are Sunni Muslim, with a Russian Orthodox minority and small Jewish communities, notably the historic Bukharan Jews. About half live in cities, and the population is young and growing, with millions working abroad, especially in Russia.
resources: Natural gas, gold, uranium and copper
Cotton, fruit, vegetables and silk from irrigated valleys
Silk Road cities — Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva — of world importance
A large, young and increasingly educated workforce
Fertile Fergana Valley
Traditions of hospitality, crafts and cuisine
struggles: The Aral Sea disaster, which has left Karakalpakstan with dust storms, salinity and health problems
Water scarcity and inefficient irrigation inherited from the Soviet cotton economy
Unemployment and dependence on labour migration abroad
Limits on political competition, independent media and civil society despite reforms
Tensions in Karakalpakstan following the deadly unrest of July 2022
The legacy of forced labour in cotton fields, largely ended only in recent years
prayFor: For the people of Karakalpakstan and the Aral Sea region, that land, water and health would be restored
For labour migrants and the families they leave behind, that they would be protected and reunited
For freedom and justice for all who speak and believe according to conscience
For young Uzbeks seeking work and purpose, that reforms would open real opportunities
For friendship and shared care of water among all the nations of Central Asia

summary.history: Uzbekistan's oases between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya were the heart of ancient Sogdiana, Khwarazm and Bactria, crossed by Alexander the Great and enriched by Silk Road trade. After the Arab conquest in the 8th century the region became a centre of Islamic learning, home to scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, al-Biruni, Avicenna and al-Bukhari. Devastated by the Mongols in 1220, it rose again under Timur (Tamerlane), who made Samarkand the capital of a vast empire in the 14th century, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built a famous observatory. The khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand ruled until the Russian conquest of the 19th century, and Soviet rule brought collectivisation, purges and a cotton monoculture that drained the Aral Sea.
summary.politicalHistory: The Uzbek SSR was created in 1924 and declared independence in 1991 under Islam Karimov, who ruled until his death in 2016 through a highly authoritarian system, including the violent suppression of protests in Andijan in 2005 in which hundreds were killed. Since 2016 the government has pursued economic opening and some reforms, including ending systemic forced labour in the cotton harvest. A 2023 constitutional referendum extended presidential terms to seven years, and the presidency remains the dominant institution, with no genuine opposition parties in parliament.
summary.art: Uzbekistan is famed for ikat silk and adras weaving, suzani embroidery, blue-glazed ceramics from Rishtan and Gijduvan, and the tilework and carved wood of its monuments. Shashmaqom classical music, shared with Tajikistan, and the Bakhshi epic singers are recognised by UNESCO. Its literary heritage includes Alisher Navoi, the 15th-century founder of Chagatai Turkic literature, and Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, whose memoir the Baburnama is a classic.
summary.monuments: Samarkand — with the Registan, Bibi-Khanym Mosque, the Gur-e Amir tomb of Timur and the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the historic centres of Bukhara and Shakhrisabz and Itchan Kala, the walled inner town of Khiva. Bukhara's Kalyan Minaret, spared by Genghis Khan, and the Ark fortress recall its long history as a centre of learning. The ruins of Khwarazmian desert fortresses in Karakalpakstan and the ship graveyard at Moynaq, on the former shore of the Aral Sea, tell stories of glory and loss.

name: Yemen
capital: Sana'a (constitutional capital; the recognised government operates from Aden)

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Modern South Arabian languages such as Mehri and Soqotri

people: Yemenis are mostly Arab, with deep tribal and regional identities, as well as Muhammasheen communities of African descent who face discrimination, and speakers of ancient South Arabian languages on Socotra and in the east. Nearly all are Muslim — a Sunni majority mainly of the Shafi'i school, and a large Zaydi Shia community in the north — while the ancient Jewish community has almost entirely emigrated. About two-thirds live in rural areas and highland villages, and the population is very young.
resources: Mocha coffee, grown on terraced highlands for centuries
Oil and liquefied natural gas
Fisheries of the Red Sea and Arabian Sea
Sidr honey, among the most prized in the world
Socotra's unique wildlife and dragon's blood trees
Ancient architecture and a deep culture of poetry and hospitality
struggles: A war since 2014–15 that has killed hundreds of thousands of people through fighting, hunger and disease
One of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with most of the population needing aid and widespread malnutrition
A country divided between the Houthi movement in the north, the internationally recognised government and southern separatist forces
Civilian harm from airstrikes by the Saudi-led coalition, from shelling and landmines, and from attacks by all parties
Collapse of public salaries, health care, a divided currency and outbreaks of cholera
Severe water depletion and the escalating Red Sea crisis since late 2023, with attacks on shipping and retaliatory strikes
prayFor: For children suffering from hunger and disease, that they would be fed, healed and able to go to school
For a just and lasting peace among all Yemenis and their neighbours, and for those negotiating it
For the injured, the bereaved and those detained, and for the release of all held unjustly
For aid workers, doctors and teachers who keep serving without pay or in danger
For water, rain and restored farms, and for the safety of fishermen and seafarers

summary.history: Yemen was the 'Arabia Felix' of the ancients, home to the kingdoms of Saba (Sheba), Ma'in, Qataban and Himyar, which grew rich on frankincense and myrrh and built the great dam of Marib. Islam came in the 7th century, and from the 9th century Zaydi imams ruled much of the northern highlands for over a thousand years, while the port of Mocha later gave its name to the world's coffee trade. The Ottomans controlled the north at intervals, and Britain held Aden from 1839, shaping a lasting division between north and south. After decades of war and division in the 20th century, the country unified in 1990, but since 2014 it has been engulfed in a devastating war and humanitarian crisis.
summary.politicalHistory: North Yemen's imamate was overthrown in a 1962 revolution, leading to a civil war and the Yemen Arab Republic, while South Yemen gained independence from Britain in 1967 and became the Marxist People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. The two unified as the Republic of Yemen in 1990 under Ali Abdullah Saleh, and a southern secession attempt was defeated in 1994. After Arab Spring protests in 2011 led to a negotiated transition, the Houthi movement seized Sana'a in 2014, and in 2015 a Saudi-led coalition intervened in support of the recognised government; since then rival authorities have governed different regions, with a UN-mediated truce in 2022 reducing but not ending the fighting.
summary.art: Yemen is renowned for its tower houses of mud brick and stone decorated with white gypsum, for the curved jambiya dagger and silverwork, and for Sana'ani song, a classical poetic music tradition recognised by UNESCO and played on the qanbus lute. Poetry is central to life, from tribal zamil chants to the work of 20th-century poet Abdullah al-Baradouni. Yemeni writers and artists, at home and in the diaspora, continue to create amid war.
summary.monuments: The Old City of Sana'a, with its multistorey tower houses, the walled 'Manhattan of the desert' of Shibam, and the historic town of Zabid are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, all now listed as in danger. The Socotra Archipelago is inscribed for its extraordinary biodiversity, much of it found nowhere else on earth. The landmarks of the ancient Kingdom of Saba around Marib, including its temples and the remains of the great dam, were added to the list in 2023.

name: Bangladesh

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Bengali is spoken by almost everyone, alongside Chittagonian, Sylheti and the languages of Indigenous peoples such as the Chakma, Marma and Garo

people: One of the most densely populated countries on earth, Bangladesh is home overwhelmingly to Bengali people, with Indigenous communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the north, and around a million Rohingya refugees sheltering near Cox's Bazar. About nine in ten people are Muslim and roughly 8% Hindu, with small Buddhist and Christian communities. Most still live in villages across the river delta, yet Dhaka is one of the world's fastest-growing megacities, and millions of Bangladeshis work abroad in the Gulf, Malaysia and the UK.
resources: The fertile Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta, with its rice, jute and fish
A vast, young and resilient workforce
The ready-made garment industry, one of the world's largest
Remittances from millions of workers abroad
Natural gas reserves
The Sundarbans mangrove forest and a rich Bengali literary heritage
struggles: Extreme exposure to cyclones, floods, river erosion and sea-level rise
Low wages and unsafe conditions for many garment workers, remembered in the Rana Plaza collapse of 2013
Deep political polarisation, contested elections and limits on free expression
Hosting around a million Rohingya refugees with no safe return in sight
Air pollution, overcrowding and congestion in Dhaka
Child marriage and unequal opportunities for girls and women
prayFor: For families on the delta's edge whose homes and fields are threatened by floods, cyclones and rising water
For garment workers, that their labour would be safe, fairly paid and honoured
For the Rohingya refugees in the camps and the host communities around them — for dignity, safety and a future
For a peaceful and just public life in which every voice can be heard without fear
For girls and young women, that they may learn, choose and flourish

summary.history: The Bengal delta has sustained rice-growing communities for millennia and was shaped by Buddhist kingdoms such as the Pala dynasty, then Hindu and Muslim dynasties, the Bengal Sultanate and the Mughal Empire. From the 18th century it fell under the British East India Company and then the British Raj, and the Bengal famine of 1943 killed millions. At Partition in 1947 the Muslim-majority east became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by India. In 1971 a war of independence followed a brutal military crackdown, with mass killings, widespread sexual violence and some ten million refugees fleeing to India. Since then the nation has rebuilt from deep poverty to become a major garment exporter, with striking gains in health and life expectancy.
summary.politicalHistory: The Bengali Language Movement of 1952 and growing demands for autonomy led to the declaration of independence in March 1971; with Indian intervention, Bangladesh became independent in December 1971 under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who was assassinated in 1975. Years of military-led rule followed under Ziaur Rahman and then H. M. Ershad, until a popular uprising restored parliamentary democracy in 1991. Since then power has alternated between, and been fiercely contested by, the Awami League and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, with periods of emergency rule and disputed or boycotted elections. It is a parliamentary republic with a prime minister as head of government.
summary.art: Bengali culture prizes poetry and song: Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem, and Kazi Nazrul Islam is honoured as the national poet. The mystical Baul minstrels, of whom Lalon Fakir is the most beloved, carry a tradition recognised by UNESCO, and hand-loomed Jamdani muslin is famed for its fineness. Nakshi kantha embroidered quilts, rickshaw painting and the colourful Pohela Boishakh new-year procession show an art that lives in everyday life.
summary.monuments: The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest and home of the Bengal tiger, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat, with its 15th-century Sixty Dome Mosque, and the ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur are also on the UNESCO list. The National Martyrs' Memorial at Savar and the Shaheed Minar in Dhaka, honouring those killed in the 1952 Language Movement, are places of shared memory and mourning.

name: Bhutan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English is the language of schooling and widely spoken

people: Bhutan's people include the Ngalop of the west, the Sharchop of the east and the Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa of the south, along with smaller Himalayan communities. Around three quarters are Vajrayana Buddhists, most of the rest Hindu, with a small Christian minority. Most people still live in farming villages in steep valleys, though Thimphu is growing fast and many young Bhutanese have recently moved abroad, especially to Australia, for study and work.

basics.roman: la (polite particle added to a request)

resources: Fast-flowing Himalayan rivers and hydropower exported to India
Forest cover of around 70% and a carbon-negative landscape
A living Buddhist culture of dzongs, monasteries and festivals
High-value, low-volume tourism
The guiding vision of Gross National Happiness
Free public healthcare and education
struggles: Large-scale emigration of young, educated Bhutanese and the strain it leaves behind
Youth unemployment and an economy heavily reliant on hydropower
Glacial lake outburst floods and climate change in the high mountains
Isolation of remote villages and the difficulty of mountain farming
The unresolved legacy of the 1990s expulsion and flight of many Lhotshampa, many of whom lived for decades in refugee camps in Nepal
prayFor: For young Bhutanese, that they find meaningful work and belonging, whether at home or abroad
For families separated by migration, and for the elders and villages left behind
For mountain communities facing floods, landslides and melting glaciers
For healing and justice for the Lhotshampa who were displaced, and for all who still carry that wound
For wisdom in pursuing a happiness that includes every person

summary.history: The Himalayan valleys of Bhutan were settled long ago, and Buddhism took root from around the 7th–8th centuries, associated with the sage Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). In the 17th century the Tibetan lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified the valleys under a dual religious and civil system and built the great dzongs. After internal strife and a war with British India in the 1860s, the country remained independent but closely tied first to Britain and then to India. In the late 1980s and 1990s, citizenship and cultural-unity policies led to unrest in the south and the departure of over 100,000 Lhotshampa to camps in Nepal, many later resettled in the West. Bhutan opened cautiously to the world from the 1960s, admitting television and the internet only in 1999.
summary.politicalHistory: In 1907 Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as the first hereditary king, founding the Wangchuck dynasty. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, abolished serfdom and created a national assembly, and the fourth, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, introduced the idea of Gross National Happiness and voluntarily began the move to democracy. The first parliamentary elections were held in 2008 under a new constitution. Bhutan is today a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and prime minister.
summary.art: Bhutanese art is devotional: thangka scroll paintings, monumental appliqué thongdrel banners and painted woodwork fill temples and homes. Masked cham dances at tshechu festivals retell Buddhist teachings, and the traditional thirteen arts (zorig chusum) include weaving, sculpture, calligraphy and woodcarving. Intricate hand-woven textiles, especially the women's kira and men's gho, remain everyday dress.
summary.monuments: Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery clinging to a cliff, marks where Guru Rinpoche is said to have meditated. Punakha Dzong at the meeting of two rivers and Trongsa Dzong are masterpieces of fortress-monastery architecture and centres of religious and civic life. Kyichu Lhakhang, one of the oldest temples, and Jigme Dorji National Park show the bond between faith and wild nature.

name: Brunei

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Brunei Malay, Kedayan, Dusun, Iban and Chinese varieties

people: Brunei's people are mostly Malay, alongside a substantial Chinese community, Indigenous peoples such as the Dusun, Murut and Iban, and many migrant workers from South and Southeast Asia. Islam is the state religion and around four in five people are Muslim, with Buddhist, Christian and traditional-faith minorities. Most live in the urbanised coastal districts, and the Kampong Ayer water village remains a cherished way of life.
resources: Offshore oil and natural gas
Intact Bornean rainforest, including Ulu Temburong
Sovereign wealth built up from energy exports
Free healthcare and education for citizens
A strong Malay Islamic cultural heritage
A peaceful, close-knit society
struggles: Heavy dependence on oil and gas and the challenge of diversifying
Limited jobs for young graduates outside the public sector
Restrictions on political participation, religious freedom and expression
Vulnerable conditions for some migrant workers
Rising rates of lifestyle-related illness
prayFor: For a future that does not depend on oil, with good work for the young
For migrant workers far from home, that they be treated with fairness and kindness
For freedom of conscience and the flourishing of every faith community
For the protection of Borneo's rainforests and those who live from them

summary.history: Brunei was a trading port on Borneo's north coast and, by the 15th–16th centuries, a powerful sultanate whose influence reached across Borneo and into the southern Philippines. Its territory then shrank under pressure from European powers and the Sarawak 'White Rajahs'. It became a British protectorate in 1888, and oil was discovered at Seria in 1929, transforming the economy. Japan occupied it during the Second World War. Brunei declined to join Malaysia in 1963 and became fully independent in 1984.
summary.politicalHistory: Under British protection the sultanate kept its monarchy, and a 1959 constitution gave it internal self-government. After the Brunei Revolt of 1962, led by the Brunei People's Party following its election victory, a state of emergency was declared and has remained in force since. Independence came on 1 January 1984. Brunei is an absolute monarchy in which the sultan is head of state and of government, guided by the national philosophy of Melayu Islam Beraja (Malay Islamic Monarchy).
summary.art: Brunei's crafts include fine brassware and bronze cannon-casting, silverwork, and the gold-threaded woven cloth known as kain tenunan. Traditional music features the gulingtangan gong ensemble and the adai-adai work songs of fishermen. Islamic calligraphy and mosque architecture are central to the nation's visual culture.
summary.monuments: The Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque, with its golden dome rising above a lagoon, is the country's best-known landmark. Kampong Ayer, a centuries-old village of houses on stilts over the Brunei River, preserves a distinctive way of life. The Jame' Asr Hassanil Bolkiah Mosque, the Royal Regalia Museum and Ulu Temburong National Park show Brunei's faith, monarchy and rainforest.

name: Cambodia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Cham, Vietnamese, Chinese varieties and the languages of upland Indigenous peoples

people: Around nine in ten Cambodians are ethnic Khmer, alongside Muslim Cham, Vietnamese and Chinese-descended communities and Indigenous upland peoples in the northeast. Theravada Buddhism is the faith of roughly 95%, with Muslim and Christian minorities. Most people live in rural rice-farming villages, and it is a young country: a large share of the population was born long after the Khmer Rouge era.
resources: The Mekong River and Tonlé Sap lake, one of the world's richest inland fisheries
Fertile rice lands
The Angkorian heritage that draws visitors from around the world
A young, hardworking population
A garment and footwear export industry
Forests and coastline of great biodiversity
struggles: The long shadow of the Khmer Rouge genocide on families and memory
Restrictions on political opposition, independent media and civil society
Land grabs, deforestation and evictions affecting rural and Indigenous communities
Heavy household microfinance debt
Landmines and unexploded ordnance still left in the countryside
Exploitation through scam compounds and human trafficking
prayFor: For healing for survivors of the Khmer Rouge years and their children and grandchildren
For farming and Indigenous families, that their land and forests be protected
For young Cambodians, for good education and work with dignity
For those trapped or trafficked in scam operations, for freedom and restoration
For honest, open public life where people can speak freely

summary.history: The Khmer Empire, centred on Angkor from the 9th to 15th centuries, was one of the great civilisations of Southeast Asia, building vast temples and waterworks. After its decline Cambodia was squeezed between Siam and Vietnam until it became a French protectorate in 1863. Independence in 1953 was followed by the spillover of the Vietnam War, including heavy US bombing. From 1975 to 1979 the Khmer Rouge emptied the cities and an estimated 1.5–2 million people died from execution, forced labour, starvation and disease. A Vietnamese invasion ended that regime, and years of conflict gave way to UN-supported peace in the early 1990s and later rapid economic growth.
summary.politicalHistory: Under King Norodom Sihanouk Cambodia won independence from France in 1953, and he dominated politics until a 1970 coup established Lon Nol's Khmer Republic. The Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot ruled 'Democratic Kampuchea' from 1975 until 1979, when Vietnamese forces installed the People's Republic of Kampuchea. The 1991 Paris Peace Accords led to UN-run elections in 1993 and the restoration of the monarchy. Cambodia is formally a constitutional monarchy with multiparty elections, though one party, the Cambodian People's Party, has dominated for decades and the main opposition was dissolved in 2017.
summary.art: Khmer classical dance, the Royal Ballet of Cambodia, is recognised by UNESCO and echoes the apsaras carved at Angkor. Sbek thom shadow puppetry, pinpeat ensemble music and the Reamker, the Khmer version of the Ramayana, carry ancient stories. Cambodian rock of the 1960s, with singers such as Sinn Sisamouth and Ros Serey Sothea, has been lovingly rediscovered after many artists were killed by the Khmer Rouge.
summary.monuments: Angkor, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, includes Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, and the Bayon with its serene stone faces. The temples of Preah Vihear and Sambor Prei Kuk are also UNESCO-listed and testify to the depth of Khmer civilisation. In Phnom Penh, the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum and the Choeung Ek killing fields preserve the memory of those who died under the Khmer Rouge.

name: China

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Chinese varieties and the languages of minority peoples such as Uyghur, Tibetan, Zhuang and Mongolian

people: Over 90% of China's people are Han Chinese, and the state recognises 55 other ethnic groups, including the Zhuang, Hui, Manchu, Uyghur, Tibetans and Mongols. Many people are not religiously affiliated, while Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, Taoism, Christianity and Islam are all practised, often within close state oversight. About two thirds now live in cities after the largest rural-to-urban migration in history, and Chinese diaspora communities are found worldwide.
resources: One of the world's oldest continuous civilisations and its written heritage
A vast, skilled and industrious workforce
World-leading manufacturing, infrastructure and renewable-energy industries
Rare earths, coal and other mineral resources
Great rivers, the Yangtze and Yellow River, and immense landscape diversity
Rich culinary, philosophical and artistic traditions
struggles: A rapidly ageing population and falling birth rate
Youth unemployment and a strained property sector
Air and water pollution and heavy carbon emissions, despite major clean-energy investment
Tight limits on speech, religion and civil society, with serious concerns about the treatment of Uyghurs in Xinjiang and of Tibetans
Rural–urban inequality and the separation of migrant workers from their children
Tensions across the Taiwan Strait and in the South China Sea
prayFor: For elderly people and for families carrying the care of parents and grandparents
For young people seeking work, purpose and hope
For freedom of conscience for believers of every faith and for those who are detained or silenced
For Uyghur, Tibetan and other minority communities, for dignity, safety and the freedom to live their culture
For peace across the Taiwan Strait and in the region, and for wisdom among all who lead

summary.history: Chinese civilisation grew along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, and in 221 BCE the Qin unified the land, beginning over two thousand years of imperial dynasties such as the Han, Tang, Song, Ming and Qing. Chinese inventions, philosophy and trade shaped much of Asia. From the 19th century the Qing suffered the Opium Wars, unequal treaties and the devastating Taiping Rebellion, and Japan's invasion from the 1930s caused immense suffering. After the communist victory in the civil war in 1949, the Great Leap Forward famine (1959–61) killed tens of millions and the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) brought persecution and turmoil. From 1978 market reforms lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and made China a global economic power.
summary.politicalHistory: The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended the Qing dynasty and founded the Republic of China, led for a time by Sun Yat-sen and later by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, amid warlordism and civil war with the Communists. In 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing, while the Republic of China government relocated to Taiwan; both sides long claimed to represent all of China, and the PRC continues to regard Taiwan as part of its territory, a claim Taiwan's government does not accept. After Mao's death, Deng Xiaoping launched reform and opening, and the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests were suppressed by the military. The PRC is a one-party state led by the Chinese Communist Party, with the National People's Congress as its legislature and the Party's general secretary as paramount leader.
summary.art: Calligraphy, ink-wash landscape painting and poetry, with masters such as Wang Xizhi, Li Bai and Du Fu, form a treasured classical triad. Porcelain, silk, jade carving and lacquerware were admired across the world, and Peking opera and Kunqu combine music, drama and acrobatics. Great novels such as Dream of the Red Chamber and Journey to the West remain beloved, and modern writers and filmmakers continue these traditions.
summary.monuments: The Great Wall, stretching across northern China, and the Forbidden City in Beijing, seat of Ming and Qing emperors, are among the world's most famous UNESCO sites. The Terracotta Army of the first Qin emperor near Xi'an and the Buddhist Mogao Caves at Dunhuang reveal ancient imperial power and Silk Road faith. The Potala Palace in Lhasa, the West Lake of Hangzhou and the karst landscapes of Guilin show the country's spiritual and natural breadth.

name: Indonesia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), the second-highest of any country, with especially great diversity in Papua

people: Spread across more than 17,000 islands, Indonesians belong to hundreds of ethnic groups, the largest being the Javanese and Sundanese, alongside Malay, Batak, Madurese, Minangkabau, Bugis, Balinese, Dayak, Papuan and Chinese-Indonesian communities. Around 87% are Muslim, making it the world's largest Muslim-majority nation, with about 10% Christian and Hindu-majority Bali, plus Buddhist and Confucian minorities. More than half live in cities, above all on densely populated Java.
resources: Extraordinary biodiversity in rainforests and coral reefs of the Coral Triangle
Nickel, coal, palm oil, tin and other natural resources
A large, young population and growing domestic economy
Hundreds of cultures united by a shared national language
Volcanic soils that feed rice terraces and spice gardens
A tradition of mutual help known as gotong royong
struggles: Deforestation and peatland fires linked to palm oil, mining and logging
Earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions and floods, and Jakarta's land subsidence
Inequality between Java and outer islands, and poverty in eastern regions
Long-running conflict and human-rights concerns in Papua
Corruption and pressures on religious minorities and tolerance
Plastic pollution in rivers and seas
prayFor: For communities living with the threat of earthquakes, eruptions and floods, for safety and swift help
For the forests, reefs and the Indigenous and rural peoples who depend on them
For peace and justice in Papua and for all who suffer in that conflict
For harmony among people of different faiths and cultures
For the poor in cities and remote islands, for fair opportunity and dignity

summary.history: The islands were home to some of the world's earliest human ancestors and later to seafaring Austronesian peoples. Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit grew rich from maritime trade, and Islam spread peacefully along trade routes from the 13th century onward. Drawn by spices, the Dutch East India Company and then the Dutch state colonised the archipelago over three centuries, with forced cultivation and harsh exploitation. Japan occupied the islands during the Second World War, and after independence was declared in 1945 a bitter war against the Dutch followed. In 1965–66 mass killings of hundreds of thousands of suspected communists marked a deep and still painful chapter.
summary.politicalHistory: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945, which the Netherlands recognised in 1949 after armed struggle and diplomacy. Sukarno's 'Guided Democracy' gave way after 1965–66 to Suharto's military-backed New Order, which ruled for over three decades and annexed East Timor in 1975. The 1997–98 Asian financial crisis and mass protests forced Suharto's resignation in 1998, opening the Reformasi era of democratisation and decentralisation. Indonesia is now a presidential republic with direct elections, and one of the world's largest democracies.
summary.art: Javanese and Balinese gamelan orchestras, wayang kulit shadow puppetry and batik textiles are all recognised by UNESCO as part of humanity's heritage. Classical dance from Bali and the Javanese courts, keris daggers and the ikat weaving of Sumba and Flores show remarkable craft. Modern literature was shaped by writers such as Pramoedya Ananta Toer, whose Buru Quartet was written in political imprisonment.
summary.monuments: Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple, and the Hindu temple complex of Prambanan in Central Java are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Bali's subak irrigation landscape of rice terraces and water temples reflects a philosophy of harmony between people, nature and the divine. Komodo National Park and the rainforests of Sumatra protect unique wildlife, while the Toraja highlands of Sulawesi preserve striking traditional architecture.

name: Laos

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Hmong, Khmu and many other minority languages

people: Laos is home to around 50 officially recognised ethnic groups: the Lao and related Tai peoples of the lowlands, the Khmu and other Mon-Khmer peoples of the hills, and Hmong, Mien and Tibeto-Burman peoples of the mountains. Most lowland Lao practise Theravada Buddhism, often alongside spirit beliefs, while many upland peoples follow ancestral traditions, and there is a small Christian minority. Most people live in rural villages, and a large diaspora lives in Thailand, the United States, France and Australia.
resources: The Mekong River and its fisheries
Hydropower potential from mountain rivers
Forests and rich biodiversity
Copper, gold and other minerals
Gentle Buddhist culture and community life
Diverse ethnic traditions of weaving and music
struggles: Heavy public debt and high inflation that have eroded household incomes
Unexploded ordnance from the Vietnam War era still killing and injuring people
Child malnutrition and poverty in remote upland areas
Dams and land concessions affecting rivers, fisheries and villages
Limited freedom of expression and civil society
Human trafficking and exploitation in special economic zones
prayFor: For families in the countryside who still live and farm among unexploded bombs, and for those clearing them
For children in remote villages, for food, health and schooling
For households struggling with rising prices and debt
For the Mekong and the communities who depend on its waters
For freedom, honesty and care in public life

summary.history: In 1353 Fa Ngum founded the kingdom of Lan Xang, the 'Land of a Million Elephants', which became a centre of Theravada Buddhism. After it split into rival kingdoms in the 18th century, much of the land came under Siamese domination, and Vientiane was sacked in 1827. France made Laos part of French Indochina in 1893. During the Vietnam War Laos was drawn into a 'secret war', and between 1964 and 1973 the United States dropped over two million tonnes of bombs, making it per person the most heavily bombed country in history. After 1975 tens of thousands fled, including many Hmong who had fought alongside the US, and others were sent to re-education camps.
summary.politicalHistory: Laos gained independence from France within the French Union in 1949 and full sovereignty in 1953 as the Kingdom of Laos. A long civil war followed between the royal government and the communist Pathet Lao, backed respectively by the United States and North Vietnam. In 1975 the Pathet Lao took power, abolished the monarchy and declared the Lao People's Democratic Republic. Laos remains a one-party socialist state led by the Lao People's Revolutionary Party, which since the late 1980s has opened the economy to the market.
summary.art: Lao music centres on the khaen, a bamboo mouth organ recognised by UNESCO, and the sung poetry of lam. Women's hand-woven silk sinh skirts, with motifs such as nagas, are among Southeast Asia's finest textiles. Temple architecture with sweeping layered roofs, gilded carving and Buddha images shows a deeply Buddhist aesthetic.
summary.monuments: The town of Luang Prabang, with its temples, colonial houses and dawn alms-giving, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Vat Phou, a Khmer-era temple complex in Champasak, and the mysterious Plain of Jars in Xiangkhouang are also UNESCO-listed. Pha That Luang in Vientiane, a golden stupa, is the national symbol.

name: Malaysia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. many Indigenous languages of Sabah and Sarawak

people: Malaysians include Malays and other Bumiputera peoples — among them the Iban, Kadazan-Dusun and the Orang Asli — together making up about seven in ten, along with large Chinese and Indian communities. Islam is the official religion and about 64% are Muslim, with Buddhist, Christian, Hindu and Chinese folk-religion communities. Around four in five people live in towns and cities, and the country hosts millions of migrant workers.
resources: Some of the world's oldest rainforests in Borneo and the peninsula
Oil, natural gas and palm oil
A strong electronics and semiconductor industry
A multicultural society and renowned shared food culture
Strategic position on the Strait of Malacca
Coral islands and marine biodiversity
struggles: Deforestation and the impact of plantations on Indigenous lands and wildlife
Ethnic and religious tensions and debates over race-based policies
Corruption, highlighted by the 1MDB scandal
Exploitation and poor conditions for some migrant workers and refugees
Rising cost of living and household debt
Seasonal flooding and haze from forest fires
prayFor: For unity and mutual respect among Malays, Chinese, Indians and Indigenous peoples
For Orang Asli and the Indigenous peoples of Borneo, that their lands and voices be honoured
For migrant workers and refugees, for fair treatment and safety
For integrity and justice in public life
For the protection of forests and the creatures who live in them

summary.history: The Malay peninsula and northern Borneo were home to ancient Indigenous peoples and to trading kingdoms linked to Srivijaya and India. The Malacca Sultanate of the 15th century became a great Islamic trading port before falling to the Portuguese in 1511, then to the Dutch, and later the British. British colonial rule brought tin mining and rubber plantations and the migration of many Chinese and Indian labourers. Japan occupied the territory in the Second World War, and a communist insurgency known as the Malayan Emergency followed from 1948 to 1960. Sabah and Sarawak joined in 1963, and race riots in 1969 led to policies aimed at improving the economic position of the Bumiputera.
summary.politicalHistory: The Federation of Malaya became independent from Britain on 31 August 1957 under Tunku Abdul Rahman. In 1963 it joined with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia, and Singapore left in 1965. The Barisan Nasional coalition governed continuously until its first electoral defeat in 2018, after which politics became more fragmented with shifting coalitions. Malaysia is a federal constitutional monarchy whose king is chosen in rotation among the nine Malay state rulers, with a parliamentary system led by a prime minister.
summary.art: Malaysian crafts include batik and the gold-threaded songket textile, intricate wood carving and keris making. Performing arts range from wayang kulit and mak yong dance-theatre, recognised by UNESCO, to the dikir barat chorus and Chinese and Indian festival traditions. The Pua Kumbu ceremonial textiles of the Iban and the novels of writers such as Tash Aw and the national laureate A. Samad Said show the country's many voices.
summary.monuments: The historic cities of Melaka and George Town on the Straits of Malacca are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, reflecting centuries of Malay, Chinese, Indian and European exchange. Kinabalu Park and Gunung Mulu National Park in Borneo protect extraordinary biodiversity and vast caves. The Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur and the Batu Caves Hindu temple are modern and devotional landmarks.

name: Maldives

languages.note: ≈ Dhivehi is the national language and English is widely used; many migrant workers speak Bengali, Hindi, Sinhala and other languages

people: Maldivians are a single island people with roots in South Asian, Arab and East African seafaring, sharing the Dhivehi language. Citizenship is tied to Islam and practically all Maldivians are Sunni Muslim. Around 40% of the population lives on the tiny, crowded capital island of Malé and its neighbours, while others live on some 200 inhabited islands; a large migrant workforce, mainly from Bangladesh and India, keeps tourism and construction running.
resources: Coral atolls, reefs and turquoise lagoons of world renown
A high-value tourism industry
Tuna fisheries using traditional pole-and-line methods
A seafaring culture and close island communities
Strategic position on Indian Ocean shipping lanes
struggles: Existential threat from sea-level rise, with most land barely a metre above the sea
Coral bleaching and pressure on reefs and fisheries
Overcrowding and housing shortages in Malé
High public debt and dependence on tourism
Political polarisation and concerns about press freedom
Youth unemployment, drug use and some radicalisation
prayFor: For island families facing rising seas, that they may have a safe and lasting home
For the reefs and the fishers whose lives depend on them
For migrant workers who build and serve, that they be treated with justice and care
For young Maldivians, for hope, healthy lives and meaningful work
For peace and fairness in public life

summary.history: The atolls were settled more than two thousand years ago by peoples from South India and Sri Lanka, and for centuries the islanders were Buddhist. According to tradition the king converted to Islam in 1153, and Islam has shaped the nation ever since. Located on Indian Ocean trade routes, the islands exported cowrie shells, used as currency far and wide. The Portuguese briefly ruled Malé in the 16th century, and from 1887 the islands were a British protectorate. Independence in 1965 was followed by the rapid growth of tourism from the 1970s, while the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami devastated many islands.
summary.politicalHistory: The Maldives was a sultanate for most of its history and became independent from Britain in 1965, abolishing the sultanate to become a republic in 1968. Ibrahim Nasir and then Maumoon Abdul Gayoom, who ruled for 30 years from 1978, governed in an authoritarian way. Protests and reforms led to a new constitution and the first multiparty presidential election in 2008. Since then politics has been turbulent, with a contested transfer of power in 2012 and a state of emergency in 2018; it is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Boduberu, a drum-led music and dance with roots in East Africa and the Indian Ocean world, is the best-loved performing art. Lacquerwork (liye laajehun), mat weaving from Gadhdhoo and intricate coral-stone carving show fine craftsmanship. The building of dhoni sailing boats remains a treasured traditional skill.
summary.monuments: The 17th-century Malé Friday Mosque (Hukuru Miskiy), built of carved coral stone, is a masterpiece of Maldivian craft. The coral-stone mosques of the islands are on UNESCO's tentative list. Baa Atoll, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, and the Old Friday Mosque's minaret and royal tombs reflect the country's faith and its bond with the sea.

name: Mongolia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Mongolian is written in Cyrillic, with the traditional vertical script being revived

people: Most Mongolians are Khalkha Mongols, with Kazakhs in the far west and Buryat, Dörvöd and other Mongol groups. Tibetan Buddhism is the main faith, often alongside shamanic traditions, while many are not religiously affiliated and there are small Muslim (mainly Kazakh) and Christian communities. Roughly half the population lives in Ulaanbaatar, many in ger districts on its edge, while a significant share still lives as nomadic herders across the steppe.
resources: Copper, coal, gold and other mineral wealth, including Oyu Tolgoi
Vast grasslands and herds of horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels
A living nomadic heritage of hospitality and resilience
Wide, wild landscapes from the Altai to the Gobi
A young and well-educated population
struggles: Severe winter air pollution in Ulaanbaatar's ger districts
Dzud disasters of extreme winter that kill livestock and push herders into poverty
Desertification and overgrazing worsened by climate change
Corruption and dependence on mining exports to China
Alcohol abuse and domestic violence
prayFor: For herding families facing harsh winters, that their animals and livelihoods be protected
For children breathing polluted winter air, for clean warmth and good health
For those who have moved to the ger districts, for homes, work and belonging
For honest stewardship of the country's mineral wealth for the good of all
For families wounded by alcoholism and violence, for healing and safety

summary.history: The steppe was home to nomadic peoples such as the Xiongnu, Turks and Uyghurs long before Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and became Chinggis Khan in 1206. His successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe, achieved through devastating conquest yet also linking Eurasia in trade. After the empire fragmented, Tibetan Buddhism spread widely from the 16th century. From the late 17th century Mongolia came under Manchu Qing rule. In the 20th century it became a Soviet-aligned state, and in the 1930s purges killed tens of thousands of people, including many Buddhist monks, as monasteries were destroyed.
summary.politicalHistory: When the Qing dynasty fell in 1911 Mongolia declared independence under the Bogd Khan, a Buddhist leader. With Soviet backing, revolutionaries led by Damdin Sükhbaatar took power in 1921, and the Mongolian People's Republic was declared in 1924, governed as a one-party communist state, long dominated by Khorloogiin Choibalsan and later Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal. Peaceful democratic protests in 1990 ended one-party rule, and a new constitution in 1992 established a multiparty democracy. Mongolia is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president.
summary.art: Mongolia's music includes khöömii throat singing, the long song (urtiin duu) and the horse-head fiddle (morin khuur), all recognised by UNESCO. Buddhist sculpture reached a high point with the 17th-century artist and lama Zanabazar. Felt-making, embroidered dress, and Naadam festival traditions of wrestling, horse racing and archery are central to cultural life.
summary.monuments: The Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape, including the ruins of the Mongol capital Karakorum and the Erdene Zuu monastery, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The petroglyphs of the Mongolian Altai and the Great Burkhan Khaldun mountain, sacred and linked to Chinggis Khan, are also UNESCO-listed. Gandantegchinlen Monastery in Ulaanbaatar is a centre of Buddhist revival, and the Gobi Desert's Flaming Cliffs are famed for dinosaur fossils.

name: Myanmar

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), reflecting the country's many ethnic nationalities

people: The Bamar make up about two thirds of the population, and the country is home to many other peoples, including the Shan, Karen, Rakhine, Mon, Chin, Kachin and Karenni, as well as the Rohingya, most of whom have been denied citizenship. Nearly nine in ten people are Theravada Buddhist, with Christian communities (especially among the Chin, Kachin and Karen), Muslims and Hindus. Most people live in rural areas, and millions have fled conflict, either within the country or abroad to Thailand, Bangladesh, Malaysia and beyond.

basics.local: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်
တောင်းပန်ပါတယ်

resources: Fertile Irrawaddy delta and rice lands
Jade, rubies, teak and natural gas
Great rivers, mountains and rich forests
A deep Buddhist heritage of pagodas and monasteries
Diverse ethnic cultures and languages
Remarkable generosity and community spirit, including a long tradition of giving
struggles: Widespread armed conflict and military airstrikes since the 2021 coup, displacing millions
The persecution and mass displacement of the Rohingya, with around a million in Bangladesh
Economic collapse, deepening poverty and hunger
Forced conscription and the flight of young people
Illicit drug production, illegal resource extraction and scam centres in conflict zones
Severe cyclones and floods
prayFor: For an end to the fighting and for a just peace among all of Myanmar's peoples
For the displaced — in camps, forests and across borders — for shelter, food and safety
For the Rohingya, for recognition, protection and a safe home
For young people whose education and futures have been disrupted
For courage, healing and reconciliation after so much loss

summary.history: The Pyu city-states and Mon kingdoms flourished in the first millennium, and the Bagan Empire unified much of the land from the 11th century, spreading Theravada Buddhism. Later Burmese dynasties, the Toungoo and Konbaung, ruled powerful kingdoms that also fought wars with Siam. After three Anglo-Burmese wars, Britain annexed the country by 1885 and ruled it as part of British India until 1937. The Second World War brought Japanese occupation and heavy fighting. Since independence, armed conflict between the military and ethnic armed groups has rarely ceased, and in 2016–17 military operations drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh amid widespread killings.
summary.politicalHistory: Burma became independent from Britain in 1948, shortly after the assassination of independence leader Aung San. A parliamentary democracy was ended by General Ne Win's coup in 1962, which imposed decades of military-socialist rule; the 1988 pro-democracy uprising was crushed and a new junta took power. A military-drafted 2008 constitution led to a quasi-civilian government in 2011 and an election in 2015 won by the National League for Democracy under Aung San Suu Kyi. In February 2021 the military seized power again, triggering mass protests and a nationwide armed resistance, and the country remains under military rule amid civil war.
summary.art: Burmese art is rooted in Buddhist devotion: gilded lacquerware, wood carving, bronze casting and the gold leaf pressed onto images of the Buddha. Traditional music features the saing waing ensemble with its circle of drums, and the marionette theatre (yoke thé) and zat pwè performances combine dance, music and comedy. Kalaga embroidered tapestries and the stories of the Jataka tales appear across many crafts.
summary.monuments: Bagan, with more than two thousand surviving temples and stupas across its plain, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Pyu Ancient Cities are also UNESCO-listed, and the golden Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is the country's most sacred Buddhist site. Mandalay's royal palace and Mahamuni Pagoda, the Golden Rock at Kyaiktiyo and Inle Lake reflect the land's devotion and beauty.

name: Nepal

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); the 2021 census recorded over 120 mother tongues

people: Nepal is a mosaic of more than 120 castes and ethnic groups, including Khas Arya, Madhesi peoples of the plains, Tharu, Magar, Tamang, Newar, Rai, Limbu, Gurung and Sherpa communities. About 81% are Hindu, around 8% Buddhist, with Muslim, Kirant and growing Christian communities. Most still live in villages in the hills and the southern Tarai plains, and millions of Nepalis work abroad in the Gulf, Malaysia and India, sending home remittances that sustain many families.
resources: The Himalaya, including Mount Everest (Sagarmatha), and their glacier-fed rivers
Great hydropower potential
Trekking and mountaineering tourism
Deep Hindu and Buddhist heritage, including Lumbini, birthplace of the Buddha
Diverse peoples, languages and festivals
The resilience and hospitality of mountain communities
struggles: Earthquakes, landslides and floods, as in the devastating 2015 earthquake
Mass emigration of young workers and the risks they face abroad
Political instability and frequent changes of government
Caste discrimination, especially against Dalits, and gender inequality
Glacial melt and climate change in the high mountains
Air pollution in the Kathmandu valley
prayFor: For migrant workers far from home, for safety, fair treatment and a joyful return
For mountain villages living with landslides, floods and earthquakes
For Dalits and all who face discrimination, for dignity and equal opportunity
For stable, honest government that serves every community
For the glaciers, rivers and the many who depend on them

summary.history: The Kathmandu valley was home to the Licchavi and later the Malla kingdoms, whose Newar artisans built extraordinary cities of temples and palaces. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini in the southern plains. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley and unified many small hill states into modern Nepal. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16 the country lost territory but was never colonised, and for over a century it was governed by the hereditary Rana prime ministers, who kept it largely closed to outsiders. From 1996 to 2006 a Maoist insurgency and state counter-insurgency cost some 17,000 lives, and in 2015 a great earthquake killed nearly 9,000 people.
summary.politicalHistory: A movement in 1951 ended Rana rule and restored the Shah kings to power, and a brief parliamentary experiment was replaced in 1960 by the party-less Panchayat system. The 1990 People's Movement brought multiparty democracy under a constitutional monarchy, but the Maoist conflict and the 2001 royal massacre were followed by direct rule by the king. The 2006 People's Movement and a peace agreement ended the war, and in 2008 an elected assembly abolished the monarchy. A new constitution in 2015 made Nepal a federal democratic republic with a parliamentary system.
summary.art: The Newar people of the Kathmandu valley are renowned for metal casting, wood carving and paubha religious painting, a tradition carried abroad by the 13th-century artist Araniko. Thangka painting in Buddhist communities, Mithila wall art made by women in the Tarai, and folk music with the sarangi and madal drum are beloved. Modern literature was shaped by writers such as Laxmi Prasad Devkota and Bhanubhakta Acharya, who rendered the Ramayana into Nepali.
summary.monuments: The Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site includes the Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, the Hindu temple of Pashupatinath and the great stupas of Boudhanath and Swayambhunath. Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, is a place of pilgrimage for Buddhists worldwide. Sagarmatha National Park around Mount Everest and Chitwan National Park, home to rhinos and tigers, are also UNESCO-listed.

name: North Korea

languages.note: ≈ one living spoken language (Ethnologue); Korean is written in the Chosŏn'gŭl alphabet

people: North Korea's people are almost entirely ethnic Korean, sharing language and history with South Korea, from which many families have been separated since the Korean War. Religious practice is severely restricted; the state promotes the Juche ideology and veneration of its leaders, while some traditional Buddhism, Cheondoism and Shamanist practice persist, and Christians are reported to face severe persecution. Around six in ten people live in cities, and life differs sharply between privileged Pyongyang and the rural provinces.
resources: Mineral deposits, including coal, iron ore, magnesite and rare earths
Mountains, forests and rivers of great beauty, such as Mount Paektu and Mount Kumgang
An educated, highly literate population
A shared Korean heritage of language, food and song
The endurance and ingenuity of ordinary families
struggles: Chronic food insecurity and malnutrition, with famine in the 1990s killing many people
Severe restrictions on freedom of movement, speech, information and religion
Political prison camps and grave human-rights abuses documented by the UN
International isolation and sanctions linked to nuclear and missile programmes
Families divided across the Korean peninsula for over seventy years
Deforestation, flooding and fragile infrastructure
prayFor: For every family in North Korea, for enough food, warmth and medicine
For those imprisoned or persecuted, including believers, for protection and freedom
For families separated across the border, for reunion and consolation
For peace on the Korean peninsula and the easing of fear on all sides
For those who have fled, that they be welcomed and find healing

summary.history: The Korean peninsula was shaped by ancient kingdoms such as Goguryeo, which ruled the north, and by later unified dynasties, the Goryeo and the Joseon, which lasted until 1910. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled harshly, suppressing language and culture and conscripting labourers. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the peninsula was divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US zones. The Korean War (1950–53), begun by the North's invasion and drawing in the United States, China and others, killed millions on both sides and ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty. In the 1990s the loss of Soviet support and natural disasters caused a famine in which hundreds of thousands are thought to have died.
summary.politicalHistory: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was proclaimed in 1948 under Kim Il-sung, backed by the Soviet Union. He built a one-party state based on the Juche ideology of self-reliance and a pervasive personality cult. Power passed to his son Kim Jong-il in 1994, who emphasised the military-first (Songun) policy, and then within the same family in 2011. North Korea is a one-party state led by the Workers' Party of Korea under hereditary leadership, and it has developed nuclear weapons despite international sanctions.
summary.art: Art is largely shaped by the state, with grand socialist-realist painting, monumental sculpture and the mass games of synchronised gymnastics. Chosonhwa, a style of ink painting rooted in traditional Korean art, and fine embroidery are notable crafts. Ancient Goguryeo tomb murals and folk songs such as Arirang, also listed by UNESCO for North Korea, connect the country to the wider Korean tradition.
summary.monuments: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs, with their vivid ancient wall paintings, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, former capital of the Goryeo dynasty, are also UNESCO-listed. Mount Paektu, revered in Korean legend, and Mount Kumgang, the 'Diamond Mountains', are cherished landscapes, while Pyongyang's monuments express the state's ideology.

name: Pakistan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Urdu is the national language and English is used in government and higher education

people: Pakistan's peoples include Punjabis, Pashtuns, Sindhis, Saraikis, Muhajirs, Baloch and many smaller communities in the northern mountains. About 96% are Muslim, mostly Sunni with a large Shia minority, and there are Hindu, Christian, Ahmadi and Sikh communities, some of whom face discrimination. It is a very young country, with most people still living in rural areas though cities like Karachi and Lahore are vast, and a large diaspora lives in the Gulf, the UK and North America.
resources: The Indus River and one of the world's largest irrigation systems
Fertile Punjab farmland producing wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane
Mountain ranges of the Karakoram, Himalaya and Hindu Kush, including K2
A large, young and entrepreneurial population
Textiles, crafts and a rich Sufi and literary heritage
Generous hospitality and strong family bonds
struggles: Severe climate impacts, including the catastrophic 2022 floods and extreme heat
Economic crisis, high inflation and heavy debt
Militant violence, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan
Political polarisation and the military's strong influence on politics
Low school enrolment, especially for girls, and widespread poverty
Discrimination and violence against religious minorities, including through blasphemy accusations
prayFor: For families who lost homes and fields to floods and heat, for restoration and resilience
For children, especially girls, to be able to go to school and learn in safety
For peace in regions affected by militant violence, and comfort for the bereaved
For religious minorities, for protection, justice and equal belonging
For honest, stable government and relief for families burdened by rising prices

summary.history: The Indus valley was home to one of the world's earliest urban civilisations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa around 2500 BCE. Over the centuries the land saw Vedic culture, the Buddhist kingdom of Gandhara, Persian and Greek influence, the arrival of Islam from the 8th century, and the splendour of the Mughal Empire based partly in Lahore. Britain conquered the region in the 19th century. The Partition of British India in 1947 created Pakistan as a homeland for South Asia's Muslims, amid mass violence in which perhaps up to a million people died and some 15 million were displaced on all sides. Pakistan has since fought several wars with India, lost its eastern wing when Bangladesh became independent in 1971, and endured years of militant violence.
summary.politicalHistory: Pakistan was founded on 14 August 1947 under Muhammad Ali Jinnah and became an Islamic republic in 1956. Its history has alternated between civilian governments and military rule, with coups by Ayub Khan (1958), Zia-ul-Haq (1977) and Pervez Musharraf (1999). Zulfikar Ali Bhutto led the country after 1971 and was executed in 1979, and his daughter Benazir Bhutto, twice prime minister, was assassinated in 2007. Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic under the 1973 constitution, with a prime minister as head of government, though the military remains highly influential.
summary.art: Sufi devotional music, especially qawwali made famous worldwide by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, is at the heart of Pakistani culture. Urdu poetry is deeply loved, from Mirza Ghalib to Allama Iqbal, the national poet, and Faiz Ahmed Faiz. Truck art, Multani blue pottery, Sindhi ajrak block printing and Mughal miniature painting are vibrant visual traditions.
summary.monuments: The archaeological ruins of Mohenjo-daro, the Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, and the Buddhist ruins of Takht-i-Bahi are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Makli necropolis near Thatta and the Rohtas Fort are also UNESCO-listed. The Badshahi Mosque in Lahore and the Faisal Mosque in Islamabad are great landmarks of faith, while the Karakoram Highway passes some of the world's highest peaks.

name: Singapore

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); four official languages, with English the common working language and Malay the national language

people: About three quarters of Singapore's citizens and residents are of Chinese descent, with Malay and Indian communities and many people of mixed and Eurasian heritage, plus a large foreign workforce making up close to a third of the population. It is one of the world's most religiously diverse societies: Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, Taoism and Hinduism are all widely practised, and about a fifth have no religion. Almost everyone lives in the city, mostly in public housing estates.
resources: A strategic location and one of the world's busiest ports
World-class education and a highly skilled workforce
A global centre for finance, trade and technology
Effective public institutions and public housing
A multicultural society and celebrated hawker food culture
Urban greenery and water innovation in a land with few natural resources
struggles: A very high cost of living and pressure on housing and families
Rapid population ageing and one of the world's lowest birth rates
Long working hours, stress and mental-health strain, especially among the young
Unequal conditions for low-wage migrant workers
Limits on political dissent, protest and press freedom
