Vulnerability to sea-level rise and extreme heat
prayFor: For families feeling the pressure of costs, work and expectations, for rest and joy
For elderly people, that they be cared for and never alone
For migrant workers and domestic helpers, for fair treatment, safety and dignity
For the young, for wholeness of mind and a sense of purpose beyond achievement
For continued harmony among people of every race and faith

summary.history: The island was known as Temasek, a trading settlement linked to the Malay world, centuries before Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company founded a trading post there in 1819. Singapore grew into a major free port of the Straits Settlements, drawing migrants from China, India and the Malay archipelago. During the Second World War Japan occupied it from 1942 to 1945, and the Sook Ching massacre killed many thousands of Chinese residents. After the war it moved towards self-government and briefly joined Malaysia, before separation in 1965. With very few natural resources, it transformed itself within a generation into one of the world's wealthiest nations.
summary.politicalHistory: Singapore became a self-governing state within the British Empire in 1959, with the People's Action Party led by Lee Kuan Yew winning power. It joined Malaysia in 1963 but was separated in 1965 amid political and racial tensions, becoming an independent republic. The People's Action Party has governed continuously since 1959, combining regular elections with tight limits on opposition and dissent, under prime ministers including Goh Chok Tong. Singapore is a parliamentary republic with an elected president as head of state.
summary.art: Singapore's hawker culture, a meeting of Chinese, Malay, Indian and Peranakan cooking, is recognised by UNESCO. Peranakan beadwork, porcelain and kebaya embroidery, Chinese opera, Malay dance and Indian classical arts flourish alongside each other. Contemporary voices include the poet Edwin Thumboo and theatre and film artists who explore a multicultural identity.
summary.monuments: The Singapore Botanic Gardens, founded in 1859, are the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. The historic districts of Chinatown, Kampong Glam and Little India preserve shophouses, temples and mosques such as the Sri Mariamman Temple and Sultan Mosque. Gardens by the Bay and Marina Bay represent modern Singapore, while the Kranji War Memorial honours those who died in the Second World War.

name: Sri Lanka

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Sinhala and Tamil are official, with English as a link language

people: About three quarters of Sri Lankans are Sinhalese, with Sri Lankan Tamils in the north and east, Tamils of Indian origin in the hill country tea estates, Muslims (Moors and Malays), Burghers and the Indigenous Vedda. Roughly 70% are Theravada Buddhist, about 12% Hindu, 10% Muslim and 7% Christian. Most people live in rural areas and small towns, and a large diaspora, including many Tamils who fled the war, lives in India, the Gulf, Europe, Canada and Australia.
resources: Ceylon tea, spices and fertile hill country
Rich biodiversity, rainforests, elephants and leopards
Beaches, reefs and a strategic Indian Ocean position
Gemstones such as sapphires
High literacy and a long tradition of free education and healthcare
Ancient Buddhist, Hindu and Islamic heritage
struggles: Recovery from the 2022 economic collapse, with debt, inflation and rising poverty
The unhealed wounds of the civil war, including the missing and calls for accountability
Ethnic and religious tensions affecting Tamils and Muslims
Hard living conditions for tea estate workers
Emigration of doctors, nurses and young professionals
Human–elephant conflict, floods and landslides
prayFor: For families still searching for loved ones who disappeared during and after the war
For reconciliation and trust among Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim and Burgher communities
For households struggling after the economic crisis, for food, medicine and work
For tea estate workers and their children, for fair wages and good homes
For honest and accountable leadership that serves every citizen

summary.history: Sri Lanka has a recorded history of more than two thousand years, with great Sinhalese kingdoms at Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa that built monumental stupas and sophisticated irrigation, and Tamil kingdoms in the north. Buddhism arrived in the 3rd century BCE and has shaped the island's identity ever since. The Portuguese, then the Dutch, and finally the British controlled the coasts and, from 1815, the whole island, bringing Tamil labourers from India to work on coffee and tea plantations. After independence, tensions over language and rights led to a civil war (1983–2009) between the state and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, marked by suicide bombings and attacks on civilians by the LTTE and, in the final phase, heavy civilian deaths in the north. The island also suffered the 2004 tsunami, the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings and the 2022 economic collapse.
summary.politicalHistory: Ceylon gained independence from Britain peacefully in 1948 as a dominion. In 1956 the Sinhala Only Act deepened Tamil grievances, and in 1960 Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first elected woman prime minister. The country became the Republic of Sri Lanka in 1972, and a 1978 constitution created a strong executive presidency; JVP insurrections in 1971 and 1987–89 were violently suppressed. Sri Lanka is a presidential republic with a parliament, and mass protests in 2022 (the Aragalaya) forced a change of government.
summary.art: Sri Lankan art is rich in Buddhist sculpture and painting, from the Sigiriya frescoes to the temple murals of the Kandyan period. Kandyan dance, with its drummers and elaborate costumes, and masked kolam and devil dances of the south are living traditions. Writers such as Michael Ondaatje and the painter George Keyt, together with the architect Geoffrey Bawa, brought Sri Lankan creativity to the world.
summary.monuments: Sigiriya, the rock fortress of a 5th-century king, and the Sacred City of Anuradhapura, with its giant stupas and sacred Bo tree, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, the ancient city of Polonnaruwa and the Dambulla cave temples are also UNESCO-listed. The Dutch-built Galle Fort and the Sinharaja rainforest show the island's colonial history and natural treasures.

name: Taiwan

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. many endangered Austronesian Formosan languages

people: Most people in Taiwan are descendants of Hokkien and Hakka migrants from southern China who arrived over several centuries, along with families who came from across mainland China around 1949 and, more recently, new immigrants from Southeast Asia. Sixteen officially recognised Indigenous peoples, such as the Amis, Atayal and Paiwan, make up about 2.5% of the population and are Austronesian in heritage. Religious life blends Buddhism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion, with Christian minorities and many with no affiliation; most people live in cities along the western plains.
resources: World-leading semiconductor and electronics industries
A highly educated, innovative workforce
Mountains, forests and coastlines of great biodiversity
Vibrant civil society, temples and night-market culture
Indigenous Austronesian heritage
Universal health insurance and strong public services
struggles: Tension with the People's Republic of China, which claims Taiwan, and the threat of conflict
Limited formal diplomatic recognition and participation in international bodies
One of the world's lowest birth rates and a fast-ageing society
High housing costs and stagnant wages for young people
Earthquakes and typhoons
Energy security on an import-dependent island
prayFor: For peace across the Taiwan Strait, and for the safety of all who live on both sides
For wisdom, restraint and honest dialogue among all who hold power in the region
For young families, for affordable homes and hope for the future
For Indigenous peoples, that their languages, lands and cultures flourish
For communities affected by earthquakes and typhoons, for protection and swift recovery

summary.history: Taiwan was home for thousands of years to Austronesian Indigenous peoples, whose ancestors are thought to have set out from here across the Pacific. In the 17th century the Dutch and Spanish established footholds, until Ming loyalist Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) expelled the Dutch in 1662 and the Qing dynasty took control in 1683, while large-scale migration from Fujian and Guangdong displaced and assimilated many Indigenous communities. After the First Sino-Japanese War, Qing China ceded Taiwan to Japan in 1895, beginning fifty years of colonial rule and modernisation. In 1945 the island came under the Republic of China, and the 228 Incident of 1947 began a period of violent repression, followed by decades of martial law known as the White Terror. From the 1960s Taiwan's economy grew rapidly, and it became a democracy in the late 1980s and 1990s.
summary.politicalHistory: After Japan's surrender, the Republic of China government took over Taiwan in 1945, and in 1949, after losing the civil war on the mainland to the Communists, Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang relocated the ROC government to Taipei. The People's Republic of China, founded in Beijing that same year, regards Taiwan as part of its territory, while the government in Taipei has administered Taiwan and nearby islands ever since; most countries maintain unofficial rather than formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, and in 1971 the UN seat passed to the PRC. Martial law, imposed in 1949, was lifted in 1987, and under Chiang Ching-kuo and then Lee Teng-hui the island democratised, holding its first direct presidential election in 1996. Taiwan today has a multiparty democratic system with a directly elected president and legislature, while its international status remains disputed.
summary.art: Taiwan treasures Chinese classical arts, with the National Palace Museum holding one of the world's greatest collections of Chinese painting, calligraphy, bronzes and ceramics. Glove puppetry (budaixi), Taiwanese opera and temple festivals such as the Mazu pilgrimage are vibrant popular traditions, and Indigenous weaving, carving and polyphonic singing are deeply valued. Modern artists include the Cloud Gate Dance Theatre, filmmakers Hou Hsiao-hsien and Ang Lee, and the sculptor Ju Ming.
summary.monuments: Taroko Gorge, with its marble cliffs, and Sun Moon Lake, home of the Thao people, are among the island's most beloved landscapes. The National Palace Museum and Taipei 101 represent Taiwan's heritage and modernity, while Longshan Temple in Taipei is a centre of popular devotion. Tainan's Anping Fort and Confucius Temple trace the island's early history, and the 228 Memorial Park honours the victims of political violence.

name: Timor-Leste

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Tetum and Portuguese are official, with Indonesian and English as working languages and many local languages such as Mambai and Makasae

people: The Timorese are made up of many Austronesian and Papuan-speaking communities, united by a shared history of resistance. Around 97% are Catholic, making it one of the most Catholic countries in the world, often alongside respect for ancestral sacred houses (uma lulik), with small Protestant and Muslim minorities. Most people live in rural villages and depend on farming, and the population is very young.
resources: Offshore oil and gas and the Petroleum Fund built from them
Coral reefs of exceptional biodiversity around Atauro island
Coffee grown in the mountains
A young population and a strong sense of community
The courage and faith that carried the nation to independence
struggles: Heavy dependence on dwindling oil and gas revenue
Child malnutrition and stunting, among the highest rates in the world
Youth unemployment and limited economic opportunity
Poor roads, water and health services in rural areas
Trauma passed down from the occupation years and gender-based violence
prayFor: For children, that they be well fed, healthy and able to learn
For young people, for work, skills and hope at home
For healing for survivors of the occupation and the families of those who died or disappeared
For wise stewardship of the nation's resources for the good of all
For women and girls, for safety and equal opportunity

summary.history: The island of Timor has been inhabited for tens of thousands of years by Austronesian and Papuan peoples organised in small kingdoms and known for sandalwood trade. Portugal established a presence from the 16th century, and the island was divided between Portuguese Timor in the east and Dutch Timor in the west. Japan occupied it during the Second World War, when many Timorese died. After Portugal withdrew in 1975 and a brief declaration of independence, Indonesia invaded and occupied the territory for 24 years; a truth commission estimated that up to around 180,000 people died from violence, hunger and disease. In 1999 Timorese voted overwhelmingly for independence, after which militias backed by elements of the Indonesian military destroyed much of the country before an international force arrived.
summary.politicalHistory: The Revolutionary Front for an Independent East Timor (Fretilin) declared independence in November 1975, days before Indonesia's invasion, and Indonesia annexed the territory in 1976. Armed and clandestine resistance continued for over two decades, and in 1996 the Nobel Peace Prize went to two Timorese advocates of a peaceful solution. Following the UN-organised referendum in 1999 and a period of UN administration, Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002. It is a semi-presidential democratic republic with an elected president and parliament, and a 2006 political crisis was overcome through dialogue and elections.
summary.art: Tais, hand-woven textiles made by women with patterns specific to each region, are the most treasured craft and are recognised by UNESCO as needing urgent safeguarding. Traditional sacred houses (uma lulik) with tall carved roofs embody ancestral identity. Music and dance such as tebe and likurai, along with resistance songs and poetry, express memory and celebration.
summary.monuments: The Cristo Rei statue overlooking Dili and the Santa Cruz Cemetery, site of the 1991 massacre that drew world attention, are places of faith and memory. The Resistance Museum and the Chega! exhibition at the former Comarca Balide prison honour those who suffered and resisted. Mount Ramelau, the highest peak and a pilgrimage site, and Atauro island with its reefs reflect the country's natural beauty.

name: Vietnam

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Tày, Thái, Khmer, Hmong and many other minority languages

people: About 85% of Vietnamese are Kinh, and 53 other officially recognised ethnic groups live mostly in the northern mountains and Central Highlands, including the Tày, Thái, Mường, Khmer and Hmong. Many people practise ancestor veneration and folk religion, often alongside Buddhism, while Catholics, Protestants and followers of Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo form significant communities, and many say they have no religion. Around 40% live in cities such as Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi, and a large diaspora lives in the United States, France, Australia and elsewhere.
resources: The Mekong and Red River deltas, among the world's great rice-growing regions
A young, hardworking and entrepreneurial population
A fast-growing manufacturing and export economy
Coffee, seafood and other agricultural exports
Long coastlines, limestone bays and mountain landscapes
A celebrated food culture and deep sense of family
struggles: Sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion and land subsidence in the Mekong Delta
Storms, floods and air pollution in major cities
Restrictions on free expression, independent media and some religious groups
Corruption and inequality between cities and ethnic-minority regions
Lasting effects of war, including Agent Orange and unexploded ordnance
An ageing population that may grow old before it grows rich
prayFor: For farmers and families in the Mekong Delta facing rising seas and salty water
For those still living with the effects of Agent Orange and wartime bombs
For ethnic-minority communities, for fair opportunity and respect
For freedom of conscience and expression for all
For healing between generations and between Vietnamese at home and abroad

summary.history: The Red River delta was home to the Bronze Age Đông Sơn culture, famous for its bronze drums, and Chinese dynasties ruled the north for about a thousand years until independence in 938. Vietnamese dynasties then expanded southward over centuries, absorbing the Cham kingdoms and parts of the Khmer lands, and the Nguyễn dynasty unified the country in 1802. France colonised Vietnam from the 1850s, and after the Second World War the Viet Minh fought for independence, defeating France at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954. The country was divided, and the war that followed, with heavy US involvement, killed perhaps two to three million Vietnamese as well as tens of thousands of Americans and others, and left lasting damage from bombs and Agent Orange. After 1975 hundreds of thousands were sent to re-education camps and many 'boat people' fled at great risk, before reforms from 1986 brought rapid growth.
summary.politicalHistory: Hồ Chí Minh declared Vietnam's independence in 1945, and after the 1954 Geneva Accords the country was split between the communist North and the Republic of Vietnam in the South, led first by Ngô Đình Diệm. The North and southern insurgents fought the South Vietnamese government and its US allies until Saigon fell in April 1975, and the country was reunified in 1976 as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Vietnam fought a border war with China in 1979 and intervened in Cambodia from 1978 to 1989. In 1986 the Đổi Mới reforms opened the economy to the market, while the Communist Party of Vietnam remains the sole ruling party.
summary.art: Water puppetry, performed on ponds in the Red River delta, and ca trù sung poetry and quan họ folk songs are cherished arts recognised by UNESCO. The epic poem The Tale of Kiều by Nguyễn Du is the national literary masterpiece, and the poet Hồ Xuân Hương is beloved for her wit. Lacquer painting, silk painting, Đông Hồ woodblock prints and Bát Tràng ceramics continue long craft traditions.
summary.monuments: Hạ Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands, and the Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng caves are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Complex of Huế Monuments, the old trading port of Hội An and the Cham temples of Mỹ Sơn reflect the country's imperial, mercantile and Hindu-Cham heritage. The Temple of Literature in Hanoi, dedicated to Confucius and scholarship, and the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long are also treasured.

name: Fiji

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Rotuman and immigrant languages

people: Around 330 islands, about 110 inhabited, are home to iTaukei (Indigenous Fijians, a little over half the population), Indo-Fijians descended largely from indentured labourers (roughly a third), and Rotuman, Banaban, Chinese, European and other Pacific Islander communities. Roughly two-thirds are Christian (mainly Methodist, with Catholic, Assemblies of God and other churches), about a quarter Hindu and around 6% Muslim. A little over half live in towns, chiefly on Viti Levu, and large diasporas live in Australia, New Zealand, the US and Canada.
resources: Coral reefs, fisheries and the Great Sea Reef
Tourism and warm village hospitality
Sugar cane, timber and mahogany plantations
Gold mining (Vatukoula)
Regional hub role: University of the South Pacific, Pacific Islands Forum, airline and shipping links
Rugby and sevens excellence, and a strong communal (vanua) culture
struggles: A legacy of coups and ethnic mistrust between iTaukei and Indo-Fijian communities
Emigration of skilled workers (teachers, nurses, tradespeople)
Very high rates of diabetes and other non-communicable diseases, including many amputations
A sharp rise in methamphetamine use and HIV infections linked to drug trafficking through the region
Cyclones, coastal erosion and sea-level rise forcing some villages to relocate
Uncertainty over land leases and a sugar industry in long decline
prayFor: For trust and reconciliation between iTaukei, Indo-Fijian and all communities, so that past coups give way to lasting peace
For families touched by diabetes, addiction and HIV — for healing, good clinics and communities that embrace rather than shame
For villages facing rising seas and stronger cyclones, as they decide whether and how to move their homes and graves
For young Fijians, that they find meaningful work and hope at home as well as abroad
For churches, temples and mosques to keep serving the poor side by side

summary.history: Fiji was settled about 3,000 years ago by Lapita voyagers, and over centuries its chiefdoms formed a culture bridging Melanesia and Polynesia, with strong ties to Tonga and Samoa. European sandalwood and bêche-de-mer traders, missionaries and planters arrived in the 19th century, bringing guns, disease and land conflict. In 1874 chiefs led by Ratu Seru Cakobau ceded the islands to Britain, which from 1879 to 1916 brought about 60,000 indentured labourers (girmitiya) from India to work the sugar plantations under harsh conditions. Fiji became independent in 1970, but differences over land and political power between iTaukei and Indo-Fijians fed coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006 and waves of emigration. Today it is the most populous of the smaller Pacific island states and a regional hub, still working through that legacy.
summary.politicalHistory: Fiji gained independence from Britain in 1970 as a parliamentary democracy within the Commonwealth. Two military coups in 1987 ended the monarchy and produced a republic, followed by a civilian-led coup in 2000 and a military coup in 2006 under Commodore Frank Bainimarama. A new constitution in 2013 introduced a single national electoral roll, and elections were held in 2014 and 2018; the 2022 election brought a peaceful change of government. Fiji today is a parliamentary republic with an elected parliament and a president as head of state.
summary.art: Fijian craft traditions include masi (decorated barkcloth), finely woven mats, carved wooden tanoa bowls for yaqona (kava) ceremonies, and the meke, which joins dance, chant and lali drumming to tell stories. Indo-Fijian culture adds its own music, festivals such as Diwali, and a literature of girmit memory. Writers such as Subramani, Satendra Nandan and Sudesh Mishra, and the Oceania Centre for Arts at the University of the South Pacific, founded by Epeli Hauʻofa, have shaped Pacific letters.
summary.monuments: Levuka Historical Port Town on Ovalau, Fiji's first colonial capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage site that shows a Pacific port where cultures met. The Sigatoka Sand Dunes hold Lapita pottery and ancient burials, and the Fiji Museum in Suva keeps canoes, war clubs and records of indenture. The Sri Siva Subramaniya Temple in Nadi and the Naiserelagi Catholic mission, with its murals of a Fijian Christ, show the islands' faith traditions.

name: Kiribati

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Gilbertese is spoken by almost everyone

people: Almost all the people are I-Kiribati, Micronesians whose life is built around the sea, extended family and the maneaba (community meeting house); a small Banaban community also has roots here. Most are Christian — roughly 57% Catholic and around a third Protestant (Kiribati Uniting Church and others) — with Latter-day Saint, Bahá'í and other minorities. About half live crowded together on South Tarawa, and others live on scattered outer atolls across 3.5 million km² of ocean.
resources: One of the world's largest exclusive economic zones and its tuna fishing licences
Phoenix Islands Protected Area, one of the largest marine protected areas
The Revenue Equalisation Reserve Fund built from past phosphate earnings
Coconut and copra, and seaweed farming
Seafaring skills and remittances from merchant sailors and seasonal workers
A strong communal culture of the maneaba, dance and song
struggles: Sea-level rise, king tides and saltwater intrusion threatening low atolls only a few metres above sea level
Overcrowding, poor sanitation and scarce fresh water on South Tarawa
High rates of tuberculosis, diabetes and child illness linked to water and diet
Few jobs for a young population and heavy reliance on fishing licence income and aid
Remoteness and costly transport between widely scattered islands
prayFor: For the people of the atolls as the sea rises — for protection, wise adaptation, and the right to stay or move with dignity
For clean water, safe sanitation and good health for children and families on crowded South Tarawa
For young I-Kiribati, that they find work and purpose at home and abroad without losing their culture
For seafarers, seasonal workers and their families separated by long distances
For the nations of the world to act justly on climate change for those who did least to cause it

summary.history: Micronesian voyagers settled the Gilbert Islands perhaps 3,000 years ago, with later Samoan influence, building societies organised around kin groups and the maneaba. Whalers, traders and missionaries arrived in the 19th century, and labour recruiters took many islanders to plantations abroad. Britain declared a protectorate in 1892, later forming the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony; phosphate mining from 1900 stripped Banaba, and in 1945 most Banabans were moved to Rabi Island in Fiji. In 1943 the Battle of Tarawa between US and Japanese forces killed thousands, and the British and US later tested nuclear weapons near Kiritimati (Christmas Island). Kiribati became independent in 1979 and now faces rising seas as a defining challenge.
summary.politicalHistory: The Ellice Islands separated in 1975 to become Tuvalu, and the Gilbert Islands became independent as the Republic of Kiribati on 12 July 1979, under first President Ieremia Tabai. Its constitution creates a single-chamber parliament (Maneaba ni Maungatabu) that nominates presidential candidates, whom citizens then elect directly. Kiribati remains a parliamentary-presidential republic in the Commonwealth, and in 2019 it switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the People's Republic of China.
summary.art: I-Kiribati dance (te mwaie, including the bird-like te kaimatoa) is famous for precise arm and head movements set to group chanting and is performed in maneaba competitions. Traditional crafts include fine pandanus mats, intricately knotted coconut-fibre armour with shark-tooth weapons, and canoe building. Oral poetry, genealogies and navigation lore carry history, and Teresia Teaiwa, a scholar and poet of I-Kiribati heritage, is well known in Pacific literature.
summary.monuments: The Phoenix Islands Protected Area is a UNESCO World Heritage site that safeguards some of the Pacific's least disturbed coral archipelagos and seabird colonies. Betio on Tarawa keeps Second World War bunkers and coastal guns from the 1943 battle. Banaba's mined-out landscape bears witness to the phosphate era, and the maneaba of villages across the islands remain the heart of community life.

name: Marshall Islands

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue)

people: Marshallese are Micronesians organised in matrilineal clans, with land passed down through the mother's line and chiefs (iroij) still respected. Nearly everyone is Christian, mostly Protestant (United Church of Christ and Assemblies of God), with Catholic, Latter-day Saint and other churches. Most people live on Majuro and Ebeye, and roughly a third or more of all Marshallese now live in the United States, notably in Arkansas, Hawaiʻi and Oregon.
resources: A vast ocean territory and tuna fishing licences
One of the world's largest ship registries
Compact of Free Association funding and trust fund with the United States
Coconut and copra
Traditional navigation knowledge, including stick charts
Strong clan and church networks across islands and diaspora
struggles: The lasting health, environmental and displacement legacy of US nuclear testing, including Runit Dome on Enewetak
Sea-level rise and flooding on atolls averaging about two metres above sea level
Very high rates of diabetes and other non-communicable diseases
Overcrowding on Ebeye and Majuro and limited jobs, driving emigration
Heavy dependence on outside funding
prayFor: For the people of Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap and Utrik, for healing, justice and a true home after the nuclear tests
For atoll communities facing rising seas, that they may find protection and wise choices for the future
For families with diabetes and other illnesses, for care, good food and strength
For Marshallese in the United States and at home, that they stay connected to language, land and one another
For young people, for education and work that let them flourish

summary.history: Micronesian navigators settled the Ratak and Ralik chains of atolls perhaps 2,000 or more years ago, mastering ocean wayfinding with stick charts of swells. Spain claimed the islands, Germany took control in 1885, and Japan ruled from 1914 until US forces captured them in 1944. Between 1946 and 1958 the United States carried out 67 nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak, including the 1954 Castle Bravo blast whose fallout poisoned the people of Rongelap and Utrik and displaced communities who have not been able to return safely. As part of the UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, the islands moved toward self-government and since 1986 have been sovereign in free association with the US. Today Marshallese carry that nuclear history and now face the threat of rising seas.
summary.politicalHistory: The Marshall Islands adopted its constitution in 1979, forming a government with Amata Kabua as first president, while still formally under US trusteeship. The Compact of Free Association took effect in 1986, giving the US defence responsibility and providing economic aid, and the UN trusteeship formally ended in 1990 when the country joined the United Nations. The system is a parliamentary republic in which the Nitijeļā (parliament) elects the president, alongside a Council of Iroij (chiefs) that advises on custom; the Compact's economic terms were renewed in 2023–24.
summary.art: Marshallese stick charts (mattang, meddo and rebbelib), made of palm ribs and shells, map ocean swells and are admired as a unique form of knowledge. Women weave fine pandanus mats, baskets and handicrafts, including the famous Kili bags, and canoe building is kept alive by programs such as Waan Aelōñ in Majel. Songs, chants and church choirs are central to community life, and contemporary Marshallese poets and artists carry the nuclear and climate story to world audiences.
summary.monuments: Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site is a UNESCO World Heritage site, with sunken warships and bomb craters bearing witness to the nuclear age. Runit Dome on Enewetak, a concrete cap over radioactive waste, is a sobering reminder of that legacy. The Alele Museum in Majuro holds stick charts and historic photographs, and wartime wrecks and remains on Mili, Jaluit and Wotje recall the Second World War.

name: Micronesia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. outer-island and Polynesian outlier languages; English is the shared official language

people: The four states — Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae — each have their own languages, clans and customs, spread across more than 600 islands; Polynesian communities live on Kapingamarangi and Nukuoro. Almost everyone is Christian, roughly half Catholic and most of the rest Protestant, and traditional chiefs remain important, especially in Yap and Pohnpei. Most people live on the high islands of Chuuk Lagoon and Pohnpei, and many have emigrated to Guam, Hawaiʻi and the US mainland under the Compact of Free Association.
resources: Huge tuna fishing grounds and licence revenue
Coral reefs, mangroves and Second World War wreck diving in Chuuk Lagoon
Compact of Free Association funding and trust fund with the United States
Lush high-island agriculture: breadfruit, taro, bananas, sakau (kava) and Pohnpei pepper
Traditional navigation and voyaging knowledge in the outer islands of Yap and Chuuk
Living chiefly and clan systems that hold communities together
struggles: Dependence on US Compact funds and uncertainty over long-term financing
Emigration draining skilled workers and young families
High rates of diabetes, obesity and other non-communicable diseases
Sea-level rise, drought and storms threatening low outer atolls
Tensions between states, including calls in Chuuk for separation
Limited infrastructure and costly travel between distant islands
prayFor: For unity and mutual respect among the peoples of Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae
For families on outer atolls facing rising seas and drought, for safe water, food and shelter
For good health care and healthy food for those suffering from diabetes and heart disease
For Micronesians abroad, that they be welcomed and stay connected to home
For young people, for education, work and hope in their own islands

summary.history: The Caroline Islands were settled over thousands of years by voyagers who developed distinct societies, from the stone city of Nan Madol on Pohnpei, ruled by the Saudeleur dynasty, to Yap's network of tribute and exchange with outer islands. Spain claimed the islands in the 19th century, then sold them to Germany in 1899; Japan ruled from 1914 and heavily settled and fortified them, and Chuuk Lagoon became a major naval base bombed by the US in 1944. After the war the islands became part of the US-administered UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. In 1979 four districts formed the Federated States of Micronesia, which entered free association with the US in 1986. Today the nation balances four distinct cultures, a far-flung geography and a large diaspora.
summary.politicalHistory: The constitution, adopted in 1979, created a federation of four states — Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae — with Tosiwo Nakayama as first president. The Compact of Free Association with the United States took effect in 1986, and the UN trusteeship formally ended in 1990 when the FSM joined the United Nations. The national Congress, with no political parties, elects the president from among its at-large members, and each state has its own constitution and government; the Compact's economic provisions were renewed in 2023–24.
summary.art: Yap is known for its rai stone money, dance performances and fine weaving, while Pohnpei and Kosrae keep traditions of canoe-making, carved storyboards, woven mats and ceremonial sakau preparation. The outer islands of Yap and Chuuk keep alive traditional ocean navigation — Satawal's master navigator Mau Piailug taught it to Hawaiʻi's Hōkūleʻa voyagers. Dance, chant and church singing mark every major celebration across the states.
summary.monuments: Nan Madol, the basalt city built on artificial islets off Pohnpei, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the Pacific's great ancient monuments. The ruins of Lelu on Kosrae are a similar royal stone city, and Yap's stone money banks display rai discs quarried in Palau. Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of sunken Japanese ships and aircraft from 1944, now a world-famous dive site and a war grave.

name: Nauru

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English is widely used in government and business

people: Most residents are Nauruans, a Pacific people of mixed Micronesian, Melanesian and Polynesian heritage organised in twelve clans, alongside workers from Kiribati, Tuvalu, Fiji and elsewhere, Chinese shopkeepers and a small number of asylum seekers and refugees. Most Nauruans are Christian, belonging mainly to the Nauru Congregational Church and the Catholic Church. Everyone lives on a narrow coastal belt around the 21 km² island, since the mined-out interior is largely uninhabitable.
resources: Phosphate (now largely depleted, with secondary mining continuing)
Tuna fishing licences in its ocean zone
Revenue from hosting Australia's regional processing centre
The Nauru Intergenerational Trust Fund
Close-knit clan and church communities
Sporting passion, especially Australian rules football and weightlifting
struggles: An interior stripped by a century of phosphate mining, leaving little land for farming or housing
Some of the world's highest rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes
Dependence on revenue from offshore asylum processing, and the hardship of those detained there
Scarce fresh water and reliance on imported food and fuel
Coastal erosion and climate risks for the narrow inhabited belt
prayFor: For the healing of the land and wise rehabilitation of the mined-out interior
For families affected by diabetes and heart disease, for health, good food and long life
For refugees and asylum seekers on Nauru, for safety, dignity and a future
For wise and honest stewardship of the nation's trust fund for future generations
For young Nauruans, for education, purpose and hope

summary.history: Nauru was settled by Pacific voyagers perhaps 3,000 years ago, and its people formed twelve clans living by fishing and tending the island's frigatebirds and lagoon fish. Contact with whalers and traders from the 1830s brought guns and alcohol that fed a ten-year civil war, ended when Germany annexed the island in 1888. Phosphate mining began in 1906, and after the First World War Australia administered the island on behalf of Britain, Australia and New Zealand. Japan occupied Nauru in 1942 and deported about 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died; the survivors returned in 1946, and on 31 January 1968 Nauru became independent. Phosphate made Nauru briefly one of the richest countries per person, but by the 1990s mismanagement and depletion had caused a severe crisis.
summary.politicalHistory: Nauru became independent in 1968 under Head Chief Hammer DeRoburt, becoming the world's smallest republic, and joined the Commonwealth. Its parliamentary system has a 19-member parliament that elects the president, who is both head of state and head of government. Governments changed frequently through no-confidence votes in the 1990s and 2000s, and Nauru took Australia to the International Court of Justice over mining damage, reaching a settlement in 1993; from 2001 it hosted Australian offshore processing of asylum seekers. In January 2024 Nauru switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the People's Republic of China.
summary.art: Traditional Nauruan culture includes string figures, dance, songs and chants, and frigatebird catching, which was once a prized sport. Crafts include woven pandanus mats and baskets, flower garlands and shell decoration. Church choirs and the nation's love of sport, from Australian rules football to weightlifting, are strong expressions of community life today.
summary.monuments: Command Ridge, the island's highest point, keeps Japanese guns and bunkers from the Second World War. Buada Lagoon, an inland freshwater lake fringed by palms, and the Moqua Well and caves are rare natural sites amid the mined landscape. The pinnacles of 'Topside', left by phosphate mining, are a stark monument to the island's history, and Anibare Bay is its most beautiful beach.

name: New Zealand

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Pacific and immigrant languages

people: About two-thirds of New Zealanders have European (Pākehā) heritage, around 17–18% are Māori, about 17% Asian and about 9% Pacific peoples, with Auckland one of the world's largest Polynesian cities. Roughly half now report no religion, while about a third are Christian, alongside growing Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist and Sikh communities and Māori Christian movements such as Rātana and Ringatū. Most people live in cities, and a large diaspora lives in Australia.
resources: Fertile pasture supporting world-leading dairy, meat and wool exports
Forests, horticulture (kiwifruit, apples, wine) and seafood
Spectacular landscapes driving tourism and film-making
Abundant renewable energy, especially hydro and geothermal
Māori culture, language revival and the Treaty settlement process
A tradition of social innovation, from women's suffrage to welfare reform
struggles: A housing affordability crisis and homelessness
Persistent inequities in health, income, education and imprisonment for Māori and Pacific peoples
Child poverty and family violence
Climate impacts such as severe floods and storms, as seen in Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023
Mental health needs and high youth suicide rates
Earthquake and volcanic risk
prayFor: For honour, healing and partnership between Māori and the Crown, keeping faith with Te Tiriti o Waitangi
For families struggling with housing costs, poverty and violence, for safe homes and support
For young people facing mental distress, that they find help, hope and belonging
For communities rebuilding after floods, cyclones and earthquakes
For welcome and unity among people of every culture and faith, remembering the victims of the 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks

summary.history: Polynesian voyagers reached Aotearoa around 1250–1300 CE, and their descendants became the Māori iwi (tribes), with rich traditions of carving, oratory and land-based kinship. Abel Tasman sighted the islands in 1642 and James Cook charted them in 1769, after which sealers, whalers, missionaries and settlers arrived, along with disease and the inter-tribal Musket Wars. In 1840 the Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi) was signed between the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, but differing understandings and land hunger led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s–1870s and vast land confiscations. New Zealand pioneered women's suffrage in 1893, fought in both world wars, and since the 1970s has seen Māori cultural renewal and Treaty settlements. It also experienced the 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks, which killed 51 people and led to new firearms laws.
summary.politicalHistory: New Zealand became a British colony in 1841, gained responsible government in the 1850s, and became a Dominion in 1907; it adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947, marking full legislative independence. It is a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a governor-general, and no single written constitution. The upper house was abolished in 1950, the Waitangi Tribunal was set up in 1975 to hear Treaty claims, and mixed-member proportional representation (MMP) was adopted by referendum in 1993, first used in 1996, with dedicated Māori electorates continuing.
summary.art: Māori art forms include whakairo (carving), tā moko (tattoo), kapa haka performance with the haka, raranga (weaving), and the decorated wharenui (meeting houses). Literature includes Katherine Mansfield, Janet Frame, Witi Ihimaera, Keri Hulme and Patricia Grace, and painters such as Colin McCahon and Rita Angus shaped modern art. Music ranges from Māori waiata to globally successful bands and singers, and film-making has won wide acclaim.
summary.monuments: Tongariro National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site for both natural and cultural reasons, holds volcanic peaks sacred to Ngāti Tūwharetoa. Te Wāhipounamu in the southwest, including Fiordland and Aoraki/Mount Cook, is another UNESCO site of glaciers and fjords. The Waitangi Treaty Grounds, where the Treaty was signed, and Te Papa Tongarewa, the national museum in Wellington, are central to the nation's story.

name: Palau

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Sonsorolese and Tobian in the southwest islands; Japanese is official in Angaur state

people: About seven in ten residents are Palauans, whose society is matrilineal and organised through clans and traditional chiefs, alongside Filipino, Chinese, Bangladeshi and other workers and smaller Micronesian communities. Most are Christian — Catholic (roughly 45%) and Protestant — and some follow Modekngei, a Palauan faith that blends tradition and Christianity. Most people live in and around Koror, and many Palauans live in Guam, Hawaiʻi and the US mainland.
resources: Some of the world's richest coral reefs, lagoons and marine life
The Palau National Marine Sanctuary covering most of its ocean zone
Tourism, especially diving and eco-tourism
Compact of Free Association funding with the United States
Matrilineal clan traditions and respected chiefly councils
A pioneering conservation ethic, including the Palau Pledge for visitors
struggles: Dependence on tourism and outside funding, as shown by the collapse of visitors during COVID-19
Coral bleaching, sea-level rise and stronger storms
High rates of obesity, diabetes and other non-communicable diseases
Reliance on imported food, fuel and foreign labour, and fair treatment of migrant workers
Pressure from great-power rivalry in the western Pacific
prayFor: For the protection of Palau's reefs and ocean, and wisdom in caring for them
For good health and healthy food for families affected by diabetes and heart disease
For migrant workers, for fair wages, dignity and safety
For Palauans at home and abroad, that their language and traditions stay strong
For peace and freedom in the western Pacific

summary.history: Palau was settled around 3,000 years ago or more, and its people built terraced hillsides, stone villages and a society of clans and chiefs that traded stone money to Yap. Spain claimed the islands in the 19th century and sold them to Germany in 1899; Japan ruled from 1914, making Koror the capital of its South Seas Mandate and settling thousands of Japanese. In 1944 the Battle of Peleliu between US and Japanese forces killed over ten thousand soldiers and devastated the island. After the war Palau became part of the US-administered UN Trust Territory, and after a long debate over its nuclear-free constitution it became independent in free association with the US in 1994. Today it is known for its marine conservation leadership.
summary.politicalHistory: Palau adopted the world's first nuclear-free constitution in 1981 and became a self-governing republic, with Haruo Remeliik as first president; he was assassinated in 1985. Because the constitution's nuclear ban conflicted with the proposed Compact of Free Association, eight referendums were held before the Compact was approved in 1993, and Palau became independent on 1 October 1994. It is a presidential republic with a bicameral National Congress (Olbiil Era Kelulau), a Council of Chiefs advising on custom, and sixteen states; the capital moved from Koror to Ngerulmud in 2006. Palau maintains diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
summary.art: Palauan storyboards, carved wooden panels that grew from the painted beams of the bai (men's meeting houses), illustrate legends and history. Traditional arts include women's money of turtleshell and Palauan bead money, weaving, chants and dances performed at ceremonies such as first-birth celebrations. Oral history and chants record clan origins, and Palauan contemporary artists and musicians blend these traditions with modern styles.
summary.monuments: The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon, a UNESCO World Heritage site, contains hundreds of forested limestone islands, marine lakes such as Jellyfish Lake, and ancient village sites. The Bai of Airai, one of the oldest surviving men's meeting houses, and the Badrulchau stone monoliths in Ngarchelong reflect ancient Palauan society. Peleliu's battlefield relics and memorials recall the Second World War, and the Belau National Museum in Koror, the oldest museum in Micronesia, keeps the nation's heritage.

name: Papua New Guinea

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue) — the most linguistically diverse country on earth; PNG Sign Language is also official

people: Papua New Guinea is home to over a thousand distinct cultural groups — Highlanders, coastal and island peoples, and the communities of Bougainville, New Britain and the Sepik — bound by clan, land and the wantok system of mutual obligation. Over 95% identify as Christian (Catholic, Lutheran, United, Seventh-day Adventist, Pentecostal and evangelical churches), often woven together with traditional beliefs. About 87% live in rural villages, many reachable only by air, foot or boat.
resources: Liquefied natural gas (PNG LNG) and oil
Gold and copper mines such as Lihir, Ok Tedi and Porgera
One of the world's largest remaining tropical rainforests and remarkable biodiversity
Coffee, cocoa, palm oil and fisheries
Unparalleled cultural and linguistic diversity
Customary land ownership that keeps most land in community hands
struggles: Tribal fighting in the Highlands, worsened by modern firearms
Very high levels of gender-based violence and accusations of sorcery leading to attacks
Weak health services, with high maternal mortality, tuberculosis and malaria
Poor roads and infrastructure, leaving many communities isolated
Corruption and unequal sharing of resource wealth, including land disputes over mines and logging
Natural disasters such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and the 2024 Enga landslide
prayFor: For peace between clans in the Highlands and an end to cycles of revenge
For women and girls, and all accused of sorcery, for safety, justice and dignity
For health workers and communities, for clinics, medicines and safe childbirth
For honest leadership and fair sharing of land and resource wealth
For the people of Bougainville as they work toward their future peacefully

summary.history: People reached New Guinea at least 50,000 years ago, and at Kuk in the Highlands people began cultivating plants about 10,000 years ago, among the world's earliest farmers. Over thousands of years, hundreds of societies developed across the island and its seas, linked by trade networks such as the Motu hiri and the kula ring. In the 1880s Germany took the northeast and Britain the southeast (Papua), which Australia administered from 1906; Australia also took German New Guinea after the First World War, and the Highlands' large populations were contacted by outsiders only in the 1930s. During the Second World War, battles along the Kokoda Track and elsewhere caused great suffering, and Papua New Guineans served as carriers and soldiers. PNG became independent in 1975, and the 1988–1998 Bougainville conflict over the Panguna mine cost thousands of lives before a peace agreement and a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly for independence.
summary.politicalHistory: Papua and New Guinea were administered together by Australia after the Second World War, gaining self-government in 1973 and independence on 16 September 1975 under Michael Somare. PNG is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a governor-general, and a single-chamber National Parliament that elects the prime minister. Politics has been marked by shifting coalitions and no-confidence motions, and the Autonomous Region of Bougainville has its own government under the 2001 peace agreement. Talks on Bougainville's political future after the 2019 referendum continue.
summary.art: PNG's art traditions include carved spirit figures and haus tambaran (spirit houses) of the Sepik, Highland body decoration and wigmanship seen at sing-sings, and the bark cloth and clay pots of the coasts. Masks, shields, bilums (string bags) and kundu drums are made across the country, and the Goroka and Mount Hagen shows bring together many cultural groups. Contemporary artists such as Mathias Kauage and writers such as Vincent Eri, whose The Crocodile was the first PNG novel, have brought these worlds to wider audiences.
summary.monuments: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site in the Western Highlands is a UNESCO World Heritage site, recording some of the earliest farming on earth. The Kokoda Track and Bomana War Cemetery honour those who died in the Second World War. Parliament House in Port Moresby, built in the shape of a Sepik haus tambaran, and the National Museum and Art Gallery celebrate the nation's cultures, while the volcanoes around Rabaul show the force of nature.

name: Samoa

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Samoan is spoken by almost everyone

people: Nearly all residents are ethnic Samoans, living by faʻa Sāmoa — the Samoan way — with extended families (ʻaiga) led by matai (chiefs) and village councils. Christianity is central to life, with Congregational, Catholic, Methodist, Latter-day Saint and Assemblies of God churches all strong. Most people live in villages on Upolu and Savaiʻi, and more Samoans live abroad, in New Zealand, Australia and the US, than at home.
resources: A living culture of faʻa Sāmoa and strong extended families
Remittances from a large diaspora
Tourism built on beaches, reefs and village hospitality
Agriculture: taro, coconut, cocoa, nonu and fisheries
Customary land held by families, about 80% of all land
Sporting talent in rugby and other codes
struggles: Dependence on remittances and aid, and few formal jobs for young people
Very high rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease
Cyclones, tsunamis and sea-level rise threatening coastal villages
Gaps in health care, as the 2019 measles epidemic, which killed 83 people, mostly children, made painfully clear
Family violence and its toll on women and children
prayFor: For families still grieving the children lost in the 2019 measles epidemic, and for strong health services
For good health and healthy food in a nation burdened by diabetes and heart disease
For coastal villages facing cyclones and rising seas
For safety and peace in every home, for women and children especially
For young Samoans at home and abroad, for work, faith and belonging

summary.history: Lapita voyagers settled Samoa around 3,000 years ago, and Samoa became one of the cradles of Polynesian culture, with powerful chiefly titles and links to Tonga and Fiji. European missionaries arrived in 1830, and by the late 19th century rival chiefs and the competing interests of Germany, Britain and the US led to civil wars. In 1899–1900 the islands were divided: the east became American Samoa, while Germany took Western Samoa, which New Zealand occupied in 1914. Under New Zealand rule, the 1918 influenza epidemic killed about a fifth of the population, and the nonviolent Mau movement for self-rule was met with violence on 'Black Saturday' in 1929, when its leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III was shot. Western Samoa became independent in 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so in the 20th century, and New Zealand formally apologised in 2002.
summary.politicalHistory: Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962 under joint heads of state Malietoa Tanumafili II and Tupua Tamasese Meaʻole, with Fiamē Mataʻafa Faumuina Mulinuʻu II as first prime minister. It is a parliamentary democracy in which the Legislative Assembly elects a head of state (O le Ao o le Malo) for five-year terms, and the prime minister leads the government. Only matai could vote until universal suffrage was introduced in 1990, though only matai may still stand for parliament; the country dropped 'Western' from its name in 1997. A constitutional crisis after the 2021 election was resolved by the courts, leading to a peaceful change of government.
summary.art: Samoa is known for its tatau (tattoo) — the pe'a for men and malu for women — which gave the world the word 'tattoo'. Siapo (barkcloth), fine mats ('ie tōga) given at ceremonies, the siva dance, fire-knife dancing and choral singing are central to culture. Writers such as Albert Wendt and Sia Figiel, and many artists and musicians in the diaspora, have made Samoan voices known worldwide.
summary.monuments: Vailima, the home of Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson (Tusitala) above Apia, is now a museum, and his tomb stands on Mount Vaea. Pulemelei Mound on Savaiʻi is the largest ancient stone structure in Polynesia. The To Sua Ocean Trench, the Alofaaga Blowholes and the lava fields of Savaiʻi show Samoa's dramatic natural landscape, and the Mulinuʻu peninsula holds Parliament House and royal tombs.

name: Solomon Islands

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), mostly Melanesian plus some Polynesian outlier languages

people: About 95% of Solomon Islanders are Melanesian, from many island cultures such as Malaita, Guadalcanal, Makira and Western Province, with Polynesian communities on islands such as Rennell, Bellona and Tikopia and a Micronesian (Gilbertese) community. Over 95% are Christian — Anglican (Church of Melanesia), Catholic, South Seas Evangelical, United Church and Seventh-day Adventist — and the churches are central to village and national life. About three-quarters live in rural villages, with Honiara growing rapidly.
resources: Tropical forests and timber
Rich tuna fisheries
Gold and nickel deposits
Coral reefs, lagoons and Second World War wrecks for diving
Customary land and strong village and church communities
Traditional knowledge, including shell money and canoe-building
struggles: Unsustainable logging and its damage to forests, rivers and reefs
Youth unemployment and rapid, unplanned urban growth in Honiara
Political instability and unrest, including the 2021 Honiara riots
Malaria, poor sanitation and gaps in health and education services
Sea-level rise and cyclones threatening coastal and artificial islands
Lingering tensions between island groups from the 1998–2003 conflict
prayFor: For peace and reconciliation between people of Guadalcanal, Malaita and all the islands
For young people, for work, education and hope
For care of the forests and reefs on which communities depend
For health, clean water and protection from malaria
For honest leadership that serves the common good

summary.history: People reached the Solomon Islands at least 30,000 years ago, and Austronesian voyagers arrived about 3,000 years ago, giving rise to many distinct island societies. The Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña arrived in 1568, but sustained contact came in the 19th century, when 'blackbirding' recruiters took thousands of islanders, often by deceit or force, to plantations in Queensland and Fiji. Britain declared a protectorate in 1893, and during the Second World War the Guadalcanal campaign of 1942–43 was one of the war's most brutal battles, with Solomon Islanders serving as scouts and coastwatchers. The country became independent in 1978, but ethnic tensions between people of Guadalcanal and Malaita erupted in conflict from 1998 to 2003, which ended with the arrival of the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI). Today it is rebuilding its institutions and economy.
summary.politicalHistory: The British Solomon Islands Protectorate gained self-government in 1976 and became independent on 7 July 1978, with Peter Kenilorea as first prime minister. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a governor-general, and a single-chamber National Parliament elected every four years that chooses the prime minister. Governments have often changed through no-confidence votes, and in 2000 an armed group forced the prime minister to resign, before RAMSI restored order from 2003 to 2017. In 2019 the country switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the People's Republic of China, followed by a security agreement in 2022, while maintaining ties with Australia and other partners.
summary.art: Solomon Islands' traditions include the panpipe ensembles of 'Are'are and other Malaitan communities, shell money made in Langa Langa Lagoon, and carvings with mother-of-pearl inlay, such as canoe-prow figureheads (nguzunguzu) from Western Province. Woven baskets, mats and dances also tell the stories of each island. Writers such as John Saunana and Celo Kulagoe and contemporary musicians have carried these cultures to new audiences.
summary.monuments: East Rennell, the southern part of the world's largest raised coral atoll, is a UNESCO World Heritage site, now listed as in danger because of logging and invasive species. The Guadalcanal American Memorial on Skyline Ridge and the Bloody Ridge battlefield recall the Second World War. The artificial islands of Langa Langa and Lau lagoons in Malaita and the skull shrines of Roviana Lagoon in Western Province reflect ancient traditions.

name: Tonga

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); also Niuafoʻou in the far north

people: Nearly all residents are Tongans, a Polynesian people with a strong sense of rank, respect (fakaʻapaʻapa) and family obligation, alongside small Chinese, European and other Pacific communities. Christianity shapes daily life, with Methodist (Free Wesleyan) churches the largest, followed by Latter-day Saints, Catholics and other denominations, and Sunday is kept as a day of rest by law. About three-quarters live on Tongatapu, and a diaspora about as large as the home population lives in New Zealand, Australia and the US.

basics.say: AH-loo AH / NOH-foh AH (to one leaving / one staying)

resources: Remittances from a large and generous diaspora
Fisheries and agriculture, including squash, vanilla, kava and root crops
Whale-watching and marine tourism around Vavaʻu and Haʻapai
A deep cultural heritage of the monarchy, nobility and ceremony
Strong family and church networks
Rugby and athletic talent known around the world
struggles: Some of the world's highest rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease
Heavy dependence on remittances and emigration of young people
Volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, cyclones and sea-level rise, as seen after the 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption
A growing methamphetamine problem linked to regional drug trafficking
Limited jobs and high debt
prayFor: For communities still rebuilding after the 2022 eruption and tsunami, and protection from future disasters
For families affected by diabetes and heart disease, for health and long life
For young people and families harmed by drugs, for healing and recovery
For Tongans abroad and at home, that the bonds of family and faith stay strong
For wise and just leadership serving all Tongans

summary.history: Lapita voyagers settled Tonga about 3,000 years ago, and from around the 10th century the Tuʻi Tonga dynasty built a maritime chiefdom whose influence reached Samoa, Fiji and beyond. Later, power was shared among the Tuʻi Tonga, Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua and Tuʻi Kanokupolu lines, and civil wars in the late 18th and early 19th centuries followed contact with Europeans such as Abel Tasman (1643) and James Cook, who called them the 'Friendly Islands'. Methodist missionaries gained a strong following, and Tāufaʻāhau, baptised as George Tupou I, unified the islands by 1845 and gave Tonga a constitution in 1875. Tonga was never formally colonised, though it was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970. In 2022 a massive underwater volcanic eruption and tsunami devastated parts of the kingdom.
summary.politicalHistory: King George Tupou I unified Tonga and issued the 1875 constitution, creating one of the world's longest-lasting constitutional monarchies, and in 1900 Tonga became a British protected state while keeping its own government. It regained full independence in 1970 under Queen Sālote's son, King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV, and joined the Commonwealth. A democracy movement grew from the 1980s, and after riots in Nukuʻalofa in 2006, reforms in 2010 gave the people a majority of elected seats in the Legislative Assembly, with nobles holding the rest. Tonga is now a constitutional monarchy with a prime minister chosen by parliament.
summary.art: Tongan culture is famous for ngatu (tapa cloth), fine mats (kie) given at weddings and funerals, and the lakalaka, a group dance-poem recognised by UNESCO as part of humanity's intangible heritage. Poetry, oratory and choral singing are highly valued, and Queen Sālote Tupou III was a respected composer of poems and songs. Epeli Hauʻofa and Konai Helu Thaman are among Tonga's best-known writers and thinkers.
summary.monuments: The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon, a massive stone gateway built around 1200 CE, is Tonga's most famous ancient monument. The Langi, terraced royal tombs at Lapaha (Muʻa), mark the old capital of the Tuʻi Tonga, and the Royal Palace in Nukuʻalofa is a symbol of the monarchy. The Mapuʻa ʻa Vaea blowholes and the islands of Vavaʻu, where humpback whales come each year, show Tonga's natural beauty.

name: Tuvalu

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Gilbertese on Nui

people: Tuvaluans are a Polynesian people, with Micronesian (Gilbertese) heritage on Nui, whose life centres on the island community, the falekaupule (council of elders) and the sea. The Church of Tuvalu (Congregational) is the faith of most people, with smaller Seventh-day Adventist, Bahá'í, Brethren and Catholic communities. About 60% live on Funafuti, and many Tuvaluans also live in New Zealand, Fiji and Australia.
resources: A large ocean zone with tuna fishing licence revenue
Income from the '.tv' internet domain
The Tuvalu Trust Fund, built with partner nations
Close-knit island communities and the falekaupule system
Seafarers trained at the national maritime school
Fatele dance and song traditions
struggles: Sea-level rise, king tides and erosion threatening atolls whose highest point is only about 4–5 metres above sea level
Scarce fresh water and reliance on rain and desalination
Limited land and crowding on Funafuti
High rates of non-communicable diseases due to imported food
Isolation and few jobs, driving emigration
prayFor: For the people of Tuvalu as the sea rises, that they may keep their land, culture and sovereignty
For fresh water and food security on every island
For good health for families affected by diabetes and heart disease
For young Tuvaluans, for education and meaningful work
For the world's nations to act justly and urgently on climate change

summary.history: Tuvalu's nine islands were settled by Polynesian voyagers, mainly from Samoa and Tonga, perhaps 2,000 or more years ago, and each island developed its own community life. In 1863 Peruvian slave raiders took hundreds of people from Funafuti and Nukulaelae, almost none of whom returned, devastating those islands. Samoan pastors of the London Missionary Society brought Christianity, and Britain declared a protectorate in 1892, later joining the islands to the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony. During the Second World War US forces built bases on Funafuti, Nanumea and Nukufetau, leaving pits that still scar Funafuti. After a 1974 referendum the Ellice Islands separated from the Gilberts and became independent as Tuvalu in 1978; today it is one of the nations most threatened by sea-level rise.
summary.politicalHistory: Following the 1974 referendum, the Ellice Islands became a separate colony in 1975 and then independent Tuvalu on 1 October 1978, with Toaripi Lauti as first prime minister. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a governor-general, and a 16-member parliament that elects the prime minister. There are no formal political parties, and island councils (falekaupule) play a central role in local governance; in 2023 Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty with Australia, covering climate mobility and security.
summary.art: Fatele, a dance and song form performed with rising tempo and box drumming, is at the heart of Tuvaluan celebrations. Traditional crafts include woven pandanus mats and fans, shell necklaces and canoe building. Oral history, chants and church singing keep each island's identity alive.
summary.monuments: The Funafuti Conservation Area protects lagoon reefs, islets and seabirds. Second World War remains, including the old airstrip and wrecked aircraft on Funafuti and Nanumea, recall the island's wartime role. The maneapa (community meeting halls) and churches of each island remain the heart of community life.

name: Vanuatu

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue) — one of the world's highest densities of languages per person

people: About 99% of the people are ni-Vanuatu, Melanesians from some 65 inhabited islands with diverse cultures, kastom (custom) and chiefly systems, plus small French, Chinese, Vietnamese and other communities. Most are Christian — Presbyterian, Anglican, Catholic, Seventh-day Adventist and Church of Christ — while some communities, such as on Tanna, keep kastom beliefs or follow movements like John Frum. About three-quarters live in rural villages, relying on gardens and fishing.
resources: Fertile volcanic soils supporting kava, copra, cocoa, coffee and organic beef
Tourism built on volcanoes, reefs, cruise visits and diving
Seasonal workers in Australia and New Zealand and their remittances
Rich fisheries and marine life
Vibrant kastom culture and community life
Customary land held by families and clans
struggles: Frequent cyclones, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, including Cyclone Pam (2015) and two cyclones in 2023
Political instability, with frequent changes of government through no-confidence votes
Gaps in health, education and infrastructure, especially on outer islands
Rising non-communicable diseases as diets change
Land disputes and concerns about the sale of citizenship
prayFor: For protection and recovery for communities struck by cyclones, earthquakes and eruptions
For stable, honest government that serves all the islands
For schools, clinics and roads reaching even the most remote villages
For families separated by seasonal work, that they be treated fairly and return home safely
For the preservation of Vanuatu's languages, kastom and land

summary.history: Lapita voyagers reached Vanuatu around 3,000 years ago — the Teouma cemetery on Efate holds some of their oldest known remains — and over time hundreds of distinct island societies developed. The Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós arrived in 1606, and James Cook named the islands the New Hebrides in 1774. In the 19th century, sandalwood traders and 'blackbirding' recruiters took tens of thousands of islanders to plantations in Queensland, Fiji and New Caledonia, while introduced diseases caused severe population loss. From 1906 Britain and France ruled jointly through an Anglo-French Condominium with dual systems of law, schools and police, which many called 'Pandemonium'. Vanuatu became independent in 1980, and in recent years has faced repeated cyclones and become a leading voice on climate justice.
summary.politicalHistory: A nationalist movement led by the Vanua'aku Pati grew in the 1970s, and Vanuatu became independent on 30 July 1980, with Father Walter Lini as first prime minister. A secessionist rebellion on Espiritu Santo, led by Jimmy Stevens, was put down with help from Papua New Guinean troops shortly after independence. Vanuatu is a parliamentary republic in which an electoral college chooses a ceremonial president, parliament elects the prime minister, and a National Council of Chiefs (Malvatumauri) advises on custom. Frequent no-confidence votes have produced many changes of government, and in 2023 the country led a successful UN General Assembly resolution asking the International Court of Justice for an advisory opinion on climate change.
summary.art: Vanuatu is known for its sand drawings, recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage, the towering tamtam slit drums of Ambrym and Malekula, and the naghol land-diving ritual on Pentecost. Masks, carved figures, woven mats and grade-taking ceremonies express kastom across the islands. Writers such as Grace Mera Molisa, a poet and campaigner, and the string band music heard in every village are also central to national culture.
summary.monuments: Chief Roi Mata's Domain on Efate, Lelepa and Artok, a UNESCO World Heritage site, preserves the home, death place and burial site of a 17th-century paramount chief. Mount Yasur on Tanna is one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes. The Vanuatu Cultural Centre in Port Vila keeps the nation's heritage, and Million Dollar Point on Espiritu Santo and the SS President Coolidge wreck recall the Second World War.

name: Algeria

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Algerian Arabic (Darja) is the everyday tongue, French is widely used in business and education

people: Most Algerians are of mixed Arab and Amazigh (Berber) heritage, with strong Amazigh identities among the Kabyle, Chaoui, Mozabite and Tuareg peoples. Around 99% are Sunni Muslim, with small Christian and Jewish communities. Roughly three-quarters live in cities along the Mediterranean coast, while the vast Sahara is thinly settled; a large diaspora lives in France.
resources: Natural gas and oil
Sahara solar potential
Phosphates and iron ore
A young, educated population
Amazigh and Arab-Andalusian cultural heritage
Mediterranean coastline and desert landscapes
struggles: Heavy dependence on hydrocarbon revenues
High youth unemployment and emigration pressure
Water scarcity and desertification
Limited space for political expression and press freedom
Bureaucracy and a small private sector outside energy
prayFor: Meaningful work and hope for Algeria's many young people
Wisdom to build an economy beyond oil and gas
Water for farms and cities in a drying climate
Healing of memories from the war of independence and the 1990s civil conflict
Freedom and dignity for every voice in public life

summary.history: Amazigh peoples have lived across this land for millennia, leaving rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer; Numidian kingdoms rose before Roman rule, and Augustine of Hippo was born here. Arab conquest from the 7th century brought Islam and Arabic, followed by Amazigh dynasties and later Ottoman rule from Algiers. France invaded in 1830 and ruled for 132 years, seizing land and settling Europeans while Algerians faced dispossession and violent repression of revolts. The war of independence (1954–1962) cost hundreds of thousands of lives and ended in independence in 1962. The 1990s brought a brutal civil conflict between the state and armed Islamist groups in which perhaps 150,000–200,000 people died.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence in 1962 was led by the National Liberation Front (FLN), which ruled as a single party under Ahmed Ben Bella and then Houari Boumediene after a 1965 coup. Multiparty politics arrived in 1989, but the army cancelled the 1992 elections that Islamists were poised to win, triggering civil war. Abdelaziz Bouteflika governed from 1999 until mass peaceful protests, the Hirak, led to his resignation in 2019. Algeria is a presidential republic in which the military remains highly influential.
summary.art: Algerian music ranges from Andalusian nouba and Kabyle song to raï, the Oran-born genre carried worldwide by artists such as Cheikha Rimitti and Khaled. Literature flourishes in Arabic, Tamazight and French, from Kateb Yacine and Mohammed Dib to Assia Djebar. Crafts include Kabyle silver jewellery, Berber pottery and carpets, and the miniature painting of Mohammed Racim.
summary.monuments: The Casbah of Algiers, a UNESCO site, preserves an Ottoman-era hillside city that was also a centre of the independence struggle. Roman ruins at Timgad, Djémila and Tipasa are among the best-preserved in North Africa. The M'zab Valley's fortified ksour and the rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer, both UNESCO sites, reveal centuries of desert ingenuity, while the Maqam Echahid in Algiers honours those who died for independence.

name: Angola

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Portuguese is official and the first language of many city dwellers

people: The largest peoples are the Ovimbundu of the central highlands, the Ambundu around Luanda, and the Bakongo in the north, alongside Lunda-Chokwe, Nyaneka, Ovambo, San and mixed-heritage (mestiço) communities. Most Angolans are Christian — roughly 40% Catholic and many Protestant and independent churches — often woven with traditional beliefs. The population is very young and increasingly urban, with Luanda home to around a fifth of all Angolans.
resources: Offshore oil
Diamonds
Fertile highlands and abundant rivers
Hydropower potential
Atlantic fisheries
A young, resilient population
struggles: Dependence on oil exports and exposure to price swings
Deep inequality and urban poverty despite resource wealth
Legacy of landmines and war damage
Recurring drought and hunger in the south
Corruption and weak public services
prayFor: Fair sharing of Angola's wealth so families can thrive
Rain and food security for drought-hit communities in the south
Safe land for farmers as landmines are cleared
Good schools and clinics for a very young nation
Continued healing and reconciliation after decades of war

summary.history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled the region over many centuries, forming states such as the Kingdom of Kongo and the Kingdom of Ndongo. Portuguese traders arrived in 1483, and for over three centuries Angola was one of the largest sources of enslaved Africans shipped to Brazil and the Americas. Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted Portuguese expansion in the 17th century, but colonial control spread inland in the late 1800s. An armed struggle for independence began in 1961, and independence in 1975 was followed by a civil war that lasted until 2002 and killed hundreds of thousands.
summary.politicalHistory: Three movements — the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA — fought Portuguese rule and then each other, drawing in Cold War powers including Cuba, South Africa, the USSR and the United States. The MPLA declared independence in 1975 under Agostinho Neto and governed as a Marxist one-party state, later led by José Eduardo dos Santos for 38 years. A 1992 move to multiparty elections collapsed back into war, which ended in 2002 after the death of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi. Angola is a presidential republic under a 2010 constitution, with the MPLA in power since independence.
summary.art: Angola gave the world semba, the forerunner of kizomba and kuduro, popularised by musicians such as Bonga. Literature includes the poetry of Agostinho Neto and the novels of Pepetela and José Eduardo Agualusa. Chokwe wood carving, especially the figure of the Pensador (Thinker), and sona sand drawings are signature visual traditions.
summary.monuments: Mbanza Kongo, the former capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Fortress of São Miguel in Luanda recalls the colonial era and the slave trade, while the National Slavery Museum near Luanda confronts that history directly. The Kalandula Falls, the Tundavala Gap and the desert landscapes of Iona National Park show the country's natural grandeur.

name: Benin

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official, Fon is widely spoken in the south

people: Benin's peoples include the Fon, Adja, Yoruba, Bariba, Fulani (Peul), Dendi and many smaller groups. Christians are roughly half the population, Muslims around a quarter, and Vodun is practised by many, often alongside other faiths; 10 January is a national Vodun day. Cotonou is the economic hub and seat of government, while much of the north remains rural.
resources: Cotton
Port of Cotonou and regional trade
Cashews and agriculture
Pendjari and W national parks
Vodun and royal cultural heritage
A vibrant creative and entrepreneurial community
struggles: Armed violence spreading into the northern border regions
Poverty and limited jobs outside farming and trade
