Narrowing space for political opposition
Coastal erosion and flooding
Gaps in health care and schooling in rural areas
prayFor: Safety and peace for families in the north
Livelihoods for farmers and young people
Open and peaceful public life
Protection for coastal communities from erosion and floods
Respect and harmony among Benin's many faiths

summary.history: The Kingdom of Dahomey, founded in the 17th century with its capital at Abomey, became a powerful state known for its royal arts and its women soldiers. Dahomey and the port of Ouidah were deeply involved in the Atlantic slave trade, through which many thousands of people were sold to European traders and carried to the Americas. France conquered Dahomey in 1892–1894 and ruled it as part of French West Africa. Independence came in 1960 as the Republic of Dahomey, renamed Benin in 1975.
summary.politicalHistory: After independence in 1960, Dahomey saw repeated coups until Mathieu Kérékou seized power in 1972 and established a Marxist-Leninist state. Economic crisis led to a landmark National Conference in 1990 that peacefully restored multiparty democracy, a model watched across Africa. Benin became known for regular peaceful handovers of power, though recent electoral rule changes have reduced opposition participation. It is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Dahomey's royal court produced appliqué cloth banners and bronze and iron sculpture, many of which were looted by France in 1892; some were returned in 2021. Vodun ceremonies, masks such as the Egungun and Zangbeto, and brass-band and Afro-funk music, popularised by the Orchestre Poly-Rythmo, are central to cultural life. Singer Angélique Kidjo has carried Beninese music worldwide.
summary.monuments: The Royal Palaces of Abomey, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserve the history of the Dahomey kings in bas-relief. The Route des Esclaves in Ouidah ends at the Door of No Return, a memorial to those sold into the Atlantic slave trade. The stilt village of Ganvié on Lake Nokoué and the Tata Somba fortified houses of the Koutammakou landscape, shared with Togo, show remarkable vernacular architecture.

name: Botswana

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. Kalanga and several Khoisan languages

people: Most citizens are Batswana, alongside Bakalanga, Basarwa (San), Herero, Bayeyi, Hambukushu and others. Christianity is the majority faith (roughly 80%), with Badimo traditional belief also present. Around 70% live in towns and the more fertile east, while the Kalahari interior is sparsely populated.
resources: Diamonds
Okavango Delta and wildlife
Stable, well-governed institutions
Cattle ranching
Kalahari landscapes and cultural heritage
Solar energy potential
struggles: Over-reliance on diamond revenues as global demand weakens
High youth unemployment and inequality
HIV, still widespread despite major progress
Drought and water stress
Land and cultural rights of San communities
prayFor: New sources of work beyond diamonds for young Batswana
Continued healing and support for those living with HIV
Rain for herders and farmers
Dignity and secure land for San communities
Wise care of the Okavango and its wildlife

summary.history: San peoples have lived in the Kalahari for tens of thousands of years, leaving rock paintings at Tsodilo. Tswana-speaking chiefdoms spread across the region from around the 14th century onwards. Pressured by Boer expansion, Tswana leaders sought British protection, and the Bechuanaland Protectorate was declared in 1885. Botswana became independent in 1966 as one of the poorest countries in the world, and diamond discoveries soon after transformed its economy.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence in 1966 came peacefully under Seretse Khama, whose marriage to Englishwoman Ruth Williams had caused a political storm under colonial rule. Botswana has held regular multiparty elections ever since and is known for comparatively low corruption and prudent management of diamond revenues. The Botswana Democratic Party governed continuously for nearly six decades. It is a parliamentary republic with an executive president elected by the National Assembly and a House of Chiefs (Ntlo ya Dikgosi) advising on custom.
summary.art: Botswana is known for finely woven baskets made by Hambukushu and Bayeyi women from mokolwane palm, and for San crafts such as ostrich-shell beadwork. Music ranges from traditional choral singing to the guitar-based Setswana folk of artists such as Ratsie Setlhako and modern kwaito and gospel. The Kgotla, the community meeting place, is also a cultural institution of open dialogue.
summary.monuments: Tsodilo Hills, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, holds thousands of rock paintings and is sacred to the San and Hambukushu. The Okavango Delta, also UNESCO-listed, is one of the world's great inland deltas. Chobe National Park, the Makgadikgadi salt pans and the Three Dikgosi Monument in Gaborone, honouring three chiefs who travelled to London in 1895, are also important.

name: Burkina Faso

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French was demoted from official to working language in 2023

people: The Mossi are the largest people, alongside the Fulani (Peul), Gurunsi, Bobo, Lobi, Senufo, Gurma and many others. Around 60% are Muslim, roughly a quarter Christian, and traditional religion remains important; inter-faith family ties have long been common. Most people farm and herd in rural areas, though Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso are growing fast.
resources: Gold
Cotton
Shea and sesame
A rich film and arts tradition
Strong community solidarity
Solar potential
struggles: Armed insurgency that has killed thousands and displaced around two million people
Hunger, especially in blockaded towns
Closed schools and health centres in conflict zones
Military rule and restricted civic freedoms
Drought and land degradation
prayFor: Peace and protection for civilians caught in the violence
Food, shelter and return home for displaced families
Schools and clinics to reopen safely
Reconciliation between communities, including Fulani neighbours often wrongly blamed
Rain and fertile soil for farmers

summary.history: The Mossi kingdoms, centred on Ouagadougou, rose from around the 15th century and resisted neighbouring empires for centuries. France conquered the region in the 1890s and created the colony of Upper Volta, drawing heavily on its people for forced labour and as soldiers. Upper Volta became independent in 1960 and was renamed Burkina Faso, 'land of upright people', in 1984. Since 2015 an armed insurgency spreading from the Sahel has caused one of the world's fastest-growing displacement crises.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence in 1960 was followed by a succession of military coups. Captain Thomas Sankara took power in 1983, pursuing a revolutionary programme of self-reliance, women's rights and anti-corruption until he was killed in 1987 in a coup that brought Blaise Compaoré to power for 27 years. A popular uprising in 2014 ended Compaoré's rule and elections followed in 2015. Two military coups in 2022 brought an army-led transitional government, and in 2024 Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formed the Alliance of Sahel States after announcing their exit from ECOWAS.
summary.art: Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, Africa's largest film festival, founded in 1969, and directors such as Idrissa Ouédraogo and Gaston Kaboré won international acclaim. Masks of the Bwa, Mossi and Nuna peoples, bronze casting and Kassena painted architecture are signature arts. Music features the balafon, djembe and griot traditions alongside modern artists.
summary.monuments: The Ruins of Loropéni, stone walls linked to the trans-Saharan gold trade, were Burkina Faso's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. The painted earthen houses of the Kassena royal court at Tiébélé are celebrated for their geometric designs. The Grand Mosque of Bobo-Dioulasso, the Sindou Peaks and the W-Arly-Pendjari protected areas (shared UNESCO site) are also important.

name: Burundi

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); nearly everyone speaks Kirundi, an unusual unity of language

people: Burundians share the Kirundi language and culture across Hutu (the majority), Tutsi and Twa identities, which colonial rule hardened into rigid categories. Most are Christian, about two-thirds Catholic and many Protestant, with a small Muslim minority. Nearly nine in ten live in the countryside on small hillside farms, making Burundi one of Africa's most densely populated and least urbanised nations; economic activity centres on Bujumbura.
resources: Fertile volcanic soils
Lake Tanganyika and its fisheries
Coffee and tea
Nickel and rare-earth deposits
Drumming and oral heritage
A shared national language
struggles: Extreme poverty and chronic malnutrition
Land pressure in a densely populated, mostly rural country
Fuel and foreign-currency shortages
Legacy of ethnic violence and restricted political space
Flooding from rising Lake Tanganyika and other climate shocks
prayFor: Enough nourishing food for every child
Healing and trust between Hutu, Tutsi and Twa neighbours
Fair access to land and work for young families
Safety for those displaced by floods and landslides
Freedom and courage for those working for justice and truth

summary.history: The Kingdom of Burundi, ruled by a mwami (king), took shape by the 17th century in the hills east of Lake Tanganyika. Germany claimed it in the 1890s, and after the First World War Belgium governed Ruanda-Urundi, entrenching distinctions between Hutu and Tutsi. Burundi became independent in 1962 as a monarchy. Waves of mass killing followed — notably in 1972 and 1993 — and a civil war from 1993 to 2005 claimed around 300,000 lives.
summary.politicalHistory: The monarchy was overthrown in 1966 and a series of Tutsi-led military regimes followed. Melchior Ndadaye, the first democratically elected Hutu president, was assassinated in 1993, triggering civil war. The 2000 Arusha Accords set ethnic power-sharing quotas, and a new constitution in 2005 ended the transition. A 2015 crisis over presidential term limits led to violence and refugee flight; a 2018 constitution strengthened the presidency, and Gitega became the political capital in 2019.
summary.art: The royal drummers of Burundi, whose ritual dance is inscribed by UNESCO, are the nation's most famous art form. Oral poetry, proverbs and the inanga trough-zither accompany storytelling, alongside the umuduri musical bow. Basketry, woodcarving and pottery, including Twa ceramics, are cherished crafts.
summary.monuments: Gishora Drum Sanctuary near Gitega preserves the royal drumming tradition, and the National Museum in Gitega holds royal regalia. Kibira and Rusizi national parks protect mountain forest and wetlands. Lake Tanganyika's shoreline, the Karera waterfalls and the Livingstone–Stanley monument at Mugere are also notable, as is the source of the southernmost Nile tributary at Kasumo.

name: Cabo Verde

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Kriolu is the everyday language, Portuguese is official

people: Cabo Verdeans are mostly of mixed African and Portuguese descent, a Creole culture formed over five centuries. Around three-quarters are Catholic, with growing Protestant and other communities. Most live in towns on Santiago, São Vicente and Sal, and more Cabo Verdeans live abroad — in the US, Portugal and elsewhere — than at home.
resources: Strategic Atlantic location
Tourism and beaches
Ocean fisheries
Diaspora ties and remittances
Music and Creole culture
Strong democratic institutions
struggles: Scarce fresh water and recurring drought
Heavy reliance on imported food and fuel
Dependence on tourism and vulnerability to shocks
Youth emigration
Rising seas and coastal erosion
prayFor: Water and rain for the islands
Good work at home for young people
Strength for families separated by migration
Protection of fragile coastlines and fisheries
Continued peace and trust in public life

summary.history: The islands were uninhabited when Portuguese navigators arrived around 1456–1460. Ribeira Grande on Santiago became an early hub of the Atlantic slave trade, where enslaved Africans were held and traded on to the Americas. Isolation and droughts brought severe famines, with tens of thousands dying in the 18th–20th centuries and many emigrating. Cabo Verde became independent from Portugal in 1975.
summary.politicalHistory: The independence struggle was led jointly with Guinea-Bissau by the PAIGC under Amílcar Cabral, who was assassinated in 1973. After independence in 1975 the islands were ruled as a one-party state, splitting from Guinea-Bissau after a 1980 coup there and forming the PAICV. Multiparty elections in 1991 brought a peaceful change of government. Cabo Verde has since been one of Africa's most stable democracies, a semi-presidential republic.
summary.art: Morna, the melancholic song form sung by Cesária Évora, and its sister styles coladeira, funaná and batuque are at the heart of Cabo Verdean culture; morna is inscribed by UNESCO. Writers such as Baltasar Lopes and Germano Almeida explore island life and migration. Pano di terra woven cloth and Mindelo's carnival are treasured traditions.
summary.monuments: Cidade Velha (Ribeira Grande), a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was the first European colonial town in the tropics and a key site of the slave trade. The former Tarrafal prison camp recalls political prisoners held under Portugal's dictatorship. Fogo's active volcano, the green valleys of Santo Antão and Mindelo's colonial harbour town are also highlights.

name: Cameroon

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French and English are both official

people: Cameroon is home to over 250 peoples, including the Bamiléké, Beti-Pahuin, Fulani, Bamoun, Sawa (Duala) and Baka forest peoples, often called 'Africa in miniature'. Roughly 70% are Christian and about a quarter Muslim, mainly in the north, with traditional beliefs widely held. Over half live in cities such as Douala and Yaoundé; about a fifth live in the two English-speaking regions in the west.
resources: Oil, gas and timber
Cocoa, coffee and bananas
Port of Douala and regional trade
Rainforests and Mount Cameroon
Immense cultural and linguistic diversity
Entrepreneurial, highly educated diaspora

Boko Haram and ISWAP attacks in the Far North
Over a million people displaced inside the country
Corruption and long-concentrated political power

prayFor: Peace and dialogue in the Anglophone regions
Safety for families in the Far North
Children able to return to school
Fair and accountable leadership for all regions
Protection of forests and the peoples who live in them

summary.history: Bantu-speaking peoples are thought to have spread across Africa from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands thousands of years ago, and kingdoms such as Bamoun and the Fulani lamidates later flourished. Portuguese sailors named the Wouri river 'Rio dos Camarões' (river of prawns), giving the country its name. Germany colonised Kamerun in 1884; after the First World War it was divided between France and Britain. French Cameroun won independence in 1960 after a bloody repression of the UPC independence movement, and Southern British Cameroons joined it in 1961.
summary.politicalHistory: Ahmadou Ahidjo led the country from 1960, turning a federation into a unitary one-party state in 1972. His successor took office in 1982 and has governed ever since, one of the longest tenures in the world. Multiparty politics returned in 1990, though the ruling party has dominated elections, and presidential term limits were removed in 2008. Since 2016, grievances in the English-speaking regions escalated into armed conflict between separatist groups and the army.
summary.art: Cameroon's music includes makossa, popularised by Manu Dibango's 'Soul Makossa', and bikutsi from the Beti people. The royal courts of the Grassfields produce beaded thrones, masks and elaborate bronze, and the Bamoun king Njoya devised his own script, Shü-mom, around 1900. Writers include Mongo Beti, Ferdinand Oyono and Calixthe Beyala.
summary.monuments: The Dja Faunal Reserve and the Sangha Trinational, both UNESCO sites, protect vast rainforests. The Royal Palace of Foumban, the Bafut palace and the chiefdom compounds of the Grassfields preserve centuries of kingship. Mount Cameroon, West Africa's highest peak, and the Diamaré-Mandara highlands with the Diy-Gid-Biy archaeological sites are also important.

name: Central African Republic

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Sango is a national lingua franca spoken by most people

people: Peoples include the Gbaya, Banda, Mandjia, Sara, Mboum, Yakoma, Fulani and the Aka (BaAka) forest peoples. Most are Christian (around 80%), with a Muslim minority of roughly 10–15%, many in the northeast, and traditional beliefs widely held. Most people live rurally, and large numbers have been displaced or have fled to neighbouring countries.

Tropical forests and timber
Fertile land and rivers
Rich wildlife in Dzanga-Sangha
Aka polyphonic singing heritage
The shared Sango language

Hundreds of thousands displaced inside and outside the country
Among the world's lowest life expectancy and weakest health systems
Hunger and dependence on aid
Exploitation of mineral wealth by armed and foreign actors

Safe return home for displaced families
Clinics, medicines and skilled carers for every region
Christian and Muslim neighbours to live and rebuild together
Children to be protected and to go to school

summary.history: The region was home to diverse farming and forest peoples, and the 19th century brought devastating slave raids from Sudanese and Wadai-based traders. France colonised the territory as Ubangi-Shari, granting vast areas to concessionary companies that used brutal forced labour. Independence came in 1960 after nationalist leader Barthélemy Boganda died in a plane crash in 1959. The country has since faced repeated coups and conflict, most severely after 2013, when violence between Séléka and anti-balaka militias caused mass killing and displacement.
summary.politicalHistory: David Dacko became the first president in 1960 but was overthrown in 1966 by Jean-Bédel Bokassa, who crowned himself emperor in 1977 before being deposed with French help in 1979. Further coups followed, including in 2003 and 2013, when the Séléka coalition seized Bangui. A UN peacekeeping mission has operated since 2014, and a 2019 peace agreement with armed groups has only partly held. A 2023 referendum adopted a new constitution removing presidential term limits; the state is a presidential republic.
summary.art: The polyphonic singing of the Aka people is inscribed by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage. Butterfly-wing pictures, woodcarving and woven baskets are local crafts. Popular music draws on Congolese rumba, and Bangui has a lively scene of choirs and bands.
summary.monuments: Manovo-Gounda St Floris National Park and the Sangha Trinational, both UNESCO sites, protect savanna and rainforest wildlife including forest elephants and gorillas. The Dzanga Bai clearing draws hundreds of forest elephants. Bangui's Notre-Dame Cathedral and the Boali Falls are also landmarks, alongside the megaliths of Bouar.

name: Chad

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French and Arabic are official

people: Chad's peoples include the Sara in the south, Arab groups, the Kanembu, Kanuri, Toubou, Zaghawa, Maba, Hadjerai and many others. Roughly 55% are Muslim, mostly in the north and centre, and around 40% Christian, mostly in the south, with traditional beliefs present. Most people farm or herd, and Chad hosts well over a million refugees, including many from Sudan's Darfur.

Livestock and gum arabic
Lake Chad fisheries

Zakouma wildlife
Hospitable, resilient communities

Severe hunger and malnutrition

Nourishment for children facing malnutrition

Just, accountable leadership that serves all Chadians

summary.history: Rock art in the Ennedi and Tibesti records thousands of years of life when the Sahara was green, and 'Toumaï', a hominin fossil about seven million years old, was found here. The Kanem-Bornu Empire, from around the 9th century, and later the kingdoms of Baguirmi and Wadai controlled trans-Saharan trade, including in enslaved people. France conquered the region by 1920 as part of French Equatorial Africa. Independence in 1960 was followed by decades of civil war and conflict with Libya over the Aouzou Strip.
summary.politicalHistory: François Tombalbaye, the first president, created a one-party state and faced a northern rebellion from 1965; he was killed in a 1975 coup. Civil war and factional fighting followed, and Hissène Habré's rule (1982–1990) was marked by grave abuses for which he was later convicted in Senegal. Idriss Déby seized power in 1990 and ruled until his death in 2021, when a military council took over. A transition ended with a new constitution in 2023 and a presidential election in 2024.
summary.art: Chad's arts include the Sara people's music and dance, griot traditions and Arab-influenced poetry and song. Filmmaker Mahamat-Saleh Haroun has won international awards with films such as 'A Screaming Man'. Crafts include leatherwork, weaving, pottery and silver jewellery.
summary.monuments: The Ennedi Massif, with its sandstone arches and rock art, and the Lakes of Ounianga, a chain of desert lakes, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Zakouma National Park has seen a remarkable recovery of its elephant population. The Tibesti mountains, including Emi Koussi, the Sahara's highest peak, and the Guelta d'Archei with its desert crocodiles are also notable.

name: Comoros

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Comorian, French and Arabic are all official

people: Comorians are a blend of Bantu African, Arab, Malagasy and Persian (Shirazi) heritage, sharing Swahili-related Comorian language varieties on each island. Around 98% are Sunni Muslim, and Islam shapes daily life and the 'grand mariage' customs of Grande Comore. Most people live in villages on Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Anjouan (Ndzuani) and Mohéli (Mwali), and a large diaspora lives in France, especially Marseille.
resources: Vanilla, cloves and ylang-ylang
Coral reefs and fisheries
Volcanic landscapes
Diaspora ties and remittances
Swahili-Islamic cultural heritage
Coelacanth waters and marine biodiversity

Political instability and the legacy of many coups
Weak health care and electricity supply
Vulnerability to cyclones and rising seas

Decent work and hope at home for young Comorians

Unity and trust among the islands
Protection from cyclones and the sea

summary.history: The islands were settled by Bantu-speaking peoples and Austronesian seafarers over a thousand years ago and became part of the Swahili trading world, linked to Arabia, Persia and Madagascar. Sultanates competed across the islands, and slave trading connected them to the wider Indian Ocean. France took Mayotte in 1841 and the other islands later in the 19th century. In 1975 three islands declared independence, while Mayotte voted to remain French, a division still disputed.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence in 1975 was quickly followed by a coup, and the Comoros endured some 20 coups or attempts, several involving the French mercenary Bob Denard. In 1997 Anjouan and Mohéli tried to secede, leading to a 2001 constitution creating a federal Union with a presidency rotating between the islands. A 2018 referendum changed the rotation system and allowed longer presidential tenure. The Union of the Comoros is a presidential federal republic.
summary.art: Twarab music, blending Arab, Swahili and Comorian melodies, is a favourite at weddings, alongside dances such as the women's wadaha. Carved wooden doors, Swahili-style architecture and embroidered caps (kofia) are fine crafts. Writers such as Mohamed Toihiri and Ali Zamir have brought Comorian stories into literature.
summary.monuments: The old medina of Moroni and its Friday Mosque recall the islands' Swahili-Islamic past. The sultanate capitals of Itsandra and Iconi, and the citadel and mosques of Mutsamudu on Anjouan, preserve historic stone towns. Mount Karthala, one of the world's largest active volcanoes, and Mohéli Marine Park, home to nesting turtles, are natural treasures.

name: DR Congo

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official, with four national languages

people: More than 200 peoples live in the DRC, including the Luba, Mongo, Kongo and Lunda, the Mangbetu and Azande, and Batwa forest peoples. Around 90% are Christian — Catholic, Protestant and Kimbanguist and revival churches — with smaller Muslim and traditional communities. Kinshasa is among Africa's largest cities, though most Congolese still live in rural areas, and millions are displaced in the east.

The Congo Basin rainforest

Fertile land

Healing and justice for survivors of violence

summary.history: Bantu-speaking peoples built kingdoms here, including the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba and Lunda empires and the Kuba kingdom. From 1885 the territory was the personal possession of Belgium's King Leopold II, whose Congo Free State forced people to harvest rubber under a regime of terror in which millions died. Belgium annexed the colony in 1908 and ruled until hurried independence in 1960. Since the 1990s, wars in the east, linked to the aftermath of the Rwandan genocide and to mineral wealth, have caused millions of deaths through violence, hunger and disease.
summary.politicalHistory: Patrice Lumumba became the first prime minister in 1960 but was murdered in 1961 amid secession crises and foreign interference. Joseph-Désiré Mobutu seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire in 1971 and ruled until rebels led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila overthrew him in 1997. The First and Second Congo Wars (1996–2003) drew in many African states. A 2006 constitution and elections followed, and the 2018–2019 elections produced the first transfer of power between civilian presidents, though conflict in the east continues.
summary.art: Congolese rumba, inscribed by UNESCO, and its offspring soukous made stars of Franco, Tabu Ley Rochereau and Papa Wemba, shaping music across Africa. Traditional sculpture includes Kuba raffia textiles, Luba stools and headrests, and Kongo nkisi power figures. Painter Chéri Samba and the Kinshasa popular painting movement, along with the sapeurs' sartorial culture, are modern icons.
summary.monuments: Virunga National Park, Africa's oldest national park and home to mountain gorillas, is one of five UNESCO natural sites, along with Kahuzi-Biega, Garamba, Salonga and the Okapi Wildlife Reserve. The Congo River and its rapids near Kinshasa are among the world's most powerful. The Lumumba memorial in Kinshasa and the Nyiragongo volcano near Goma also hold deep significance.

name: Republic of the Congo

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official, Kituba and Lingala are national languages

people: The Kongo peoples form nearly half the population, alongside the Teke, Mbochi, Sangha and Indigenous forest peoples such as the Aka and Baka. Most are Christian — Catholic, Protestant and revival churches — with traditional beliefs often blended in and a small Muslim community. Around two-thirds live in cities, mostly Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire.

Tropical forests and timber
Peatlands of the Congo Basin

summary.history: The Kingdom of Loango on the coast and the Teke kingdom inland traded with Europeans from the 15th century, including in enslaved people. In 1880 the Teke king signed a treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, opening the way to French colonisation. As the capital of French Equatorial Africa, Brazzaville was also the base of Free France in the Second World War, while concession companies exploited the people harshly. Independence came in 1960, and civil wars in the 1990s caused great suffering, particularly in Brazzaville and the Pool region.
summary.politicalHistory: Fulbert Youlou, the first president, was toppled in 1963, and from 1969 the country became the Marxist-Leninist People's Republic of the Congo. A 1991 national conference restored multiparty politics and Pascal Lissouba won the 1992 election. Civil war in 1997 returned to power the leader who had ruled from 1979 to 1992. A 2015 constitutional referendum removed term and age limits; the state is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Brazzaville is a cradle of Congolese rumba, shared with Kinshasa across the river, and the Poto-Poto school of painting, founded in 1951, became internationally known. Writers include Sony Labou Tansi, Alain Mabanckou and Tchicaya U Tam'si. Teke and Kongo carving and Pygmy polyphonic song are deep traditions.
summary.monuments: The Sangha Trinational, a UNESCO site shared with Cameroon and the Central African Republic, protects forest elephants, gorillas and chimpanzees. Odzala-Kokoua National Park is one of Africa's oldest parks. The Basilica of Sainte-Anne in Brazzaville, the Loango slave port memorial and the Diosso Gorge are also important.

name: Côte d'Ivoire

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official, Dioula is a widespread trade language

people: Over 60 peoples live in Côte d'Ivoire, broadly grouped as Akan (including Baoulé), Voltaic (including Senufo), Mandé (including Malinke and Dan) and Kru, plus many people of Burkinabè and Malian origin. Roughly 40% are Muslim, mostly in the north, and about 40% Christian, mostly in the south, with traditional religions also practised. More than half live in cities, with Abidjan the economic heart.

Cashews, coffee and rubber
Port of Abidjan

Child labour on cocoa farms

Every child free to learn rather than labour
Peaceful elections and continued reconciliation
Protection for families in the northern border areas
Restoration of forests

summary.history: Akan, Mandé, Kru and Voltaic peoples built states such as the Kong Empire and the Baoulé and Abron kingdoms. European traders came for ivory and enslaved people, and France made the territory a colony in 1893, developing cocoa and coffee plantations through forced labour. Independence in 1960 was followed by two decades of strong growth known as the 'Ivorian miracle'. Disputes over national identity ('ivoirité') led to civil war in 2002–2007 and post-election violence in 2010–2011 in which around 3,000 people died.
summary.politicalHistory: Félix Houphouët-Boigny led Côte d'Ivoire from independence in 1960 until his death in 1993, under a one-party system until multiparty elections in 1990. A 1999 coup, a contested 2000 election and a 2002 rebellion split the country between north and south. The disputed 2010 election led to armed conflict before a new government took office in 2011. A 2016 constitution created a vice-presidency and senate; the state is a presidential republic, with Yamoussoukro the official capital and Abidjan the seat of most institutions.
summary.art: Ivorian music includes zouglou and coupé-décalé, born in Abidjan, and reggae stars such as Alpha Blondy. Baoulé and Dan masks, Senufo sculpture and Korhogo painted cloth are celebrated arts. Writers include Bernard Dadié and Ahmadou Kourouma, author of 'The Suns of Independence'.
summary.monuments: Grand-Bassam, the first colonial capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the Sudanese-style mosques of the north and the parks of Taï, Comoé and Mount Nimba. The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is among the largest churches in the world. The Plateau skyline of Abidjan and the Banco forest also mark the nation's identity.

name: Djibouti

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French and Arabic are official, Somali and Afar are most spoken

people: Djibouti's two main peoples are the Somali (mostly Issa) and the Afar, with Arab, Ethiopian and European communities. About 94% are Sunni Muslim, with a small Christian minority. Most people live in Djibouti City, while Afar and Somali pastoralists move through the arid interior; the country also hosts refugees and migrants crossing toward the Arabian Peninsula.

Ports and the railway to Addis Ababa

High unemployment and poverty outside the port economy

Food insecurity and heavy import dependence
Risks faced by migrants crossing to Yemen and the Gulf

Work and opportunity for young Djiboutians

Peace with neighbours in a volatile region
Open and fair public life

summary.history: Afar and Somali pastoralists have lived here for centuries, and the coast was linked to the ancient Land of Punt trade and later to Islamic sultanates such as Adal. France acquired Obock in 1862 and built Djibouti City in the 1880s–90s, creating French Somaliland. The railway to Addis Ababa, completed in 1917, made the port Ethiopia's main outlet to the sea. After referendums in 1958 and 1967 the territory, renamed the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas, became independent as Djibouti in 1977.
summary.politicalHistory: Hassan Gouled Aptidon became the first president in 1977 and ruled a one-party state from 1981. An Afar-led rebellion (1991–1994) and later fighting were ended by peace agreements, and limited multiparty politics was introduced in 1992. Gouled's chosen successor took office in 1999, and presidential term limits were removed in 2010. Djibouti is a presidential republic hosting several foreign military bases.
summary.art: Somali oral poetry and song are central, and the band Groupe RTD and singers such as Abdo Xamar have shaped Djiboutian music. Afar dance, ritual songs and the dhaanto dance of the Somali are performed at celebrations. Writer Abdourahman Waberi is internationally known, and woven mats and silver jewellery are traditional crafts.
summary.monuments: Lake Assal, the lowest point in Africa, and Lake Abbe, with its limestone chimneys, are striking natural wonders. The Day Forest on the Goda mountains and the Moucha and Maskali islands with their coral reefs are protected areas. In Djibouti City, the Hamoudi Mosque and the old European quarter around Place Menelik recall the city's history.

name: Equatorial Guinea

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); the only Spanish-speaking country in sub-Saharan Africa

people: The Fang make up the large majority, especially on the mainland (Río Muni), with the Bubi on Bioko island and Ndowe, Annobonese and Bujeba communities. Most people are Catholic, a legacy of Spanish rule, with Protestant and traditional beliefs also present. Most live in cities, especially Malabo and Bata.

Tropical forests

Fisheries

Freedom to speak and gather without fear

summary.history: Bantu peoples, including the Fang and Bubi, settled the mainland and Bioko over centuries. Portugal claimed the islands in the 15th century and ceded them to Spain in 1778; Bioko (Fernando Po) later became a centre of cocoa plantations worked by contracted labourers under harsh conditions. Spain governed the territory as Spanish Guinea until independence in 1968. Oil discoveries in the 1990s transformed the economy, but most citizens have seen little of the wealth.
summary.politicalHistory: Francisco Macías Nguema, the first president, imposed a brutal dictatorship (1968–1979) during which a large share of the population was killed or fled. He was overthrown in a 1979 coup by his nephew, who has led the country ever since. A multiparty system was formally introduced in 1991, but the ruling party dominates every institution. Equatorial Guinea is a presidential republic, with a new capital, Ciudad de la Paz, under construction on the mainland.
summary.art: Fang culture is known for its mvet epic poetry and harp-zither, its masks and its reliquary (byeri) figures. Bubi dances such as the balélé and Annobonese song are cherished traditions. Writers include Donato Ndongo and Juan Tomás Ávila Laurel, voices of Spanish-language African literature.
summary.monuments: Malabo's Spanish colonial old town and its twin-spired Cathedral of Santa Isabel are landmarks. Bioko's Caldera de Luba and Pico Basilé, and the beaches of Ureca where sea turtles nest, are natural treasures. On the mainland, Monte Alén National Park protects rainforest with gorillas and forest elephants.

name: Eritrea

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); nine recognised ethnic groups each have their own language

people: Nine recognised peoples live in Eritrea: Tigrinya and Tigre (together the large majority), Saho, Afar, Bilen, Hedareb, Kunama, Nara and Rashaida. Christians (mainly Eritrean Orthodox, with Catholics and Lutherans) and Sunni Muslims are roughly equal in number; other churches are restricted. Most people farm or herd, and a large share of young people have left the country, forming a sizeable diaspora.

Gold, copper, zinc and potash
Potential fisheries
Asmara's modernist architecture

Multi-faith heritage

Severe restrictions on freedom of speech, press and religion

Release and reunion for prisoners and their families

Freedom of faith for all believers

summary.history: The highlands were part of the ancient Aksumite kingdom, whose port at Adulis traded across the Red Sea, and the region later saw Ethiopian, Ottoman and Egyptian rule. Italy made Eritrea a colony in 1890, building Asmara and a railway, until Britain took control in 1941. In 1952 the UN federated Eritrea with Ethiopia, which annexed it in 1962, sparking a 30-year war for independence. Eritrea became independent in 1993, but a border war with Ethiopia in 1998–2000 killed tens of thousands and was followed by two decades of 'no war, no peace' until a 2018 peace agreement.
summary.politicalHistory: The Eritrean People's Liberation Front won the independence war in 1991, and a referendum in 1993 confirmed independence with near-unanimous support. A constitution was ratified in 1997 but has never been implemented, and no national elections have been held. Since 2001, when senior officials and journalists critical of the government were detained, the state has been a one-party system under the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, led by the same president since independence. National service, intended to be 18 months, has often been extended indefinitely.
summary.art: Eritrean music features the krar lyre and the guayla dance, with singers such as Helen Meles and Yemane Barya much loved. Coffee ceremonies, injera-based cuisine and embroidered white zuria dresses are cultural cornerstones. Asmara's 1930s Italian modernist buildings, such as the Fiat Tagliero service station, are celebrated works of architecture.
summary.monuments: Asmara, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the world's finest collections of early modernist architecture. The ancient port of Adulis and the Aksumite ruins of Qohaito recall the region's ancient civilisation. The Ottoman-era port city of Massawa, the Dahlak Archipelago and the mountain monastery of Debre Bizen are also significant.

name: Eswatini

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); siSwati and English are official

people: Most people are emaSwati, sharing one language and a strong monarchy-centred culture, with Zulu, Tsonga and smaller European and mixed communities. Around 90% are Christian, especially in Zionist and other African independent churches, often alongside traditional beliefs. Around three-quarters live in rural homesteads.

currency.name: Swazi lilangeni (South African rand also accepted)

Mountain landscapes and wildlife reserves

summary.history: Bantu-speaking ancestors of the emaSwati migrated south and, under King Sobhuza I in the early 19th century, unified clans into a kingdom in the hills of the present country. Pressure from the Zulu, Boers and British shaped its borders, and it became a British protectorate after the South African War in 1903. Much land had been granted to European concessionaires, and the nation worked for decades to buy it back. Swaziland became independent in 1968 and was renamed Eswatini in 2018.
summary.politicalHistory: Independence came in 1968 as a constitutional monarchy under King Sobhuza II, who in 1973 suspended the constitution and banned political parties. Under the tinkhundla system, candidates stand as individuals rather than for parties, and the monarch holds wide executive power. A new constitution was adopted in 2005, but parties still cannot contest elections. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were met with deadly force; Eswatini remains Africa's last absolute monarchy.
summary.art: The Umhlanga (Reed Dance) and Incwala (kingship) ceremonies are vibrant national celebrations with song, dance and dress. Crafts include grass baskets, candles, glass-blowing, and the batik and soapstone carving of craft centres such as Ngwenya. Choral music, both traditional and gospel, is woven through daily life.
summary.monuments: Lobamba holds the royal kraal, parliament and the National Museum, along with the memorial to King Sobhuza II. The Ngwenya Mine is among the oldest known mines in the world, worked for ochre tens of thousands of years ago. Mlilwane, Hlane and Mkhaya reserves and the Sibebe Rock granite dome are natural highlights.

name: Ethiopia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Amharic is the federal working language, with several others official regionally

people: Ethiopia's largest peoples are the Oromo and Amhara, followed by the Somali, Tigrayans, Sidama, Gurage, Welayta, Afar and dozens of others. Around 43% are Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, about a third Muslim and about a fifth Protestant (P'ent'ay), with traditional faiths in some regions. Most Ethiopians live in rural highlands, though Addis Ababa and other cities are growing fast.

basics.roman: ebakih (to a man) / ebakish (to a woman)

Coffee, Ethiopia's gift to the world

Food, safety and return home for the displaced

Hope and work for its young generation

summary.history: Ethiopia is one of humanity's oldest homelands, where fossils such as 'Lucy' (3.2 million years old) were found. The Aksumite kingdom traded across the Red Sea and adopted Christianity in the 4th century, and Ethiopia welcomed early Muslims fleeing persecution in Mecca. Under Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopia expanded and defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, remaining uncolonised apart from Italy's occupation of 1936–1941. Famine, revolution and civil war marked the late 20th century, and the 2020–2022 Tigray war caused immense loss of life.
summary.politicalHistory: Emperor Haile Selassie ruled from 1930 until he was overthrown in 1974 by the Derg, a Marxist military junta under Mengistu Haile Mariam whose 'Red Terror' killed many thousands. The Derg fell in 1991 to the EPRDF coalition led by Meles Zenawi, which introduced ethnic federalism in the 1995 constitution. Mass protests from 2015 brought a change of leadership in 2018, a peace deal with Eritrea and the dissolution of the EPRDF into the Prosperity Party. Ethiopia is a federal parliamentary republic.
summary.art: Ethiopian Orthodox church painting, illuminated manuscripts in Ge'ez and processional crosses are treasures of Christian art. Music ranges from liturgical zema, attributed to Saint Yared, to the 'Ethio-jazz' of Mulatu Astatke and the voices of Mahmoud Ahmed and Aster Aweke. The coffee ceremony, eskista shoulder dance and the Ethiopian calendar and script are distinctive cultural legacies.
summary.monuments: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, carved from solid stone in the 12th–13th centuries, are a UNESCO site still used in worship. Aksum's giant stelae, the castles of Gondar, the walled Muslim city of Harar Jugol and the Konso cultural landscape are also UNESCO-listed. The Simien Mountains and the Danakil Depression show the land's dramatic natural beauty.

name: Gabon

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official and widely spoken

people: Gabon's peoples include the Fang (the largest group), Punu, Nzebi, Myene, Kota, Teke and Baka and Babongo forest peoples, plus many West African migrants. Most are Christian (mainly Catholic), with a Muslim minority and the Bwiti spiritual tradition practised by many. Around 90% live in cities, especially Libreville and Port-Gentil.
resources: Oil and manganese
Rainforest covering nearly 90% of the land
National parks with forest elephants and gorillas
Timber and sustainable forestry
Atlantic coast and marine reserves
Bwiti and other living cultural traditions
struggles: Dependence on oil and inequality despite high average income
Youth unemployment and poverty in cities
Political transition after decades of dynastic rule
Poor roads and public services outside the main cities
Human–wildlife conflict for rural farmers
prayFor: A just and peaceful transition that serves all Gabonese
Shared prosperity and work for young people
Good schools and clinics everywhere
Rural farmers living alongside wildlife
Wise care of the great rainforest

summary.history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled the region's forests over many centuries, and the Mpongwe and Orungu traded along the coast. Portuguese navigators arrived in the 1470s, and the coast became a source of ivory, timber and enslaved people. France established Libreville in 1849 as a settlement for freed captives and colonised the interior, later making Gabon part of French Equatorial Africa. Gabon gained independence in 1960, and oil made it one of Africa's wealthiest countries per person, though benefits were unevenly shared.
summary.politicalHistory: Léon M'ba, the first president, was briefly overthrown in 1964 and restored by French troops. Omar Bongo succeeded him in 1967 and ruled for 41 years, mostly under a single party until multiparty politics returned in 1990. His son Ali Bongo succeeded him in 2009 through disputed elections. In August 2023 the military seized power after another disputed election, ending the Bongo family's 56-year rule and launching a transition.
summary.art: Fang reliquary figures, Punu white-faced masks and Kota guardian figures are among the most admired works of African sculpture and influenced European modern art. The Bwiti tradition uses the ngombi harp, song and dance in all-night ceremonies. Musicians such as Pierre-Claver Akendengué have blended traditional and modern sounds.
summary.monuments: The Lopé-Okanda landscape, a UNESCO site, combines rainforest and savanna with ancient rock carvings, and Ivindo National Park is also UNESCO-listed. Loango National Park, where hippos and elephants walk the beaches, is a famous wildlife area. Albert Schweitzer's hospital at Lambaréné and Libreville's St Michael's Church, with carved wooden columns, are cultural landmarks.

name: Gambia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English is official, Wolof is the lingua franca around Banjul

people: Gambians include Mandinka (the largest group), Fula, Wolof, Jola, Serahule, Serer and others, with much intermarriage and joking-cousin relationships between peoples. Around 95% are Muslim, with a small Christian community and longstanding interfaith harmony. Most live along the river and in the fast-growing urban area around Serekunda and Banjul.
resources: The Gambia River
Groundnuts and fisheries
Atlantic beaches and tourism
Birdlife and wetlands
Strong family and community networks
Rich griot and kora traditions
struggles: Poverty and few jobs, driving dangerous migration toward Europe
Food insecurity and dependence on imported rice
Coastal erosion and salt intrusion into farmland
Healing and justice after two decades of dictatorship
Limited electricity and health services
prayFor: Hope and safety for young people tempted by perilous journeys
Justice and healing for victims of past abuses
Fertile fields and full fishing nets
Protection of the coast and river communities
Continued peace among peoples and faiths

summary.history: The Gambia River valley was part of the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires' trading worlds, and Mandinka and Wolof kingdoms flourished along its banks. Kunta Kinteh Island (formerly James Island) became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade under British and other European traders. Britain claimed the river in the 17th century, outlawed the slave trade in 1807 and made the Gambia a colony and protectorate. It became independent in 1965 and a republic in 1970.
summary.politicalHistory: Dawda Jawara led the country from 1965, as prime minister and then president, maintaining a multiparty system. A short-lived confederation with Senegal (Senegambia) existed from 1982 to 1989. In 1994 Yahya Jammeh seized power in a coup and ruled for 22 years, marked by serious human rights abuses. He lost the 2016 election and left in January 2017 under regional pressure; a Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission has since documented past abuses.
summary.art: Griots (jali) preserve history through song, accompanied by the 21-string kora, with masters such as Foday Musa Suso. Mbalax and Afro-manding music are popular, and Kankurang masked figures appear at Mandinka initiations, a tradition recognised by UNESCO. Batik and tie-dye textiles, woodcarving and wrestling festivals are part of daily culture.
summary.monuments: Kunta Kinteh Island and related sites, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recall the transatlantic slave trade. The Wassu and Kerbatch stone circles, part of the Senegambian Stone Circles UNESCO site, are ancient megaliths. Arch 22 in Banjul, the Abuko Nature Reserve and River Gambia National Park, with its chimpanzee sanctuary, are also notable.

name: Ghana

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English is official, Twi is widely spoken

people: Ghana's peoples include the Akan (including Asante and Fante), Mole-Dagbani, Ewe, Ga-Adangbe, Gurma and Guan. Around 70% are Christian, with many Pentecostal and charismatic churches, about a fifth Muslim, mostly in the north, and traditional faith practised by some. Over half live in cities such as Accra and Kumasi, and a large diaspora lives in the UK, US and elsewhere.
resources: Gold
Cocoa
Oil and gas
Strong democratic tradition
Vibrant arts, music and fashion
Forests, beaches and Lake Volta
struggles: Debt crisis and high inflation weighing on families
Illegal small-scale gold mining (galamsey) poisoning rivers and land
Youth unemployment
Gaps between north and south in services and income
Coastal erosion and flooding
prayFor: Relief for families facing rising prices
Clean rivers and land healed from destructive mining
Work and opportunity for young graduates
Fair development for the northern regions
Continued peaceful democracy

summary.history: Ghana takes its name from the medieval Ghana Empire to the northwest, while within its borders the Asante Empire and Fante, Ga, Ewe and Dagbon states rose. European traders arrived in the 15th century, building castles along the 'Gold Coast' through which countless enslaved Africans were shipped to the Americas. Britain fought a series of wars against the Asante and made the Gold Coast a colony. In 1957 Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, inspiring liberation movements across the continent.
summary.politicalHistory: Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana to independence in 1957 and became president of a republic in 1960, but turned it into a one-party state before being overthrown in 1966. Coups and short-lived civilian governments followed until Jerry Rawlings seized power in 1979 and again in 1981. A 1992 constitution restored multiparty democracy, and Ghana has since seen several peaceful transfers of power between the two main parties. It is a presidential republic.
summary.art: Kente cloth, woven by the Asante and Ewe, and adinkra symbols are iconic Ghanaian art forms. Highlife music, with legends such as E.T. Mensah, gave rise to hiplife and Afrobeats-influenced sounds. Sculptor El Anatsui, writer Ama Ata Aidoo and Ga fantasy coffins are celebrated worldwide.
summary.monuments: The forts and castles of the coast, including Cape Coast and Elmina, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and sombre memorials of the slave trade. The Asante traditional buildings near Kumasi are also UNESCO-listed, and the Manhyia Palace remains the Asantehene's seat. The Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, Kakum's canopy walkway and the Larabanga mosque are much-visited landmarks.

name: Guinea

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); French is official

people: Guinea's largest peoples are the Fula (Peul), Malinke and Susu, alongside Kissi, Kpelle, Toma and others in the forest region. Around 85% are Muslim, with Christian and traditional-faith minorities, mainly in the southeast. About a third live in cities, mostly Conakry, and many depend on farming.
resources: Bauxite (among the world's largest reserves)
Simandou iron ore and gold
Rivers that feed the Niger, Senegal and Gambia
Fertile land and hydropower
Rich Mandé musical heritage
Fouta Djallon highlands
struggles: Poverty despite vast mineral wealth
Military rule and restricted civic freedoms
Environmental harm and displacement from mining
Weak health care, still recovering from Ebola
Power cuts and poor infrastructure
prayFor: A peaceful return to civilian, accountable government
Mining that benefits local communities and protects land and water
Health care for every family
Education and work for young Guineans
Unity among Guinea's peoples

summary.history: Parts of Guinea lay within the Mali Empire, and the Fula founded the Islamic state of Fouta Djallon in the 18th century. Coastal peoples were drawn into the Atlantic slave trade, and Samori Touré's Wassoulou Empire resisted French conquest until 1898. France ruled Guinea as part of French West Africa. In 1958 Guinea alone voted 'no' to France's proposed community and became independent immediately, after which France abruptly withdrew support.
summary.politicalHistory: Ahmed Sékou Touré ruled from 1958 until his death in 1984 as head of a one-party socialist state, during which many political prisoners died in Camp Boiro. Lansana Conté then seized power in a coup and ruled until 2008, introducing multiparty elections in 1993. After another coup and a 2009 stadium massacre, Alpha Condé became the first democratically elected president in 2010. He was overthrown by the military in 2021 after changing the constitution to seek a third term, and a transitional military government has led since.
summary.art: Guinea is a heartland of Mandé music: the balafon, kora and djembe, the griot tradition, and the national ensembles Les Ballets Africains and Bembeya Jazz. Singer Mory Kanté brought Guinean music worldwide with 'Yé ké yé ké'. Writer Camara Laye's 'The Dark Child' is a classic of African literature, and Baga masks such as the D'mba are renowned sculpture.
summary.monuments: The Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve, shared with Côte d'Ivoire, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Sosso Bala, a sacred balafon kept in Niagassola, is inscribed by UNESCO as intangible heritage. The Fouta Djallon waterfalls, the Grand Mosque of Conakry and the Îles de Loos are also notable.

name: Guinea-Bissau

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Portuguese is official, Kriol is the lingua franca

people: Peoples include the Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Manjaco, Papel and the Bijagós islanders, with a Creole urban culture. Around 45% are Muslim, roughly a fifth Christian and many follow traditional faiths, often combined with other beliefs. Most people live in rural areas, growing rice and cashews.

Fisheries
Bijagós Archipelago biodiversity
Rice paddies and fertile land
Rich, diverse cultural traditions
Mangroves and coastal wetlands

Drug trafficking through the country
Dependence on a single crop, cashews
Weak health and education systems
Rising seas threatening coastal rice fields

Freedom from the harm of drug trafficking
Fair prices for cashew farmers
Schools and clinics for every village
Protection of the islands and mangroves

summary.history: The region lay on the edge of the Mali Empire, and the Mandinka kingdom of Kaabu dominated much of it for centuries. Portuguese traders arrived in the 15th century, and the coast became a source of enslaved people for the Atlantic trade. Portugal only established effective control of the interior in the early 20th century. A liberation war from 1963 to 1974 led to independence, recognised by Portugal in 1974.
summary.politicalHistory: The PAIGC, founded by Amílcar Cabral, led the independence struggle; Cabral was assassinated in 1973, and his half-brother Luís Cabral became the first president. A 1980 coup brought João Bernardo 'Nino' Vieira to power, and multiparty politics arrived in 1994. A civil war in 1998–1999 and repeated coups and attempted coups have followed, and no elected president served a full term until 2014–2019. Guinea-Bissau is a semi-presidential republic.
summary.art: Gumbé music and the songs of artists such as José Carlos Schwarz and Super Mama Djombo are national treasures. The Bijagós islanders are known for vaca bruto bull masks and ritual sculpture. Carnival in Bissau and woven pano di pinti cloth are vibrant traditions.
summary.monuments: The Bijagós Archipelago, a UNESCO biosphere reserve and World Heritage Site, is home to saltwater hippos and nesting turtles. The Fortaleza d'Amura in Bissau holds the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, and Cacheu's fort recalls the slave trade era. Cantanhez National Park protects forests with chimpanzees.

name: Lesotho

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); Sesotho and English are official

people: Nearly all citizens are Basotho, sharing the Sesotho language, with small Xhosa, Phuthi and other communities. Around 90% are Christian, roughly half Catholic, often alongside respect for ancestors. Most people live in the western lowlands and mountain villages, and many work or have worked in South Africa.

currency.name: Lesotho loti (South African rand also accepted)

resources: Water exported via the Lesotho Highlands Water Project
Diamonds
Wool and mohair
Mountain landscapes
Textile manufacturing
Strong national identity and culture
struggles: Very high HIV prevalence
High unemployment and dependence on South Africa
Food insecurity, drought and soil erosion
Political instability and coalition crises
Job losses in the textile industry
prayFor: Health and care for all living with HIV
Work and hope for young Basotho
Rain, harvests and healthy soil
Stable and peaceful government
Strength for families separated by migrant labour

summary.history: San peoples lived in the region for thousands of years, leaving rock art in mountain shelters. In the early 19th century, amid wars known as the Difaqane, Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees on the mountain fortress of Thaba Bosiu and founded the Basotho nation. Facing Boer encroachment, he sought British protection, and Basutoland became a British protectorate in 1868, losing much fertile land to the Orange Free State. Lesotho became independent in 1966, entirely surrounded by South Africa.
summary.politicalHistory: Lesotho became independent in 1966 as a constitutional monarchy with Leabua Jonathan as prime minister; he annulled the 1970 election and ruled until a 1986 military coup. Civilian rule returned in 1993, but a disputed 1998 election led to unrest and a South African-led intervention. Since 2012 coalition governments have been frequent and fragile, including an attempted coup in 2014. Lesotho remains a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary government.
summary.art: The Basotho blanket and the conical mokorotlo hat are national symbols, and litema patterned wall painting decorates homes. Music includes the famo accordion style and the lesiba mouth-bow of herdboys. Writer Thomas Mofolo's 'Chaka' (1925) is a classic of African literature.
summary.monuments: Thaba Bosiu, Moshoeshoe I's mountain stronghold and burial place, is the cradle of the nation. Sehlabathebe National Park, part of the Maloti-Drakensberg UNESCO site, protects highland wetlands and San rock art. Maletsunyane Falls, the Katse Dam and the dinosaur footprints near Morija are also remarkable.

name: Liberia

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); English is official and Liberian English the everyday lingua franca

people: Liberia is home to about sixteen ethnic groups, among them the Kpelle, Bassa, Gio, Mano, Kru, Grebo, Loma, Vai and Mandingo, alongside descendants of the freed African-American and Caribbean settlers known as Americo-Liberians. Roughly 85% are Christian and about 12% Muslim, with traditional religion and initiation societies still woven through village life. About half live in towns, a third of the population around Monrovia, and a sizeable diaspora lives in the United States.
resources: Iron ore of the Nimba and Bong ranges
Upper Guinean rainforest, the largest remaining block in West Africa
Rubber plantations
Gold and alluvial diamonds
The world's largest ship registry by tonnage
A resilient, church- and market-centred community life
struggles: Deep poverty and youth unemployment after two civil wars
Weak health system, still marked by the 2014–16 Ebola epidemic
Corruption and fragile public institutions
Deforestation and concession disputes over land
Drug use among young people, including the synthetic drug kush
Poor roads that cut rural areas off in the rainy season
prayFor: For lasting healing and reconciliation among families scarred by the civil wars
For young Liberians caught in addiction, and for the people working to bring them home whole
For honest leadership and institutions that serve ordinary people
For nurses, midwives and teachers in rural clinics and schools
For the forests and the communities who depend on them

summary.history: The coast was home for centuries to Kru, Grebo, Vai, Bassa and other peoples, linked by trade in pepper (the Grain Coast) and later scarred by the Atlantic slave trade. From 1822 the American Colonization Society settled freed Black Americans at what became Monrovia, and the settlers declared the Republic of Liberia in 1847, Africa's first. For over a century the Americo-Liberian minority dominated power, while indigenous peoples were excluded and, in the 1920s, subjected to forced labour exports that caused an international scandal. Two civil wars (1989–1997 and 1999–2003) killed perhaps 250,000 people and displaced most of the population, with widespread use of child soldiers. Since 2003 Liberia has kept the peace, weathered the Ebola epidemic of 2014–16, and rebuilt slowly with help from its diaspora and partners.
summary.politicalHistory: Liberia was a settler republic modelled on the US constitution, ruled for most of 1878–1980 by the True Whig Party. Samuel Doe's 1980 coup ended settler rule but became a brutal dictatorship, and Charles Taylor's 1989 uprising opened the civil wars; Taylor was later convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone. The 2003 Accra peace agreement led to elections in 2005 that made Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Africa's first elected female head of state. Liberia is now a presidential republic, and the 2017 and 2023 elections both brought peaceful transfers of power to the opposition.
summary.art: Liberian art is rich in carved masks of the Dan, Mano and Sande and Poro societies, and in country-cloth weaving and basketry. Music ranges from traditional drumming and hipco, Liberia's Liberian-English rap, to gospel that fills churches every Sunday. Writers include the poet Bai T. Moore, whose novella Murder in the Cassava Patch is a national classic, and the novelist Wilton Sankawulo.
summary.monuments: Providence Island in Monrovia marks where the settlers first landed in 1822 and is a site of complex, shared memory. Sapo National Park and the East Nimba Nature Reserve protect some of West Africa's last primary rainforest, home to pygmy hippos and chimpanzees. The Centennial Pavilion and the old Ducor Hotel ruin in Monrovia, and the beaches and colonial-era houses of Robertsport, tell the country's layered story.

name: Libya

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), incl. migrant languages

people: Most Libyans are Arabic-speaking and of mixed Arab and Amazigh (Berber) heritage, with distinct Amazigh communities in the Nafusa Mountains and Zuwara, and Tuareg and Tebu peoples in the far south. Nearly all are Sunni Muslim, largely of the Maliki school, with a small Ibadi Amazigh minority. Around 80% live in cities along the Mediterranean coast, and the country hosts several hundred thousand migrant workers and people in transit from sub-Saharan Africa and beyond.
resources: Africa's largest proven oil reserves
Natural gas
The Great Man-Made River and Nubian Sandstone Aquifer
Mediterranean coastline and Saharan landscapes
Some of the finest Greek and Roman ruins in the world
A young, educated population
struggles: Political division between rival governments in east and west since 2014
Armed groups and foreign interference that undermine security
Abuse and exploitation of migrants and refugees
Heavy dependence on oil revenue and a frail public sector
Aftermath of Storm Daniel and the 2023 Derna dam collapse
Water scarcity and ageing infrastructure
prayFor: For the families of Derna, still grieving thousands lost in the 2023 floods
For a unified, peaceful Libya where young people can build lives without fear of militias
For migrants and refugees held in detention or crossing the sea, and for those who help them
For wise and honest stewardship of the country's oil wealth
For reconciliation between regions, tribes and communities

summary.history: Amazigh peoples lived across what is now Libya for millennia, and the Garamantes built an irrigated civilisation in the Fezzan desert. Phoenicians founded Tripoli's ancient cities, Greeks settled Cyrenaica, and Rome made Leptis Magna and Sabratha into great cities before Arab Muslim armies arrived in the 7th century. Ottoman rule from the 16th century was followed in 1911 by an Italian invasion and a brutal colonial war in which tens of thousands died in camps, and Libya became a major battlefield of the Second World War. Independence in 1951 was followed by the oil boom, four decades of authoritarian rule under Muammar Gaddafi, and the 2011 uprising and NATO intervention that ended his regime. Since then Libya has suffered civil conflict, division and suffering among Libyans and migrants alike.
summary.politicalHistory: Libya became independent in 1951 as a federal kingdom under King Idris I, the first country to gain independence through the United Nations. In 1969 a military coup brought Gaddafi to power; he proclaimed the 'Jamahiriya', a state of the masses that in practice concentrated power in his hands. After the 2011 revolution an elected General National Congress and then a House of Representatives took office, but contested elections in 2014 split the country between rival authorities in Tripoli and the east. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 2020 reduced fighting, yet national elections planned for 2021 were postponed and the country remains divided.
summary.art: Libya's prehistoric rock art in the Tadrart Acacus, showing giraffes, cattle and dancers, is among the oldest in Africa. Traditional crafts include silver jewellery, woven textiles and carpets, leatherwork, and the music of the malouf, an Andalusian-rooted tradition, alongside Amazigh and Tuareg song. Modern literature includes the novelist Ibrahim al-Koni, whose desert novels are widely translated, and Hisham Matar, whose memoir The Return won the Pulitzer Prize.
summary.monuments: Leptis Magna, birthplace of the emperor Septimius Severus, is one of the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere. Sabratha and the Greek city of Cyrene, with its Temple of Zeus, are also UNESCO World Heritage Sites, as are the rock-art sites of Tadrart Acacus. The old desert town of Ghadames, 'pearl of the desert', with its shaded covered lanes, shows how people adapted to the Sahara; all five Libyan sites are on UNESCO's list of World Heritage in Danger.

name: Madagascar

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue), mostly Malagasy varieties

people: The Malagasy descend from Austronesian seafarers from Borneo and from East African peoples, a heritage visible in language, rice farming and features; some eighteen ethnic groups are recognised, including the Merina of the highlands, the Betsimisaraka of the east coast and the Sakalava of the west. Most people are Christian, roughly evenly divided between Catholic and Protestant, while honouring the ancestors (razana) through rituals such as famadihana remains central; there are Muslim and traditional-religion minorities. About 60% live in rural areas, mostly growing rice.
resources: Extraordinary endemic biodiversity — lemurs, baobabs, chameleons, orchids
Vanilla, of which it is the world's leading producer
Nickel, cobalt, graphite and ilmenite
Rice terraces and fertile highlands
Coral reefs and long coastlines
A deep culture of fihavanana — kinship and solidarity
struggles: One of the highest poverty rates in the world
Deforestation, slash-and-burn agriculture and soil erosion
Drought and hunger in the Grand Sud; frequent cyclones
Chronic child malnutrition
Political instability and corruption
Insecurity from cattle raiders (dahalo) in rural areas
prayFor: For families in the drought-stricken south, that rain, food and water reach them
For children growing up malnourished, and for those who feed and teach them
For the forests and wildlife, and for farmers who need livelihoods that sustain the land
For peaceful, honest politics that serve the poor
For communities rebuilding after cyclones

summary.history: Madagascar was among the last major landmasses settled by humans, by Austronesian voyagers who arrived perhaps 1,500 years ago and later mixed with Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab and Swahili traders. Kingdoms such as the Sakalava and the Merina rose, and in the 19th century the Merina kingdom unified most of the island and embraced Christianity under Queen Ranavalona II. France invaded in 1895, abolished the monarchy and imposed colonial rule, crushing the 1947 uprising at the cost of tens of thousands of Malagasy lives. Independence came in 1960, followed by decades of political turbulence and economic decline, even as the island became globally celebrated for its unique wildlife.
summary.politicalHistory: Madagascar became independent from France in 1960 under Philibert Tsiranana's First Republic. A period of military rule from 1972 gave way to Didier Ratsiraka's socialist Second Republic, and popular protests in 1991 brought a new democratic constitution. Disputed elections in 2001–02 and an unconstitutional seizure of power in 2009 led to a long transition and international sanctions until elections in 2013. It is a semi-presidential republic whose elections, including those of 2023, have often been contested.
summary.art: The highlands are known for lamba silk and cotton cloths, Zafimaniry woodcarving (inscribed by UNESCO as intangible heritage), and the hiragasy, a travelling performance of music, dance and oratory. Malagasy music features the valiha bamboo tube zither and the fast salegy dance rhythm of the north. Jean-Joseph Rabearivelo is the founding poet of modern Malagasy literature, and the ancestral tombs of the Mahafaly, with their carved aloalo posts, are celebrated works of funerary art.
summary.monuments: The Royal Hill of Ambohimanga, a sacred seat of Merina kings, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Rova palace complex crowns Antananarivo. The Tsingy de Bemaraha, a forest of razor-sharp limestone pinnacles, and the Rainforests of the Atsinanana are also UNESCO-listed. The Avenue of the Baobabs near Morondava and Isalo National Park are among the island's most beloved landscapes.

name: Malawi

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue)

people: Malawians include the Chewa (the largest group), Lomwe, Yao, Ngoni, Tumbuka, Sena and Tonga peoples, and the country is known as 'the warm heart of Africa' for its hospitality. About 77% are Christian and around 14% Muslim, the latter concentrated among the Yao near Lake Malawi, while Chewa Gule Wamkulu traditions remain vital. More than four in five people live in rural areas and farm small plots of maize.
resources: Lake Malawi, with more fish species than any other lake
Fertile soils for maize, tobacco, tea, sugar and groundnuts
Hydropower from the Shire River
Mulanje Mountain and Nyika Plateau
Uranium and rare-earth deposits
Strong traditions of community and hospitality
struggles: Widespread poverty and recurring food insecurity
Dependence on rain-fed maize amid droughts and cyclones such as Freddy (2023)
Deforestation for charcoal and firewood
Foreign-exchange shortages, high inflation and fuel scarcity
Cholera outbreaks and strained health services
Rapid population growth and youth unemployment
prayFor: For farming families facing failed harvests, and for rain in its season
For communities still rebuilding homes and fields after Cyclone Freddy
For health workers, and protection from cholera and malaria
For girls to stay in school and young people to find meaningful work
For integrity in public life and wise use of scarce resources

summary.history: Early hunter-gatherers were joined from around the 1st millennium by Bantu-speaking farmers, and from the 15th century the Maravi confederacy of the Chewa dominated the region. The 19th century brought upheaval: Ngoni invasions from the south and a brutal Arab-Swahili and Yao slave trade through the lake region, which David Livingstone's reports helped publicise. Scottish missions were followed by the British Central Africa Protectorate in 1891, renamed Nyasaland, from which many men left to work in Rhodesian and South African mines. John Chilembwe's 1915 uprising was an early act of resistance, and after a struggle against the Central African Federation Malawi became independent in 1964.
summary.politicalHistory: Nyasaland was joined to the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953 despite African opposition, and became independent as Malawi in 1964 under Hastings Kamuzu Banda. Banda declared himself President for Life and ruled a one-party state marked by repression until a 1993 referendum restored multiparty politics. A new constitution in 1994 made Malawi a presidential republic. In 2020 the Constitutional Court annulled a flawed presidential election and the rerun was won by the opposition, a landmark for judicial independence in Africa.
summary.art: The Gule Wamkulu masked dances of the Chewa are inscribed by UNESCO as intangible heritage, and the Vimbuza healing dance of the Tumbuka is also recognised. Woodcarving, basketry and pottery thrive, and the Chewa and Tumbuka make music with drums, the bangwe board zither and choirs. Writers include the poets Jack Mapanje and Steve Chimombo and the novelist Legson Kayira.
summary.monuments: Lake Malawi National Park, at the southern end of the lake, is a UNESCO site for its hundreds of colourful cichlid fish species. The Chongoni Rock-Art Area preserves Batwa and Chewa paintings and is also UNESCO-listed. Livingstonia mission on its escarpment, the old colonial capital of Zomba, and the granite massif of Mulanje Mountain speak of the country's faith, history and natural beauty.

name: Mali

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue); since 2023 thirteen national languages are official and French a working language

people: Mali's peoples include the Bambara, Fulani (Peul), Soninke, Malinke, Songhai, Dogon, Senufo, Bozo, Tuareg and Moors, many bound by joking-cousin (sanankuya) ties that ease tensions between groups. About 95% are Muslim, mostly Sunni, with small Christian and traditional-religion communities. Most people live along the Niger River in the south; about 45% are urban, and Malians abroad, especially in France and neighbouring countries, send home vital remittances.

basics.local: I ni ce / A ni ce

resources: The Niger River and its inland delta
Gold, Africa's third- or fourth-largest producer
Cotton and livestock
Lithium and other minerals
A great manuscript and griot heritage
Music that has shaped the world's blues
struggles: Armed jihadist insurgency and intercommunal violence in the north and centre since 2012
Millions in need of humanitarian aid and hundreds of thousands displaced
Military rule and restricted political freedoms
Desertification, drought and floods that threaten farmers and herders
Low school enrolment, especially as schools close in conflict zones
Deep poverty and food insecurity
prayFor: For peace in the centre and north, and protection for villagers caught between armed groups
For displaced families, and for those who share their homes and food with them
For children whose schools have closed, that they may learn again
For herders and farmers sharing scarce land and water
For leaders who seek justice, dialogue and the common good

summary.history: The middle Niger was home to some of Africa's earliest cities, such as Djenné-Djeno. Three great empires rose here: Ghana (Wagadu), the Mali Empire founded by Sundiata Keita in the 13th century and made legendary by Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca, and the Songhai Empire, which fell to a Moroccan invasion in 1591. Timbuktu became a world centre of Islamic learning, while Bambara kingdoms and the jihad states of the Fulani and Umar Tall arose in later centuries. France conquered the region in the late 19th century as French Sudan, and Mali became independent in 1960; since 2012 it has suffered rebellion, jihadist insurgency and successive coups, with great civilian suffering.
summary.politicalHistory: French Sudan briefly joined Senegal in the Mali Federation before becoming independent as the Republic of Mali in 1960 under Modibo Keïta's socialist one-party government. Moussa Traoré seized power in 1968 and ruled until a 1991 popular uprising and coup opened the way to multiparty democracy under a 1992 constitution. A 2012 coup and northern rebellion led to French and UN intervention, and further coups in 2020 and 2021 installed military-led transitional authorities. A new constitution was approved in 2023; French forces and the UN mission left, and in 2024 Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announced their exit from ECOWAS and formed the Alliance of Sahel States.
summary.art: Mali's griots (jeliw) carry history in epic song, notably the Sundiata epic, accompanied by kora, balafon and ngoni. Its modern musicians — Ali Farka Touré, Salif Keita, Oumou Sangaré, Toumani Diabaté and Tinariwen — are among Africa's most celebrated. Bogolanfini mud cloth, Dogon masks and sculpture, and the photography of Seydou Keïta and Malick Sidibé are treasured worldwide.
summary.monuments: The mud-brick Great Mosque of Djenné, rebuilt in 1907 and replastered each year by the community, is the largest earthen building in the world and part of a UNESCO site. Timbuktu's Djinguereber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia mosques and its manuscripts recall its golden age of scholarship; mausoleums destroyed in 2012 were rebuilt by local masons. The Cliff of Bandiagara (Land of the Dogons) and the Tomb of Askia in Gao are also UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

name: Mauritania

languages.note: ≈ living languages (Ethnologue)

people: Mauritanians include Arabic-speaking Moors — Bidhan (White Moors) and Haratin, descendants of formerly enslaved people — and Black African Halpulaar, Soninke and Wolof communities along the Senegal River. Almost all are Sunni Muslim of the Maliki school, and the country is known for its scholarly and Sufi traditions. Once largely nomadic, Mauritania is now over half urban, with about a quarter of the population in Nouakchott.
resources: Iron ore from the Zouérat mines
Some of the richest fishing grounds in the Atlantic
Gold and copper
Offshore natural gas (Greater Tortue Ahmeyim)
Banc d'Arguin's migratory-bird wetlands
Centuries-old traditions of Islamic scholarship and poetry
